items.title: The Look-at-Me Spectacle of Actors Playing Actors in “Elsinore” and “I Play Rocky”
items.description: The bluest of peepers, framed in the tightest of closeups, can be found staring out at you from a movie screen. No, not Elizabeth Holmes’s in the hotly debated documentary “You Can See Everything,” though her eerily unblinking stare, somehow both insinuating a
items.author: Justin Chang
paragraphs: The bluest of peepers, framed in the tightest of closeups, can be found staring out at you from a movie screen. No, not Elizabeth Holmes’s in the hotly debated documentary “You Can See Everything,” though her eerily unblinking stare, somehow both insinuating and vacant, certainly runs a close second. I speak of Andrew Scott in the muddled biographical drama “Elsinore,” in which he plays the London-based Scottish actor Ian Charleson in the autumn of 1989, during some of the unbearable and extraordinary final months of his life. Ian, who’s forty, is living with AIDS in an era when the diagnosis is a death sentence, and he already has a ghostly white pallor that brings out the intensity of his eyes, which sparkle like deep-set sapphires. (Scott, whose eyes are brown, wore blue contact lenses during production.) His complexion also contrasts starkly with a lesion that appears, early in the film, near his right temple—one of many that will eventually cover his body, though it’s the only one that worries him for now. A skin growth on an arm or a leg can be covered, but a blotch on Ian’s face, even when obscured with makeup, might catch a viewer’s attention.

Ian is used to getting noticed on stage and off, though the source of such recognition can be exasperating. He’s best known for his performance as the Olympic-champion runner Eric Liddell in “Chariots of Fire” (1981), a film that is itself best known for a musical score that most would call iconic and Ian would term incessant. He can barely promote a new project on a talk show without being assaulted on the air by the composer Vangelis’s overweeningly cosmic synths; in a cab, he nods along indulgently as the driver hums the whole damn theme. Ian has resigned himself to the fact that “Chariots of Fire” will lead his obituaries, and also to the likelihood that those obituaries are not too far away. But then he learns that Daniel Day-Lewis, a star on the rise, has mysteriously dropped out of the role of Hamlet at the National Theatre—and the director, Richard Eyre (a fine Johnny Flynn), asks Ian to take over, mid-run. Famously, the production marked the last time that Day-Lewis ever appeared in a play; for infinitely sadder reasons, it also gave us the last role of Ian Charleson’s life. (He made it through twenty-four performances of “Hamlet” at the National and died weeks later, in January, 1990.)

“Elsinore,” directed by the Australian filmmaker Simon Stone and written by Stephen Beresford, seeks to make a heroic spectacle of Ian’s refusal to go gentle into that good night. He already lives, breathes, and often quotes “Hamlet”—he played the prince of Denmark before, in 1974, at a theatre in Cambridge—and he’s determined to summon every last reserve of his energy, which is waning, and his talent, which is considerable. He has the unflagging support of his closest friend, the casting director Patsy Pollock (Billie Piper), but also the stern disapproval of his doctor, Margaret Johnson (Olivia Colman), who knows that the stress of rehearsals and performances will only hasten Ian’s physical decline. Johnson is a real-life pioneer in H.I.V. and AIDS treatment, and Colman plays her with a bracing dash of vinegar; the pleasure of her scenes with Scott lies in the sugary grace notes that gradually seep into their interplay. Doctor and patient reach a respectful impasse when Margaret tells Ian that her priority is the preservation of life, to which Ian replies that life can also be measured in quality, not quantity.

This is a worthy sentiment, though I’m not sure that Stone, a more-is-more kind of filmmaker, grasps its value as an aesthetic principle. The movie is built around an almost mathematical sense of amplification—it’s a mortality-driven tearjerker and a testament to the power of art—and it mashes together Ian’s onstage triumphs and behind-the-scenes travails in a monotonous manner that eventually leeches both of meaning. The montages in “Elsinore” go on forever; more than once, I longed for Stone to slow down and let an extended scene of rehearsal play out—to have Ian puzzle over a particular line reading or a bit of blocking, unadorned by crosscutting or music. Instead, “Hamlet” is reduced to a collage of high-flown sound bites, interrupted and sometimes drowned out by fits of coughing and retching. The plague’s the thing.

A cynic might observe that, for an actor, the chance to declaim some of Shakespeare’s greatest lines and showily waste away from terminal illness amounts to two thespian challenges rolled into one—a kind of Oscar-qualifying biathlon. If so, no one could deny that Andrew Scott is in intensely competitive shape, and he grabs hold of you so thoroughly as to send your skepticism into retreat. The part calls for extremes of suffering and showmanship, but Scott finds room for modulation; his Ian retains two qualities—a core of tenderness, and a persistently impish wit—that somehow survive every setback that AIDS can hurl at them. Is it churlish to note that Scott was even better, and rather less effortful, in “All of Us Strangers” (2023), in which he brought a delicate, haunting interiority to the role of Adam, a lonely gay Londoner? Adam undergoes the quietest yet most transformative of spiritual and emotional journeys; he isn’t the same person at the beginning, the end, or, indeed, at any point in the movie. Ian, by contrast, is all dogged determination from start to finish. He flails, suffers, and ultimately transcends, but he doesn’t expand.

Ian’s one decisive shift concerns the matter of visibility: although he’s kept his sexuality private, he decides that, once he’s gone, the cause of his death will be made known. He arrives at this decision through a tense reckoning with the pioneering gay director Derek Jarman (David Dawson), who bitterly resents Ian for essentially disavowing their collaboration on the queer-punk film “Jubilee” (1978) and for suppressing his sexuality publicly in a bid for Hollywood acceptance. The film’s depiction of Charleson and Jarman’s spats, however rooted in truth, is corrected and diminished by Theo Rollason’s excellent recent documentary “Queer Edward II,” which features newly discovered archival footage from the set of “Edward II,” Jarman’s period drama from 1991. Like “Elsinore,” Rollason’s documentary—which premièred at the Venice and London film festivals and is still, as of this writing, seeking a U.S. distributor—addresses Jarman’s passionate commitment to art and activism, and also his controversial willingness to pressure closeted celebrities into outing themselves. Yet the real Jarman, even at his most confrontational, is shown to possess an infectious warmth, ebullience, and largeness of spirit—all of which render the glaring, vitriolic Jarman of “Elsinore” almost unrecognizable by comparison. Not for the first time in this movie, the truth seems to overwhelm the filmmaker’s imagination.

I invoked the Oscars flippantly, but not unreasonably. It’s hard to avoid the subject in the case of “Elsinore,” partly because the film has been widely tipped to earn Scott a nomination for Best Actor, but also because the legacy of the Academy Awards looms over the story itself: “Chariots of Fire” won Best Picture in 1982, a choice that hasn’t aged half as well as Vangelis’s score. By curious if just-short-of-fascinating coincidence, there’s a new film in theatres that unfolds under the shadow of another Oscar winner, “Rocky” (1976)—a better-regarded champ than “Chariots,” though it, too, features more than its fair share of musically charged sprinting. “I Play Rocky,” directed by Peter Farrelly from a screenplay by Peter Gamble, exalts the making of an improbable yet immortal American classic—and the birth of a movie star, Sylvester Stallone, played here by a charismatic and enormously likable young actor named Anthony Ippolito.

We encounter the young Stallone as a cash-strapped nobody in mid-nineteen-seventies New York City, working at a fishmonger’s, auditioning for nothing parts, and calling himself Mike. His deeply supportive girlfriend, Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), encourages him to write his own scripts—and to go by Sylvester, a name that once made him a target of childhood bullies. Sylvester isn’t an obvious moniker for a working stiff with a wink-wink taste for raw eggs, but the incongruity is the point. This guy, who tries out for roles such as Thug No. 2 by day and recites Walt Whitman’s “I Sing the Body Electric” by night, has unexpected poetry in him, and it bursts forth in his stubborn desire to be an actor and a screenwriter. In time, he and Sasha marry and move to Los Angeles, where he charms and hustles his way into the offices of the producers Irwin Winkler (P. J. Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell), a pair of savvy industry gatekeepers who, like most everyone else, feel dubious about Sylvester at first. By the film’s end, they will believe in him as passionately as he believes in himself.

“I Play Rocky” wants us to believe in Sylvester, too, which is easy enough to do. Ippolito, magnetizing the camera with a sleepy-eyed stare, and mumbling his lines with a deft approximation of Stallone’s slightly slurred delivery, is an astounding physical and verbal match for Stallone, and you can’t take your eyes off him—or close your ears to him—even when the movie pulls its narrative punches. Given what Stallone has revealed in interviews, some of them to promote his recent memoir, “The Steps,” the character’s home life feels patchy and sanitized. Gone is anything more than a hint of emotional turbulence between Sylvester and his father, Frank Stallone, Sr. (an almost unrecognizable Matt Dillon), who cruelly disparages his son at every turn.

Sylvester’s big eureka moment takes place in an L.A. bar, where he catches an epic fifteen-round boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner—and then immediately races home to write “Rocky” in a three-and-half-day burst of inspiration. This backstory is the stuff of Hollywood legend, and “I Play Rocky” reprints it gleefully, with nary a concern that legend alone might not suffice. Sylvester, a movie nut, knows a thing or two about what makes a picture work, but where did he get his writerly instincts, his sense of narrative drive and structure? A title card from earlier in the film—“SIXTEEN MONTHS AND EIGHT SCREENPLAYS LATER . . .”—doesn’t exactly tell the story.

The best scenes in “I Play Rocky” arrive shortly after the script is written and triumphantly presented to Winkler and Chartoff—at which point Sylvester delivers the ultimatum of the title. Sandy Maddox (a rudely amusing Tracy Letts), an executive at United Artists (and a composite of several real-life individuals), wants a bankable star such as Robert Redford or Burt Reynolds, and the tug-of-war negotiations that ensue open up an engrossing, sharply satirical window onto the frivolity and arbitrariness that so often govern Hollywood. Farrelly and Gamble attempt a deeper process dive once the film is green-lit, though it’s here that “I Play Rocky” goes on making-of-“Rocky” autopilot, stuffed with reënactments of beloved scenes and recognizable setups. Here is Sylvester in gray sweats, lunging up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and there he goes, tottering after Talia Shire on an ice-skating rink—a scene that nearly gets axed at the last minute, against Sylvester’s protests. Here, too, is the film’s journeyman director, John G. Avildsen (Jay Duplass), who has a talent for passing off thrift as realism, and whose cost-cutting instinct threatens to derail Sylvester’s ambitions as often as it helps realize them. Those ambitions will pay off, of course, and how: the finished “Rocky” will bring audiences to their feet, become the highest-grossing film of 1976, and prove the smirking Sandy Maddoxes of the world wrong.

“I Play Rocky” isn’t just an underdog story; it’s practically an underdog shelter. Rocky Balboa is an underdog in the boxing ring, “Rocky” is an underdog at the box office and the Oscars, and Stallone is an underdog in Hollywood—and, in his case, an underdog with a literal underdog, an abandoned bullmastiff that he finds on the streets of New York and adopts as his own. No doubt Farrelly’s film fancies itself an underdog, too—a scrappy, feel-good David of a picture, going up against the industry’s many shiny prestige Goliaths, and seeking to honor an earlier tradition of nervy but popular American filmmaking. For all that, I’m not convinced the film entirely buys, or successfully sells, its own mythmaking. Again and again, Farrelly, who unwittingly revealed the toxic side of nostalgia in the slickly retrograde, Best Picture-winning “Green Book” (2018), sacrifices real suspense and drama on the altar of fan-service reënactment. Beat by beat, “I Play Rocky” leans so complacently on the audience’s assumed love and knowledge of “Rocky” that it defeats its own stakes. It takes the triumph of the underdog too easily for granted. ♦

items.title: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” Is Tarantino Minus Tarantino
items.description: In a way, the most engrossing thing about “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is what it isn’t: a film directed by Quentin Tarantino. It’s a sequel to his 2019 movie “Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood,” which he both wrote and directed. For the new f
items.author: Richard Brody
paragraphs: In a way, the most engrossing thing about “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is what it isn’t: a film directed by Quentin Tarantino. It’s a sequel to his 2019 movie “Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood,” which he both wrote and directed. For the new film, he wrote the script but farmed its direction out to David Fincher, and I found myself watching the movie psychodramatically, with an eye for the aversions it may have aroused in Tarantino, the symptoms it may have triggered. To some extent, the movie encourages this kind of diagnostic viewing, because for all its enticements—starting with the cast, led by Brad Pitt and Elizabeth Debicki—it’s a movie of cinematic riffs and asides that calls attention to its artifices and, especially, to its personalized artistic quirks and obsessions.

“The Further Mis-Adventures” is centered on the earlier movie’s main supporting character, Cliff (played by Brad Pitt). In “Once Upon a Time . . . ,” set in 1969, he’s the stunt double for an actor named Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio), whose career is in a downturn. The new film picks up with Cliff, again played by Pitt, in June of 1977; Rick has departed for Australia, and Cliff, at the margins of Hollywood, is a sometime projectionist at the New Beverly Theatre (which, in real life, Tarantino now owns). He also works as a part-time bartender and does favors for friends as something of a fixer. Cliff is first seen doing his technical duty in the projection booth, seeing a scant audience out after the last show, and then welcoming, into the empty theatre, a pair of crooks (played by Karren Karagulian and Corey Fogelmanis), with whom Cliff negotiates the return of a bag of valuables (including an Oscar statuette) that they’ve stolen. Eventually, negotiating no more, he guns one down and makes the other help dispose of the body.

So much for the projecting; it’s the fixing that interests Tarantino. The next day, Cliff is surprised to be summoned to a meeting with a TV actor named Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), because Charlie is both famed for doing his own stunts and too short to use Cliff as a double. The job Charlie has in mind turns out to be offscreen: in a plot with a coincidental similarity to James Gray’s new film, “Paper Tiger,” Charlie has naïvely become involved with gangsters who are threatening his wife, Toni (Carla Gugino), and he wants Cliff to get them out of the jam. Cliff’s first idea, the simplest, is to pay them what they want. His second idea is to, um, negotiate, and it’s clear what that implies. But these gangsters, ruthless and bloodthirsty, promise an altogether more dangerous showdown.

Unfortunately, this tense setup proves more or less to be a live-action MacGuffin. Tarantino’s script dangles a gaudy array of decorative events and tangy characters, florid dialogue and snappy gestures that are more than the movie’s raison d’être—they’re its main matter. Like a Rube Goldberg contraption, the digressive screenplay is devised to do its job as circuitously, as idiosyncratically, and as ornamentally as possible. The narrative adornments are at least clever, and even when they’re hollow, noisy, and vain they’re, above all, symbolic incarnations of a world view.

Compared with Fincher’s other recent films, “The Further Mis-Adventures” must have been a blast to make. “Mank,” his bio-pic of the classic-Hollywood screenwriter Herman J. Mankiewicz, from 2020, had the heavy weight of real history looming over it, testing Fincher’s artistic superego rather than his expressive powers. “The Killer,” his action movie from 2023, buried both its pulp vigor and any connection to the real world in an overcooked dourness. By contrast, “The Further Mis-Adventures” has the typically Tarantinian explosive action and calibrated slow burns, the motormouth dialogue, the whimsical yet logical twists, the humor, and, above all, the light-footed, hearty energy and exuberant glee that Pitt brought to the original role. His reprisal of Cliff comes with even more self-aware snap, because it comes after a run of disappointing parts, including “Babylon” and “F1,” that risked turning his laid-back charm into a routine and a cliché.

In “Once Upon a Time . . . ,” Tarantino’s direction was at its best in catching the character’s verve in casual action, and in “The Further Mis-Adventures” Fincher captures similar moments with joyful wonder—if not with the palpable physicality that Tarantino brought to the job. Whether Cliff is handling reels and keeping an eye on the projector, the screen, the concession stand; dispensing jazzy pours and non-stop patter at the rowdy bar he tends; or taking sure command of stressful situations, he is essentially a boss in workingman’s garb, a big man in circumstances too small for him. Cliff’s commonplace heroism conceals his real heroism, which is hinted at in the wartime actions that he speaks of, and in his enforcer-like battles on his friends’ behalf. He’s a hidden version of the character played by Bradley Cooper in Clint Eastwood’s “American Sniper”: a protector—albeit one who, by contrast, is portrayed as untroubled by guilt, unburdened by responsibility, indeed lacking any inner life or psychology at all.

Why wouldn’t Tarantino want to return to direct his own sequel, and to help Pitt imbue Cliff with his characteristic swing or some new flair? The answer might be that, in recent years, Tarantino’s focus has tilted so drastically toward the gratifications of his own writing that the aesthetic gratifications he once found in the visual side of filmmaking appear to have dissipated. This shift was evident in his methodical filming of “The Hateful Eight,” which treated the screen largely as a proscenium, and even in “Once Upon a Time . . . ,” which provided a podium for the proclamation of his own old-Hollywood nostalgia. In “The Further Mis-Adventures,” Tarantino uses the same premise to put forward a new idea that amounts to a fascinating renunciation of the art of directing—and yet another mode of nostalgia.

Tarantino’s old-Hollywood veneration is centered on people like Cliff, the rugged characters of rich life experience who, without fame or acclaim, give the movie town its soul. The expression of that soul is in their glorious talk, in the stories they tell. Cliff is a formidable raconteur, who even in high-stakes negotiations spins fabulistic yarns in which to entangle his prey. He tells behind-the-scenes tales about actors in movies that his father, Gus (Peter Weller), a pawn-shop owner, watches on TV. He riffs on some of his derring-do as seen in “Once Upon a Time . . . .” He tells stories about sex. “The Further Mis-Adventures” is a story of stories: where they come from, what they’re for, and what they have to do with movies. And what the film reveals, doubtless unawares, is that a story on its own is a narrative that ends too soon and leaves out too much. It’s not enough to film one. (The shibboleth that filmmakers are mere storytellers is meant to keep producers happy.) What turns a story into a finished work is its transformation, its expansion beyond storytelling itself—which is exactly what “The Further Mis-Adventures” is missing.

“The Further Mis-Adventures” is a Tarantino film not despite the fact that he didn’t direct it but because he didn’t direct it: by not directing, he has given us a manifesto of his new artistic perspective. He has effectively become his own showrunner, with Fincher as a hired hand who thus becomes something like the parody of the auteur that Pauline Kael describes in her 1963 anti-auteurist screed “Circles and Squares”: someone who “expresses himself by shoving bits of style up the crevasses of the plots.” Speaking of Kael, there’s a great love story embedded—indeed, smothered—in the crime drama and the sidebar antics of “The Further Mis-Adventures.” The meeting with Charlie, the actor in need of Cliff’s help, is arranged by the actor’s agent, Karen Crosby (played by Elizabeth Debicki). She’s no ordinary agent but an agent with a prior career as a film critic, which was launched, she explains, with Kael’s help. At one of the meetings (which also includes Toni), Karen is coaxed into delivering, for Cliff’s benefit, her signature riff, which, in short, is that Hollywood movies aren’t and can’t be art—that, even in the best cases, a Hollywood film, as she puts it, isn’t Albert Camus’s “The Stranger” and “isn’t even Kerouac” but the artistic equivalent of hamburger—and she mocks critics for considering it art when all they’re doing is comparing Big Macs to Whoppers.

Whether true or not, it’s at least a convenient view for an agent to hold. What matters to the drama, however, isn’t Karen’s view of movies but her view of Cliff, and vice versa. Theirs is exactly the sort of romance that, Cliff says, would be a high-school cliché—the rough-hewn jock and the regal brainiac—and, apparently, neither Tarantino nor Fincher could get past clichés in working it out. Still, it’s there in the movie, as emotional raw material of extraordinary volatility, ready to produce a spectacular romantic conflagration at the slightest spark, and instead left undeveloped, essentially unused. Debicki, bringing commanding elegance and athletic grace to the role, opens a door and offers a glimpse of cinematic possibilities—and, more important, human ones—that both filmmakers at the joystick boyishly shy away from. ♦

items.title: Raye’s Theatrical Pop Nostalgia
items.description: The British singer and songwriter Raye presents her retro big-band act through a mesh of knowingness, often breaking the fourth wall to provide a meta-text. “I had hoped you’d find your way to this piece of music / And that would mean, oh my friend, we have ma
items.author: Doreen St Félix
paragraphs: The British singer and songwriter Raye presents her retro big-band act through a mesh of knowingness, often breaking the fourth wall to provide a meta-text. “I had hoped you’d find your way to this piece of music / And that would mean, oh my friend, we have made it to the end,” she sings, in the final song on her sophomore studio album. Never does she allow her listeners to feel anything like abandon; she is always reminding them, as she is always reminding herself, of the intractable frame of entertainment, that we are all plodding through our private dramas on a public stage. Although she is deep in a phase of mid-century drag, with her banana-curled bouffant and her corseted silhouette, she is as painfully contemporary as they come, by which I mean, preoccupied with being understood. Her breakthrough mini-album, “Euphoric Sad Songs,” released six years ago, when Raye, born Rachel Agatha Keen, was twenty-three, was, as its postmodern title ironically suggests, competently produced generica, a collection of mid-to-up-tempo dance-pop melodies that served as vessels for her melancholy. The music she has made since then—two albums, “My 21st Century Blues” and “This Music May Contain Hope,” the latter of which has just garnered her the most nominations of any artist for the 2027 Grammys—only deepens the impression that this is a musician trapped in her idea of what it means to be a musician.

But another fact persists: everybody loves Raye. Why wouldn’t they? She’s got that city charm. She provides the comfort of the legacy act, and the light perversity of the theatre kid. She can do what Sabrina Carpenter does, make us succumb to camp and humor, as in her enormous hit “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!” She is a Christian, but she knows what it is to have lost one’s faith.

Born in South London to a Ghanaian Swiss mother and a white English father, she grew up with three sisters, two of whom are also professional musicians who sometimes join her onstage, and all were trained in the way of praise singing in the church. Jazz—the scatting of Ella Fitzgerald, the blowing of Louis Armstrong—was an early obsession. As an adolescent, Raye had a clear view of pop success and how to attain it; she dreamed of attending the BRIT School, an institution that had been a way station for many singers, including Adele and Amy Winehouse, idols whose extraordinary presence Raye sought to emulate. She got in. And then she dropped out, at sixteen, perhaps feeling creatively stifled. (She was one year ahead of another British star, Olivia Dean.) The disillusionment with the institution introduced Raye to the general disillusionment experienced by the female singer, who is confronted again and again with the cold reality of the industry, its hostility to her art.

A teen-aged Raye entered a limbo. At seventeen, she signed with Polydor Records, a sub-label under Universal. She released a body of work on SoundCloud, called “Welcome to the Winter”; it tried out lo-fi, Rihanna-esque vocals, set against gothic beats that call to mind the Weeknd. You can hear, too, the stamp of Lily Allen. (She is not ready, at this stage, to bring out the full influence of Winehouse, but you can feel it under the surface.) Raye was forced to divert her songwriting skills to other artists, a soul-killing kind of ventriloquism for some, that also had the effect of teaching her versatility. Her credits include work for Beyoncé, John Legend, and her cultural peer Charli XCX. Memorably, in 2021, Raye—who was becoming a darling among the keen-eyed observers of her evolution, from the development of her performer’s armor to the stylized stage name—posted on X, “I have been on a 4 ALBUM RECORD DEAL since 2014 !!! And haven’t been allowed to put out one album. ALL I CARE ABOUT is the music. Im sick of being slept on and I’m sick of being in pain about it this is not business to me this so personal.”

To my ear, the extraction from that bad deal hasn’t exactly facilitated freedom for Raye. “My 21st Century Blues,” released in 2023, is a likable record choked by its music-student stridency, the compulsion to prove she is the inheritor to any number of blues women. It’s in the title of the album. It’s in the titles of the songs, all of which are punctuated with a period, as if to say that there is nothing up for discussion. In the tradition of Brits who have molded themselves in genres born across the Atlantic, Raye is an acolyte; she isn’t a raider, the sort of nostalgist who picks diamonds from corpses and pretends as if they were hers all along. She wants to pay her respects—to Sarah Vaughan, to Fitzgerald, to Dionne Warwick. She has to, as this album addresses her past addiction, and how it nearly destroyed her, along with her experience of sexual assault, by a music producer, and how it fed a season of self-abnegation. This is personal and exhibitionistic songwriting, on subjects that mid-century singers could have only found expression for through metaphor. Raye sings it straight, hyperverbal, multisyllabic, like she’s a bad-bitch Sondheim: “Codeine / silent, marvellous codeine.” But genuflection creates a stasis, which we feel on “The Thrill is Gone.,” and “Mary Jane.,” with its overwrought guitar. The album is torn, seesawing between nostalgia play and up-to-the-minute “issues” music. (There is a song on it called “Body Dysmorphia.”) Vocally, Raye is most interesting when she is playing sedate, closer to rapping than belting, like on the viral single “Escapism.,” a nocturnal track about desire and regret, featuring the crooner 070 Shake. She is most interesting when she is of her time.

Then again, what is her time but the age that the British cultural theorist Mark Fisher called “the slow cancellation of the future”? I kept asking myself that question while listening to Raye’s most recent album, the international crowd-pleaser “This Music May Contain Hope.” In spoken interludes throughout, Raye is the maestra, nesting explanations and analyses about the album’s four-season structure, which she has, of course, borrowed from Vivaldi. The twenty-twenties are beginning their slow end, and Raye’s recombinant maximalism—her need to be vaudeville and to be Fosse and to be dance hall and to be trip-hop, to feature Al Green, to feature Hans Zimmer, to know everything—is the picture of a present rushing pathologically into the bosom of the past. Fifteen years ago, the music critic Simon Reynolds provided a term for this condition: “retromania.” At the time, I had many issues with Reynolds’s thesis: the Freudian undertone, the inadequate engagement with hip-hop and sampling. These days, I have fewer. ♦

items.title: The Former Trump Official Who Thinks Trump’s Staff Has Let Him Down
items.description: In his new book, “The President Deserves Better: Leadership and Accountability to Keep America Great,” John Ullyot argues that President Donald Trump’s advisers and appointees have let him down in his faltering second term. As Ullyot, a former deputy assistant
items.author: Isaac Chotiner
paragraphs: In his new book, “The President Deserves Better: Leadership and Accountability to Keep America Great,” John Ullyot argues that President Donald Trump’s advisers and appointees have let him down in his faltering second term. As Ullyot, a former deputy assistant to Trump at the White House who has held several government jobs during Trump’s Administrations, including as chief spokesman for the National Security Council, writes “The bottom line is this: The President deserves better.” He adds, “And it’s not just from his Cabinet Secretaries. Many individuals and groups work behind the scenes to block or slow-roll Trump’s reform agenda. You often hear about how liberal media outlets and the foot-dragging, antireform, bureaucratic Deep State try to stop Trump. This book provides a first-hand account of how that happens on a day-to-day basis.”

Recently, in The Atlantic, Ullyot called for the resignation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whom he had advised at the Pentagon in 2025, saying that Hegseth had mismanaged the Iran war and was becoming an embarrassment to the President. (In April of that year, Ullyot detailed the chaos at the Pentagon under Hegseth in Politico.) I recently spoke by phone with Ullyot about his time working with Trump, and the source of the problems in the President’s Administration. Our conversation, edited for length and clarity, is below.
I read your Atlantic piece calling for Hegseth’s resignation. What is it that you think he has done wrong?

Hegseth has done a lot of damage to the Pentagon and to the military. I volunteered to stand up his press operation just for a short period of time at the start of his term last year, and he and I got along very well. When I left, as planned, after standing up his operation and turning it over to his friend—a friend of his that he had selected to run the operation—he thanked me for doing a good job, et cetera. And then it was after that that things got very crazy. I didn’t notice a lot of crazy things going on when I was there, but it was after that point, after I left, that I decided to write that op-ed in Politico. And that was because things had gotten so crazy that he had two of my friends marched out of the building by security, and he accused them of leaking material to the press, and he just had become very paranoid about the leaks.

Hegseth is the least qualified and most polarizing Defense Secretary in modern memory. And as a Marine veteran, and as someone who has spent a lot of time in both the Senate Armed Services Committee and at the National Security Council working with senior members of the military and senior Pentagon leaders, I felt the need to speak out, because he was doing real damage and it was hurting the President as well.
He was appointed to the job by President Trump, right?
So how do you understand President Trump’s decision to appoint him, and also to keep him in the job, even as he’s doing this tremendous damage that you referenced?

So, the President hired him. In his first term, President Trump hired people based on recommendations from many people who were outsiders. And he felt, I believe, that he was not well served by several of them. In his second term, it has been different. He’s hired more on loyalty and hired more people who are going to pursue his agenda rather than those who have a résumé.
So is Hegseth pursuing Trump’s agenda?

I think he is in a lot of ways. The President decided to go to war in Iran, and the Secretary reportedly pushed him into that. I do not think that the President has paid attention to the damage that Hegseth has done on either the cultural front or the self-promoting front, or to the damage that he’s done in taking out very good leaders of the military. I think that the President is mainly briefed on what’s going on at the Pentagon by Pete Hegseth, and doesn’t have people around him who have apprised him of the job that Hegseth’s doing and the damage that he’s done.
If Trump could focus a little more, sit down, read a briefing book on what Hegseth was doing, it might be easier to get him to come around to what you’re saying.

Yeah, I think that’s right. But I really do think that the President hired Hegseth without really looking under the hood. He watches Fox News a lot, and Hegseth, he’s very bombastic, outspoken; he really shouts into the camera on Fox News. And I think President Trump said, “Hey, this guy must be a real military hero. He’s a man’s man, et cetera.” I doubt that he looked at his résumé much, because a lot of people are surprised that Hegseth was not a SEAL Team Six door-kicker or something like that. But he has a persona, and he wrote three books about lethality in the military. I read all three of them before going to work for him.
Yeah, and basically they all say the same thing, and they can be summed up with one page: The military’s gone woke. And, No beardos, no weirdos, no trannies, no fatties, this type of thing.

Did that message appeal to you when you first joined the Administration, but then you thought, Oh, maybe the “no beardos, no weirdos” thing is not actually the way to carry out the running of the Pentagon?

I wrote an op-ed back when Hegseth was still in high school, when I left the Marine Corps, about the need to keep high physical standards, because that was going out, particularly with integrating women into Marine units. Anyway, so I’m not agreeing with him. He’s not the person who invented the idea of high physical standards. And then, in terms of his criticism of how identity politics were woven into the military, I agreed with that. But I wouldn’t make it a big deal. I would just get it done. So I didn’t think you needed to beat your chest about restoring . . . whether it’s in any government position, I agree with eliminating identity politics or identity-based hiring. So I was on board with both of those, but I wasn’t screaming about it.
“Talk softly and carry a big stick” kind of thing.
Yeah, just make the changes and don’t make a big deal about it.

It does occur to me that people who write books that, as you say, can be summarized by lines like “No beardos, no weirdos” might not be so laser-focussed on really running the department as well as they should, and might be more focussed on being obnoxious and things like that. I don’t know. I’m just speculating.

Yeah, I think that’s right. I mean, with his résumé and his bombast, I think that he was probably qualified to be the Pentagon spokesperson, or since he spends a lot of time P.T.ing with the troops, he could have been head of the Presidential physical-fitness council, like Arnold Schwarzenegger was. But, actually, you need a manager or somebody with real management experience to run the largest department in the federal government.

Let’s just go back to President Trump, because your book is very interesting on this idea that Trump has been let down by the people around him in his second term. Is the problem Hegseth, or is the problem more that Trump didn’t do his due diligence?
I don’t think he did due diligence. I think President Trump just saw him on Fox News, liked what he saw, and didn’t say, O.K., let’s look into his background.

Is that then the fault of people around Trump, or is it more Trump’s fault? Because your book is saying that Trump himself is a very effective leader, but that he’s been let down. So I’m curious how you think that through.

So I think that ultimately the buck stops with the President. So, when I say the President deserves better, yes, he deserves better from his staff, but above all he deserves better from himself. Let’s say you’re a friend of a pro golfer and the pro golfer knows that he can do better. You would say, “Hey, look, I think you deserve better than that. You deserve to train a little more or to work on your swing with a swing coach,” et cetera. It’s not a great analogy.

Like any C.E.O., the President is the steward of his own brand. And his brand has slipped badly. But he needs to have staff that are not yes-men. He never did this in the first term, but if you look at these scripted or televised Cabinet meetings where they’ll go on for an hour, the Cabinet meetings with the cameras rolling, they’ll just go around while all the Cabinet members are trying to outdo each other. Each Cabinet member’s trying to outdo the others in praising the President. And that’s not serious. The President doesn’t need that, but ultimately he’s responsible.
Trump’s first Cabinet meeting, in 2017, five months into his term, included a lot of praise, if I remember correctly.

Well, I mean, that could have been the case, but now every Cabinet meeting is televised. I mean, in the first term there were some serious people there who were supporters of the President, but they were not seal clappers the way you see a lot in this Administration.

I am looking now, and in June of 2017, at that first Cabinet meeting, they did go around the room praising him. But, as you say, there’s going around the room and praising him, and then there’s going around the room and really praising him. So you have to draw distinctions, which I think is what you are trying to do.

That’s right. I’ve been in and out of the private sector and advise C.E.O.s, and I say a good C.E.O. surrounds himself with people who are strong enough to tell him what he doesn’t want to hear. And one of them that I worked with was Alan Mulally, when he was C.E.O. of Ford, and they were doing the auto-bailout hearings, back in December of 2008. Mulally was great to work with, and, famously, when he took over Ford, he had his first review of the business units and all the charts, and he said, “Put a green, yellow, or red chart based on how your business unit is doing.” So it was all green while the company was losing billions. And then one executive finally put up a red slide, and Mulally just started applauding him, and later that executive became C.E.O. and replaced Mulally. Mulally wanted to hear the bad news, probably before the good news.
Does it seem to you that Trump wants to hear the bad news before the good news?
No, I don’t think so. I think he deserves better from himself on that. He deserves to look under the hood much more than he has been doing in his second term.

Your book is about how the President deserves better from his staff, but it seems like one of the things you’re saying in this conversation is that the President deserves better from himself, which is a little different.

Yes, that’s right. He made three promises when I worked for him as a senior adviser on the 2016 campaign: no more forever wars, drain the swamp, and put America first. In his first term, when I worked for him in the White House, he was new to Washington and very laser-focussed on delivering on those priorities.

When I remember the first term, it was a lot of tweeting in the middle of the night. It was a lot of staying in the residence to watch Fox News. It was a lot of golfing. I’m not saying things are exactly the same as this term, but when you say the President was laser-focussed on his priorities, I’m trying to remember that.

No, you’re right about his tweeting and his watching TV and staying up late. That hasn’t changed, but what I think has changed in this second term is that he has lost focus on implementing his promises.
I think the ballroom is distracting him. Honestly, I think that’s one of the problems.
Yeah, exactly. So, anyway, things slipped in the second term. Now you’ve got former aides who are cashing in on his name.
Is he cashing in, too, do we think?
I don’t think he is, but certainly there are allegations that his family is. I mean, I think that he’s not personally—
Oh, so you think it’s more his family than him?

Well, it’s his family, but it’s also, let’s look at the ballroom or the library. He is building these big projects that need a lot of money, and so any donor to any President does not contribute to their projects five years after they’ve been President. They’re all lining up to contribute when the President has the power. But, in draining the swamp, that was his promise to be a different President, and now you’ve got his aides.

But do you think that flows from the top? Maybe this gets back to what you say about the fact that he himself deserves better. Maybe he should tell himself to tell his family not to focus on business deals.

Right. This was not a visible embarrassment in the first term. Now it’s a visible embarrassment, and, in fact, he’s reportedly surprised by some of these revelations. So, when we come back to “the President deserves better,” he should have set the tone in the second term and said, “No more of this B.S., I’m different. That’s why I was elected in 2016, because people wanted me to drain the swamp, and I don’t want to have anybody, whether it’s my family or anybody else, riding on my name.”
I think one important thing about your book is getting the message out there that he needs to do this.

Yeah. I appreciate that. That’s what I was trying to do in writing the book. And I had no idea when I started writing it a year and a half ago that the Republican Party would take the shellacking that it did. I mean, nine Senate seats. I worked in the Senate for seven years, and nine seats is seventeen per cent of all the senators. I looked it up—seventeen per cent of the entire collection of senators in the chamber.
Wouldn’t nine Senate seats be nine per cent of the Senate?
Of the Republicans. Republicans had fifty-three. If you divide nine out of fifty-three—
Of course, yeah, my mistake.

Yeah, no worries. So, anyway, nine seats is a lot of seats. Anyway, when I started writing this book, I was saying it is maybe intended for future Presidents, but now it has become a lot more relevant to this President.

Well, honestly, if there’s a theme to this conversation, I think it’s that if Trump had read Hegseth’s books, or if he reads your book now, things could be better. Maybe Trump reading more books is the solution here.
Yeah, maybe that’s the solution.

Last question for you: What if someone said, “Look, this Donald Trump, he’s got a little older, he’s surrounded by more loyalists, but fundamentally, this is the guy who, from the start, talked about Obama’s birth certificate, and then he talked about ‘Mexican’ judges, and then he insulted people all the time, and there are all these accusations about how he assaults women, and then there were all these things that he said about Haitians, and January 6th, and then you go to the second term, and he’s posting the video of the Obamas as apes, and actually he is just the same guy who never really had any sense of how to run the country or a sense of the national interest”? I’m not saying there’s any merit to this idea, but what do you think of it?

Well, no, I think that’s a very good point. What I would say is he’s the same man, but, politically, voters were once willing to overlook this pugilistic, crude character tweeting about the Obamas as apes and all of that business.

It seems as if you wish Trump would remind himself, and remind people, that fundamentally he was a businessman who came to shake up Washington. If he could get back to that, maybe he could get back on the right track.
Yeah, absolutely. There’s still a runway for him to get things done. ♦

items.title: Is Science Accelerating?
