items.author: Joshua Rothman
paragraphs: What was American life like a hundred years ago? The economist Robert J. Gordon offers a vivid picture in his book “The Rise and Fall of American Growth,” from 2016. In 1926, Gordon writes, there were almost no paved roads west of the Mississippi. Fewer than one in ten homes had an electric refrigerator. (A typical one cost the equivalent of ten thousand dollars today.) If you lived in Muncie, Indiana, the odds were one in four that your house had no running water, and one in three that it had no sewer connection. Life was rough by our standards. And yet, Gordon shows, scientific and technological progress was obvious everywhere. Thousands of new hospitals were being constructed, many with cutting-edge X-ray departments. Ninety-three per cent of Iowa farmers owned automobiles, even though the automobile itself had begun to appear only three decades before. 1926 was the year it became possible for an ordinary person to travel on an airplane; it was also when an inventor named Clarence Birdseye perfected frozen food, making the consumption of fish affordable in landlocked places. The way people lived was clearly better than how their parents had lived.

This rapid “epochal transformation,” Gordon writes, actually continued for a whole century, stretching from 1870 to 1970. It was powered by five “Great Inventions”—electricity, urban sanitation, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, internal-combustion engines, and signal transmission. The Great Inventions, in turn, were based on foundational discoveries in physics, biology, medicine, chemistry, math, and other fields. “What makes the period 1870–1970 so special is that these inventions cannot be repeated,” Gordon writes. The germ theory of disease, which Louis Pasteur advanced in the eighteen-eighties, led to sweeping changes in pretty much every aspect of life, and yet it could be discovered only once. The principle of electromagnetism unlocks everything from engines to radios, but there aren’t infinite, similarly powerful principles to uncover and apply. The staircase of science—or at least this flight of it—appears to have only so many steps.

What happens after the biggest discoveries have been made, explored, and put to use? Arguably, the rate of progress slows, and dramatic transformation becomes harder to achieve. The practice of science itself also changes. In recent decades, economists and other researchers have explored a field that they call “metascience”—the study of why the pace of scientific discovery increases or decreases. They point out that, although more scientific papers are being published, fewer are truly disruptive; more patents are granted, but a smaller number are for “breakthrough” inventions. Increasingly, science is conducted inside enormous bureaucracies that favor cautious, incremental research. Grants are awarded mainly to sure bets; power concentrates among august institutions and scientists. In a 2020 paper, the economists Nicholas Bloom, Charles I. Jones, John Van Reenen, and Michael Webb asked, “Are ideas getting harder to find?” They observed that the number of researchers required to double the speed of computer chips was eighteen times larger than it had been in the early nineteen-seventies. For a long time, they concluded, progress had emerged from “a constant flow of new ideas.” Now that flow has slowed.

Is this how life feels in 2026? Does it seem to you that scientific and technological progress has plateaued? It’s true that the iPhone Duo is only somewhat exciting. But, on the other hand, there is now a pancreatic-cancer pill and a melanoma vaccine. In Massachusetts, a man named Tim Andrews lived for the better part of a year while relying on a gene-edited kidney grown inside a pig. Norwegian salmon farms now use underwater A.I.-controlled laser robots to kill sea lice; in France, a startup has made tiny drones that can do the same for mosquitoes in your back yard. “Technological evolution is still accelerating,” the computer scientist John von Neumann wrote, in a 1955 essay, toward the end of Gordon’s spectacular century. In that particular essay, von Neumann was thinking mainly of nuclear power, machine automation, and climate control—technologies that have progressed slowly or fizzled out. And yet computer science, a field to which he made foundational contributions, has made steady—and now startling—new advances. The question of whether science is slowing or accelerating is complicated by its essential unpredictability. And because science is an interpersonal, interwoven enterprise, progress in one area can enable it in others, in ways that might not be easy to foresee.

A cartoon equation for science might go like this: B (brainiacs) + M (money) x T (technology) = D (discovery). Needless to say, it isn’t that simple. The brainiacs can be arranged in all sorts of organizations and hierarchies; the money can flow to the right ones or the wrong ones. The technology can be employed correctly or incorrectly; the discoveries can result in smarter brainiacs, more money, and better technology, or they can die on the vine. Fields and methods, meanwhile, can be young or grown-up, flexible or ossified, fashionable or passé. “At the time I was starting, lots and lots of things were just opening up,” Eve Marder, a neuroscientist who began her career in the nineteen-seventies, told me. “I started just after the time when someone could put an electrode anywhere in any nervous system and see something that no one had ever seen before—which is very, very different from the much more mature science that we have today.” For neuroscientists now, she went on, “what constitutes ‘success’ or ‘new knowledge’ has changed, and the incentive structures have also changed.” Marder recalled going to her first neuroscience conference, which had around five hundred attendees, allowing her to meet many of the most important figures in the field. Today, the big annual meeting put on by the Society for Neuroscience typically hosts around twenty thousand researchers.

Marder is now an eminent scientist: her lab, at Brandeis University, studies how individual neurons connect to create stable circuits that can survive and function over time. She has won major awards, supervised large numbers of scientists and graduate students, and participated in research projects of varying sizes. “We have a very complicated challenge in science today, which is that there are some things that can only be done by ‘big science,’ ” she said. “If you’re doing ‘small science,’ with small groups of people, then the ones who make mistakes can be very easily corrected or can self-correct. But, if you do big science poorly, somebody can make a bad decision and take everyone down a bad path.”

In a big-science world, researchers often work in large consortia that cross institutional and disciplinary lines. They collaborate to gather vast quantities of data, hoping that it will be amenable to analysis now and in the future. Young scientists can find themselves assimilated, Borg-style, into these expansive projects and the institutions that make them possible. “A student who goes into a field is captivated by ideas,” Marder said. “They want to discover something, to create something, just like a philosopher wants to think something no one’s ever thought. And then they are socialized by having to get to the next step, or get the next fellowship. They start worrying about who they have to please—and that can flow down and change the science that they’re willing or able to do.” Some young scientists “are very stubborn, and will continue to be independent and innovative, and become leaders in their fields,” Marder went on. But “a lot of very creative people get driven out.”

If the scale of modern science can dwarf individual scientists, it can also sideline their contributions. “Right now, on my desk in my office, I have a huge pile of really important papers by brilliant people that I don’t have time to read—there’s too many of them,” Michael Levin, a biologist at Tufts, told me. “I conclude, by symmetry, that nobody has time to read my papers, either. That raises the question: Who the hell am I writing all this for?” Levin, who studies bioelectric computation—the process through which cells communicate and make collective decisions—believes that science is, in fact, accelerating: one sign is that “it’s becoming more and more difficult to stay apprised of the important things.” In a 2005 paper titled “The Burden of Knowledge and the ‘Death of the Renaissance Man,’ ” the economist Benjamin F. Jones explored this paradox. Since “knowledge accumulates as technology progresses,” he wrote, there is ever more to know, and so the “educational burden” on researchers increases; eventually, it becomes harder not just to know everything but to know what’s needed for you, in particular, to push knowledge forward. Ironically, science may be slower precisely because it’s moving quickly in too many directions.

Organizational and communicative challenges exist alongside what might be called problems of ambition: science can be slow simply because, at this point, its aims are Olympian. Kristin Persson, a materials scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, explained one overarching goal in her field: predicting how different arrangements of atoms will behave under different conditions, so that they can be combined into new and useful materials. “For a very long time, we’ve been trying to do what some people call multi-scale modelling,” she said. “You start out with atoms and electrons, and you have an equation for behavior on that length scale and time scale. Then you take those properties and you feed them into higher-scale equations.” The approach, she said, has “never really taken off, because of what’s lost in translation every time you move from one set of equations to the next.”

It’s hard, in other words, to precisely predict the behavior of matter at every scale. The theoretical basis for such predictions was established a century ago—in 1926, as it happens—by the physicist Erwin Schrödinger, who devised a single equation describing how electrons interact under the laws of quantum mechanics; it’s relatively simple to solve for small numbers of electrons, but becomes unwieldy as atoms add up. If you want to use it at a large scale, you can solve it only approximately, unless you want your computer to calculate for billions of years. Science is full of such bottlenecks: places where dramatic insights, some long-standing, can’t yet yield practical results.

Today’s computers may not be fast enough to effortlessly apply Schrödinger’s Equation—but they are, apparently, fast enough to read and think. Accordingly, Levin told me, scientists are using artificial intelligence to respond to the burden of knowledge. “They take that stack of papers and put it through an A.I., and say, ‘Summarize this for me,’ ” he said. Levin regards it as a useful innovation, wielded by experts, that might itself be accelerated. “If all my work is going to get filtered through an A.I., then why am I putting out a traditional paper, with all of this stuff we do for each other—with the freaking grammar, and the PDFs, and the figures, which the A.I. has to take apart?” he asked. He anticipates a near future in which the form of the scientific paper becomes A.I.-ready, with old knowledge ably surfaced by artificial intelligence alongside new work. “There are amazing authors with amazing sets of papers from twenty, thirty years ago that nobody knows today,” he said. “Theoretically, that information is there somewhere, but, if nobody knows it and nobody uses it, then do we really have it?”

It could be that some version of this transformation is already under way. Scientists are increasingly using large language models not just to read papers but to write them: studies from last year, when A.I. was less capable, found that many researchers had experienced writing-productivity boosts of between thirty-three and fifty per cent, and submissions to journals and to conferences are up, in some cases dramatically. Meanwhile, in a study titled “AI Article Reviews Dominate Human Peer Reviews at Their Best,” two Harvard researchers, Gary King and Steven Worthington, show that peer reviews performed by L.L.M.s “are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts”; they’re even “judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors.” It’s possible to discern, in these developments, a new rhythm of scientific communication.

L.L.M.s work with language: it’s not surprising that they can be used to process information. But what about the actual labor of science, which is concrete, empirical, and often outrageously time-consuming? “There’s a lot of ‘donkey work,’ ” Persson, the materials scientist at Berkeley, said. Experiments must be done painstakingly, over and over, for years, and even then they can produce unpredictable results; a brilliant young researcher might spend her whole postdoc on the creation of a statistical model that’s immediately bested by someone else’s. Scientific progress is slow, in part, because there aren’t that many passionate, hyper-educated people willing to devote themselves to hands-on, detail-oriented, ruthlessly competitive, and often fruitless labor.

It’s clear, at this point, that A.I. can automate some of the donkey work. “We have a bunch of computational neuroscientists in my lab, and every last one of them says, ‘I can now do in a week what would have taken me six months,’ ” Marder, the neuroscientist at Brandeis, told me. Materials scientists use computer simulations that can easily run off the rails. “When I was a graduate student, I logged in late at night to see if my simulation had worked out,” Persson said; she’d then spend untold hours troubleshooting. Now, she explained, “L.L.M.s are learning from errors in the simulations and applying their corrections autonomously to keep them on track.” This leaves time-constrained researchers free to focus on higher-level questions.

The advantages may go beyond vibe coding. A.I. systems “are so helpful at solving problems because they can try lots of things,” Michael Brenner, a professor of applied math and physics at Harvard who also helps direct A.I. science efforts for Google, told me. At Google, Brenner led the development of a system called Empirical Research Assistance (ERA), which scientists can use to create data-analysis tools. In many ways, ERA also addresses the burden of knowledge: researchers pose questions to it, and provide it with data, and it responds by trying and mixing different extant methods of analysis in numberless combinations, discovering new paths to progress. (Researchers have used ERA to create improved disease-forecasting models, for example.) “It’s like swapping and flipping, flipping and swapping the pieces, and trying to figure out something that actually works,” Brenner said. The power of the system, he went on, was “not Einsteinian but Edisonian”: it consisted in the novel application of known ideas.

Could A.I. offer even more in the way of novelty, contributing to the automated production of new data, new knowledge, and new theories? Both Levin and Persson described automated laboratories as a logical next step. Currently, Persson said, the creation of new experimental data is extraordinarily expensive and time-intensive—but robots, she argued, could be used “to produce data at scale,” which could then be analyzed by existing A.I. models or used to train new ones. (This data, she noted, might also have the advantage of being unusually consistent and free from human error.) “We’re going to get lab automation,” Levin said. “Then there’s going to be no more concern with hallucination or confabulation—the A.I.s are going to try stuff, and it either works or it doesn’t. At that point, once they have the ability to actually test out the consequences of their hypotheses, the loop is going to accelerate, and all this is going to go exponential.” This vision—in which A.I. speeds up not just the collection and analysis of data but the generation of hypotheses and the design of experiments—represents one of the more radical acceleratory possibilities for science. Levin suggested one major obstacle: “A.I. has been obviously trained on human output where conventional theories are overrepresented,” he said. To arrive at “unconventional ideas”—the kinds that lead to full-throttle acceleration, and to world-changing invention—it would have to become less consensus-driven.

If dramatic scientific acceleration occurs, it will be significant on at least three levels. First, there’s the question posed by John von Neumann, the computer scientist, in his 1955 essay: “Can we survive technology?” Today, the concept of a technological “singularity” is easily taken to refer to a single Promethean moment, such as the invention of superintelligent A.I. But the concept, which is often credited to von Neumann, can have a simpler meaning. New technologies are frequently hard to manage; as more of them pop up, their management gets more and more difficult, until they become, in aggregate, unmanageable. How many simultaneous “upgrades” can society withstand? This problem concerned von Neumann precisely because he was writing toward the tail end of the century of invention described in “The Rise and Fall of American Growth.” If we are entering such a period again, we need to be as concerned as he was with the problem of technology management. We need to shift from a fetishization of disruption to a fascination with control.

Second, there’s the question of growth. In his book, Gordon shows how much life can improve when Great Inventions are changing the world. During the hundred years he describes, people got healthier and ate better; worked less and travelled farther; moved into bigger, more comfortable houses; and grew increasingly educated while exercising more personal freedom. The economy expanded because lives were expanding. But today, the United States, along with most of the Western world, is facing a crisis of growth. Populations are aging, and the ratio of workers to pensioners is falling. The costs of housing, food, education, health care, and other necessities are rising, as are our debts. “What are we going to do?” the economist Tyler Cowen asked, recently. “Plan A is that A.I. will help us grow more quickly, and we will manage to pay our bills. . . . There is no Plan B.” We need some new Great Inventions; an acceleration in science, enabled partly by A.I., is our most promising path to getting them.

Finally, there’s the not-unimportant matter of human knowledge. Progress in science is good—but it doesn’t always feel good. Often, it centers not on the arrival of answers but on the proliferation of difficult questions. The same may be true for progress in the practice of science. Sudden advances in mathematics have led some mathematicians to say that their field has been “broken” by artificial intelligence. “I don’t think math is broken,” Brenner told me. “It’s hard for the community, and some of my math colleagues might disagree with me, but I think it’s a very exciting time in mathematics, a time to really rethink things and break new ground.” Persson agreed: “Maybe the mathematicians are having a rough time, but honestly I would congratulate them,” she said. “You should talk to some of my students: They see a lot of their mundane work going away. They can focus on fun things; they can do simulations they could never do before.” It was, she suggested, a great time to become a scientist. ♦

items.title: Jared Kushner’s Wars
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Andrew Rice
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

At 45, Jared Kushner is no longer young, but he still presents as a man in a hurry. His thin face rests in an expression of impatience: lips pursed, nostrils flared, eyebrows arched. He has no formal office in President Donald Trump’s government, only a wedding license, but on any given day he may be anywhere in the world, tending to his father-in-law’s diplomatic business. On one tropical morning in late September, he can be found at his home outside Miami — the city that, under Trump, has become an unofficial hub of American foreign policy. When I first see him through the enormous front windows of his sleek modernist mansion in the Village of Indian Creek, a private island in Biscayne Bay, Kushner is standing by the front door, cell phone to his ear. At this moment, he is simultaneously giving his attention to three global crises, each of which is critical and overwhelming in its own right.

On top of that, Kushner has a day job at his private-equity firm, Affinity Partners, which does business in some of the same countries where he practices diplomacy. He sees no conflict in this, only virtuous synergy, but it does require some toggling.

Kushner opens the door, invites me inside, then hoists a backpack over his shoulder. He is dressed casually in a lightweight sweater and throwback Air Jordans. He bounds down the white marble front stairs to his car, an unfancy Jeep Cherokee. Its wheels crunch the driveway gravel as we circle a bubbling fountain and head out through the hedges with his Secret Service detail trailing behind. The island — known to tabloids and celebrity real-estate agents as the “Billionaire Bunker” — is separated from the mainland by what is effectively a moat, which we cross via a gated bridge, and Kushner turns in the direction of the Affinity office.

“I’m a fairly all-in personality, so when I’m in something, it consumes all of me,” Kushner says as he drives. “It takes a big toll on me to do one of these, let alone three.” Crisis No. 1 is Gaza, which Kushner took on last year by inserting himself into the middle of cease-fire negotiations between Hamas and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “Not only getting the war stopped — getting all the hostages home, getting the bodies of the hostages home. It was a crazy operation,” he says. “Bibi didn’t think we could do it.” Since then, Kushner has been working on the future of Palestine — without much substantive input, critics say, from actual Palestinians — while also trying to resolve crisis No. 2, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and navigating crisis No. 3, Trump’s war of choice with Iran.

“Fixing Iran-U.S. relations, that’s something that has been broken for 50 years, so it’s not like there’s a precedent for success,” Kushner tells me. He’s oversimplifying the history, but he doesn’t think history matters much anyway. His cell phone rings. It’s his brother, Josh, the tech venture capitalist who is buying a piece of the Los Angeles Lakers. He sends Josh to voice-mail so he can concentrate. Over the months we’ve been talking, Kushner has explained his theory of statecraft, which prizes the innate ability of “deal guys,” who he says can think up solutions that elude the cautious, protocol-bound, and past-obsessed professionals of the diplomatic corps. Although he collaborates closely with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s old friend and official peace envoy, and they are both technically overseen by Marco Rubio, who is national security adviser and secretary of State, Kushner effectively works as an unpaid freelancer, relying on the back channels he opened as a senior White House aide during Trump’s first term and later solidified through his business.

Earlier in the drive, I told Kushner that, the way I saw it, one big question was arising from all his efforts: “What’s this guy’s angle?” One common and plausible answer is money. A couple of weeks before, The New Yorker published a long article about what it labeled Kushner’s “dollar diplomacy,” looking into the ways in which — even as he participated in fateful foreign-policy decisions about the Middle East — he had cultivated investment from some of the same governments he has been meeting with on behalf of the U.S. The funds managed by Affinity, which currently has some $6 billion in assets, mostly came from sovereign-wealth funds controlled by the royal families of the Persian Gulf. Kushner invested in an AI start-up in Silicon Valley and a rental-car company in Israel and Burger King franchises in Brazil and even a real-estate development in Albania, where his involvement has inspired widespread anti-government protests. The New Yorker article was just the latest installment in a decadelong series of reports, books, and official investigations about his business dealings, but the latest implication that he had been bought off got under Kushner’s skin so much that he tells me he is putting together what will turn out to be a 6,800-word footnoted rebuttal.

“The accumulation of more wealth is not my top objective,” he tells me. He says he could be making more money if he weren’t giving his time away, and his standard answer to critics is to challenge them to find any instance when he acted contrary to American interests. “Having the resources that I need to live my life makes me more independent to pursue the things that I want to pursue,” Kushner says. “I’ve been doing this for ten years, and my business has been an objectively successful business. My diplomacy’s been successful diplomacy. Nobody’s ever identified any case where I’ve done one thing to benefit the other.”

It is still a few weeks before the midterms, and Democrats are promising to test his catch-me-if-you-can defense when they retake Congress, and with it, subpoena power. But Kushner claims he is unfazed. “I sleep well at night,” he tells me, “because I know what the laws are, I know what the rules are, and I don’t come close to violating them.”

At the entrance to the open-plan office of Affinity, I see evidence of another possible motivation. Behind the reception desk is his “power wall,” where an array of pictures and mementos are hung. Some of the photos are of Trump, and others are inscribed by him. JARED, GREAT JOB reads the distinctive Sharpie scrawl atop a map of Israel, memorializing a peace initiative Kushner pushed in the first term. (It was unsuccessful.) Another photo, of Trump’s border wall, bears the underlined word PAINT. (Trump had put Kushner in charge of building it and wanted it to be black.)

Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump — who also served as an aide to her father during his first term — spent four tumultuous years in the West Wing. Working from a tiny office that linked to the Oval Office through an inner passageway, Kushner served as Trump’s actualizer, translating his gut feelings into government action, and his soft-voiced interpreter to Congress, Wall Street, and world leaders. After the first term ended in a haze of tear gas and disgrace, Kushner wrote a White House memoir called Breaking History, in which he placed himself at the center of all that went right and none of the wrong. “I left Washington with a new understanding of the world,” Kushner told me when we met for our first interview this past summer. “A lot of new relationships that were mostly earned in the trenches, chasing impossible goals, and a deep belief in myself.”

During the first term, Kushner would sometimes advise colleagues not to try to control Trump — he makes the waves, Kushner says, and you can only try to surf them. He swears he didn’t want to get pulled back into the water. When pressed, Kushner concedes that he may be excited to exercise power, but he claims he doesn’t want it for its own sake — rather, he wants the power to do good in the world. The signature foreign-policy promise of Trump’s comeback campaign was “No new wars,” but now it’s wars all over. Who would choose to take that on? “No. 1, there’s a high likelihood of not succeeding,” Kushner says as we talk in his corner office, where his standing desk looks out onto the Atlantic. “And No. 2, a high likelihood of people screaming at you and people accusing you of crazy things.”

Many of the accusations leveled at Kushner are not at all crazy, though, and to the Democrats who recently reclaimed control of Congress, they potentially involve a rich vein of corruption to mine in their coming investigations of the Trump administration. “I think Kushner is going to be a huge focus,” says a Democratic staffer on one of the congressional committees about an investigation that is now gearing up. “The scale of Jared Kushner’s corruption makes what Hunter Biden did look like food-stamp fraud.”

News reports have already identified some potential conflicts of interest, including Affinity’s interest in Arxis, a Connecticut defense contractor that sells to the U.S. military, and Phoenix Financial, a large firm in Israel that has invested in companies supplying that country’s army with ammunition, drones, and other matériel. (Kushner contends Phoenix is just an asset manager comparable to an American company like Vanguard and has declined to comment on Arxis.) The incoming Democrats believe they will turn up more damaging information once they start compelling witnesses to testify under oath.

Kushner is quick to point out that many previous investigations have failed to pin anything illegal on him. Still, there remains the separate question of what he has actually done with his power. In the Kushner belief system, there is no more shameful sin than ineffectiveness. But as a diplomat, he is at least partly responsible for the debacle in Iran — the “biggest self-own in the history of foreign policy,” as one expert described it to me — and Democrats hope to show he has made money while botching the assignment. To them, he looks like a caricature of Trump-era corruption, the walking, slim-suited embodiment of two of the things a majority of the Americans who voted to repudiate Trump in the midterms hate the most about his administration: the war and the greed. How does Kushner justify what he has done and what he has failed to do? To a remarkable degree, he is insouciant in the face of disaster and its consequences.

When he worked in the West Wing, the Secret Service gave him the code name “Mechanic,” and he expresses boundless confidence in “my ability to problem-solve, my ability to manifest impossible things.” In our conversations, this self-assurance is undiminished by the harsh reality that most of his diplomatic initiatives have been going nowhere and, in some cases, have left the world in worse condition than it was before.

Kushner’s master plan for Gaza — a scheme to build the strip into a coastal metropolis — is stalled and cannot proceed until Israel allows it to move forward, which won’t happen unless Netanyahu or a successor is convinced that Hamas is serious about disarming. In Ukraine, the recent strategy of offering economic carrots to Vladimir Putin while using the stick on Volodymyr Zelenskyy has yielded little in the way of concessions from Russia, the aggressor. It has been bombarding Kyiv as viciously as at any point in the war. And in the Persian Gulf, the region of the world where Kushner has concentrated both his foreign-policy and fundraising efforts, the American position has deteriorated over the past year, despite — or maybe because of — his involvement. Trump went to war with Iran only after Kushner judged that negotiations with the Iranian regime over its nuclear program were not worth pursuing. In retrospect, walking away and launching air strikes looks like a catastrophic mistake. Despite the death of Iran’s supreme leader, the hard-liners in the country appear to feel they have emerged stronger from nine months of on-and-off conflict. Kushner has tried to address the problem, but it has defied all his powers as a deal-maker. Once you break history, it’s tough to put it back together.

It is tempting to describe Kushner’s role in government as unprecedented, but if you take the long view, it’s not so strange. “I feel like I’ve been going back to early-modern history,” says Fiona Hill, who worked with Kushner when she was on the staff of the National Security Council in the first Trump term. “Jared is a prince, and he plays a kind of a function that would have been not unfamiliar in the 18th century.” Hill, who oversaw Russia policy before she resigned in 2019 and later became a witness against Trump in his first impeachment, recalls being summoned to the Oval Office to listen to a call between the president and Putin. When Trump hung up, he ignored her, the expert, and instead asked Jared and Ivanka for their takes.

To Hill, this was striking to see in the West Wing, but there are plenty of places where the ruler turns to family first. “In the context of international diplomacy,” says Ben Rhodes, a former foreign-policy adviser to President Obama, “it is actually not unusual to have a son-in-law who is a power broker who mixes business and profit.”

In Kushner’s own telling, family obligation has been the driving force in his life. He had to grow up fast, taking over the Kushner real-estate business, established by his grandfather, when he was still in his 20s. (His father, Charlie, had been sent to prison for crimes connected to a feud with his brother-in-law. He was pardoned by Trump in 2020 and is now the U.S. ambassador to France.) When Jared married Ivanka, he entered a new family with new obligations. In his memoir, he portrays his decision to take over Trump’s disorganized 2016 campaign as a matter of duty. Then he says duty sent him to Washington. Kushner’s ego, and the power he wields, is couched in the language of noble service. If he wanted to make money, he says, he did not need to do it in a roundabout way by going into government. When he took his White House position, Kushner had to sell his interests in various private investments, including an early one he had made in Thrive Capital, the venture firm his brother, Josh, founded. It’s gone on to such success that the shares he sold would’ve been worth many billions today. “I believe he and Ivanka would pass a lie-detector test,” says a first-term White House staffer. “They believe it to their core: If you asked them whether this made them richer or poorer, they would say ‘poorer.’”

“I think that for whatever reason, I’ve always been underestimated in my life,” Kushner says. In reply, he can cite a list of unquestionable achievements he pulled off during Trump’s first term, such as launching Operation Warp Speed, which produced a COVID vaccine in a miraculous seven months. But no assignment was more meaningful, he says, than the one Trump gave him at the start of the administration: figure out Israel and Palestine. His grandparents survived the Holocaust in the forests of Belarus. As a teenager, Jared once vacated his bedroom for Netanyahu when he stayed over as a houseguest. Given that prior rounds of negotiation had yielded failure after failure, it made for an easy joke: Jared was going to bring peace to the Middle East? But Kushner took the possibility seriously and approached diplomacy as another form of networking.

Back when he was just another striving young businessman, he had become acquainted with Tony Blair, the former British prime minister. (He has a knack for befriending older Davos Men.) In 2016, Blair was pushing a plan to address both Palestinian demands for statehood and Israel’s desire to thaw its political and trade relations with Arab nations. Blair told Kushner he saw an opening and it ran through the Persian Gulf.

Traditionally, the public-facing appointees who represented America to the world were backed up by a seasoned army of Foreign Service officers and area experts inside the federal bureaucracy. The National Security Council used a methodical interagency process to explore and weigh changes in policy. Kushner went about things his own way. Through a friend, an American asset manager who has dealings in the United Arab Emirates, he made a connection to that nation’s ruler, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, commonly known as MBZ. He became close to MBZ’s brother and national security adviser, Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who controls a sovereign-wealth fund that has more than $1 trillion in assets. Early in the administration, Kushner met Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, or MBS, with whom he would form a key alliance.

MBS was in a struggle with another potential successor to the Saudi throne who had close ties to the CIA. The Middle East experts in the White House were cautious, thinking MBS was cocky and inexperienced, but Kushner saw him as a disrupter like himself. “MBS knew right away that Jared was his flunky,” says a senior National Security Council official from Trump’s first term, who describes Kushner as “a completely loose cannon with respect to any interagency coordination.”

Kushner arranged for Trump to make a presidential visit to Saudi Arabia in 2017. At a banquet during the trip, MBS made introductions for Kushner and Ivanka. Kushner recounts in his book that MBS took him to his table and said, “These were the ‘Jared Kushners’ of the Middle East,” and that “they didn’t all have obvious titles, but if I needed to get anything done in their countries, I should call them.” Kushner soon began paying visits to his new acquaintances in the region. He traveled with a small entourage, usually without the inclusion of translators or U.S. Embassy staff on the ground.

There is little in the public record about what transpired in Kushner’s private meetings, which has led to much speculation about the nature of his conversations. In October, the investigative journalist Matthew Cole published a book called Princes and Thieves, in which he alleges (based on confidential sourcing) that MBZ and MBS bribed Kushner by jointly putting billions of dollars into overseas bank accounts that were intended both to enrich him personally and to create a “slush fund” to advance secret U.S. military and intelligence objectives. Cole writes that Kushner’s compromising financial relationships eventually became known to various parties, including the government of Qatar, the Russians, and even hackers working for the Dutch intelligence service. These extraordinary claims lack extraordinary evidence, and Kushner has described them as “completely insane.” He points out that this time coincided with special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation, when he was “one of the most scrutinized people in the world.” Kushner says he is preparing a defamation lawsuit, yet to be filed.

It’s really not necessary to resort to bribery, though, to explain the affinity between Kushner and the Jared Kushners of the Middle East. Foreign-policy experts have a term for this, mirroring — seeing your own values and preconceptions in your counterpart. Kushner believes the Gulf rulers found his family-to-family outreach “familiar and reassuring.” In the Gulf, “they feel very, very comfortable with the idea that the leader of the United States has a family member who is out representing him personally in negotiations,” says a former diplomat stationed in the region at the time. “That aligns with the way that Gulf ruling families do business.”

Kushner spent the time it took to build trusting relationships. He bonded with MBS at one of the crown prince’s estates in the desert, staying up all night and watching the sun rise over a fire. Kushner was impressed with his vision for modernizing Saudi Arabia and his willingness to spend his oil money on transformative projects. When they weren’t together, Kushner and MBS would talk and text on WhatsApp. MBS loves video games, and sometimes they’d play together. (“League of Legends,” Kushner specifies. “He’s a big League player.”) When MBS was implicated in the grisly assassination of a Washington-based dissident, Kushner refused calls to repudiate him. “It’s a real friendship,” Kushner says.

It took nearly four years for Kushner’s personalized approach to come to fruition in an act of diplomacy that, at the time, even his skeptics described as nimble. In 2020, he unveiled a new land-for-peace plan to the Israelis and the Palestinians. The Palestinian Authority leadership immediately rejected it, saying it offered them no substantive assurance they would ever attain statehood while providing the thinnest of smoke screens for Israel’s annexation of West Bank settlements. But the setback created an opportunity. From their interactions, Kushner had concluded that Gulf leaders were weary of supporting the Palestinian struggle and ready to drop their pretense of hostility toward Israel. He met with Yousef Al Otaiba, the Emirati ambassador in Washington, who had become another friend. (“Whether it’s on WhatsApp or Signal or whatever the method is, he speaks to you like a normal person,” Al Otaiba tells me. “He actually listens, and he doesn’t come in with preconceived notions.”) The Emiratis were ready to propose an alternative approach. They wanted economic and security ties with Israel. If Netanyahu would agree not to annex West Bank settlements, there could be a new framework: peace without the Palestinians.

Kushner flew all over the region to broker the resulting agreement, known as the Abraham Accords. “I actually say to people he is probably the best natural political mind I have come across,” says Blair. “And I have come across quite a few.” The accords demonstrated not just the value of Kushner’s relationships but his willingness to go big, Blair tells me. “One of the things he is extremely good at is that when a problem is in quite a narrow compass and there is a blockage, he creates an enlargement of the matrix of issues to be decided that allows you then to unlock the problem.” The Abraham Accords soon expanded to encompass more than just one set of concerns. After the UAE became the first Arab nation to normalize diplomatic relations with Israel in more than 25 years, several other Muslim-majority countries jumped aboard.

In the final months of Trump’s term, Kushner spent much of his time traveling the Gulf region, promoting economic development and trying to lay the groundwork to bring Saudi Arabia into the accords. (MBS assured Kushner he might join down the line.) Airline routes opened between Tel Aviv and Dubai. Commerce began to flow. “I’m always trying to focus on the economics,” Kushner says. “Everyone’s focused on the historical grievances, whereas my view is the past is the past.”

On January 6, 2021, Kushner was flying home from Saudi Arabia, where he had been attending an economic summit, when he learned that rioters had broken into the Capitol. Although he has never stated unequivocally that Trump lost the election, Kushner had concluded weeks before that any effort to overturn it was hopeless. He left it to Rudy Giuliani and others to pursue legal challenges. Still, after his plane landed, Kushner went to the White House to support Ivanka, who has since said she was trying to persuade her father to call on his supporters to disperse. While Kushner would personally condemn the attack as “wrong and unlawful,” he never uttered a critical word about Trump himself. “You’ll never, ever read a public thing where I distance myself from him,” Kushner says to me one morning in July. “I won’t do that. I’d rather suffer.”

We are at Bedminster, where he and Ivanka usually spend part of the summer with their three children in their house across the club’s pool from Trump’s own. By Kushner standards, it’s a relaxed time. His son Joseph has been learning to caddie for his grandfather on the golf course, which is festooned with banners for the Saudi-sponsored (and soon to go bust) LIV tour. Ivanka is out taking their youngest, Theodore, to a STEM camp. (Ivanka declined to be interviewed.)

“In the first term,” Kushner tells me, “80 percent of the people in the White House thought they were trying to save the world from Trump and 20 percent of us thought Trump was saving the world.” He and Ivanka decided that if Trump won a second term, they wouldn’t go back to work for him in the West Wing. After January 6, Kushner helped coordinate damage control. “I joke with him that we’re 2-0 on impeachments,” he says. But he was ready to get out of Washington. As he now tells the story, one morning soon after the election, he woke up and told Ivanka their next move had just dawned on him.
“Let’s go to Miami,” he said.

Jared and Ivanka had spent four years trying to live with one foot in Trumpworld and another in elite society. “That is like the narrowest tightrope in history,” a former White House staffer says. January 6 severed the line completely. In Miami, the weather was warm, crypto was booming, the restaurants were open in spite of COVID, and no one judged. They bought their house in Indian Creek in 2021 for $24 million and immediately tore it down to the studs, turning what was previously a gaudy South Florida villa into something more reflective of their taste.

When I visit on a weekday morning, the house is quiet and sunbathed. Through the glass double doors of the living room, I can see a backyard pool and a thatch-roofed sukkah the family has erected for the holiday season. Beyond that stands a large covered patio with a grill for alfresco dining and a gym with weight machines and a sauna. (“Set the cold plunge at 42 degrees, and just go for it,” Kushner says. “After that, the day’s easy.”) A boat is docked at the rear of the property. The boys fish, and Ivanka likes to paddleboard. It’s a good life, and their market timing was impeccable. Since they purchased on the island, they’ve acquired new neighbors, including Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg.

“Now it’s become a place for immortals, but we were some of the last mortals to be able to buy there,” Kushner says. He has served as a member of the Indian Creek Village council, and the family recently was accepted into the island’s country club after a cooling period on the wait list. To some of their old friends in New York, it looked like they were retreating to a temporary place of exile, but Kushner doesn’t look at the island as an Elba. It’s become his family’s home. “A narrative people were writing is that we were running away from New York, but we didn’t view it like that,” Kushner says. “We viewed it like we were running toward the lives we wanted to live. We stopped giving a shit what other people say, and we just started living for ourselves.”

Soon after he settled in, Kushner founded Affinity Partners, which served as a landing spot for some of the aides who worked for him in the White House. He returned to the Gulf as a private citizen and pitched Affinity in the same places where he’d put together the Abraham Accords. A Saudi sovereign-wealth fund put in $2 billion after MBS overruled management objections about its nonexistent track record. The Emiratis and Qataris followed, bringing the fund’s initial capitalization to around $3 billion. Kushner contends that at that time, he had “no desire, plans, or prospects to return to diplomacy,” and Trump was out of office, so there was no way his investors could have thought they were buying his influence. Perhaps, to infinitely rich monarchs, a few billion is a small price to pay for past performance and future insurance. “I said this at the time,” Ben Rhodes told me, “that the payoff is on the back end in the Gulf.”

Affinity has deployed its billions in ways that reflect both Kushner’s priorities — promoting the economic conceit of the Abraham Accords by channeling the wealth of the Gulf into Israeli companies — and those of his benefactors. When MBS wanted to buy a video-game-maker, Kushner introduced him to a managing partner of Silver Lake, a huge technology-investment firm. Together with the Saudi sovereign-wealth fund, they all joined in a $55 billion deal to take Electronic Arts private, the largest leveraged buyout in history.

In 2024, when the Senate Finance Committee was last under Democratic control, it conducted an investigation that found Affinity had by that point collected $157 million in fees for managing its fund. (Kushner claims that the figure is inaccurate and that he charges an industry-standard amount that covers costs like personnel and overhead.) In the subsequent two years, the reported value of Affinity’s assets under management doubled to $6 billion — an increase Kushner attributes to the positive performance of its investments. He says he has not raised any funds since Trump’s reelection. But earlier this year, the New York Times reported that Affinity was exploring the possibility of starting a second fund with new capital from the Middle East. Kushner claims Affinity ceased to consider that “the instant the actions in Iran began.”

“My brain right now is not very much in my Affinity role,” Kushner says when I talk to him at his office. He claims that for the past year, he has hardly been involved in managing his fund at all, a decision he portrays as a costly diversion from his original plan. “I started a business when I left government. I focused on that business. I worked really, really hard. I did a good job with that business. Circumstances changed, where my father-in-law became president again. I intended to stay out but got pulled back in.”

For a while, Kushner says he acted only as a discreet sounding board to members of Trump’s second-term inner circle, including the (now deposed) chief of staff Susie Wiles and Rubio. Trump decided to give the portion of Kushner’s old portfolio that focused on the Middle East to Steve Witkoff, a developer (and strong Israel supporter) the president had met in the New York real-estate business. items.title: Trump’s Huang Games Show the Midterms Meant Nothing to Him
items.description: Whatever else they meant, the 2026 midterm elections were a direct and unmistakable signal to Donald Trump that he needed to change his priorities, his policies, and most of all, his ways. We know this from almost too many sources to count. Midterms are always
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Whatever else they meant, the 2026 midterm elections were a direct and unmistakable signal to Donald Trump that he needed to change his priorities, his policies, and most of all, his ways. We know this from almost too many sources to count. Midterms are always principally referenda on the president currently occupying the White House. It’s the only way Americans can register a demand for a course correction for the ship of state, particularly when the captain ignores or denies other signs of discontent. Moreover, Trump did everything within his power to personalize the election, imposing his will and his brand on the Republican Party constantly, and even personally insisting that voters imagine his own name was on the ballot. In addition, every bit of evidence we have about why the GOP suffered such a debacle on November 3 indicates that a lot of 2024 Trump voters felt he broke repeated promises to lower living costs, avoid wars, and limit mass deportations to violent criminals, while also defying popular concerns about AI and data centers in order to lead cheers for both.
So how has the 47th president, so often described as a “populist” with an uncanny eye and ear for what Americans want, responded to this direct rebuke? The term that comes to mind is “with contempt.”

There has been no course correction at all. Trump’s major moves since being slapped around by the midterm electorate have been to place the living symbol of MAGA extremism and the father of indiscriminate mass deportations and ICE violence, Stephen Miller, in charge of the White House; to double down on the Iran war and defend Pete Hegseth; and to illustrate his continuing indifference to domestic tranquility by consorting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in a manner that was both grandiloquent and obsequious.

And now, the president has capped off midterm election month by personally intervening to protect preeminent tech baron Jensen Huang for the consequences of his own terrible behavior. That this behavior might have included compromising U.S. national security has not given Trump a moment’s pause. Indeed, in the bizarre assassination-survival meme he posted on Truth Social today, he both proclaimed and at the same time dismissed as insignificant the idea than Huang was just another Epstein-era horndog whose indiscretions were nothing as compared to his great contributions to the NASDAQ.

You don’t have to attribute great political skill to Trump’s advisers to imagine that this latest power move must have horrified them. Of all the people on the planet for Trump to have conspicuously embraced in the wake of the midterms, he has chosen Miller, Hegseth, Xi, Putin, and Huang. Each maneuver seems calculated to insult the voters who repudiated him so recently, along with the newly empowered Democrats and the duly chastened Republicans, who must wonder if Trump is determined to sink their odds in 2028 as well. Has the president who is so emboldened to lecture the board of Nvidia on its leadership lifted a finger to help make people’s lives more affordable, head off a possible government shutdown on December 11, or to address the many challenges he will face in dealing with a Democratic Congress in the remaining two years of his tenure in office? If so, it’s hardly apparent, and Trump’s conduct since November 3 has not rewarded any hopes that he was paying attention.

items.title: 11 Insights From Our New Profile of Jared Kushner
items.description: We’ve published a sweeping profile of Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and one of his go-to diplomats for no less than three separate wars. Andrew Rice spent months reporting the story, including having several conversations with Kushner. Below are
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: We’ve published a sweeping profile of Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and one of his go-to diplomats for no less than three separate wars. Andrew Rice spent months reporting the story, including having several conversations with Kushner. Below are 11 highlights, including Kushner’s thoughts on Israel, mixing business and diplomacy, the forthcoming probes by congressional Democrats, and playing video games with MBS.
He sees no problem mixing diplomacy and business
Kushner’s day job is running Affinity Partners, a private-equity firm with more than $6 billion in assets that “does business in some of the same countries where he practices diplomacy.”

“The accumulation of more wealth is not my top objective,” he tells me. He says he could be making more money if he weren’t giving his time away, and his standard answer to critics is to challenge them to find any instance when he acted contrary to American interests. “Having the resources that I need to live my life makes me more independent to pursue the things that I want to pursue,” Kushner says. “I’ve been doing this for ten years, and my business has been an objectively successful business. My diplomacy’s been successful diplomacy. Nobody’s ever identified any case where I’ve done one thing to benefit the other.”
Kushner also told Rice he’s all in when tackling each of the wars:

“I’m a fairly all-in personality, so when I’m in something, it consumes all of me,” Kushner says as he drives. “It takes a big toll on me to do one of these, let alone three.” Crisis No. 1 is Gaza, which Kushner took on last year by inserting himself into the middle of cease-fire negotiations between Hamas and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “Not only getting the war stopped — getting all the hostages home, getting the bodies of the hostages home. It was a crazy operation,” he says. “Bibi didn’t think we could do it.” Since then, Kushner has been working on the future of Palestine — without much substantive input, critics say, from actual Palestinians — while also trying to resolve crisis No. 2, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and navigating crisis No. 3, Trump’s war of choice with Iran.
“Fixing Iran-U.S. relations, that’s something that has been broken for 50 years, so it’s not like there’s a precedent for success,” Kushner tells me.
He thinks Israel took the wrong path after the October 7 attack

“I feel like the fork in the road,” Kushner tells me, “is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status.”
“My brain right now is not very much in my Affinity role”

He says he has not raised any funds since Trump’s reelection. But earlier this year, the New York Times reported that Affinity was exploring the possibility of starting a second fund with new capital from the Middle East. Kushner claims Affinity ceased to consider that “the instant the actions in Iran began.”

“My brain right now is not very much in my Affinity role,” Kushner says when I talk to him at his office. He claims that for the past year, he has hardly been involved in managing his fund at all, a decision he portrays as a costly diversion from his original plan. “I started a business when I left government. I focused on that business. I worked really, really hard. I did a good job with that business. Circumstances changed, where my father-in-law became president again. I intended to stay out but got pulled back in.”
On life in in the “Billionaire Bunker” of Indian Creek, Florida

When I visit on a weekday morning, the house is quiet and sunbathed. Through the glass double doors of the living room, I can see a backyard pool and a thatch-roofed sukkah the family has erected for the holiday season. Beyond that stands a large covered patio with a grill for alfresco dining and a gym with weight machines and a sauna. (“Set the cold plunge at 42 degrees, and just go for it,” Kushner says. “After that, the day’s easy.”) A boat is docked at the rear of the property. The boys fish, and Ivanka likes to paddleboard. It’s a good life, and their market timing was impeccable. Since they purchased on the island, they’ve acquired new neighbors, including Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg.

“Now it’s become a place for immortals, but we were some of the last mortals to be able to buy there,” Kushner says. He has served as a member of the Indian Creek Village council, and the family recently was accepted into the island’s country club after a cooling period on the wait list. To some of their old friends in New York, it looked like they were retreating to a temporary place of exile, but Kushner doesn’t look at the island as an Elba. It’s become his family’s home. “A narrative people were writing is that we were running away from New York, but we didn’t view it like that,” Kushner says. “We viewed it like we were running toward the lives we wanted to live. We stopped giving a shit what other people say, and we just started living for ourselves.”
He won’t say if he opposed the Iran war

“Look, you can’t rerun the simulation. So you learn from what’s occurred. I think there’s been a lot that’s been achieved. Our job is to engage and try to create the best deal possible for the president.”
He’d rather “suffer” than publicly distance himself from Trump

On January 6, 2021, Kushner was flying home from Saudi Arabia, where he had been attending an economic summit, when he learned that rioters had broken into the Capitol. Although he has never stated unequivocally that Trump lost the election, Kushner had concluded weeks before that any effort to overturn it was hopeless. He left it to Rudy Giuliani and others to pursue legal challenges. Still, after his plane landed, Kushner went to the White House to support Ivanka, who has since said she was trying to persuade her father to call on his supporters to disperse. While Kushner would personally condemn the attack as “wrong and unlawful,” he never uttered a critical word about Trump himself. “You’ll never, ever read a public thing where I distance myself from him,” Kushner says to me one morning in July. “I won’t do that. I’d rather suffer.”
He also said all you can do is surf Trump’s waves:

During the first term, Kushner would sometimes advise colleagues not to try to control Trump — he makes the waves, Kushner says, and you can only try to surf them. He swears he didn’t want to get pulled back into the water. When pressed, Kushner concedes that he may be excited to exercise power, but he claims he doesn’t want it for its own sake — rather, he wants the power to do good in the world.
Trump is a “very special” everything

“Look, he keeps everyone off balance — at this point, I accept that,” Kushner tells me. “I think he’s got a very special deal instinct, and he’s a very special politician and a very special leader and a very special boss and a very special father-in-law. So you kind of buy the package, and it’s not my job to say, ‘Oh, do this’ or ‘Don’t do this.’ I think you have to follow his instincts and then use his instincts to try and take advantage of whatever uncertainty he wants to create.”
Jamie Raskin says the subpoenas are definitely coming

Jamie Raskin, the incoming chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, tells me he will use his subpoena power to examine (among other things) the allegations in Cole’s book. “If the key policy person in the Trump administration on Middle East issues is in business with foreign powers that are deeply invested in those issues and has been for essentially a decade, then we need to know about that,” Raskin says. “Either he’s being unfairly maligned or he’s a billion-dollar bagman for the Trump family.” And even if there were no secret bank accounts, Raskin adds, it’s undisputed that Kushner has profited from the legal investment in Affinity. “He keeps wanting to have it both ways. The whole point of conflict-of-interest laws and the Emoluments Clause is that if you represent the U.S., you owe 100 percent undivided loyalty to the United States.”

Kushner claims he is willing to entertain “serious questions” about his alleged conflicts of interest if the Democrats in Congress really have any to ask. But, he adds, “if they want to do political theater, then we’ll engage accordingly.” His definition of theater seems expansive enough to rule out any substantive cooperation with the legislative branch if it tries to examine his quasi-governmental role and anything he has done overseas.
And he claimed he was unfazed at the prospect of Democratic oversight
“I sleep well at night because I know what the laws are, I know what the rules are, and I don’t come close to violating them.”
Tony Blair thinks Kushner is “probably the best natural political mind I have come across”

“I actually say to people he is probably the best natural political mind I have come across,” says Blair. “And I have come across quite a few.” The accords demonstrated not just the value of Kushner’s relationships but his willingness to go big, Blair tells me. “One of the things he is extremely good at is that when a problem is in quite a narrow compass and there is a blockage, he creates an enlargement of the matrix of issues to be decided that allows you then to unlock the problem.”
He used to play League of Legends with Mohammed bin Salman

He bonded with MBS at one of the crown prince’s estates in the desert, staying up all night and watching the sun rise over a fire. Kushner was impressed with his vision for modernizing Saudi Arabia and his willingness to spend his oil money on transformative projects. When they weren’t together, Kushner and MBS would talk and text on WhatsApp. MBS loves video games, and sometimes they’d play together. (“League of Legends,” Kushner specifies. “He’s a big League player.”) When MBS was implicated in the grisly assassination of a Washington-based dissident, Kushner refused calls to repudiate him. “It’s a real friendship,” Kushner says.

items.title: Trump Shouts About Corrupt Huang Intervention From the Rooftops
items.description: President Trump personally strong-armed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO.
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: President Trump personally strong-armed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO.

This seems like the kind of thing we’d learn days after the fact, from some bombshell report featuring half a dozen anonymous sources. After all, the case against Huang was pretty strong. He resigned less than two weeks ago after it was reported that he was having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence had identified as a Chinese spy. Since then, he’d also been accused of having extramarital affairs with at least one subordinate executive at his company, and of engaging in a wide variety of abusive behavior in the workplace. Oh, and the American people just signaled quite clearly that they don’t love what Silicon Valley is up to these days:

But the source for this wild story about the president’s intervention is actually Trump himself. He’s gone to absurd lengths to make sure everyone knows that he was personally involved in getting his pal reinstated.

Trump began publicly reveling about this almost immediately. On Monday morning, just moments after the news broke that Huang was back at Nvidia, Trump took to Truth Social to praise the company’s board for making the “correct and proper decision.” He also shrugged off concerns about Huang’s involvement with Chinese spy, saying, “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security”:
Less than an hour later, Trump posted a second, more succinct note of congratuations:

Then Trump called in to CNBC to take credit for this “absolutely GREAT decision.” In a 50-minute interview, Trump revealed that he contacted Nvidia’s board directly and urged them to bring back Huang.
“I spoke to them. Let me just put it that way, and I convinced them,” Trump said. “I made the deal.”
Trump went on to say he “felt very strongly that he should come back” because “we have to protect our geniuses, and he’s clearly a genius.”

As for whether Huang could face criminal liability for his relationship with the alleged spy, Trump said he’d been “exonerated.” He explained that “a very thorough investigation” by his administration concluded that Huang “did nothing wrong,” aside from having “bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents.”

For those who prefer their presidential bragging administered via meme, Trump then posted this image, which manages to simultanously belittle concerns about Chinese spying, inappropriate workplace relationships, and his own near-assassination:
Huang’s reinstatement was quickly denounced by both Democratic and Republican lawmakers. So why was Trump eager to shout about his involvement from the rooftops?

There are multiple possible explanations. Trump and Huang have forged a close personal and professional relationship over the past two years (it probably didn’t hurt that the CEO donated $25 million for Trump’s White House ballroom). Trump also owns Nvidia stock, and probably profited from the surge in the company’s shares on Monday — though as the New York Times reported, we don’t know by how much:

At the end of last year, Mr. Trump owned at least $12 million worth of Nvidia shares, according to his financial disclosure report, and his brokerage accounts have continued to buy and sell Nvidia shares as recently as September.

It is impossible to determine the current size of President Trump’s position in Nvidia, or any company, because there is a lag between when trades occur and when they must be disclosed under federal law.
During his CNBC interview, Trump seemed excited to see another powerful man succeeding despite his illicit affairs:
Trump explained that the midterm elections left him little choice but to pressure Nvidia into reinstating Huang.
“I’m doing it for the country,” he said. “After the election, I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election. And I wasn’t on the ballot, but it was still a bad election.”

Maybe the election was the primary motivating factor — but not because our benevolent leader wanted to save us from the consequences of our poor choices three weeks ago. Trump’s about to lose a lot of power, and nothing says “I’m still in charge here” like proudly shouting your corruption.

items.title: Vance Wants Credit for Reinstating Huang, Too
items.description: Remember J.D. Vance? The vice-president was once President Trump’s would-be successor, at least until the chances of that dropped precipitously this year after American voters wholesale rejected Trump and the GOP, and Vance tried to blame it all on Trump’s fav
items.author: Chas Danner
paragraphs: Remember J.D. Vance? The vice-president was once President Trump’s would-be successor, at least until the chances of that dropped precipitously this year after American voters wholesale rejected Trump and the GOP, and Vance tried to blame it all on Trump’s favorite war. That hasn’t gone over well for him. A year ago, the prediction markets rated Vance’s odds of being the 2028 Republican presidential nominee at better than 50 percent. Now it’s down to 30 percent, and Trump is clearly entertaining the idea that Secretary of State Marco Rubio would make a better standard-bearer.

Regardless, J.D. Vance is still trying to get everyone to remember J.D. Vance. There are reports about how he’s humbled but resolved to win back everyone’s good favor. He’s doing rhetorical gymnastics to back away from his own comments criticizing Trump’s Iran war. He even inserted himself into one of last week’s terrible AI-generated Grand Theft Auto political memes.

This morning, Nvidia shockingly (or not shockingly at all, depending on how cynical you are) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO following a pressure campaign from Trump and Huang’s Silicon Valley buddies. It’s blot-out-the-sun tech, business, and politics news. Nvidia’s stock price is surging. Elon Musk is psyched. And we know Trump was instrumental in this because he’s going on and on about it, talking about how he convinced Nvidia’s board to reverse course, and how this was the best thing for America, and posting stuff like this:

A lot of people are thrilled, including those who hero-worship Huang, and/or back American AI dominance, and/or don’t care about wealth-creator misconduct, and/or love red-bra theft, and/or think Trump is just the best. So it may come as no surprise that by midday in the news cycle, we had suddenly learned that J.D. Vance helped too!
Reports Semafor’s Shelby Talcott:

VP JD Vance was deeply involved in the process to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia. He and POTUS were “personally engaged” over the weekend to resolve the situation, a source familiar tells me — Vance used his relationships in Silicon Valley + business community to help move the Nvidia board along. Vance and Trump believe that Huang is an effective counterbalance against the incredible and increasing power of OpenAI and Anthropic, as the administration seeks to diversify model providers and support open source models.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation. Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed that the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk. Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. … In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley.
Take it from sources familiar with how integral and important J.D. Vance still is: J.D. Vance is still integral and important. Take that, Rubio!
This post has been updated with more information about how integral and important Vance is.
