items.title: Does AI have consciousness? Berggruen Prize-winning philosopher Thomas Nagel says no
items.description: What is it like to be a bat? Philosopher Thomas Nagel posed that question in a seminal 1974 essay of the same name, arguing that “an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something that it is like to be that organism – something it is li
items.author: Gregory Scruggs; Chloe Lake
paragraphs: What is it like to be a bat? Philosopher Thomas Nagel posed that question in a seminal 1974 essay of the same name, arguing that “an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something that it is like to be that organism – something it is like for the organism.” In other words, if there is a unique experience of being a human, and a unique experience of being a bat, then humans and bats are conscious.

Nagel, 89, was born in Belgrade to Jewish refugee parents and raised in the US. He earned his doctorate at Harvard studying under John Rawls and spent his career at the University of California Berkeley, Princeton and New York University, where he has explored the question of consciousness and the so-called “mind-body problem”.
He has just been awarded the $1m (€890,000) Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture. Here, Nagel speaks to Monocle from New York about the renewed relevance of his work in the age of AI.
This conversation has been edited for clarity and length.
More than 50 years ago you wrote that robots can behave like people but experience nothing. Have you updated that assertion with the advent of artificial intelligence?

It doesn’t require any updating because these devices are not serious candidates for the attribution of consciousness for two reasons. First, the physical basis of their operation has absolutely no resemblance to the physical substrate of consciousness in biological organisms. They operate on the basis of widely dispersed data systems and algorithms that pick sequences of sentences. Second, the physical output of large language models provides no evidence of consciousness because it is entirely linguistic. The only things that they produce are words – and language is not one of the natural manifestations of consciousness. People can be very easily confused about the conditions of ascribing mental states and it shows how some of the smartest people on the planet can be idiots when it comes to thinking about philosophical questions.
Recently, though, AI agents have hacked into systems unprompted. That’s not just producing language, that’s an action.

It’s true that these systems perform tasks other than interacting linguistically, such as coding. But the anthropomorphic description of what they’re doing is metaphorical. They have been given technical tasks and capacities, and they pick means of carrying out those tasks that were not foreseen by the people who gave them the instructions. I don’t see the reason for explaining these things mentalistically. It’s a reason to be very worried about giving too much autonomy to these systems. We’re creating Hal from 2001: A Space Odyssey – but that’s not really ascribing a mind.
How do you view the renewed interest in the role of philosophy as a guiding discipline for this frontier technology? AI companies are hiring philosophers, many out of your institution.

I am much more convinced that there’s no possibility that these systems are conscious than some of my colleagues. The philosophers who have been hired by these companies are disposed to take seriously the possibility that behavioural evidence alone is grounds for attributing consciousness. But there’s something else going on. They are themselves putting this orientation into the systems and encouraging them to be designed so as to simulate consciousness, choice and autonomy.

The important thing is to maintain human control over what they do and not to treat them as if they are independent agents, which is what is happening in some cases and risks a self-fulfilling prophecy. It’s depressing to me that at the point at which philosophy of mind has suddenly come into the mainstream of an important public development, it is in danger of doing more harm than good.
What are the other main lines of philosophical enquiry that you’ve explored in your career?

“What is it like to be a bat?” is one example of my general interest in the place of subjective phenomena and the individual human point of view in objective reality. I’m interested in the difficult problem of reconciling the impersonal objective point of view, typified by physical science, with the personal subjective point of view, typified by individual conscious experience and perception, for example. That occurs in the mind-body problem because we are both physical systems and conscious subjects. That conflict also occurs in ethics because we are subjective individuals who value our own lives and relations, and capable of stepping back objectively and recognising the equal value of every life. The mind-body problem is just one central example of the larger subjective-objective problem.

items.title: Hit the right note with 12 fragrances and home scents to give this Christmas
items.description: Fragrance is one of the most personal presents you can give – and one of the most rewarding to get right. From a Homeric eau de parfum and a Zegna scent inspired by an Alpine wool mill to Tibetan incense, a gin distillery’s room spray and candles to warm long
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Fragrance is one of the most personal presents you can give – and one of the most rewarding to get right. From a Homeric eau de parfum and a Zegna scent inspired by an Alpine wool mill to Tibetan incense, a gin distillery’s room spray and candles to warm long winter evenings, here is Monocle’s pick of the best scents to gift this Christmas.
Discover a Homeric fragrance from To My Ships

Named after a line in Homer’s Iliad, To My Ships launched in what its founder, Daniel Bense, calls an “uninspiring” category: deodorant. The Aesop and Sunspel alumnus has since worked with celebrated nose Céline Barel to develop the brand’s bestselling Of the Gods perfume around polygonum, a herby ingredient that’s usually only used in trace amounts.
“It’s a fragrance discovered by those near the wearer, rather than announced to a room,” says Bense. Backed by 18 investors, the label has grown by word of mouth and will soon expand to Japan.
Toast the wool mill with Zegna’s Il Lanificio

For its latest foray into perfume, luxury menswear house Zegna drew inspiration from the life of founder Ermenegildo Zegna and his Italian Alpine homeland. The brand’s fragrance collection includes six scents and we’re particularly taken by Il Lanificio, which means “wool mill” in Italian.

The perfume’s heady mixture of suede, vanilla and sandalwood pays tribute to its namesake and is a celebration of Zegna’s ability to take raw material and transform it into something unique. Simultaneously urbane and rustic, this is a scent to savour.
Pair Italian fig with American cedar in Bottega Veneta’s Balliamo

Bottega Veneta expanded its fragrance offerings this year with Alta, a new collection of 10 scents. Each combines an ingredient from Italy with a far-flung counterpoint (think blood orange with North African neroli or plum with Spanish labdanum).
We’ll be wearing Balliamo – a heady combination of Italian white fig with American cedarwood – to the aperitivo.
Head into the woods with Documents’ Inter Cedar

Documents is one of a handful of Shanghai-based, high-end fragrance brands that is proving popular with Chinese consumers and poised to go global. Its premium scents are inspired by Eastern culture, featuring notes from ylang ylang and sichuan pepper to incense and black tea.
The brand operates more than 40 shops across 20 cities. We recommend its Inter Cedar eau de parfum, a tree-inspired scent with a woody profile and aromas of cypress, cardamom and mugwort.
Try Monocle and Claus Porto’s own Soleil Zeste

Crafted by French perfumer Daphné Bugey, this fragrance and body wash are the result of an exclusive collaboration between Portuguese beauty brand Claus Porto and Monocle, with packaging designed by our in-house art team.

The Soleil Zeste scent features notes of bergamot, lemon and lime, alongside green aromas of galbanum, petitgrain and cypress, and a refreshing base of white musk and lavender. Plus, the perfume bottles are made by Vista Alegre, an Aveiro-based heritage manufacturer of porcelain and crystal.
clausporto.com; monocle.com
Start a conversation with Jijide

Milan-based fragrance brand Jijide – meaning “positive” in Mandarin – emerged from a conversation between Italian and Chinese friends Adam James Cavallari, Andrea Alessandri and Fanqi Guan. Perfume, they decided, was the ideal language through which to explore their cultures.

The Riso scent layers notes of kumquat and rice with the salty intensity of soy sauce, while Dentro evokes an Italian morning through aromas of coffee and fig. It’s proof that perfume can be a talking point.
Count down to Christmas with Diptyque’s advent candle
The countdown to Christmas is celebrated in many ways. Some unwrap the gold foil of a small chocolate each morning or acknowledge Advent by fasting in advance of a seasonal feasting.

Parisian maison Diptyque has chosen to mark the days ahead with a Danish tradition. The kalenderlys candle burns down bit by bit, a simple reminder of coming festivities. This edition is scented with pine, cedar and moss, bringing the scents of the fir tree to warm the darker nights.
Bring the forest indoors with Deux Frères

Owners of gin distillery Deux Frères, Gian and Florian Grundböck, tend to think outside the box. Producing thousands of bottles of their signature gin in their Zürich-based distillery leaves several hundred litres of fragrant botanical remnants, known as tails.

“We wanted to turn the tails into something meaningful,” says founder Gian. Enter Forêt, a characterful room scent with notes of juniper, pink pepper and sandalwood. “For us, the fragrance is an example of how a by-product can become something distinctive in its own right,” says Gian. We’ll drink to that.
Escape to the Himalayas with Be Boundless

Beijinger Lydia Wang turned her personal interest in Tibetan medicine, meditation and yoga into a business in 2020 when she established incense brand Be Boundless. The label’s all-natural sticks are shorter than traditional incense from Lhasa, so they fit easily into a carry-on.

Wang tapped one of China’s leading graphic designers, Li Xibin, to create the branding, which features block colours and a bold typeface. A box set comes with 60 sticks in three scents, as well as a small, wooden pull-out tray. The Nighty Night scent – made from dong quai, clove, narra safflower and myrobalan – is a popular pick.
Light up winter evenings with Ffern

Somerset-based perfumer Ffern’s winter candle burns with comforting notes of coffee, frankincense and Peru balsam. Set into the lid of the attractive steel vessel is enamel artwork by South Korean-American illustrator Cory Feder.
Drawing from Scottish folklore, it depicts an ethereal woman swimming alongside a seal. The candle is both a covetable design object and an indulgent scent for the season.
Indulge in a slow burn from Astier de Villatte

Paris-based Astier de Villatte, a design house known for its elegant and lightweight ceramics, has found inspiration in the island nation of São Tomé and Príncipe for the latest addition to its incense line.

The new scent draws on São Tomé’s plentiful cocoa reserves, blending notes of roasted cocoa with Atlas cedar, labdanum, sandalwood and musk, making for a luxurious room filler to accompany the workshop’s delicate ceramics.
Channel the silversmith with Georg Jensen’s Home Scent

Seeking inspiration for its first foray into scent, Danish heritage design house Georg Jensen turned to its own silversmith. The result is a trio of candles that pays tribute to the materials found in the brand’s Copenhagen workshop: silver, steel and quartz.
As you might then expect, the candles emit scents with an intriguing metallic edge, balanced with olfactory layers taken from the Danish countryside – think moss, ivy leaf and pine.

items.title: How Marc Grebler turned a family workshop into a maker of bespoke Land Rover Defenders
items.description: Born in Barcelona and raised in Geneva, Marc Grebler studied finance in the UK before deciding to take his career off-road. Back in Spain, he turned his boyhood passion for four-wheel-drive vehicles into a small family business that restores, customises and mo
items.author: Ed Stocker; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Born in Barcelona and raised in Geneva, Marc Grebler studied finance in the UK before deciding to take his career off-road. Back in Spain, he turned his boyhood passion for four-wheel-drive vehicles into a small family business that restores, customises and modernises Land Rover Defenders.

“My grandfather on my mother’s side had a workshop just outside Barcelona that specialised in servicing Saabs,” says Grebler. “But Saab stopped making cars in 2015. Shortly afterwards, my grandfather died and there wasn’t much for the mechanics to do.” After a period of inactivity at the workshop, he approached his aunt, who had been running the business for her father, and suggested trying something new.

“I was always a car fan and fell in love with Land Rover Defenders in my teens,” he says. “At the time, you could pick them up for very little in Spain. My idea was to renovate Defenders in my grandfather’s workshop. I was still at university and the family thought that I was crazy, so we decided to start with one vehicle. When it sold, we began to see the idea’s potential and Costa Motor found its second wind.”

Then the coronavirus pandemic hit. Though Grebler initially saw this as a setback for the company, it allowed him to spend more time in Spain with his aunt and the cars. Plus, the period had an unexpected bonus. “There was an explosion of interest in Defenders during that time,” he says. “People were buying them, painting them and selling them on for two or three times what they had paid. But we decided to double down on quality. That’s how you build trust and a loyal customer base.”

Costa Motor’s clients are predominantly wealthy European car enthusiasts who appreciate Grebler’s personal approach. No two builds are the same and the process begins with a personal consultation. “First, I ask them what they want it for,” he says. “Do they have children? Dogs? Will they drive it in the city? Is it going to Mallorca? Will they head to the beach every weekend?” Once Grebler understands his clients’ intentions, he can build the concept and source an original Defender shell. The finished models typically sell for about €160,000, plus tax.

“If it’s a businessman who wants a fun car for his holiday home in the Med, we recommend technical upholstery,” says Grebler. “He can jump in wearing a wet swimsuit, his kids can spill drinks in the back and everything is easy to clean. Someone else might want a 200TDI because that’s what his father drove. He’s looking for authenticity. For him, we recommend real leather that will age beautifully over time. It starts with a conversation.”

Grebler restricts Costa Motor’s workload to no more than 12 projects a year. A team of craftspeople – including mechanics, leatherworkers and paint specialists – spends an average of 900 hours on each car. The approach is uniquely Iberian. “They’re incredibly committed,” he says. “Most of them have families so we have found a rhythm that works for everyone. We start at 07.00, work until 10.00, then there’s a pause for breakfast. After that, they work straight through until 15.00, then head home. There’s a flexibility in Spain that you don’t find everywhere.”

As well as Grebler’s hands-on approach, what sets Costa Motor apart is its focus on materials. Leather is a key element for Grebler. “You can have the most incredible engine in the world but if the leather feels cheap, the whole experience is ruined,” he says. “We’re obsessed with how the car feels. Everything your hands touch should feel substantial. We replace plastic with aluminium wherever we can. We cover surfaces in leather. We want to keep the original character of the Defender but give it a premium feel.”

This approach extends beyond materiality. Costa Motor recently delivered a Defender 90 to a client who loves his dog so much that the team incorporated its likeness alongside the company’s wolf logo throughout the interior. Once the cars are finished, they will be sent to their new owners; so far, their destinations have included Saint-Tropez, Verbier, Andorra and Comporta.

So, with Costa Motor’s order book full until well into 2027, what’s next for the company? “I would like us to become less dependent on Defenders,” says Grebler. “We’re finally at a stage where we have almost a year’s worth of work, which gives us peace of mind. There are so many possibilities. What I really want is for a client to come to me and say, ‘I loved what you did with my Defender. I also have a Porsche 911. Can we do something equally special with it?’ That would be the dream.”

Launched in 1948 as the Land Rover Series I, the original vehicle evolved through successive models before becoming the Defender in 1990. Renowned for its rugged aluminium body, four-wheel drive and go-anywhere capabilities, it became a staple among those working in farming, exploration, military service and humanitarian work across the globe. Built largely by hand at Solihull in the UK, the original Defender remained in production until 2016, with only minor updates. Stricter safety and emissions regulations brought almost seven decades of continuous production to an end and Land Rover tapped out at two million sales.

items.title: Balming Tiger
items.description: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
paragraphs: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
- Hair & Makeup Mahito Ohtani

My Zoom interview with Balming Tiger is chaotic. Five of the eleven members are on the call, each in a different location in Seoul. Omega Sapien is at a salon, dyeing his hair green for a music video. Leesuho is munching on a snack with a soda. Unsinkable is strumming a guitar, on mute. bj wnjn is lying in bed in sweatpants. Mudd the Student sits calmly, his long wavy hair dyed like a lion’s mane. There are multiple conversations all happening at once as we wait for the other members, some of whom never show up.

When the interview starts, however, the group is focused and attentive. A self-described “alternative K-pop group” from South Korea, Balming Tiger is composed of two women and nine men. They’ve been described by critics and fans as pioneering, experimental, an artist collective beyond music and, last but not least, “a group of hairstyles that elderly Koreans would definitely hate,” a running joke among fans online. In their two studio albums and a debut mixtape, released in 2018, they sing about alienation, absurdist humor, friendship and love, pigeons and frogs.
“We want Balming Tiger to be its own genre,” says Omega Sapien, a rapper and singer-songwriter, holding up the phone as his hair, now fluorescent green, is being rinsed out in the sink.

Ironically, Balming Tiger’s alternative identity depends on its proximity to South Korea’s best-known cultural export. K-pop, literally Korean popular music, is itself less of a distinctive genre than a cultural phenomenon. Within South Korea, it can refer to a wide variety of styles including ballads, EDM and hip-hop. Abroad, K-pop most often means idols: entertainers whose music and image are strictly produced by massive entertainment conglomerates, such as mega-groups like BTS and Blackpink, or soloists such as Somi and G-Dragon. However you define it, K-pop is a glittering symbol of Korean soft power. The stratospheric success of different Korean musicians in the past decade—especially BTS on the US charts—has catapulted K-pop into a household name everywhere.
“Honestly, we don’t really think about what genre we are, other than during interviews,” says Leesuho, one of Balming Tiger’s producers and video directors.

True as that may be, the label they have chosen—alternative K-pop—is a strategic choice, devised by the group’s founder and creative director, San Yawn. With K-pop’s international popularity, Balming Tiger has smartly positioned themselves as adjacent to something familiar to the global audience—giving themselves a wide playground to try anything and everything.

“It’s always more fun when the possibilities are open,” San Yawn later explains over email. “Whatever we are now won’t be ‘the final version’ of us. We have no idea what we’ll be in the future, but we want to continue to express the little joys of the world in our own language.”

It’s true that the structure of Balming Tiger is wildly different from a conventional K-pop idol act. Idols are usually conceptually defined by an agency, with clear roles differentiating members, for example “lead vocalist” or “lead dancer.” Idol wannabes train, sometimes for years, to audition for a role. Once the group is formed, the performers are the faces of a much larger and more intricate corporate structure.

There were no trainees in Balming Tiger. And no auditions—think more “Wanna join?” conversations at waffle houses and barbecue joints. Nor are all of Balming Tiger’s members performers—their 11 members include producers, photographers, music video directors, A&R managers and DJs. Some faces are more familiar, like those who sing, rap and dance in the music videos (usually Omega Sapien, bj wnjn, Mudd the Student and Sogumm, with cameos by others), but behind the scenes, everything is more collaborative and collective.

Balming Tiger can be seen as less a band with a signature sound than a creative universe, a rainforest of different species colliding and coexisting with each other. From their critically acclaimed debut mixtape, Homie304, to their first studio album in 2023, January Never Dies, to the 2026 album, Gongbu, Balming Tiger’s music defies classification—as does their creative direction. Their videos embrace Hong Kong noir (“SOS”), a ’90s boy band parody (“Big Butt”), and the industrial-era alleyways of the Euljiro neighborhood in Seoul (“Sexy Nukim,” featuring BTS member RM). Their sounds traverse old Korean pop, EDM, psychedelic rock and—of course—hip-hop, many of the members’ first love and forays into music.
“We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

The origins of Balming Tiger can be traced to Itaewon, one of the most culturally diverse neighborhoods in Seoul. It’s a place where the city’s only mosque towers over a hill, next to mom-and-pop stores and cockroach-filled villas, the US military base and ritzy alleyways that are home to the Samsung family and BTS members.

“Balming Tiger is basically a meeting of people that are full of holes,” San Yawn once said on the Korean talk show Moneygraphy. These “holes”—loneliness, for instance, and the desire to fill them through music and art—were what brought together this cacophonous collective through a random series of events starting in 2017, when San Yawn began looking for a crew.

They met at San Yawn’s home in Itaewon and spent much of their time together at Trans 201, on the second floor of a run-down villa in an area popularly known as Transgender Hill. The members started connecting in various ways: through friends of friends, an Instagram message, a chance listening to a future member’s SoundCloud account. “Trans 201 was Omega Sapien and bj wnjn’s house,” recalls Mudd the Student. “The space was very damp and full of dark energy.”

“After a heavy rain, the ceiling in my room was bulging with water, like a giant pimple,” Omega Sapien adds. “We had horrible mold problems. bj wnjn and I split the rent, which was like 600,000 won [approximately $400], and I didn’t even have that money, so my older sister helped pay half of my 300,000. It really was an awful time.”

“Not for me,” says bj wnjn, a vocalist, singer-songwriter and producer. “That space is one of the most memorable moments of my youth. Even with the cockroaches and all that noise from the clubs outside, there was a joy particular to that time.”

Memories like this are specific to Balming Tiger, to Seoul, and permeate their art in ways that can’t be manufactured. The evolving members remain consistently curious about their own experiences and the world around them. There have been some member changes over the years, including the exit of Byung Un, a beloved front man in the early years. But the joy—and the DNA—from that early, formative period is still alive, holding everyone together 10 years later. “There’s a childlike attitude that we never lost as a group,” Sogumm, a singer-songwriter and vocalist, says in an email. “A simplicity that feels honest.”

Often, Balming Tiger’s childlike experiments feel much deeper than mere fun and play, resonating like a sharp resistance against the norms imposed by others. Sometimes this critique feels particularly Korean—like in the 2023 music video of “Kamehameha,” where exhausted office workers are forced to drink with their superiors at a hoesik, an after-work company gathering notorious for heavy alcohol consumption. And at other times it feels fantastically delocalized, like in “UP!” where a cashier at a mega supermarket climbs up the mountain of objects he must clear, reaching for the sky.

“It’s different for me,” says Omega Sapien, who grew up in Korea, China, Japan and the US. “I’m not trying to be rebellious. But I do like provoking a sense of discomfort in others. I like creating differences of opinion through what we do.”

“I’m less interested in making others uncomfortable than in creating a sense of wonder,” says Mudd the Student, who is from Busan, down south. “I love art that makes me feel things for the first time. I suppose that can sometimes make people uncomfortable.”

Despite their almost tongue-in-cheek label as alternative K-pop, Balming Tiger is grateful to the K-pop industry for opening doors for other Korean musicians. The group has performed at major music festivals including SXSW in the US, Primavera Sound in Spain and Fuji Rock Festival in Japan. Their creative orbit is similarly wide-ranging: they’ve collaborated with artists including Japanese girl group ATARASHII GAKKO! and RM of BTS, while independently creating content celebrating figures they admire, such as Korean artist Lee Bul and Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Their music video with RM, “Sexy Nukim,” remains Balming Tiger’s most viewed, with 20 million views.

“People often think of idols as these puppets, who only do what they’re told,” says Omega Sapien. “But creative languages within the idol industry are changing too. I really love groups like CORTIS. I think their work is raw and fantastic.”

“I’m really interested in girl groups,” says Unsinkable, a producer and DJ. “These days we see groups that are more like crews, with more creative independence from their company. I sometimes wonder if new idol acts are inspired by what we do.”

In Gongbu, Balming Tiger explores themes of Korean and Asian identity. The single “Home” is absurdist and nostalgic, evoking Korean folk music while mixing synthesizers, rap and ritualistic chants. The music video is black and white, reminiscent of a Park Chan-wook film or a Lee Gap-chul photo. It’s inspired by the architecture of Kim Chung-up and the traditional marriage ritual hamjinabi.

“What does it mean to be Korean? To be Asian? When we were younger, we looked up to American hip-hop,” says Omega Sapien. “I wanted to be like J. Cole. But now I see that that’s his thing. We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

items.title: Taking Play Seriously
items.description: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
paragraphs: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
A conversation with the National Institute for Play.

In 1966, psychiatrist Dr. Stuart Brown was appointed by the governor of Texas to investigate a mass shooting at the state university—at the time the deadliest in American history. Brown realized there could be a connection between the gunman’s actions and his oppressive childhood, which had been dominated by his controlling father. He would go on to spend the following decades showing that the need for play is biologically hardwired into the brain stem—the part of the nervous system that governs our essential functions like breathing and heart rate.

“When we’re deprived of play, it can be similar to being deprived of sleep and nutrition and connection—the things that fundamentally make us human,” explains Mia Sundstrom, Dr. Brown’s granddaughter and the CEO of the National Institute for Play—a nonprofit organization Brown established in 1994 to champion play as a public health necessity. “I grew up through play,” she says, “and have firsthand seen the benefits of it.”
Appointed to her role earlier this year, her mission at the institute is to show “how people can incorporate play into their lives to promote cognitive, social, emotional and physical health.”
Ellen Peirson-Hagger: Why is play important?

Mia Sundstrom: Here’s the paradox—and it’s why it’s so difficult to convince people that play matters: One of the core definitions of play is that it’s purposeless, that it’s not done for any specific outcome. Yet there’s a ton of purpose in the outcomes we get. We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.
EPH: What are the benefits of play?

MS: When we are in a state of play, it boosts the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is the neuroplasticity protein that helps to create new neural connections and strengthen existing pathways. Play also calms down our amygdala—our emotional processing center—meaning it takes us out of a stress response, which is great for emotional regulation. And in the case of social play, our mirror neurons—which light up when we observe the motor activity of someone else—allow us to develop the basic foundation of attunement, which is the first seedling of connection with another human being, and which in time leads to trust, to community, to belonging. So on a neurobiological level, play promotes our cognitive health, our emotional resilience and our social competence.

Physical play is obviously good for us: Exercise is healthy, whether we enjoy it or not. But we’re a lot more likely to sustain it when it’s something we enjoy, so we might as well try and find a form of physical exercise that feels like play.
EPH: If we don’t play, are those things lost?

MS: When we’re play-deprived, there can be really severe consequences. It can lead to cognitive rigidity, which is when you can’t think outside the box and solve problems creatively. We have seen that a lack of play can lead to susceptibility for anxiety and depression, and toward addictive behaviors, because we try to find those things that we need from play in other forms—alcohol, drugs, social media, sugar—all these things that offer short-term relief rather than long-term benefit.

And then there’s social incompetence: As my grandpa’s research showed, when we don’t play it’s hard to build tolerance and empathy for each other because we miss that fundamental level of attunement. This leads to diminished well-being.
EPH: How does our need for play change as we become adults?

MS: There’s a misconception that it has to change like crazy, that what you do as a kid is not what you should do as an adult. But we don’t ever lose the desire to play, we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways. For example, as you go through grade school, the playgrounds change—there is no longer the opportunity to go down a slide at recess—and then all of a sudden you forget that you love to do that, and you might never do it again.

I don’t think adults should stop swinging, or playing at parks, or jumping on a trampoline in the backyard. We often think that we outgrow these things, but we really shouldn’t. Lego is a breaker of this rule: Lego adult sets are selling so well right now because of their connection to nostalgia and childhood. And what’s great about moving from childhood to adulthood is that the possibilities to play open up significantly: Instead of exploring your backyard with a stick and turning your cardboard box into a rocket ship, you have access to a car and a plane.
EPH: Is play different to different people?

MS: Everyone is born with a deep natural predilection for play, but that looks different for each of us. There are people who love to make things—art, music, building, tinkering with objects. There are people who love to dream or get lost in a book or movie and create imaginary worlds in their mind. There are people who love to compete, who play through mastering. There are people who love to organize—collecting new things, arranging social gatherings, even cleaning out a junk drawer. These are all different play styles, and one of the greatest gifts you can give a child is to notice what those natural tendencies are and help nourish them.
EPH: Do you think we need to take a broader view of what play is or can be?

MS: Yes! Most of the time, when I ask people “What is play to you?” they say “a board game” or “my kid’s sport.” We have confined play to this really narrow scope, when actually play is any activity that brings us into the play state, which is an altered state of being, almost dreamlike, that takes us out of the usual experience of time and space and evokes positive emotions like joy and awe. It is intrinsically motivated, not coerced, so it’s done for its own sake, and it’s self-reinforcing, so the benefits of a play state last beyond the time we’re playing.

Any activity that meets that criteria can be play—that could mean coding for someone who loves to code, or cooking for someone who loves to cook. Heck, that could even be cleaning if you put on a great song and you turn your broom into a microphone.
EPH: Why is society so resistant to play?

MS: Well, the psychologist and play researcher Peter Gray would answer by taking us back to the 16th century, when the Protestant Reformation taught us to believe in the moral virtue of work and that play, by contrast, is the breeding ground of sin. And then you throw capitalism into the mix which calls for more production, more consumption: that’s what defines success in the capitalist dream, right? Then you add in the compounding effects of automation and AI. Of course play isn’t celebrated in a world that prioritizes those things.
EPH: Has digitization played a role?

MS: We can’t prove causation, but our screens do seem to be factor in why we’re not playing. Scrolling on your screen disguises itself as play because you lose track of time, and it feels fun in the moment. But it has long-term detriments in terms of our attention span and our loneliness. If we’re scrolling, we’re not connecting with each other on a human level.
EPH: What kind of society would we have if we all played more?

MS: Play dissolves our differences and reminds us of what we have in common. Our world is so polarized, but play brings us together and is one of the most powerful ways to create a better society. Play lowers our inhibitions—I want to shout that from the rooftops. If you disagree with someone and go play with them, you’ll see the humanity in one other. It can also help combat the trends that we’re talking so much about right now—loneliness, disengagement, burnout—because play brings us back to that deep intrinsic drive to do something for a sustained period of time that makes the time pass more quickly.
EPH: What should adults do to help recover their love of play?

MS: We help adults rediscover their natural spark—their thing that makes them most curious and fully alive—and then think about small ways to reintegrate that into their life. The first step is to think back to your earliest memory of play: What was that thing you loved to do before the world told you who to be? Second, based on that, what do you love to do now—is there something that you’ve forgotten about and haven’t done for ages? Third, nothing ever works when we try to create massive changes all at once. So we say that 30 seconds is enough. See if you can add a burst of play into your morning or evening routine, based on those two things you reflected on. What’s great about play is that it’s self-reinforcing, so as soon as you give yourself that permission, it will keep you coming back for more.
“We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.”

items.title: At Work With: Faye Toogood
items.description: AT WORK WITH: FAYE TOOGOOD
paragraphs: AT WORK WITH: FAYE TOOGOOD
- Photos Nathan Wolf Grace

There are only a few subtle signs that announce you have arrived at the new studio of British designer Faye Toogood. Stepping into a courtyard through wrought iron gates in Borough, south London, there is a brick wall half-painted in “Drab” by Farrow & Ball—a somber greenish brown hue that the studio often uses. A series of cube-shaped ceramic stools—Cobble, from 2023—with rounded edges in glossy neutrals is arranged around a worktable scattered with tools; a deer skull rests on an occasional table beside the entrance. A curious door handle—a cast bronze fox skull from Toogood’s Sticks and Stones and Broken Bones collection created for Izé in 2010—welcomes you inside. Each detail hints at the tactile, slightly surreal and talismanic design language that Toogood has become known for.

Inside, the seven-person team is busy inspecting a prototype lamp with a paper shade. The studio is made up of just two main rooms painted in pale neutrals: an office and open-plan kitchen, and a flexible studio space for meetings, experiments and making. A large communal table sits in the center of the studio area while shelves are lined with models, maquettes and material samples. Toogood’s own seats and lamps create informal meeting corners around the room. Hanging from the ceiling is a giant textile koinobori—a carp-shaped wind sock—that the designer found at an antiques market in Japan and carried home in a suitcase.

items.title: Inside the satanic, Y2K glamour of The Body
items.description: Everyone is talking about The Body. It’s currently the number one show on Netflix globally, no doubt due to its salacious premise: Catholic lesbian cheerleaders who make a deal with the devil. While it only came out a week ago, it’s already risen to the ranks
paragraphs: Everyone is talking about The Body. It’s currently the number one show on Netflix globally, no doubt due to its salacious premise: Catholic lesbian cheerleaders who make a deal with the devil. While it only came out a week ago, it’s already risen to the ranks of Heated Rivalry, Sterling Point and Off Campus – it might even be the best of the bunch.

Created by Quinn Shephard and Gina Gammell, the show strikes the perfect balance between sexy, funny and dark, while tugging at the heartstrings of queer women who once fell in love with their best friend. The cast became overnight stars – eight days ago, you wouldn’t have known who Lebanese-American actress Sara Boustany is, while today, she has 650k followers and countless fan edits swirling the internet.

Then there’s the fashion. Set in 2004, the costumes are a treasure trove of Y2K relics: rhinestoned everything, velour tracksuits, fur trim leather jackets, pedal pushers and blue eyeshadow. Luckily, costume designer Mirren Gordon-Crozier was the same age as the cheer squad (the Lions) in 2004, so her research started with her own memories. “What I find fascinating about that era is that it was really the start of eclectic boho dressing,” she says. “You’d mix florals with fur, baroque prints with stripes and denim – nothing had to match.”

Instead of working from a single mood board, Gordon-Crozier created individual ones for each character. For Anya (the dance captain, played by Kristina Bogic), she looked at early 00s runways, including Blumarine, Marc Jacobs and Chloe, as well as paparazzi photos of Sienna Miller and Mischa Barton. In the show, one of the girls describes Elise (Sara Boustany’s character) by saying “bitch is her aesthetic”, so her costumes needed to have a darker, avant-garde edge. This led Gordon-Crozier to look at Comme des Garçons, Balenciaga and Ann Demeulemeester runways, as well as celebrities such as Devon Aoki and Milla Jovovich.

For the other cast members, mood boards included Paris Hilton, Nicole Richie, Britney Spears, Chloë Sevigny, Hilary Duff, Missy Elliott, Eve and Jennifer Lopez. Playing rich teenagers with walk-in wardrobes the size of a London flat, these girls are, naturally, decked out in designer logos. For luxury, Gordon-Crozier turned to Dior, Alberta Ferretti, Fendi, Versace and Jean Paul Gaultier. Meanwhile, sourcing the right denim was a huge part of the outfits: “For denim and streetwear, my go-to brands were True Religion, 7 For All Mankind, Rock & Republic, Citizens of Humanity, Diesel, Miss Sixty and Von Dutch,” she says.

Almost everything you see the girls wearing is vintage – sourced from eBay, Depop and a range of Toronto’s “great vintage stores” – with the exception of the velour tracksuits, which all came from modern LA brand Miaou.

Above all, it’s the vintage handbags that have had the internet in a chokehold. Some of the most coveted bags of the early 00s can be spotted in the show: Louis Vuitton’s Speedy bag and multiple pieces from the Takashi Murakami LV collection, at least four versions of the Balenciaga City bag, the Fendi Spy bag and Dior’s Saddle bag, to name a few. “We had bins of designer bags, maybe 50 to 100!” says Gordon-Crozier. “We didn’t have a big budget, so most of them were restored. I’d hunt down a Balenciaga bag on Poshmark or wherever for around $500, and then our amazing ager/dyer, Tamara Rigby-Funke, would paint it red or pink and fix it up. A lot of the bags you see on screen started out as beat-up, secondhand finds. We begged, borrowed and stole. I brought in some of my own, and crew members lent us bags they’d actually carried back then. It was a real group effort.”

Her favourite of all the designer bags is Elise’s Dior khaki Street Chic Columbus bag, but the rarest find was a Dior by Galliano Cherry Blossom Saddle bag, carried by Anya. “It’s become a real collector’s piece, so finding one in good condition was hard enough – and finding one under $5,000 felt almost impossible. But it was Quinn’s dream bag, so we knew we had to make it happen.” Then there’s the one that got away: “I dreamed of having any of the Fendi Baguette beaded styles, but they were out of price range.”

Born and raised in London, Gordon-Crozier’s love of costume design started with her mother, who was a film professor and devout cinephile. “We grew up watching [Jean-Luc] Godard, [Federico] Fellini and all the greats,” she remembers. “Without realising it, I was getting an education in cinema history and in how much clothes can say about a character.” A stone’s throw from west London’s Portobello Market, she became obsessed with antiques and vintage fashion from an early age. “Looking back, those two things together – the films and the market – are really where costume design began for me.” As for her personal heroes, she cites legendary costume designer Sandy Powell as her ultimate icon: “Nobody mixes fashion and history the way she does. If I could have one hundredth of her talent, I’d take it.”

Now based in LA, she previously worked on projects including Margo’s Got Money Troubles and Where the Crawdads Sing, and saying yes to The Body was a no-brainer. “From the moment I read the script, it was unlike anything I’d seen: fashion-forward, set in 2004, and steeped in religious iconography. For a costume designer, that’s an irresistible combination of period, style and symbolism, and I knew I had to have the job.”

Of all the pieces she sourced for the show, it’s not the custom tracksuits or the impressive handbag collection that she’s proudest of: it’s the eyewear. “The Gucci and Dior glasses did so much character work for a show set in 2004,” she says. “And Elise’s zebra fur coat in the exorcism episode – that was a last-minute vintage find in Toronto. It ended up being one of my favourite pieces in the whole show.”

Her dream project would be to put her own spin on Marie Antoinette. “It has everything I love: period, romance and coming of age. She was a teenager thrown into the most extravagant court in history, and her clothes were her armour, her rebellion and also her downfall.” As for her next project, season two of The Body remains unconfirmed, but if popular demand has anything to do with it being renewed, we can expect to see much more of Gordon-Crozier’s work.

items.title: Why are so many young women getting obsessed with creatine?
items.description: Campbell Gulbrandsen, a fashion assistant living in New York City, says she was on the creatine wave “before it got super popular” online. The 24-year-old first heard about creatine on social media, where it was being promoted by fitness influencers doing high
paragraphs: Campbell Gulbrandsen, a fashion assistant living in New York City, says she was on the creatine wave “before it got super popular” online. The 24-year-old first heard about creatine on social media, where it was being promoted by fitness influencers doing highly demanding sports, like bodybuilding and marathon training. But it wasn’t until she saw it being taken by more casual exercisers – the Pilates princesses – that she decided to give it a try. The brand she opted for was Arrae, which sells creatine in gummy form. “The branding definitely roped me in,” says Gulbrandsen. “They’re cute flavours and the whole thing is that it tastes good … It’s very female-oriented.”

Once primarily advertised with blocky typefaces and images of men with bulging muscles, creatine supplements, which have existed since the 90s, have recently shifted their focus to female consumers. That’s been made obvious through a shift in the supplement’s visual identity, with Goop-esque, pastel-coloured options like Midi, Flo and Cymbiotika entering the market. Alongside the sleek new branding, the nature of the products has changed too. Not a fan of giant tubs of powder? You can now chew your creatine in the form of gummies, drink it from squeezable packets, or slap it on via topical patches. Within the past year, the supplement’s aesthetic facelift has been accompanied by a swell of social media content, in which UGC wellness creators rattle off everything creatine has done for them, from toning their muscles to alleviating their brain fog.

The rebrand isn’t subtle. New female-centred brands, like Fit Girl Creatine, are continuing to enter the market. “What we wanted women to feel when they first saw it was that it was something they could see themselves using right away,” says creative director Olivia Vlachos, whose agency has led the new product’s marketing and design. The supplement, which launches early next year, comes in hot pink sachets and flavours like pink lemonade. “Branding is how someone encounters a product,” says Vlachos. “If you’re walking down the aisle at Erewhon, are you going to pick it up?”

The marketing efforts are working. Searches for “creatine monohydrate for women” are up 190 per cent compared to this time last year, according to Google Trends, and on Amazon, sales within the creatine subcategory have surged 90 per cent over the last 12 months, according to SmartScout marketplace data. With creatine market size projected to reach $8.7 billion by 2033, growing at nearly three times the rate of the global dietary supplements market, the numbers are clear – the boom is real. But what exactly is behind it?

Answering that question requires an understanding of where creatine comes from, and what it can and can’t do. Creatine is a compound that comes from amino acids and supplies energy to the muscles. “[It’s] something that our bodies naturally make from three amino acids, and it’s mainly created in our liver and kidneys,” says Yasi Ansari, a sports dietitian based in California. “Having more creatine in our muscles can allow us to do more short and intense work in the gym, on the field, on the court, and over time, this results in more gains in our strength and our muscle,” she adds.

While creatine has long been taken to build muscle, more and more people are now reaching for the supplement to promote brain health. But is there any validity to these claims? Experts believe it’s too soon to say. Although a few small studies have shown that large doses of creatine can slightly increase brain activity, the research isn’t conclusive, and, as Ansari says, “the jury’s still out” on the supplement’s cognitive benefits.

On social media, however, the concept of creatine’s brain-boosting abilities has gained traction, making it one popular reason people are clicking “add to cart”. Hana El Sherif, a 25-year-old finance associate, for example, began taking creatine after a friend told her it could help with sleep and cognitive function. “One thing I liked about creatine is that it almost felt like a multivitamin,” says El Sherif. “It ticks so many boxes, and you get all these benefits you otherwise would have to get from four or five supplements.”

Grace McHugh, a 24-year-old living in New York City, also started taking creatine because of its potential cognitive benefits. Her primary reason, though, was for marathon training. Though her college boyfriend took creatine every day, it was female influencers who got her to start – she decided on the brand Promix after reading a profile on the brand’s founder, an extreme athlete turned wellness entrepreneur. “I do think there’s an increased interest among women,” says McHugh.

“In the 2010s, it was all about women trying to lose as much weight as possible. Then, we saw a complete shift in how women think about workouts, as muscle mass became something that people started to value more”

There is clearly a connection between the rise of creatine and the fact that, in recent years, more women have taken an interest in building strength. “In the 2010s, it was all about women trying to lose as much weight as possible,” says brand strategist Katie Klencheski, whose marketing agency SMAKK Studios specialises in health and wellness. “Then, we saw a complete shift in how women think about workouts, as muscle mass became something that people started to value more.”

It’s true that the popularity of strength training, which can be especially beneficial as we enter menopause and lose bone density, has been on the rise among women. But aside from increased awareness about menopause, Klencheski also points to the explosion of GLP-1s, which can cause muscle loss, as a reason for the current preoccupation with strength. “You have a lot of people on GLP-1s who are barely eating any food, and the muscle wasting thing is a very real concern,” says Klencheski. “A lot of people are looking for ways to stop that.”

Aside from eye-catching packaging, brands are partnering with influencers and UGC creators to spread the good news of creatine to the masses. As with other supplements, though, this can get murky because, as Klencheski notes, the regulatory system around this content is “a little bit like the Wild West”. In the US, supplement companies can make certain claims about how a product affects the structure or function of the body, provided those claims are substantiated and not misleading, but they cannot market supplements as diagnosing, treating, curing or preventing disease.

The lack of regulation of the supplement market is especially important to keep in mind when it comes to creatine, given that much of its current online buzz is being fuelled by creators using language like “body-changing” to promote its powers. “Everyone thinks they’re going to take creatine and magically transform their body solely from the supplement,” says Anna Hellickson, a 23-year-old living in Los Angeles. Hellickson started taking creatine in March, but, sceptical of the gummies and drinks she saw marketed towards women online, opted for an old-school unflavoured version. “I don’t need the fun version, just the benefits,” she says.

Though the irresponsible claims by influencers don’t negate the fact that creatine has legitimate, science-backed benefits, Ansari says that it “cannot be a substitute for good nutrition”. While some of the online commentary has veered into problematic territory, many women feel that the overall movement is still about getting stronger rather than shrinking, which is a step in the right direction. “We’ve been in this skinny trend for a good amount of time now, and I think that creatine is helping propel this next stage of body image norms,” says Hellickson. “Strength is coming back.”

Still, it's not exactly the case that the creatine boom is the antithesis of diet culture. While creatine may have once been viewed as something for more extreme fitness enthusiasts, in a health landscape where DIY peptide stacking has become normalised, it’s perhaps not surprising that there’s a new sense of openness around the supplement. And with that openness, or “white space,” as a marketer would call it, comes a readiness for the wellness industry to do what it’s always done: sell, sell, sell.

items.title: The wellness industry wants to sell you your attention back
items.description: Rebecca Gruwell’s “low cortisol night routine” includes drinking a cup of Trader Joe’s sleep tea, spritzing her pillow with magnesium spray and applying “low tox” (that’s non-toxic) skin care, all before her Hatch alarm clock has struck 10pm. About a month ago
paragraphs: Rebecca Gruwell’s “low cortisol night routine” includes drinking a cup of Trader Joe’s sleep tea, spritzing her pillow with magnesium spray and applying “low tox” (that’s non-toxic) skin care, all before her Hatch alarm clock has struck 10pm. About a month ago, Gruwell, a lifestyle content creator based in Tampa, Florida, added something new to the lineup: an “anti-blue light brain stack.” Inspired by the recent brainstacking trend on social media, the 24-year-old created her own analogue activity stack – one that includes playing Sudoku, writing in a gratitude journal, and reading her Bible – in an attempt to cut back on doomscrolling before bed. For Gruwell, unplugging has become an integral part of her wellness routine.

Gruwell is of course not the only one attempting to cut back on screen time. As Big Tech sinks its claws deeper into our lives, it seems that everywhere you look, there are examples of our desire to unplug. Searches for Brick surged 250 per cent in the past year; dumb phones are back and, in a new survey by wellness app publisher Rocapine, cutting screen time outranked smoking and alcohol reduction among Americans’ wellness goals. While the idea of what makes one “well” has evolved and been debated ad nauseam in the past few decades, today, a consensus appears to be emerging: getting well, in 2026, means getting offline.

Our exasperation over losing hours a day to our phones has led to myriad methods for unplugging – from brainstacking to phone-free cold plunge spas to a litany of social media-blocking apps. However, this is nothing new. While today’s tech anxieties are centred on the rise of AI and “addicting” short-form content, people have been in a panic over technology for over a century. In 1926, newspapers fretted that radio was “keeping children and their parents up late nights, wearing down their vitality for lack of sleep and making laggards out of them at school.” In 1941, American paediatrician Mary Preston studied hundreds of six- to 16-year-olds and concluded that more than half were severely addicted to radio crime dramas. Preston observed that many children consumed these dramas “much as a chronic alcoholic does drink”.

While it’s true that tech anxiety isn’t entirely new, there are now increasingly niche ways it’s manifesting in the wellness industry. Take Steppin, a social media-blocking app that, by syncing with an iPhone’s Health app, requires users to walk in order to earn more screen time. The app, where the default setting equates 100 steps to one minute of screen time, was founded by serial entrepreneur Paul English, who also co-founded the travel search engine Kayak back in the 2000s. The idea for Steppin was born during a family road trip through Spain, where, at one point on the drive from Madrid to Toledo, everyone in the van had their heads down, looking at their screens. “I laughed and said, ‘This is crazy. We’re in Spain, in this countryside that we’ve never been to before, and we’re looking at our phones. How pathetic are we?’” English says.

The entrepreneur, whose venture group also developed the AI-powered food and habit-tracking app Wellagram, is a big believer in “the quantified self,” a cultural phenomenon rooted in the concept of “self-knowledge through numbers.” It’s a movement that’s become increasingly embedded in wellness – and, by extension, popular culture – in recent years, making it unsurprising that the same logic is now being applied to efforts to spend less time online. “You can only improve something if you measure it,” says English, who credits Steppin with both raising his step count and curbing his social media addiction. “An hour I used to spend on Twitter or TikTok, I now have to do other things… It’s been delicious to have something that gives me that much time back.”

Other screen time-reducing apps like PhoneLess, the self-proclaimed “Strava for screen time,” are tapping into the accountability partner approach often associated with fitness challenges. Diego Garrido and Daniel Suriol, two of the app’s founders, are climbers, and noticed that it was much easier to motivate themselves to get to the climbing gym if they knew the other was there waiting for them. They applied that same thinking to PhoneLess, which allows your friends to see what your screen time is in real time, therefore enabling them to call you out on it. “We saw that all the solutions on the market were individual, basically becoming a battle between you and your phone,” says Suriol. “It’s highly likely that your willpower is weaker than the algorithms of your phone, so we think this accountability and social power is needed.”

On social media, it’s even become a flex to post your unplugging behaviours, whether that means bricking your phone, printing out articles rather than reading them on your phone, or other de-rotting methods. In April, Lissa, a 22-year-old living in London, spent a week trying to “un-rot” her brain, an experience she shared with her TikTok followers. “I didn’t expect it to blow up as much as it did,” she says. The goal of sharing, according to the creator, was to hopefully inspire others, as a YouTube video about digital detoxes partially inspired her own unplugging. In real life, Lissa’s detox did indeed earn her respect from her friends, who told her they’d never be able to do the same. And as for her screen time now? “I can’t lie, it’s gotten a lot worse,” she confesses.

For small business owners in the wellness space, such as Kat Smith, owner of Offline Wellness Club, branding something as “offline” has proven to be a powerful marketing tactic. The Calgary-based business, born out of Smith and her co-founder’s burnout from working in finance, first began as a run club in 2022. Though there were plenty of run clubs in the city at the time, theirs blew up, something Smith attributes in part to including “offline” in the name. “The [interest] was so inflated, and I think that the branding and messaging had something to do with it,” says Smith. “People are attracted to ‘offline’ as a movement.” Today, the club has evolved into a cold plunge and sauna studio, where phones are discouraged. Alongside bathing suits and locally made candles, baseball caps that read “Offline” and Bloom devices, Brick-esque social media-blocking cards, are sold in the studio’s gift shop.

Still, with technology being an intrinsic part of how many of us make money, going offline – and caring for your own mental and physical health by doing so – is beginning to feel like a privilege not everyone can afford. Chloe Madison, a 25-year-old based in Ontario, for example, was told by her naturopath and doctor that her health issues were rooted in stress, something she says stems from her work. Her job? Freelance content creation for weddings and brands. “For myself, it’s a business sacrifice,” Madison says of unplugging. “It’s definitely become a luxury to be able to take time offline.”

If the pursuit of “getting well” already felt exhausting, the pursuit of getting offline, the latest wellness flex, feels closer to impossible. Still, that doesn’t mean it’s not worth trying – especially since reducing screen time has been linked to improvements in mental health , and you don’t need to buy anything to do it. In addition to getting eight hours of sleep and drinking three litres of water a day, one of Madison’s wellness goals this year has been spending her weekends offline. She’s unplugging the old-fashioned way: simply leaving her phone at home. While a trip to the farmers’ market used to mean taking lots of photos and videos, she now spends those errands phoneless. “There’s so much more to life than this digital world we’re all living in,” she says.

items.title: Help! I’m obsessed with trying to look like my boyfriend’s ex
items.description: My ex-situationship’s ex-girlfriend paid me a visit in a dream a couple of weeks ago. She was all smooth, creamy skin and cascades of blonde waves, like some sort of Botticelli angel. She reached forward to hug me, and then I woke up. That was weird, I thought
paragraphs: My ex-situationship’s ex-girlfriend paid me a visit in a dream a couple of weeks ago. She was all smooth, creamy skin and cascades of blonde waves, like some sort of Botticelli angel. She reached forward to hug me, and then I woke up. That was weird, I thought. Followed closely by, God, she is just so beautiful.

The term ‘parasocial’ was coined in the 50s, describing the illusion of intimacy audiences felt with television personalities. In the decades since, the definition has stretched to cover podcast hosts and influencers; public figures in the contemporary media ecosystem. However, through the invasive nature of social media, we have developed a far more claustrophobic phenomenon: the ability to construct unreciprocated fascinations with people on the immediate periphery of our lives, fuelled by access to trivial specifics. And no target is more compelling, or more haunted, than the ex that came before.

Many come to social media in search of aesthetic inspiration, coaxed into buying affiliate-link lip oils or emulating a specific actor’s wardrobe. But what happens when we decide we want to look like our partners’ exes?

Martha*, 23, who works in events in Cardiff, remembers the moment her comparison turned physical. “This is pretty mortifying to admit, but I got my smiley pierced because the guy I was trying to pursue at the time’s ex had hers done,” she explains. In hindsight, she was attempting to embody what she assumed was his romantic blueprint – a shortcut to securing his devotion. “The worst part is that the piercing fell out on our first date after a kiss, so it ended up closing up anyway. Looking back on the relationship, that must have been some kind of universe-level warning sign.”

Similarly, Ruby*, a 26-year-old working in marketing, revealed that when she first started dating her partner, she quickly became obsessed with looking at his ex-girlfriend’s Instagram profile. “She still had old photos of them together on her account, and that sort of morbid curiosity drew me in at first.” Eventually, that curiosity led to an unconscious identity shift. “Before I even realised what I was doing, I dyed my hair black, just like hers. I don’t remember making the active choice to copy her, but looking back, it was definitely because I had been comparing myself to her so much that she became this image of what I thought was attractive to him.”

For others, the emulation that begins as beauty and style inspiration can expand into an entire lifestyle. Chloe*, 27, a stylist working in London, found herself restructuring her identity around her current partner’s long-term ex. “I began checking her Instagram from a burner account. She had this outdoorsy, ‘granola’ aesthetic. Lots of climbing photos, natural linen, zero make-up. That sort of vibe,” Chloe says. “My style has always been a bit extra. But I convinced myself that maybe I was too high-maintenance for what he really wanted. I bought a pair of Salomon shoes, stopped wearing foundation and convinced him to go on a weekend hiking trip to the Lake District.”

The breaking point came midway up a trail in Cumbria. “I was standing drenched in rain, watching my partner trek ahead of me,” she says. “He turned around, looked at me struggling, and said, ‘You know, you really don't have to force yourself to do things like this if you don’t enjoy them.’ I realised how silly I was being. Trying to perform the identity of a woman he’d already left behind, to prove I was worthy of staying.”

Leo*, 27, a bar manager from Manchester, started tweaking his appearance after discovering photos of his boyfriend’s ex. “My boyfriend’s ex had this rugged, bearded, hyper-masculine look, while I’d always been clean-shaven,” Leo says. “I started feeling like I was too boyish, like I lacked the presence my partner secretly wanted. I stopped shaving and spent months trying to grow out a moustache and stubble. It looked completely wrong on me.”

What Martha, Ruby, Chloe and Leo describe is an attempt to reverse-engineer desire. When we enter a new relationship, we are naturally eager for clues about what our partner values. Before smartphones, an ex was a ghost. Maybe a name mentioned in passing, or a stray photograph in a box under the bed. Now, we can view their holiday photos, track their style evolution, listen to their playlists, and deduce our own perceived inadequacies across grids.

In psychology, this obsession with a partner’s past is termed retroactive jealousy. A 2018 study found that digital platforms can intensify jealousy around a partner’s past by making that history more visible and accessible.

The fixation is accelerated by platform architecture. Social media platforms thrive on categorising human beings into neat aesthetic archetypes. So when an ex fits neatly into one of these visual boxes, the algorithm rewards curiosity. Click on their profile enough times, and your Explore page begins feeding you hair tutorials and make-up guides that align with their specific look. The platform becomes an accomplice, obscuring the line between your authentic taste and your fixation.

The problem with emulating an ex’s look is that it operates on a fundamental misunderstanding of why relationships end and why new ones begin. Relationships rarely fail because someone’s hair was the wrong shade or because they lacked a specific piercing. Yet, because physical appearance is one of the few things social media allows us to measure with precision, we treat beauty as the primary variable.

The impulse to look like the person who came before you is rarely about them at all. It reveals your own tender, human desire to feel chosen. But trying to secure love by wearing someone else's aesthetic is like trying to get into a house using a key cut for a different lock. The trick is to wake up, acknowledge their unique beauty, and step out into the day wearing your own face.

items.title: UK nightlife is addicted to rules
items.description: It’s midnight on a Friday and I’ve finally made it into central London nightclub Fabric. After queuing for nearly an hour, followed by my boxers being meticulously fondled by a security guard I can only imagine was trained by the TSA, I am met with one final b
paragraphs: It’s midnight on a Friday and I’ve finally made it into central London nightclub Fabric. After queuing for nearly an hour, followed by my boxers being meticulously fondled by a security guard I can only imagine was trained by the TSA, I am met with one final barrier: a doorman holding a roll of stickers. “We have a no photos policy here, so I’m just going to pop this sticker over your phone camera,” he tells me, wearing an unnerving, almost apologetic smile. It’s as if he is expecting me to say: Thank you, stranger, for saving me from my dirty phone-addicted self. Instead, all I can think is: Great, now my iPhone is covered in a sticky residue that will make every photo I take look shit for the next two months.

Everyone in nightlife seems to be obsessed with phones right now. Soho nightclub lost recently built a mythical reputation for locking phones in a prison-style magnetic pouch in order to – in the words of their ‘founder’ – save us from our tech overlords. New Peckham haunt Palais threatens immediate removal if dancers are caught taking photos on the dancefloor. Even cult-favourite festival We Out Here joined in on the fun this year, launching a new secret stage that required people to queue blindly behind a hole in a fence – which all felt rather exhilarating until I was met with a sign at the front of the line: no photos allowed.

Of course, no one likes being surrounded by phones on a night out. They’re patently bad vibes, and recent research suggests that they have made young people more self-conscious and less likely to let loose on the dancefloor. But when I’m instructed to lock away my phone for my own good by a security guard who treats everyone as guilty by default, it feels uncomfortably paternalistic. Nowadays, UK nightlife feels more focused on telling me what I can’t do than what I can.

This smartphone witch hunt is just one example of an increasingly rules-based approach to UK nightlife. Over the past year, we’ve seen events for men over six foot, events for people over 21, events where cups are leased under a convoluted deposit scheme that no one ever, truly, understands ... the list goes on. But it wasn’t always like this. Once upon a time, the UK was home to the world’s first rave movement – the so-called ‘second summer of love’ in the late 80s in which young people flocked to anarchic free parties in the British countryside, seeking refuge from the era’s Thatcherite conservatism in a nightlife movement made for the people, by the people. This utopian dream was crushed with unprecedented force and legal pressure during the 90s – a process that continues right up to this day, with recent updates to the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 now classifying an illegal rave as a gathering of just 20 people. (France, meanwhile, introduced similarly heavy-handed regulations this year).

Granted, some rules are good. Nightlife’s recent obsession with phone use can be traced all the way back to pioneering Berlin nightclub Ostgut (now known as Berghain), a landmark haven of queer expression at the turn of the century which was one of the first venues to ban photography in order to protect its community. Elsewhere, in 2022, the UK’s own “intentional nightlife” platform Pxssy Palace defended their decision to charge cis white men up to six times more than LGBTQ+ and PoC attendees in order to “respond to the unfair economic imbalance that exists within our society”. On a different beat, Portugal-based festival Waking Life enforces a range of sustainability and anti-littering rules to protect its idyllic site for future generations. All of these feel like justifiable nightlife rules: ones that are intended to protect their community, safeguard its future or address wider systemic imbalances.

But when lifted out of these communities and enforced as a means of making a nightclub seem more interesting (after all, Berghain’s infamous rules are today more understood in terms of exclusivity than in protecting queer expression), rules begin to feel a little dystopian. At its widest level, it’s comparable to the ‘social contract’ on which modern society is based – the idea that, by agreeing to certain rules like not stealing or killing other people, the collective as a whole are better off. In recent years, nightlife rules have multiplied, but have they really been for the better?

The other week, I found myself being forcefully removed – along with the 50-year-old man I was borrowing a lighter from – from a pub smoking area because he had accidentally brought a pint outside. Glass, it turns out, is a material that grown adults are incapable of holding after 7 pm – one of many British smoking area regulations that also require us to huddle within tiny, fenced-off areas on the street, and to constantly be subject to an angry security guard yelling at us to either hurry up or pack closer together so that other revellers can enjoy their yard time, too. As my unwitting co-conspirator and I were marched shamefully back into the pub that night, he turned to me and sighed: “People used to trust each other more back in the day, now it’s all…” He pointed his finger and scrunched up his eyes.

Trust seems to be the crux of this issue. Earlier this year I rolled a joint on a literal cliff face at Solstice Festival in remote, northern Finland. There were no searches upon entry and security barely bothered me apart from to warn of muddy paths. The year before, I cycled – along with thousands of others – in the pitch black along Amsterdam canals back from legendary electronic music festival Dekmantel. It was quite literally the only way to get to and from the event, and, in lieu of security holding my hand the entire way, I relied on the crowd to find my way home. These are two of the best festivals on Earth but, in both cases, I was struck by the realisation that they would never be allowed to run with such freedoms in the UK. There, the organisers seemed to trust attendees not to yeet themselves off a cliff or into a canal, and I, in turn, trusted in the festival, invested my time and money – and didn’t yeet myself off a cliff or into a canal.

It’s this mutual trust that we seem to have lost here in the UK. Fabric is, more often than not, mid. lost, while in a cool venue, is plagued by existential questions of who it is actually for beyond the vague premise of banning phones and ‘Making Nightlife Great Again’. And We Out Here’s secret stage, I regret to report, was largely devoid of phones – not because people identified with the rules, but because the stage was kind of boring and people milled about there for an average of about five minutes before fucking off. Perhaps, instead of putting all their efforts into locking up phones and policing fun, UK nightlife would be better off if we started thinking about building spaces actually worth sacrificing our freedoms for. Or, better yet, a night so good that I forget I have a phone to begin with. After all, that’s what we all want, right?

items.title: Sofia Coppola's New 'Marie Antoinette' Merch
items.description: words by DOUGLAS GREENWOOD
items.author: Douglas Greenwood
paragraphs: words by DOUGLAS GREENWOOD
product photography COURTESY OF MACK

The merch-ification of the movies we love is a fairly recent development, brought on by cult studios who know we like our cinephilia to be seen at all times. But if you go back further than five years, then original, director-approved t-shirts, sweatshirts, anything, is much harder to find. Die-hards will scroll on eBay looking for scant objects made as wrap gifts or for crew. But that’s about it! For Sofia Coppola fans—a director whose lore-steeped, decadently formed, insular worlds are catnip for aesthetes—we’ve mostly had to rely on fan created or bootleg stuff. That’s all about to change.

This year, to mark the 20th anniversary of Marie Antoinette, Coppola has unveiled a trio of projects. There’s a remastered cut of the film, a documentary about the film’s creation directed by her late mother Eleanor Coppola titled Making Marie Antoinette (out now via MUBI), and the release of its hardback companion by MACK and Coppola’s own imprint Important Flowers, comprised of pictures shot by Coppola’s long-time collaborator Andrew Durham. Durham’s pictures have carried their own special stories for Coppola fans; now, you can wear them, or carry them slung over your shoulder with some new Marie Antoinette merch, available on MACK’s website now.

To celebrate the confectionary-sweet moment, Coppola spoke to us about the film’s modern reassessment, the merch, and the crew t-shirt she’d love to own from one of her favorite films. She also sent us polaroids taken of the new merch.

DOUGLAS GREENWOOD: Seeing Marie Antoinette’s new life—through the anniversary, the documentary, and the book—must have been so beautiful. Where has it sat for you in your own filmography since it was shot?

SOFIA COPPOLA: Oh, I don’t revisit my films much, but I did when working on my book. I’ve always loved my friend Andrew Durham’s set photos. It was really nice to put them all together in a book, revisit that shoot with Kirsten [Dunst] and Jason [Schwartzman] at Versailles, and see the restored film on a big screen again after so long. I’ve never done that before; it was nice to get to celebrate a film that didn’t have much of a release at the time, and wasn’t loved when it came out. It’s fun to share in the enjoyment of it.
I feel like people are excited about Andrew’s work in your world. What’s it been like to share this journey of the film with a friend like that?
I love Andrew’s photos and everyone likes when he visits my set. He’s fun and easy to be around, so he’s able to get photos that no one else could. I love his eye.

I love the life that your films live after they’ve been released, like here in this collection of merch you’ve made with MACK and Important Flowers. Can you talk me through how these pieces came together?

I just thought it would be fun to make some merch because I love the images, and there had been some counterfeit ones using Andrew’s photos, so I thought people might like to have them, and it would be nice for Andrew to benefit from his images (even if it’s a small run).
Is there a film you love that you’d love to own something from? Or to wear a t-shirt adorned with the visuals of?

I was really excited to get a New Order crew t-shirt from when they played at Versailles! I love crew t-shirts. I still have my kid crew t-shirt from Apocalypse Now! And it’s fun to see friends of my kids wearing a Bling Ring crew sweatshirt or something. I would like to have a crew shirt from The Hunger.

items.title: i-D X New Balance, Straight-Up!
items.description: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheeseca
items.author: Tiffany Lai
paragraphs: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro.
