Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheesecake before the party continued downstairs at the Knave of Clubs for pub drinks and a boogie.

At 8 p.m., a new billboard was unveiled outside the pub, celebrating version 7 of New Balance’s iconic 990 silhouette, set to release globally on November 6. Made in the USA, the 990 has been a proud “dad shoe” since 1982, so naturally, we had to ask our guests: who is your favorite American? And which celebrity dad has the best style?

Who is your favorite American? Kim Kardashian or Adam Sandler. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Rey Mysterio from WWE. What’s an album that’s on repeat right now? The new Worldpeace DMT album. What are you doing this weekend? Spreading optimism and premature Christmas cheer!

What do you do? I’m a stylist. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Ford Bronco cars. What are you wearing today? Mules, which aren’t very practical for walking in the rain, an old pair of Our Legacy jeans, a cashmere jumper to keep me warm, and a vintage bomber. My hat is made by my friend Biddyish. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Brad Pitt.

What’s an item of clothing you’d never part with? My 1960s vintage McGregor jacket that I picked up in Paris a few years ago. What are you drinking tonight? Guinness. Who’s your favorite American? Jim Carrey. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My granddad, actually. What’s your favorite form of exercise? Running, because of the mental clarity and the long and steady journey I’ve had with New Balance.

What do you do? I’m a photographer, director, and DJ. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? A secondhand leather jacket from a market in Paris. What album is on repeat right now? Choke Enough by Oklou. What’s a color that you’d love to wear more of? Green.

What do you do? I make music, but I like saying my job is just connecting the dots because there’s no laws or limits to art. Tell us about your outfit. My outfit’s steady but also flex-y, smart-casual. What are you doing this weekend? I’m always creating. I’m working on some new music, shooting cool videos, fun stuff. Who first taught you to tie your shoes? My mum. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? I’m in a black era right now.

What do you do? We’re freelance stylists. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Jacob: Jeff Goldblum. His personality is the style. If you had to run between two Tube stops, which ones would you choose? Jacob: Bethnal Green and Mile End because they’re the closest ones together. Lauren: Custom House to Canning Town. Nice scenic run. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? Lauren: A big fur coat.

Who’s your favorite American? Fred Hampton. He was one of the leaders of the Black Panther Party. What’s your side hustle? I’m rebranding my friend’s fashion brand. Doesn’t mean I give it less attention than a main hustle, but that’s the thing that I’m supporting right now! What’s your favorite form of exercise and why? Push-ups and pull-ups at home. I hate going to the gym. What are you doing this weekend? I’m seeing my friend who’s leaving for Australia. I’ve got to sort his Moonpig out ASAP!

What do you do? I’m the editor-in-chief of i-D Magazine. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Me. Which celebrity dad has the best style? My dad. He’s modeled in the Chopova Lowena show, he wears New Balance 990s, and he loves a Ralph Lauren polo. Best grail? This Prada scarf. Who’s your favorite TV dad? Michael Bluth from Arrested Development.

What do you do? I’m a fashion designer. What’s an item of clothing you’ll never part with? This pair of jeans that my boyfriend gave me. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? Gray. What’s your favorite form of exercise? I go to the gym, but I want to pick up tennis.

What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Black music. What are you wearing tonight? Made in the USA 2040 V5 New Balance shoes, Supreme Made in Japan denim, and a Bleue Burnham ring. What are you drinking tonight? Chili margarita, some red wine, Guinness, and water. Got to stay hydrated. What are you doing this weekend? This weekend, it’s the Amsterdam Dance Event where I live. My partner’s going clubbing, so I’m taking care of the kids.

What do you do? I’m a musician, and I play the harp. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? My 1800s Victorian body that is falling apart, but I’ll never let her go. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My dad. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a cemetery walk date with my girlfriend in Abney Park. Who’s your favorite American? Lana Del Rey.

What are you wearing? Hysteric Glamour boots with pink studs, a skirt that my ex-boyfriend gave me, a nice, warm Supreme jacket, and a Goldwin jumper. What are you drinking tonight? Two spicy margaritas, a glass of white wine, and a glass of red wine. Who’s your favorite American? Martine Syms. I like her exhibition at Sadie Coles. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a first date to a wine bar in Hoxton. Do you have a side hustle? Hustling!

What do you do? I work for Homer Jewellery and Louise Konrad Jewellery. Who’s your favorite American? The Tiger King. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? My sweatpants. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Zendaya’s Mugler outfit for the Dune premiere. What are you drinking tonight? Vodka soda.

items.title: The Story of Cécred
items.description: photography BLAIR CALDWELL
items.author: Eni Subair
paragraphs: photography BLAIR CALDWELL
hair NEAL FARINAH FOR CÉCRED
colour direction MASON POOLE

Haircare was always one of the many ways Beyoncé’s family expressed love. Watching her mother Ms. Tina Knowles care for everyone from doctors and judges to the unhoused in her now-famous Houston salon Headliners, Beyoncé saw firsthand how hair can empower and instill confidence in others—and in herself. It was in Ms. Tina’s salon chair, at just 9 years old, where Beyoncé’s appreciation for haircare began.

Decades and dozens of House of Deréon looks later, Beyoncé and Ms. Tina decided to bring their love and appreciation for haircare to the world. In 2024, they turned their lifelong shared passion into Cécred, with Beyoncé as the sole investor, founder, and Chairwoman and Ms. Tina as Vice Chairwoman. Years in the making, the brand was an endeavour worth perfecting—with Beyoncé and Ms. Tina personally testing every product.
Limited copies of the zine are available here.
The quality speaks for itself: Take the Restoring Hair and Edge Drops, which has become the number one hair product in the United States, driven by hair growth testimonials all over social media.

Meanwhile, a heartwarming Father’s Day short film of JAŸ-Z’s loc takedown process, using the brand’s signature Detangling Spray, has offered an intimate glimpse into the family. The love poured into the products only amplifies the scientific truths: These serums, shampoos, and gels really work for you.
This autumn, Cécred jumped across the pond from Los Angeles to London, offering its wide range of products for us Brits at Space NK stores.

To celebrate the UK launch, Beyoncé and Ms. Tina opened up about their hair and their lives. It’s a full-circle moment for the mother-daughter duo, who are sharing the lessons in hair confidence passed down through generations with a whole new audience. For Beyoncé, it’s about more than hair. It’s about continuing her mother’s legacy and making sure everyone feels their best in their hair.
ENI SUBAIR: What has been the most rewarding part of building Cécred?
BEYONCÉ: My mother and I poured decades of experience, tradition, and love into Cécred, so seeing our community grow across every ethnicity, texture, generation, and gender is so fulfilling.

In the beginning, it took some conditioning from the world’s perception of how to launch a brand founded by someone like me. I’m the founder, visionary, and sole investor—not the face or model for this brand. I had a vision to build something that solved real problems and performed so incredibly that the people who can’t stand my music still use Cécred, haaaa! … because it works.
Cécred has been years in the making, so why did 2024 finally feel like the right time to launch?

MS. TINA: Well, we tried to launch it two years earlier, and Beyoncé, you know, she’s a perfectionist. So, with the products, I thought they were amazing, but then I would give them to her, and she would test them on herself, her friends, and her daughters. Then, if one person didn’t have an excellent experience, she would give it back to me. She drove us crazy, and the team was like, “Oh my God!” But I’m so happy that she was so picky about it because it just got better and better. And our testing, research, and development is where we put a lot of money. I was like, this is so crazy expensive because we’re researching and testing so much. We’ve tested on three continents to get all types of hair textures, to make sure that it works on all hair. I had a salon in the ’80s, and what I was told all the time was that our hair was strong because they think that because our hair is coarser, it is stronger. But that is a myth surrounding Black hair. It’s just the opposite. Our hair is the weakest, most fragile hair, and the curlier your hair is, the more texture you have.

And I’ve always studied the science of hair: what it was made of and what it needed. Even making sure to reduce the molecular weight of products so that it can get through the cuticle and build and strengthen the hair.
What lessons have you learned from your mum that have helped you on this journey?

BEYONCÉ: Growing up I saw my mom pour love into others at her salon, and she still does this every day. I love that she trusts that the world is for her. She trusts God. She approaches things with humanity and love. I love my mother’s rebellious spirit. She can spark an idea and make it come to life. She’s fearless and I get that from her. It was in her salon that I witnessed stylists transforming women and helping them get their confidence back and see their beautiful potential. It was more than just getting their hair done, it became a sacred space where they were cared for. That impact resonated so deeply, and I wanted that to be reflected in Cécred and the community we’re building. Your heart carries energy and wisdom from your fingertips.

Recently my mom decided to surprise me by visiting a hair salon in the UK. No calls ahead, no warning. She packed a bag of Cécred, got into the car, and showed up without any pre-planning. Even though one of the managers told her she couldn’t be there, she stuck around and made the owner come. She was determined to build a relationship with the salon owners and clients and ended up spending almost a whole day doing hair there, ha!
What’s your first memory of experimenting with your hair?

BEYONCÉ: One day I decided to cut my own hair. I think I may have cut the whole ponytail off and also cut bangs! I walked in with my ponytail and said, “Mom, put this back on please.” And she was like, “I can’t.” But I thought she could, because I’d seen her be such a hair magician, especially when she would bond hair. Those crazy memories were the foundation of my childhood.
Both you and your mum love Tottenham—where do you like to go? What are your favourite spots?

BEYONCÉ: One of my favourite things about London is the drive to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and passing through Seven Sisters. I love seeing all the communities with their kids, the barber shops, and all the culturally diverse restaurants. As I get closer to the stadium, I start to see the fans who put so much effort into attending the show, either dressed in metallic silver, glistening in the streets and sunshine, or in full cowboy gear, boas, and boots. I can spot my Hive from miles away. When I’m onstage and see all the ethnicities, all the beautiful and fabulous outfits and families, there’s no other experience like it. The melting pot of beautiful diversity in London, particularly at my shows, is something magical to witness.

I love the music scene in the UK. I’ve watched Sienna Spiro grow up from a beautiful young girl to an extraordinarily talented young woman. I’ve known her family well for quite some time. I heard her sing when she was a kid discovering her voice and I can’t articulate the pride she brings me. What a God-given talent! I’m also so proud of Raye, who wrote some of the songs on The Gift. She has had such an anointing. You hear the vulnerability and wisdom in her voice. I also love and respect Olivia Dean. These beautiful women are all kind, have grace, and write and produce their own music. It gives me goosebumps. I just burst with pride when I see them.
Looking back, what was your favourite hairstyle during the B’DAY era, and your favourite look created by your mum?

BEYONCÉ: My favorite hair look was the B’DAY cover updo. That’s stood the test of time and has had such a renaissance this year. I love seeing everyone’s interpretations, and videos and the evolution of the early 2000s look.

My favourite dress my mother designed was my wedding dress—it was gorgeously simple and made with her love. We had a very small wedding in our home. We told the guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends. Wearing a dress, she designed was very important to me, and more important than any designer dress.

You recently re-wore a House of Deréon top that you wore back in 2006 to mark 20 years of B’DAY. What did you love about House of Deréon then that you still love now? What can we find in your archive?

BEYONCÉ: Yes, haaaa! I pulled out the Deréon archive for the Hive for the B’DAY 20th Anniversary re-release. I also had so much fun recreating some of my and my mother’s designs. We brought back the Deréon hoodies and metallic Freakum dresses. I’ll never forget calling my mum the day before the “Freakum Dress” shoot, asking her to make more dresses in more colours because I envisioned match-cutting the colours during the choreography. She was frustrated that I tasked her with making them so last minute, but she and Ty (Tyrone Hunter) got it done. I’m so very thankful for her. I’m so excited to pass all my archives to my kids, especially now that they’re all discovering their own personal style. I’m going to enjoy seeing how they pull from their parents’ carpets and tours if they’re ever interested. Rumi’s favourite place to shop right now is Ross and TJ Maxx these days.

items.title: Bebe Rexha Burns Down the Asylum
items.description: “You’re going to gag,” Bebe Rexha says, squinting in the glare of late afternoon sunshine as she scrolls through her phone.
items.author: Joan Summers
paragraphs: “You’re going to gag,” Bebe Rexha says, squinting in the glare of late afternoon sunshine as she scrolls through her phone.

A moment earlier, the singer was juggling her laptop as she flipped over the edge of her hot pink bikini top to proudly show her publicist her tan lines. Bebe has brought her computer out onto a balcony overlooking Ibiza — a work from home setup fit for a pop star. Now she’s on her phone, hunting down a photo she took on set the day of her PAPER magazine shoot. It’s taking her a minute, but she’s determined. Then her face lights up as she finds what she’s looking for. Bebe holds her phone up to her computer camera. “I have a picture of me burning down the asylum,” she beams.

The proverbial in-patient program in question is The Khia Asylum, named perhaps unfairly after the rapper Khia, whose 2003 hit “My Neck, My Back (Lick It)” peaked just outside top 40 but lives on in infamy via this piece of pop terminology, used to describe any whiff of commercial under-performance. Since pop fans started using the term a couple of years ago, prior residents like Sabrina Carpenter, Charli XCX and Zara Larsson have all graduated from perceived flopdom, thus breaking out of the asylum. Could Bebe Rexha be next?
Bodysuit: Noscenegirls, Gloves: Wing & Weft, Shoes: Jean Paul Gaultier x Lotta Volkova courtesy of Gabriel Held Vintage

The 36-year-old Brooklyn-born, Staten Island-raised singer and songwriter has an unlikely CV for a flop: she’s written megahits, including Eminem and Rihanna’s enduring smash “Monster,” plus songs for Selena Gomez and Nick Jonas. She’s collaborated with everyone from Dolly Parton to Snoop Dogg, Cardi B, Doja Cat and Pitbull. And she’s got her own hits, too – four top 10s and five songs with more than one billion streams, including her most recent to join the billions club, a 2022 EDM smash with David Guetta, "I'm Good (Blue)."

But Bebe’s often been seen more as a voice on a hook than a superstar in her own right. Now she’s trying to change that. Early this year, Bebe announced her exit from Warner Records after three albums and more than a decade, instead striking a deal with an independent label and distributor, Empire. Then she started dropping dance floor fillers like “New Religion,” a searing EDM song built around a sample from the nineties dance classic “Insomnia” by Faithless and the propulsive “Çike Çike,” which sees Bebe embracing her roots by singing in Albanian. Finally, in June, she dropped her fourth studio album, Dirty Blonde, complete with a music video for every song.

So far, Bebe’s bet on herself has paid off: Dirty Blonde debuted atop the Billboard Top Dance Albums chart, having moved 19,000 album equivalent units its first week. On Spotify, she currently has 43 million monthly streams and not long after the album release she was one of the 100 most streamed acts on the platform. And she’s in Spain for a major moment — she joined David Guetta to sing their latest collab together, “Sad Girls” for 80,000 screaming fans.

PAPER catches up with Rexha shortly afterwards, fresh out of burning down the asylum for this very cover story. The pop phenom talks to PAPER about Dirty Blonde, going independent and having a party girl moment in her thirties.
Read our latest cover story below.
Dress, Corset, Blazer: Jane Wade, Shoes: Gianvito Rossi

It’s gorgeous. It’s amazing. I performed with David Guetta the other night and I got to watch his show. I was on stage with him mid-way through the show, so I got to go into the crowd to watch after. I was like, wow. This motherfucker is amazing. The whole show was amazing, like top to bottom, wow.
Congrats on Dirty Blonde topping the Billboard dance chart.
Thank you. I was like, “Oh, shit. That’s cool!”
You were with your old label for more than a decade. How does it feel to be independent?

It feels great. It feels refreshing being with a group of people who believe in me and want the best for me and see my vision and help me execute it. It’s a rebirth. Music feels exciting again and for a long time it didn’t feel exciting.
You recently said you were mourning the way your career had drifted. What had been frustrating you?

I was always scared of making the wrong decision. I was always worried about making everyone else happy and chasing what could be a hit. I feel like I lost my DNA. I wanted to be successful for everyone around me, you know? But what I learned is, even when I did have success on some songs, it didn’t even make me happy. I was like: this is not who I am. I am really grateful for “Meant To Be” and the way the country community accepted me, that was really nice. I was happy and I love “Meant To Be” but I didn’t feel like it was a reflection of my artistry even though I wrote it.
Bodysuit: Noscenegirls, Gloves: Wing & Weft, Shoes: Jean Paul Gaultier x Lotta Volkova courtesy of Gabriel Held Vintage
I thought your last album, 2023’s Bebe, was underrated. It was kind of slept on. “Call On Me” should have been a hit.

I love that album too. But you know what a lot of people say to me about that album? They’ll be like, “I didn’t even know you had an album out.” I was like, damn. Maybe I should have pushed it more. But I was also in a funk. I knew where I stood with my label and I knew I wasn’t a priority. I had kind of already given up.
Earlier this year, you posted that video of you running on the treadmill, joking about trying to exit the Khia Asylum. Do you feel like you’ve now broken out?

I’m the type of person who just likes to create music. I’m such a Virgo – I’m trying to celebrate that the album went number one on the dance chart, but I’m the type of person who is like, “Oh my god, I could still write better songs. I could do more.” More, more, more.

Every day, I don’t wake up being like, “Did I break out of The Khia Asylum?” I’m doing my thing. Once I hit a stride, I’ll know and it will feel good, but I still feel like I’m in the building stages of what I’m trying to build.
In terms of your stats, your streams are way up, Dirty Blonde moved 19,000 album equivalent units in its first week. The response to this record feels good. Does it feel good to you?

It feels good to me. Look, compared to where I was at, for a long time I was – I don’t want to say dead in the water, because that’s very dramatic – but I didn’t feel the energy. With this album, Dirty Blonde, the energy is different this time. It hasn’t felt like this in a long time.
Corset & Skirt: Andrew Curwen, Necklace: Stylist's own Gas Bijoux
The industry has changed so much and now you can get a big moment years into your career, like Charli XCX and Zara Larsson. What has it been like to watch those women have big moments?

It’s extremely inspiring. I’ve been in the industry for quite some time now and I’ve heard the things people have said about other artists and they’re not always nice. People always want to count women out, say “They’ve already had their chance,” or “They’ve already been signed before, they’ve had a certain number of singles.” What I’ve seen with Charli and Zara is they’re work horses. They never stopped.
To see them do what they’re doing is fucking awesome.
You chopped your hair off right before the start of this era. Did getting a blonde bob change everything?

Long hair is sexy. I get it. I love having a good extension in, you know what I mean? It makes you feel like Rapunzel. But for me personally, I’ve tried so many hair colours. I was trying to find my identity in hair colors and all these lengths. What I really like, when I feel the most me, is when my hair is a blonde bob. When I first dyed my hair, everybody said, “No, no, no.” I booked the appointment, went to the salon, spent 14 hours and everybody was like, “Oh my god, this looks unreal.”
I want to die blonde. Please, make sure my hair is blonde. No roots when I’m in my casket.
Let’s talk about “New Religion” with Faithless and what it took to get that sample cleared. I heard you had brunch with Sister Bliss.

I did. It took me a very, very long time to get that sample cleared. I didn’t know if I was going to get it cleared. I wrote some other songs with them. I spoke to Rollo, I spoke to Sister Bliss. I had brunch with Sister Bliss. I got to know her. She’s really cool, she’s very smart.
The original is such an amazing record. I feel really lucky they allowed me to use their sample.
Dress: Bach Mai, Shoes: Gianvito Rossi
You wrote and recorded this album while globetrotting from one nightclub to another, from Ibiza to London to Tokyo. What brought you out to the clubs?

I was never a party girl. Even though I’m in my thirties, I feel like it’s never too late. I feel like there’s a resurgence in partying in your thirties now. I was in Zurich and it was my birthday the next day…I went out that night and I went out the night after. I was up until like four in the morning. I was the last person in the club. Literally the last person. It was me, some random girl who was drunk and these two guys and I somehow ended up in the back of the DJ booth. It was so fun.
I love that your songs have big vocals. With so much pop music today, the vocals are restrained, they’re smaller. I love that you’re a singer’s singer.

I hope that actually comes back, because I agree with what you’re saying. We’ve gone into this world of small singing. It is beautiful, I actually love it, but I just feel like what I’ve noticed is that with my songs, they have big hooks and that’s what people love about me most. I guess maybe it makes them feel something. I’ve been noticing that more than ever at my shows and in my writing session, everybody always wants that big moment, they love when I hit the octave, it’s big, high choruses.

The only thing about that I don’t love is when I do it live, it’s like, you’re having all these songs that are super high. And I’m like, ah, shit, at the end of the show, I’m like “Why the fuck are the songs so high?” I literally had my music director look at me and go, “I guess talk to yourself?” I was like, shit. I need to start writing these songs a little lower.
You asked your fans on Twitter if they could find you a man. Were there any strong contenders?
Single as a Pringle! There’s nothing happening. I always think about Cher’s quote about her not needing a rich husband.

Ya! “Mom, I am a rich man.” I’m in Ibiza right now and I was trying to find somebody to get a yacht for me, just to be on the yacht. I was like, let me see what the vibe is. I came to a point where I was like, “I’m working so hard, I’m going to get the fucking yacht myself.” I did what I wanted to do with nobody else and that was so much more fulfilling than being on somebody else’s dime, on somebody else’s yacht.
I love how you embraced your Albanian heritage on, “Çike Çike.” Do you have any theories on why so many pop girls are Albanian?

There’s a hardness to Albanian women, but in the best way. We’re fighters. All the women that I’ve met who are Albanian, they’re crazy hard workers. They won’t take no for an answer. Insane work ethic. When I was getting to know Dua and Rita, they both had an insane work ethic. Not stopping, very hungry, focused energy.
You need a lot of tenacity to be a pop star.
I would say so. You have to be very strong mentally.
The lyrics for “I Like You Better Than Me” are very vulnerable. What type of experiences led to that song?

Being in the music industry and struggling, even when I was thinner, I always struggled with my image. Being on the red carpet, I always felt off or not good enough. And beyond the red carpet, it could be pictures people take of you on stage or being around other female artists in the industry who seem to always have it together. That gets to you. Comparison is the thief of joy, it really is.
Is it true you used to offer songs to artists but only if you could sing the hook?

Yeah, of course. I didn’t know that in the beginning. After I’d written a couple big songs for other artists, then I was like, “Sure, you can have this song but I have to stay on it.” I call it the power of the pen!
You clearly could stick to working behind the scenes, you have the talent to be a songwriter. Diane Warren has done it her whole career.
And she’s rich! What drives you to continue in the pop game, pursuing your own career as a pop star?
I really, really love performing live. I love feeling a crowd’s energy, I love when they sing along.
Are you still writing songs for other people?

I really want to but I really don’t have time. People ask me all the time. I’d love to write some more K-Pop songs, it’s really fun. What I love about K-Pop is there’s so many different melodies and you can be more fun and kitschy with the titles.
Do you have plans for live shows to support the album?
Yes. We’re working on it. Everybody keeps asking. Nothing is set yet but we’re working on it. I definitely want to tour Dirty Blonde.

items.title: Prince William Reportedly Wants to Strip Prince Harry of His Titles
items.description: Prince William is reportedly actively considering a plan for a “far-reaching restructuring” of the British monarchy, which he would implement once he ascends to the throne. His brother, Prince Harry, would be at the forefront of these changes: The future monar
items.author: Séraphine Roger
paragraphs: Prince William is reportedly actively considering a plan for a “far-reaching restructuring” of the British monarchy, which he would implement once he ascends to the throne. His brother, Prince Harry, would be at the forefront of these changes: The future monarch reportedly wants only active members of the royal family who carry out duties on his behalf to retain their royal titles and the style of “Royal Highness.” These titles would therefore no longer be an “automatic privilege of birth” but would instead be equivalent to a “job title.”

The plan was detailed by Tom Sykes, a journalist and writer specializing in the royals, in his book Dukes of Hazard, to be published next February, excerpts of which were published by the Mail on Sunday on Saturday, November 21. The author, “a royal authority with impeccable society contacts” as the newspaper puts it, is said to have obtained confessions from friends of Prince William.

“If you are a working royal—going out, touring the country, doing diplomatic work, doing government work, having a public role, pressing the flesh, getting out of bed on a wet Wednesday to go to Sheffield—then you will be an HRH and you will have a prince or princess title. You will also get an allowance, a salary, and a place to live. One place to live,” the associate of the prince explained to Sykes. “If you are not doing those things and you are not a working royal, you will not get to be an HRH, you will not get a free or subsidized place to live, and you will not get any special favors. You will, however, be a private citizen free to get on with your life and make money any way you choose.”

By implementing this measure, Prince William hopes to prevent potential media scandals regarding the legitimacy of certain individuals’ right to retain their titles if they are not prominent members of the Firm (Prince Harry) or if they are under legal scrutiny (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor). But also, and above all, the Prince of Wales hopes to offer an option to his children, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, eight, who could easily renounce their titles to pursue independent careers. The question does not arise for the eldest child of the Prince and Princess of Wales, Prince George, 13, whose future as heir to the throne is “guaranteed.” In fact, none of the three use their royal titles, preferring simply to be called by their first names and the surname Wales.

Under the rules established by King George V in 1917, the title of prince or princess, along with the predicate, is granted at birth to the sovereign’s children and to the children of the sovereign’s sons, as well as to all the children of the Prince of Wales’s eldest son. Prince William’s children, therefore, received these titles at birth, while Prince Harry’s children, Archie and Lilibet (ages seven and five), did not become prince and princess until King Charles III ascended the throne.

They may have to give them up if Prince William carries out his plan. “Under William’s current plan, the prince and princess titles of Harry and Meghan’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, would be legally removed, along with the royal styles and princely titles of Harry and Meghan themselves,” writes Tom Sykes in his book. To do so, according to Sykes’s book, constitutional advisers have told William that he could issue letters patent, an official document authorized by the king. Such a decision could strain the relationship between the two brothers.

Sykes is convinced that Prince William would garner the approval of his subjects and “enormous public support in a country increasingly impatient with the cost and perceived excess of a sprawling royal household,” according to those close to him.

In October 2025, Prince William confided to actor Eugene Levy—whom he was hosting at Windsor Castle for the taping of Levy’s show The Reluctant Traveler—that “there are points when you look at tradition and go, Is that still fit for purpose today? Is that still the right thing to do? Are we still doing and having the most impact we could be having?”
Kensington Palace, however, declined to comment on the rumor. “As a matter of policy, we don’t comment on books or claims made within them.”
Originally published in Vanity Fair France.

items.title: Miley Cyrus Marries Maxx Morando at Frank Sinatra's Famous Palm Springs Mansion
items.description: It's official: After more than five years together and nearly a year of engagement, Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando have tied the knot. The couple were married in the desert hot spot of Palm Springs, California on Saturday, November 21, an outdoor ceremony held a
items.author: Diego Parrado
paragraphs: It's official: After more than five years together and nearly a year of engagement, Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando have tied the knot. The couple were married in the desert hot spot of Palm Springs, California on Saturday, November 21, an outdoor ceremony held at Frank Sinatra’s former mansion, with Wayne Coyne, frontman of The Flaming Lips and a Cyrus collaborator, officiating.

The 33-year-old singer and the 28-year-old musician—Morando is the drummer for the band Liily—had kept their plans a secret until Friday, when TMZ broke the news. Confirmation of the impending celebration emerged that same evening, during the dinner that capped off the rehearsal, when Miley’s half-sister, Lily-Rose Purcell, posted a photo on her Instagram Stories of a menu featuring the couple’s initials. This is Cyrus’s second marriage, following her alliance with actor Liam Hemsworth from 2018 to 2019.

According to images published in outlets including People, the ceremony venue was decorated with white flowers and large candles, with Sinatra’s pool in the background. Miley Cyrus wore a long-sleeved white satin dress with a plunging back and no veil, while the groom opted for a classic black tuxedo with a bow tie.

Among the guests were the bride’s mother, Tish Cyrus, accompanied by her husband, actor Dominic Purcell, and Miley's sister, Noah Cyrus. Also in attendance was the singer’s father, Billy Ray Cyrus, along with his rumored fiancée, British actress Elizabeth Hurley, and her son, Damian.

As the bride has recounted in past interviews, her relationship with her now-husband began in 2021 following a blind date organized by mutual friends. That same year, they went public by attending the singer’s New Year’s Eve TV special in Miami together. Their engagement came to light in December 2025, when, during another of those joint appearances, Miley Cyrus posed on the red carpet wearing a diamond ring that turned out to be her engagement ring.

One of the most emotional moments of the ceremony took place just before the couple exchanged their vows, when—according to multiple outlets— Dolly Parton’s “Love Is Like a Butterfly” began to play. The nod follows a similar one Miley made last month, when she broke down in tears over Parton's death during a performance at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles.

“Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart, and I’m gonna see her again,” Cyrus told the stadium crowd in October, per The Hollywood Reporter. “And I can’t fucking wait because I miss her,” Cyrus tearfully continued. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, performed by my Aunt Dolly."

items.title: Kate Middleton Announces Surprise Documentary About Her Cancer Journey
items.description: “Cancer does change you,” Kate Middleton says, emotion clear in her voice. “It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” These words come not at as an Instagram post or at a pu
items.author: Alessia Arcolaci
paragraphs: “Cancer does change you,” Kate Middleton says, emotion clear in her voice. “It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” These words come not at as an Instagram post or at a public event. Instead, they're the voice-over in a previously unannounced documentary about the Princess of Wales and her life since she disclosed a diagnosis of cancer in 2024.

According to Kensington Palace, which announced the film on Saturday, Heal is “a deeply personal new documentary from The Princess of Wales, exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness.” It will air on the BBC in the UK on November 29, and in the US on NBCUniversal on November 30.

Heal follows Kate Middleton during her participation in one of the United Kingdom’s most demanding endurance events: The National Three Peaks Challenge, which she completed this summer. In less than 24 hours, the princess climbed the three highest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales: Ben Nevis (4,413 feet), Scafell Pike (3,209 feet), and Yr Wyddfa–Snowdon (3,559 feet). The undertaking wasn't just a personal effort, as it was also in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization that supports people living with cancer before, during, and after the disease.

The documentary will also support that organization, Kensington Palace notes, saying “All funds received through the documentary's distribution have been directed to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity to help people living with and beyond cancer.” The Royal Marsden Hospital, at which Middleton received treatment, is also referenced in the film, as Middleton's brother, James, asks her “Isn’t it when you leave the Royal Marsden, you ring the bell?”

But while many patients participate in the bell-ringing ritual at the conclusion of treatment, Middleton says she missed out on that moment. “Yeah, but I didn’t ring the bell,” she replies. “So maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” James responded, suggesting her Three Peaks experience was that symbolic peal.

While Prince William is no stranger to documentary work, nor are Prince Harry and wife Meghan Markle, this is Kate Middleton's first venture into the format. Perhaps to ease her into the project, Heal's Director of Photography is a face quite familiar to the Princess: Will Warr, the filmmaker behind her video announcement marking the end of her chemotherapy treatments.

“Through this documentary, The Princess hopes to help others navigate diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer and transform access to holistic cancer care which supports wellbeing, resilience and quality of life during and after diagnosis,” Kensington Palace says of Heal, a message underscored by Middleton's words in the trailer. “You know, healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”

“It’s clear we're not meant to face life’s challenges alone,” the princess says as the trailer concludes. “Things can renew and grow. Often it is through pain that we realize that there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that."
Originally published by Vanity Fair Italy

items.title: Who Will Be The Next Bond Girl?
items.description: Since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, new Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation
items.author: Valentine Ulgu-Servant
paragraphs: Since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, new Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation and months of intense rumors, the next James Bond now has a new face. Now, the next question on everyone’s mind: Who will be the next Bond girl?

The exception in thie great debate is Léa Seydoux. The actor, who seems to be everywhere this year, played Madeleine Swann in Craig's final Bond films, Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021). Her magnetic performance made Madeleine an unforgettable Bond girl, especially since her character plays a decisive role in the arc of Craig’s character: at the end of No Time to Die, the famous spy sacrifices himself to save her and their daughter, Mathilde. For the first time since its creation in 1953 by British author Ian Fleming, the secret agent in Her Majesty’s service was gone.

In a recent interview on Vogue's The Run-Through podcast, Seydoux was candid about how little interest she had in her successor. “I don’t really care,” she said with a laugh. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”

When pressed on who Pattinson's female lead might be, Seydoux expressed mixed feelings about the British spy's latest iteration. With the purchase of the Bond IP by Amazon, “It became American," Seydoux said. “But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve, who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great.”

The online megamart took control of the storied franchise in 2023, after which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos controversially sought feedback on the title character's casting via X. The announcement of Villeneuve as the next film's director brought things back from the brink.

Bezos, who confirmed that he was “very involved” in the film's casting process, also seems to give Seydoux pause. In an interview with Variety, she admitted “was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold (…) but now that it’s Denis, I was like, Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema.”

Denis Villeneuve, who directed Seydoux in Dune: Part Two, will release the final installment of this epic science-fiction trilogy will be on December 16. After that, he'll be free to focus on his next major project: reviving the world’s most famous secret agent. It remains to be seen who he will choose to star opposite Robert Pattinson as his female companion—but we know that despite her fondness for the director, Seydoux will not return: Just last month, the French actress told People “I really loved being on this franchise, but now it’s ... done.”
Originally published by Vanity Fair France

items.title: Behold, the Most Disastrous Thanksgivings in Sitcom History
items.description: Ah, Thanksgiving. A time for family; a time for food; a time for trying very hard not to overdo it on the Xanax. While we love the holiday, this is a safe space: we can also admit it’s kind of stressful, right?
items.author: Laura Bradley
paragraphs: Ah, Thanksgiving. A time for family; a time for food; a time for trying very hard not to overdo it on the Xanax. While we love the holiday, this is a safe space: we can also admit it’s kind of stressful, right?

But never fear: your lamest Thanksgiving will never compare to the disasters we’ve seen on some of our favorite sitcoms. Because even if you burn every item on the table, we’re guessing you still won’t have to utter the words, “As God is my witness, I thought turkeys could fly.”
Friends, “The One Where Ross Got High”

This episode might be better remembered as “The One Where Rachel Makes a Trifle That Is Also Shepherd’s Pie.” A runner-up from the Thanksgiving-loving sitcom: “The One with All the Thanksgivings,” which gave birth to this iconic image:
Full House, “The Miracle of Thanksgiving”

The Tanners’ first Thanksgiving dinner without the girls’ mother does not exactly go as planned. D.J. forgets to defrost the turkey, and in their efforts to cover her mistake, the men of the house accidentally set fire to the poor bird. Stephanie drops the pumpkin pie. All is lost—until Danny reminds D.J. that her mom would be proud of her for pulling everyone together for a home-cooked meal.
Cheers, “Thanksgiving Orphans”

This is yet another episode in which an undercooked turkey poses a dilemma. The Cheers patrons gather together, since they have no one else to spend Thanksgiving with—but as the gang waits for food, everyone gets testy. The result? The beginnings of a food fight. Diane, in peak form, scolds everyone for being so childish—until Sam hurls some cranberry sauce her way, at which point the battle takes off. The bright side? By the time the war is over, the turkey is ready.
WKRP in Cincinnati, “Turkeys Away”

Mr. Carlson’s idea for a promotional turkey give-away turns disastrous thanks to one major oversight. His idea: give away live turkeys by dropping them out of a helicopter. The problem: turkeys are flightless birds. After Les recounts the horrors he witnessed on the ground, Mr. Carlson delivers one of the best lines in TV history: “As God is my witness, I thought turkeys could fly.”
Seinfeld, “The Mom & Pop Store”

As with most Seinfeld episodes, there are a lot of threads going on here at once. The important one in this case? Jerry crashes a Thanksgiving party, where he accidentally knocks a trophy off the window ledge and damages a Macy’s Thanskgiving Day Parade Woody Woodpecker balloon below.
The Bob Newhart Show, “Over the River and Through the Woods”

An oldie but a goodie: when Bob’s patient expresses anxiety about the holidays, Bob decides it’s best not to leave town—but his wife, Emily, does so anyway, leaving him alone. So he invites the patient, Elliot Carlin, to his house for the holiday, along with one of his associates. They all get drunk, exposing the fact that even the usually straight-laced Bob has a sillier side. Oh, and as you might expect, none of them has a clue how to cook a turkey either. Bob sums up the episode pretty well when he says, “I knew it was going to be bad, but I didn’t know it was going to be this bad this early!”
The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, “There’s the Rub”

This one’s a two-parter in which Will accidentally lands Uncle Phil in jail. No big deal! Turns out, the massage parlor where Will takes Phil in the hopes of healing his injured back is not just any massage parlor. The police burst in after the women offer the two more than just a massage. Thankfully, Phil is able to spring them loose just in time, by laying down the law as only Uncle Phil can.

items.title: Slushy Noobz Gives Us a Crash Course in All Things Gen Z
items.description: Slushy Noobz Gives Mel Ottenberg a Crash Course in All Things Gen Z
items.author: Mel Ottenberg
paragraphs: Slushy Noobz Gives Mel Ottenberg a Crash Course in All Things Gen Z

In less than two years, Hamzah Al-Emad and Martin Andrijasevic have gone from boxing each other on a livestream to their first Paris fashion show, bringing the same loose banter and obvious fondness for each other to both. As Slushy Noobz, the Toronto duo started out as self-described bad gamers and have turned that friendship into a YouTube channel with 1.7 million subscribers who tune in to watch the pair make an event out of whatever it is they do. On the day the Gen Z sensations talked to Mel Ottenberg, Hamzah was about to head to the airport for his first trip to America in seven years, new passport in hand. Mel wanted to know how to clip farm.
MONDAY 2PM OCTOBER 26, 2026 TORONTO
HAMZAH AL-EMAD: Yo, Mel. It’s me, number 13.
MEL OTTENBERG: Hamzah! Number 13! What’s up?
AL-EMAD: I’m number 13 now because I just got my citizenship. That was my number from the ceremony.
OTTENBERG: I’m really sorry America deported you while Donald Trump was president.
AL-EMAD: That’s okay, I’ve been neutralized now. Wait, naturalized, not neutralized.
OTTENBERG: Look at you now, motherfucker!
MARTIN ANDRIJASEVIC: Hey, Mel.

OTTENBERG: Hey, Martin, what’s up? I’m so happy to interview both of you guys today. Slushy Nudes. Noobz. I just said nudes. It’s Slushy Noobz, Canada’s hottest Gen Z YouTube sensation duo! How did you guys actually meet?

AL-EMAD: We first met on the internet. I thought Martin was really mean at first, but then we met in person when he went to an EDM festival in Toronto he didn’t have tickets for, and he ended up sleeping on my couch.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Hamzah didn’t have a blanket, so he gave me—
AL-EMAD: I gave him a rug.

ANDRIJASEVIC: And then for a good year, we didn’t really do anything. We just hung out and smoked weed and filmed a few TikToks here and there, and people were like, “You guys are so funny together.” When I wasn’t visiting Hamzah in Toronto, we were playing a lot of Overwatch together.

ANDRIJASEVIC: It’s a shooter game. We were always looking for something to do because we weren’t making money off TikTok, so we randomly thought of the fact that we play a lot of video games and could start a YouTube gaming channel.
OTTENBERG: Can you tell me what games are good? I haven’t played a video game since eighth grade because I realized I was too ADD and it was going to fuck me up forever.
ANDRIJASEVIC: You’re asking two people who are really bad at video games. We just like to play them while we talk.
OTTENBERG: You told me that in Paris and it’s what made me like you. What game should I play?
AL-EMAD: Have you ever tried just driving around in GTA?
OTTENBERG: Wait, wait, wait, hold on. Oh, Grand Theft Auto.
AL-EMAD: Grand Theft Auto, yes. They have Grand Theft Auto VI coming out. You should download that.
OTTENBERG: Okay, I’m going to get them to send me that game and I’m going to get a PlayStation. What games are great and what games suck right now?
AL-EMAD: Halloween sucks. Wolverine sucks a little bit.
ANDRIJASEVIC: The new Resident Evil is insane. Me and Hamzah beat that pretty much as soon as it came out.
OTTENBERG: Have you guys ever had psychic or astrology readings?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I just did one last week in Salem, Massachusetts. She said I have to start a company because I have the potential to become a billionaire like Jeff Bezos.
OTTENBERG: Wow, then I’m so glad I’m talking to you, and I’m extra sorry Hamzah got deported. By the way, I want to ask you guys how to clip farm.
AL-EMAD: Clip farm me talking about getting deported, or just in general?
OTTENBERG: I don’t know. Wait, remind me what clip farming is. Oh, that’s when they take all your clips and they post them?
ANDRIJASEVIC: That’s kind of a farm. Is this being recorded?
OTTENBERG: Of course, babe. This is your interview in motherfucking Interview magazine.
ANDRIJASEVIC: I’ll do a clip farm right now.
OTTENBERG: Okay, let’s do it.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Mel, don’t ever ask a question like that again or this interview is over.
OTTENBERG: Right, because you nailed the drama and the tea and you made it so people will want to read this fucking interview. I see what you’re saying. I want to record it myself.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Let’s do it.
OTTENBERG: This is why this interview is so important for me.
ANDRIJASEVIC: So, what you’re going to do first is ask some slightly intrusive question.
OTTENBERG: Okay. Hey, Martin, how do you feel that Hamzah’s early life is so much more exciting than yours on Wikipedia?
ANDRIJASEVIC: What a stupid question. Okay, if you ever ask a question like that, this interview’s over, genuinely.
OTTENBERG: Wait. Hold on. I have to do it again. Hey, Martin, why Crumbl? Crumbl cookies suck.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Is he serious, Hamzah? This is ridiculous.
AL-EMAD: Yeah, I don’t know what it is.
ANDRIJASEVIC: I’m going to end this interview if you ever say that again.
AL-EMAD: Sorry. He’s just sensitive about that.
AL-EMAD: It’s a science. Have you ever watched a Twitch stream, Mel?
OTTENBERG: No, but I mean to because it sounds great. Are you guys on Twitch?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I stream sometimes for fun, but it’s not a career thing for me because it’s hard. Live streaming is really hard. That’s why we love YouTube.
OTTENBERG: I’m with you. I love to edit. Why not? Editing is better.
ANDRIJASEVIC: That’s where the comedy comes from.
OTTENBERG: As a Slushie, I wanted to ask you: If I was going to have a YouTube show, what would it be?
AL-EMAD: You seem to tell it how it is. Am I right?
OTTENBERG: I like to, yes.
AL-EMAD: Do you like to do it to a fault?
OTTENBERG: No, definitely not.
AL-EMAD: Would you mind making people uncomfortable?
OTTENBERG: I think I should make people more uncomfortable than I already do.
AL-EMAD: I could see you doing some kind of travel series.
ANDRIJASEVIC: He’s only saying that because you look like Anthony Bourdain.
OTTENBERG: You’re the fifth person to tell me this, and honestly, it’s a huge compliment.
ANDRIJASEVIC: I think you could have a show where you have guests on and you completely revamp them in terms of style. You give them a rebrand.
OTTENBERG: Like random people?
AL-EMAD: Just pull people off the street.
OTTENBERG: Now that you can come back to America, you can help me pick some people out of the park.
ANDRIJASEVIC: That would be fun.
AL-EMAD: What’s your favorite thing about Interview?
OTTENBERG: One of my favorites for real is working with Gen Z people and getting to know what’s up.
AL-EMAD: Do you think young people’s voices are underrated, overrated, or rated?
OTTENBERG: I guess underrated, because Gen Z people are so funny. It’s interesting that the world is such total diarrhea, but you guys are still cool.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Check it out, I just got an Hermès belt.
OTTENBERG: I like it. Do you know who Wayne and Garth are?
OTTENBERG: They’re from my generation. It doesn’t matter. Wait, I have a clip farming question for you.
OTTENBERG: And by the way, I just want to say I did not write this question the way it was written, but I thought it was so funny.
OTTENBERG: Do you know Dan Constable at UTA? Dan is the guy that’s going to get you your Gucci deal.
OTTENBERG: You guys look great in Gucci by the way. You look great in all your outfits.
ANDRIJASEVIC: That was our favorite.
AL-EMAD: Did you like our photos?
OTTENBERG: I liked them all, but obviously, the all-denim with UGGs is surprisingly—you don’t expect that to be so…

ANDRIJASEVIC: It’s so funny, because we actually shot at the same location years and years ago when we made our own calendar. We were wearing denim then too because we recreated the Brokeback Mountain poster.
OTTENBERG: How are some straight guys able to make fun of gay guys in a way that gay guys love, but other straight guys make fun of gay guys and we don’t fuck with it? [Laughs]
AL-EMAD: Wait, Mel, why are you laughing?
OTTENBERG: Because that question just came to me.

ANDRIJASEVIC: I guess it’s the energy behind it, but you also got to put your money where your mouth is. You got to pop out at Pride or something. Jack Harlow is a good example of someone who does that. You can tell his energy is sincere.
OTTENBERG: Yeah, he’s friends with the gays. Do you guys have plushies mad at you now after “The Video with No Plan”?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Oh, like furries?
OTTENBERG: Furries, excuse me.
AL-EMAD: My answer would be no, the furries weren’t mad. I was surprised by how happy they were in the comments.
OTTENBERG: You guys looked great as furries.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Yeah, it’s actually weirdly comforting. You put it on and it’s like you do really get into embracing the character you’re in. Cosplay is becoming cooler as well, so it’s not that far.
OTTENBERG: Have you ever really felt it while cosplaying?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Well, we just did it recently.
OTTENBERG: I guess I didn’t watch that.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Hamzah was dressed up as Gojo, his favorite anime character.
AL-EMAD: Gojo’s from Jujutsu Kaisen, but I also dressed up as Vanillamace. Do you know her?
OTTENBERG: I do. Don’t you think we should do Vanillamace in Interview?
OTTENBERG: I keep telling everyone, “We got to do Vanillamace.” Can you explain why, because no one’s listening to me.
ANDRIJASEVIC: She is Gen Z at its core right now. She’s the number one girl on Twitch.
ANDRIJASEVIC: The number one female streaming on Twitch right now.

AL-EMAD: She’s also very kind and charismatic and she’s a really awesome success story of just someone who wasn’t planning on having it happen to them and then filling out the role of content creator very well.
ANDRIJASEVIC: And her lore is crazy and her style is insane.
OTTENBERG: Wait, hold on. Again, I did not write this question, but it needs to be asked.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Mel, you keep saying, “I didn’t write it,” and it makes it sound like you actually did write it. Did you write it?
OTTENBERG: No, I didn’t. My assistant Sofi is a big Slushie. She was like, “I want to write out a bunch of questions for you.”

OTTENBERG: And she did a really good job. I was just planning on doing it myself and she did do a good job, but this question was really funny to me. The Robert Pattinson and Skyler Gisondo interview, people and even fans hated this, and it was admittedly a very hard watch.
AL-EMAD: Yes. Is that the end of the question or does it keep going?
OTTENBERG: I guess there wasn’t a question. I just wanted to talk to you about it.
AL-EMAD: I’ve heard mixed reviews. I think I’m an acquired taste, baby.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Well, it could have been watchable if we didn’t decide a day before to just throw on a British accent. That was a last-minute decision.
OTTENBERG: But that was the right decision.
AL-EMAD: You’re right. I just wish I could have said something to him either before or after. I wish I could have given him some context to tell him I’m not weird, but it’s whatever.
OTTENBERG: The interview’s excellent. Is it also a flop? Maybe, but is it great? Yes. The accents made it.
ANDRIJASEVIC: There’s so many press junkets, and every interview is the same. They always ask us the same things. So we’re just like, “How do we add a little bit of spice to this?”
OTTENBERG: Am I asking you different questions than most people ask you when they ask you questions or are they exactly the same?
ANDRIJASEVIC: No, for the most part, pretty unique. Also, off the record…
[OFF THE RECORD CONVERSATION REDACTED]
OTTENBERG: Guys, we’re back on the record. Do you guys understand fashion?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I don’t think anyone understands fashion. A lot of people pretend to understand it, and it’s about how good you are at pretending.
OTTENBERG: Right. Do I understand fashion? No.
ANDRIJASEVIC: You have a lot of experience in the fashion world, but it’s like fashion’s literally changing in front of your eyes every second. How can you possibly understand it?
OTTENBERG: Even though you don’t understand it and nobody else does either, is there something you want to see more of in fashion?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I wear a lot of wrinkled clothing, and if I saw more wrinkled clothes in fashion, I would feel more confident.

OTTENBERG: What do you watch on TV? You were recently talking about that doc with that evil preacher and his wife who committed suicide and the bums were nutting on her, and then he went back to preaching.
ANDRIJASEVIC: We watched that recently. It was insane.
AL-EMAD: I’ve just been watching a lot of spooky stuff. I watched Longlegs last night. Watched Carrie, watched Widow’s Bay.
ANDRIJASEVIC: I’m rewatching Dance Moms.
OTTENBERG: Oh, wow. With JoJo [Siwa]?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Yeah, but I’m not at the part with JoJo yet. I think she’s coming in next season, if I remember.
OTTENBERG: I’m inspired by that. What about you, Hamzah? Are you watching Dance Moms as well?
AL-EMAD: My reality TV is bodycam footage on YouTube.
OTTENBERG: Do you know about the house of horrors in Philly?
AL-EMAD: Is that the one with the grandpa who killed nine people?

OTTENBERG: It’s this guy with a patch over his eye who’s really evil and was killing all these women and then his son got caught with drugs and a chick with a fake ID. It’s just really crazy. Anyway, I’m asking because I was like, “There’s
got to be amazing YouTube coverage of it.”
ANDRIJASEVIC: Yeah, probably. Now I want to watch that.
AL-EMAD: True crime YouTube is really good.
ANDRIJASEVIC: Bodycam footage is something me and Hamzah watch a lot of whenever we’re eating food, before or after recording.
OTTENBERG: Can I give you my number? Will you send me some bodycam footage to watch?
OTTENBERG: You don’t have to send it right now. I just mean I’ve never watched that and I want it.
AL-EMAD: I’ll send it to you.
OTTENBERG: Okay, my phone number is 646-[REDACTED].
ANDRIJASEVIC: Hamzah, put us in a group chat and I’m going to send my recos over.
OTTENBERG: Your record? What record?
ANDRIJASEVIC: My recos. My recommendations.
OTTENBERG: Oh, your recos. Thank you, guys. I really think this is important for me. Were you guys always popular?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Popular in life or on YouTube?
ANDRIJASEVIC: I was just friends with a lot of people in school, but I didn’t have my own friends. I didn’t have a friend group.
AL-EMAD: So you’re like a popular loner, you’re saying?
ANDRIJASEVIC: No, I wasn’t. Okay. I was that.

ANDRIJASEVIC: I’m a pretty charismatic guy, but when I get online I really feel like I’m a loser. It’s like, if I’m ever playing video games with my friends, they’re always bullying me. If I’m in a public lobby in a game or something and I’m on the voice chat, I always get flamed. I feel like I’m more of a loser online, a cooler guy in real life.
OTTENBERG: Do you guys have any favorite Slushy Noobz episodes?
ANDRIJASEVIC: The easy answer is all of them, but I think our favorite one of all time is the Comicon on shrooms one, just because it was so ambitious.
AL-EMAD: It’s the camping vlog for me, our first time camping.

ANDRIJASEVIC: First time camping was also really iconic because we actually got lost and could have died and that video might’ve never came out because there were bears and stuff. Then I think when we went to that abandoned mall, which was a top 10 experience because I didn’t know what to expect. Hamzah’s like, “Oh, there’s this abandoned mall in Toronto. We have to go,” and so he was showing me around and then we got sucked into this weird world of this mall that was selling counterfeit stuff and they had an amusement park in there that was also weirdly empty and we just got to ride a bunch of rides.
OTTENBERG: Do you guys ever go to live shows? Are you into music?
AL-EMAD: We go to a lot of live shows, a lot of music. The most recent one was Overmono.
OTTENBERG: I don’t know what that is.
ANDRIJASEVIC: They’re U.K. DJs. Really cool.
OTTENBERG: What else are you guys into music-wise?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Underground rap.
OTTENBERG: Can you give me some shout-outs?
ANDRIJASEVIC: Yeah, Nettspend. Fakemink.

AL-EMAD: My radio’s been stuck on country in my car for three days and I’m hearing stuff that’s blowing my mind. The lyrics were really profound. The way they describe a sunset is not like anything I’ve heard around these parts.
ANDRIJASEVIC: “These parts.” It looks like country radio has rubbed off on you a little bit.
OTTENBERG: This interview comes out in December. If you were looking at a crystal ball, what’s December’s like?
AL-EMAD: Hopefully some of our best YouTube videos out by then. We always like to end off the year with a bang.
ANDRIJASEVIC: We actually might be bigger than the program in December. We don’t even know.
OTTENBERG: Hamzah, what are you doing for the rest of the day?
AL-EMAD: I’m going to get an Uber to the airport and I’m going to America for the first time in seven years.
OTTENBERG: That’s beautiful. Don’t forget your new passport.
OTTENBERG: Great talking to you guys. See you soon.
AL-EMAD: Okay. Thank you so much for the time.
