items.title: The Center of the News Universe Has Shifted to CNBC
items.description: On Monday morning, CNBC senior Washington correspondent Eamon Javers was driving in his car when the President of the United States called.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: On Monday morning, CNBC senior Washington correspondent Eamon Javers was driving in his car when the President of the United States called.

Javers pulled over to the side of the road, and within minutes he and President Trump were live on Squawk on the Street to talk about Nvidia‘s shock decision to bring back CEO Jensen Huang. Trump was on the show for nearly an hour, revealing his central role in securing Huang’s return.
In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter Monday afternoon, KC Sullivan, the president of CNBC, called this morning’s coverage of Huang and Nvidia a “really special moment.”

“The President was so generous with his time, but it was fun to see Eamon bring that in, and then to have [Jim] Cramer jump in, Sarah Eisen jump in, Carl Quintanilla jump in, David Faber jump in, and to be able to get all those different perspectives, I just think it made such a rich discussion,” Sullivan said. “I was really just so proud of the team and how they delivered.”

For months, the news business has been focused on the 2026 midterm elections, and for good reason. But the midterms are over, and suddenly it seems the most consequential stories of this moment in time are happening on CNBC.

Nvidia stock soared 31.8 percent on Monday after the news, and the entire stock market rallied. Huang and Nvidia are not only a business story, they are an economic story, a political story, a national security story. It’s a story of our time. For CNBC, it was also the second highest hour of web traffic this year, behind only SpaceX’s IPO in June.

“In the world of media now, it’s those who are essential to their audience and really understand their brand promise and deliver on that are the ones that are going to going to thrive,” Sullivan says. “I do think that there’s a lot of attention on the business world right now, and I don’t think there’s anybody who can compete with us in that arena.”

For CNBC, that audience includes Trump, as well as seemingly every CEO of note in America. “I want to congratulate you guys. You covered it really well,” Trump told the Squawk on the Street hosts during his marathon interview.

Huang, of course, is just the latest news. Last week, it was Cramer’s exclusive interview with Nvidia’s interim Colette Kress as the company reported its first (and only?) earnings report without Huang at the helm. Two days later Andrew Ross Sorkin had an exclusive interview with Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei as the AI company IPOd.

“It’s not like those things just happen. Those are long-term, trusted relationships,” Sullivan explains. Eamon has been working that relationship to the President for many months, which put him in a position to do that; Cramer’s relationship and trust with Nvidia is what allowed him to get that first interview with Colette; [Joe] Kernen’s got a really important, longstanding relationship with the Treasury Secretary so when he was playing a major role over the last two weeks, to be able to have him come on our air; Sorkin has the relationship into Anthropic. Those aren’t gimmes. Those aren’t just things that happen.”
Those moments all delivered double-digit ratings increases for CNBC on linear TV, and secured millions of social views and engagements, where they were shared, analyzed and moved the markets.

“At CNBC we pride ourselves on this, but we’re the place that the most influential people go to at the most important times and most important moments,” Sullivan says. “I think what it comes down to is that our audience wants to understand what is changing, what does it mean, and what do they do with that information? And that’s everything from the midterms to the AI trade. When they’re trying to to figure out what’s going on, they turn to us. And I think our guests know that as well.”

The TV news business can be fickle. General interest brands like CNN and NBC News can benefit immensely when major global news is happening, but tend to be consistent on a day-to-day basis. More partisan-leaning cable news channels like MS NOW and Fox News can rise and fall with the outcome of elections, or how people on the right or left side of the spectrum are feeling.

In the case of CNBC, the news cycle today is simply in their wheelhouse, and it is poised to continue over time as OpenAI weighs its own IPO, and with investigations into Nvidia assuredly coming from Congress (MS NOW may benefit from those too).

The CNBC boom also comes at a good time for the news brand, which is set to launch a new direct-to-consumer offering in the coming months. Sullivan is coy on what that specific offering will entail, but he notes that it will lean into its brand attributes of trust, and the live exclusives that the channel has become known for, be it an exclusive interview with the Amodei siblings, or having the President on the phone for nearly an hour.

“I think that what you’ll see when we roll out our direct-to-consumer product early next year is that we’re doubling down on that to deliver for the audience where and how they want it, making CNBC more useful and making CNBC easier to interact with and more rich for the consumer where and how they want it, but all built off of the same tenets that you saw today or over the last few weeks.”

items.title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Lands Season 5 Renewal at Apple TV
items.description: Ted Lasso, the series, is returning — even if Ted Lasso, the character, might be stepping away (slightly) from the soccer pitch.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: Ted Lasso, the series, is returning — even if Ted Lasso, the character, might be stepping away (slightly) from the soccer pitch.

Apple TV has picked up a fifth season of the Emmy-winning comedy, which remains one of the streamer’s biggest shows. Season four, which concluded in early October, is on track to be one of the most viewed original streaming series of 2026; it spent 12 weeks on Nielsen’s top 10 streaming charts, drawing about 9.8 billion minutes of viewing time in that span.

Not yet nailed down is who among the show’s large ensemble will be returning for season five: Final determinations about which castmembers will continue have yet to be made. A writers room for season five opened recently.

The season four finale of Ted Lasso set up a number of avenues for the show to explore. After being lured back to London to coach AFC Richmond’s women’s team, Ted (Jason Sudeikis) stepped back from the job in the final episode, demoting himself to assistant manager so that Alice (Tanya Reynolds) could take the head job. Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham) also successfully fended off a challenge to her ownership of the club, and Roy (Brett Goldstein) took the reins at Chelsea while waiting to become a parent with Keeley (Juno Temple).
The season four cast also features Brendan Hunt, Jeremy Swift, Jude Mack, Faye Marsay, Rex Hayes, Aisling Sharkey, Abbie Hern and Grant Feely

Warner Bros. TV and Universal TV produce Ted Lasso. Sudeikis and Hunt executive produced season four with Joe Kelly, Jane Becker, Jamie Lee, Bill Wrubel, Jack Burditt, Goldstein, Leann Bowen, Bill Lawrence, Jeff Ingold and Liza Katzer. Sarah Walker and Phoebe Walsh served as writers and producers for season four, with Sasha Garron as co-producer. The writers room also included Julia Lindon and story editor Dylan Marron. Sudeikis, Lawrence, Kelly and Hunt developed the series, based on characters created for NBC Sports.

items.title: Amanda Seyfried, Robert De Niro and Timothee Chalamet to Host ‘SNL’ in December
items.description: After leading the New York Knicks to their first NBA championship in more than half a century, Jalen Brunson will add another accomplishment to his career highlights this fall: Saturday Night Live host.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: After leading the New York Knicks to their first NBA championship in more than half a century, Jalen Brunson will add another accomplishment to his career highlights this fall: Saturday Night Live host.

Brunson is set to host the Sept. 26 season premiere of SNL and will be joined by musical guest KATSEYE. He’s the first athlete to host the show in more than three years (Travis Kelce was the most recent one, in March 2023) and the first active NBA player to take center stage at studio 8H since LeBron James back in 2007.

Dakota Johnson (Oct. 3) and Shane Gillis (Oct. 10) will each host SNL for the third time in the fall. Johnson will be joined musical guest Turnstile, and Rosalia will be the musical guest for Gillis’ episode. SNL then takes a couple weeks off before returning on Halloween with Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette making her debut as host and musical guest Gracie Abrams.

On Nov. 7, comedian and online/social media creator Druski will make his hosting debut (his booking was first reported at Puck). He’s the first person to make the leap from the online creator world to hosting SNL, though Druski has also had several TV, movie and commercial roles and hosted the BET Awards in June. The Strokes will be the musical guest for the episode, the band’s fifth time on the show.
A week later, comedian and former SNL writer John Mulaney will host for the seventh time. Phoebe Bridgers will make her second appearance as musical guest.

The show will close out 2026 with three shows. Amanda Seyfried will host on Dec. 5 with musical guest Don Toliver; it will be the first time for both. On Dec. 12, Robert De Niro hosts for the fourth time, with Slayyyter debuting as the musical guest. Timothee Chalamet hosts the Christmas show on Dec. 19 (also his fourth time), and Charli xcx will make her fourth appearance as the musical guest.

The cast of SNL will be fairly stable — at least compared to the sizable overhaul prior to season 51 last year. Chloe Fineman announced her departure from the show in July after seven seasons, and writer and occasional performer Martin Herlihy left after five seasons. The rest of last season’s cast, however, is returning, and Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter are joining the show as featured players.
The full list of hosts and musical guests for season 52 of SNL is below. This story will be updated as more shows are announced.
Sept. 26: Jalen Brunson, KATSEYE
Oct. 3: Dakota Johnson, Turnstile
Oct. 10: Shane Gillis, Rosalia
Oct. 31: Inde Navarrette, Gracie Abrams
Nov. 7: Druski, The Strokes
Nov. 14: John Mulaney, Phoebe Bridgers
Dec. 5: Amanda Seyfried, Don Toliver
Dec. 12: Robert De Niro, Slayyyter
Dec. 19: Timothee Chalamet, Charli xcx
This story was first published on Sept. 9, 2026.

items.title: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ Review: Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer Lead Amazon’s Visually Rich, Emotionally Deficient Sci-Fi Sequel
items.description: In a striking early sequence of Blade Runner 2099, Amazon’s new sequel to Ridley Scott’s 1982 adaptation of Philip K. Dick’s Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, LAPD partners Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (Hunter Schafer) follow a lead into Body Body, from
items.author: Angie Han
paragraphs: In a striking early sequence of Blade Runner 2099, Amazon’s new sequel to Ridley Scott’s 1982 adaptation of Philip K. Dick’s Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, LAPD partners Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (Hunter Schafer) follow a lead into Body Body, from all outward appearances just your run-of-the-mill seedy sex club.

A glimpse behind the shimmering curtains, however, reveals not naked bodies but false ones. Replicants pay to strap themselves into pregnancy prosthetics to caress distended bellies or cradle mechanical babies, indulging in the impossibility of natural reproduction. But if the impulse is an understandable one, proprietor Muller (Arben Bajraktaraj) also sees it as restricting. It’s only by refusing to define themselves against human capabilities, he argues, that replicants can truly become “what we were meant to become.”
Cast: Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schaffer, Dimitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Tom Burke, Johnny Harris, Matthew Needham, Sheila Atim, Katelyn Rose Downey, Amy Lennox

I thought back to this scene often as I made my way through the rest of Blade Runner 2099, itself trapped by the effort to emulate what’s come before it. Superficially it succeeds, with moody jazz-set visuals that could pass almost as outtakes from the first film. Yet without any distinctive identity or purpose to call its own, it’s only able to achieve respectful imitation, not exciting evolution.

In-universe, the world has advanced somewhat since the earlier movies. In creator Luisa Silka’s 2099 — 80 years since the events of Blade Runner and half a century since those of Blade Runner 2049 — society has come out the other end of a violent and definitive power shift. Following a brutal series of wars, it is now the replicants who run the world and the humans who are oppressed, forced to endure the second-class existences or brutal off-world assignments they’d once outsourced to the replicants.

It is in this context that Olwen, a replicant blade runner with just eight days left in her predetermined life span, meets her new partner Marian — actually Cora, a human passing as a replicant. Olwen is looking for Marek (Johnny Harris), a fellow blade runner who recently disappeared without a trace. Cora is seeking a mysterious artifact to trade to the human rebels in exchange for passage to Mexico City, reportedly the last human-run enclave in the whole wide world. Wouldn’t you know it — it turns out their missions are, essentially, one and the same.

As an extension of the Blade Runner aesthetic, the drama functions very capably; apparently, these new robot overlords have done little to overhaul Los Angeles’ grimy streets or ramshackle technology. The city still glitters white and neon under oppressive clouds of smog. Interiors are still cramped, dirty, stuffed to the gills with ancient rusted equipment. By day, light does not so much flood a room as pierce through like pale blue spears. A wailing jazz score, courtesy of Leopold Ross, sets a plaintive, lonely tone.

A gal could get lost in a vibe this thick, and 2099 frequently does, lingering on empty landscapes or crumbling neighborhoods as its characters make their way from one location to another. Or perhaps 2099 is just trying to fill time, given that the actual plot has the feel of a movie spread across a TV season for vague business reasons.

Olwen and Cora roam around searching for Marek, for a MacGuffin, for other people who are also searching for this Marek and this MacGuffin. Olwen conceals from Cora her terror of dying and her emotional history with Marek. Cora hides from Olwen her humanity, her secret agenda and her secret past. About once an episode, they’re forced into violent altercations too dimly lit to look as cool as they probably ought to. I started to grumble to myself that Harrison Ford’s Rick and Ryan Gosling’s K seemed to accomplish just as much in less than half the time.

While the ideas that drive Cora and Olwen and their story are broadly palatable — the desire for immortality, the dream of a better tomorrow, the question of what (if anything) really separates humankind from their synthetic children — 2099 never manages to meaningfully complicate them, let alone take them in truly new or daring directions. Meanwhile, the existential anguish that powered the earlier movies only occasionally flickers through in brief detours like the Body Body investigation.

The advantages of small-screen storytelling are ignored in pursuit of some vague cinematic grandeur. The luxurious run time of a full TV season is given over to pacing that could generously be described as deliberate and less generously as plodding. The potential for intimacy afforded by a medium that invites viewers to lean into their screens chapter after chapter is squandered on characters who exist to move the plot along or parrot the show’s big themes, but who seem to have no real motives or personalities of their own.

Olwen at least has the benefit of being played by Yeoh, who can imbue a lifetime of regret into a moment as small as seeing a goat for the first time in her soon-to-be-ended life. But the backstory that should bring us closer to her is painted in strokes too broad to merit deep emotional investment. Schafer has possibly an even tougher job playing a character we barely know at all beyond the disguise she’s donned on pain of death, though she capably captures the scrappy desperation that underlies every one of Cora’s moves.
The world surrounding them feels flimsier still, in ways that may or may not be forgivable in a two-hour feature but definitely aren’t in an eight-hour series.

Theoretically major characters like Elias (Lewis Gribben), Cora’s brother, are given no inner life to speak of; his frequently ill-advised actions are dictated only by the need to motivate or complicate her mission. Generically dystopian backstories for characters like Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey), a human girl sold into working for the LAPD, or Bebeto (Dimitri Abold), Cora’s human ally, technically provide more information about the events that made this world, but also feel too obvious to offer any better sense of what it’s like to exist within it.

Without that emotional specificity, without textured world-building or provocative ideas or complex characters, what remains feels like a simulation of the real thing. This Blade Runner might look the part, might act the part, might even be trying very hard to be the part as best as it can. But you don’t need a Voight-Kampff test to see it hasn’t quite managed to replicate the soul.

items.title: The Las Vegas Grand Prix Kicks Off With a Disco Bash by SkinCeuticals
items.description: Outside, the city of Las Vegas is readying its streets for this weekend’s Formula One Grand Prix, when the world’s fastest drivers in the world’s fastest cars will tear down the Strip at 200-plus miles per hour. But inside Sin City’s hot spots, the starry F1 e
items.author: The Editors; GQ
paragraphs: Outside, the city of Las Vegas is readying its streets for this weekend’s Formula One Grand Prix, when the world’s fastest drivers in the world’s fastest cars will tear down the Strip at 200-plus miles per hour. But inside Sin City’s hot spots, the starry F1 events are just getting started—and everyone at the SkinCeuticals Las Vegas Grand Prix Party quite literally had their (glowing) game faces on.

On Wednesday night, SkinCeuticals, as the official skincare partner of Scuderia Ferrari HP, hosted an exclusive bash at Baby Disco, the intimate, moody lounge tucked away within Zero Bond at The Wynn Las Vegas.

With the space aglow in Ferrari Rosso Scuderia red under a shiny mirrored disco ball and a checkered-flag DJ booth, guests snacked on wagyu bites and gourmet caviar-topped chicken nuggets and sipped on-theme cocktails. (Also served: SkinCeuticals’s top-shelf favorites, including the P-TIOX and C E Ferulic serums, passed around on silver trays.) The model Kelly Piquet, partner of F1 star Max Verstappen, posted up on the green velvet banquette, as other attendees played around with SkinCeuticals-branded poker chips and cards around the room.

On the venue’s outdoor terrace overlooking the glowing marvel that is Sphere, actor Chace Crawford and his dad, dermatologist Chris Wayne Crawford, took a moment to enjoy the view. The two were doing a little father-son bonding—a perfect setting since F1 is “a male, testosterone-fueled sport,” joked Chris. As a Texas native, Chace (who also came through GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party in LA last week) has seen the F1 Grand Prix in Austin, but he’s excited to catch his first race under the megawatt Vegas lights. “It’s surreal out here,” said the The Boys star, looking out over the Strip.

Inside, sportscaster and former Seattle Seahawk superstar Russell Wilson, a big F1 fan, couldn’t wait for lights-out-and-away-we-go on Sunday. He’s attended F1 races in Monaco and Montreal, but he really digs the Vegas experience. “I’m racing around the track tomorrow night,” he said, “so I’m fired up about it.”

At 9 p.m. the party kicked into high gear as Alex Pall and Drew Taggart of the Chainsmokers took to the DJ booth, easing into their set, kicking off a remix of thesynth-pop classic “Don't You Want Me” then incrementally dialing up the heat until Taggart took to the mic himself to perform “Paris,” the DJ duo’s 2017 hit. When the musician Sooin, of the K-pop group Meovv, hopped into the booth to chop it up with the Chainsmokers, the room lit up.

The nostalgia was at a full tilt as the duo played MGMT’s millennial-optimism anthem “Kids” while guests were offered trays of warm chocolate chip cookies. When the Chainsmokers teed up “Roses,” their first top 10 hit, Taggart cued the crowd by saying, “I need all the 2015 energy you still have left inside you.” Then they brought the whole house down with their 2016 Halsey duet “Closer.” At this point, the Chainsmokers were flying, indulging the crowd with an anthemic dance version of Miley Cyrus’s “The Climb” and a dubstep mix of “Spectrum” by Florence + The Machine.

They closed out their set with some on-theme bottle service, as the Baby Disco crew made their way through the crowd hoisting magnums of Champagne and a strobe-flashing disco ball shaped like SkinCeuticals’s iconic serum dropper bottle. Time for the cooldown lap.
“I just want to say, everyone has really nice skin in here,” Taggart told the room with a grin. “Shout out to SkinCeuticals.”

items.title: This Piping Hot Zenith Collaboration Explains the Future of the Watch Market
items.description: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.
items.author: Cam Wolf
paragraphs: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

In early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November. The latest Zenith G.F.J., made in partnership with the Los Angeles-based independent watchmaker J.N. Shapiro, is a gorgeous timepiece that combines the former’s mechanical know-how with Shapiro’s meticulously handmade dials. Over four months before the watch was even unveiled to the public, Marietta shared that 20 of the 25 pieces produced had already been sold. Of all the releases from the major Swiss brands in 2026, none better represent the future of luxury watchmaking than this high-end, fussily made, independent-adjacent, sold-out-before-you-ever-heard-about-it G.F.J.

Zenith recently announced that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market. “All of us in our segment, which is described as mid-range, are going through a very difficult period,” Zenith CEO Benoit De Clerck told staff as he explained the restructuring, according to Le Temps. The brand has been shifting upmarket since last year, when it released a rainbow gem-set version of its flagship sport watch. The G.F.J. is the cornerstone of that new business. As the economy tilts even further in favor of the uber-rich, it’s also altering where the bulk of the profits come from for watchmakers. “Wealthy people are still wealthy, and even more wealthy,” Marietta said. “It’s easier [now] to sell high-end watches than watches for 3,000 to 5,000 Swiss francs.”

That’s true. Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Company, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year. Not for the brand’s flagship Chronomaster, which remains firmly in the starter luxury watch zone at $12,300, but for the far more expensive G.F.J., which starts at $49,900. “The luxury direction is the game changer,” Monroy said. Feldmar only received three G.F.J.s to allocate in 2026 and they were all quickly snapped up. There’s now a waitlist building at the retailer for the upscale model.

When it comes to the G.F.J., Zenith has acted like MacGyver, finding endless uses for its smash-hit model. First released in the spring of 2025, the watch received two very pretty, well-received sequels earlier this year. In March, I got to test out the new onyx-dial version for just a few hours before I had to send it along to Hollywood stylist Fabio Immediato, who promptly strapped it on Simu Liu’s wrist for the Oscars.

Over the summer, Zenith also launched this double-signed program, which allows the brand to work with independent makers like J.N. Shapiro. Before this latest release, the Swiss brand linked up with Japan’s beloved Naoya Hida.

That watch was a fascinating representation of the project—the spotlessly clean dial was straight out of the latter’s workshop. Zenith, a historic brand backed by LVMH, ceded control entirely to the small Japanese indie. It was a massive success. To allocate the pieces, Marietta said they narrowed the list to 10 clients, mainly from the Naoya Hida side, then sent an email that included the price tag of 60,000 Swiss francs but zero images of the watch. “They said yes right away, trusting us with the design,” Marietta said. “And that’s a great testimony of how the trust can be at that level when you buy a piece for [$75,000] without even seeing it, not even a picture.”

One of those clients was Eric Ku, the influential dealer and collector behind online auction platform Loupe This, who has been buying Naoya Hida for years. “There hasn’t been a Zenith release so limited and oversubscribed at the same time in recent memory,” he said. Another buyer was super-collector Eric Peng Cheng, the global CEO of Undefeated, who owns multiple Naoya Hida pieces but had never purchased a modern Zenith directly from the brand until their collaboration with the Japanese maker.

In the topsy-turvy world of watches in 2026, it’s much sexier to be an independent brand than one in the stable of the world’s largest luxury conglomerate. Marietta calls the G.F.J. “an independent brand within our global lineup,” pointing to the high-level finishing and historic movement inside the piece—the type of nerdy details that appeal to the most seasoned collectors driving the industry. “The G.F.J. collection itself is bringing us new clients,” Marietta said. “It's attracting clients who did not really have Zenith on their radar. These guys were more A. Lange & Söhne clients or with independents.”

Zenith created irresistible bait for this new stripe of collectors. The new J.N. Shapiro-designed G.F.J. is absolutely gorgeous. The partners leverage the LA independent’s dedication to creating its dials by hand through a technique known as engine turning. I got to visit Shapiro’s workshop a few years ago and was charmed by the contrast of the brand’s cavernous industrial warehouse and the row of almost medieval-looking engine-turning machines lined up at the front of the room.

The dials of the new collaborative watches were painstakingly made on those very machines—on which a single mistake means tossing the whole thing in the bin—and then shipped off to Switzerland, where Zenith watchmakers installed them into cases. There are three different patterns on the dial, including a basketweave at the center and Shapiro’s signature invention, the Infinity Weave, inside the subdial. Much like on the Naoya Hida version, the dial is all Shapiro. Marietta notes, however, that it already resembles the brick pattern seen on the original G.F.J., which is based on the exterior of Zenith’s manufacture in Le Locle.

Zenith plans to release two collaborative versions of the G.F.J. annually moving forward. According to Marietta, a couple of years down the road, the brand may allow their indie partners to go beyond the dial and play with the case and movement as well.

With the G.F.J., Zenith has created something that is tailor-made for today’s collectors. Seven-figure pieces are currently booming at auction, and it would take Moses himself to part the money flooding into the market right now. These deep-pocketed collectors are most interested in watches from independent makers: Auction houses have sold more million-dollar F.P. Journe watches this year than they have from either Rolex or Patek Philippe. As collectors search for the next hot watchmaker, they’re finding exactly what they’re looking for in a 161-year-old Swiss luxury brand.

items.title: APC Just Dropped a Pair of Incredibly Clean Casios
items.description: We’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japa
items.author: Josiah Gogarty
paragraphs: We’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japanese giant has just followed up its 2024 collab with APC. The pair are perfectly matched: Casio watches are known for being beautifully functional and understated—adjectives that fit APC’s spartan aesthetic too.

The first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch. That release stripped back a lot of the original’s markings and added the APC logo on the dial. This time around, it's the AQ-240 getting a makeover. The case is squarer than the rectangular A1000, and while there’s a narrow window for a digital display, the watch maintains the traditional analog format with hands and hour markers. Here, you get the best of both worlds. The watch is sold out on APC's website but still available through Casio, so act fast if you want one. The silver variant is $110, and the gold goes for $135.

What about the APC-ness of it all? That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation. We’ve got the APC logo on the dial and the buckle, plus the brand’s guitar-and-dagger insignia engraved out of sight on the caseback. Casio already offers the regular A1000 in a bunch of different colorways, but these two new ones are made specifically for the APC collab. The release includes a silver case with a dark-green dial and another in gold on gold. Both of the pieces have a brushed sun-ray effect on the dial. The vibe is refined and stripped back; this is a fashion watch that almost feels anti-fashion.

Maybe the best way to think about it is as the reverse side of the coin to the excellent new G-Shock 2500 Series. Both come from Casio, and both are minimal and functional. But the G-Shocks are big and bulky, with a design that seems to tip its hat to Patek Philippe’s Nautilus. These new ones are slim and nearly dressy. Put the two new releases together, and you’ve got pretty much all bases covered. And if those aforementioned Timex collabs felt a bit too classicist for you, then the Casio-APC partnership takes things in a more modern direction. Far from just being a cash grab, the “fashion watch” is now one of the best routes into affordable, on-point horology.
This story originally appeared on British GQ.

items.title: David Corenswet Wore a Cult-Favorite Seiko on the Red Carpet
items.description: Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

One of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI Welcomes a New Wave of (Virtual) Gym Bros
items.description: After a 13-year drought, Grand Theft Auto VI has finally hit the masses. Predictably, a large swath of guys have called off work to give themselves just enough time to explore the immersive fictional land of Leonida, where players can do just about everything
items.author: Tyler Chin
paragraphs: After a 13-year drought, Grand Theft Auto VI has finally hit the masses. Predictably, a large swath of guys have called off work to give themselves just enough time to explore the immersive fictional land of Leonida, where players can do just about everything they can in real life—from driving cars and renovating homes to playing video games within a video game. In Grand Theft Auto VI, that now also includes hitting the gym. And if you want to progress through the story as efficiently as possible, becoming an in-game gym rat might be the best thing you can do.

Expanding on a gameplay mechanic introduced in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, working out in GTA levels up your character to help with progressing through the story. The fitter you become in the game, the more stamina you have to sprint, the more health you have before you’re Wasted, and the more focus you have to take down enemies. Just like in real life, pumping iron makes daily life a whole lot easier.

To get fit, you can use the weights in Jason’s outdoor gym, which features the big three full-body lifts: squats, bench presses, and deadlifts. While your character handles the heavy lifting, all you have to do is carefully time your button presses to complete reps without causing an injury. Once you have enough money, you can purchase memberships at gyms across the city, giving you access to treadmills, free weights, and workout machines. The exercise options are so extensive (you can even do zone 2 cardio) that gamers have already started trading tips to the best GTA 6 workouts for maximizing your character’s gains.

As your character gets stronger, their avatar transforms accordingly, developing more defined muscles, a six-pack, and even a chiseled face. Neglecting your fitness and overeating (a real thing you can do in the game) has an alternate effect as your player visibly gains weight and adopts a “dad bod.”

Inevitably there will be many players that skip the gym this weekend so they can pump a little virtual iron with their thumbs. There’s something undeniably ironic about looksmaxxing your GTA character while spending hours sitting on the couch playing a video game. But don’t think that just because it’s all on a screen that you won’t walk away from a session with a little back pain, so maybe schedule a few breaks in between. You could even build a home gym of your own like Jason’s—it’s already got one fitness expert’s approval.

items.title: 60 Luxury Holiday Gifts for Your Chicest Loved Ones
items.description: Most gift guides promise something for everyone. But this one is for the people who have everything—your friends, family, and loved ones with impeccable taste, the ones you’d happily give the moon (if only the moon met their standards. But some Louis Vuitton w
items.author: Maryam Lieberman
paragraphs: Most gift guides promise something for everyone. But this one is for the people who have everything—your friends, family, and loved ones with impeccable taste, the ones you’d happily give the moon (if only the moon met their standards. But some Louis Vuitton will do, of course). We’ve done the hunting, from small luxuries that punch above their price point to showstoppers worth gushing over. Below, peruse our compilation of recent and forever favorites that will make even the most discerning recipient light up.

This is the beauty gift for the person who truly has everything, except perhaps a good reason to get out of bed and do their skincare routine. Chanel’s Sublimage L’Extrait de Crème is obviously some serious skin indulgence, but we must say the real pièce de résistance is the lacquered case. It’s so beautiful, you’ll keep it long after the product is done.

It bears repeating that a little old-school glamour still goes a long, long way. Inspired by a design from Tiffany & Co.’s 1962 archives, this 18-karat yellow gold necklace with Akoya pearls and turquoise has that rare, untouchable chicness that’s never dated. Wear it long or doubled up (our preference). This is a piece for a lifetime.

Consider this your permission to put something spectacular under your own tree. A little reward for all those hours of hard work, this silver python Horsebit is equal parts sexy, statement-making, and endlessly tempting for evening.

Make your home gift memorable—why settle for the obligatory silver frame or crystal piece? The Louis Vuitton Diago High Vase, designed by Patricia Urquiola in lilac or seafoam green glass with LV perforated leather detailing, is a far more striking proposition. It’s sculptural, unexpected, and compelling with flowers inside (or not!).

Because she has super-sharp taste and her entrances are studied by everyone in the room, this Cartier necklace is pure provocation, and perfect for her. Fashioned in 18-karat gold with onyx accents and emerald eyes, this long necklace features a chic panther medallion with tassels.

This one is clearly for someone with a strong point of view on dressing, with just the right amount of fashionable edge. We love this chic, substantial accent that works as well with a crisp white shirt as it does with a black evening gown.

Smaller in scale but singular in presence, this season’s most coveted Louis Vuitton beauty-centric launch turns up the volume on glam traveling. The monogrammed piece is a gorgeous, timeless color and defines what luxe leather collectables are all about.

These beauties are stylish, pared-back, and impossible to overdo. Dior’s four-inch pumps are a fabulous gift to elevate her jeans-and-black-turtleneck look—or give her Little Black Dress effortless élan.

Because subtlety is overrated, especially when it comes to holiday gift-giving. Guerlain’s glow-inducing pearls of multicolor makeup arrive in a jewel-worthy case, complete with its own kabuki brush. This product is entirely too gorgeous to hide in a makeup bag.
A little irreverence goes a long way, particularly when Chanel is involved. These gold-tone metal-and-resin earrings from the house’s cruise 2026/2027 collection are both playful and polished.

We all know the Love bracelet needs no introduction. But this pink-gold version, set with diamonds and designed with a flexible construction, offers a more unexpected take on a familiar icon. Wear it solo, without another bracelet in sight (a little Parisian insouciance, if you will).

The effortless edge here is undeniable—the distressed tasseled leather gives this piece a lived-in, rock-and-roll feel from day one. Pair with your jeans and thigh-high boots and you’ve got a look you will reach for season after season.
Meet the everyday bag finally done right in a beautiful leather. Jonathan Anderson’s Dior proves elegant and easy can be the same thing.

Gucci’s recent fragrance game has been especially strong, and this whimsical jasmine-and-gardenia blend is no exception. Effortlessly feminine, the set includes an eau de parfum, body lotion, and travel-size spray.

The Flamenco bag is a stunner, with luminous shades and a shape that will outlast every trend. Give it to the woman who lives for color, or the one who’s worn nothing but black for years. Both will fall in love with the accessory instantly.
Never lose track of your lip pencils while traveling again. This gorgeously, timeless case houses ten beautiful colors, from perfectly curated nudes to classic reds and everything in between.

We love this piece for a multitude of reasons: it’s a little Aspen, a little Gstaad, and entirely Chanel. The neutral palette has an après-ski nonchalance, but there’s nothing ordinary about it. The zip closure keeps essentials tucked away, while the silhouette does the fashion talking. It’s practical, yes, but that’s hardly the first thing you’ll notice about this bag.
For the lipstick devotee, here are 12 (yes, 12!) perfected shades from Pat McGrath Labs. This gift is like a years-long celebratory wardrobe for the lips, with liners to match.

The most memorable beauty gifts are the ones that blur the line between vanity and collecting. Inspired by Estée Lauder’s 1965 holiday collection, this turquoise compact—with its mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell hues—has the appeal of a vintage jewel. Inside, the solid scent of Beautiful Magnolia lends a soft, feminine finish that is impossible not to love.

This is one of Ferragamo’s most refined seasons yet—and the mini Hug handbag is another fabulous example of creative director Maximilian Davis’s chic vision. This piece is plush, luxe, and totally covetable.

We can’t stay away from a little everyday luxury in the prettiest shade of pink. Bottega’s buttery-soft leather is in a class of its own, and the signature Intrecciato weave makes this far more than just a cardholder. It is a work of art!

A La Mer devotee is not easily tempted elsewhere, and this set only reinforces that sense of loyalty. Packed with the brand’s complexion essentials, it’s a welcome excuse to replenish their favorites. And for what it’s worth, it’s a very satisfying gift to unwrap.

Someone has clearly been very good this year. With eleven full-size Augustinus Bader formulas for face, body, and hair, this will be a Christmas morning to make even Santa reconsider his own skincare routine.

The best part? You don’t have to go anywhere. This at-home sauna is your own private indulgence, whenever you want it. No booking, no crowds, just you, the heat, and a door that transports you to glowing skin, detoxification, muscle recovery, better sleep, and less anxiety (seriously).

Some gifts are destined to elicit an audible reaction, like this one—a nod to the Bulgari archives, a little modernist bravado, and coming in an utterly covetable shade of blue. This 18-karat yellow gold Tubogas necklace, set with a central blue topaz and pavé diamonds, epitomizes enduring style. It needs no occasion, of course, but Christmas makes for a very good excuse.

For the fashion iconoclast who loves a statement and wears it with confidence, this Giorgio Fachini ring is impossible not to love. Eighteen-karat yellow gold is capped with a disc-shaped onyx that will stun from the moment it’s on the hand.

This is beyond good taste on every level: Sisley for the skin, Christofle for the home. Two icons of French luxury come together in a set that pairs Sisley’s exacting approach to skincare with a beautifully etched Christofle tray designed by Christine d’Ornano.

This is a gift duo that balances thoughtful formulation with understated polish. The LV Ombrés 150 Beige Memento refillable eyeshadow compact pairs squalane and camellia seed oils with a texture designed to help keep creasing in check, while the LV Rouge 105 Nude Nécessaire lipstick brings a complementary wash of color that you simply can’t get wrong (because who doesn’t love a good nude lip?).

The unexpected fashion pick of the person who already owns all the basics. In animal print, the Ferragamo Gancini belt polishes a white shirt and jeans and can cinch beautifully on a dress if you’re feeling daring.

No one can touch an iconic French scent, and Hermès is always a sure winner in the fragrance game. Barenia is fast becoming a modern classic, with sensual notes of chypre, oakwood, and patchouli. The set comes with a full-size bottle and travel spray, so you are never without the aromatic mood.

Gucci is testing everyone’s spending willpower this season. This one’s for the woman who has every It bag and shoe on the planet. Gucci’s buttery-soft nappa leather turtleneck is pure fashion attitude—sleek and subversive.
Meet the bag to carry on repeat from fall through the New Year. We assure you it will be worn straight out of the gift box and never make it the closet, because that’s what happened to us.

When it comes to red light masks, Celluma is in a league of its own, bringing decades of photobiomodulation research to its newest product, which delivers precisely calibrated wavelengths and has energy output designed to deliver red-light therapy where it counts. A standout gift for the skincare devotee who wants the best, with the added appeal of red-light benefits for the scalp (!).

Mahjong shows no sign of losing its hand, and while there are plenty of luxe sets on the market, La DoubleJ’s is an especially fun choice. The color schemes are bold, the design has that unmistakable Italian flair, and it brings colorful joy to the game wherever you are playing.

A gift for a new home, a guest bathroom in need of personality, or anyone whose getting-ready space deserves as much attention as the rest of the house. Missoni’s signature fiammato (zigzag) print brings an unexpected jolt of pattern and color.

Here’s something for the clean-beauty devotee with high standards. This set brings together four of Tata Harper’s formulas for exfoliation, hydration, replenishment, and barrier support. Organically sourced ingredients and sustainable packaging round out the offering, housed in a verdant box that makes a beautiful first impression.

For someone who knows that the objects on a table are part of the pleasure of gathering around it. FoundRae’s sculptural brass double candle holder brings a touch of gold and a strong design to a dinner table or coffee table.

For the beach-house hosts who have received their share of wine and flowers, a pair of artfully designed beach rackets is a welcome change of pace. A little unexpected, genuinely fun, and likely to see far more use than another hostess bouquet.

A fragrance gift that always lands, this for the woman with timeless taste. Baccarat Rouge 540 is an iconic scent for a reason (it is, notably, Rihanna’s favorite), and pairing it with body oil makes an already exceptional fragrance gift that much better.
Here’s a beautiful and pleasing scent for all to love. This is a delightful pear and lotus incantation that comes with a full-size bottle and a cute travel size option.

For the fragrance obsessive and the perpetually undecided, this set is an excuse to experiment. Seventeen 1.5ml samples, plus a 50ml bottle, cover plenty of olfactory ground, from the heady Jasmine 17 and understated Lavande 31 to the cult-favorite Santal 33.

Some gifts are a gamble, but this is a guaranteed home run, especially if your recipient is on the more youthful side. Hourglass has packed four of its greatest hits into one very luxe package: a full-size Phantom Volumizing Glossy Balm in Slip, Unlocked Instant Extensions Mascara in Ultra Black, Ambient Lighting Edit Unlocked in Hope, and a limited-edition Ambient Lighting Edit Brush II in Love. It all comes tucked inside a vegan leather makeup pouch.

In this clever home gift, the brass has just enough polish to work in both modern and traditional interiors. Plus, there’s something satisfying about giving a gift that won’t be relegated to the back of a cupboard. Anyon Atelier’s match holder comes in a small and large option, and unlike the candle it accompanies, this product has staying power.

Some skincare gifts are best judged a few weeks after Christmas, when your loved one starts noticing the difference in their complexion. Bonjout’s pairing of face cream and balm is an invitation to discover a new favorite, and the sort of introduction to a brand that can turn a first-time user into a serious loyalist. Trust us, this French label is worth checking out.

The Knesko Sculpting Set pairs its beloved glow-giving face oil with a heart-shaped rose quartz gua sha for facial sculpting and lymphatic drainage. It’s perfect for pre-party prep or an evening ritual to boost circulation and de-puffing.

Whoever gets this gift will fall in love with this fabulous and unique fragrance that has a limited-edition bottle designed by painter Abel Macias. Forest Sounds feels destined for cult-classic status especially for those who find gourmands a little too dessert menu and florals a little too basic. This yuzu green masterpiece has a transportive depth that hits just right.

Give the candle lover something to watch while they enjoy the flaming aroma: Diptyque’s’s pine tree lantern dotted with golden stars turns the flame skyward, throwing dazzling moving shadows around the room.

For the person whose home should smell as considered as their personal style, this set pairs three of Byredo’s signature fragrances with an engraved wooden incense holder. A welcome departure from the predictable candle, it offers a different way to scent a room.
Because it’s so pretty in presentation and on the lips, it’s a lovely gift. Dries Van Noten offers two fine lipsticks and a sheer balm in this set.

A toothbrush may not strike everyone as a sexy holiday gift, but there might be someone in your life who takes their oral hygiene very seriously. If so, Dyson’s new CameraJet is an elevated option, all the way. Using a microscopic camera and AI to identify gaps between teeth, it combines brushing and precision-flossing in one rather ingenious kit.

If they’re the type to cancel plans for a proper hair night, the T3 Aire 360 is a gift that understands their need for perfection. The new Rouge edition combines a compact, dual-voltage design with ceramic attachments for bouncy curls or a voluminous blowout.

Good skin is a gift that keeps on giving. Biologique Recherche brings together its iconic Masque Vivant and blemish-control serum here—two serious players in the complexion department, and a proper skincare splurge.

If they can happily lose an hour (or two) in a bath, Santa Maria Novella’s Melograno bath salts are a healing indulgence with panache. There is something gratifying about gifting a pleasure that rarely makes it onto anyone’s to-buy list, particularly when it comes from one of Florence’s most storied apothecaries.

Because one catchall is never enough, these botanical-print porcelain beauties bring a little Gucci glamour to every room. You can use this to coral rings, bedside odds and ends, or whatever deserves a prettier landing spot.
For the peel devotee who takes their skincare seriously, this is a high-mark skincare set from iS Clinical that’ll provide a skin-renewing and rejuvenating regimen all winter long.

Here’s a makeup gift that punches well above its price tag. Beckham’s Bordeaux collection makes a case for the burgundy palette on everyone, whether they’re blonde, brunette, blue-eyed or brown-eyed. The set includes a refillable eye compact that works all year, black mascara, and the new Bordeaux Pavé kajal liner flecked with gold and ruby.

There’s no shortage of shimmer oils, but after testing so many, this one gets the balance just right: a beautiful, subtle gleam without veering into disco-ball territory. The Sublime scent is another selling point—the title says it all. Adding a little shimmer to our holiday outfits? Don’t mind if we do.

This is hand wash for people who notice all the details while inspecting your powder room. Housed inside plant-derived, sustainable packaging, this set comes with a nourishing hand cream that earns its place in your purse, too.

If you’re seeking an elevated gesture to gift that isn’t too loud, we recommend this little slice of Tuscan escape, minus the ten-hour flight and airfare. Seed to Skin, the spa-world insider favorite, brings its particular brand of indulgence home with the Borgo Air Candle and Cloud Nectar bath treatment.

They’ll use it for every holiday, guaranteed. The deep tan iteration of this bag is especially beautiful for leisurely getaways, and it’s a favorite among the jet-set crowd for good reason. It’s the sort of bag you’ll spot everywhere, from beach escapes to hotel restaurants.

items.title: Courtney Applebaum Opens a World of Her Own in Tribeca
items.description: The essence of Courtney Applebaum’s new Tribeca showroom coalesces through textures and materials: luminescent silver. Soft brown velvet cushioning with a sleek, dark frame. Delicate embroidery. Weathered wood surfaces.
items.author: Rachel Summer Small
paragraphs: The essence of Courtney Applebaum’s new Tribeca showroom coalesces through textures and materials: luminescent silver. Soft brown velvet cushioning with a sleek, dark frame. Delicate embroidery. Weathered wood surfaces.

“Part of me is very polished and likes a very clean aesthetic. And then part of me is disheveled, patina-ed,” says the designer, who is originally from Los Angeles and has been bicoastal since launching her studio in 2011. “I’ve always tried to keep a balance, and I think in the last few years, I’m okay with more of a mess.” Take the soaring metal birdcage that greets visitors, encircled by mesh and topped with a point, filled with branches skillfully arranged to look as though they simply fell there. “It has that Miss Havisham energy,” jokes Applebaum of her affinity to the eccentric, wealthy spinster from Charles Dickens’s Great Expectations. Fluttering around inside, a flock of Parson finches represents “joy and positivity, happiness, optimism, and celebrating life's simple pleasures, and I love that,” she adds.

Still, the showroom’s white walls establish a neutrality that Applebaum ultimately finds liberating. “It’s freedom to experiment,” she says—especially within the range on display. “I want the pieces to interact with one another, not with the space.” The items are old and new, mixing Applebaum’s designs alongside selections from an ever-evolving collection of vintage and antique pieces. Delicate vignettes across the gallery evoke, say, a bedroom, a study, or a living room. “I wanted a space that gives my context to these pieces, and shows how I would have them interact, and create a world in that way,” she says.

In one spot, a game table, her own original design, with a smooth mahogany frame and seeded-glass top, is flanked by four chairs with pink cushions and floral embroidery; the set sourced from a Paris gallery and extensively restored. Elsewhere, a newly designed bed frame, made of thin, black-lacquered slabs, is complemented by an antique gold-embroidered spread. A matching pair of Adirondack deck chairs, dating to the late 20th-century and attributed to Westport, sport a slightly chipped painted surface. Visitors might also notice miniature frogs perched here and there. “I kept thinking, Why am I drawn to this?” says Applebaum. Then she realized: “When I was a child, my mom would have little frogs throughout the backyard garden, and I would stumble upon them. I always loved that kind of whimsy.”

Applebaum, whose big break came in 2014 when The Row commissioned her to help design the brand’s first store on Melrose Place in Los Angeles, further built her reputation on highly curated, antiques-forward residential interiors, often set against restrained backdrops. She first launched her namesake line in 2021, rolling out terra-cotta lighting fixtures, mahogany nightstands, and shelving, among other items. Now, with the opening of the Tribeca space, Applebaum unveils new silver objects—including a table, a lamp, and sconces—in forms that echo her earlier designs. For these, she partnered with a multigenerational family of silversmiths in Mexico. Their expertise was a revelation, she explains, due to the difficulty of working with silver on a larger scale.

From here on out, Applebaum trusts that the future of her space will unfold in the right direction—all anchored in her “love of design and beautiful things,” she reflects. “Everything has always been intuitive and natural and not necessarily planned. And so I want to just let things unravel.”

items.title: For Mariko Mori, Science and Spirituality Are Interconnected
items.description: Mariko Mori’s boundary-pushing art practice is defined by juxtaposition. In her photography, sculptures, videos, and installations, she examines all things ancient and futuristic, the scientific and spiritual, technology and nature. “However, my intention is n
items.author: Stephanie Sporn
paragraphs: Mariko Mori’s boundary-pushing art practice is defined by juxtaposition. In her photography, sculptures, videos, and installations, she examines all things ancient and futuristic, the scientific and spiritual, technology and nature. “However, my intention is not to emphasize these oppositions, but to explore the possibility that they are fundamentally interconnected,” the artist, who splits her time between New York, Tokyo, and Miyako Island (about 180 miles southwest of Okinawa Main Island), tells W. Mori notes her upbringing was similarly marked by dualistic thinking: “Growing up in Japan, I was surrounded by a culture where ancient spiritual traditions coexist with an extraordinary enthusiasm for technological innovation. The worlds of anime, science fiction, Buddhist philosophy, and Shinto beliefs were all part of the cultural landscape that shaped my imagination.”

These sources of inspiration have fueled Mori’s practice for more than three decades, rendering her work as awe-inspiring and relevant now as when it was first created. This fall, the Mori Art Museum—founded by the artist’s uncle in 2003—celebrates her multifaceted oeuvre with Mariko Mori: All That Shines, the artist’s first major retrospective in Japan since 2002 (open through March 28, 2027). The exhibition is a highlight of Art Week Tokyo, an annual citywide platform encompassing museum and gallery presentations, performances, talks, and more. Conceived in collaboration with The Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, the show presents some 40 career-defining works, from early photographic experiments in self-portraiture to the iconic Wave UFO (1999-2002), and a new video incorporating AI. Organized chronologically, the show is curated by Alexandra Munroe, senior curator at large of global arts at the Guggenheim Museum and Foundation; and Mami Kataoka, director of the Mori Art Museum.

Mori calls the homecoming “deeply meaningful and emotional. Although I have spent much of my life living and working internationally, Japan remains at the heart of my cultural and spiritual identity,” she says, noting how she was “struck by the philosophical continuity” of the works upon seeing them together for the first time. “This exhibition has allowed me to see my artistic journey not as a series of separate chapters, but as one continuous exploration.”

Many of the questions Mori’s work examines stem from her father’s passing during her early 20s. “His death made me confront the fragility of human existence for the first time,” she says. “I began to wonder whether consciousness truly disappears when our physical body dies, or whether we might be part of something much greater.” Mori studied Buddhism and astrophysics to better understand humans’ place in the universe, and has continuously collaborated with scientists and engineers, as well as architects, programmers, and craftspeople, in her practice. Mori also found herself drawn to sacred sites and ancient ruins, such as Giza, Angkor Wat, and Machu Picchu. “I came to understand that our physical existence is never separate from the universe. From a scientific perspective, the elements that make up our bodies were formed within stars and released into the universe when those stars died,” says Mori, who believes science and spirituality are not opposing fields but rather “different ways of approaching the same mysteries of existence.”

With the issue of existence at her practice’s core, Mori describes her work’s evolution as shifting “from the individual to the collective.” Early works, such as her “Cyborg” series (1994-95), in which Mori photographed herself in everyday urban settings, critique contemporary society and gender roles. In Play With Me (1994), for example, Mori, donning a metallic anime-robot-like costume, stands outside a gaming store, blurring the boundaries between real and fictional characters (while challenging the traditionally submissive role of a Japanese woman). In another series, titled “Esoteric Cosmos” (1996-98), Mori uses advanced digital imaging to create mystical scenes in which she, embodying deities, is superimposed onto barren landscapes, dotted with cartoon-like lotus blossoms and aliens. The series also features orb-like forms, which are echoed in 3-D as the exhibition progresses. A four-channel video installation produced between 1995 and 2006 depicts performances in which Mori lies in a transparent capsule situated in different public spaces, inciting an array of reactions from onlookers.

Mori’s biomorphic capsules peak with her largest installation, Wave UFO, which was the first artwork to ever use brainwave biofeedback. Three people can simultaneously lie down inside the pod, where headsets use electrodes to measure the electrical activity in their brains. Their electrical brain rhythms are then converted into colors and shapes, and, after a few minutes, the participants can watch an accompanying Mori-made video of the abstracted imagery. “What interests me is not simply creating a spectacular visual environment, but offering an experience that may lead to an inner transformation,” the artist adds.

Technology “has always been a medium through which I explore much older and more fundamental questions about existence, consciousness, and spirituality,” Mori says. “In that sense, my work is not so much about the future as it is about exploring what is timeless and universal.” In the case of Wave UFO, the work reflects the concept that all existence is interconnected, which the artist argues is especially urgent now that “we are living in a time of profound division, marked by conflict, environmental crises, and increasing social fragmentation.”

All That Shines spotlights the Faou Foundation, established by Mori in 2010 to engage local communities by permanently installing artworks that encourage connection between nature and humanity. So far, Mori has realized sculptures on Miyako Island and Rio de Janeiro. On view in the exhibition, Peace Crystal (2016-24)—an over-five-foot-tall diamond-shape sculpture of transparent crystal glass—is planned for installation in Ethiopia.

Iridescent materials and crystals have become a signature of Mori’s. For the artist, “light symbolizes the continuity of existence, as well as love, compassion, and the possibility of transcendence.” She adds, “If there is one thought I would like to share through All That Shines, it is that each of us carries a light within. And perhaps, by recognizing that light in ourselves and in others, we can begin to understand that we are all part of one greater existence.”

items.title: How Fetish Fashion Went From the Dungeon to the Runway
items.description: In 1961, when The Avengers debuted on British television, the sexy spy series gave rise to one of the most persistent style trends in modern history: fetish fashion. After Diana Rigg and Honor Blackman appeared in suburban living rooms wearing laced corsets, l
items.author: Jenny Comita
paragraphs: In 1961, when The Avengers debuted on British television, the sexy spy series gave rise to one of the most persistent style trends in modern history: fetish fashion. After Diana Rigg and Honor Blackman appeared in suburban living rooms wearing laced corsets, leather catsuits, and over-the-knee boots, dominatrix wear climbed out of the dungeon and into the closets of everyday women.

Clothing-centric kinks have likely been around since cavewomen started swathing themselves in animal hides, but many of the earliest recorded examples date to the Victorian era. In London, a trend for cinching one’s corset to the point of swoony near-asphyxiation was widespread. In 1887, the French psychologist Alfred Binet coined the term “sexual fetishism.” One famous case: “It’s said that Napoleon III had to have women wear black stockings,” says the fashion historian Valerie Steele, director of the Museum at F.I.T. and the author of Fetish: Fashion, Sex & Power. In the 1920s, Brits who got a thrill from doing it in rubber rainwear—a practice known as “macking”—formed the Mackintosh Society, one of the first-known fetish organizations.

Such clubs were hush-hush, but at least a few fetish fashionistas were openly marketing their designs. In early-1900s Paris, the wife-and-husband team Nativa and L. Richard founded Yva Richard, a line of metal bras, chastity belts, whips, and ball gags. The Nazi occupation in the 1940s put them out of business, along with their main competitor, Diana Slip, a boutique that employed the likes of Brassaï to photograph its fishnet thigh-highs and crack-revealing panties. But fetish culture reemerged after the war, with magazines such as Bizarre featuring S&M-inflected imagery.

In 1974, Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren rebranded their London boutique as Sex, introducing British teenagers to bondage pants. Around the same time, the photographer Helmut Newton was shooting fashion editorials in which, he later enthused, “the ladies look like whores and the whores look like ladies!”

The ’80s saw plenty of kink on the runways, with Thierry Mugler metal bustiers, Azzedine Alaïa bandage dresses, and Jean Paul Gaultier cone bras. Dominatrix chic came to a climax with the fall/winter 1992 Versace collection, which Anastasiia Fedorova—author of Second Skin: Inside the Worlds of Fetish, Kink, and Deviant Desire—considers “the most powerful intersection of fetish with fashion.” Titled “Miss S&M,” the show had top models in high-neck bodices, studded leather skirts, and buckles galore. “It was huge!” says Steele. “And the look has continued to reemerge every few years since.”

Most recently, in fact, at this fall’s collections. Hermès showed strict leather jumpsuits that, says Steele, “turn the wearer into kind of a visual phallus.” At Gucci and Schiaparelli, getups featured skin-revealing slashes. And at Vaquera, a scowling model wore an extremely low-rise black thong, from which emerged a bright green heart-shaped patch. Was it a merkin? The model’s own dyed and coiffed pubic hair? The beard of a tiny leprechaun? Whatever the case, the trend did not come off as shocking to Steele. “There’s a pendulum swing between sexy and less-sexy fashions, and fetish has come to be one of the key synonyms for sexy,” she says.

Back, too, are the same questions that preoccupied critics after “Miss S&M”: Are these looks degrading to women or empowering? “We’re past the naivete that it’s purely objectifying,” says Steele. As Fedorova points out—and as any dominatrix can tell you—being a sex object comes with its own brand of power. “Wearing something revealing can be a way of seizing control through sexual expression,” she says. “Especially in this moment of toxic masculinity, fetish-wear can be a form of armor.”

Runway, From left: Victor Virgile/Getty Images; Victor VIRGILE/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images; Estrop/Getty Images; Lyvans Boolaky/Getty Images; Courtesy of Hermès. Center: Movie Poster Image Art/Getty Images.

items.title: Kate Madden, Nicole Richie’s Daughter, Enters the Spotlight With Balenciaga
items.description: Kate Madden, daughter of Y2K icons Nicole Richie and Joel Madden, is ready to introduce herself to the world. And what better way to do so than with a Balenciaga Le City Bag bag campaign? Twenty-five years ago, Richie helped turn the accessory into one of the
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: Kate Madden, daughter of Y2K icons Nicole Richie and Joel Madden, is ready to introduce herself to the world. And what better way to do so than with a Balenciaga Le City Bag bag campaign? Twenty-five years ago, Richie helped turn the accessory into one of the era’s defining It bags. Now, mother and daughter have both been tapped to star in its anniversary campaign, making the moment less a passing of the torch than a shared family affair.

“I’ve wanted to model since I was young, but I felt like, now that I’m 18, and I have a very specific look, it’s the perfect time for me to start,” Madden told W ahead of the campaign launch. That look includes recently dyed black hair in place of her natural blonde, giving her style a darker, goth-inflected edge. Along with Madden’s large, captivating eyes—which have already drawn comparisons online to Tim Burton characters—the transformation is on full display in the campaign.

The Le City itself dates back to 2001, when Nicolas Ghesquière bucked the era’s prevailing logomania with a design inspired by the classic motorcycle jacket. Its supple lambskin body, metal buckles, and long leather laces quickly caught the eye of early-aughts style—and tabloid—fixtures, Richie among them.

For Madden, the bag has simply always been around. Growing up with a fashion-designer mother and a musician father has clearly shaped her aesthetic, which lands somewhere between the feminine eclecticism of Richie’s House of Harlow and the rock-forward attitude of Good Charlotte. Below, Madden talks about how her parents influence her style, raiding her mother’s closet, her makeup secrets, and career ambitions.
How would you describe your style?
I wear a lot of vintage stuff—a lot of black and pink. I love being girlie, but I also love to dress in darker pieces.
That really seems like an amalgamation of both your parents’ styles. Do they inspire you?
I would definitely say they influence my style. My dad basically only wears black, and I love to wear black. And then I take inspiration from my mom’s style when she was younger.
Do you shop your mom’s closet a lot?
Yeah, I’m always borrowing my mom’s stuff. It’s literally amazing. She’s so nice about letting me borrow whatever I want. Sometimes, she borrows things from me too.
What is the best style advice you’ve gotten from your parents?
They tell me to just be myself with my style. I love unique stuff, so they tell me to wear what I want. They’re always very supportive of whatever I want to wear.
Have you watched A Simple Life?
I haven’t. I guess I haven’t thought about watching it, but I see clips on TikTok. I don’t know, maybe I’ll watch it eventually.
Let’s discuss your makeup, because your big, bold eyes are so unique. I’ve seen people online say that you look like a Tim Burton character. What do you think about that comparison?

It’s the best thing ever. I love hearing that. I grew up as a dancer, so I learned how to do my makeup and my hair at a young age. I mostly focus on my eye makeup because I already have big eyes, so I try to accentuate them as much as possible.
How do you achieve the doe-eyed look? Do you use white eyeliner?
I don’t. My eyes just look like that. But I do wear fake eyelashes and dark eyeshadow.
Let’s talk about Balenciaga. How many Le City bags do you and your mom own? Do you have a favorite?

I have no clue how many my mom owns. I borrow hers a lot, but I have three of my own right now. I love my white one. It goes with everything and I basically wear it every day. It works when you’re trying to dress more fancy, but also when you’re trying to be casual.
What does it mean to be in this campaign with your mom, and to represent a bag she helped make famous?
It was so fun to do it with my mom. It was good for me to do my first campaign with her because I had someone who has more experience helping me through it.
I definitely want to keep modeling, and eventually I want to start acting.
Who do you look up to in those industries?
In the modeling industry, I definitely look up to Amelia Gray and Gabbriette.

items.title: Congratulations to WIRED’s Class of 2026
items.description: For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.
items.author: WIRED Staff
paragraphs: For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.
ANIMATIONS BY LUKTHIS STUDIO ILLUSTRATIONS AND PHOTO TREATMENT BY ROB VARGAS

An internet devoured by AI. Surveillance at every traffic light. Global leaders who seem determined to bring about dystopia. At the end of a year like 2026, it’s tempting to conclude that there’s little room for idealism. Don’t give in! After all, this year we also saw a new generation of filmmakers challenge Hollywood, teenagers take on AI companies, and scientists make once-unimaginable breakthroughs. We saw activists fight surveillance, astronauts do the impossible, and an adorable raccoon melt the internet’s black heart. So for the first time, we’re publishing a WIRED Yearbook: our very subjective, occasionally ridiculous, always enthusiastic collection of the people, institutions, inventions, and moments that offered optimism in 2026. I hope it gives you a healthy kick of bullishness—and the vigor to keep fighting for the future you want to see.
—Katie Drummond, Global Editorial Director

From the ecstatic night the Knicks won the NBA championship to the surprising ease with which New York absorbed the chaos of the World Cup to the record-low violent crime—it’s been a huge 2026 for the greatest city in the world. WIRED first sat down with Zohran Mamdani in 2025, when he was still just a candidate for mayor. A year later, as the midterm elections loomed, we returned.
KATIE DRUMMOND: We talked last year about social media as a tool for campaigning. How are you thinking about social media now as a tool for governance?

ZOHRAN MAMDANI: You have to continue to recognize the fact that for many New Yorkers, this is how they engage with the world. It is yet another medium that has to be treated with the same legitimacy and respect as traditional mediums.
What’s your point of view on the data center movement? Why do you think that specific issue has become such a flash point?
The movement to oppose data centers is one that gives me a real sense of hope.

It’s a bipartisan fight. What you’re seeing from Americans across the country is an opposition to what these data centers would mean for their day-to-day lives, what they would mean for their electricity rates, what they would mean for the environment. It’s also a repudiation of what has been governing politics for the last few years when it comes to AI, which is: Our risk, their reward.
You worry that we’re in a bubble?
You worry that bubble’s gonna pop?
Last year I asked you if technology was making democracy stronger or weaker. You said weaker. What about today?

I have family members sending me AI videos of me, thinking that they’re real. One complimented me on a 45-minute debate that I had with a European member of parliament. I was like, “This is not me.” There is a real crisis of faith as to what is real right now.
What do you hope the Democratic party looks like in, say, 2036?

I hope that party looks like one that realizes the only majority in this country is the working class, and fights for it. An ambitious version of the party cannot only be one that we find in history books. We need that to be a living, breathing politic. The people who run it have to be the American people.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

AOC’s Egg-Freezing Journey

In early August, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced that she was freezing her eggs. “Usually I keep my private life quite private,” she said in an Instagram video, before opening up about the process and sharing videos of the self-administered hormone injections.

This wasn’t an extraordinary event—more women than ever are making the same decision—but the internet exploded anyway. “This desire to start having children late in life is completely baffling to me,” wrote the far-right commentator Matt Walsh on X. “Totally backwards and ridiculous.”

Republicans weren’t all on the same page: Katie Miller, wife of the man recently promoted to White House chief of staff, defended AOC, writing on X, “If one woman wants to preserve her right to have children, which means more than having none—we should celebrate that.”

It is true that the Republican party has been intensely focused on women’s fertility. The expectation of motherhood, along with the proliferation of pro-natalism, has become core to the party. For conservative commentators to bash the New York representative felt incongruous at best. The White House itself reportedly didn’t love Walsh’s take.
Meanwhile, in an interview with ABC, Ocasio-Cortez said it was important to “normalize” the procedure at a time when “this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country.”

As the 37-year-old congresswoman considers a presidential run in 2028, expect more of this. Conversations about her body, her health, and her possible maternal well-being will be front and center no matter what. She could have 100 children, and Republicans would spend time complaining about their names. —Leah Feiger
