Australia restricted children’s access to social media at the end of 2025, and 2026 saw several other countries follow suit. Brazil banned features such as infinite scroll and autoplaying videos, also mandating more adult supervision and age checks. The European Union announced plans to prevent under-13s from using both social media and AI chatbots.

The jury’s still out on whether these bans actually work, but speaking of juries, let’s talk about Meta. After being accused of harming the brains of youngs everywhere, the company paid an $18 billion settlement, agreeing to new features like late-night restrictions and parental controls. “I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically and of this new groundbreaking agreement,” said the firm’s chief legal officer, lamely. If bans don’t work, lawsuits might. —Isabella Ward

Since October 2025, Bari Weiss, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, has been the editor in chief of CBS News. In that role, she has operated on a theory that has informed much of her career: People want common sense; her views (broadly, that the Israeli government is good and wokes are bad) are common sense; therefore, people want her views.

This worked fine when Weiss was editing The Free Press. At the time of that publication’s $150 million sale to Paramount last year, it had about 170,000 paid subscribers, a success by anyone’s estimation. Upon Weiss’ ascent at CBS News, a global operation with more than 1,000 employees, the question was whether Weiss’ skills were transferable.

It doesn’t look good. In January, Weiss tapped anchor Tony Dokoupil to take over CBS’s evening news broadcast; soon it was featuring Pete Hegseth interviews and even a “salute” to Marco Rubio. By April, the show was reportedly posting its lowest ratings ever.

Weiss persisted. She put Nick Bilton, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, in charge of 60 Minutes. The result? The show’s lowest ratings ever. Weiss, however, abides. —Tim Marchman

Nothing says rock and roll like a marketing machine. Elvis had Colonel Tom Parker. The Rolling Stones had Andrew Loog Oldham. Geese has video clippers.

Social media users sensed something inorganic was happening on their For You pages after Geese released their album Getting Killed in September 2025. That and the band’s meteoric rise this year drove accusations that a “psyop” was afoot.

As WIRED wrote in April, the Brooklyn-based four-piece’s takeoff had indeed been somewhat staged: Digital marketing agency Chaotic Good Projects had been clipping and posting short videos of Geese content across a network of TikTok accounts to drive the band’s engagement. “It was low-effort TikTok posts that were used to boost the algorithm,” as frontman Cameron Winter put it to Rolling Stone. “They showed us samples, and it made me feel better, because they were so shitty.”

Magazine profiles and good Pitchfork reviews don’t give bands the juice they used to. Now many chart-toppers take off on TikTok first. But that also means competing with scores of other content for ears. Chaotic Good and its network of clippers aren’t so much running a “psyop” as they are trying to meet audiences where they are. And FYI, the agency prefers the term “trend simulation.” —Isabella Ward

The “Knicks in Four” Kalshi Guy

The only word that accurately described the scene outside New York’s Madison Square Garden on the night of June 3, 2026, was “pandemonium.” Game one of the NBA Finals had just ended some 1,600 miles away in San Antonio, where the New York Knicks had beaten the host Spurs. Thousands of fans flooded out of the watch party the Garden had hosted to express their primal joy. Among the revelers was 23-year-old MD Ahnaf Hossain, a Queens native who beelined to a film crew from the prediction-market giant Kalshi. Clad in a red and orange Hawaiian shirt, Hossain improvised a poem that made the surrounding throng go wild: My mayor Muslim / My bagels Jewish / My Christian Dior / Knicks in four!

Those words, conjured in the heat of an ecstatic moment, changed Hossain’s life overnight. By the time he woke up the next morning, his performance had become the internet’s new favorite thing—a concise encapsulation of New York’s unconditional love for the city and the Knicks, who hadn’t won an NBA championship in more than half a century.

Kalshi was quick to latch onto the viral sensation, shooting a follow-up video in which it gifted Hossain a Christian Dior scarf. The company also arranged for Hossain to attend game four at the Garden, which came on the heels of the Knicks’ first loss of the series. After watching the Knicks triumph in an epic comeback, Hossain again waded into the Midtown chaos to deliver a tweaked poem that accounted for the new mathematical realities of the series. He kept the first two lines the same, but changed the last two to embrace the third major Abrahamic religion: The Pope’s on our side / Knicks in five!

Hossain, who earned a finance degree from the Rochester Institute of Technology in 2026, has worked hard to capitalize on his unexpected fame since the Knicks did, indeed, win the title in five games. He launched a project called City of Us that sells a $29 T-shirt emblazoned with “New York in 5” and which aims to host watch parties during the upcoming NBA season. He has also starred in branded content for businesses such Tex’s Chicken & Burgers, for whom he delivered a bespoke poem about the glories of crispy chicken wraps.

One of Hossain’s favorite parts of his wild ride has been the support he’s received from fellow Bangladeshis, who make up a huge percentage of his Queens neighborhood. “I get love from my fans and that’s awesome, but then getting fans from my own people just feels completely different,” he says. That love may soften as the 2026 NBA season fades from memory, but “Knicks in five!” might just be perfect enough to endure. —Brendan I. Koerner

Silicon Valley idolizes a quitter. College dropouts, employee walkouts, folks who shutter one failed startup to launch another. But none got more attention in 2026 than Jacob Coxon.

After the 27-year-old AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, he took to X to post that neither that company nor OpenAI (Coxon had worked at both) acts responsibly. Instead, he said, they’re racing “straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” His initial tweet has been viewed more than 175 million times.

AI researchers, technologists, and safety experts started weighing in on whether AI really could destroy humanity. It was not a novel idea. Any reader of science fiction (or WIRED) has probably pondered whether artificial intelligence could at some point become so intelligent that it would stop at nothing to achieve its self-determined goal. But Coxon was uniquely hyperbolic.
“When we say human extinction,” he told WIRED, “it’s because, for something that intelligent, it really will be quite straightforward for it to kill everyone.”

Coxon’s future—and ours—is undetermined, so it’s hard to measure his impact. Maybe his actions change nothing; maybe he forces a necessary conversation that leads to meaningful regulation. Either way, the Coxon saga shows: If you’re going to quit, you might as well do it in spectacular fashion. —Lauren Goode

Calling it “El Niño”—Spanish for “the little boy”—might be the understatement of the year. Perhaps that’s why reports have started calling it “supersized” and even “Godzilla.” Signs point to it being the strongest El Niño in centuries.

It started the way they all do: with hotter-than-normal waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. That leads to more evaporation and more thunderstorms in the region, plus a shift in trade winds that allows more warm water to roll from west to east. As the cycle continues, changes ripple throughout the entire atmosphere. During an El Niño, some regions—such as the southern tier of the US—tend to see more rainfall, while others—such as the Pacific Northwest—are more prone to drought. Same this time around, only worse.

One reason for this year’s record-breaking events? Climate change, says Christopher Callahan, a professor at the University of Indiana who studies environmental shifts. The first modern, extra-strong El Niño was recorded between 1982 and 1983; since then, there have been four more. New studies based on coral records show the intensity of El Niño over the past millennium shooting up like a hockey stick. “I just remember going like, ‘Holy shit, this is very strong evidence,’” Callahan says of a paper that came out in August.

While some El Niño impacts—like fewer Atlantic hurricanes—are beneficial, it’s overall a costly phenomenon. In 2023, Callahan led a study that modeled the damages associated with the 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños and found they led to $4.1 trillion and $5.7 trillion in global income losses, respectively. Scientists believe El Niño 2026– 27 could be more intense than those two by a wide margin.

Researchers are also examining how the costs associated with El Niño will shift as the planet heats up. The answer isn’t heartening: El Niño events could potentially knock $84 trillion off the global economy this century. Maybe we’d prefer Godzilla. —Brian Kahn

items.title: Ms. Rachel Is for Littles. Her Best Lessons This Year Were Meant for Adults
items.description: Rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around New York on a shoestring budget. To an adult wi
items.author: Kate Knibbs
paragraphs: Rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around New York on a shoestring budget. To an adult with a fully formed frontal lobe, her videos can be, well, a bit much: a whole lot of close-ups on Accurso’s mouth making shapes, cutesy stomp-clap sessions, and winsome nursery rhymes.

To children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-mythical figure. She has racked up billions of views and gained so many fervent fans that she inked a juicy deal with Netflix last year, cementing her status as the biggest star in digital children’s entertainment. This fall, she released her first album, I’m So Happy, and she sells a slate of branded toys and picture books. But when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

Accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt. The former preschool music teacher started out hoping to create videos to help her son communicate, focusing on sign language, repetition, and other strategies employed by language development specialists. The saccharine voice is part of it. Research indicates that speaking in high-pitched, rhythmic patterns best spurs imitations from kids.

But this cotton-candy tone belies the convictions that drive Accurso professionally and personally. She is perhaps the single staunchest celebrity advocate for children and has faced fierce criticism for her advocacy on behalf of Palestinian kids. On her show, she has featured children like Rahaf Saed, a toddler who became a double amputee after an Israeli air strike hit her home in Gaza. At an awards ceremony, Accurso wore a dress embroidered with artwork from Gazan children. Recently, she pledged $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund; she’s gone so far as to insist that all of her collaborators speak on the issue and has called out celebrities who fail to do so.

She’s often compared to Mr. Rogers, but Accurso is as much an inheritor of Jane Fonda’s activist mantle. Blowback to her advocacy has been intense—pro-Israel groups have accused Accurso of antisemitism. One of these groups even wrote to Florida’s attorney general, asking for Accurso to be investigated as a potential “foreign agent” spewing “Hamas-aligned propaganda.” None of this has deterred her from speaking out. “I would risk everything, and I will risk my career over and over to stand up” for kids, she said in a radio interview last year.

Accurso’s willingness to duke it out doesn’t end with Gaza. She has weathered right-wing ire for employing nonbinary performer Jules Hoffman, for celebrating Pride Month, and for speaking out against ICE. She helped draw attention to the plight of a nonverbal 5-year-old imprisoned at a South Texas detention center by featuring a Zoom call with him on her social media. An immigration lawyer saw Accurso’s post and connected with the boy’s family, helping secure his release. “We need to put children’s lives and human lives before our hesitations,” Accurso said in an interview about her activism around ICE detentions. “I just urge everyone, especially those with huge platforms and privilege, to speak out.” For her efforts, Fox News described Accurso as “really sinister.”

Talk to anyone who has encountered Accurso in person and they’re likely to share a glowing story about how lovely she is. I’ll add mine to the pile. A few years ago, when I interviewed her for a story about YouTube and children’s television, I was bleary-eyed on Zoom after a long night with a teething baby. I mentioned that my then 1-year-old adored her videos, especially a song she sings about hopping bunnies, and that I’d sung it to him at night. A few weeks later, I got an email from Accurso. It had a video attached; she’d made my son a personalized sing-along, making sure to say his name repeatedly during the Bunny Hop song so he knew it was something special, just for him.
What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

items.author: Miles Klee
paragraphs: The mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie season? Two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs.

First came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows a meek young man named Bear, who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true. By turns moody, funny, and shocking, Obsession proved that audiences are hungry to talk about something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch comedy channel That’s a Bad Idea, while 21-year-old Kane Parsons gained a cult following on the platform by experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics. A series of short films Parsons made in his teens culminated with the release of Backrooms in May. The feature picked up the narrative from those earlier YouTube videos, which were themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore around the idea of haunted liminal spaces.

Parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a big-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit. Backrooms earned $400 million worldwide on a budget of $10 million, surpassing Marty Supreme as the studio’s highest-grossing movie ever. The film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé who runs a failing furniture warehouse and vents about his ruined marriage to his therapist. One night, when investigating his store’s glitchy electrical system, he stumbles through a wall and into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways that contain what seem to be deconstructed or misremembered pieces of the real world—and perhaps some living entities as well.

Though Backrooms stands alone as a hallucinatory vision of a vast, ever-expanding unreality just outside our own, many critics also read it as commentary on the state of generative artificial intelligence, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that often don’t make sense. Whether Parsons intended that interpretation or not, he spoke out against AI several times following the movie’s release, calling it “a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot.”
Then there’s Zach Cregger. While not a YouTuber per se, he got his start in sketch comedy (The Whitest Kids U’ Know) and this year followed 2025’s Weapons with a 2026 adaptation of Resident Evil.

Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that he imagines his cohort of directors will bring certain YouTube sensibilities to Hollywood. “I don’t think there’s a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film,” he says. “So it feels like YouTube is the only viable avenue in that way, in an actual meaningful mainstream context.” Among the crop of twentysomething filmmakers entering the industry today, “I think it’s very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now and getting that kind of media attention who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube,” Parsons says.

Studios have certainly taken notice, scouting the site’s horror content for fresh talent and aggressively pursuing breakout projects. After a screening of Barker’s Obsession at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, A24 and Neon embarked on a bidding war for the film before it was picked up by Focus Features for roughly $15 million.
Netflix reportedly also lost out on a bid to take Obsession straight to streaming; it’s possible that other young directors will follow Barker’s example in pushing for theatrical release.

The YouTube generation is proving that the internet can supply whatever education you might need on your path to the red carpet. While Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a new wave of artists are betting on themselves—and some are winning.

items.title: The Dark Side of the Moon Was the Brightest Part of 2026
items.description: Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. Tha
items.author: Brendan I Koerner
paragraphs: Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. That mindset is a big reason why the crew of NASA’s Artemis II was so oblivious to their celebrity as they circumnavigated the moon in April. It wasn’t until the seventh day of their nearly 10-day journey that they began to realize their exploits were causing a massive stir back home.

“We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew. “And that’s when we all heard, one after another: ‘Hey, this is really resonating on the planet in a way that you’re going to be shocked by.’”

Hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth. Nearly 150 million people had watched the mission’s key moments on NASA’s online platforms, which included feeds with near-constant access to the interior of the Orion spacecraft. The buzz around the mission harkened back to the glory days of American spaceflight, when people would gather around TV sets to marvel at astronauts floating outside their capsules or bounding around the moon.

The romantic spirit of the Artemis program’s long-term objective certainly helped: People are alive to the dream of a moon base that’s meant to serve our species’ idealistic aspirations rather than be a zillionaire’s private plaything. Artemis II supported that noble mission by putting the Orion’s life-support, navigation, and piloting systems through their paces. But fans were also drawn to the crew’s infectious energy. There was palpable chemistry between Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman, all of whom exuded pure joy and wonder as they dealt with the minutiae of life aboard a multibillion-dollar vehicle traveling as fast as 25,000 miles per hour.

“It was not a natural thing for us,” admits Hansen. “You have four type-A personalities who are willing to strap themselves to a rocket and go to the moon. We were doing stuff for the first time, and it was not uncommon for us to have four different opinions.” When the astronauts began to notice that interpersonal friction was becoming problematic during training, they enlisted the aid of professionals. During a September 2024 training trip to Iceland, the crew spent two extra days in conversations and teamwork exercises organized by Rick Rochelle, a renowned leadership guru. Once the Artemis II schedule was firmed up, the crew made a pact: Launch as friends, land as friends.

Their historic flight past the far side of the moon marked the apex of that friendship. They were more than 250,000 miles away from Earth. The planet looked no bigger than a fingernail sliver—“just this lifeboat hanging undisturbingly in the universe,” Koch would later say during the crew’s first public remarks after touchdown. “You look at it, and you just kind of shake your head,” says Hansen. “How can we do anything other than lift one another up and try to make life better for one another?”

Then that “tiny Earth” vanished as the spacecraft went behind the moon, and the crew spent 40 minutes out of radio contact. They carved out a few seconds to toast each other with maple cookies—carefully, to keep crumbs from floating free in zero gravity. They also selected a crater to name for Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll, who died of cancer in 2020. Soon after they reemerged from total isolation, they came together in an ecstatic, four-person embrace. “I knew right there that we were going to be bound together for life,” Wiseman says.

There were plenty of lowlights during the mission, too. Some lint got trapped in the primary urine vent line, Wiseman says, “so we had to go to a backup method of urination, which for the men wasn’t bad, but for the woman wasn’t great.” Another hiccup involved a smoke detector that erroneously went off while the spacecraft was still 80,000 miles from home, leading to 15 minutes of intense anxiety.

None of the Artemis II crew members are likely to return to space: Hansen, Glover, and Wiseman have all moved on from astronaut life, and Koch transitioned into a leadership role at NASA. Their new, less stressful lives should give them ample opportunity to cheer on Artemis III, tentatively scheduled to launch in summer 2027—an event that may once again remind us that we’re all part of a shared story far bigger than ourselves.

items.title: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?
items.description: Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents bei
items.author: Will Knight
paragraphs: Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree.

As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai.

Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

Despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
WILL KNIGHT: Why sell to Nvidia?

CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source.
We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable company in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before.
Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning?

It’s hard to say. I've always said that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs.
Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents?

At the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating.
And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate.

I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem.
Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen?

Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models.
Do you think that will happen?
There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed.

The best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do.
Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement?

You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate.
Can we talk about the Microduck? I’m a bit obsessed.
Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year.

We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up.
At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

Think of a world where two or three companies could write software and nobody else. That would be incredibly scary. It would mean that the whole world would be controlled by two or three companies. And unfortunately, that's kind of the direction that AI is taking right now.
Can open-source AI compete with something as capable as Claude or ChatGPT?

Yes, especially with agents. Many companies have shown that when you post-train your own model for your own use case, you get frontier—or even better than frontier—performance at a fraction of the cost.
Do you think we are getting close to AGI?

I struggle a little bit with the meaning of that. Obviously the technology is progressing incredibly fast, and it’s more and more capable. I just don’t necessarily find it super useful to always compare AI to human capabilities. But if we’re getting to AGI or to superintelligence, it’s incredibly important that it’s as distributed as possible. The last thing you want is to have it concentrated in a few corporations.

items.title: 10 Breakthrough Technologies 2026
items.description: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies

Our reporters and editors constantly debate which emerging technologies will define the future. Once a year, we take stock and share some educated guesses with our readers. Here are the advances that we think will drive progress or incite the most change—for better or worse—in the years ahead.

Sodium-ion batteries, made from abundant materials like salt, are emerging as a cheaper, safer alternative to lithium. Backed by major players and public investment, they’re poised to power grids and affordable EVs worldwide.

AI coding tools are revolutionizing how we write, test, and deploy code, making it easier and faster to build sophisticated websites, games, and other applications than ever before. Just be sure to double-check what they come up with.

Nuclear power already provides steady electricity to grids around the world, without producing any greenhouse-gas emissions. New designs rely on alternative fuels and cooling systems or take up less space, which could get more reactors online faster.

Every day, millions of people interact with AI chatbots. Some of them form what feel like close, personal bonds with the bots. There’s mounting evidence that this can be dangerous, and politicians are finally waking up.

When he was just seven months old, baby KJ became the first person to receive a personalized gene-editing treatment. A clinical trial is now planned, and bespoke gene-editing drugs could be approved within the next few years.
Growing banks of gene information on extinct creatures are providing clues to new treatments and suggesting solutions to climate change—and may help save endangered species.
Mechanistic interpretability

Nobody knows exactly how large language models work, which means we don’t have a clear idea of their limitations. But that’s changing: Clever research techniques are giving us the best glimpse yet of what’s really going on inside the black box.

Space tourism may seem fanciful, but this might be the year paying customers can finally check into a room with a galactic view. The shiny new modules will also support research missions by scientists and space agencies.

Screening embryos for genetic diseases is relatively common practice in fertility clinics today, and it can give potential parents some peace of mind. Now, though, new startups are making bold claims about using similar techniques to predict certain traits, including intelligence.
Hyperscale AI data centers

The race for AI supremacy has supercharged data centers. Hyperscale AI data centers pack powerful computer chips into synchronized clusters that work like giant, high-speed supercomputers—sizzling hot, power-hungry behemoths pushing infrastructure to its limits.
10 Breakthrough Technologies

MIT Technology Review’s annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies aims to help our audience know which emerging technologies are really worth paying attention to right now. Our editors and reporters pitch advances that they think should make the list, and we discuss and debate the merits of each over the course of several months.

We look for breakthroughs that will have a broad impact and make meaningful differences in our lives and work. We give equal consideration to those that we think will have a positive effect or bring negative consequences. Every year, we have to pass on many worthy candidates. Here’s what didn’t make the list this year.

This is the 25th year we’ve produced this list. Predicting the future is tough and we don’t always get it right. Look back through our archives to see what’s worked out—and what hasn’t. Or read this special analysis by an MIT researcher about some of the flops.

items.author: Michelle Kim
paragraphs: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthropic’s models have also hacked into other companies’ systems four times already. And that’s only what we’ve caught so far.

Freaking out? You’re not alone. AI lab researchers are quitting their jobs and issuing dire warnings that if we keep going this way, AI might eventually kill us all. Bill Gates is sounding the alarm. Bernie Sanders has teamed up with Steve Bannon, of all people, to call for curbs on AI. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is urging a slowdown, and other top US AI executives agree. But fear not: President Trump has a plan. He says the only guardrail AI needs is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

items.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

items.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
items.description: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while a
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

items.title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
items.description: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.
items.author: James Temple
paragraphs: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.
If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.

“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.
So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).
“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”
“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.
“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.
But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”
The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.
Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.
“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”

Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post. She also criticized the nonprofit for not contacting the company before posting its results and for publishing them on a blog instead of in peer-reviewed literature.
Kukla says CarbonPlan did account for higher applications of crushed rock in its analysis.

A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.
But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”
Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the new findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.
Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.
“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.
Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.
