items.title: Kelley Curran Approves of Your Social Climbing
items.description: Sign up for The Gilded Age Club, a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.
items.author: Michel Ghanem
paragraphs: Sign up for The Gilded Age Club, a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.

“You either really love Enid or you don’t,” The Gilded Age actress Kelley Curran says of her onscreen character. It’s Enid’s divisiveness in the sumptuous 1880s period drama that makes her such a magnetic character to watch and equally exciting for Curran to play. Before being cast in an initially minor role, Curran was a newcomer to television with a background in New York theater. Now, she relishes the opportunity to play Enid’s unexpected arc, emerging as a fan favorite — if you support her social-climbing antics.

Once a maid unhappily working for Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon), a failed seduction of the robber-baron patriarch George Russell (Morgan Spector) sent Enid scurrying into the night. She eventually reemerged as Mrs. Winterton in the second season, having successfully risen in class status through a strategic marriage despite her scandalous past. “It made sense to me that she would have the savvy and Machiavellian skills to marry into the culture and marry up,” Curran says.

By the fourth season and after the death of her husband, Enid is making her best decision yet — a lavender marriage to eligible gay bachelor Oscar van Rhijn (Blake Ritson). This sets Enid and Oscar up as formidable foes to the Russell family, who are vying to surpass the van Rhijns in high society. Enid is finally thriving: throwing lavish art salons with her gay husband; moving their bodies to the mazurka, a lively Polish dance style; and dressing more provocatively. Her style evolution away from the “armor” of high necklines and toward a visible décolletage suggests she is finally able to be her truest self in this partnership. “She’s been cosplaying as very conservative,” Curran says. “This is Enid when she’s no longer performing for the old-money audience.”
Do you enjoy playing Enid’s snarky side on The Gilded Age?

I like that she’s a character who is provocative. That’s really fun for an actor because she’s very high-impact whenever she is onscreen. She’s been such a desperate character, her need is so great, and she’s been so resentful because her expectations for her life are not matching her reality. To play a thriving side of her this season that is really having fun and is more comfortable with her history … she’s more comfortable in her own skin now. She’s been in this echelon of society for a little while. She’s learned how to navigate it, and now she has the full support of the van Rhijn name behind her. She’s living her best life. I definitely prefer dancing the mazurka to trading barbs and throwing tantrums, but they’re all really fun to do.
Speaking of the “Mazurka, mazurka!” — how did that moment come about?

Blake and I were filming all day long on location at Reid Castle, and that scene was going to be the last scene in the day that we were filming. He and I do a lot of homework together, over Zoom, or we’ll call each other to try to understand the architecture of the scenes. I was like, “Blake, I can’t get it out of my head that they’re still dancing.” It’s been the best party, they’re tipsy, and they’re just not done dancing yet. He immediately latched on. He was like, “Let’s go learn some steps of the mazurka,” because we hadn’t yet filmed the actual mazurka scene. Our choreographer was on set that day, and we grabbed him to teach us a few steps. Salli Richardson-Whitfield, who’s been directing us since season one, trusts us enough to know that we have juicy ideas at times. Sometimes they won’t work, and sometimes they will. All season long we would do the mazurka to each other, but nobody in the cast knew what we were doing because only the two of us filmed that scene. Now everybody can join in, and that’s great fun.
Who is a gay man you would want to be in a lavender marriage with, dead or alive?

Well, I have gay men in my personal life that I absolutely would. But if we’re talking iconic gay men throughout history, oh, good heavens! There’s something about Rock Hudson, that old Hollywood glamour, like yes, give it to me. There’s just something so marvelous about him.
Getting into our “Rules to Live By” questions — what’s your No. 1 rule for a successful dinner party?

Greet everyone at the door. I once went to this party, and the host opened the door, and he said, “Kelley, everyone is so excited you’re here.” It was the nicest feeling in the world. I immediately relaxed. You can’t underestimate the power of greeting someone at the door, having a mocktail or a cocktail in hand, and then directing them to the snacks. That, to me, is aces.
What’s a Gilded Age–era etiquette rule you wish was followed today?

Well, I think people’s names should be announced at the door when you come into a house. I love that. I love that it’s like Mrs. So-and-So. It’s so grand and excellent. Of course, not everyone has butlers, nor would everyone want one. But it would be a funny thing if we just all started doing that in this kitschy way. That could be kind of delightful.
What’s your No. 1 rule for advice-giving?

To know whether it’s welcome or not. Unsolicited advice is one of my least favorite things. A lot of times people just need to talk a thing out, and they just need to be heard, and they just need to be witnessed. So to be able to calibrate whether the advice is welcome, or when you’ve just got to sit back and be that friend who’s a sounding board. In some ways, it can be more productive because oftentimes people will solve their own problems if they can work through it.
Did you receive any particularly good advice regarding your career?

One of my earliest teachers at Fordham University said that making a life in the arts is equal parts luck and endurance. Keeping that in mind all these years has been incredibly helpful because it certainly cycles. Like any career, it’s not a steady climb up a ladder — I think that’s a real fiction that we’ve invented — and so that was great advice.
Is there a way to gossip tastefully?

Absolutely. I love good, healthy gossip. It can be bonding. I think the line is when it starts to get into judgment. Like, if you can gossip and manage to leave your judgment at the door, you are nailing it. That is exactly what we want. We want to know the details of who, where, when. But if you start to get too deep into the whys and then start to judge the whys, then it’s tiresome.
The Gilded Age is basically a show about gossip.

It sure is! The stakes were high for these people. One of the craziest things I’ve learned about the time period in terms of etiquette was that if a social faux pas happened, like if you were at a dinner and somebody spilled something all over themselves, they would just completely ignore it. Obviously a servant would come help, but they would act like it didn’t happen, and that to me is wild. That’s one thing I can’t quite get onboard with, because I feel like for us now you have to acknowledge these moments. We’re deeply vulnerable all the time, so we’re all subject to these moments of utter humiliation constantly. To acknowledge them is giving yourself a little more grace than having to pretend like everything’s totally fine. I can’t imagine living in that kind of atmosphere.
What’s your No. 1 rule for canceling plans?

I tend to overexpress my regrets. I tend to be like, “I’m so sorry. This has happened, and this has happened, and my cat, and …” It’s not white lies, it’s just feeling so guilty to have to renege on somebody. I think if I were a better version of myself, I would just be like, “I’m so sorry, I don’t have the capacity, but we’ll make plans down the line.” I think people who can be that direct, they’ve got it figured out.
My favorite Enid line is, “I don’t want other dukes! I want this duke!” What’s your No. 1 rule for dating?

Arrive there when you want to be there. If it’s not a full-body yes, maybe it’s not time to be dating. You want to show up as your grounded, courageous, full self when you’re dating, because otherwise, why waste anybody’s time? Why waste your own time? If you’re in a place where you can be that self and then be generous with that self, then you’re gonna have a good time. Unless it’s a really bad date, unless it’s a real stinker.
You come from a theater background. What is your No. 1 rule when attending a play?

Cell phones off! I know that’s the most basic thing in the world, but you are there. You have paid the money. You have taken hours of your time to be there. You are in a room full of people who have made the same investment, in a digital world, to say I’m going to present in this room for a couple hours. Turn it off. And unwrap your candy first.
How do you feel about social climbers?

Go for it. I think playing one has made me much more empathetic toward them. She’s just trying to make her way in the world and live to her fullest potential! As long as you’re causing no harm, live your best life. Enid is building it from nothing. You have to admire the grit.
What’s your No. 1 rule for meeting famous people?

I was recently on a flight and Katie Couric walked in right behind me. I was having trouble getting my luggage up, and she was like, “Oh, you know, if you put it over here, it should go in.” I was like, “Oh, thank you so much. I admire you deeply.” Then I left her alone for the rest of the flight. I think if you have genuine enthusiasm for someone and their work, usually expressing that is welcome. But be respectful of physical and verbal boundaries.
What is your No. 1 rule on the set of The Gilded Age?

Don’t eat until you’re out of the corset. I’ve made the mistake of doing snacks halfway through the morning or late at night. One night, I decided to go for the late-night treat of vegan ice cream. It was one of the worst decisions I’ve ever made on set. The discomfort was astronomical, so I learned from that. Once that corset gets off, eat as much as you want.

items.title: The Reasonable Person’s Guide to Preparing for the Apocalypse
items.description: Last Friday, when the planes were grounded, I was already in one, a little less than halfway to Minneapolis from Los Angeles. I received the news via cautiously worded texts from my parents, who assured me, a fearful flyer, that there were “no known threats” a
items.author: Katie Heaney
paragraphs: Last Friday, when the planes were grounded, I was already in one, a little less than halfway to Minneapolis from Los Angeles. I received the news via cautiously worded texts from my parents, who assured me, a fearful flyer, that there were “no known threats” and “no problems” (besides more than 20,000 flights being canceled).

Ultimately, I was lucky: My plane had to sit on the tarmac for an hour after landing, but I wasn’t stranded. Did it make me feel confident about boarding my return flight four days later? Not particularly. Did I wonder — as Microsoft, Chase, Apple, and, briefly, United Airlines again also faltered in the span of five days — if the end might be really nigh? Yes.

Many of us are feeling skittish, whether about AI, hackers, espionage, or just a broader crumbling of our every institution. You might be wondering, What’s the best course of action for a rational person? Someone aware of the extent that frenzied coverage of an issue makes it seem more acute, yet still feeling an ominous chill while entering banking passwords?

Lisa Bedford of the Survival Mom, a family-focused survivalist blog, says whatever you do, don’t panic. “My concern is that people will start doing really extreme things,” she says. “People are sitting on years’ worth of freeze-dried food they’re never going to use. Or they paid $5,000 for a backyard bunker. My first piece of advice is to take a deep breath.”

For more practical, pragmatic guidance about what to do if SHTF (as the preppers say), I consulted survival and cybersecurity experts. Here’s their advice on disaster preparedness, which ranges from “pretty chill” to “I am already in the bunker.”
What’s the very first thing I should do, right now, to protect myself from system failures?

If you’re anything like me, you’ve received a half-dozen emails informing you that a company you have no memory of has exposed your “personal information” in a data breach. Also like me, maybe you didn’t do much about this. It’s time. “My advice is the same as it was before AI risks emerged. Take steps to protect your own access to your systems, which means turning on multifactor authentication, and use a password manager,” says Tyler Moore, department head of Cyber Studies at the University of Tulsa.

To secure your online accounts, you definitely shouldn’t use the same password for everything, but don’t think you can memorize 20 different ones, either. “Rely on technology to help you,” Moore says. He suggests a password manager, like those recommended by security experts here. When I ask what happens if the password manager itself were to become inaccessible, Moore says that’s pretty unlikely. “They have copies of the information in the cloud, but there are also locally stored copies on your devices.”

While Moore is not not worried about large-scale financial cyberattacks, he says there’s not much you or I can do to stop them, and there are more commonplace risks to guard against. “We can imagine a very significant event that could disrupt the entire world order, but the more common threat is that billions of dollars are lost each year to financial scams,” Moore says.
What should I buy if I’m only able to spend $100 on prepper stuff?

At the moment, you might be thinking about going ham at the nearest Lowe’s. How should you prioritize supplies, though, when it comes to your budget? Bedford suggests a form of prepper’s mindfulness when it comes to stashing rations. “Over the 15 or 18 years I’ve been doing this, I’ve moved away from a lot of advice,” she tells me. “I told my husband last week, ‘Honey, I can’t remember the last time I used duct tape.’ But you see duct tape on every single list of survival supplies you need.”

According to survivalist Thomas Coyne, of Thomas Coyne Survival Schools, a California-based survival-training program, it’s all about water, food, and fuel. “I would get as much as much water as I can, and then some canned food,” he advises. “Then it depends on your climate control needs. If you’re in Minnesota, and the grid goes down, it’s 20 below zero. Your house is a death trap. So you want some kind of improvised heat generation, like a Mr. Heater Buddy.” For warmer climates, he says, a fan goes a surprisingly long way. You should also have a basic first-aid kit.
Let’s say there’s no power for a while. What should I have on hand?

A prepper’s first order of business should be securing alternate sources of power, says Coyne. If you’re not the type to keep a generator at home (same), it’s a good idea to keep a good flashlight (or even headlamp) on hand, plus a lighter, matches, and candles or lanterns.

If you want to get serious and have the space for a generator, Coyne says, “I’m big on the solar ones, because they always have fuel.” His favorite is the Jackery, which looks like a big printer on wheels. “Solar panels still work on cloudy days; they’re not as efficient as sunny days, but they still work. You’re not dependent on storing fuel, and fuel does go bad. You have to put a fuel stabilizer in it, or your fuel will go bad.” Solar power can also fuel power banks, which can be used to charge phones and other devices.
How much water should I keep stocked?

You should keep extra water at home, according to all the experts I spoke to. Coyne, the survivalist, is on the more intense end. According to him, water should be distilled to kill microbes and particles (either in pots on the stove or in a countertop water distiller), put through a reverse-osmosis device, then put through a Brita or similar carbon filtration. Then you store it in a 55-gallon water barrel and treat it with a water stabilizer. When asked what a person who will never do all that might try instead, Coyne concedes that bottled water is okay, though it doesn’t last forever, and isn’t impervious to contamination, long-term. He recommends replacing it yearly.

As for ideal quantities, while the Red Cross advises one gallon of water per person per day, Bedford suggests aiming for two gallons per person per day, plus more for pets. She adds that it’s worth remembering the global crisis we all lived through not so long ago. “During COVID, people could still get water,” she says. “I ask myself, Lisa, Do you really need to have multiple 50-gallon water drops? That would be for a drought.”
What about food? Do I need to learn canning?

Though there’s been a lot of innovation in dehydrated food over the last decade, Coyne warns that going that route will cut into your water supply. It’s wiser and more cost-efficient to stick with a week or two’s worth of canned goods. “You don’t have to have the yummiest stuff,” he says. “You can get the cheapest brands.”

By this point, I’m wondering where all this stuff is supposed to go. Coyne insists that people living in one-bedroom apartments have more storage space than they might realize, at least for little stuff, if not a full generator. “You have the space under the bed, you have under your couch,” he says. “One small couch that holds three people — you can put, like, 200 pieces of canned food under that.”
Do I need to buy an atlas? Or a local map, at least?

Like many millennials, there was a time I knew how to get around without looking at my phone, but it has long since passed. (Even then, I was printing out a lot of MapQuest directions.) If Google Maps were to go out, it might be helpful to keep an atlas on hand, Coyne says. “There are still Thomas Guides around, like the ones you find in gas stations,” he says. “But with a large-scale grid disruption, you’re mostly dealing with a shelter-in-place-type thing.” With fires or floods, you’d flee, but if it all goes down, internet wise, you’re more likely to be stuck at home. “A grid event might not necessarily make your domicile unlivable,” Coyne explains. “It just doesn’t have power, or water, or things like that.”
Should I keep cash on hand? If so, how much?
For the short term, Coyne recommends setting aside about $100 per person in your household. “$300 to $500 can get a lot of food and gas,” he adds.

Moore agrees that a modest stash has practical uses but warns against going overboard. “Taking your money out of your bank account and keeping it in your house makes you a greater target for theft,” he says.

Even without access to online banking, most of us probably shouldn’t worry about whatever bills are set to autopay or otherwise electronically transferred. “You can’t really go to PG&E and be like, ‘Here’s $200 in cash,’” Coyne says. As far as he’s concerned, you can worry about all that later.
Should I get a battery or hand-crank radio for emergency news?

If it works for your budget: Sure, it can’t hurt. When shopping for a portable radio, Coyne says, “You want AM, FM, shortwave, and NOAA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. What that does is constantly give you updates to the weather in your location, but it’s also used for emergency communications in the event of a major emergency.” He likes this one by Kaito. It also comes with a flashlight, reading lamp, and five sources of power, including a hand crank.
How can I keep in touch with my family if the phones go down?

In most cases of an emergency, Bedford says some form of technology should still be available. “It’s like when you’re in an airplane, and you can use WhatsApp or internet-based messaging, but not iOS text messaging,” she says. For families and loved ones you need to keep in contact with, she recommends making a shared Google doc, where people can update each other as to their whereabouts if necessary. (That’s also a great place to list any planned disaster-meetup spots the family has, as well as other in-case-of-emergency info.)

Bedford also likes the Zello app, which turns your phone into a push-to-talk (PTT) walkie-talkie, and enables free communication using any Wi-Fi hotspot with or without cell service. If all tech is truly unavailable? “Then you’re just talking about pigeons,” she says. Talking through a meeting place ahead of time is your better bet.
What if the grid fails and my kid is in school?

Every school is different, so Bedford recommends having a chat with your kids’ teachers about general emergency preparedness. “I once had a principal tell me their rule was that, no matter what happens, they cannot let people claiming to be a parent or a guardian just show up to grab a kid,” she says. “That would be a nightmare, so you need to know the requirements in advance.”

For younger kids especially, school is a relatively safe place to sit through shorter-term emergencies like storms. “I would tell the kids: ‘If there’s a big storm, or if the power goes out, your teachers tell you exactly what to do,’” Bedford says. “‘Just know that I’m here, and they’re going to keep you safe, and when it’s safe for me to come get you, I will.’”
What if I’m a billionaire with access to the most advanced prepperism money can buy?

The ultrawealthy love to hoard, including their penchant for building underground doomsday bunkers in which to live out the end times (or, at least, that’s their hope). But even the world’s richest rich are dependent upon other people for survival, says Moore. “No man is an island. There are billionaires who try to build their own compounds that are completely off the grid, and even then, I’m not sure that’s a world that’s going to be very sustainable,” he adds. There’s a silver lining for you!
Are tech outages only going to get more frequent?

This almost certainly isn’t the end of large-scale outages, according to Moore. “Many companies have built infrastructures that prioritize efficiency over resilience, which has led to a lot of these brittle failures,” he explains. “We’re seeing multiple trends that all point towards increased outages.”

As for the much-speculated-upon role of AI in technological failures, Moore says it’s not necessarily the “rogue AI” takeover we imagine. “AI tools make it much cheaper and easier to find bugs and vulnerabilities in software, and that can be exploited,” he says. Even well-intentioned uses of these tools can cause issues. “If you find a bug or a vulnerability, you have to issue a patch, which means going through a process to update the systems.” Every time you do that, there’s a chance of an outage or disruption to service, he says.

Moore cautions against reading too much of a “trend” into the past week. “The human mind wants to extrapolate that something much worse is happening,” he says. “It could very well just be that we had this series of independent events that all compressed together, and they’ll spread out again in the coming months and years. That’s as likely, or more likely, than further acceleration.”

Moore also points out that many prepper tactics risk creating more problems than they solve, particularly when they result in overspending. “The cure is worse than the disease,” he says. The best way to be sensible in the face of an uncertain future? Not draining your savings account on fishing line and hazmat suits.

items.title: Guess Who’s Back?
items.description: It turns out that if your board loves your vibe, you can just come back to work after allegedly having affairs with two of your employees and an accused Chinese spy. After vaguely addressing widespread reports of his infidelity — one of which was recently refe
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: It turns out that if your board loves your vibe, you can just come back to work after allegedly having affairs with two of your employees and an accused Chinese spy. After vaguely addressing widespread reports of his infidelity — one of which was recently referred to by Senator John Kennedy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy” — Jensen Huang was able to overcome all of that and was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday.

According to a statement from the AI-chip company, Nvidia’s board of directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back after he resigned two weeks ago amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs. The board was, apparently, “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” That’s an interesting choice of words, considering that Huang’s “lack of candor” was cited as one of the reasons the board accepted his resignation during an Nvidia all-hands meeting earlier this month. I guess Huang has adjusted his level of candor appropriately over the past few weeks.

Huang said that he is “honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution.” He thanked board chair Harvey C. Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress for leading the company during his little sabbatical. Huang added that he is approaching his comeback with “the greatest humility and renewed commitment.” “Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family,” he said. “I can’t wait to get back to work.”

This is, above all else, an inspiring story for all men. You guys can really get away with anything. If you’re a man and you’re really important at your job, feel free to do something totally wild today. It won’t matter! If you’re a woman, I cannot offer the same advice. Maybe one day your boss will have to step down and you’ll get to be CEO for two weeks during the lowest moment in your company’s history. He’ll come back, but you’ll still get to put “Interim CEO” on your résumé.

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

paragraphs: Happy (almost) Thanksgiving break to all. You’re so close to slamming that laptop shut for the long holiday weekend … you can do it! I will unfortunately not be slamming my laptop shut because it’s also almost Cyber Weekend. But luckily for you, that means myself and my fellow Cut editors are going to be sharing all the best Black Friday deals you won’t want to miss. We’ve been working overtime for weeks, searching high and low for the best early Black Friday deals across all categories — from beauty and fashion to home and tech.
Read on for the best deals from Amazon, Sephora, Levi’s, Walmart, and more. Some sales aren’t live quite yet, but check back here throughout the week to take advantage of them when they start.
Stock up on essentials or splurge on luxury beauty
The Best Black Friday Beauty Deals
Bezos never skips a sales event, which is great news for those of us who like to save money on K-beauty and everyday essentials, like UGGs and Bose headphones.

The K-beauty skin-care brand behind our beauty writer Carol Lee’s favorite skin-barrier cream is up to 45 percent off on Amazon.

Take 20 percent off Laneige skin care products and 25 percent off the brand’s viral lip products through November 30.
Get up to 65 percent off sleep accessories and silk hair scrunchies.
Get 25 percent off site wide at Ouai through December 1, and from November 27 to December 1, get a free four-pack of air fresheners with any purchase.
The namesake beauty brand of Dua Lipa’s makeup artist, Katie Jane Hughes, is offering 20 percent off site wide this week.

Through November 30, take 20 percent off everything (including bundles) sitewide at Summer Fridays. And from November 27 to November 30, the brand is also offering a gift with purchase: Receive a complimentary Cherry Lip Butter Balm when you spend $100 or more.
Therabody’s biggest sale of the year is here. Save on so many of the brand’s best-selling devices, including the Theragun and the TheraFace Depuffing Wand.

The Best Black Friday Fashion Deals
