items.title: Naomi Osaka, Amber Glenn, & 8 More Athletes Who Defined Sports In 2026
items.description: A true game changer makes a lasting impact. In women’s sports this year, there were plenty of athletes who did just that and made it look easy. Maybe it was by signing a record-breaking contract that laid the groundwork for the future of their sport. It could’
items.author: Alexis Morillo
paragraphs: A true game changer makes a lasting impact. In women’s sports this year, there were plenty of athletes who did just that and made it look easy. Maybe it was by signing a record-breaking contract that laid the groundwork for the future of their sport. It could’ve been by uplifting their competitors in an Olympic event with a reputation of pitting women against one another. At times, changing the game can be about simply spreading love during a specific moment in time or being the best at something unapologetically yet with humility.

This year, women in sports showed all of the above — and then some. Rookies and veteran players alike broke WNBA shooting records. Athletes who had sworn off their sport returned to it and soared. There were exciting moments on the scoreboards and in the fan cams that spread afterward online. And that energy is sure to exist in 2027 and beyond. But before then, it only feels right to honor the women who made this year in sports so memorable.
Below are 10 superlatives of 2026 that showcase the variety of ways female athletes have made an impact this year.

Naomi Osaka has long served groundbreaking looks on the court (who can forget the bedazzled Labubu?). This year, she transcended the game when she started working with the legendary Law Roach, best known as the mastermind behind Zendaya's red carpet looks, before the 2026 US Open in August. Her range of outfits throughout the tournament included threads from Thom Browne, Monse, KidSuper, and more.

Personal stylist Aricia Symes says tennis inherently allows for special fashion moments in a way many other sports do not, since players enter the court by themselves rather than with a team. “There's this wonderful, almost runway-like moment when a player emerges onto the court with all eyes, and cameras, on them,” she says. “Naomi isn't bringing fashion to a sport that never cared about clothes. She's pushing the boundaries of a sport that has always cared about them.”
Her looks, though all different — from billowing layers on power suits to an Allen Iverson tribute — brought the drama.
“She can make this extraordinary entrance, remove the dramatic layers, and then get down to playing world-class tennis,” Symes says.
Power Couple: Hilary Knight & Brittany Bowe

Hilary Knight, captain of the United States Women’s Hockey team, met Team USA speedskater Brittany Bowe during the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics. Four years later, their love story came full circle when Knight proposed to Bowe during the 2026 Winter Games in Milano Cortina.

“I remember the day [they got engaged] was a really exciting day. People came in and were talking about it at the bar,” says Chandler Robertson, a co-founder of Blazers, a women’s sports bar in Brooklyn. “The Olympics are obviously centered around pride in your country and it was really cool to have a queer couple representing during this time in the United States.”
During this year’s Games, two-time medalist Bowe skated her last race for Team USA and Knight helped the women’s hockey team bring home the gold.
“Celebrating women in sports and getting to see queer representation felt really special,” Robertson says.
Most Likely To Break A Record: Trinity Rodman

At 23 years old, forward Trinity Rodman made history after signing a record-breaking contract with the Washington Spirit in January. It’s worth over $2 million annually, including bonuses, and ended several months of the star player’s free agency. Her contract was created in line with the High Impact Player Rule (colloquially referred to as the “Rodman Rule”), which is an official NWSL salary cap exception that helps teams recruit and retain talent.
“It feels amazing, I'm very happy, I'm very blessed," Rodman previously told the media after signing.

USWNT head coach Emma Hayes also said of the historic contract: “When I see a landmark moment like yesterday, of course I'm happy for Trin. But I'm happy for the whole, because it means that the people are investing, one; and two, I'm always about ‘let's keep raising the bar.’ I think it's a monumental achievement for NWSL.”

"I lost a lot of my motivation. I was barely going to the rink, not doing off-ice [workouts]. Then I grew a lot and got injured quite a bit,” Alysa Liu told the press in 2022 when she announced her retirement from competitive figure skating at age 16.

Two years later, she rewrote her story. Liu returned to the ice in 2024 — for the first time taking control of her training schedule, diet, and costumes — leading to a 2025 World title and an exceptional 2026 Olympic run. Her women’s individual free skate performance to Donna Summer’s “MacArthur Park” helped earn her a near-perfect total score of 226.79 and a gold medal — the first for the United States in that event in 24 years.

Off the ice, she became a sensation, too, with people trying out her signature striped hair for themselves and Zara Larsson’s reaction to her Exhibition Gala skate to PinkPantheress’ “Stateside” going viral.

“This comeback, whether it was the music that she was skating to, the things she wore, how she presented herself... It just very much felt like she was saying, ‘If I'm going to come back and un-retire, it's going to be on my terms,’” says sports content creator Aliyah Funschelle. “It was really empowering, especially as a woman, to see someone being able to do things the way they want to.”
Olivia Miles, Minnesota Lynx guard and 2026 Kia Rookie of the Year, was a force on the court and brought levity to the league.

Whether she was curled up in a ball mid-possession or mopping the court herself, Miles’ delightfully unserious nature was fodder for funny moments that made their way into TikTok edits throughout her first season in the W. Sure, her dancing during games and high-fiving her opponents after they blocked her were fun moments to watch, but the numbers she put up this year — breaking the all-time WNBA rookie single-season scoring record with 790 points (previously held by Caitlin Clark in 2024 with 769 points), for one — are an exciting sign for her future in the league.
Most Viral Social Media Moment: Kelsey Pfendler

If you were online between May 21 and July 4 of this year, you likely came across Kelsey Pfendler’s story. She broke the solo row record from California to Hawaii, completing her trek in just 43 days (the previous record was 52 days, and held by a man) and documented much of her journey on her TikTok account with over 1.8 million followers.
According to TikTok, toward the final leg of her journey from June 28 to July 4, TikTok posts across the United States using the hashtag #kelseyrowingtracker grew more than 74 times.
Most Likely To Succeed: Eileen Gu

Eileen Gu, the most decorated women’s freestyle skier in Olympic history, charmed fans new and old during her 2026 Olympic run. Viewers loved her post-event interviews during the Games, with interviewers praising her eloquence as well as her poise and wit when asked if winning silver felt like losing a gold. “The two medals lost situation, to be frank with you, I think is kind of a ridiculous perspective to take,” she responded at a press conference.

“She says the quiet things out loud. I think that's a very great quality to have, especially in women's sports. You want an athlete who not only speaks out, but articulates herself in such a way that really gets heard and felt,” says Funschelle.
Dynamic Duo: Gisele & Alyssa Thompson

Sisters Gisele and Alyssa Thompson became the third pair of sisters to be named to the USWNT (after the Fairs and the Mewises), but their side-by-side soccer story didn’t start there. They also became the first sister duo to combine for a goal when Alyssa assisted Gisele’s first professional goal during a May 3, 2025, game with Angel City FC. Gisele previously told Bustle that moment was “surreal.”

“To see two siblings playing at the highest level is just such a fun thing,” Funschelle says. “They seem so down to earth and even though they're literally competing at the very highest level, they still seem just like your average pair of siblings.”
The duo was named in the USWNT training camp announcement ahead of the 2027 World Cup, so there may be more historic Thompson sister moments to come.
In 2024 and 2026, Wilson scored 1,000 points during the regular season, making her the only WNBA player to do so twice.

“It's really exciting to be able to be a sports fan in the time of A’ja Wilson,” Robertson says of the five-time WNBA MVP winner. “Women's sports have had such incredible trailblazers with careers that we’re very lucky to be able to look back on, but at the same time we’re always like, ‘If only the fandom and the money had been there behind them.’ I think that's what watching A’ja Wilson feels like.”
“She's the all-around person, on and off the court, who is so respected by fans and the players,” says Meg, the artist behind the viral WNBA fan account @wnbaart. “There is no weak point for her.”

Meg also noted Wilson’s success off the court, particularly the popularity of her Nike collabs and how the league’s fan base loves her allyship. “Every year in June, she has the most incredible Pride cakes made for her gay teammates. It shows what a great teammate and a person she is on top of her being the best player we've seen, if not ever, in a very long time. I don't think you can find anyone who would dispute you on that.”
Biggest Cheerleader: Amber Glenn

Headed into the 2026 Milano Cortina Olympics, Amber Glenn was a top competitor for the women’s figure skating podium. But an invalid element during her short program performance was ultimately a costly error. Still, she rooted for her teammates with admirable grace. “I’m so proud of you,” Glenn told Liu during a hug after the final scores of the free skate, which won Liu an individual gold, were announced. When another competitor, Japan’s Kaori Sakamoto, got emotional after a tough run, Glenn told camera people to give her space.

“Having an example of someone like Amber who is incredibly competitive and talented, but who doesn’t let that get in the way of the general camaraderie of the sport, was such a great example,” Robertson says. “She showed that even if you don't end up on the podium, you can still be happy for other people.”

Off the ice, Glenn is known for speaking openly about her pansexuality and her experience with depression and anxiety to normalize the subjects for other athletes. She also supports the Trevor Project, a nonprofit for LGBTQ+ youth in crisis.
“A quote that I love to live by as a woman in sports is ‘we rise by lifting others,’” says Funschelle. “[Glenn] is such a positive person. The more she uplifts others, the more she's also ascending.”

items.title: How Barbara Kingsolver Wrote The Steamiest Scenes In Her New Book, ‘Partita’
items.description: When Barbara Kingsolver enters my Zoom room, she’s clad in a chunky gray cable-knit, cupping a warm mug between two hands, and standing at a desk in front of floor-to-ceiling mahogany shelves housing hundreds of books in every size and color. “These are my fic
items.author: Sophie Fishman
paragraphs: When Barbara Kingsolver enters my Zoom room, she’s clad in a chunky gray cable-knit, cupping a warm mug between two hands, and standing at a desk in front of floor-to-ceiling mahogany shelves housing hundreds of books in every size and color. “These are my fiction shelves,” she says, stepping back and gesturing proudly.

It’s an apt backdrop for the author who, in lieu of a formalized MFA program and writing classes, calls novels her teachers. Kingsolver has been a fixture on bestseller lists for over 30 years, and her 2022 novel, Demon Copperhead, landed the top slot on the New York Times readers’ pick best books of the 21st century list.

But before she was a Pulitzer and two-time Women's Prize for Fiction winner, Kingsolver says she was a spy. At 18, just months into her music coursework at DePauw University, she realized she “didn’t have the right stuff” to make it as a professional pianist. Waiting to see if her scholarship would transfer to the biology department, she observed her classmates as they struggled through grueling practices and the mounting expectation to make it.

“I learned how cloistered it is, how you have to just put all of your eggs into the music basket. You can't really let yourself be interested in much of anything else, including the daily news and the state of the world," says Kingsolver, 71. “Little did I know that 50 years later, I would be using that information.”

Livia Cable, the protagonist of Partita, Kingsolver’s 10th novel and 19th book, has this kind of singular focus. At present, middle-aged Livia is a piano teacher and wife of a dairy farmer in her rural Tennessee hometown. But when a phone call from a past lover calls her quiet life into question, Livia is forced to confront the choice she made when she was Livia Bohusz, an Appalachian college freshman on a piano scholarship.

Studying alongside wealthier peers at Indiana University, Livia is what Kingsolver describes as a “class migrant.” She learns to hide her Appalachian accent and lie about gaps in her formal training to earn respect from her teachers. While many of her classmates have safety nets to lean on, Livia is isolated in her fear that working as a concert pianist is her only way out from rural poverty. She balances school with work and lives off of hunks of government-supplied cheese, a scrappiness Kingsolver can relate to. “That sense of being an imposter, I carry to this day,” she says.

Sitting down to write Partita shortly after she turned in Demon Copperhead, Kingsolver set out to answer a question: Why do we need art? “It’s what Ann Patchett calls an ingredient in the pantry. My life has all these different experiences that I can pull out and use as ingredients once I decide what kind of soup I'm going to make,” she says. “It's not that I wrote about music because I knew about it, I wrote about music because I had interesting questions to ask about it and I had this information I could bring into the story.”

Living on a farm in southern Appalachia, Kingsolver is proud to come from “a culture of artists.” “It's mostly homemade things. We make quilts, we make music on the porch, we make our own art,” she says. “But art has been siloed, and there are a lot of rural and working-class people who may have internalized this kind of shame of thinking, ‘Well, that's not for me. I wouldn't feel comfortable going to a piano, a symphony concert, or an art museum.’"

At the same time, she pushes back against the idea that Southerners aren’t interested in pursuing so-called fine art. “In every rural place I've lived, I've known kids who want to play Bach, who just take to the piano like Livia did,” she says. “I think that we all should have access to this art because it's so helpful to be in touch with the most beautiful things that our gifted humans have made over the centuries to remind us of the greatness of human civilization.”

Traveling the country for her 20-stop book tour, she’s spoken in front of audiences that outnumber the population of her hometown of Carlisle, Kentucky (roughly 2,200). “It makes me feel really good about the state of reading in our country, and just the state of people's hearts,” she says.

After we speak, she’ll head to two final engagements. “I've got to do Raleigh and then Charleston. So the blue state of North Carolina and the blue state of South Carolina,” she says. “I’ll be celebrating the new South.”
Below, Kingsolver opens up about the books she’s loving right now and the ones that she turns to for inspiration.
Dolly: My Life and Other Unfinished Business by Dolly Parton
Right now I'm writing an obituary of Dolly Parton for the New York Times. So I'm reading all things Dolly Parton, including several of her own.
Labor: One Woman's Work by Dr. Mary Fariba Afsari

Afsari is an OB-GYN working in rural Oregon, and it is a story of the heroic work that medical care workers are doing to support women's reproductive health. The climate of today is like a war zone, and it's so moving. It's something that I think all of us should read to be more cognizant of how much we need to rethink the way healthcare is delivered in our country.
Miss Benson's Beetle by Rachel Joyce

I have just fallen in love with Rachel Joyce. A couple of years ago, she published a novel called Miss Benson's Beetle, which is both funny and heartbreaking and beautiful. I took that book on vacation and every member of my extended family read it. That's my recommendation because the teenagers loved it, the old people loved it, and the kids loved it.
Hamnet by Maggie O’Farrell

Often when I'm working on a particular scene, I'll remember a scene in a novel that I've read maybe even 10 years ago and reread it to find the juice. I'm looking for the technique that made it work, and then I can apply that.

There are some very steamy sex scenes in Partita. It's a story of young love, so of course it's going to be very sexual and it's going to be very sensual. It’s difficult because the language has been co-opted by pornography, so we have to find new language to write about sex.

I was trying to think about the most memorable sex scenes I've ever read that have really stayed with me. And I thought of two, and I went back and reread them both. One is in Hamnet when Will and Agnes had their first encounter and it's in an apple shed. The trick she used is we're not looking down at them on the floor against the wall of this apple shed. We're looking up at all these apples on the shelves and they're turning, just bump, bump, bump. All the apples are rotating in unison, and it's so sexy because it just puts you in the scene.
Snow Falling on Cedars by David Guterson

The other one that I read was David Guterson's Snow Falling on Cedars. It has a really beautiful and moving sex scene right in the middle, and it takes place in a hollow tree. It gave me that idea of, OK, go for an unusual place that has both a sense of privacy and a sense of exposure.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Exclusive: Ben Wang Says There's More To His 'Hunger Games' Character
items.description: Ben Wang is probably a bigger Hunger Games fan than you. No, really. When the 29-year-old actor was a preteen, he bought his copy of Suzanne Collins’ dystopian novel the day it came out, before it became a billion-dollar franchise.
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Ben Wang is probably a bigger Hunger Games fan than you. No, really. When the 29-year-old actor was a preteen, he bought his copy of Suzanne Collins’ dystopian novel the day it came out, before it became a billion-dollar franchise.

“I was a fan of Suzanne from her previous book series, Gregor the Overlander,” he tells Bustle. “For some people, it's a deep cut. For me, that's part of the canon. When I heard she was writing a new book, I was like, ‘Oh, is it... Are there rats and elves?’ And it was like, ‘No. It's a dystopian future.’ The concept was crazy to me at 11.”

After working on projects like American Born Chinese and the Mean Girls musical film, Wang nabbed a part in Hunger Games director Francis Lawrence’s 2025 film The Long Walk, calling it “one of the most artistically fulfilling experiences I've ever had.” Upon learning that Lawrence would adapt the new prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping, Wang hoped he would be considered for a role.

Although the director had read the manuscript, Wang couldn’t get an early copy of the book. “Even Francis was like, ‘It’s kept under lock and key.’ If you wanted to see it, it's in a vault, and you have to scan your thumb and give them your DNA. Then they clone you, and that clone gets to read the book, and then they shoot him,” he jokes.

On the book release day, Wang immediately identified with Wyatt Callow, a District 12 tribute whose family specializes in oddsmaking during the Games, and enters the 50th Quarter Quell alongside eventual victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada). “Wyatt is someone who, when you first meet him, especially through the eyes of Haymitch, is cold and calculated,” he says. “He's a gambler. He's an outcast. But you find out he's a lot more than that.”

As fans expect in the world of The Hunger Games, Wyatt eventually meets his demise. “Wyatt ends up doing something that is completely irrational, from the gut instead of from the head, which is what you would expect him to do,” he says. “That contradiction of human nature is compelling to me. Wyatt's true talent is perception. He's intelligent, but he’s very sensitive and has a big heart.”
Oddly enough, it wasn’t the first time Lawrence gave Wang’s character a heroic but gruesome death. “I hope it‘s a pattern,” he says with glee.

Naturally, filming his death came with equally gruesome circumstances. Wang and his castmates filmed the arena scenes on a remote UNESCO World Heritage Site in the mountains of Spain, making the cast feel as isolated as the actual tributes.

“It was awesome if you're the kind of actor that really likes grit. Jo was eating that up, and I was a little bit too. But you have to understand, it's kind of miserable,” he says, explaining how they had to slog through the mud and take rocky bus rides to set. “We showed up at our hotel the first day in the mountains. They had a paper bag with saltine crackers, a bag of nuts and olives, and brine. I was like, ‘Where's the nearest grocery store?’ And they were like, ‘It's two and a half hours away.’”

Wang has no regrets, though, crediting his co-stars Zada and Mckenna Grace for getting him through. “Thank God I had all of them around to keep me sane,” he says. “It felt like going to summer camp with your best friends. There's no adventure without a little bit of misery.”
I'm a tea guy. If I’m at a coffee shop, I like the chai latte. But otherwise, I prefer green tea.
What are the saved weather locations on your phone?
Los Angeles, where I am now, and New York, where I live. And there's Minnesota, which is my home. Oh, and Beijing, which is where my mom lives.
I'm a Virgo. I don't follow astrology much, which I'm told is very Virgo.
What is your favorite overused movie quote?
"Luke, I am your father.” But it’s not actually what Darth Vader says in Episode V. The quote's incorrect, so it makes me a little peeved when people use that as a shorthand for Darth Vader.
What was your favorite cartoon as a kid?
I came to the U.S. from China when I was 6. I learned English over the course of one summer by watching Cartoon Network nonstop. My favorite shows were Ed, Edd n Eddy and Powerpuff Girls.
What's one movie or TV show that you're currently obsessed with?

It's John Adams on HBO. It's one of the best miniseries ever made. It's niche. Everybody is turning off the broadcast now because they're like, "I don't care about the second president." But you want to know an actor that inspires me? Paul Giamatti. I hope I get to meet Paul one day.
Other than him, who is your celebrity idol?

I've had the privilege of working with so many of my heroes — Michelle Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, Jackie Chan. With each of them, I learned a new lesson about what it is to be an actor and how to operate through the industry with grace and dignity.
If you had to go on a reality TV show, what would it be?
Oh, God, I hate reality television. It scares me a lot. Maybe a cooking show, but one where I could be a judge, so I can just eat stuff and be like, "I don't like it."
What is your go-to karaoke song?
I just went out to karaoke last night with the cast, and I sang “Lovesick Blues” by Hank Williams. I also love “Vienna” by Billy Joel.
What's something that's been inspiring you lately?

My castmates, doing all this press with them. Jo, this is his first big thing. He’s handling all of this stuff with such playfulness, but he knows when to lock in. And Mckenna's been doing this since she was essentially in the womb. I don't know when her first credit was. It might have been an ultrasound on Grey's Anatomy, and apparently, she took direction great. To be in the room with these guys and watch them absolutely nail this thing, I didn't start working until I was older than they are now, so it's very inspiring to see.
What is something you would want people to say about you?

He lived a good life. He lived. He died. I don't know. I don't care what people say about... That's not true. I do care what people say about me, but I shouldn't care what people say about me, so say what you want, guys.

items.title: Kelly Rowland Has Been Taking Tina Knowles’ Beauty Advice For Years
items.description: Kelly Rowland Is Trying To Crack The Collagen Code
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: Kelly Rowland Is Trying To Crack The Collagen Code
The singer opens up about eczema, her blush obsession, and the drugstore mascara she swears by.

In Bustle’s Beauty Detail, we dive into the beauty bags of our favorite celebrities and talent for intel on the rituals that keep them glowing. Ahead, Kelly Rowland talks collagen-maxxing, blush blindness, and the beauty advice she got from Beyoncé’s mom.

Kelly Rowland has always been serious about her skin care. Even in her 20s, she wasn’t one to cut corners — something she credits to Tina Knowles. “My Mama T told me, ‘If you go to sleep with makeup on, that’s aging your skin 10 years,’” Rowland says. “I don’t know if it’s true or not, but I’ve never, ever done it since.”

When we get on Zoom, the advice seems to have served her well. Her skin looks incredible, but as Rowland tells me, it hasn’t always been so cooperative — even when she was doing everything right. After becoming a mom, she was diagnosed with eczema, which sent her down a rabbit hole of treatments and home remedies: prescription topicals, oatmeal baths, even a specific type of shea butter someone had recommended. “A lot of it worked, but temporarily, and then it just didn't anymore,” she says.

Now, as a partner with Ebglyss, a prescription treatment by Lilly, Rowland has a better handle on her eczema — which, in turn, has given her a healthier relationship with her skin overall. And at 45, that also means embracing the changes that come with aging, or “evolving,” as she puts it. “I'm just grateful, number one, for the skin I'm in and confident in the skin I'm in. I’m trying to preserve it, not in a way where I want to be younger — preserving it with time.”

First up on the agenda: collagen-maxxing. “I'm trying to figure out how to drink it, how to put it in a shake, how to do something,” Rowland says, laughing. Keeping her stress levels in check is another priority, especially when it comes to managing her eczema flare-ups. Her favorite way to unwind? When she’s not binge-watching Nobody Wants This, a 25-minute sauna session will do. “I come out of there, and you can ask me for anything, and I'll say yes,” she jokes.
Ahead, she takes Bustle through her go-to beauty products — from the sunscreen she wears every day to the blush that’s taken over her makeup routine.

“I swear by sunscreen, but it’s really tricky to find one that won’t break me out. I’m obsessed with this one and always keep it stocked. It has a little tint to it as well, so it's a nice start to my makeup routine.”

“I cannot live without Cécred’s Moisture Sealing Lotion. I use it not just for myself, but also [on] my babies. It locks in the very ends of the curl — everything. Also, the Hair & Scalp Balm. Those two are game changers.”

“I’ve been applying more blush than usual recently, inspired by one of my makeup artists, Esther Edeme. She set the trend so beautifully. Daiquiri Dip by Fenty is my go-to. It’s orange and just so pretty.”

“Bobbi Brown’s skin corrector stick in the shade Deep Peach has been a game changer for me. I always put a little moisturizer on, then the color corrector and Nars’ concealer over it — that’s my holy grail.”
“Some products just work better than others. It doesn’t matter what the price point is — if it works, I want it. I love drugstore mascara. My favorite is L’Oréal’s Voluminous. It’s a good buy.”

items.title: Exclusive: Leon Thomas Reveals He Almost Reprised His ‘Victorious’ Role
items.description: Leon Thomas Is Victorious In More Ways Than One
items.author: Gabrielle Bondi
paragraphs: Leon Thomas Is Victorious In More Ways Than One
The Grammy winner talks R&B music, his dream collaborators, and whether he'd ever reprise his Nickelodeon character.

It’s been quite a year for Leon Thomas. The 33-year-old musician and actor — who many might recognize as Andre from Nickelodeon’s 2010s hit Victorious — won the Grammy for Best R&B Album for his 2024 smash, Mutt, in February. Now, as 2026 comes to a close, he has even more to celebrate.

Just a little over a week after chatting with him at T-Mobile’s T-Mix House event in Los Angeles, Thomas picked up six more Grammy nods, including recognition for his 2025 EP, Pholks, and several high-profile collabs.

“I feel like there's always pressure in the room when you're trying to make music for people in this generation because everybody's a critic. But it was a blessing to be able to receive the Best R&B Album Grammy,” Thomas tells Bustle during the Nov. 5 event, reflecting on his win earlier this year. “To this day, I have to pinch myself when I see it at the house. It represents a lot of hard work, and a lot of no's before I got that wonderful yes with the Grammy board.”

Thomas seems to be on a big “yes” spree. Along with his new nominations, the artist performed at Lollapalooza this past summer and just booked a coveted spot in Coachella’s 2027 lineup. He also has a new album on the way and plans to take it on tour. Even with all that on his plate, it hasn’t stopped people from asking whether he’d ever return to acting.

“There have been a lot of people trying to get me back into it. I've been very focused on building my touring company, building my artistry,” Thomas says. “I want to make sure I finish this chapter properly before I start another one with acting again. It can be a lot to balance both at the same time.”
Below, Thomas opens up about exploring new themes in his upcoming music, his dream collaborators, and whether he’d ever revisit the world of Victorious.
Tell me about being part of T-Mobile’s T-Mix House event and working with the brand.

It's an amazing opportunity to find brand synergy. It's really tough sometimes to find brands that understand your music and you as an artist. It was fun working with them at Lollapalooza. I threw a little party at the festival, which was cool, and now we get to throw another one here in LA, where I live.
R&B has evolved over the decades. What are you experimenting with in the genre?

R&B definitely raised me, so it's a huge part of who I am as an artist. But what's great about how R&B is evolving these days is that people are bending genres more and more often in 2026, and I'm definitely one of the trailblazers who does my best to try to mix a little hip-hop, rock and roll, and other genres to create something that feels different and brand new.
Is there one genre or subgenre that you want to try out next?
Someday I would love to try to do an R&B jazz album. But my biggest thing is I still want to make sure that I'm making music that can reach the world and make hits.
In your last album, you sang about heartbreak. Are there different themes that you're looking to explore in your upcoming music?

I'm definitely looking forward to exploring deeper themes. This year I lost my stepfather, so I've been toying with a lot of different themes conceptually, from mortality to success, and the effects of survivor’s remorse. All of my co-writers have been helping me express myself in a way that's going to be amazing for the world to hear.
I'm sorry for your loss. I lost my dad too, so I'm excited to hear what you're working on because I've been looking for something that can speak to that grief.
I try not to hit it right on the nose, but I don't know. There are definitely a couple of records that are very personal to me.
Tell me a little bit about your approach to working and collaborating with other artists, like Baby Rose.

It's really fun. R&B can be a very competitive genre. One thing that I've been bringing to the game is that I like to collaborate. I like to have fun and make records with whoever, and it's been dope working with a lot of people I've looked up to over the years.
When I'm in the studio, I'm almost like a little kid. I'm very playful, and it's my happy place. So when artists come to create with me, they can feel that fun energy, and it shows in the records.
Is there an artist in particular that had you pinching yourself?

Yeah, I was working with Jazmine Sullivan recently. We haven't released anything we're working on, but I'm a huge fan of her voice, and she's so amazing. I was definitely pinching myself the whole time while she was doing her ad-libs and writing with me. It was a beautiful situation.
That's amazing. Do you have a dream collaborator?
I'd love to work with Beyoncé and Pharrell. I feel like one day it'll happen.
Looking back at Victorious, how do you reflect on that time and how you've evolved and grown since then?

I’m reminded of it every day because all of my castmates have done so many amazing things out there in the world. Today I was on Sunset Boulevard, and there was a huge billboard of Ariana Grande's new movie Focker-In-Law. It's so beautiful to see all of us find our way in this world. That can't be said about a lot of other casts from children's shows. We talk a lot, and I definitely celebrate that time period in my life because it's been the building blocks for who I am today.
Daniella Monet recently returned to playing Trina in Netflix’s new show, Hollywood Arts. Are you open to returning to the Victorious universe?

We talked about it. They actually had an episode ready for me, but I was on tour at the time, so it was literally impossible for me to go out there, shoot it, and get back on the road. But if I have a pocket of time for the next season, I'd love to come and do my thing.
You got your start on Broadway. Would you ever want to go completely full circle and act on stage again?

That's definitely been on my mind. It's no joke. It's a lot of hard work to get up there and to knock it out eight times a week. So I would definitely have to prepare myself for the brutal schedule that Broadway brings.
Of all the things you have coming up, what are you most excited for?

Honestly, I'm most excited for my new album coming out next year, and the ability to transfer that body of music to the stage and give people more than a show. I want to give them an experience, something that they remember for a lifetime.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Sagittarius Season Is Here — & It Will Bring Less Drama & More Function
items.description: Sagittarius Season Is Here — & It Will Bring Less Drama & More Function
items.author: Lisa Stardust
paragraphs: Sagittarius Season Is Here — & It Will Bring Less Drama & More Function

Adventure and curiosity will be at the forefront of our minds because we are experiencing the combustible nature of Sagittarius. On one hand, we will be restless, but on the other, we'll get everything on our to-do list done efficiently. The yearning to be honest, witty, and not bogged down by rigidity will consume our minds; however, we'll find it vital to keep a plan on the back burner so we don't get lost in the process of our joviality.

Uranus retrograde in Gemini opposes the Sun in Sagittarius on November 25th, the day after the Super Full Moon in Gemini. The vibes will reflect the uncertainty we are all feeling as we wrap up 2026. Collectively, it'll feel like instability and rebellion are happening on all fronts. We'll be a little edgier in how we express ourselves because we are exhausted by the same old existence and yearning for change; personally, we may see shifts in dynamics as we enter or exit relationships and change how we present ourselves to the world. Uranus calls us to embrace our personal freedom, which can lead to breakups or changes in our friendship circles. We may try a new fit or hairstyle to enhance our appearance and stand out from the crowd.

Another standout astrological aspect is that, for the first time in years, we aren't going to be dealing with a ton of Pisces energy, particularly Pisces in Saturn and Neptune. Previously, these planets brought confusion to the mix. Sagittarius season is going to get a dash of fiery passion from Saturn and Neptune in Aries, which are highlighting our desires. We are stepping up to the plate and asserting our goals. The caveat is that we’ll want to attain greatness and power ASAP without taking the necessary protocol. Rather than working our way to an amazing level of success, we’ll ask for it immediately. Basically, the fiery element brings no chill and patience.

To sum it up, Sagittarius season 2026 is about healing. We are manifesting a new way of being based on what has transpired in the previous months. This is the moment to plan for the future with a completely different vision than before.

All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.

My cart is already having an identity crisis. There are hot-pink running tights with five pockets for the version of me who has her Saturday miles mapped out, oversized Dance Studio pants for the version who considers a coffee walk with her husband a date, and a green ringer tee that makes me want to dress like I have a standing tennis match. (It might help to learn to serve first.)

The Define Jacket is an easy place to start, but the sleeper hit for me is the crinkle-nylon barrel-leg pant. I'd wear it with a slim tee and sneakers, then swap in a big sweater when it gets cold. And if you're shopping for someone else, the blue-trimmed canvas tote and the pink-and-cream Dual Pouch Wristlet are the kind of gifts I'd have to wrap immediately so I don't start using them myself.
Ahead, I've narrowed the early deals down to 12 picks I'd actually make room for, from the joggers I'd wear on a holiday flight to the marbled yoga mat I'd happily leave unrolled in my living room.

I’m the kind of person who reads the entire menu and orders fries. So when a vibrator has 30 settings, my first thought is, okay, but which one am I actually going to use? This is where Lily Allen's Love, Lily edit with Lovehoney makes things easier. Take the peach and the heart-shaped toys. With the Womanizer Peach, you can find the intensity you like and call it a night. With the Heart Duo, you can switch between air pulses and direct contact and see which one you’re in the mood for. I can see the appeal of both, depending on how much decision-making I have left in me by bedtime.

Allen had the rare opportunity to figure out her preferences before putting her name on anything. According to Lovehoney's press materials, the brand delivered a batch of toys to her hotel during her run at the London Palladium. She cleared the outlets so she could leave everything charging while she went to work. As tour stories go, it's refreshingly practical. If you're going to spend your evening onstage, it makes sense to have something waiting for you afterward that requires very little effort on your part.
Most of us are making this decision with a few browser tabs and an actual budget. So, which of Allen's six picks would earn its spot in your nightstand?

The Heart Duo is the one I'd look at if your shopping history consists of reading the words "clitoral suction," wondering whether you'd like it, and closing the tab. The heart separates into two magnetic pieces. One delivers pulses of air around the clitoris. The other uses a moving tip for direct contact. Having both gives you a way to compare two distinct sensations without committing to two separate purchases.

The Womanizer Peach is for the person who's happy to stick with air pulses and would like a little more say over how strong they feel. There are 14 intensity levels, and its charging stand gives it a designated place to live. If you already like air pulses and want to add vibration, the Womanizer Enhance let's you adjust the air pulses and vibration individually. That's the feature I'd consider paying more for. Once you know you like a particular setting, it's nice to be able to change one thing at a time.

The Pleasure Trip Wand has a broad head and a curved handle, which are the details I'd pay attention to here. A wand makes sense if you like vibration spread over a wider area or find it fiddly to hold a smaller toy in precisely the right spot. This one also has a flexible neck, so you have some room to change the angle as you go.

Then there's the Polka Dot Plug. If the pattern looks familiar, you may have seen the West End Girl USB, a piece of album merch shaped like the toy referenced on the record. The Lovehoney version is a rechargeable vibrating plug. The reference is a fun detail for fans who were already curious about this category. I'd give the dimensions more attention than the dots when deciding whether it belongs in your cart.

The Enjoy Advent Calendar includes a mini wand, a bullet vibrator, and a Womanizer Starlet 3, along with smaller accessories across 24 compartments. Before you buy it, ask yourself how many of those things you'd be excited to try on a random Tuesday. If you're interested in a few different toys, there's a case for the box. If you're mentally circling the mini wand, you've already narrowed the search. There's a particular satisfaction in knowing exactly what you want, even when the thing you want happens to come in peach.

The first thing I want to know when someone tells me they found a good deal on diamonds is what they mean by "good." Are we talking earrings I could buy with the budget I already set aside for a holiday gift or a tennis bracelet that requires a quick meeting with myself and my checking account? Both can be good deals. Only one is making it into my cart without consulting my husband.

So I took a look at Ring Concierge's lab-grown diamond collection with an actual dollar amount in mind. Here's what I found: You can get diamond studs for as low as $103 or a mini tennis bracelet from $558 during the brand's 30% off Black Friday deal.

I know that's a crazy good deal for fancy jewels. If you're wondering if they are natural or lab-grown diamonds, Ring Concierge sells both. So you can toggle back and forth to see the price point difference on some of the styles. We love a fiscally responsible baddie.

As for what I'd actually wrap up this holiday season? Well, the round studs are my pick for the person whose taste I know well enough to buy jewelry for but whose ring size remains a mystery. I'd go with the mini tennis bracelet for someone who wears the exact same watch every day and could use a little razzle-dazzle on their wrist. And if you've been dropping increasingly specific hints about a classic investment-piece your self, consider this your opportunity to send this story directly to you-know-who.
Ahead, shop the lab-grown diamond gifts I’d buy from Ring Concierge while they’re 30% off.

items.title: My dog had separation anxiety, I had PTSD. How did we cope?
items.description: I slip my feet into my sneakers, the laces pre-tied. My coat lies in the crook of my elbow. I slide my forearm through my purse strap and lift my keys off the entryway hook, the blades clinking ever so slightly. I wince and hold my breath, praying he didn’t he
items.author: Tracy Strauss
paragraphs: I slip my feet into my sneakers, the laces pre-tied. My coat lies in the crook of my elbow. I slide my forearm through my purse strap and lift my keys off the entryway hook, the blades clinking ever so slightly. I wince and hold my breath, praying he didn’t hear and won’t rush from the living room barking his orders, demanding I stay.

I’ve performed this routine hundreds of times, and yet adrenaline runs through my fingers like a current of electricity, paradoxically paralysing and mobilising me, as my knuckles bend around the door handle.
I tell myself go, though I’m afraid of the consequences.
You might be thinking that I live with an abusive spouse, but I don’t. I live with a dog who has separation anxiety. Some days I felt like his prisoner.

At 52, I haven’t lived a traditional woman’s life: I’ve never been married or close to engaged. I’ve never had kids, never raised a family. I’ve never allowed myself to fall in love, though not for lack of wanting.

When I was a teenager and my parents’ marital problems grew vocal and visible, relatives and friends stopped visiting. Isolation and silence overtook our home. I felt as if I’d been shipwrecked with my mother and father on a toxic abandoned island.
My mother told me she had nightmares about the house I’d grown up in

Behind closed doors, my father was abusive. Living in our house didn’t feel safe, but neither did leaving. I wanted to meet my peers for ice cream at Friendly’s, but the idea of going out gave me a stomach ache.
‘Go,’ my mother said, her glassy blue eyes dodging my gaze. ‘I’ll be fine.’

Decades later, long divorced and before her death, my mother told me she had nightmares about the house I’d grown up in: ‘He’s always there,’ she said, though my father had left and my mother had sold the house and moved. ‘I can never leave.’

Sometimes I’ll have this nightmare: I’m running from my childhood bedroom, down the stairs of our split-level suburban ranch, to the bolted front door, my heart pounding as my hand grasps, then turns, the doorknob. I pray I can escape.

When I was a girl, I begged my parents for a puppy, a companion. What I was really looking for was love. The answer was no, but my father said he could be my pretend dog. He got down on all fours and panted and pawed my body. He pushed me over and got on top of me. He assaulted me. My childhood dream of love, and family, died hard.
As an adult, I thought I could right my wrong.

Unpartnered and almost 47, during the acute loneliness of the COVID-19 pandemic I adopted a puppy: Beau was a sweet, smart, playful yellow Lab mix found under a drug house in Mississippi, though when we met I didn’t know his history. He was transported to New England, and came to live with me in my small city condo, just outside of Boston. I imagined he and I would do everything together: he’d be my jogging buddy, my backseat driver, my soul mate.
Going out on a date, or just to check the mail, was out of the question

But Beau barked and lunged at people on rollerblades and skateboards, so jogging together wasn’t feasible. In the car, when he saw scooter riders on our congested streets, he punctured the side door’s interior with his claws.

While I was at the supermarket, he self-destructed – barking, hyperventilating, and soiling himself. Going out on a date, or just to check the mail, was out of the question. My friends told me not to worry, just let him cry it out, like a baby. But Beau didn’t have run-of-the-mill separation anxiety. His, as I came to learn, was a severe clinical case requiring medication and intense training, which I diligently, doggedly pursued. I didn’t fathom that when everyone I knew had long left their pandemic quarantine, I’d still be living in relative isolation. My friends began to suggest I re-home Beau.
But I loved him. I couldn’t bear to give him up, or give up period.

Vowing to find a solution to what seemed an impossible problem, I hired a behaviourist trainer who specialised in separation anxiety. We spent 10 months on pre-departure cue desensitisation – approach the door; put on your coat; put on your shoes, pick up your keys – and 18 months on leaving the premises with Beau home by himself for a few seconds, working our way to 20 minutes.
The first time I left my building without Beau, the trainer watched the pet camera video feed for me from her home, so that I could take a walk without constant monitoring.

‘I’m at the bakery,’ I texted the trainer as the smell of coffee, chocolate croissants, pecan muffins and cheesecake brownies awakened my desire to be out in the world, to live. I felt anxious and eyed the clock. I might not have time to wait my turn. ‘There’s a line. Should I stay or go home?’
‘Stay,’ the trainer replied. ‘Beau’s calm. He’s lying on the floor with his eyes closed.’
For an entire year his anxiety regressed to the point I couldn’t leave him alone

When I reached the front of the line, I ordered not one but a handful of baked goods, thinking I’d better stock up since I wasn’t sure when or if I’d be able to come again. As the cashier handed me my bag-to-go, I felt as if I was both receiving an Olympic medal and robbing a bank.
A simple outing felt both extraordinary and forbidden.
Twenty minutes solo eventually led to 45.

Just when I thought we were almost home free, the unthinkable happened: while I was at work, Beau was attacked at doggie daycare. He needed emergency surgery to repair the physical damage. His emotional wounds were more complicated to heal, and for an entire year his anxiety regressed to the point I couldn’t leave him alone. He panicked with sitters, even people he knew well. Daycare was no longer an option. What was I going to do?
Beau’s assault and the aftermath called up my past, the event I thought I’d put behind me: the violation, the betrayal, the fear that I might never recover, that all hope, that love, was lost.
I didn’t know if I was in denial or just being persistent, but I didn’t quit. Love fuelled me.

Slowly, we climbed our way back to 20-minute absences, then one hour, then two hours. Through it all, I kept waiting for everything to fall apart again. I kept looking for the sign that said I didn’t deserve my dog or my freedom, or anyone’s love.

It’s March 2025, and I turn on the television and also a calming instrumental music station, having discovered that not one but two layers of sound help block out the city and building noises, and I leave the condo, locking the door behind me, walking down the hallway, toward the building stairwell, watching Beau via the pet camera video feed on my phone.
I pray Beau will self-soothe but as I get into my car, his barking escalates

Hypervigilance is a symptom of my PTSD, and Beau’s. I watch as he trots his 80-pound body to the entryway, which he usually does after I exit and before he returns to the couch, his ‘go-to’ spot, which he selected for himself over our almost four years of separation-anxiety training.

But today he doesn’t go to his spot. Something triggers him – a noise, a sense, something. He fixes his eyes on the door. His ears bend forward. He stands erect, staring in the direction of where I’ve gone. His jaw tightens.

I start sweating. I can’t return – I’m scheduled to teach a Zumba class at a local gym, my hard-won part-time gig that I did for fun and some extra money, a job I almost lost when I was housebound after we lost daycare. I pray Beau will self-soothe but as I get into my car, his barking escalates. I feel powerless to the destruction of what I’ve built, a house of cards caving in. I drive to work, my palms clammy. I’m afraid of an irreversible regression. I’m afraid of getting fined for a neighbour’s complaint. I’m afraid of seeing the truth: that I’m still caught in the grip of my past, and I don’t know the way out.

For years, I hid my body underneath layers of baggy clothes. When I was 40, I watched a Zumba class from a treadmill outside the dance studio, telling myself I could never do those moves, could never let go of my fear of being in the world – of being seen.

Now, 11 years later, I’m standing on the studio stage, wearing neon spandex pants and a lacy sports bra, shaking my booty, leading a Latin-inspired dance fitness class while my phone blinks with barking notifications. I don’t stop dancing, even as anxiety chews my gut, spitting out the question: how will I bear this disaster?

‘Disaster?’ my therapist will say at my next session. I know it’s an extreme word to characterise a dog anxiously barking. Did Beau harm himself or my home in my absence? No. Did anyone get hurt or die? No.
It will be the worst day for separation anxiety in two years, but it won’t be disastrous. By the time my class ends, the dog walker will have picked up Beau, texting ‘he’s fine’.

Later, I’ll review the footage: 21 barking incidents, one almost a minute long, the others 15-30 seconds. I won’t discount the three 7-10 minute intervals when Beau napped on the couch. I’ll remind myself that a really bad day doesn’t mean everything is lost.
After 1,000 separation anxiety sessions, I stopped training Beau and started living.

items.title: The house my father built was resilient and rickety, like him
items.description: I watched the excavator eat into my childhood home one bright fall. Its steely fangs bit into the cedar my father had nailed in more than four decades earlier. Windows burst inward. A slanted roof buckled. One wall heaved before folding into another, disappear
items.author: Henrick Karoliszyn
paragraphs: I watched the excavator eat into my childhood home one bright fall. Its steely fangs bit into the cedar my father had nailed in more than four decades earlier. Windows burst inward. A slanted roof buckled. One wall heaved before folding into another, disappearing in plumes of sawdust, glass and sheetrock.

I expected grief. I awaited a distinctive pain that comes only from watching the place that held your formative memories disappear into a pile of timber and insulation. But instead, I felt relief. Watching the structure come down meant seeing the building that organised my inner life begin to fade.

My father called the house a refugee. He meant it as a joke, though not entirely. Like him, it appeared foreign in a town where families had lived for generations. Built on pilings above the marshes of Broad Channel, a narrow island in Jamaica Bay on the edge of New York City, it looked as though it landed there by chance.
He built it in the early 1980s after spotting a burned-out lot on his way to Rockaway Beach. Where others saw a charred garage and overgrown, wheat-coloured grass, he saw possibility.
Soon, he recruited fellow eastern European immigrants and paid them in cash, six-packs of Coors Extra Gold and Marlboros. Together, they built a three-storey house with a slanted roof.

Nothing was quite straight. Tiles never lined up. Rain always found a way inside. During winter, without central heating, rooms warmed only with space heaters while elsewhere you could see your breath. The house squealed in high winds and shivered through nor’easters.
We retreated upstairs as if on a lifeboat while the house swayed on its pilings
The birdhouse-like structure was never beautiful, but it was well-constructed and refused to surrender to its surrounding elements. Whenever a big storm hit, it proved its strength.
My father fit this same resilient archetype.

He’d spent his earliest years moving through refugee camps in postwar Germany after his family fled what is now western Ukraine. His six brothers and sisters moved through seven refugee camps in five years. They slept in divided classrooms as ‘displaced persons’. My father grew used to hunger while his parents struggled to survive. My grandmother, Kunegunda, would smuggle her silverware into each camp while my grandfather, Ignacy, would cradle his vodka-bootlegging gear as a moveable business. They both held on to what little they could, convinced they might have to leave again tomorrow.

The United States promised a stability my father’s family had never known. Yet he never trusted this belief. Ever since arriving in the US, he relied on chaos over peace, endurance instead of comfort. The house he built reflected this mindset.

During one nor’ easter in the early 1990s, bay water flooded the first floor of the house while wailing winds rattled the windows so violently I thought they would implode. We retreated upstairs as if on a lifeboat while the house swayed on its pilings. Long after the storm passed, I lay awake listening to the building judder in the darkness.
Looking back, the house came with two competing realities: it showed me wonder while teaching me to expect instability.

I remember the seasons most. In summer, the home became a treehouse hovering over the lapping water. My sister and I fed swans, netted blue crabs, and learned to windsurf. In winter, we laced on skates and crossed the frozen channel to the nearby Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge where we spotted greater snow geese with our golden retriever, Blondie, slipping and sliding his way along the ice.

When my sister and I returned from our winter adventures, my mother made us hot chocolate while my father poured himself a vodka. My mom drank wine and played Simon and Garfunkel’s live concert from Central Park on the tape deck as we sat thawing by the fireplace.
The place felt alive and I loved it severely. It also felt as though it might come apart at any moment and riddled me with worry
‘This is Xanadu,’ my father liked to say. On the rickety, water-warped dock overlooking the bay, he would insist: ‘You can travel anywhere from here.’
The entire place felt alive and I loved it severely.
It also felt as though it might come apart at any moment and riddled me with worry.

Years later, the writer Andrew Solomon put words to what I felt. ‘Nirvana occurs when you not only look forward to rapture, but also gaze back into the times of anguish and find in them the seeds of your joy,’ he wrote in Far from the Tree: Parents, Children and the Search for Identity (2012). ‘You may not have felt that happiness at the time, but in retrospect it is incontrovertible.’

My mother tried to make the house feel steadier than it was. She’d grown up in Montreal, had studied art, travelled widely, and met my father by chance in Mexico while sailing from Portugal. She filled the crooked rooms with colour, music and food from places my father only imagined visiting. She introduced me to Nina Simone, French, and Campari. She rolled sushi on the kitchen counter, and painted the walls in vivid shades while my father disappeared with his brother to hunt in Connecticut. Whenever he embraced disorder, she responded with a cool serenity.

On Friday nights, after I started university, I would take the A-train from Manhattan to see my father. We’d sit by the fireplace drinking vodka while the cherry wood snapped over old newspaper in the fire. A cigarillo rested between his fingers, filling the room with its sweet and bitter scent.
One winter evening, he stared into the flames longer than usual.
‘My father wanted to get rid of me,’ he said.

A story followed about him being sick on a train in Germany while transferring camps. His father thought an unhealthy child would end their chances of emigrating, but his mother saved him from being thrown off the train. It was the closest I ever saw him to crying.
Compared with his childhood, mine was easy. But kids don’t compare their lives with history they didn’t live through. They compare it with their homes.

My family’s breaking point came during that first year of college. My mother had been diagnosed with breast cancer. On Christmas Eve, an argument erupted that ended with a shattered glass table. Pierogies slid across the floor. Wine-hued borscht bled into the carpet. Before midnight, my mother packed her things and left.
I knelt on the floor gathering shards of glass while my father sat near the fire, a cigarillo glowing between his fingers.
Without looking at me, he said: ‘Your mother wanted to throw you in the garbage when you were born.’
The words felt pent up and and arrived like a gut punch.

Pain like this can change form but often carries import for years. Psychologists now recognise that trauma can even extend beyond a single lifetime. This transmission occurs through emotional patterns and parenting styles. It can happen in the way a man treats his home and those who reside within it. It can transpire in how he transfers pain to his own child.
I didn’t recognise I was still staring through the scuffed-up windows of my father’s house

Looking back, I’m not sure if he was trying to wound me as much as connect. The rejection he felt as a child had become part of a dialogue through which he was forced to understand love, disappointment and family. He handed me a pain that voyaged across generations. It journeyed through wars, triumphs and tragedies until it landed near a shattered dinner table in Queens that Christmas Eve.

I visited, I awaited the worst, even when nothing happened. I mistook frenzied caution for astute awareness. I thought staying alert could prevent the next disaster. Over time, such experiences can produce what psychologists call hypervigilance, a heightened sensitivity to threat. The neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett has described the brain as a prediction organ, continually using past experiences to anticipate what will come next. Environments play a central role. At home, I was always on the lookout for the next calamity or volatile indiscretion. This habit would follow me for years after leaving Broad Channel. I expected relationships to fracture, success to dissolve, good fortune to reverse. Moments of happiness often carried a wary mistrust. I assumed this was a clear view of the world. What I didn’t recognise was I was still staring through the scuffed-up windows of my father’s house.

Wedged between Howard Beach and the Rockaways, Broad Channel existed in a perpetual negotiation with its surrounding waters that acted as both a threat and a neighbour. Every storm seemed capable of redrawing the map; every stunning sunset promised a celebration for the eyes.

When Hurricane Sandy tore through the island in 2012, things changed. Five feet of saltwater poured into my father’s house. The dock splintered. Furniture floated before setting into a thick grey sludge. I drove to the island first as a journalist covering the storm and then as a son trying to salvage what remained, carrying waterlogged boxes to the curb, and rescuing family photos.

The house had survived again but there was a shift. Around the same time, my father’s health began to fail. A quintuple bypass became stents that turned to medications he resisted taking. Slowly, a frailer version of the man who’d once built an impossible house with his own hands would greet me when I visited.
The room where Christmas exploded was gone. I stood where the fireplace once was

Buckets appeared beneath new leaks, instead of caulking. Shingles went unreplaced. Whenever I did work on the house, I would come back to see more leaks and more lost shingles to replace. Both the house and the man seemed engaged in a battle with time and its environmental pressures. Both refusing to surrender, and each losing more ground each day.

My father died of heart failure in late 2023. The house sat empty through a lengthy probate while vandals stripped the home of copper wiring, smashing windows and looting what they could. After years of storm damage, the city deemed it unsafe and ordered an emergency demolition.
Two years later, the house still stood, hovering defiantly over the bay even as it was getting torn down.

I gripped a cigarillo like the ones my father smoked. While the house broke off in pieces, I saw Blondie barking at the snow geese. My mother laughing at the bright yellow she painted the kitchen. My sister and I balling bagel dough to feed swans. My father shirtless telling stories of Germany from his water-logged Xanadu.

By late afternoon, there was nothing left of the structure except industrial trash heaps full of memories. The room where Christmas exploded was gone. I stood where the fireplace once was. The marsh had grown peaceful. Without the house, Jamaica Bay seemed larger, as if the horizon zoomed in.

I waited for the familiar tightness in the chest, the racing of the mind. I lit the cigarillo. The tide was about to rise again across the marsh. Planes climbed into the chalky blue sky from JFK. I paused for heartache but something else came. I rolled my shoulders, exhaled a cloud of smoke, and felt an unexpected release.
As the sun hovered, for the first time I could remember, I wasn’t bracing for the next storm.

I expected grief. I awaited a distinctive pain that comes only from watching the place that held your formative memories disappear into a pile of timber and insulation. But instead, I felt relief. Watching the structure come down meant seeing the building that organised my inner life begin to fade.

My father called the house a refugee. He meant it as a joke, though not entirely. Like him, it appeared foreign in a town where families had lived for generations. Built on pilings above the marshes of Broad Channel, a narrow island in Jamaica Bay on the edge of New York City, it looked as though it landed there by chance.
He built it in the early 1980s after spotting a burned-out lot on his way to Rockaway Beach. Where others saw a charred garage and overgrown, wheat-coloured grass, he saw possibility.
Soon, he recruited fellow eastern European immigrants and paid them in cash, six-packs of Coors Extra Gold and Marlboros. Together, they built a three-storey house with a slanted roof.

Nothing was quite straight. Tiles never lined up. Rain always found a way inside. During winter, without central heating, rooms warmed only with space heaters while elsewhere you could see your breath. The house squealed in high winds and shivered through nor’easters.
We retreated upstairs as if on a lifeboat while the house swayed on its pilings
The birdhouse-like structure was never beautiful, but it was well-constructed and refused to surrender to its surrounding elements. Whenever a big storm hit, it proved its strength.
My father fit this same resilient archetype.

He’d spent his earliest years moving through refugee camps in postwar Germany after his family fled what is now western Ukraine. His six brothers and sisters moved through seven refugee camps in five years. They slept in divided classrooms as ‘displaced persons’. My father grew used to hunger while his parents struggled to survive. My grandmother, Kunegunda, would smuggle her silverware into each camp while my grandfather, Ignacy, would cradle his vodka-bootlegging gear as a moveable business. They both held on to what little they could, convinced they might have to leave again tomorrow.

The United States promised a stability my father’s family had never known. Yet he never trusted this belief. Ever since arriving in the US, he relied on chaos over peace, endurance instead of comfort. The house he built reflected this mindset.

During one nor’ easter in the early 1990s, bay water flooded the first floor of the house while wailing winds rattled the windows so violently I thought they would implode. We retreated upstairs as if on a lifeboat while the house swayed on its pilings. Long after the storm passed, I lay awake listening to the building judder in the darkness.
Looking back, the house came with two competing realities: it showed me wonder while teaching me to expect instability.

I remember the seasons most. In summer, the home became a treehouse hovering over the lapping water. My sister and I fed swans, netted blue crabs, and learned to windsurf. In winter, we laced on skates and crossed the frozen channel to the nearby Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge where we spotted greater snow geese with our golden retriever, Blondie, slipping and sliding his way along the ice.

When my sister and I returned from our winter adventures, my mother made us hot chocolate while my father poured himself a vodka. My mom drank wine and played Simon and Garfunkel’s live concert from Central Park on the tape deck as we sat thawing by the fireplace.
The place felt alive and I loved it severely. It also felt as though it might come apart at any moment and riddled me with worry
‘This is Xanadu,’ my father liked to say. On the rickety, water-warped dock overlooking the bay, he would insist: ‘You can travel anywhere from here.’
The entire place felt alive and I loved it severely.
It also felt as though it might come apart at any moment and riddled me with worry.

Years later, the writer Andrew Solomon put words to what I felt. ‘Nirvana occurs when you not only look forward to rapture, but also gaze back into the times of anguish and find in them the seeds of your joy,’ he wrote in Far from the Tree: Parents, Children and the Search for Identity (2012). ‘You may not have felt that happiness at the time, but in retrospect it is incontrovertible.’

My mother tried to make the house feel steadier than it was. She’d grown up in Montreal, had studied art, travelled widely, and met my father by chance in Mexico while sailing from Portugal. She filled the crooked rooms with colour, music and food from places my father only imagined visiting. She introduced me to Nina Simone, French, and Campari. She rolled sushi on the kitchen counter, and painted the walls in vivid shades while my father disappeared with his brother to hunt in Connecticut. Whenever he embraced disorder, she responded with a cool serenity.

On Friday nights, after I started university, I would take the A-train from Manhattan to see my father. We’d sit by the fireplace drinking vodka while the cherry wood snapped over old newspaper in the fire. A cigarillo rested between his fingers, filling the room with its sweet and bitter scent.
One winter evening, he stared into the flames longer than usual.
‘My father wanted to get rid of me,’ he said.

A story followed about him being sick on a train in Germany while transferring camps. His father thought an unhealthy child would end their chances of emigrating, but his mother saved him from being thrown off the train. It was the closest I ever saw him to crying.
Compared with his childhood, mine was easy. But kids don’t compare their lives with history they didn’t live through. They compare it with their homes.

My family’s breaking point came during that first year of college. My mother had been diagnosed with breast cancer. On Christmas Eve, an argument erupted that ended with a shattered glass table. Pierogies slid across the floor. Wine-hued borscht bled into the carpet. Before midnight, my mother packed her things and left.
I knelt on the floor gathering shards of glass while my father sat near the fire, a cigarillo glowing between his fingers.
Without looking at me, he said: ‘Your mother wanted to throw you in the garbage when you were born.’
The words felt pent up and and arrived like a gut punch.

Pain like this can change form but often carries import for years. Psychologists now recognise that trauma can even extend beyond a single lifetime. This transmission occurs through emotional patterns and parenting styles. It can happen in the way a man treats his home and those who reside within it. It can transpire in how he transfers pain to his own child.
I didn’t recognise I was still staring through the scuffed-up windows of my father’s house

Looking back, I’m not sure if he was trying to wound me as much as connect. The rejection he felt as a child had become part of a dialogue through which he was forced to understand love, disappointment and family. He handed me a pain that voyaged across generations. It journeyed through wars, triumphs and tragedies until it landed near a shattered dinner table in Queens that Christmas Eve.

I visited, I awaited the worst, even when nothing happened. I mistook frenzied caution for astute awareness. I thought staying alert could prevent the next disaster. Over time, such experiences can produce what psychologists call hypervigilance, a heightened sensitivity to threat. The neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett has described the brain as a prediction organ, continually using past experiences to anticipate what will come next. Environments play a central role. At home, I was always on the lookout for the next calamity or volatile indiscretion. This habit would follow me for years after leaving Broad Channel. I expected relationships to fracture, success to dissolve, good fortune to reverse. Moments of happiness often carried a wary mistrust. I assumed this was a clear view of the world. What I didn’t recognise was I was still staring through the scuffed-up windows of my father’s house.

Wedged between Howard Beach and the Rockaways, Broad Channel existed in a perpetual negotiation with its surrounding waters that acted as both a threat and a neighbour. Every storm seemed capable of redrawing the map; every stunning sunset promised a celebration for the eyes.

When Hurricane Sandy tore through the island in 2012, things changed. Five feet of saltwater poured into my father’s house. The dock splintered. Furniture floated before setting into a thick grey sludge. I drove to the island first as a journalist covering the storm and then as a son trying to salvage what remained, carrying waterlogged boxes to the curb, and rescuing family photos.

The house had survived again but there was a shift. Around the same time, my father’s health began to fail. A quintuple bypass became stents that turned to medications he resisted taking. Slowly, a frailer version of the man who’d once built an impossible house with his own hands would greet me when I visited.
The room where Christmas exploded was gone. I stood where the fireplace once was

Buckets appeared beneath new leaks, instead of caulking. Shingles went unreplaced. Whenever I did work on the house, I would come back to see more leaks and more lost shingles to replace. Both the house and the man seemed engaged in a battle with time and its environmental pressures. Both refusing to surrender, and each losing more ground each day.

My father died of heart failure in late 2023. The house sat empty through a lengthy probate while vandals stripped the home of copper wiring, smashing windows and looting what they could. After years of storm damage, the city deemed it unsafe and ordered an emergency demolition.
Two years later, the house still stood, hovering defiantly over the bay even as it was getting torn down.

I gripped a cigarillo like the ones my father smoked. While the house broke off in pieces, I saw Blondie barking at the snow geese. My mother laughing at the bright yellow she painted the kitchen. My sister and I balling bagel dough to feed swans. My father shirtless telling stories of Germany from his water-logged Xanadu.

By late afternoon, there was nothing left of the structure except industrial trash heaps full of memories. The room where Christmas exploded was gone. I stood where the fireplace once was. The marsh had grown peaceful. Without the house, Jamaica Bay seemed larger, as if the horizon zoomed in.

I waited for the familiar tightness in the chest, the racing of the mind. I lit the cigarillo. The tide was about to rise again across the marsh. Planes climbed into the chalky blue sky from JFK. I paused for heartache but something else came. I rolled my shoulders, exhaled a cloud of smoke, and felt an unexpected release.
As the sun hovered, for the first time I could remember, I wasn’t bracing for the next storm.

items.title: A screenshot is precious when my family in Iran is out of reach
items.description: It was one of those suspended moments – I sat still, my thumb scrolling across the screen. The strange thing is this: you know no one is online, no new messages, no new stories. And, still, you scroll, in hopes that something – anything – might confirm the wor
items.author: Elaheh Shabani Afarani
paragraphs: It was one of those suspended moments – I sat still, my thumb scrolling across the screen. The strange thing is this: you know no one is online, no new messages, no new stories. And, still, you scroll, in hopes that something – anything – might confirm the world you left behind hasn’t simply vanished.
Everything on my feed felt irrelevant – until, suddenly, it wasn’t.

I came across a cooking video my mother had liked before we lost the connection. Seeing her name beneath the post struck me, as if someone had brought news. My eyes filled. I read the recipe for pasta with white sauce in the caption. She must have saved it for one of those evenings when she didn’t know what to cook. I took a screenshot, as if I might need to return to it – something I didn’t want to lose: yadgari, a keepsake, a trace of her touch pressed into a screen.

After 10 years of living in India, my connection to home in Iran had settled into a rhythm. Each morning, I checked our family groups on the messaging app Telegram to see what had unfolded while I slept. During the day, a message from my mother, a brief pause in the flow of things, felt like a small gift.

At night, I scrolled through Persian Instagram – jokes, cooking videos, fragments of humour that make sense only in our language. I would laugh until I cried, then fall asleep with a quiet reassurance: somewhere, my world was still alive.

We had an almost-fixed time for a video call, the holy hour of 6 pm. My parents would already be there, waiting. Behind them, the red carpet framed on the wall; in front of them, a bowl of seasonal fruits. Sometimes my mother would say: ‘Add your sister.’
We spoke every day. Nothing new – just exchanging words, routines and meaning.
‘What did you cook today?’
‘Did you go to the bazaar?’
Nothing important. Everything important.
These calls – the pictures, voices, messages – were part of life, like tea

My father had established this unwritten rule: we had to talk every day, even if only for two minutes. He described it as a kind of dependency, a small but necessary interruption to the weight of his routine. Our conversations moved easily between memories, what we made of them, and laughter. Always laughter.

My mother’s connection to me was different. Our conversations were built from the small details of her day: what she cooked, what she cleaned, the news of a cousin or a neighbour. In return, I gave her the only thing I could: an audience. I listened to the rhythm of her life and offered my voice back to her: Khaste nabashi. ‘May you never be tired.’ In those moments, her daily work wasn’t just chores; it was a story we shared.
These calls – the pictures, voices, messages – were part of life, like tea, like the fading light of evening. We watched each other’s days unfold.
Then, almost within a few minutes, the flow stopped.

It was 28 February, a Saturday morning, project day at my child’s school in Bengaluru. I was holding my phone, recording my son’s presentation – already imagining sending it to my parents. Although I tried to stay present, my attention kept drifting back to the screen. For weeks, I had been checking updates and watching tensions rise in the Persian Gulf.
Then, on our family Telegram group, a message stopped me: Bacheha, jang shoro shod! ‘Guys, war has begun!’
At first, it felt unreal, like the many rumours that circulate in tense times. I checked state news channels. This time, it was confirmed. War had begun. Tehran was attacked.

I stepped out of the hall into the yard, searching for a corner of quiet. My eyes were already burning. I returned to the family group chat immediately.
