items.title: Joseph Zada Is Following in Some Very Big Footsteps
items.description: Joseph Zada would describe himself as a bit of a rebel. “More so than other people,” he clarifies. When asked for examples of his defiance, however, he gets coy, or more accurately, a little cheeky: “If I told you, I’d probably be in trouble.”
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: Joseph Zada would describe himself as a bit of a rebel. “More so than other people,” he clarifies. When asked for examples of his defiance, however, he gets coy, or more accurately, a little cheeky: “If I told you, I’d probably be in trouble.”

As he says this, his lips lift into a smirk, and his eyebrows rise slightly, giving his sharp blue eyes more room to draw you in. All he’s missing is a bomber jacket and a cigarette dangling from his mouth to become a modern James Dean. It’s an apt comparison, considering he just stepped into a role once played by the late heartthrob in Netflix’s new East of Eden adaptation.

Zada is making a habit of taking on roles originated by greats. This month, he stars as Haymitch Abernathy in the Hunger Games prequel Sunrise on the Reaping, playing the younger version of Woody Harrelson’s character.

When talking to Zada, it’s easy to see why director Francis Lawrence chose him to lead the prequel, based on Suzanne Collins’s fifth book in the popular series. Zada is suave, but in a way that feels natural, not manipulative or artificial. His golden curls fall haphazardly across his forehead as he gets wrapped up in a point he’s trying to make with that mesmerizing Australian lilt, but he always concludes his thought with a smile and a direct look into your eyes.

That charm is just as perceptible in Zada’s portrayal of a 16-year-old Haymitch. Fans first met the character through Harrelson, who played him in the original four films as a browbeaten, cynical middle-aged man more interested in getting drunk on the Capitol’s dime than supporting Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss or Josh Hutcherson’s Peeta. But the Haymitch of Sunrise is worlds away from Harrelson’s depressed and snarky alcoholic. Zada’s Haymitch is in love (and sober), and throughout the film we see him gradually unravel from a youthful mama’s boy making do in the neglected District 12 to the jaded, lonely mentor of those original films.

Sunrise takes place 24 years before we meet Katniss Everdeen, during the 50th Hunger Games, or the second Quarter Quell, when the Capitol chooses twice the usual number of tributes. When Haymitch gets plucked as one of District 12’s unfortunates, he must leave behind his family and girlfriend, Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), to face certain death alongside 47 other innocent kids.

Zada himself is just a kid in many ways. The 21-year-old Sydney native is endearingly earnest, which is striking given his recent successes. Aussies will know the actor from the drama series Invisible Boys, in which he played an aspiring musician who is outed as gay. YA fans caught him in season one of Prime’s We Were Liars (he just finished filming season two). But Zada really broke into the mainstream this fall, when he starred in the final two episodes of Zoe Kazan’s East of Eden. Sunrise hits theaters on November 20, and the franchise has a history of turning young actors into stars, including Lawrence, Rachel Zegler, and Tom Blyth. If all goes to plan, it will do the same for Zada, whose career has been in the works since he was a young boy.

“From the time I was five years old, my mom was like, ‘He’s going to be an actor,’” Zada recalls. His mother, film producer Jessica Brentnall, took the prediction seriously. “I wasn’t allowed to play rugby,” he says. “You can’t have a broken nose as a movie star.”

She knew that fact all too well. Zada’s father, Jeremy Cumpston, is a director and actor, and his older brother started performing at a young age. Today, several of the five Cumpston siblings have IMDb pages. (Zada, who was born Joseph Cumpston, adopted his grandmother’s surname professionally when he was 18. The name traces back to his great-grandfather, an Afghan cameleer, and Zada has said he felt a “spiritual connection” to the family history it carries.)

When he was 15, Zada decided to pursue acting himself. “It’s the most random story ever,” he says of meeting his first agent, Mags Stewart. He agreed to star in his then-girlfriend’s short film for a school project. When she presented it over Zoom, Stewart walked by her daughter’s laptop and caught a glimpse of Zada’s performance. In that moment, she decided, “I want to be that kid’s agent.”

Zada’s career has been filled with these sorts of kismet moments. He says his audition for We Were Liars was the last one the casting team watched. From there, his costar, Mamie Gummer, helped push his tape through to Kazan for East of Eden. He auditioned for Sunrise just days after wrapping the Steinbeck adaptation. “The role came at the perfect point,” Zada says of Haymitch. “I never would have been as ready as right after East of Eden when I worked with Florence [Pugh].”

Sunrise is Zada’s first movie, and it proved to be a baptism by fire. He joined a beloved series whose director and crew had worked together for more than a decade, with a legacy to uphold and a set to lead. “There was a lot of pressure,” Zada admits. In many ways, though, that pressure put him right in his character’s headspace.
“Haymitch is someone who gets thrust into a position where people look towards him, though he doesn’t know what to do,” Zada says. “He has to stand up and take charge.”

Once the initial jitters wore off, Zada naturally took a leadership role on set. “I have three younger siblings, so I’m very good at hanging out with younger kids, taking care of them, and being a leader,” he says. “That was the core of the character, uplifting younger actors and these younger characters.”

With just a handful of projects under his belt, Zada is still figuring out his process. Right now, he’s dabbling in being over-prepared. Before Sunrise, he filled up five journals with prep work. “I was a madman,” he says. He also tried method acting, which helped when working with industry veterans like Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, and Jesse Plemons. “In order to not get too freaked out, I spent most of my time in the character,” he says. “I didn’t want to be fangirling in the middle of a scene.”

His main model, of course, was Harrelson. Zada didn’t meet his predecessor until after filming wrapped, but he studied Harrelson’s many roles. “He gave me a performance to mirror,” Zada says. “I mean, my job for a while was to watch Woody Harrelson movies. That’s not a real job.”

Zada also looked to Mickey Rourke’s work, specifically in the 1987 neo-noir Angel Heart, for young Haymitch’s flirtatious streak. His heart belongs to Lenore Dove, but that streak comes out with Elle Fanning’s Effie Trinket. “There was a little bit of flirtatious energy with Elle,” Zada admits. “It makes their scene together come alive and adds a nice dynamic.”

His relationship with fellow District 12 tribute Maysilee (Mckenna Grace) runs deeper. What begins as an icy acquaintance melts into an attachment born from hardship. “It’s a lot like soldiers who return from war,” Zada says. “There’s a bond between Haymitch and Maysilee because of the traumatic events they’ve gone through.”

Off-screen, the two have become fast friends. They’re currently on a worldwide press tour together, Zada’s first. “Mckenna is one of my favorite people in the entire world,” Zada says of his costar. “I leaned on her so much during the shoot. She’s such a pro.” Grace has shared similarly flattering statements about Zada. She told Variety Australia that Zada is “about to become one of the biggest stars ever.” Harrelson echoed the opinion to Vanity Fair, saying, “he’s about to be a big star.”
“It’s nice to hear, but I don’t have a job right now,” Zada says, humbly countering with another Harrelson quote: “It’s all well and good until you start believing it.”

Still, Zada is optimistic others will share Grace and Harrelson’s view when Sunrise hits theaters. “My hope is that filmmakers and studios feel the same way,” he says, laughing. He also knows that stepping into a beloved franchise means plenty of opinions will follow. For now, Zada has vowed to stay off the Internet, especially after the release, in order to maintain some distance from the online discourse. “I’ve become too aware of what everyone is saying,” he says. “I just need to stay away and keep to myself.” Instead, he’ll occupy his time with the script he’s writing with his brother, a drama comedy about half-siblings.

“I only want to do what I want to do,” Zada says of future projects, finally revealing a bit of that rebellious spirit. “I’m not willing to be pushed into anything that I’m not wholeheartedly in love with, whether that means making money or not. I just want to explore and go way off the deep end.”
Zada wears Calvin Klein throughout; styled by Jason Bolden.

items.title: Hailey Bieber Rewears an Iconic Carolyn Bessette Kennedy Look
items.description: There’s been no shortage of Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy references over the past year, but Hailey Bieber’s latest look might be the most impressive yet.
items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: There’s been no shortage of Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy references over the past year, but Hailey Bieber’s latest look might be the most impressive yet.

On Wednesday, the Rhode founder took the stage at the New York Times DealBook Summit in a vintage Yohji Yamamoto blazer that looked identical to the one owned by CBK. The tightly-buttoned black jacket, from the brand’s spring 1998 collection, features a mock-neck silhouette and a subtle peplum flare. Bessette first wore it to the Robin Hood Foundation Benefit with JFK Jr. in 1998. For her take, Bieber kept the white pencil skirt the same, but updated the vibe with glossy black pumps and a ’90s-style headband, though thinner than Bessette-Kennedy’s favored C.O. Bigelow accessory.

At the annual DealBook Summit, which gathers industry leaders in commerce, government, tech, and culture, Bieber sat down with journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin to talk mental health, social media, and selling Rhode to e.l.f. Beauty for $1 billion. The 29-year-old model was something of an outlier among the program’s guests, which also included Elon Musk, Zohran Mamdani, and Sam Altman. After all, she’s certainly the only one who can pull off a niche ’90s It girl reference and talk billion-dollar acquisitions. Along with getting some backstage support from her husband Justin, having the perfect power dressing ensemble was key to success, and for Bieber, that of course meant a spot-on CBK recreation.

It’s been a fashion-filled, Rhode-focused few days for the star, who, just yesterday, accepted the Brand of the Year award at WWD’s Beauty Inc Awards. For that appearance, she did not go archival, but instead wore a fresh-off-the-runway slip from Calvin Klein—which is, famously, Bessette’s former place of work. Looking back, perhaps it was a chic little hint at the iconic recreation look to come.

items.title: Black Friday Mattress Deals Are Already Wide Awake
items.description: Mattress sales come and go so often that it’s hard to determine what’s an actual deal. The times of year when we see the most legit mattress deals are Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Memorial Day, and Labor Day. And this year is no different. We’re already seeing
items.author: Molly Higgins
paragraphs: Mattress sales come and go so often that it’s hard to determine what’s an actual deal. The times of year when we see the most legit mattress deals are Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Memorial Day, and Labor Day. And this year is no different. We’re already seeing our favorite WIRED-tested bedding and mattress brands offering early Black Friday deals leading up to the big weekend. I’ll be on the lookout for more deals as we approach the actual event, so be sure to check back often for fresh discounts on these often-pricey purchases. Note that all mattress prices below are for queen sizes, and discounts on Shop may only appear once you're in the checkout menu.
Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Amazon, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and Black Friday Deals at Home Depot.
- Our favorite adjustable smart bed: Sleep Number ComfortNext Lux Smart Bed for $3,199 ($800 off)
- A combination sleep tracker and sunrise alarm clock: Hatch Sleep Clock for $188 ($62 off)
- The best sleep mask for most people: Bearaby Tree Dreamer for $62 ($27 off) (go to the checkout screen to see the discount)
Updated November 20, 2026: I've updated the mattress sales with new dates and promo codes, updated prices, and added new deals from Sleep Number, Naturepedic, Hatch, Zinus, and Bearaby.

This Helix mattress has been our top pick for years and remains one of the most popular bed-in-a-box options for good reason. Its plush pillow top and medium-firm feel make it comfortable for nearly any sleeper, whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach.

We love Helix in general, and right now the brand has 20 percent off site-wide when you use the Helix promo code BF20. It also offers special discounts, including 25 percent off Luxe mattresses with promo code LUXE25 and 30 percent off Elite mattresses with code ELITE30. (All listed Helix promo codes are valid through November 29.)

We really love this organic mattress. When we tested the Luxe model above, we found it offered a lovely balance of plush comfort and pressure relief, with just enough bounce to make it a great choice for back sleepers seeking a little extra support. But all of Birch's models are made from natural materials like wool, latex, and cotton, without any polyurethane-based foams.
Birch's Black Friday sale runs through November 29, with 25 percent off site-wide when you use the Birch promo code BF25.

The firm Bear Elite Hybrid has long been one of our top picks for back pain. Both reviewers who tested it agree that you love it more the longer you sleep on it. Bear mattresses also keep you cool, with phase-change material that absorbs body heat and copper-infused memory foam that wicks it away.
Bear Mattress has a Black Friday Sale running through November 29, with 35 percent off site-wide and a free bundle of two pillows and a mattress protector with promo code BF35.

This was former WIRED reviewer (and sleep expert) Julia Forbes’ all-time favorite mattress. She appreciated that its extra springiness provided added support and firmness, making it ideal for side sleepers.
Nolah Mattress’ Black Friday sale runs through November 29, with 35 percent off site-wide; no promo code needed.

We on the WIRED Reviews team love hybrid mattresses because they bring together the best of both worlds—memory foam and the support of inner coils. The Sapira Chill is the best hybrid mattress we've tested to date, bringing relief to our tester's back pain while absorbing excess heat through the temperature-regulating cover.
Leesa Sleep’s Black Friday Sale runs through December 8 and offers 30 percent off mattresses and 35 percent off adjustable base bundles, with no promo code needed.

Hybrids run cooler in general due to the open-spring design, and this cooling hybrid bed has a pillow top to provide a memory-foam-like feel—the best of both worlds. The initial pillow-top layer is made of ThermoPhase “cooling foam,” and the deep dimples on the top create extra airflow to keep things cool. There are 8-inch zoned coils below to give more solid support, and these beds tend to run on the firmer side, so keep that in mind when choosing between soft, medium, or firm.
During Brooklyn Bedding’s Black Friday Sale, you’ll get 30 percent off site-wide through November 29.

Instead of air chambers on each side of the mattress, as most smart beds use, Bryte uses a more traditional foundation of coils and memory foam layers. They call their coils “Bryte Balancers,” which can be adjusted for things like lumbar support or contouring, down to individual zones, in the connected app. There are also 100 firmness levels, so you can really dial in the settings to optimize for anything, stomach sleepers or folks with back pain included. The bed also tracks your sleep and provides sleep metrics like sleep phases, hours of sleep, heart rate, respiratory rate, and the number of bed rebalances.
The Bryte mattress sale offers 20 percent off site-wide and a free Cozy Earth Bamboo Cooling Sheet Set with purchase, through November 29.

We love these smart beds from Sleep Number. (Read our review of the ComfortNext Lux Smart Bed here.) The smart beds offer balanced pressure that’s ideal for side sleepers, cushioning for pressure points, motion isolation, helpful sleep tracking, and customizable firmness. The ComfortNext even has built-in sleep tracking, which monitors your nightly sleep score, called your “Sleep IQ” number, within the app. That data is compared with the firmness level you choose, known as your “Sleep Number” setting. This helps you fine-tune the firmness that, based on your sleep-tracking data, helps you sleep better.

The ComfortNext line, including the Lux Smart Bed model above, is 20 percent off. Sleep Number's Climate Collection is 25 percent off, and sheet sets and pillows are BOGO 50 percent off—check out all of Sleep Number's current sales and eligible items here. The offer runs through December 7, and no promo code is needed.

This is probably the most luxurious smart bed the WIRED Reviews team has tested. (Read our review here.) You're probably not planning to drop 10 grand on a bed today, but if you've been curious about smart beds, this may be a good one to check out. It has a unique design centered on temperature control, with built-in fans that make its surface noticeably cooler to the touch. The bed also monitors your bedroom's air quality and analyzes sleep metrics with an AI-powered sleep coach to give you feedback.

You can save $500 and get a $300 credit toward a future purchase when you buy a TEMPUR-ActiveBreeze System, TEMPUR-Breeze, or TEMPUR-LuxeAdapt mattress and a TEMPUR-Ergo Smart Base through December 1, with no promo code necessary.

When I die, bury me with this modular, supremely cooling mattress. It's part of Bedgear's new Night Ice collection, the coolest beds I've ever slept on. It has a silky cover that's cool to the touch, top cooling layers that work together to dissipate heat effectively, and side mesh vents to increase airflow throughout the mattress. With this modular design, you can choose the same or different levels of firmness on both sides.
The M5 above, plus Hybrid Performance and Sport Performance models below, are all discounted, and you can get a further discount if you buy one with an adjustable base. Sales run through December 7.

Former WIRED reviewer (and sleep expert) Julia Forbes thought this responsive hybrid mattress delivered firm support that helped with spine alignment and good pressure relief. (Read the review here.) The quilted top foam layer contours the hips and chest, and the layers of foam and pocketed coils offer good lumbar support, making it ideal for stomach sleepers or those with back pain.
During DreamCloud's Black Friday Sale, you can get up to 60 percent off mattresses and $100 off all memory foam mattresses.

If you suffer from back pain or are a stomach sleeper, we recommend a firmer, more supportive mattress like the ones above from Plank. The firm model above is very sturdy, and the firm luxe version is a hybrid mattress that adds coiled support and is flippable, with different levels of firmness on each side.
During Plank’s Black Friday Sale, you’ll get 30 percent off site wide through November 29.

This luxe model from Essentia was the first organic mattress I tested, and I’ve been spoiled since. The Tatami is vegan, so it contains no wool or other animal byproducts. It also has a nontoxic, allergy-free Kevlar fabric barrier. It doesn't have springs, but it's super comfortable, and its foam gently conforms to your body’s curves and pressure points.
Essentia’s Black Friday sale runs through November 29, with 25 percent off site-wide, and you’ll get two free latex Cloud pillows (a $399 value) with the purchase of a mattress.

We recommend this customizable organic mattress for side sleepers as an especially great option for couples. Its modular design lets each person choose a different firmness level, with a top cover that holds separate layers of foam and wrapped coils in place. You can adjust the firmness on either side of the bed to suit your individual preferences. Plus, you can swap out any of the five latex layers for free during the 100-night trial to ensure you've found the perfect feel.
Naturepedic's Black Friday Sale runs through November 7 and offers 20% off sitewide, plus 25% off all bedding and the Concerto Organic Pillowtop Mattress, with no promo code needed.

This was the first bed I tested for our guide to the best cheap mattresses, and I'm still impressed by how comfortable it was for roughly the price of a nice dinner out. It feels plusher—perhaps medium-plush—than its listed medium firmness, so I'd recommend this bed to people who prefer a softer feel. It has four layers of hypoallergenic, green-tea-infused gel memory foam, along with low motion transfer, cooling technology, and a breathable design to help you sleep cool.
Zinus's Amazon deals offer up to 30% off select mattresses and bed frames and run until November 30.

items.title: The Robot Vacuum I Refuse to Part With Is on Sale for Black Friday Already
items.description: Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with many models from popular brands like Dyson and Shark starting at $1,200. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and with early Black Frid
items.author: Nena Farrell
paragraphs: Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with many models from popular brands like Dyson and Shark starting at $1,200. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and with early Black Friday deals already kicking off, it's one of the best times to shop for one.

One of our favorite robot vacuum brands, Roborock, began its early Black Friday deals yesterday, and some of our favorite models we've tested are available for the best prices we've seen. Here's which models I'd snatch up while the prices are low.
- Roborock's best budget vac at its best price: Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro for $450 ($350 Off)
- A powerful, but still affordable roller mop vac: Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow for $600 ($400 Off)
- If you want Roborock's arm attachment: Roborock Saros Z70 with OmniGrip for $950 ($700 Off)
The Best Early Black Friday Vacuum Deals from Roborock

The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro launched in late summer as the newest addition to the brand's more affordable Qrevo line, and it quickly landed as a pick on my guide to the Best Robot Vacuums. It's often on sale for around $600, and thanks to Black Friday it's down to the lowest price I've seen it for: $450, nearly half off.

Overall, Roborock's vacuums are great, but I've been especially impressed by this one's corner cleaning, thanks to its extendable mop arm. It won't always spot cords, but it does a better job at navigating furniture and getting underneath my cabinets than more expensive robot vacuums I've tested.

If you'd rather have a roller-mop-style robot vacuum, the Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is another great option from Roborock's Qrevo line. This one came out in January of this year, and our reviewer instantly loved it.

The Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is a more expensive robot vacuum than the Qrevo 2 since it comes with the brand's SpriaFlow roller-mop. The internal roller spans nearly the entire width of the vacuum and can extend to edge-clean your home. It even has a built-in scraper to move dirty water into the tank instead of rolling it back onto the floor. If you're looking for an affordable mopping powerhouse, this is the one to choose. It's also nearly half off, down to $600 off the $1,000 price tag.

There's the affordable Qrevo line from Roborock, and then there's the higher-end Saros line. While both I and former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So weren't particularly impressed with the Saros 20, I've been much happier with the performance of the Saros 20 Flow. Like the Curv 2 Flow, it has a roller mop instead of spinning mop pads and did well in my mopping tests. It also didn't leave debris around, even with its high suction of 36,000 Pa.

It's one of Roborock's most expensive vacuums, and it comes across while using it—it feels very premium. I've been preferring it over the new Dyson robot vacuum I've been testing. Luckily, you can get it on sale right now for Black Friday. It still isn't cheap at $1,300, but it's one of my all-time favorites and one I have kept coming back to after trying other models.

If you're looking for something truly unique in a robot vacuum, Roborock's Saros Z70 might be what you're looking for. It has a mechanical arm built into it to pick up small items like socks while it vacuums, which feels handy, but didn't work as well as we'd hoped during testing. Still, maybe you feel that's the solution you've been dying for. If that's the case, it's available for a nice discount right now at $950.

It also packs 22,000 Pa of suction (not as powerful as the Saros 20 Flow, but still plenty of suction to clean carpets and rugs alike!) and still executes fast, effective cleaning. But the battery life on this vacuum isn't as long as that of other Roborocks we've tested. Again, you're mostly getting this one for the mechanical arm.

items.title: The 36 Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals
items.description: REI's 2026 Holiday Sale kicked off November 13 and lasts until November 23. There are plenty of great deals to help you restock your backpacking, hiking, biking, camping, outdoor loving gear quiver. REI members can use the code HOLIDAY2026 to save an extra 20
items.author: Scott Gilbertson
paragraphs: REI's 2026 Holiday Sale kicked off November 13 and lasts until November 23. There are plenty of great deals to help you restock your backpacking, hiking, biking, camping, outdoor loving gear quiver. REI members can use the code HOLIDAY2026 to save an extra 20 percent off one full-price item and an extra 20 percent off one REI Outlet item. Below are the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more.
There are also sales at Backcountry.com and some of our favorite cottage industry brands like Six Moon Designs, Zenbivy, and more. Not sure what you need? Check out our many outdoor gear guides.

The 650 Down Jacket is one of the best budget three-season puffer jackets you can buy, more so at this price. At 10.9 ounces, it's reasonably lightweight and has large hand pockets and some very nice internal pockets for stashing a hat or gloves. The kids' version is also on sale in a nice yellow color that's handy for spotting your child in the snow.

The Ghost Whisperer Down Jacket is my top pick for a backpacking puffer jacket. It weighs just 6.7 ounces for a men's medium (7.3 ounces for the men's large I tested), packs down to a tiny little thing (stuffing into its own pocket), and the 1,000-fill-power goose down offers one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios on the market. The men's version is technically on sale right now, but the only size available is small and XXL.

This is my favorite puffer jacket, especially in the shoulder seasons when temps dip a little lower. It features 4.5 ounces of 1,000-fill down (men’s medium), which is half the weight of the overall jacket. The internal TILT lining (short for Thermo Ionic Lining Technology) may or may not do anything; I haven't been able to devise an effective test, but even if it did nothing, the amount of 1,000-fill-power down combined with the scant weight makes this an appealing option for ultralighters. The 7D fabric (which is what keeps the weight low) does need babying, but I haven't had any issues in over a year of use.

This is great deal on a very warm down parka. It's thigh-length, which helps keep drafts up your back to a minimum, and it fits pretty well, though it's definitely boxy (what do you want from a 650-down-fill parka that's designed primarily to keep you warm?). I did find that the main two-way zipper can be fiddly, and does sometimes snag, but it's hardly a deal-breaker, especially at this price.

This 850-fill down hoodie makes the honorable mentions section of our puffer jacket guide. The cut is roomy and its gusseted around the shoulders for climbing. Our main gripe is that it's pricey, but this deal takes some of sting out of the price. The women's version is unfortunately not on sale.

The Rainier is our favorite budget rain jacket, especially when it's on sale. Unlike most rain jackets in this price range, the Rainier uses high-quality three-layer, seam-taped, laminate waterproofing that's non-fluorinated (meaning no PFAS). It has some other features rare in budget rain jackets, like pit zips or venting, a weatherproof center zip, and an adjustable, stowable hood.

It's a little weird to shop for sun hoodies with snow on the way, but if you're looking to avoid the sun next summer, REI's Sahara Shade hoodie is a great alternative to sunscreen. I don't often use a sun hoodie myself, but I have worn this one and it does do a good job of protecting you without feeling too stuffy on a hot day (it's definitely better for protecting against high altitude sun rather than humid, Florida sun).

When these were an REI Outlet deal earlier this year I got nervous that they might be discontinued, but apparently not because they are back. REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides when I'm riding my bike, but if you prefer, the regular top is also on sale for $64, as is the base layer bottom.

Smartwool's 100 percent merino base layer is my top pick for cooler weather in our guide to the best base layers. It's a great all-around choice, and the loose fit makes it work as a long-sleeve T-shirt in the shoulder seasons. That extra bit of roominess makes it possible to use it as a second light layer over something thinner. The pants are also on sale for $94 ($31 off).

Keen's Targhee Apex has finally found a look that isn't bad by Targhee standards. Perhaps more than any other shoe we've tested, these look like the trail-running Gorpcore icons they are. At just 0.75 pounds each, they are light without being fragile, and the generous footbed lets your feet spread comfortably on long days.

The La Sportiva Prodigio combines trail-running agility with boot-level protection, delivering surprising versatility on rugged terrain. They're one of our favorite light hiking boots. The fit is a little on the snug side—much like La Sportiva climbing shoes—but they should be fine even for wide feet thanks to the generous footbed width. At 1.65 pounds for the pair, these aren't terribly bulky, either.

These are my favorite barefoot sandals. I always refer to these as the barefoot equivalent of Chaco sandals. They're not as robust—I'd still bring Chacos for white-water rafting—but for everything else, these are perfect. Z-Trails flex and bend as you walk, giving your feet the freedom of movement you'd expect from a barefoot shoe, though these do have 10 mm of cushioning, which makes them a good option if you're just starting out with barefoot shoes. The even more minimal Z-Trek sandals are also on sale for $45 ($15 off).

These Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers are my favorite hiking pants thanks the thigh zips that deliver excellent ventilation. The Vidda Pros uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere, and nice reinforced knees (with openings for pads). There's even a hatchet loop on the leg.

Six Moon Design's Lunar Solo is one of the best single-wall ultralight solo tents you can buy. It's not without its quirks (read the pitching tips), but if you want something more than a tarp, that still weighs just 26 ounces (740 grams), this one is hard to beat. Use the Code YULEHIKE to get the 25 percent off.

Nemo's Hornet tents are some of the lightest freestanding tents around. The 1-person model is my go-to for situations where I might have to pitch on rock or concrete slabs (like staying in towns on a longer bike-packing trip). It's roomy enough for you and all your gear, light enough at 2.25 pounds (without stakes), and packs down remarkably small. It's also held up well in storms, though you will want some extra guy-outs if the wind is really howling (I like Zpacks 1.2-mm dyneema cord for lightweight guy lines).

This is the bike-packing version of Big Agnes' popular Copper Spur tent, one of the best backpacking tents around. The only difference, aside from color, is that the pole segments on this model are shorter (to make it easier to store on a bike). The Copper Spur line is very nearly the lightest freestanding tent around (it's just slightly heavier than the Hornet above), and if you happen to use it with trekking poles, you get what I think is the best feature, the covered awning modification for the vestibule. While this is the best deal, the 2-person model is also on sale for 20 percent off.
Sleeping Bad and Sleeping Pad Deals

This is one of my favorite ultralight sleeping bags. There are lighter quilts out there, but when you need the warmth of a mummy bag on those colder nights, this is what I use. It also has the smallest pack size of any bag I've tested in this temperature range. With the included compression sack, this thing is truly tiny. The down fill is PFC-free, 850+ hydrophobic down. The zippers are on the small side, but they slide well and rarely (if ever) snag on the bag. I've slept in this bag down to 20 degrees and never been the least bit cold.

Closed-cell foam pads like the Therm-a-Rest Z-Lite Sol are a must-have. They weigh next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), fold up small enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and double as a chair, extra padding on cold nights, table, you name it. I am too old and too soft to be the sort of ultra-minimalist who gets by with just a Z-Lite, but I still have one around on almost every trip I take.

Nemo's Tensor-insulated sleeping pads have the best R-value-to-weight ratio of anything I've tested. The Tensor All-Season featured here sports an R-value of 5.4 and weighs 18.2 ounces. That alone is impressive, but what I love about the Tensor is that it's thick, comfortable, and most importantly, nearly silent. The lighter Trail model is also on sale at REI. Its R-value is only 2.8, though.

I love my MegaMat, it is hands down the best sleeping experience I've had car camping (I have the auto version that fits in the back of your car). While it's not our absolute favorite mega sleeping pad (that's the slightly lighter, smaller MondoKing), I like the MegaMat better it has slightly better insulation. This deal is on the duo model, which is 72 inches long and 41 inches wide. The single wide MegaMat is also on sale for $195 ($75 off).
Deals on Camping and Backpacking Gear

I don't usually bring a chair backpacking—I just sit on the ground. But for some reason, I do love a chair when I'm bike packing, which is where I've used this Nemo the most. It's quite pricey, but it's very light and packs down to a tiny package. The genius part of this chair is that the cover is also a mat that keeps it from sinking into soft ground.

The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI-brand gear is the company's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works quite well and has generated some really great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example of that. It's not as nice as the Nemo above—it does wobble a bit, side to side, when you move—but it's still comfortable and half the price.

This camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is a bit big, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.

I sincerely hope you never have any need for one of these Sea to Summit bug head nets, but if you do, boy do you. I once did not have one and tried to go backpacking in Michigan’s UP in early May. I lasted about two hours. When I got home, I bought one of these and … still haven't ventured back to that marshy bog of a hike. But I could, and possibly even retain some of my sanity thanks to this thing.

What I said about the chair above goes for this day pack as well; it's an excellent value, especially on sale. I was surprised by how comfortable this thing is, especially because, to look at it, the straps are very lightweight and there's almost no padding. It still managed to carry loads up to 10 pounds without straining my shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. The Flash 22 is made of 70-denier recycled ripstop nylon, which is on the lighter side, but mine has held up well, even coming through some rough canyon hikes in Utah without any more than mud stains.

These two pots are my go-to cooking vessels for larger group meals. I find they're just about perfect for boiling up enough water to rehydrate four servings. I don't take the bowls and silverware into the backcountry, but they're handy for camping.

Sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's new inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

The Stash is our favorite all-in-one backcountry cook system. The heat diffuser design is what speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I was only able to match indoors in still air), but the real appeal here to me is the way this kit all packs down into itself. For weekend trips, this is the simplest system I've tested when it comes to cooking for two.

Jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger-capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.

These dry bags from Sea to Summit have double-stitched, tape-sealed seams that have held up well over the years. I also really like the external lash loops that make it easy to strap to anything with a tie-down anchor.

I like these dry bags for organizing things in my pack. They're not dry bags in the sense that you can submerge them and your gear will be fine, but the 30D silnylon with PCF-free DWR easily sheds a little rain. And they make finding your stuff easy. I put all my cooking gear in a red bag (red for fire), all my water-filtering stuff in a blue bag for, wait for it, water—and so on. I find the 3- and 5-liter bags the most useful, but you can get all the way up to 35L.

I've noticed that, when trying to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter-weight backpack, people then struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which takes my favorite sleeping bag (the Sea to Summit Spark above) and smashes it down to about half the size of the included stuff sack. You can do the same thing to clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino to some extent, to free up more room in your pack.

REI’s Big Haul duffel is a durable, water-resistant, gear-swallowing bag for carrying, well, just about everything. It's one of our favorite ways to schlep your gear when flying. It hits the right balance of robust build materials and pockets without being too heavy to lug around all day. The strap system is cleverly customizable, and you can convert it to a backpack.

Once upon a time, in a galaxy far, far away, I traveled around Southeast Asia with an early version of this Osprey pack, living out of it for almost a year. It stood up well to the abuse of overland travel—more than once, I watched a bus driver tie it to the roof of a bus by cinching it down with a rope, pulling with all his weight right down the middle of my pack, like a cheese cutter. The Farpoint survived, and my gear inside did as well, thanks in part to the thickly padded sides, which provide considerable extra cushioning.

items.title: Amazon Is Giving You More Time to Shop During Black Friday. Here’s What’s on Sale
items.description: Amazon’s Black Friday deals are a go. Its “Black Friday Week” sale runs November 19–30 (Cyber Monday), giving shoppers a head start on holiday shopping. The retailer has already discounted many items since last week and has now added even more to the sale. Eve
items.author: Les Shu
paragraphs: Amazon’s Black Friday deals are a go. Its “Black Friday Week” sale runs November 19–30 (Cyber Monday), giving shoppers a head start on holiday shopping. The retailer has already discounted many items since last week and has now added even more to the sale. Even better, we’re seeing some items with even lower prices. To help you sift through the products, we’ve highlighted some of our favorites below. If you’re a big Amazon shopper, now is a great time to fill those holiday wish lists and spend Black Friday with friends and family.
Check out our guide to the best Early Black Friday deals, plus standing desk deals, Home Depot appliance savings, and early tech deals.
Updated November 19: Amazon’s Black Friday deals start today. We’ve updated this story to reflect that and added more products we’ve recommended in our guides and reviews.
Best Amazon Black Friday Tech Deals

With a WIRED rating of 9 out of 10, the XM6 is one of our favorite over-ear headphones, combining comfort with great sound quality and noise cancellation. This is the lowest price on Amazon; however, it has dropped to this price before. Note that Walmart and Best Buy are also offering the XM6 at this sale price.

Good gaming laptops are never cheap, and they’ve become even more expensive this year. If you need a recommendation that balances performance and budget, we recommend the Asus ROG Strix G16 with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060, one of our favorite budget gaming laptops. We prefer the RTX 5070 option, but it’s nearly $3,000. This on-sale model is more attainable.

The latest Echo Show 11 is our recommendation for the Best Alexa Smart Display. WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell found the screen bright and crisp, with immersive sound quality. Since the sale price matches the regular price of the smaller Echo Show 8, it’s a good deal—just $5 more than the sale price during Amazon’s October Prime Day event.

The Pixel 11-series phones from Google are among our favorite Android devices. Loaded with the latest software and Gemini AI features, the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro XL are our pick as the smartest Android smartphones. They’re also the only non-iPhones to support Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic mounting, so you can use MagSafe accessories. During Black Friday, you can get all for under $1,000 each—a terrific deal for a flagship phone—and they’re at their lowest price ever on Amazon.

The Series 12 model is not only cheaper than the high-end Ultra 4, but it’s also the best Apple Watch you can buy, period. It has the latest health-sensing features, including a Readiness score that summarizes your recent health and activity. Its Amazon sale price is currently the lowest since its introduction.
High-quality three-in-one charging stands look terrific on a bedside table, but many cost over $100. This one from Mophie is one of our favorites, and it’s 49 percent off on Amazon right now.

The AirTag seems to be on sale all the time, but no matter—it’s currently the lowest price on Amazon and cheaper than buying from Apple. It’s one of the best Bluetooth trackers. If you can swing it, go for the four-pack.

Alongside the AirTag, the AirPods Max 2 and AirPods Pro 3 are also on sale. These are well-regarded among WIRED testers, but we recommend waiting until after Thanksgiving to see if they drop further—don’t worry, they are often on sale.

Phone accessories are aplenty on Amazon, but few look as good as Moft’s. You can pick up this ingenious wallet-kickstand hybrid that attaches to an iPhone via MagSafe, or peruse the rest of Moft's Black Friday deals.

You can expect Amazon’s own devices to go on sale during Black Friday. While Blink’s security cameras didn’t make our short list, WIRED reviewer Simon Hill still thinks they’re worth considering, especially if you’re on a budget. A downer is that they only work with Alexa, but if that’s you, it’s NBD. The latest version of its pan-tilt camera is usually $40, but it’s 50 percent off right now.

WIRED’s audio editor won’t stop praising Soundcore products, but he’s not wrong: This nascent brand (soon to be rebranded as Anker, its parent company) makes terrific audio products without the premium price. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe included this Bluetooth boom box in a roundup of her favorite festival gear. It’s the lowest price ever on Amazon currently, but it’s not the cheapest—keep an eye out at other retailers during Black Friday.

This EcoFlow portable battery is WIRED reviewer Simon Hill’s pick as the best power bank for laptops. It has a large 27,650-mAh capacity, which is plenty for charging smaller devices too. It’s great for travel since it’s allowed on a plane, and it has a retractable USB-C cable, so you can leave extras at home.

At $359, the second-gen Bose QuietComfort over-ear headphones seem overpriced considering the competition. But when they’re on sale at $199 to $219 (depending on the color), they suddenly become a great buy. As expected from Bose, the noise cancellation and sound quality are excellent. They are also comfortable, making them great travel companions. Note that the first-gen version is also on sale for $169 (it’s frequently at this price), but it’s outdated, and we think you should spend $30 to $50 more on the latest version instead.
Amazon Early Black Friday Home and Kitchen Deals

Love them or hate them, but pod-based coffee makers are popular for their convenience. The Nespresso Vertuo Pop+ is our recommended espresso pod maker, and the Deluxe model is under $100. It has a larger water tank than the standard version, and the Vertuo pods are recyclable. For more savings on coffee-related products, check out our Early Black Friday Espresso Machine Deals.

WIRED’s home-cleaning expert, Nena Farrell, recommended only three robot vacuums, naming this Eufy floor-sweeping automaton her budget pick. It’s 43 percent off right now for a robovac with great suction power and a self-cleaning roller mop.

With quality espresso machines costing $500 and more (way, way more), a budget option seems improbable. Yet, this De’Longhi fits the bill. One of our recommended models, it usually costs around $200 or just a little more, but you can snag one for $150 if you’ve been wanting to get into the third-wave coffee game. It’s a great price, but we’ve seen it go as low as $120 in past sales.

items.title: Don’t Sleep on This Hatch Sleep Clock Deal
items.description: If you’re still using your iPhone’s “Radar” sound as an alarm, it might be time for an upgrade. The latest Hatch Sleep Clock is designed to make both falling asleep and waking up a little more pleasant. It combines a sunrise alarm clock, dimmable bedside light
items.author: Boutayna Chokrane
paragraphs: If you’re still using your iPhone’s “Radar” sound as an alarm, it might be time for an upgrade. The latest Hatch Sleep Clock is designed to make both falling asleep and waking up a little more pleasant. It combines a sunrise alarm clock, dimmable bedside light, sound machine, and contactless sleep tracking into one bedside gadget. And for the first time, it’s going on sale (early) as a Black Friday deal.

From November 19 through November 20, the Sleep Clock is 25 percent off at Hatch and Amazon. Normally $250, it’s down to $188, which is just $18 more than the Hatch Restore 3’s $170 retail price. And unlike its predecessor, the newer Hatch adds passive sleep monitoring, which is pretty compelling for anyone who hates wearing wearables to bed. Or maybe you’re like me and occasionally forget to wear your Oura Ring to bed, in which case, you wouldn’t have to worry because the Hatch is already quietly tracking your sleep in the background.
Hatch Sleep Clock for $188 ($62 Off)

I’ve been testing the Hatch Sleep Clock for over two months, and it’s earned a permanent spot on my nightstand. As someone who already wears a smart ring and smartwatch to bed, I’m not exactly short on sleep-tracking data. But I’ve never owned a sunrise alarm clock, and I instantly became a convert. Unlike my iPhone or Amazon Echo Dot, it doesn’t wake me up by blaring an obnoxious alarm in my pitch-black bedroom. Instead, it gradually illuminates the room within my scheduled wake-up time. You can customize the sunrise's duration and brightness, and pair it with a soundscape of your choosing. It truly makes getting out of bed feel less jarring, especially as the mornings get darker.

Most notably, the Sleep Clock also doubles as a contactless sleep tracker, using a built-in motion sensor to detect your movements and breathing throughout the night. I compared its readings against my Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch Series 12, and while sleep duration estimates were generally aligned, the sleep-stage readings were less consistent. The device doesn’t measure physiological metrics like heart rate, and it can’t detect snoring or other audio-based sleep disruptions. I also found that placement significantly matters. My nightstand tends to collect clutter, so I had to rearrange my trinkets to make room for the clock.

Each morning, the Hatch app gives you a breakdown of when you went to bed, when you fell asleep, when you woke up, and how much time you spent in different sleep stages. The color-coded reports are easy to understand without burying me in random metrics. Plus, unlike most sleep trackers, Hatch doesn't require a subscription to access your sleep data. (You will need that Hatch+ membership ($6 per month) if you want to access the full audio library, however.)

Overall, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the best all-in-one bedside device. I wouldn’t recommend replacing your dedicated wearable with it if detailed health tracking is your priority. But if you’ve been wanting a sunrise alarm clock that can also offer a little insight into your sleep, do not sleep on this Black Friday deal.
If you don’t care for sleep tracking, Hatch is also offering discounts on several other products across its lineup.

items.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
items.description: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
items.author: Grace Huckins
paragraphs: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

items.title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
items.description: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
items.author: Antonio Regalado
paragraphs: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”
“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

items.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
items.description: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)
I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”
