The second body to be uncovered was that of a woman in her sixties who had dark, curly hair. An implanted port, allowing for the infusion of chemotherapy and other medications, was visible on her upper chest, suggesting that she may have died of cancer. “She looks like my sister,” Hedley said.

The third body was that of a slender older man with exceptionally long legs, a relatively short trunk, and large hands. I guessed that he’d had a connective-tissue disorder known as Marfan syndrome. “People want you to learn from their differences,” Hedley told the group. He attempted a wisecrack: “My dad wanted to make sure everyone saw his giant testicle!”

The class split into three groups, each of which selected a body and named it. I joined the table with the male cadaver, which we decided to call Aristotle. (The women were dubbed Nonna Marcy and Starla Marie.) Next, Hedley instructed us to stand the bodies up. “In life, we meet people vertically,” he explained. At first, I thought he was joking, but he grabbed Aristotle and started to hoist him off the table. Hedley and an assistant lifted the torso while a fellow-participant and I knelt to lock his knees in place. The body, which was heavier than I expected, nearly toppled over. I stared up at the dead man towering over me and wondered what the hell I was doing.

Most medical schools teach what’s known as regional anatomy. Students might spend a day isolating the brachial plexus—the intricate network of nerves that animate the shoulder, the arm, and the hand. Another session might focus on tracing the arteries that run through the abdomen, supplying blood to the liver, the spleen, and the gut. Medical dissectors clear away connective tissue from structures of interest; instructors sometimes insert pins or flags for identification. In this way, doctors develop a common language to talk about the body, and a precise mental map that enables medical interventions. Hedley’s “integral anatomy,” by contrast, does not necessarily isolate or name the structures that doctors care about. Integral anatomy is concerned primarily with the body’s continuities and textures, and treats connective tissue not as extraneous material to be discarded but as a system worthy of sustained attention.

After a cursory presentation on how to handle a scalpel and hemostatic forceps, Hedley directed us to remove the cadavers’ skin. “You only get one first cut,” he said. “Make it count.” Even though I was wearing a mask, the smell of formaldehyde singed my nostrils, and my eyes started to burn. I ran my gloved fingers over Aristotle’s right thigh, which felt firm and smooth, like cold leather. I made an incision from near the groin to above the knee. I was surprised by how thin the skin was—just a millimetre or two deep—and, as I worked to peel away the layer, I accidentally took part of the fatty yellow tissue below. “Got a little carried away there!” Hedley said over my shoulder. He helped me scrape the underside of the skin clean, revealing a delicate network of fibrous tissue that looked like cantaloupe rind, then gestured toward a metal bucket marked with blue tape which sat by my feet. Every bit of tissue that we removed from the body was to go in there; the remains would be cremated and returned to the family. Hedley brought over a flap of abdominal skin from Starla Marie. He shone a flashlight behind it to emphasize narrow bands of damaged collagen and elastin—stretch marks. Near the head of the table, someone cut into Aristotle’s armpit, and blood-tinged embalming fluid flowed onto the metal surface. The lab’s director sucked it up with a turkey baster. A woman working next to me indicated that she felt lightheaded and excused herself.

Madhav Gramke, a chiropractor who serves as one of Hedley’s assistants, joined our group. He had a bald head, a black beard, and lively eyebrows. As he cut away the thick skin of Aristotle’s heel, I noticed the names of the Hindu deities Radha and Krishna tattooed on Gramke’s forearm. Gramke was born in Houston, and his parents, who were Catholic, named him John. “But I always felt more like a Madhav than a John,” he told me. As an adolescent, he became an atheist, but one night in college he took LSD and watched the sun rise over the ocean. That’s God, he remembered thinking. A few weeks later, a Hare Krishna gave him the Bhagavad Gita, and Gramke eventually went to India to study with a guru who called him Madhav. Gramke said that his faiths had instilled in him a deep appreciation of the human form. Christianity teaches imago Dei—humans are made in the image of God. Some Hindus consider the body a temple for the soul. “Christian, Hindu, evolutionary biologist, whatever,” Gramke said, placing a flap of skin into the bucket. “If you pay attention, you’ll see that the body is amazingly elegant. It’s an extraordinary thing.”

The history of dissection is full of sordid episodes. A few centuries ago, many cadavers were obtained by “resurrection men,” who dug up freshly buried bodies and sold them to anatomists. Surgeons and for-profit body collectors fought over corpses after public executions. In 1752, England passed the Murder Act, which allowed for the bodies of convicted killers to be hung in chains and left to decay or to be “dissected and anatomized,” for “better preventing the horrid crime.” The first known full-body nerve dissection, conducted in 1888 and still on display at Drexel University, was reportedly performed on a Black woman named Harriet Cole; there is no record of her having given her consent. The famed Scottish anatomist John Hunter, a father of modern surgery, once hired someone to follow a nearly eight-foot-tall Irish man in the days before his death. The man, who had a pituitary disorder, did not want his body to be dissected, and arranged for his corpse to be thrown into the ocean. But Hunter conspired to bribe the undertaker, so a coffin full of stones went into the ocean instead. Hunter kept the man’s skeleton at his home.

Misconduct continues to this day. In 2024, an NBC News investigation revealed that a Texas university had been using unclaimed bodies—many of them from nursing homes, hospitals, and homeless encampments—for its anatomical-dissection program. In one case, a deceased veteran’s body was classified as unclaimed, despite the fact that his family lived nearby. Some medical companies use body parts to help them develop products; the veteran’s torso was sent to a medical-education company, one of his legs went to a Swedish device-maker, and a pair of bones from his head went to the U.S. Army. The man’s family later said that he never wanted to be a donor. Last year, a former morgue manager at Harvard Medical School was sentenced to eight years in prison for helping to steal and sell body parts that had been donated to the university, and Harvard recently agreed to a fifty-three-million-dollar settlement to compensate the families of the donors. Not long ago, the operators of a funeral home a few hours away from the Institute for Anatomical Research were sentenced to prison for harvesting and selling parts of hundreds of bodies that they’d promised to prepare for cremation.

James Pulciani, the Institute’s director for the past decade, is in charge of procuring bodies for dissection. He described the recent scandals as “a constant challenge.” “I am always trying to destigmatize this work,” he said. “I want people to see labs like ours as a third destination for the body after death. It should be burial, cremation, and anatomical dissection.” Pulciani has a graying goatee, three earrings in his left earlobe, and a boisterous laugh; in the lab, he could usually be found in purple scrubs and SpongeBob SquarePants socks. Recently, a student asked Pulciani how he should alter his diet so that his colon would not look as diseased as that of a cadaver on display. “Now that’s what I call preventative care!” Pulciani said, chuckling.

In the U.S., people who wish to donate their bodies can register with their state as organ donors (which means that the donation could directly save lives) or as whole-body donors (which is sometimes described as a donation “to science.”) Debra Szuster, who manages the whole-body donation program at the Colorado State Anatomical Board, told me that medical and dental schools are generally the first to receive donations. When there are sufficient donations, however, bodies can go to professional-development programs like those at the Institute; they are generally used within two or three years so that the remains can be returned to families. Szuster personally inspects many such organizations, to make sure that they store and treat the donations with care.

The Institute acquires about forty bodies per year. Many that do not come from the Anatomical Board come from the Institute’s direct-donation program. Pulciani often retrieves the bodies himself in a van, at times driving to morgues and funeral homes as far as three hundred miles away. “A lot of programs try to anonymize donors,” he told me. “We tend to take the opposite tack.” A few years ago, a brother of one of Pulciani’s close friends was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. The man, who’d cycled in and out of prison, learned of Pulciani’s work during his treatment. Initially, he was reluctant to offer up his body, but Pulciani framed a donation as a way to give back. Money also played a role. The man didn’t want his family to bear the expense of his burial; if he donated his body, the lab would cover the cost of cremation. When I spoke with one of the man’s sisters, Debbie, she told me that their mother never felt comfortable with his decision. “I can’t believe they’re cutting into him like that,” she remembered her mother saying. But Debbie was moved “beyond measure” by her brother’s donation. She occasionally watches videos of his dissection and recognizes his tattoos; she thinks of the people who might learn from him. She has since filled out paperwork to donate her own body to the Institute when she dies.

Sometimes the relations are even more intimate. Hedley’s whole-body nerve-dissection project was performed on Gramke’s father, whom Hedley called Captain. Gramke, who participated in the dissection and helped film it, described the experience as intense and strange, but also “beautiful in its own way.”

Dissecting the body of someone you’ve known in life can be seen as an act of devotion or as a profound transgression. During my time with Hedley, I tried to decide which it was. Medicine discourages practitioners from treating their family and friends, and has strong norms in favor of professional boundaries, but Hedley’s work is often personal. Some anatomists I spoke to questioned whether anyone can make an objective decision to donate his body to someone he knows. “I worry about conflicts of interest,” Champney, the University of Miami professor, told me. “You don’t want situations where it’s ‘Oh, I’m not sure about this—but I’ll do it for my friend.’ ” James Cray, who directs the anatomy graduate program at Ohio State University, said, “Good stewardship is all about consent. It’s important that donors really understand how their bodies will be used and make decisions based on what’s important to them.”

In an article on best practices for body donation, the Swiss anatomist Beat Riederer wrote that dissecting a friend or a family member “seems unimaginable.” I felt the same way. Still, I had to admit that my aversion was more visceral than rational. Hedley emphasizes the distinction between a body and a person: “Cadavers are not people. They are records of people.” I could not detect anything coercive or exploitative about the lab and its work. Staff members spoke of donors with respect, even reverence. Direct donors to the Institute sign a letter of intent that encourages open conversation with loved ones, “so that everyone feels informed and comfortable” with their wishes. (It can be withdrawn at any time.) The organization’s website tells the public, “When you make a whole body donation, your legacy will live on as your body becomes a teacher in our lab.”

After the skin had been removed from the cadavers, they looked as though they were encased in buttery yellow bubble wrap. This was the superficial fascia, which sits just beneath the skin. When I cut into it, my blade advanced with a succession of tiny pops: we were severing the fibrous material that separates lobules of fat. I pulled the layer up like it was a carpet and saw a thin white sheet of dense, collagenous tissue underneath—the deep fascia. I was surprised by how much of the firmness of the muscle below seemed to come from this layer. After I removed it, the muscle felt like lumpy hamburger meat.

Lower down the body, one of my tablemates had filleted the quadriceps, four reddish-brown straps that converge at a white tendon above the kneecap. Pulciani pointed out that, contrary to many people’s expectations, two of the straps actually extend around the thigh and partially attach to the back of the femur. When we turned the body face down, we also saw a glistening silver ribbon running up the back of the thigh. It was the connective tissue atop the hamstrings, and it looked almost like aluminum foil. I made a mental note to stretch more.

As I worked, I thought about how abstract my sense of the human body had become. When I examine a patient who has neuropathy, my mind immediately turns to drugs and doses; I couldn’t remember the last time I’d conjured an image of the neurovascular bundle that I was now pinching between my thumb and forefinger. In my practice, cardiovascular disease is represented by risk scores, imaging studies, and cholesterol blockers. But in the lab I could lift up a man’s neck muscle and feel that a once supple carotid artery was rigid with gritty calcium deposits. The dissection reminded me that as medicine grows more digitized, and more artificially intelligent, it will become only more divorced from the material reality of sickness and health.

The novelist Ayad Akhtar has noted that, in French, two words can be translated as “to know”: savoir, to know about, and connaître, to know directly. Dissection, it seemed to me, was an exercise in moving anatomical knowledge from the realm of description to the realm of experience. One massage therapist in the room said that she’d never realized how deep she needed to press to access the psoas-major muscle, which connects the lower spine to the thigh. Another said that she changed her technique massaging the iliotibial band after she saw how it ran along nearby structures. But knowing how to cut open a body is different from knowing how it works. When we opened a donor’s abdomen, Hedley spoke admiringly of the visceral fat lining certain organs—“Don’t be hating on your visceral fat!”—even though scientists have associated it with such conditions as diabetes, stroke, and cancer. Later, he characterized the liver and the spleen as “friends,” saying that, when the liver fails, the spleen enlarges in order to assume some of its jobs. In fact, the spleen grows because blood has difficulty passing through a scarred liver; it can’t, in any meaningful sense, take over the liver’s functions.

Hedley has a special interest in the fascia, which in alternative-medicine circles is seen as a key driver of pain and stiffness. In a 2009 YouTube video titled “The Fuzz Speech,” which has been viewed more than a million times, Hedley pulls back a layer of muscle and uses his finger to disperse wispy tissue that looks like cotton candy. “Each night when you go to sleep, the interfaces between your muscles grow fuzz,” he says. “In the morning, when you wake up and you stretch”—he reaches his arms overhead and groans—“the fuzz melts.” Failure to stretch, Hedley claims, makes us “all fuzzed over,” which can be treated with massage and other forms of bodywork. Paul Ingraham, a science writer and a former massage therapist,

items.title: Gifts for Food Lovers and Loved Ones Who Eat
items.description: Something I’ve always loved about gift-giving is how sneakily selfish it can be. There’s so much satisfaction in browsing, buying, and presenting—not to mention in realizing, on those rare, intoxicating occasions, that you’ve utterly nailed it. You have succes
items.author: Helen Rosner
paragraphs: Something I’ve always loved about gift-giving is how sneakily selfish it can be. There’s so much satisfaction in browsing, buying, and presenting—not to mention in realizing, on those rare, intoxicating occasions, that you’ve utterly nailed it. You have successfully perceived your loved one’s essence and translated it into an everyday commercial object. You are the bringer of joy! This satisfaction is felt all the more keenly when it comes to gastronomic gifts. As the English essayist Charles Lamb once wrote, “I love to taste them, as it were, upon the tongue of my friend.” I’ll leave the specifics of your relationship with your friend’s tongue up to you (and your friend). But, even in a more hand-to-hand situation, consider this selection of objects wild, wonderful, delicious, and delightful—a pleasure to receive, and an equal pleasure to give.

One of the incontrovertible truths of holiday gift-giving is that size matters. A teddy bear? Fine. A teddy bear that’s six feet tall? Now we’re talking! A box of pasta under the tree? Weird. A five-and-a-half-pound sack of rigatoni? Magnificent! Bizarre! A gift never to be forgotten! Pastificio Gaetano Faella, a Campanian manufacturer that’s more than a century old, makes some of the nicest pastas on the market, and, lucky us, they sell some of their best shapes in 5.5-pound bags, most of which are available from the Italian importer Gustiamo. I’m partial to the rigatoni ($52 for that big bag), which has ideally rough-edged ridges for bolognese to cling to, and the gigantic, tubelike mezzi paccheri (same price), which collapse in an elegant flop under a creamy sauce.

The late artist John Baldessari was famous for many things—dropping colored dots over the faces of found photographs and film stills, writing “I will not make any more boring art” over and over again, incinerating every painting he made prior to his turn to conceptualism. But of all his works I’m most charmed by “Miracle Chips,” a slim artist book published by Steidl in 2009. A puckish sendup of our tendency to see faces in inanimate things, the volume presents a series of photographs of potato chips that bear uncanny resemblances to some very famous faces: Is that Ludwig Wittgenstein? Che Guevara? Frida Kahlo? “Can one look at a potato chip and not see some image hidden within its surface?” Baldessari writes, in a brief note at the end of the otherwise textless volume. “Do not people’s faces often look like potato chips?” The book is now out of print, but a few copies are still available at decent prices: the New York-based rare-book dealer Dividing Line has one for $150, and I’ve spotted them on AbeBooks, now and again, for under $100. If you’re giving it as a gift, you’ll naturally want to pair it with some potato chips (don’t get fancy; Lightly Salted Lays are as good as any) or, perhaps, with an homage to the potato itself: a humble spud sculpted from Carrara marble ($57 and “fairly life-like”).

Speaking of art books: Carl Middleton’s Fruit Sticker Album ($6) is pure delight. A simple chapbook intended as a receptacle for each produce sticker you peel off your apples, oranges, bananas, peaches, mangosteens, jackfruits, plums, and so on, up to three hundred pieces of fruit. Why collect your fruit stickers? Listen: why not? What a thing it is to eat a peach!

And, then, on the matter of fruit: I simply cannot imagine anything more devastatingly chic at the center of a dinner table than a bowl of juicy red cherries, interspersed hither and thither with these trompe-l’oeil cherry candles ($33 for a set of eight), whose wick-stems the host could, perhaps, nonchalantly set alight in the middle of the soup course.
Tinned Fish, for Real Heads

Heartbreaking, isn’t it, to see something excellent and eternal—say, fish, packed in tins with oils and salts and herbs and other tasty elements, and heat-treated for extraordinary shelf stability—become a fad, and thus a punch line? We anchovy-heads and sardine stans rejoiced as fish in cans started taking our social-media feeds by storm a few years back, and we’re still here, even as the tides of trendiness recede. I’ve been especially enamored, of late, by the products of Great Lakes Tinned Fish, a Michigan-based outfit that smokes and packs whitefish from North America’s own inland, saltless seas. A sampler trio ($45 for three ninety-gram tins) includes whitefish with garlic and shallot, with lemon and dill, and simply on its own.

My go-to housewarming gift is a round metal tin of Danish butter cookies—once you’ve eaten its contents, it’s a sewing kit, get it? I’ve been thinking, lately, about committing even further to the bit, with the addition of a plastic tub of margarine, the most timeless leftovers container there is. Honor both proud traditions with Little Shop of Pins’ sewing-kit lapel pin and leftovers lapel pin—the former an enamelled Royal Dansk butter-cookies container whose hinged lid flips up to reveal a sewing kit, the latter a little tub of Country Crock, with a swirl of saucy spaghetti inside ($16 each; also available in sour cream).
The Most Beautiful Grater in the Whole Entire World

An oroshigane is a grater for daikon radish, but it works just as well for grating ginger, garlic, and any other tender root. This moody glazed ceramic design ($58, available in three colors) collects your grated mush in a little vessel below the grater, for easy use. It’s so bewitching, in its tones and shapes and textures. I love it so much.

I’m a kids’-cookbooks hater, and I won’t apologize for it. In my experience, they’re either histrionically enthusiastic or excessively nonchalant, and it’s ridiculous to me that so many use standard recipe formatting, a mode of technical writing so infamously imprecise and incomprehensible that even literate adults struggle to decipher it. If you’re buying a gift for a big kid—we’re talking knife-wielding and stove-using—then just give them a grownup cookbook. For littler ones, try one or two or three of Phaidon’s ingenious Cook in a Book series ($23 each, or $110 for a set of six). Created by the Finnish designer Lotta Nieminen, each brightly colored, splendidly illustrated book describes the preparation of a single dish (pancakes, black-bean tacos, spaghetti with red sauce) using interactive elements: pull tabs, spinning wheels, pop-out pieces, and more. Reading them—over and over and over and over, if your kid is anything like mine—really teaches the what and the why of cooking, demystifying the act of cooking in a way that might benefit some adults, too.
There Bundt for the Grace of God

Earlier this year, I found myself deep down a Bundt-cake rabbit hole. Did you know that the term “Bundt” is a registered trademark of the Nordic Ware kitchenware company, which developed the pan—a more lightweight version of Europe’s heavy Kugelhopf molds—and other manufacturers need to call their copycats “ring molds” or “ring pans”? Did you know that the Bundt pan became famous when one Ms. Ella Helfrich, of Houston, Texas, took second place at the 1966 Pillsbury Bake-Off with her Tunnel of Fudge cake, which became a sensation? Did you know that, when Pillsbury discontinued its Double Dutch Fudge Buttercream dry frosting mix, a key ingredient for the Tunnel of Fudge, the recipe no longer worked as advertised? Did you know that Nordic Ware holds that a Bundt cake’s beauty lies in the cake itself, and not in any frosting or secondary garniture, and consequently the company has designed and manufactured dozens of pans of stunning artistry? There’s a deeply geometrically pleasing three-dimensional swirl ($46), an arched design reminiscent of a Renaissance cathedral ($46), a dizzying fractal checkerboard ($48), a freaky wheel of spiky ridges ($48), a pleasingly naturalistic laurel wreath ($50), and a snappy little ring of pineapples ($60). The trick is to get your cake to release cleanly from these intricately detailed pans, for which there is Nordic Ware’s own Baker’s Joy spray ($11), as essential as good butter, a good oven, and a sprinkle of powdered sugar at the end.

No one will ever turn up her nose at a beribboned jar of homemade Chex Mix (add a pinch of adobo seasoning—it’ll change your life), but there’s something splendidly luxurious about buying a fancy snack confection that could never be found in standard grocery-store aisles. Good Mix, a collab between the L.A.-based chocolatier Valerie Confections and the mega-cool L.A. design studio Commune, is dreamy and rough and weird and wondrous, with almonds, pumpkin seeds, and cocoa nibs held together in a sea-salted matrix of bittersweet chocolate ($14 for a bar, $30 for a box). If your giftee is not a chocolate person, Commune’s house-label tea ($30 for a cannister of sixteen tea bags) is also a very special thing: a hazy-bright blend of sencha, sage, lemon peel, and peppermint, in characteristically gorgeous packaging.

Chocolate-covered golden berries, tart and sweet ($7 for a hundred grams). Salty, savory peanuts roasted with sea moss ($8 for 5.5 ounces). Old-fashioned saltwater taffy in a nineteen-twenties-style box ($19 for sixteen ounces). A five-pound metal bucket of Hammond’s hard pretzels ($68). Fancy Italian sugar candies from Romanengo, a nearly two-hundred-and-fifty-year-old Genoese confectioner ($32 for a hundred grams). Raw honey in a paint tube ($16 for six ounces). Chicago-style-hot-dog-flavored potato chips ($33 for ten one-ounce bags). Artisanal rainbow sprinkles ($16). Or, if they prefer to do their own grocery shopping, a sprightly mortadella tote ($39), from the witty design studio Produce Aisle, is perfect for carrying items home. (For the vegetarian or the charcuterie-averse, it is also available in onion.)

Everybody feels like they need a better pepper grinder. How about you just get the best one? The Pepper Cannon ($200) is an object of almost cartoonish male-codedness: there’s the name, for starters, and the fact that it’s a heavier-than-it-looks hunk of matte-black metal, with the approximate heft of a tactical Maglite. And then there’s the fact that the company that makes it is called Männkitchen—though that, they say, is intended to mean “My Kitchen” in Old Norse. Its insistent virility notwithstanding, the Pepper Cannon is genuinely phenomenal: it pulverizes your peppercorns with the gentlest flick of the wrist, and feels sturdy enough to last well beyond the apocalypse. Fill it, if you’re inclined, with peppercorns from Milly ($42 for a set of three), whose green, white, and black berries come in cute little tins and each have their own distinct, bright, dusky, piquant sharpness.

When it comes to truly dedicated cooks, don’t test their patience with a specialty knife; don’t oblige them to smile over a spice blend that they promise they’ll absolutely use. Spark their joy, instead, with an entirely new way of thinking about the things they already know: Isobel Chiang’s “Colour Palate” ($34), an utterly lovely meditation on the relationship between cooking and color, whose spiral-bound color cards produce thousands of visual, conceptual recipes. Go even deeper with “A Dictionary of Color Combinations” ($24), a set of palettes organized by the painter and costume designer Sanzo Wada, published in Japanese in the nineteen-thirties and reissued in a bilingual edition just a few years ago.

Physical cookbooks! So immersive, so important, so endlessly frustrating to actually cook from, owing to the irritating tendency of the pages to roll and flip at precisely the moment you’re elbow-deep in a heritage chicken. I used to weigh down the pages with cans of beans, or strategically wedge the book under the lip of my countertop fruit bowl, but it turns out they make actual tools for this sort of thing: on one end of the aesthetic spectrum, a smooth, minimalist Ukanmuri book clip ($10); on the other, Awkward Auntie’s cast-concrete Donut Bookmarks ($20 each), which are weighty enough to lay across the open pages and keep things in place. If you prefer a vertically perched book, behold the satisfying modernism of a powder-coated metal book stand ($28; available in several colors), or the easy efficiency of a folding stainless-steel model ($39), with its jaunty little leg spirals.

Something about a carafe set feels so correct: a modestly sized pouring vessel, a harmonizing cup or two. It’s moment-size, human-scale, intimate—set on a side table, or in a little conversation corner, ready to send off the evening with a nightcap. And, done right, it’s just brilliant: I like this black-into-white ombre-glazed set ($160 for a carafe and two cups) from the Tunisian ceramicist Nesrine Ouertani, of NOA Atelier, or a dramatically bulbous, dramatically tapered bedside carafe set ($40 for a carafe and one cup), whose cup bottom has a clever little protrusion that makes it work as a sturdy bottle-stopper, and it also looks sleek as hell. I’m charmed, too, by this cut-glass, vintage-inspired bedside carafe ($138 for a carafe and one glass); its floral design would lend a real sense of gentility to an otherwise prosaic afternoon hydration break.

I first encountered Zojirushi’s electric countertop fish roaster ($215) last winter, at a friend’s home, and it’s haunted me ever since. I found it simultaneously absurd and perfect: a tidy metal box ideally sized to broil, say, a smallish trout, or a meaty hamachi collar, with heating elements above and below, and internal reflectors for maximum crisping. Temp controls? Who needs ’em! Especially when you’ve got an ultra-lo-fi mechanical timer and an on-off switch. This device is not for everyone, but for the right person it’ll be a gift of exquisite, specific perfection.

For the bread baker: a sourdough-starter whisk ($20)—hook-shaped, small in scale, ideal for aerating and stirring in smaller containers—designed and sold by the bona-fide bread genius Andrew Janjigian, the author of the excellent new cookbook “Breaducation” ($45). For the cookie baker: a slice-and-bake-cookie-dough keeper ($35), which shapes, scores, and stores your dough, so that fresh cookies are bakeable at a moment’s notice. For the pastry cook: a five-wheel pastry cutter ($57), for making lattices, ribbons, twists, and twirls. For the baker of any stripe: Doap ($29), a silicone scrubber whose specific knobbly design seems, in my experience, to summon some strange and eldritch magick that gets all the stubborn, sticky bits of gluelike dough off your bowl, workspace, and person.
It’s a disco-hot-dog kit! ($55.) ♦
This article is periodically updated to reflect price changes and availability. Some items may have sold out.

items.title: Gifts for Discerning Design Lovers
items.description: In Vincenzo Latronico’s novella “Perfection” (originally published by Fitzcarraldo, and, in the U.S., by New York Review of Books), Tom and Anna, two young digital creatives, aspire to an idealized life plucked from discerning social feeds: modernist seating i
items.author: Nicholas Blechman
paragraphs: In Vincenzo Latronico’s novella “Perfection” (originally published by Fitzcarraldo, and, in the U.S., by New York Review of Books), Tom and Anna, two young digital creatives, aspire to an idealized life plucked from discerning social feeds: modernist seating in an industrial urban loft, a black metal side table with the latest issue of Monocle, an Anglepoise lamp with house plants positioned just so to look like the pages of Apartamento. The writing is deliberately superficial and deeply relatable—a painfully accurate depiction of a curated life that feels only ever quasi-real. What are the things that become meaningful over time, and that last? Which objects do I like enough to give to the people I love? The objects listed here come from the studios of friends, designers, illustrators, and makers I admire. They follow some of Dieter Rams’s principles of good design: they are utilitarian, durable, minimalist, and aesthetic.

Warning: some of the items are made in limited quantities and will sell out quickly, but I encourage you to browse the sites they are listed on. Labour and Wait, Best Made, Wms & Co., and Florentine are among my favorite sources for gift-giving.

The most prominent object on our kitchen table is an analog calendar. Filling out my family’s daily pursuits (Ultimate Frisbee practice, choir lessons, dinners out) is a family ritual. Manufactum sells a minimalist weekly calendar ($19) that is our organizational bible. Crispin Finn makes a wall calendar ($39) for the entire year that’s aesthetic enough to function as a poster. Seeing the whole year at once is a wonderful way to visualize time. John Lennon was a devout user of the New Yorker Desk Diary ($60), which includes cartoons and covers of the magazine, in addition to a monthly planner. Best Made, which began as a shop centered on high-end painted axes, sells a traditional Japanese daily calendar ($68) that includes the lunar phases and zodiac signs; it’s screen-printed by hand, with bold typography on a semitransparent vellum. You can see the next day underneath, as if peering into the future. Or, instead of starting each day with a number, begin with an image—a watercolor landscape, or a witty drawing—with the illustrator Christoph Niemann’s new calendar Every Day ($52). The celebrated Dutch designer Karel Martens uses metal shapes and found objects to create abstract and colorful numerals in Every Day Is a New Day ($45).

Designers tend to be obsessed with watches because they are both aesthetic and utilitarian, equal parts form and function. The legendary graphic designer Tibor Kalman (who created Colors magazine) designed a collection of watches in the nineties that are now being reissued as they were originally produced, by M & Co Labs ($250). One of the watch designs, Askew, playfully scrambles the positions of the numbers; Onomatopoeia replaces numerals for tiny spot drawings; and the most minimal design, 10-1-4, in a classic exercise of the design mantra “Less is more,” uses only three numbers. (It’s in the MOMA design collection.) No watch is coveted by designers as much as the Max Bill watch ($1,030). Bill, a Bauhaus-trained Swiss designer with work in the permanent collection of MOMA, created this piece for the German company Junghans, in 1960. It is exceptionally elegant and restrained, with every line and mark carefully considered. I’ve always loved military watches for their no-nonsense design and easy-to-read numerals knocking out of a black background, like the instruments in the cockpit of an old airplane, and my favorite on the market is made by the Canadian company Marathon ($575). One thing that makes military watches so fun is that you can demilitarize them by customizing the bands with bright colors through the Strap Tailor ($37). On a larger scale, Mondaine makes an iconic wall clock ($345) using a design developed for the Swiss Railways. Mine hangs on the kitchen wall and keeps my family on track. In an expression of Swiss precision, the red second hand is the most prominent element. If you are not really in it to tell time, the German artist Sarah Illenberger makes Slowlex ($845). It’s a piece of jewelry disguised as a watch, and completely nonfunctional. It’s subversive, sexy, and literally timeless.

My favorite kinds of gifts, to receive and to offer, are from art-supply stores. The Toronto Ink Company offers handmade inks ($25-$32) using elements from the urban environment: rich hues of blue from oxidized metals, and old railway spikes foraged from the streets of Toronto. Sample color swatches, called “test prints,” are works of art in themselves. Inks are useless without paper, and I always have a few sketchbooks stacked on my desk ready for use. My favorite is a German Pasteboard sketchbook ($20-$40), made with a blank chipboard cover, a bright cloth spine in a selection of Bauhaus colors (red, yellow, and blue), and natural white paper suitable for ink drawing. Because of the cloth binding, it opens flat. The typesetter in me loves the Japanese rubber-stamp set ($147), possibly drawn by hand in a serif font similar to Cheltenham Condensed, sold by Wms & Co. Beyond the creative potential (think of the rubber-stamp drawings of Saul Steinberg), it would make an eye-catching object on your shelf or desk. Another printmaking gift is a mini linocut set ($41), sold at the British home-goods store Labour and Wait. It has everything you need to print multiple editions of whatever you design. Create your own holiday card! The holy grail of mini ballpoint pens is the Lamy Pico ($39), available in neon colors, and half the size of a normal pen, with a sleek design and an ingenious telescopic mechanism for releasing the tip. Pantone, a universal system for accurately specifying colors, and worshipped by designers and printers around the world, sells a straightforward ruler ($29). It comes in a variety of colors (of course), and would look great on any desk; my favorites are Red 2035 and Yellow 012.

For most of the nineties, my wardrobe was black (with the occasional navy so dark that it might as well have been black). Since then, I’ve been on a mission to bring more color into my life. One of the most stunning pieces of product design I’ve come across is the Tex-Lock ($169), a cloth-covered bicycle lock designed by art students in Leipzig. It’s theft-proof: saw blades get ensnared in the fabric covering, and clippers can’t cut through the fibres. The lock comes in bright orange and looks good looped around your neck during transit.

Anticipating the colder weather about to descend on New York, you might check out the Dutch furnishing brand Suite702’s reinvention of the hot-water bottle ($62). The unique rounded-rectangle shape, with bold colors and racing stripes, may just make you want to hibernate. But, if you decide to brave the elements, keep in mind the German proverb “There is no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing.” Lloyd’s made-to-order Canadian-fleece toque with a massive brim ($62) will make you feel invincible. My favorite colors are red and “epoca” blue. To fill in awkward silences at holiday cocktail parties, the San Francisco artist Tucker Nichols created a set of hand-lettered napkins ($36), printed in pink and red, on linen, with suggested topics of conversation: “Where birds go in big storms,” “fear of escalators,” “smog v. fog.” As a companion piece, he designed subjects to avoid: “Root Canals,” “When was the last time you wore that sweater,” “Cloth diapers.” I was happy to discover that Karel Martens also collaborated, with Suite702, on a series of modernist towels with bold stripes and blocks of color ($28-$229), inspired by the colors on the beach in Le Havre, France. On the other side of the Channel, in Cornwall, the illustrator Tabby Booth designed the Odessa throw ($250), for Slowdown Studio, depicting a mermaid staring at a red fish. It’s remarkably primitive, and powerful.

To draw, I need a really good light. Anglepoise invented the now ubiquitous and widely imitated adjustable-spring desk lamp in the nineteen-thirties. Paul Smith refreshed the design by introducing primary colors to the steel arms of the Type 75 Mini Desk Lamp ($370). This simple design move transforms an understated lamp into a fun object. Another great use of color can be found in the Dutch coffee-brewing machines made by Moccamaster ($369). Designed in the nineteen-sixties to bring high-quality brewing to Scandinavian homes, the red, orange, yellow, and green machines are surely intended as an antidote to the monochromatic, dark Nordic winters. They remind me of the colorful houses often seen in traditional Scandinavian towns. For those who drink tea, the Japanese enamel kettle Noda Horo ($41), with its simple forms and bright colors, is another design classic. If you want to make this gift more special, pair it with Taiwanese tea ($8-$46) from Té Company, a shop in the West Village. Florentine sells an affordable designer butter knife ($35) engraved with an abstract illustration by Oded Webman, which transforms a mundane kitchen utensil into a small work of art. Its dull edge and playful motif make it suitable for children. The Kiridashi knife ($128), sold through Best Made, looks more dangerous. Unlike a jackknife, it has a penlike cap (also known as a scabbard cap). Made of steel, iron, and magnolia wood, the knife has an elemental quality, and adheres to Rams’s principle “Good design is as little design as possible.”

After my cloth pencil cases deteriorated, owing to wear and tear and leaking black ink, I upgraded to a steel box ($39) from Toyo. I pack pens, brushes, erasers, inks, pencils, and earbuds in this box, but it can hold anything, and versatility is one of its virtues. It’s also lightweight and durable. (I’ve had mine for two years, and it does not have a scratch.) The box comes in a variety of colors and sizes, and is handcrafted in Japan in a retro style. As someone who tends to lose art supplies, I can tell you that this inexpensive item has improved my life. Another Japanese steel company, Nakamura Seiko, makes a beautifully proportioned toolbox ($48). Not as bulky as those from heavy-duty American brands such as Stanley, it comes in bright powder-coated red, green, and blue. Conceal a bottle of locally distilled Kings County Bourbon ($23-$84) inside for a bonus surprise.

The extra-large River Café tote bag ($54), from Ruthie Rogers’s legendary London restaurant, is the perfect urban bag for running errands. Whether Yves Klein blue or bright yellow, this bag radiates joy. Ruthie’s late husband, the architect Richard Rogers, incorporated color into all of his buildings, notably the Pompidou Center, and I can’t help but think that his ethos is woven into the fabric of this bag. The designer Deborah Ehrlich, known for her exquisitely sculpted handblown glassware, released a super-light travel bag ($750) made of reused sails. Because sails are made to withstand gale-force winds, the bag is structurally strong, yet looks light and luminous. Ehrlich is not the first to make bags from old sails, but she is the first to make them this refined. They’re handcrafted in Florence with sustainably made materials, including leather from Blue Hill at Stone Barns. ♦
This article is periodically updated to reflect price changes and availability. Some items may have sold out.
An earlier version of this article included an inaccurate price for the watches sold by M & Co Labs.

items.title: The Best Gifts for Kids Are Small. Or Big. Or Lots. Or Stomp
items.description: When you are a kid, time can seem to organize itself around occasions for receiving treats—and, above all, presents. This is not because children are materialistic monsters (mostly) but because they have a limited ability to treat themselves. Generally speakin
items.author: Molly Fischer
paragraphs: When you are a kid, time can seem to organize itself around occasions for receiving treats—and, above all, presents. This is not because children are materialistic monsters (mostly) but because they have a limited ability to treat themselves. Generally speaking, an eight-year-old cannot reward herself, at the end of a tough week, by doing a little window-shopping and deciding that she deserves a cute bag, or its third-grade equivalent (glowing slime?). The calendar can become a series of buildups and letdowns around the prospect of surprise delights. This is the golden age of gift-getting. No one cares as much about presents as kids do. No pressure!

Fortunately, choosing a gift for a child comes with fewer shades of social nuance than picking something for an adult. The goal is pure pleasure, not a statement or message; the worst-case scenario is indifference or mild disappointment—not, say, horror at your fundamental misunderstanding of a long-standing personal relationship. You are going for FUN. Think about the experience of seeing the present and opening the present, and about whom the present is actually going to please.

If you are buying a present for a person who lacks object permanence, that present is for their parents. Shop with this fact in mind. Clothes are an excellent gift, in a way that they won’t be again until the child’s adolescence—here is your chance to jazz up the Center of the Universe. Buy something that’s more expensive than anyone thinking about the cost of child care could justify buying themselves, but that’s still functional enough for everyday use. No to tiny buttons, the color white, and lace; yes to $64 balloon pants. Yes to leopard-print anything. (It’ll hide stains!) Yes to seasonally appropriate comical hats ($55-$99).

Parents spend a lot of time gazing upon their babies (how would the Center of the Universe look in pink sunglasses?), and they also spend a lot of time reading to their babies, at least if they are overachieving millennials who have imbibed the requisite parenting expertise. It is important that they have books to read aloud that are not bad. My husband, a bookseller, often notes that most books are bad, and this may be doubly true for children’s books, whose brevity leads foolhardy would-be authors to underestimate the difficulty of their task. Before you give a children’s book, think: Is this book fun to read aloud? Will it be fun to read aloud twelve million times? Rhythm counts for everything, subject matter for almost nothing. Babies do not care about “art” or “science,” and you can’t make them. What you’re after here is fluid prose and pictures that contain lots of interesting items to identify and talk about. There’s a reason everyone already has “Goodnight Moon.” Instead, consider “The House in the Night,” by Susan Marie Swanson, or “All the World,” by Liz Garton Scanlon, both sold in chompable board-book editions. Richard Scarry’s “I Am a Bunny,” though not explicitly bedtime-oriented, is another durable hit. (If you want to give a new parent something to read to themselves, consider “And Now We Have Everything,” by Meaghan O’Connell, a funny and unsparing account of parenthood’s earliest days.) ($9-$40)

As for toys: true infants are scarcely capable of “play” in any sense that requires accessories or equipment; they’re still realizing that they have hands. Something with fabric that produces a crinkly sound ($10) when pawed inexpertly is pretty much the upper limit of possibility.

Not long ago, my husband and I asked our three-and-a-half-year-old what we should get his grandfather as an eightieth-birthday present. “Cars and cars and cars and cars and cars,” he replied. It was an instructive answer: the sorts of gifts that people imagine giving others are a good indication of the gifts that they themselves enjoy receiving. In general, I’m all for quality, but when attempting to please a small child there’s something to be said for quantity. Sheer, dazzling quantity: cars and cars and cars and cars and cars ($7-$30). Present them loose in a bag or in a box; remember that it’s always nice to have spares to lose, or for a visitor to take home.

By a similar token, stickers and stickers and stickers and stickers and stickers ($9-$31). The recipient can stick them on a giant roll of paper ($33) (how giant? That’s up to you), taped out on the floor. The effect is something like an off-season approximation of a sidewalk, and, your winter climate permitting, sidewalk chalk (tons of it, for $18) is another good option. And books are not excluded from the thrill of scale. Richard Scarry’s “Biggest Word Book Ever!” ($45)—about twenty-four by thirty-two inches when wide open—is irresistibly grand, full of many quintessentially busy Scarry characters, and large enough for a small reader to literally climb inside.

The appeal of something to climb inside is a valuable reminder of another language that kid gifts can speak: the charm of little. It can be fun to be small and to feel small, and this is why it is nice to build forts. Technically, doing so only requires a blanket, but you don’t need a gift guide to direct you to your linen closet. Expand your household’s fort horizons with the Nugget ($249-$299), a “play couch” made of sturdy, rearrangeable cushions that can be used to construct cozy reading corners and nooks for playing pretend. (A chair called the Smore, at $199-$239, from the same company, offers a similar concept, with a smaller footprint.)

It is also fun simply to think about small things. And so, to stock the fort’s library: the author and illustrator Phoebe Wahl produces books full of magical tiny beings, stories that are beautiful and sweet without being precious or twee. “Little Witch Hazel: A Year in the Forest” ($20) collects four stories—one for each season—about a witch who lives in a mossy stump and is small enough to ride on the back of an owl. Her friends and neighbors include the Mole Sisters, Mousepappa, and a frog named Wendell (who might plausibly have been named for Wendell Berry). Wahl’s “Backyard Fairies” ($19) depicts a kid who is sure that there are fairies just out of sight, in the woods behind her house, and tries to find them. For children inclined to such expeditions—or who just want to read in a dark spot—a camping headlamp ($35) makes an inexhaustibly useful accessory.

Becoming a parent, and shopping for a child, is a constant reminder that everything and nothing changes. I can easily recall the joy of forts; I would have loved “Backyard Fairies.” Yet certain stalwart kid pleasures have been reimagined in the intervening decades. Take training wheels and tricycles: they’re out. Now children have balance bikes, which are two-wheelers without pedals—an arrangement that supposedly makes for an easier transition to riding the real thing. Based on the anecdotal evidence of my local playground, I’m convinced. The little guys get good at gliding, fast. These new versions of that classic Big Present, a bike, can be procured from such manufacturers as Guardian ($169) and Woom ($249) (branding keyed to a target market of anxious parents).

Even crayon technology has somehow improved in the years since I was coloring. Have you tried gel crayons ($20)? Instead of hard and waxy, they’re as soft as oil pastels, but miraculously smudge-proof once dry, with colors bright and opaque enough to draw on dark construction paper. And, for kids approaching the age of phones, Tin Can ($100) has given the humble landline a contemporary reinvention: it permits calls to preselected phone numbers using home Wi-Fi, and has (yes) a cord.

When I set out to make a list of gifts for kids, there was only one thing I was sure I wanted to include. If you take nothing else from this guide, know this: a Stomp Rocket ($30) is the perfect present.

One kid can have fun with a Stomp Rocket; two kids can execute some impressive teamwork; three or four kids can share effortlessly. The learning curve is nonexistent. The payoff is immediate. The only way to improve it is to buy extra rockets ($10), which you should do. (And do not go off-brand with these—you want genuine Stomp product. Amazon imitations can get stuck on the launch tube, an unacceptable defect, and one that I discovered the hard way.) I have never seen a group of children get bored of a Stomp Rocket. I have seen a group of adults sipping early-evening drinks on a patio, idly Stomping and chatting, enjoying the beginning of a spring thaw and the return of sunlight. ♦
This article is periodically updated to reflect price changes and availability. Some items may have sold out.

items.title: What 2026 Means for Democrats in 2028
items.description: The unexpectedly big wave election of 2026 has understandably lifted Democratic spirits everywhere, in part simply because Donald Trump will spend the last two years of his presidency dealing with a Congress that isn’t inclined to do him any favors. We are als
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The unexpectedly big wave election of 2026 has understandably lifted Democratic spirits everywhere, in part simply because Donald Trump will spend the last two years of his presidency dealing with a Congress that isn’t inclined to do him any favors. We are also already in the throes of a wide-open 2028 presidential contest that will give Democratic voters a lot of options for the first time since the pandemic election of 2020.

But before parading too far down the road to total victory, Democrats should take a look at the historical precedents for how the party that wins big in midterms fares in subsequent presidential elections. Midterm wins, even big waves, haven’t necessarily carried over to the next presidential election. There are two post-World War II examples that make this point with particular force.

In 1946, Republicans flipped both congressional chambers, adding 12 Senate seats and 55 House seats. There was lots of talk about the New Deal Era ending and a new period of conservative ascendancy, particularly with Democrats deeply divided over civil rights and the Cold War. Harry Truman, an “accidental president” who had ascended to the Oval Office on the death of FDR, had job approval ratings in the low 30s just prior to those midterms.

So what happened in 1948? Truman was reelected, carrying 28 states and piling up over 300 electoral votes, and Democrats re-flipped Congress, gaining nine Senate seats and an incredible 75 House seats.

Another example of a big post-midterm U-turn occurred in 1982. As unemployment soared and Washington went into shock over the new Reagan administration’s radical tax and social policies (and its unprecedented use of an all-powerful new tool called budget reconciliation), Democrats made big midterm gains in the House. They won the national House popular vote by 11.8 percent (nearly as large as the 2026 win) and added 26 seats, giving them a 269-165 majority, larger than the one they will take into 2028.
So what happened in 1984? Ronald Reagan carried 49 states (including New York, Massachusetts, Illinois, and California) and won the popular vote by 18 percent.

There’s no obvious pattern connecting these two examples of big midterm wins turning into big presidential losses. In 1948, Truman managed to turn his own reelection campaign into a referendum on the record of the “do-nothing 80th Congress,” while exploiting fears that a triumphant GOP would repeal popular elements of the New Deal, especially farm price stabilization programs. Yet four years later the pro-GOP trend that was so evident in 1946 resumed with Dwight D. Eisenhower’s landslide election, accompanied by a reconquest of Congress. In 1984, the country was undergoing a strong economic recovery (hence Reagan’s “Morning in America” thematics) and a partisan realignment of the South (which had been temporarily interrupted by Jimmy Carter) towards the GOP was fully underway. It took until 1992 for Democrats to retake the White House with a southern candidate who also represented a fresh ideological take on liberalism.

There have been other occasions when positive midterm trends continued right on into the next presidential election. In the 1962 midterms, with JFK in the White House, Democrats held their own (gaining a few Senate seats, losing a few House seats), and then two years later LBJ headed up a massive Democratic landslide.

Perhaps the most promising midterm-to-presidential precedent for Democrats was quite recent: Democrats followed up their big 2006 gains (flipping Congress and winning the National House popular vote by eight percent) with Barack Obama’s breakthrough presidential win. He won the popular vote by 7.3 percent, and Democrats gained 21 House seats (winning the House national popular vote by 10.6 percent) and eight Senate seats — momentarily giving their party both a mandate and the means to accomplish big things like the Affordable Care Act. In both 1964 and 2008, Democrats were aided by a feckless opposition and built an unusually broad–and as it happens, entirely temporary–voter coalition (both 1966 and 2010 were banner years for the GOP, in part because there was so much low-hanging fruit in the way of Democrats occupying hostile territory).

The abiding lesson is that parties enjoying a midterm wave election cannot rest on their laurels, and need to pay attention to the underpinnings of their majority. Today it would behoove Democrats to take a long look at the swing voters who backed Trump in 2024 and then repudiated him in 2026. For the most part, these voters aren’t fond of Democrats either, and must be persuaded to vote Democratic in a presidential election that involves a choice rather than a referendum.

No matter what happens in the presidential election of 2028, however, Democrats remain likely to hang onto their control of Congress for at least another two years. Big swings in House and Senate contests occur most often in midterms. In fact, the last time either party lost control of the House in a presidential election year was in 1952. Heading into 2028 with a House majority of 40 seats or more makes a flip of that chamber very unlikely. Meanwhile, the Senate landscape for 2028 looks much less forbidding for Democrats than the 2026 map on which they so massively over-performed, particularly given their cushion of five to six seats:

Yes, big changes in the Senate have occasionally happened in presidential election years, notably 1980 (when Ronald Reagan trounced Jimmy Carter and Republicans won every single close Senate race, netting an incredible 12 seats) and 2008 (when Democrats won a fragile Senate super-majority after gaining eight seats). So it would be prudent of Democrats to choose at least a competitive presidential candidate in 2028. If they pick a winner, then a governing trifecta is almost certain to follow.
