items.title: Anatomy of a Torch Pass: Like Father, Like Son
items.description: Where have all the male pop stars gone? The internet certainly wonders. There are think pieces and Reddit debates all centered on the idea that we, as a music-consuming public, have spent this decade deprived of male pop stars. I’m not sure I buy that, though.
items.author: Joan Summers
paragraphs: Where have all the male pop stars gone? The internet certainly wonders. There are think pieces and Reddit debates all centered on the idea that we, as a music-consuming public, have spent this decade deprived of male pop stars. I’m not sure I buy that, though.

The boundaries of who a pop star is, or what a pop star is considered to be, have only continued to expand with time. Pop itself has become increasingly decentralized, focusing on microgenres and subcultures, which makes the Main Pop Boys a little harder to discern. Kendrick Lamar is a pop star. A.G. Cook is a pop star.

But the same kind of Pop Motherdom family tree exists with fathers and sons, too (the fully realized tree itself isn’t ruled by gender, but more on that soon.) Most importantly, ‘50s rocker Little Richard is a crown atop any and all flow charts concerning pop influence. His rambunctious stage persona, his theatrics, his capes and his pompadour inspired everyone from Elvis to Bowie to Prince. There would be no male pop stars without Little Richard.

Much of today’s discourse surrounds who seems to be copying whom, rather than who is mothering (fathering) whom. Benson Boone’s jumpsuits and sparkles got him coined Mormon Harry Styles, while Yungblud’s leather pants, eyeliner-clad, sweaty onstage persona often gets him referred to as Evil Harry Styles, or an Even Eviler Matty Healy (Healy himself is undoubtedly a Brian Eno/Peter Gabriel/Mick Jagger lovechild.) Someone like Justin Bieber has sons who have evolved as his sound has, slowly moving out of Shawn Mendes territory and into Mk.gee and The Kid LAROI land.

So what follows aren’t perfect mirrors as much as spirits of: So-and-so is the so-and-so of the 2020s. And boy, did our last list cause all sorts of conversation! (We're looking right at you, Pop Base and Pop Crave!)

Remember, these lists are not definitive, or final. It is starkly gendered in a way that doesn’t necessarily align with reality or leave room for nuance. Influence is not bound by gender; gender is just part of this specific form.
And so, without any more ado, let’s discourse!
Paul McCartney & Harry Styles

The Boyband Heartthrob to Most Successful Solo Act pipeline is alive and well in Paul and Hazza. Both Head Bitches of their respective groups, McCartney and Styles have each grown into the most corporatized of their former bandmates (you rarely catch either without a PR-approved response on the tip of their tongue) with a kind of machine approach to music output that still remains explorative. Harry Styles is McCartney’s Band on the Run (in their expected lane, maybe a little more rock-centric than their group work), where Kiss All The Time is full-blown McCartney II “Temporary Secretary.” This one feels so aligned and uncanny that it almost feels like cheating.
Julian Casablancas & Cameron Winter

Yes, Julian Casablancas and Cameron Winter look kind of similar. But this pairing is more than that. It’s in their New York nepo-adjacentness, in how young they both were when their respective bands took off (Casablancas was 23 when Is This It dropped; Winter was 21 for Geese’s 3D Country and 22 when he dropped Heavy Metal), and in both exuding their own kinds of frontman energy from the jump. The way Winter slips between Geese and his solo work mirrors how Casablancas moved through his career, dropping solo LPs and later forming a whole different group with The Voidz. Winter’s presence ensures Casablancas’s New York City rock lives on.

If Daddy Yankee broke reggaeton and Latin pop into the mainstream, Bad Bunny launched it into the stratosphere. Benito has repeatedly cited Ramón Rodriguez as a source of inspiration since the start of his career, and they feel like two harbingers of Latin pop for two different generations of listeners. With “Gasolina” and the rest of his 2004 LP Barrio Fino, Daddy Yankee helped transform reggaeton into a global commercial force, bringing club-focused energy and dembow rhythms into the undeniable mainstream. Bad Bunny has since surpassed Daddy Yankee in popularity and longevity (the latter feels stuck in time, with a recent pivot toward Christianity, while the former is primed for a decades-long career), but his career feels like a second coming of the Latin hip-hop renaissance that Daddy Yankee kicked off in the early aughts. They both approach their music with a multifaceted mix of loverboydom, grit and pointed cultural commentary.

The more I look into Elvis and Bruno Mars, the more I think Mars is the definitive Elvis incarnate. In 1991, a six-year-old Mars went on the Arsenio Hall Show dressed in a full blue studded jumpsuit to flaunt his Elvis impersonation. He was the youngest Elvis impersonator of his time, and in the years since, he’s built a career almost as massive and notorious as The King himself, keeping and morphing some of Elvis’s most well-known iconography (his quiff, his aviators) for the 2010s. And he’s certainly followed in his footsteps in a mid-to-late-career pivot to Vegas residencies. (Elvis did 636 sold out shows at the Westgate in seven years, while Mars, who just completed his ninth year at Park MGM, has done over 100. Both grossed in the hundreds of millions.) Elvis’s inexplicable attachment to Mars’s home state of Hawaii makes it all the more uncanny.
Calvin Harris & KAYTRANADA

words to share on X (then Twitter) about Calvin Harris: “Like straight up, pop stars and edm dj collabs are like boiled chicken with no-seasoning,” referring to Harris’s songs with everyone from Ellie Goulding to Dua Lipa to Rihanna. He later elaborated, saying, “The pop stars collab with the big edm djs…. MUSICALLY it hasn’t evolve[d] since 2011. All I’m saying is that it would’ve been much cooler to see someone on the come-up collaborating w/ them instead of doing the same thing.”

But I’d argue that Kaytranada operates similarly to Harris, albeit with more experimentation and genre-bending (he seems to have followed his own advice.) Kaytranada’s responsible for a similar mainstream-ification of R&B descendant, turntable-centric club pop to what Harris was with 2010s dance music; Kaytranada’s Rihanna and Ellie are Kali Uchis, H.E.R., Ravyn Lenae, Tinashe and Rochelle Jordan. Both know how to work a hook, make a catchy tune and flaunt their collaborators’ strengths. They’re more alike than maybe even Kaytranada would like to admit — and that’s not a bad thing!
Michael Jackson & The Weeknd

Michael Jackson’s presence, good and bad, is felt in endless facets of the music industry. Any time someone has impeccable dance skills, takes creative risks in music videos or drops an album that disrupts genres and tingles ears. But his spirit, and the complicated legacy attached to it, lives on most obviously in The Weeknd. (A horrific legacy too, no fault of Tesfaye, in light of resurfaced allegations from Jackson's victims.)

Still, like Jackson, Abel Tesfaye has grown into one of the biggest acts in modern music history, his blend of R&B and dance pop making him one of the most listened to artists of this generation (he recently became the first artist to have 30 songs on Spotify with over one billion streams, and at 5.2B streams, “Blinding Lights” is the most listened to song on the platform.) Their falsetto-leaning vocals blend with their crisp, sleek production, and both expanded from more traditional R&B into increasingly maximalist, synthpop-adjacent work over time, while also foraying into film, TV, and other multimedia-centric projects throughout their careers (Tesfaye in Uncut Gems; Jackson in The Wiz and Moonwalker).
George Michael & Troye Sivan

The definitive and self-proclaimed “Father Figure,” George Michael (his artistry, songwriting and overall career) is integral to why and how artists like Troye Sivan exist today — and can exist so unequivocally out.

Sivan’s music mirrors the emotional depth that’s at the core of so many of Michael’s songs (especially post-AIDS crisis, post-being outed.) Tracks like “How To Stay With You” and “One of Your Girls” hide vulnerability in funkier club beats. The former, specifically, hit a certain part of the 2020s pop sphere as I imagine “Careless Whisper” did for the ‘80s mainstream.
Dijon has unintentionally filled a Frank Ocean void in the 2020s, and I didn’t realize how many people feel the same way until I dug deeper into their paths.

Both of them deal with heartbreak and anguish with poeticism; their music is centered on love but is emotionally expansive, diving into the more specific emotions that lie beneath. Both of their music feels like dream states, warm and fuzzy like you could wrap yourself in a sweater of their sounds. Faraway vocals and slowed, molasses-type ambiance mix with endless reverb and bleeding instrumentation. Their catalogs and collaborations show a genreless approach to songwriting, Dijon leaning into guitar-based, rootsy Americana (across Absolutely and in his production work with Bon Iver), while Ocean toyed with rap and hip-hop with Odd Future in his early years and A$AP Rocky later on.

If any of these father-son pairs are evil renditions, The Dare is categorically Evil Gen Z Mark Ronson. These two producer-forward, DJ-adjacent, NYC lore-fests have made their own impact on pop with their solo discographies, but more importantly, with their production work. While Ronson has worked with Dua Lipa, Lady Gaga and Amy Winehouse, The Dare’s hyperpop flirtations with Charli XCX, PinkPantheress and ADÉLA have made him left-of-center pop’s favorite collaborator. I’m not sure if we’ll see Harrison on the next Barbie soundtrack, but maybe he’ll be on Jordan Firstman’s nonexistent-but-probably-already-in-the-works Club Kid follow-up.

Bruno Mars, son of Elvis, is also, almost unavoidably, a father to many. But no son is more legitimate than Benson Boone. Boone is spiritually Bruno Mars, even if people conflate him with Harry Styles. It’s in the way I'm force-fed their music in grocery stores and airports everywhere. The way they both have undeniably strong voices (Boone covering Adele really did something to me.) But their songs just couldn’t fall flatter, couldn’t feel more like staring into a commercialized pop void.
Tell me you can’t picture Boone doing endless Vegas residencies in 15 years, backflipping into oblivion.

Prince built an entire career around refusing categorization, never staying in one place sonically long enough for everyone else to catch up to him. Chaz Bear takes this sensibility into Toro y Moi, blending and morphing between funk, rap, indie rock and psych pop (Bear has noted that Prince’s drums had a specific impact on his drum programming.) Born in the ‘80s, Bear takes to the time’s synth emphasis and hyper-electric, wah-heavy guitar tones. Mood and momentum drive each of their sounds, both artists maintaining a kind of ubiquitous presence where you broadly know what you’re gonna get, even if it could realistically sound like anything.

I actually don’t care if Shawn Mendes is two years younger than ROLE MODEL. I literally could not care less. You just can’t tell me Tucker Pilsbury isn’t the 2020’s version of “Lost in Japan”-era Shawn Mendes. It’s in their white boy of the month-ness, the way I can barely tell their songs apart, the way they permeated into cultural consciousness almost without a trace. And most importantly, the way their relationships are constantly superseding their musical output.

items.title: The Method-Dressing Madness Behind Mckenna Grace‘s 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Press Tour Looks
items.description: Before the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour began, Mckenna Grace knew she wanted to be method dressed for her appearances. Made a household term by Law Roach and Zendaya, method dressing is when actors wear looks that pay homage to the film or s
items.author: Wisdom Iheanyichukwu
paragraphs: Before the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour began, Mckenna Grace knew she wanted to be method dressed for her appearances. Made a household term by Law Roach and Zendaya, method dressing is when actors wear looks that pay homage to the film or show they’re promoting: See Zendaya’s on-theme looks across red carpets for Dune, Spiderman, and The Odyssey for a slew of examples.

With the new Hunger Games film, it’s Grace’s turn to adopt the trend. A super fan of the Suzanne Collins book series and their film adaptations, Grace—who plays District 12 tribute Maysilee Donner—took a hand in the styling for her press run, weaving easter eggs into every look. Her stylist, Molly Dickson, was up for the challenge of translating Grace’s deep-cut references into custom and archival looks from Monique Lhuillier, Gucci, Celine and more.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Dickson breaks down all the looks that set the Hunger Games fans’ hearts aflame, from Rue’s blue dress to Katniss’ Mockingjay gown, and all the threads that came together for Grace’s most memorable press appearances yet.
Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

Molly Dickson: I went to college in Minnesota and my major was advertising. Two weeks before I graduated, I called my mom and said, "I'm not into this. I don't wanna do advertising." She said, "Well, what do you wanna do?" I told her, "I wanna do fashion. I wanna go to New York." She said, "No, absolutely not."

Right after I graduated, I went to LA, this was 2009 during the recession, and no one was hiring. I got an internship at Marie Claire in New York, and enrolled back into college to get school credit to intern at Hearst. I worked at Marie Claire as a market assistant for almost two years, and then I left and assisted Leslie Fremar for seven years. That's when I fell in love with celebrity. Then ten years ago, I went off on my own.
What would you say are your aesthetic influences as a stylist?

My personal style relates very similarly to Sadie Sink's style, very effortless. She always wants to be very comfortable and easy, never anything frilly or over the top. Just a simple, beautiful dress, and you let it speak for itself.
Mckenna is a big fan of the original film series, so it’s clear you’re pulling from there as influences when dressing her. Is it a collaborative process when coming to one of these referential looks?

She's obviously a very huge fan of the franchise. We actually started having conversations about this tour in April, which is very early to start having conversations. I could just sense her excitement around it. She started sending me mood boards, and I actually looked back today at the mood board and it was, it was a lot of Katniss Everdeen. It had Joanna on it, and it was filled with these really strong female characters from the franchise.
What she really wanted to hit was Katniss’ wedding gown look and the Mockingjay look with the wings. I was really stumped on how to pull that off without making it overly costumey.

Mckenna kept asking, "What's going on with those?" I knew the vision, but I didn't know how to execute it. I was working with Keke Palmer and the designer Michael Ngo. He was making some cool music costumes for Keke, and I asked, "Michael, could you make this silver piece?" 'Cause I really had no idea how to get it done.

He said, “I don't think I can do that. You know what? Just give me a day, let me play around with it." That night, he said, "I figured it out." We got the piece and I thought, "Okay, it needs to be a wedding dress under,” so I reached out to all the bridal houses. I wanted it to be vintage because it would tell a pretty story. Monique [Lhuillier] ended up sending a ton of wedding gowns, and the day before Mckenna came in for the fitting, I actually tried the wedding dresses on myself with the silver piece.

I sent Mckenna five dresses, and the one that she ended up wearing, she said, "That's it. I don't even need to try anything else. That's the one I'm gonna wear." Then, it was a matter of finding the right event to wear it to because it’s pretty nice, very dramatic.

She was in Paris for the Miu Miu show, and I brought it there because she had the Hunger Games Museum event. It was a whole conversation with her team, like, "Is it the right moment? Is it too much for this event?" Her PR said, "No, this is the perfect moment. It's the best way to kick off the tour." The response with the Hunger Games fans—I have never seen anything like it before, ever.
What was the experience of having her be such a big part of the styling process?

It makes my job so fun because she is so passionate about it and she loves Hunger Games so much, even just finding subtle nods back to the movie. She would say, "I wanna do a ladybug look." Thom Browne did that amazing ladybug dress, I thought, "That's so cool, but it's not really her personal aesthetic." So it’s finding ways to keep it still true to her personal style while maintaining the nods to the film.

The way you seem to understand Mckenna feels something similar to the connection between Katniss and Cinna in The Hunger Games. When pulling looks for her, what comes into play? How do you make her come through and not be lost in the lore of the stories or the dress?

Mckenna had said that she maybe wanted to do a red or a dark pink feather look because in the books [Maysilee] gets attacked by the red birds which are like flamingos. I'm pulling in all these red feather dresses and on the runway, this one dress looked amazing. Mckenna said, “That's perfect for the flamingo reference.”

But we put it on her and it was so big, and she's so petite so she was just getting swarmed. I said, “Let"s not force it.” The goal was for her to feel comfortable in the look rather than just getting each reference.
The public has been really excited about these looks. Are you thinking about the response to the looks when you’re putting them together?
There's been some conversations in a fitting, like, "Oh, the Hunger Games fans are gonna get this." They're gonna see the inspiration, they're gonna understand it.

But I wouldn't say we're choosing a look because ‘Oh, this is gonna go viral to the Hunger Games community.’ Mckenna is a super fan herself so if she's getting excited about the look, everyone else that's a fan of the franchise is gonna get excited about the look.
Do you feel any pressure to top the last outfit after each premiere?

Yes. I think it was Paris because that wedding dress did get so much press. In that fitting, it felt like, "We gotta keep our game up high." It's been really fun for my team and market assistants because a lot of the girls that work with me are huge fans of the movie. They're not even seeing it as work. They're like, "Oh my God, this is so exciting. Look at this. This looks like this from the movie."
What was the inspiration to do method dressing for this press run? What do you think is the value?

Mckenna knew back in April, she said, "I wanna do method for this." I personally did not read the books. I'm a visual person, so I've seen all the movies. Lionsgate was able to let me go with the cast when they first saw the movie because my agent was like, "Molly needs to go to the movie to get inspired before this press tour. She can't do a method dressing press tour without seeing the movie."
Even as the tour was going on, Mckenna kept sending me new references and quotes from the book and stuff like that.

What made you take it to the next level? From paying homage to not only characters, but the actual actors from the films like Jennifer Lawrence at the 2011 Oscars to even dressing like set pieces from the film.
That was all Mckenna's vision. On her first mood board, she had a lot of Jennifer Lawrence's red carpet moments because she's such a huge fan of Katniss and Jennifer Lawrence.

With the Rue reference, Mckenna thought that color was just very Hunger Games. It wasn't until she put the dress on, her mom said, "Wait, this is Rue's dress." So that was just fate. I would love to take credit for that.
Why do you think that this styling has generated so much attention?

I think it’s when you do method dressing for such a big franchise and you really are passionate about it. The thing is that Mckenna is so excited and passionate about this movie. She has said, “I didn't think that I would love doing fittings so much. I used to hate doing fittings.”

Because every look is so intentionally tied back to Hunger Games and she's such a big fan, it's literally like playing dress up with her. I think the fans see it, she's so relatable because she's a fan that all these fans think, "Wow, like, she's a fan and she got to do this." She’s the fangirl living out her dream, and the fans are excited for her that she finally gets to do this.
What do you think are the best kinds of projects to implement method dressing with/works best with? What does it work best with?

I think the big movies that already have a fan base, like Barbie or Wednesday, Being able to pull inspiration from existing books or films makes it so much easier for a stylist rather than a movie that no one's seen before. There's no curiosity or momentum about it because you're starting from scratch, whereas Hunger Games, Barbie, Wednesday, there's already a level of expectation.
The looks for this press run have been a mix of archival, new, and custom pieces. How do you make that choice? How important is it for you to create an archive for Mckenna?

It kind of is a mix of what we’re able to source. McKenna really wanted to pay homage to Joanna's character with that scene where she's like, "My stylist is always putting me in trees." She's like, "I wanna do a tree reference." And I'm like, "How in the world am I gonna find a fashion reference that's a tree that's not a costume?"

I love the challenge of sourcing the market, and so do the girls on my team. I think it was 2011 Phoebe Philo where Celine did some tree references in the collection. But just because we find it online doesn't mean that we can get it. So then it's reaching out to every vintage dealer, every rental house, asking, "Do you guys have anything like this?" And they might have it, but they're like, "It's already gone, someone has it." I ended up actually finding the Celine tree dress on the RealReal, and I bought it. I love RealReal.
What is your approach to dressing different clients? For instance, you mentioned Sadie Sink earlier, can you walk me through how that process differs from Mckenna?

It's very different between each girl. I let them set the pace. If they wanna be involved, great. If they just wanna show up to the fitting and not even know what's gonna be there, I try to accommodate whatever direction they wanna go. I have one client that literally last week has sent me over 200 references of dresses that she wants, and another girl that's like, “I really don't care. Whatever you tell me to wear, I'll wear it.”

Every girl is different, and what makes my job so interesting is that it's not the same. Everyone has very different styles. I think the most important part of a job as a stylist is to keep their style true to them and not just force my style onto them. McKenna's way more girly, Sadie is a little bit more casual, it’s just taking their style and elevating it a little bit.

Will you do any looks inspired by Mckenna’s character Maysilee? The looks have been mostly referential to things and people from past stories. Are there influences of Maysilee in the looks that fans haven't been able to pick up on because the film wasn’t out yet?

In a couple days, she’ll be in Miami for press, and she's wearing a very Maysilee inspired, purple Miu Miu dress that has a white collar. When she wears it, everyone's gonna be like, "Oh, that's Maysilee." She really wanted to have flowers and necklaces because Maysilee is really into jewelry, so it’s very light and flowery.
Can you break down the outfit for the New York City premiere?

We are doing the Mockingjay dress, the one with the wings, and that was another thing that I was very stumped on. I'm like, "What designer's gonna make these wings?" I had this woman in LA who does wings, she's done Halloween costumes and music videos.

In the first fitting, I pulled this navy Pamella Roland gown. The fabric is really, really cool. It's like a shimmery kind of organza. I thought, "That's the right color,” but I wanted it to be strapless. I went back to Pamella Roland and they were like, "We can make it in strapless." Mckenna was very keen on having some sort of embellishment to replicate Katniss because she had screen printing on the gown and it kind of looks like wings in a way.

Pamela then drew all these CADs with diamond wings on it, and then we got the wings made. We did the final fitting and I almost started to cry. Her mom's taking videos and it's epic. It's so exciting because the fans were doing polls on what she's gonna wear to the premiere.
It's full circle, we started with the wedding dress, Mckenna did the fire gown, and then we ended with the Mockingjay dress.
What was the hardest look to pull together?
I think design-wise, it was the fire gown.

Getting the fire printed on the fabric was really hard. I had a while back done a custom Cong Tri gown for Cami Mendes for the Masters of the Universe tour. It was like a gold beaded gown, and I remember I really liked the fabrics that they used for it.

So when I was thinking of who could do this fire gown, I reached out to them first, and I'm like, "Can you guys do something that looks like a fire? Like, she's literally on fire." And they're like, "No. We don't think we can." And again, they were like, "Give us some time." They came back and said, "We did all these testing on the fabric." I'm like, "Yeah, you did it. You did it."

What's really funny is we were at a fitting at Mckenna's house with the fire gown in a garment bag, and one of her friends stopped by. It was just a tip of the dress showing and her friend said, "Oh my God, you got a fire gown." Then I thought, "Okay, people are gonna get it."

items.title: This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur
items.description: Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unp
items.author: Nate Freeman
paragraphs: Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unpredictable; when I went there this summer for lunch with a movie producer, we spotted a powerful name-brand media executive, an architectural bigwig who designs the homes of billionaires, and a two-time Academy Award–winning actor. A few nights later, I sat near Walter Isaacson, who’s a regular. And don’t just take it from Elon Musk’s biographer. Matthew Schneier, the chief restaurant critic at New York magazine, recently named Borgo the city’s best all-around restaurant.

On one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

The twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

After launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had shows recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.
As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

“I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”

The studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They showed figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

The studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

“It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” says Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”
Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

“I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”
He told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

“What are the processes? Like you said, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”

Diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.
“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

Tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some new development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few shows. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

“I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”

Sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

Sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”

As a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

“I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he said. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”
Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

“I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”

The show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

The showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he said. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

“I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew said, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy says. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”

Like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy says, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.
And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

“I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he said. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”
Have a tip? Drop me a line at nate_freeman@condenast.com. And make sure you subscribe to True Colors to receive Nate Freeman’s art-world dispatch in your inbox every week.

items.title: 'GTA VI' Sets New Record With Nearly $4 Billion in Sales on Launch Day
items.description: The highly anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI shattered video game sales records, earning $3.79 billion in the first 24 hours of its launch.
items.author: Cheyenne Roundtree
paragraphs: The highly anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI shattered video game sales records, earning $3.79 billion in the first 24 hours of its launch.

Already, the 13-year wait for the latest installment of the crime spree series had racked up more than 32.5 million pre-orders, according to Rockstar Games and GTA parent company Take-Two. After Thursday’s numbers came in, the companies dubbed the franchise the “highest-grossing entertainment property” and the “biggest entertainment launch in history.”

“It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Sam Houser, president and founder of Rockstar, said in a statement, per The Hollywood Reporter. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world, and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.”

GTA VI was already competing against itself for the highest release-day sales. Its predecessor, GTA V, earned $815.7 million within 24 hours of its September 2013 release, while Call of Duty: Black Ops II pulled in $500 million in its first day on shelves in November 2012.

The video game has earned rave reviews, including an aggregated score of 99 on Metacritic and perfect scores from gaming critics. “It raises the bar at every level that matters,” Gene Park wrote for The Washington Post. “Grand Theft Auto VI is the most extraordinary game I’ve ever reviewed.”

items.title: Box Office: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $56 Million on Friday, ‘I Play Rocky’ Follows With $3.8 Million
items.description: The odds were ever in the favor of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest entry in the storied franchise, which ruled the box office on Friday.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: The odds were ever in the favor of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest entry in the storied franchise, which ruled the box office on Friday.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” generated $56 million from 4,018 North American theaters on Friday, taking the No. 1 spot on its opening day. It’s a strong start for the prequel, which looks to pull in around $120 million by Sunday. (That number far exceeds the cautious $85 million start the studio had projected.)

The Francis Lawrence-directed film takes place 25 years before the original “Hunger Games” series and follows the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy as he’s forced to compete in the second Quarter Quell. Joseph Zada, McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning and more star, with appearances from original “The Hunger Games” cast members Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woodey Harleson.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is the second prequel in the series, following 2023’s “The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” which finished its theatrical run at $363 million globally, making it a commercial success against a $100 million budget. With the new release, the “Hunger Games” franchise has generated more than $3.437 billion at the worldwide box office.

Amazon MGM’s “I Play Rocky” landed in second place on Friday, grossing $3.8 million from 2477 North American theaters following its wide expansion. The film is expected to gross $9.3 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative total to $10.419 million. “I Play Rocky” previously brought in just under $1 million after two weekends in limited release.

The biopic-type film tells the true story behind the tumultuous making of the 1976 boxing classic “Rocky.” Anthony Ippolito portrays a young Sylvester Stallone, with AnnaSophia Robb, Kiki Seto, Matt Dillon, Stephan James and more also starring.

Paramount Pictures’ “Ebenezer” took the No. 3 spot with $2.04 million from 3,545 North American theaters in its second weekend in theaters. The Johnny Depp-led drama is eyeing another $7.775 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative gross to $32.62 million.

“Ebenezer” reimagines the Christmas classic “A Christmas Carol,” this time starring Depp as Scrooge. Directed by Ti West, the description simply reads: “The name you know, the story you don’t.” Alongside Depp, “Ebenezer” boasts an ensemble including Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman and Ian McKellen.

“The Cat in the Hat” followed in fourth place with $1.6 million from 3,26 locations. Rival estimates expect Warner Bros.’ animated film to add $7 million by Sunday, bringing the animated film’s cumulative gross to $47.26 million.
Bill Hader voices the titular character in the cartoon, which follows the shenanigans that occur after a mischievous, hat-wearing cat arrives to cheer up two siblings who move to a new town.

Finally, in fifth place was Columbia Pictures’ “Ghost Soldier.” The William Eubank-directed film earned $700,000 on Friday, coming in just ahead of GKids’ “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which brought in $680,000 on Friday. That puts the “Godzilla Minus One” follow-up at more than $51 million domestically.

items.title: ‘GTA 6’ Hits Massive $3.79 Billion in First-Day Sales
items.description: Crime pays: Rockstar Games’ “Grand Theft Auto 6″ preorder and first-day sales reached $3.79 billion, the game developer announced Friday.
items.author: Jennifer Maas
paragraphs: Crime pays: Rockstar Games’ “Grand Theft Auto 6″ preorder and first-day sales reached $3.79 billion, the game developer announced Friday.
Per Rockstar Games parent company Take-Two Interactive, that total sets “a new record for entertainment across any medium” and makes “GTA 6” “the biggest entertainment launch in history.”
A spokesperson for Take-Two Interactive declined to comment on the number of “GTA 6” copies sold.

For the sake of comparison, Sony Pictures’ “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” reaped $2.52 billion at the global box office in 2026, the No. 1 movie of the year to date. Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster “The Odyssey” has taken in just over $1.8 billion to date.

On its first day of release, “GTA 6” made roughly as much as James Cameron’s last two “Avatar” movies, “The Way of Water” and “Fire and Ash,” have grossed combined. With just Day 1 sales, “GTA 6” has already out-grossed the highest grossing movie of all time, “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion), in one day.
The game cost a reported $1.5 billion to produce over more than a decade of development.

“GTA 6” launched Thursday for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S and was also available on Xbox One via Xbox’s Cloud Gaming service. The game retails at $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the ultimate version. Preorders for “GTA 6” opened June 25.

With a reported total gameplay time of approximately 80 hours to complete its main storyline, “GTA 6” follows duo Jason and Lucia as they navigate their way through criminal life in the fictional Leonida.
“GTA 6” has reached a 99 Metacritic score (tying it for the highest-rated video game of all time) and received a nomination for Game of the Year at The Game Awards this December.

“It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI,’” Rockstar Games president and founder Sam Houser said. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.”

items.title: Princess Kate Cancer Documentary ‘Heal’ Sets BBC, NBC and International Premiere Dates
items.description: “Heal,” a documentary from Princess Kate on her cancer diagnosis and living life in the face of serious illness, will debut in the U.K. on Nov. 29, with international premieres to follow.
items.author: Mya Copeland
paragraphs: “Heal,” a documentary from Princess Kate on her cancer diagnosis and living life in the face of serious illness, will debut in the U.K. on Nov. 29, with international premieres to follow.
The documentary will premiere on the BBC in the U.K. on Nov. 29, via NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30, Channel 9 in Australia on Dec. 1 and CTV in Canada on Dec. 7.
The Princess of Wales was diagnosed with cancer in early 2024 and announced she was in remission in January 2025 after undergoing chemotherapy.

The documentary follows Princess Kate as she undertakes the National Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours in support of The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity. During her challenge attempt, she reflects on her experience alongside others navigating their health journeys, exploring the impact that illness has on a person and the people, places and experiences that can aid in healing.

The documentary shines a light on navigating diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer. Princess Kate aims to transform access to holistic cancer care that supports resilience and quality of life during and after diagnosis. All funds received during the documentary’s distribution have been directed to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity to support those living with and beyond a cancer diagnosis.
In the U.S., “Heal” will be available on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on NBC and at 11:30 p.m. ET/PT on Bravo. It will also be available to stream next day on Peacock.
“Heal” was produced by Detail Films and directed by Benji Jackson.
