items.title: Robert Pattinson’s Bond Ascent: How Pricey Screen Tests and Amazon Execs Landed a Starry 007
items.description: What does an actor do in the quiet moments before the announcement that will change his life?
items.author: Matt Donnelly
paragraphs: What does an actor do in the quiet moments before the announcement that will change his life?

For Robert Pattinson, there were about 12 hours between the Sunday phone call confirming he’d landed the role of James Bond and Amazon MGM’s Monday-morning release of the first image of the actor rocking a tuxedo and pistol. He spent it, rather predictably, watching an arthouse horror film.

His longtime friend and collaborator Robert Eggers told Variety this week that Pattinson was screening the director’s forthcoming genre drama “Werwulf” when the Bond news broke. Nothing like a stark naked Aaron Taylor-Johnson terrorizing a quaint village to pass the time.

But after months (years, really) of toiling and speculation over who would replace Daniel Craig in the film adaptations of Ian Fleming’s spy novels, Pattinson took the crown. It buttons up a delicious, messy and very public guessing game over which lucky man would land the iconic role. When Amazon MGM bought out rights to James Bond from longtime custodians the Broccoli family in 2025, intentions were set for a young star who could shoulder the franchise for a decade or two. An A-list team of producers (Amy Pascal of “Spider-Man” and David Heyman of the “Harry Potter” movies) recruited Denis Villeneuve to direct. Together, with significant influence from Amazon execs Courtenay Valenti and Mike Hopkins (and yes, Jeff Bezos), they screen-tested a laundry list of virile performers — including Callum Turner, Tom Francis, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor — earlier this year.

For the curious, the batch of screen tests cost Amazon MGM between $300,000 and $500,000 to pull off, ostensibly in secret (everyone found out), sources familiar with the process say. But two wildcard actors who tested at the last minute — “Superman” star Nicholas Hoult and the DCU’s reining Batman, Pattinson — tipped the scales. Villeneuve’s voice became the most trusted in the room on the matter of Bond’s casting, two insiders tell Variety.

His shorthand with Pattinson from working on “Dune: Part Three” made the choice inevitable, according to industry insiders — especially after Turner, the early favorite, came under scrutiny against more established names like Hoult and Pattinson. Lowden, the heat-seeking star of “Slow Horses,” was even the subject of a suspected sabotage campaign when paparazzi footage circulated showed the actor bungling an on-set motorcycle stunt just two weeks before the Bond casting was confirmed.

A sect of the internet lost its mind when Variety reported earlier this month that Harry Styles and Theo James were both in talks for the role. It’s rare, even by tentpole movie standards, that such a long list of candidates would flow so freely through public channels. The studios hate it because it makes them seem indecisive, one exec says. Talent absolutely hates it because the also-rans will have to answer for almost being James Bond on talk show couches and podcasts for the next 10 years.
“Whatever, it’s really fun,” one top talent rep tells Variety of the audition merry-go-round.

While there will be detractors, it’s inarguable that the Bond gig now enshrines Pattinson in the upper echelons of movie stardom. He was already well on his way, with even civilian social media pundits having commented on the “generational run” Pattinson has been living out onscreen in films like “Primetime,” “The Odyssey,” “The Drama,” “Die My Love” and, obviously, “The Batman.” That’s to say nothing of the deeply indie era (“Good Time,” “The Lighthouse”) that followed major franchise moments like his star-making turn in the “Twilight Saga” movies and a prominent role in “Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.” The new job also represents a major win for Pattinson’s agent of more than 20 years, Stephanie Ritz of WME. Ritz and team have managed to populate massive IP with Pattinson’s face while still allowing the actor to take risks and brand himself a maverick for the cross-generational devotees of studios like A24.

Given the shocking November news that DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran had been jettisoned by the David Ellison regime, it’s doubtful Pattinson would linger long as Matt Reeves’ caped crusader — freeing him up to embody the sultry British charm and execute the bare-knuckle action audiences have come to expect from 007. Art-house horror movies may have to take a back seat.

items.title: Hudson Williams and His Hairstylist Aika Flores Really Are That Close
items.description: It was early December 2025 when actor Hudson Williams met celebrity groomer Aika Flores. His queer Canadian hockey series, Heated Rivalry, had been out for just over a week, but the show was already catching fire on social media and at workplace water coolers.
items.author: Nicole Fell
paragraphs: It was early December 2025 when actor Hudson Williams met celebrity groomer Aika Flores. His queer Canadian hockey series, Heated Rivalry, had been out for just over a week, but the show was already catching fire on social media and at workplace water coolers. The pair met when Flores was hired by her close friend to do grooming for a cover shoot with Timid Magazine.

“[My friend and editor-in-chief] Henry was telling me, ‘It’s this show that’s on the second episode. I think it’s going to get big. People are already talking about it. He’s hot,’” Flores tells The Hollywood Reporter about the pitch on Williams.

Flash forward 11 months, and she and Williams are sprawled out on a couch in the green room of THR’s New York photo studio. It’s a rare break in filming for Williams, who’s knee-deep in filming the second season of Heated Rivalry. As predicted, the show blew up, became a cultural phenomenon and launched the 25-year-old Canadian actor into an overnight sensation and a certified heartthrob. It didn’t take long for Williams’ authentic appreciation for skin care to land him a brand ambassadorship with his favorite Korean skin care company Skin1004.

But Williams has had virtually no time over the past year between returning to the hockey romance series, his latest show, AMC+’s Yaga, and a slew of other roles he’s booked in the wake of his breakout. It’s been intense. And Flores has been by his side the entire time.
“The vibes were so good,” says Williams of their first meeting. “I was so tired that day, but we were already getting into our early lives, where we grew up.”

That one-day booking for a U.S. press day turned into jet-setting around the world together in the past year for media appearances and red carpets. “[His team] wanted to see first if we got along, and then they booked [me for the rest of the tour] while we were doing the shoot,” Flores says.

“She was grounding, chill, funny,” says Williams. “Sometimes overtalkative people are just a little bit much in the morning, especially when [there are] always late nights. Those people that always have energy. I’m like, whoa, whoa, whoa.”
Flores reminds Williams that he’s pretty high energy — except when he’s in her chair, getting ready. “Quiet time,” he says.

This is in high contrast to only minutes earlier, when the pair were joking around while shooting video content: Williams taking a stab at being the one to pamper Flores for a change, Flores attempting to get the actor ready as he jumped out of the chair and dodged her hands. The horseplay on set might make one assume that they are close friends. “We’re like family now,” Flores says. Williams describes how he’s become “Uncle Hudson” to Flores’ son. “He made me brush his teeth,” he says, fondly.

Uncle Hudson has been known to prep for bedtime stories with the same dedication he applies to scenes, using voices for the characters, something Flores jokes that she and her wife don’t even do. “I was sort of nervous, I had to play Santa,” Williams says. “I was like, ‘I hope he’s not judging me.’”

That almost familial closeness helped Williams through a whirlwind year. After Heated Rivalry finished airing around Christmas, his schedule exploded with late night tapings, Golden Globes presenting, Olympic torch-bearing, Milan runway walking and more life-changing experiences. Through it all, Flores, along with his CAA branding agent Leilani Houston and stylist Anastasia Walker, has been by his side. “It’s been great because, honestly, we call our group chats the quad squad,” Williams says.

“Yesterday we hung out until 3 a.m., after a day where we were up in the morning and it was a 12-hour shooting day, because we just love each other so much,” Williams adds. “We all take care of each other. It’s kind of like a maternal energy toward everyone. It feels like we’re sisters braiding each other’s hair or something — with alcohol.”

Williams leans on the quad when online commentary gets intense. “A lot of times, social media is just inherently mean, and so everyone gets shot at online,” he continues. “We always have each other, and there’s a feeling that since we’re always aligned and we always have this group that we will always be together.” Flores says they often laugh the hate off because it’s the only way to go about it. “It’s outrageous, so it’s so funny,” Williams says. “It’s like speculation, or they make it up,” adds Flores.

“When we come across it, we’re like, ‘Oh my God, did you know that I got shot yesterday? Did you know that I’m actually really problematic, I guess?’ We just laugh because it’s so stupid,” she continues. “That’s what’s nice, is having each other,” adds Williams.

Even as Williams’ signature heartthrob hair has been a hit online, plenty of people have speculated that Flores is somehow forcing Williams into looks he doesn’t want. “I want my hair to be the same,” the actor clarifies, with Flores adding, “It’s how he likes it, and I just elevate it, and then we bounce off ideas.”

The pair also like to take risks, and his daring Met Gala look of exaggerated cat eyes and sculpted wet hair landed on many best-of lists. “She popped off with the Met,” says Williams. “We like to have fun and not take anything too seriously. [We] just try things, be bold.”

Heated Rivalry is taking up much of his time lately, rejoining his co-star Connor Storrie to film the show’s highly anticipated next season in Toronto. “It’s going good, but it’s sad,” Williams says, referencing the material they’ll be tackling in the next season. It’s based on author Rachel Reid’s follow-up The Long Game, which show creator Jacob Tierney has previously referred to as “Sex Scenes From a Marriage.”

There’s not much Williams can say about what they’re getting up to on the set, but he did note that the return made him a little nervous. “Leading up to [filming], I was getting kind of scared of how it’d feel, but it’s the same crew. Jacob does a really good job of making it feel just as small and intimate,” he says.

“Even the joining cast, they immediately picked up on the vibe and were so sweet. We’re all supportive of each other. It’s just a really fun time. Still feels tiny, [it’s] just crazy,” adds Williams. “It’s just a bigger family now.”

For The Hollywood Reporter’s 10th Beauty Issue, Williams and Flores talked about “evil” hair, that time he got scolded by a security guard (and the internet) for lighting a smoke on the streets of Milan, and why, in times of exhaustion, Williams likes to “take a nap on Aika.”
What’s been your favorite look?
AIKA FLORES I think my favorite look has to be the Met [Gala].
HUDSON WILLIAMS She popped off with the Met.

FLORES It was so collaborative between me and [stylist] Anastasia that for, I feel like months, we were planning it. As soon as [Hudson] got invited, we were [planning]. We knew from the beginning we weren’t going to do a black suit. That’s just not his personality [or any] of our personalities.

WILLIAMS We like to have fun and not take anything too seriously. [We] just try to take risks and try things, be bold. That was my favorite too, as far as [it being] fun and getting the whole team to be working together so cohesively. I do like how nice I looked at the Oscars, as far as my face and hair. It’s one of my favorites just because my hair was wet-looking. My skin was great. You elevated my skin. I liked the hair you did when I was going to the Armani show.
FLORES Oh, the cigarette that he got in trouble for.

WILLIAMS I wasn’t even trying to smoke that in the street, but I was like, “Will I have time to smoke it there?” I think it was Lei Lei who was like, “I don’t think you have time.” So I asked, “Should I just smoke it while I’m walking?” But I felt like with the suit, how we worked with Armani to make that. Then how you worked with my hair, I thought that was cool.
Is there a recent look you’ve loved?
FLORES The Yaga premiere at TIFF, where his hair was like … He looked evil.
WILLIAMS That was fun too.
What look have you been trying lately?
FLORES We’ve been toying a lot with wet hair because it’s cool.
What do you like most about working with one another?

WILLIAMS My favorite thing is — we just did a shoot yesterday for something I can’t say — but I got really tired in the middle of the shoot. It was a long shoot, and I had to do a bunch of stuff. I just took a nap on Aika, and that’s always fun. Whenever I have these big moments, I can just literally grab onto her and fall asleep. We’re always giggling and laughing and not taking it too seriously, which is fun. I feel like we always find something to laugh at. The vibes never go left. I feel like we’re very respectful of each other’s moods.

FLORES My favorite, and I think this goes to just you being a person, is he can’t remember months or dates or anything that happened. But as soon as he sits in the chair, he remembers our last conversation, what we talked about last time. Obviously, we don’t really do small talk anymore, but we can appreciate silence together. We can just chill together. I don’t feel like I’m performing when I’m working with you.
Is there a look you’ve been dying to try?
WILLIAMS My hair is going to change for parts, so there’s definitely other styles I want to try. For one of these roles, I want to cut it into a crop sort of fringey thing, for a future part.
FLORES He never told me this.
WILLIAMS I have another thing that I might do where I’d have long-ass hair, and if I had it, if it was real long hair, not a wig, learning how to style that would be fun.
What’s a beauty trend you want to see get popular next year?

WILLIAMS I’ve been putting barrettes [in my hair]. When I wear a hat, sometimes my hair wings out and sticks out like crazy, so I have little chrome heart and star barrettes. I put my little star clips in my hair. The ones for meant for 5-year-old girls. I think men should get on the barrettes [trend] because they’re so cute.
FLORES I second that. That’s dope.
A version of this story appeared in the Nov. 18 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: Celebrity Beauty Brands (Even Kim’s) Are Failing. Here Are the New Rules
items.description: Gwen Stefani’s GXVE Beauty is gone. So are Scarlett Johansson‘s skin care line The Outset and Serena Williams’ Wyn Beauty cosmetics. Even Kim Kardashian‘s KKW Beauty and SKKN by Kim have been retired. Blake Lively‘s Blake Brown Beauty hair care is struggling,
items.author: Elycia Rubin
paragraphs: Gwen Stefani’s GXVE Beauty is gone. So are Scarlett Johansson‘s skin care line The Outset and Serena Williams’ Wyn Beauty cosmetics. Even Kim Kardashian‘s KKW Beauty and SKKN by Kim have been retired. Blake Lively‘s Blake Brown Beauty hair care is struggling, and Jennifer Lopez‘s JLO Beauty has quietly exited Sephora. Yes, the celebrity beauty business is crowded and unforgiving, but that still hasn’t stopped Cardi B and Jennifer Lawrence from joining the fray.

Cardi B, for one, remains undeterred. “People are always going to have something to say, but I didn’t create Grow-Good just to put my name on a bottle. Hair care has always been personal to me. I’ve been sharing my hair routines, my homemade treatments and my hair journey with my fans for years, way before I ever thought about launching a brand.”

With a stake in a brand worth potentially far more than a movie deal as production slates threaten to continue shrinking, it’s easy to understand why Hollywood keeps lining up. The success stories are seductive: Rihanna‘s Fenty Beauty helped make her a billionaire, Selena Gomez‘s Rare Beauty has been valued at $2.7 billion, and Hailey Bieber’s Rhode sold to e.l.f. Beauty in a deal worth up to $1 billion.

But fame doesn’t always bring fortune — or an easy ride. In October, Lawrence launched Mes (pronounced “mess”) with Arcaea CEO Jasmina Aganovic, generating plenty of buzz and a fair amount of backlash over what online critics complained was another example of celebrity overreach.

The partnership reportedly began after Lawrence watched Aganovic deliver a TED Talk about the future of cosmetics. Aganovic leads Arcaea, a biotech company developing sustainable, high-performance cosmetic ingredients that has counted Chanel among its investors, and she brings serious beauty credentials, having previously worked at Living Proof and led skin-microbiome brand Mother Dirt. Mes embraces an “unbothered beauty” philosophy, with the enticing promise of achieving great hair without putting in lots of time or effort. It also plays into Lawrence’s public persona as the rare A-lister with genuinely self-deprecating, what-you-see-is-what-you-get candor. The actress introduced the line, which includes a hair mask, serum and volume mist, on Instagram as one for “nice people who don’t leave mean comments.” It was almost as if she knew what was coming. (Per her reps, Lawrence was not available to comment for this report.)

After years away from social media, Lawrence made her debut Sept. 9, just weeks before the launch, and the timing didn’t go unnoticed. Some commenters smelled a calculated sales pitch. Others questioned the fit, noting she’s never been especially known for her hair. To skeptics and Reddit users, it looked like one more celebrity chasing a Rhode-sized payday. Lawrence, for her part, said the line grew out of years in the glam chair, when she would wash her hair only once a week.

“At this point in the life cycle of celebrity brands, the initial reaction is always going be the eye roll,” says Aliza Licht, marketing veteran and author of On Brand. “We all have the playbook now and everybody knows what’s behind the curtain.” Often, that’s a licensing deal, a manufacturer, a hefty marketing budget and a carefully crafted backstory, with the star’s name as the cherry on top. “Consumers are good at recognizing an engineered marketing narrative dressed up as a personal passion project.”

Beauty publicist Marie-Laure Fournier, founder of Fournier PR + Consulting, believes the criticism around Mes is still manageable. “A candid, even humorous video with Aganovic, whether with a magazine or on social media, could go a long way toward humanizing the launch and addressing the skepticism head on,” she says. “The public wants to see that you’re listening, learning and willing to adapt.”

Despite some of the backlash, the early industry read on Mes is cautiously optimistic. Lawrence’s working with Aganovic is “a good move, to partner with a brand like Arcaea that is well established in the beauty industry,” says Clare Hennigan, principal analyst for beauty and consumer goods at global research firm Mintel. Hennigan also sees promise in the products, particularly a gel hair mask that can be applied to dry hair and doubles as a styler. No need to wait for wash day. “They are solving a pain point of convenience, a key motivator for purchases,” she says. “Anything that makes life a little easier is something shoppers will pay more for.”

Kate Hudson would applaud this solution-oriented approach for the consumer. The celebrity entrepreneur co-founded Fabletics in 2013, remains a shareholder and watched the activewear company reportedly surpass $1 billion in revenue in 2025. “You can have the most beautiful vision in the world, but once you put something out there, you have to pay attention to what they need, what they love and what they don’t,” she says.

Delivering effective products is one thing; fostering a genuine connection with the consumer is another. Cardi B out of the gate demonstrated a keen understanding of the latter with marketing Grow-Good. Her grassroots strategy focuses on neighborhood beauty supply stores, including shops in her native Bronx. The hair care line, following three years of development, debuted in April and reportedly sold out in less than 35 minutes. “Listen, I know my people because I am my people!” she says. “I grew up going to beauty supply stores. Those stores have always been part of our community, and I wanted Grow-Good to be there too. For me, it was about making sure the products were accessible to the people I created them for.” Lisa Motzko Hamilton, former vp of merchandising at Ulta Beauty and co-founder of Breakthru Beauty consultancy, says brands perform best when the entertainer is “showing up, engaging with their community and sharing a part of themselves beyond their celebrity status.” The Business of Fashion reports a promising 40 percent return-customer rate for Grow-Good.

Even more critically, the celebrity and the product need to make sense together. Lady Gaga’s Haus Labs cosmetics draw on her reputation for artistry and creative expression, while Selena Gomez built Rare Beauty around supporting mental health for young people, a cause she has publicly owned as a personal issue, with 1 percent of sales going to Rare Impact Fund.

Hennigan cites Jennifer Aniston‘s LolaVie as a brand that gets it very right. Aniston’s hairstyles have been a cultural fixture for decades, making hair care a natural fit. She spent several years developing the line before launching in 2021 and has since expanded to Ulta and Credo. “LolaVie is very personal to me. My relationship with my hair, the products I’ve tried over the years and the challenges I’ve experienced are what inspired the brand in the first place,” says Aniston. “I didn’t want to simply put my name on something; I wanted to be part of building something that I truly believed in.”

The Morning Show star also makes a point of keeping a conversation going with customers. “I love hearing how other people incorporate the products into their routines and about the results they’re seeing. We’ve made changes to product in the past based on consumer feedback,” she says. (She’s also extended LolaVie into pet shampoo: “My dogs are such a big part of my family, and I wanted to bring the same thoughtfulness and attention to detail that goes into our human hair care.” All profits benefit The Clydeo Fund, which supports animal rescue and rehabilitation.)

Author Licht points to Kardashian as someone who has spent years cultivating “a parasocial bond with followers, so a new brand lands with people she already knows, even the haters.” Stars who suddenly surface hawking new products are a harder sell. “It’s odd when we hear from celebrities out of the blue,” she says. “We don’t have social relationships with them, they’re movie stars.” Licht adds that Lawrence, who had no public social media presence until weeks before the launch, “seemed to come out of thin air,” she says. “We are missing a bit of evidence there.”

Johansson’s The Outset offers another cautionary tale. “We didn’t have historical commentary from Scarlett around skin care,” says Licht. “The consumer needs to find a germ of a connection between the celebrity and the brand.” Hennigan sees another issue: “The problem was proof. The efficacy and science may not have been as visible to shoppers.”

Lopez faced a different kind of disconnect with potential consumers. A merchandising executive at a beauty retailer, speaking on condition of anonymity, questions JLO Beauty’s origin story. “Jennifer hung the age-defying ‘JLo Glow’ on a family olive oil secret, but doubters online, including a chorus of dermatologists, weren’t convinced it was the whole story with JLO Beauty,” creating an issue with consumer trust.

Blake Lively’s Blake Brown Beauty hair care line launched to considerable fanfare at Target, only to face a more complicated reality as the actress became embroiled in the fallout surrounding It Ends With Us and her legal battle with Justin Baldoni. Lively went quiet on social media, and sales have reportedly dropped sharply. “The war with Justin was likely a huge detriment to sales,” says Licht.

Distribution matters, too. Lady Gaga’s Haus Labs initially launched exclusively on Amazon, a challenging fit for color cosmetics, where shoppers want to try on shades before buying. Its move to Sephora introduced the brand to a broader beauty audience.
Then comes the most important question of all: Does the world really need another beauty line?

Fenty Beauty answered that question nearly a decade ago with an expansive and inclusive shade range that addressed a glaring gap in the cosmetics market. Rhode found its opening with accessible pricing on ingredients that had become associated with more expensive skin care. “Peptides were drawing a lot of attention, with many brands charging a premium for them, while Bieber offered high-performing peptide products at a more affordable price,” notes Hennigan. For Mes, even in light of its messy debut, Hennigan sees an opportunity to shift the conversation toward time-saving efficiency with education: “Help consumers understand how these products fit into their existing hair care routines. Since the hair mask comes with a learning curve, the brand needs to drive the how-to aspect home” with tutorials and partnerships with pro stylists who can demo the products, she advises.

Ultimately, the biggest challenge of the enterprise may be the least glamorous part: remaining involved long after the cameras and launch parties. Hudson, who joined HealthyCell supplements as an investor and creative strategy partner in October, says patience is the X factor. “I’ve learned that building a business is a long game,” she says. “You have to love the process, not just the excitement of launching something.” Licht doesn’t mince words: “Most of the time celebrities are just not cut out for the daily grind required to build a brand, and that’s why a lot of these lines fail.”
Additional reporting by Beth Landman.
This story appeared in the Nov. 18 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando Are Married
items.description: Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando are married.
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando are married.
The couple tied the knot Saturday in Palm Springs, California, according to Entertainment Tonight. TMZ first reported that Cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, were expected to wed over the weekend.

On Friday, the Grammy winner’s stepsister Lily-Rose Purcell shared photos on her Instagram Stories from the couple’s rehearsal dinner. One photo showed the dinner tables decorated with crimson flowers, along with a menu featuring “M+M,” the couple’s initials, printed at the top.

The “Flowers” singer and Morando, also a musician, met on a blind date in 2021, she told British Vogue in 2023. The pair have also worked together, collaborating on her albums Endless Summer Vacation and Something Beautiful.

The couple’s engagement was confirmed in December 2025 after Cyrus debuted a shiny gold band on her left ring finger while posing for photos with Morando at the premiere of Avatar: Fire and Ash, for which she contributed the song “Dream as One.” People confirmed the engagement the following day.
More than two weeks after the news of their engagement broke, Us Weekly reported that the couple had “talked about eloping” instead of having a traditional wedding.
“Miley is really happy right now and in such a good, calm place,” an insider told the publication. “She’s not super into the idea of doing another wedding.”

Cyrus was previously married to Hunger Games actor Liam Hemsworth, whom she met while filming the 2010 film adaptation of Nicholas Sparks’s novel, The Last Song. After a decade-long, on-again, off-again relationship, the pair married in 2018 and divorced in 2020.

items.title: The Best Early Black Friday Deals on Laptops I’ve Tested Myself
items.description: It's not Black Friday quite yet, but I'm already on the hunt for Black Friday laptop deals, and this week, they're finally getting good. I know some people will want to wait until the weekend of Black Friday to ensure they're getting the best Black Friday deal
items.author: Luke Larsen
paragraphs: It's not Black Friday quite yet, but I'm already on the hunt for Black Friday laptop deals, and this week, they're finally getting good. I know some people will want to wait until the weekend of Black Friday to ensure they're getting the best Black Friday deals, but there's no guarantee that the discounts will stick around until then. I'll be carefully following laptop deals through Black Friday and the holiday shopping season, so make sure to come back for more hand-picked deals on some of the best laptops I've tested this year.
Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Amazon, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and the Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals.
The Biggest MacBook Neo Discount Ever

The MacBook Neo was already cheap, so Apple hasn't been eager to give much in the way of price cuts—despite the laptop having been out for seven months. But finally, the MacBook Neo's price has dropped by $50, bringing it down to $649. That's a great deal, especially if you're looking for an affordable laptop that feels premium, with a metal chassis and quality display. The 8 GB of RAM is limiting, but if your needs aren't overly heavy, the MacBook Neo should do the trick—especially at this price.
An Excellent 15-Inch Laptop for $900

These days, you'll be hard-pressed to find a laptop for under $1,000 that doesn't have any major compromises. That's even more uncommon for a laptop with a larger screen. But the IdeaPad Slim 5x is just that. It's a 15-inch laptop with great performance, long-lasting battery life, lots of ports, a solid trackpad, and a high-resolution OLED screen. It even comes packed to the brim with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. It's not as thin as the 15-inch MacBook Air, no, but then again, it's hundreds of dollars cheaper.
Microsoft Surface Laptop for $900

It might be well over two years old, but I still find myself recommending the Surface Laptop from 2024. The price is down to $900 right now, which is a good deal for these specs, performance, and battery life. You're limited to only the blue color option (also known as Sapphire), but it's the best price I've seen on this laptop this year so far. My favorite feature will always be the 3:2 aspect ratio screen, which gives the display a taller shape for more vertical space to work with.

There is a newer version, which comes with the Snapdragon X2 Plus/Elite chips, but I've found that it's still quite expensive. The IdeaPad Slim 5x listed above is the better option if you're OK with a larger device, since it uses those next-generation Snapdragon chips and twice the storage. But if you're sold on the more premium design of the Surface Laptop, this is the one to get.

With the MacBook Neo selling for $649, you might look at something like the HP OmniBook 5 with suspicion. Even on sale for $750, being $100 more than the MacBook Neo doesn't seems like a great position to be in for an entry-level Windows laptop. And while this laptop is on sale often, this is $100 cheaper than I've seen it over the past few weeks.

The HP OmniBook 5 is a special device, with its OLED display, very thin chassis, and 16 GB of RAM. It very much looks like a laptop that should cost hundreds more. Battery life is great too, thanks to the Snapdragon X chip inside. The 16 GB of RAM is still the main selling point here—if it was any less, I would recommend the XPS 13 in nearly every scenario (but it's not on sale right now). It's only real downfall is the touchpad. It feels frustratingly clumsy to use, making precise movements difficult.

items.title: Have You Packed Your Go-Bag for the End of the World?
items.description: Gina Arconti was getting ready to board a flight at San Diego International Airport last Friday when the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop. The 28-year-old medical-device rep had been planning a weekend trip to San Jose to visit a friend, but when she hea
items.author: Erica Schwiegershausen
paragraphs: Gina Arconti was getting ready to board a flight at San Diego International Airport last Friday when the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop. The 28-year-old medical-device rep had been planning a weekend trip to San Jose to visit a friend, but when she heard the news, she immediately called an Uber home. “I was feeling pretty uneasy,” she says. As soon as she got back to her apartment, she started checking her emergency supplies to see if she had enough water and toilet paper on hand. Then she pulled out the Béis weekender bag she keeps under her bed and started filming, showing off the first-aid kit, hand sanitizer, Pedialyte, deodorant wipes, spare batteries, solar chargers, human anatomy guidebook, road atlas, and compass she keeps packed and ready to go at a moment’s notice. “I was like, ‘If people haven’t thought about these things before, maybe now is a good time.’” An hour later, her phone started pinging. Friends were texting telling her they’d just gone to Costco to make their own go-bags. “I was like, Okay, so we’re all really anxious right now.”

Over the past week, an unsettling series of outages not only temporarily grounded flights but also took out Microsoft Outlook, disrupted major banking services, shut down the NSA’s internal communications network, and caused issues with Apple Pay and iCloud. People are on edge. “Every day my friends and I get a news alert of something being shut down, and we are all kind of like, ‘What’s happening?’” says Mabel Dustin, a 27-year-old who works in influencer marketing. “It’s definitely scary, since we don’t have any information.” Add to that months of headlines warning that AI is becoming powerful enough to destroy the world and the fact that we’re currently at war with Iran, many people are finding their minds spiraling to worst-case scenarios. As a sense of impending doom sets in, some women have found an outlet for their ambient anxiety: They’re posting videos of their apocalypse hauls and comparing notes on the supplies they have ready to go in their doomsday bags.

For many, the recent system failures were a terrifying glimpse at just how screwed we’d all be without Wi-Fi or our phones. On Tuesday, Emma Botti, a 27-year-old songwriter who lives in Williamsburg, was talking with her boyfriend while she walked to a bar to meet friends. “He lives in Denver, and I kept asking him, ‘In an emergency, how am I gonna get to you?’ Like, we need to find an imaginary state we would meet in,” she says. He was making fun of her, but then he asked if she’d seen the news about the NSA outage. “I was like, ‘That’s it.’” When she got to the bar, she started shopping for rations and emergency water pouches on Amazon Prime. “I told my best friend, ‘If your phone signal goes out, you know the code to my apartment. Our plan is to meet there, and I’ll have some supplies.’”

Madeleine Scheffs, a 23-year-old who works in real estate in Virginia, says the recent headlines inspired her to stock up on candles, fire starters, body wipes, bleach, and dog food. She also ordered some SOS bars, a 3,600-calorie food ration that claims to taste like a coconut cookie and has a five-year shelf life. Scheffs lives near data centers and is paranoid about power outages. She looked into buying a generator, but it was $10,000. Her algorithm has no shortage of ideas, though. “I saw this video the other day of a woman who was collecting her rainwater in case of an emergency,” she says. She asked her boyfriend if he could set something like that up for her, but he said no. “He was like, ‘You need to reel it in and calm down.’”

But Scheffs isn’t alone in finding comfort in preparing for the worst. The doomsday-prep business has set its sights on anxious women, with Instagram serving up ads for hot-pink first-aid kits. For $1,450, the luxury emergency-supply brand Preppi sells a sleek silver fireproof backpack that comes stocked with a respirator mask, tent, three-day supply of water packs, Marvis toothpaste, and Malin+Goetz soap. After Dustin posted about the walkie-talkies her dad bought her and her siblings so they can communicate if the grid goes down, her DMs were flooded. “Everyone was like, ‘I want the radio,’ or asking how far of a range it can go. They’re like, ‘I have family that lives in upstate California. Will I be able to talk to them?’” She added an affiliate link to her bio; they’re currently on sale for $439 for a two-pack. Arconti told me that since she posted her go-bag video, the “emergency preparedness” collection on her Amazon storefront has been blowing up, with people rushing to buy water-filter straws and a 318-piece survival kit.

None of the women I spoke to were convinced we’re really on the brink of the apocalypse. “If I’m supposed to go without power for like 90 days, I think I can count myself out on being able to survive that,” says Botti. And with no imminent threat, it’s hard to say where exactly you would go with your go-bag. But they also don’t think it’s a bad idea to be prepared. Arconti was in college when COVID hit. “I went shopping a little too late, and by the time we got there, a lot of stuff was gone from the shelves, and it was really chaotic,” she says. Now, she has a storage unit with extra water jugs, spare batteries, camping supplies, and a crank radio. “I always keep my gas tank filled up so if I need to get out quickly and the roads are accessible, I can leave as soon as I hear a news break,” she says. At the end of the day, she doesn’t think a massive grid outage is likely. But living in Southern California, the threat of wildfires feels much closer to home. The go-bag under her bed gives her peace of mind.

“It’s very valid to be freaking out right now,” says Jen Heller, the creator of The Disaster Playbook, an emergency prep guide. But she told me she worries less about potential end-of-the-world scenarios and more about climate change. “What’s far more likely is a local breakdown, like what happened after Hurricane Helene” in 2024, when floodwaters shut down roadways and outages left people without power for weeks. “Even climate scientists are freaked out by the speed with which everything’s collapsing,” she says. “Every night I go to sleep in my comfy bed with my running water and wonder how long I’ll be able to have this life.”

items.title: What These Miss Universe Contestants Want the World to Know About Their Countries
items.description: Does anyone get more excited about the Miss Universe pageant than Latines? Every year, when the competition takes over our screens, families across Latin America and the diaspora gather to watch, cheering on the women representing their countries and celebrati
items.author: Raquel Reichard
paragraphs: Does anyone get more excited about the Miss Universe pageant than Latines? Every year, when the competition takes over our screens, families across Latin America and the diaspora gather to watch, cheering on the women representing their countries and celebrating the pride and possibility of seeing one of their own take home the crown.

This year, the pageant takes place in San Juan, Puerto Rico, marking the competition’s first return to the archipelago in 24 years. The 75th Miss Universe competition airs live on Tuesday, November 24, on Telemundo, with a new queen set to be crowned by reigning Miss Universe Fátima Bosch of Mexico.

Ahead of the competition, we spoke with some of the women representing Latin American and Caribbean countries about what they wish more people knew about their homelands, how they plan to use their platforms to uplift women in their communities, and what they hope their presence on the Miss Universe stage will mean to the women and girls watching back home.
What's one interesting fact about your country you wish more people knew?

Well, in my country, approximately 36 Indigenous languages are spoken, and I think it is wonderful to have such cultural diversity. I believe it is important for people to learn more about the history of these languages and the communities they represent. To me, this is something that should never be overlooked, and I hope to help further promote it through tourism in my country as well.
What is an issue affecting women in your country that you would like to support and advocate for through your platform?

I believe every country faces challenges, not only related to gender but in general. However, women today have certainly gained access to many more leadership positions and opportunities. Still, I believe the gender pay gap remains. Therefore, I think we need to focus on education so that women can continue occupying these positions while moving toward greater fairness and equality, where women's true value is genuinely recognized.I believe this is something we need to work on, and education is how we can achieve it.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage will communicate to the women and girls in your country who are watching you?

Well, I hope to represent us with strength, joy, and great commitment, just as Bolivian women are known for. Because beyond our beauty, we have a history behind us and a voice that can tell so much more than just what is traditional or cultural. And I believe it is our voices and our purpose that will allow us to shine on that stage. Today, I am Valeria Mena, but above all, I am Bolivia. And I have a commitment to carry with me not only my own dream, but also the dreams of all those women and little girls who dream of one day standing there themselves, of having their voices heard. And through every little step I take at Miss Universe, I want to show that a woman can be strong and capable of achieving whatever she sets her mind to — and that every one of them can do it, too.
What's one interesting fact about your country you wish more people knew?

Well, I'd like people to learn a little more about our history, especially the story of Julia de Burgos, a Puerto Rican woman who helped pave the way for Puerto Rican women's rights. Although she had a short life — she died in her 30s — she left behind an incredibly meaningful legacy. And I would love for people, especially now that we're at Miss Universe, a platform for leaders and global ambassadors, to have the opportunity to learn about a Puerto Rican woman who was also a leader in her own right.
What are some issues affecting women in your country that you'd like to use your platform to champion?

There are many challenges. One of them is that we live in a society that wants to confine women to traditional social roles, even though women have demonstrated throughout history that they can be everything they choose to be. In addition to that, there's the gender pay gap, which still stands at 22%. I would love to bring greater visibility to these issues.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage says to the women and girls back home who are watching you?

Authenticity and elegance, and the idea that many things can coexist at the same time. I can be a woman who is approachable but also commanding. I can be intelligent but also beautiful. And I am a woman who isn't perfect, but wants to be memorable.
What's one interesting fact about your country you wish more people knew?
We don't have an army. So we are a really peaceful country. That's something I'm really proud of.
What's an issue affecting women in your country that you'd like to use your platform to champion?

I think access to great education. I was talking about my social project, which is Manos Amigas de Talamanca. It's a project about people from the South Caribbean of Costa Rica. It's called Limón, Bribri to be exact, and we work with them in different schools, and one of my targets with this project is helping them to have better access to education.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage says to the women and girls back home who are watching you?

Actually, when I was a little girl, I didn't have the self-esteem to dream about being Miss Universe, not even a model. So I want to inspire young girls that they don't have any limitations. They can have whatever they dream of. We as women, we don't have real limits. Our limits are in our head.
What is an issue affecting women in your country that you would like to support and advocate for through your platform?

Certainly, one of the challenges we face in my country, and I think in every country, but especially in Brazil, is violence. I don't understand how we can walk out into the street and feel so afraid, or how we can be in certain environments and feel so afraid. Having experienced domestic violence myself, I was able to feel firsthand what it means to live with that fear on an even deeper level. I would really love to share my stories and some of my thoughts so that women can empower themselves and so that, together, we can work and fight every day for a better country.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage will communicate to the women and girls in your country who are watching you?

I would like to show that hope is something alive, something that exists right in front of us. I tried competing in Miss Brazil other times, and I didn't win. Now, being able to stand on this stage representing a country that is in my heart feels like a story of overcoming adversity. It's a story of determination that never faded with time, and a reminder that you can always return to pursuing a dream because some dreams never die and never grow old. I hope that, through my story and my life, women can see that determination really can lead to something beautiful. And, of course, I would also like to show the most beautiful thing we have to offer, which is my heart, and everything I am willing and open to give.
What's one interesting fact about your country you wish more people knew?

One of the things I would like to show people is that we are the cradle of Mayan culture and how interesting it is to see the traditions go through generations and how our people are keeping them alive. It's just so beautiful.
What's an issue affecting women in your country that you'd like to use your platform to champion?

One of the things that I like to show around the world with people and use this platform is that women around the world, not only in my country, but we are still very underestimated in our capability and our leadership. And we are women. We are capable of doing anything we wish to.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage says to the women and girls back home who are watching you?

Well, the thing I would like to say to the women and girls is that they should really follow their dreams. And this is not about me. This is not about you looking at me. Don't look at me. I would like to tell them, don't look at me. Look at yourself. Look at yourself in the mirror and see all the potential you have and that you're capable of doing anything you wish for if you work hard enough.
What's one interesting fact about your country you wish more people knew?

One fact about my country that I wish more people knew is that we have more than 60 nationalities, but at the end of the day, we're one. We are all called daughters and sons of Curaçao, and we carry that name with a lot of pride.
What's an issue affecting women in your country that you'd like to use your platform to champion?

For me, the issue that I already champion for is we tend to forget about ourselves. We focus so much on the people that we take care of, especially in the world of caregivers, nurses, doctors, any version of caregiver that you have in the female world in general. We tend to put ourselves on the back burner and we get burnt out. And when we do, we get labeled as a disgruntled woman, someone that doesn't want to do her work, a woman that doesn't take care of those around her. But it's more than that. It's just we weren't heard when we were asking for help. So I want to be that voice.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage says to the women and girls back home who are watching you?

There's no limit. Trust me, do not label yourself with one title. Do not put yourself in one box. Explore life. Find what you love, and once you find that thing, go all in. And once you're done with that one thing, once you've reached your goal, you have many more to go. Live your life
What's one interesting fact about your country you wish more people knew?

Well, I think a lot of people don't know this, but we have the tallest waterfall in the world, Salto Ángel, and it's a beautiful place. I had the opportunity to go about, I think, three years ago now, and it feels literally from another planet. I recommend everyone, if you can, go visit, see it, because your life will be changed. You're gonna feel like you're in a movie.
What's an issue affecting women in your country that you'd like to use your platform to champion?

I think child or teenage pregnancy is a very big issue facing women in my country, and unfortunately, this might stop them from pursuing an education or, you know, pursuing a career. I had the privilege throughout this year of working with Aprendiendo Querer, which gives reproductive or sexual reproductive classes and programs to kids and teenagers, and I think that's an incredibly valuable and important way that we can help young adults stay informed about how they can best take care of themselves and then in order to, well, you know, give themselves the best future possible.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage says to the women and girls back home who are watching you?

That we don't have to be perfect to start chasing our dreams, that we can start today, right now. You are good enough. And also to never listen to other people trying to limit you, because I think society is going to try to limit us a hundred different times in a hundred different ways, but it's important to remember that we are capable.
What's one interesting fact about your country you wish more people knew?
One interesting fact that my country has is that we have the second biggest dam in Latin America. It’s actually in the place that I come from, Joho, it's called Represa Hidroeléctrica El Cajón.
What's an issue affecting women in your country that you'd like to use your platform to champion?

I think one of the main issues that is impacting women in my country is the lack of access to education. It's a topic that, you know, has been around for many years, but I honestly want to use my platform to let them know that I am a voice for them. I hear, I see what's going on behind closed doors, and here I am as the queen trying to represent that kind of, or trying to represent what Honduran women go through, and all the things that we have to go through as well in order to aim for education, in order to get a job, you know. I want to open up a little bit more using the Miss Universe platform to show the world that there is, in fact, a problem going around, but there's also a solution, and I am here for this.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage says to the women and girls back home who are watching you?

I hope that my presence on the Miss Universe stage can let women know that they're able to reach out for their dreams. They just have to work hard. They have to show the world, to show the light that they deserve to be there. But there's a lot of sacrifice and a lot of learning first. It's not easy. It's not an easy step, but definitely women are able to conquer their dreams, fulfill their dreams as well, and become the woman they want to be, even if that's a beauty queen, if that's an engineer, if they want to be an astronaut, whatever you want to be, a painter, you can do it.
What's one interesting fact about your country you wish more people knew?
We have the lowest tax burden in the region, and Paraguay is an excellent country for investment.
What's an issue affecting women in your country that you'd like to use your platform to champion?

Gender-based violence. In the first week of 2026, Paraguay experienced seven cases of femicide. That's why I decided to raise my voice and create a podcast, in addition to my social project, that’s called Voces que Sanan, where I interview women who have experienced violence. We also help them transform themselves and become a light for their communities.
What do you hope your presence on the Miss Universe stage says to the women and girls back home who are watching you?
I hope to embody the image of a woman leader who dares to dream and inspire them to become the best versions of themselves.

items.title: The story behind R.E.M.'s album covers
items.description: Chris Bilheimer and Michael Stipe first met, 35 years ago, over a whirring photocopier and a mutual interest in visual art. It was the tentative start of professional relationship that would (literally) change the face of record sleeve artwork in the Peak CD e
items.author: Craig McLean
paragraphs: Chris Bilheimer and Michael Stipe first met, 35 years ago, over a whirring photocopier and a mutual interest in visual art. It was the tentative start of professional relationship that would (literally) change the face of record sleeve artwork in the Peak CD era. And, as it turned out, in the last hurrah for albums as a physical medium.

At the time Bilheimer was studying art at the University of Georgia in Athens, Georgia. A decade earlier, in 1980, Stipe had embarked on the same course, before dropping out to concentrate on the band he’d formed with fellow students Bill Berry, Peter Buck and Mike Mills: R.E.M.

Back then, recalls Bilheimer, 'Kinko's was the college town copy shop where students in bands would go to make their flyers. It was a creative epicentre for people who didn't have studios.' Ahead of the March 1991 release of R.E.M.’s seventh album Out of Time, Stipe 'had a bunch of disparate things that he wanted to make copies of to send to the record label. I ended up helping him collage those pieces together, because I happened to be at Kinko's when he was there.'

Then, 'a couple of years later, as computers started becoming more prevalent, I was at Kinko's working on [artwork] for a small band. Michael came in and wanted to do some reference material for [1992 album] Automatic for the People, and had me typeset what became the back cover of the album. I laid out the typography for the sign painter to hand paint that on glass.'

These 'little threads of connections to the artwork' were then braided together into a full-time position on 1994’s Monster, 'to assist Michael the way I had been assisting him at Kinko's. And it just grew from there.'

Having been forged in the 1990s, the decade when R.E.M. became one of the biggest bands in the world, the Bilheimer/Stipe visual partnership is still creating, three-and-a-half decades on. For the new, 25th anniversary release of 2001’s Reveal, the graphic designer and the former frontman have collaborated on a fresh iteration of the sleeve artwork for the band’s 12th album. It’s the latest in a run of quarter-century reissues – all beautifully pimped out with new imagery and unreleased and/or not-widely-available recordings – that began with a freshening up of R.E.M.’s 1983 debut, Murmur.

'It's been an interesting journey going through the reissues as a designer,' reflects Bilheimer, 55, from his home in Austin, Texas. 'When we started, it was Murmur, Reckoning, Fables of the Reconstruction – I was now re-designing albums that I grew up listening to. And I tried to keep them very faithful as a fan to how they felt when they came out.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

'But as this process has gone on, and we've gotten further along in the catalogue, Michael has wanted to fuck with it more. I have never asked him exactly what his feelings are, but there's been increasing desire in him to toy with the legacy. Or just have fun with it. More so than holding our breath and faithfully honouring the original.'

Bilheimer – once a fanboy, always a fanboy – admits to conflict about the legacy of a cherished group who split in 2011, 31 years young. 'There's part of me that wants to keep the [sleeves] as a timepiece. And there's a part of me that's like: “Oh, this is fun. We get to reinvent something we already did.” And Reveal is a really good example of that…'

The original, bleach-yellowed cover is a Polaroid that Stipe took on tour, with the shadow of the distinctively chrome-domed singer, camera in hand, in the bottom left corner. 'The first thing Michael said to me was: “What would that look like if it were infrared photography?” So, imagine what it would be like through different technology. Just fuck with the colours, give it a completely different vibe.' Hence the pinkified new look.

For his original work on Reveal, Bilheimer received the first of three Grammy nominations that would come his way, alongside Stipe, for his artwork for the band. Here he, yes, reveals the stories behind the other R.E.M. sleeves he worked on.
R.E.M.’s grunge-era album, dedicated to actor and friend River Phoenix, who died the previous year, with not-so-monstrous candy-coloured sleeve

'It’s funny you say candy-coloured because the starting point was fruit-flavoured cereal boxes from the early 1970s. Then it’s photography by either Michael or [frequent band collaborator] Jem Cohen – except the cover. That came from a weird balloon that Michael bought at a store. It was a full-body bear. But for some reason, its head and its body were separated on the balloon. So it's this very surreal-looking creature.

'We were photographing the bear, and the first picture I took was an accident, totally out-of-focus, and that's the one we ended up using on the cover. It’s copyright of The Tilly Balloon Company and we contacted them to see if they'd let us have rights to it. We were half-expecting them to see that this huge band wants to use their artwork and then have dollar signs in their eyes. They said: “Yeah, you can totally use it. But can you send us a couple copies of the album? Also, if you want to buy some balloons…” So we ended up buying a promotional amount of balloons from them.'
New Adventures in Hi-Fi (1996)
Trailed by suitably greyscale single ‘E-Bow the Letter’, a collaboration with Patti Smith, and with a black-and-white cover photograph, taken through a tour bus window, of a desert-scape

'That whole album was recorded during the Monster tour, and all of those photos were taken by Michael during that time period. Then we were in the studio in Seattle, and we had all these photographs spread out over the floor. And Peter Buck walked by and pointed at the one of the hill and goes, “That one should be the cover” and just kept walking. I think that was the one and only time Peter ever had an opinion about the artwork. So we're like: well, if Peter says it, then that's got to be the cover!
'I actually got to drive by that hill on the cover during the pandemic – someone texted me the GPS coordinates. It's in New Mexico or Arizona.'
Blocky colours and an R.E.M. logo hand-drawn by Bilheimer

'I found a bunch of reference images to show Michael of what I was really into in that era, and still am. There's a thing called spot colour – you mix a purple ink, and you mix a green ink, and you print each colour one at a time. You'll often print one colour on top of another colour accidentally, and you see through it, and you see the texture of the ink. It was very, very analogue.

'The “up” came from a book where someone had collected every version of the “up” arrow on cardboard shipping boxes. Originally, they wanted to call the album Up, Up, Up, Up, Up. But then somewhere along the line, it got shortened to just Up. Titling the records was always a thing, and it always came way late in the process. But it was different every time. Out of Time is called that because they ran out of time to come up with a title.'
Blurry aliens walk amongst us…

'Those are all overexposed photos of Michael taken on a sunny day. And he had this little plastic stencil that you could stick a pin in and make lettering. He just drew the alphabet, and gave me these photos, and said: “That's all I want for the album.” So it's really simple. That was an example where I just put the thing together. I didn't have any design input on it. Michael knew exactly what he wanted.'
A hellish metropolis on the front, David Carson-esque typography design on the inside…

'Michael sent me hundreds of photographs of buildings that he took while he was travelling. He said: “I want you to mash up these buildings into a dystopian landscape.” Every picture's taken from a different angle, nothing lines up. And it's very disorienting to try and create [a cityscape] out of buildings that are all at different angles.

'After Around the Sun, musically it was a rawer, more straightforward album. So I went with the punk rock flyer [aesthetic], back to Kinko's. Those were all full-colour photographs and I made them black and white on a Xerox machine, cut and pasted them together, and built a big diorama. And the R.E.M. logo was pen and ink.'
An R.E.M. album sleeve that – shocker – features the band on the cover, Stipe with his hand in the air. What could it possibly mean?

‘I did not know, when we were making that record, that it was going to be their last one. And it's really interesting, in retrospect, the things that Michael gave me as prompts. He gave me this photo, where he's waving goodbye. Then I poured on acetone, which is a solvent, to eat away the ink on the paper, so it was degrading and disappearing. The other element he gave me was that concept in illustration where things go off to a vanishing point in the horizon. That's why there's lots of lines going off into different directions.

'And it never occurred to me that him waving goodbye, us disappearing the band with chemicals and the vanishing point were all symbolic. R.E.M. are going off, away, into the distance. And I've never asked how intentional that was. I imagine it was probably pretty intentional.'
Reveal (25th Anniversary Edition) boxset is released on 20 November 2026

London-based Scot, the writer Craig McLean is consultant editor at The Face and contributes to The Daily Telegraph, Esquire, The Observer Magazine and the London Evening Standard, among other titles. He was ghostwriter for Phil Collins' bestselling memoir Not Dead Yet.

items.title: John Lautner’s modernist buildings just got turned into cake
items.description: Have you ever wondered what architecture could taste like? Well, Friends Of Residential Treasures: LA (FORT: LA) has. The non-profit organisation dedicated to celebrating Los Angeles’ residential architectural history presents a bake-off to celebrate the works
items.author: Tianna Williams
paragraphs: Have you ever wondered what architecture could taste like? Well, Friends Of Residential Treasures: LA (FORT: LA) has. The non-profit organisation dedicated to celebrating Los Angeles’ residential architectural history presents a bake-off to celebrate the works of the late American architect John Lautner.

The bake-off is part of a wider public event titled ‘Architecture Uncorked: Lautnerpalooza’, which took place at Barnsdall Gallery Theatre in Los Angeles, in collaboration with the John Lautner Foundation to celebrate the organisation’s 30th anniversary.
Discover the winning John Lautner-inspired cakes

Lautner is best known for his modernist architecture that was futuristic and organic at the same time, utilising large glass walls to welcome the outdoors in. Now, over 30 years after his death, his work has been turned into baked delights for the event, featuring, variously, frosted façades, sponge-cake walls, and chocolate rocks, enjoyed by architecture enthusiasts hungry for something a little different.

The entries were whittled down to five finalists, whose bakes were presented on 14 November 2026 for panellists to judge. Best of Show went to ChocoLaut Nervana by Andrei Pogany and Deborah Gorman, respectively, the head of an architectural design studio and a chef and owner of Deborah’s Table. They chose to create various details of their favourite Lautner buildings (the Sheats Goldstein residence in Beverly Hills, Silvertop in Silverlake, and Arango House in Acapulco) and combined them into a new vision.

Best Architectural Cake and Audience Choice award went to the 'Cherry' Garcia House by Abigail Lodevico, owner of the custom cake shop Abs of Cakes in East Los Angeles. She chose to incorporate the siting and structure of Lautner’s Garcia House in the Hollywood Hills to create a round cake. The flavour was inspired by Ben & Jerry’s Cherry Garcia Ice Cream with vanilla, chocolate, and cherry.
Pearlman Cabin Pistachio Cake by Grace Davis and Katie Horak, architects and former co-workers who are also avid home bakers, won Best Flavour. They looked to the Pearlman Cabin, completed in 1957.

Other entries included Silvertop Hearth Cake by Allise Matsuno, a designer and writer. She aimed to create a cake that combined elements of the fireplace at Silvertop in Silver Lake, highlighting Lautner’s use of materials. The cross-section of the cake references an architectural section, while flavours are of roasted berry, chocolate and mousse.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Nougat Googie by Julia Berkson, an energy-industry contracts manager, created a cake inspired by the shapes of the Foster House in Sherman Oaks and the colours of the Schaffer House in Glendale. Her flavours were inspired by the local area, including almond, orange and tangerine.

Russell Brown, FORT: LA founder and board chair, says of the event, ‘John Lautner spent his career challenging conventional ideas about how we live. We thought it would be fun to see what happens when you give that same challenge to a group of cake makers. At FORT: LA, we're always looking for unexpected ways to bring people into the stories of Los Angeles architecture, and sometimes the best way to appreciate a building is to eat it.’

Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer. When she isn’t writing extensively across varying content pillars, ranging from design and architecture to travel and art, she also helps put together the daily newsletter. She enjoys speaking to emerging artists, designers and architects, writing about gorgeously designed houses and restaurants, and day-dreaming about her next travel destination.

paragraphs: В «Снобе» мы используем и развиваем собственные информационные технологии. Это не просто часть нашей работы, а основа всего проекта. В нашем IT-отделе мы решаем следующие задачи:
- Создаем, улучшаем и поддерживаем все наши веб-ресурсы, включая сайт Snob.ru.
- Консультируем по вопросам, связанным с веб-разработкой и работой сайтов.
- Предоставляем онлайн-доступ к нашему контенту и различным цифровым сервисам.
- Разрабатываем собственные инструменты для работы с интернет-рекламой — от размещения до аналитики.
Ядро нашей IT-системы — это, конечно, федеральное сетевое издание Snob.ru.

Для того, чтобы вы могли удобно читать нас, а редакция — быстро и эффективно публиковать материалы, мы создали мощную собственную платформу. Это не стандартное коробочное решение, а наша уникальная разработка:
- Удобная система управления контентом (CMS), которая позволяет нашим редакторам создавать материалы в самых разных форматах, легко менять дизайн и структуру главной страницы и разделов.
- Автоматическая публикация контента не только на сайте, но и в наших социальных сетях и новостных агрегаторах.

Эта платформа полностью разработана нашей командой с использованием современных технологий: на фронтенде (то, что вы видите) используются HTML, CSS, TypeScript и JavaScript (с фреймворками Vue 2 и Vue 3); бэкенд (основная логика) написан на Python (с Django), а данные хранятся в базе PostgreSQL. Такая «кухня» позволяет нам быть гибкими и постоянно развивать функционал.

Сайт Snob.ru полностью кроссплатформенный. Это значит, что вы можете комфортно читать нас с любого устройства — компьютера, планшета или смартфона, на любой операционной системе (Windows, MacOS, Linux, Android, iOS). Мы позаботились о том, чтобы контент выглядел отлично везде.
Наша собственная разработка и круглосуточная поддержка в режиме 24/7 обеспечивают стабильную работу всего проекта, позволяя обрабатывать более 2 500 000 уникальных визитов в месяц.
Описание функциональных характеристик программного обеспечения
Программное обеспечение представляет собой современную систему управления контентом (CMS) сайта snob.ru, которая предназначена для следующих целей:
1. Работа редакции и контент-команд
- Позволяет оперативно создавать и публиковать материалы в различных форматах (новость, статья, интервью, тест и др.).
- Даёт возможность легко настраивать дизайн, менять структуру главной страницы и разделов без необходимости программирования.
- Поддерживает совместную работу над контентом, включая редактуру, модерацию и планирование публикаций.
2. Онлайн-платформа для авторов и читателей
- Предоставляет инструменты для ведения личных блогов, публикации авторских материалов и взаимодействия с аудиторией.
- Включает функции рейтингов и обсуждений, что помогает пользователям находить единомышленников и формировать сообщества.
- Подходит как для индивидуальных авторов, так и для организаций, желающих создать удобную площадку для обмена мнениями и контентом.
3. Онлайн-платформа для программы лояльности — Клуб «Сноб»
- Размещения анонсов акций, спецпредложений и привилегий.
- Редактирования и обновления контента в режиме реального времени.
- Включения материалов в email-рассылку по базе подписчиков клуба.

Специализированный лендинг для взаимодействия с партнерами медиапроекта, позволяющий собирать и публиковать эксклюзивные предложения для зарегистрированных пользователей. Каждый партнер получает персональный профиль с возможностью:
4. Платформа для Премии «Сделано в России»
- Прием заявок. Пользователи могут номинировать собственные проекты, реализованные не ранее октября предыдущего календарного года, через форму на сайте.
- Онлайн-голосование. Система с защитой от накрутки, отсеивающая некачественный и роботизированный трафик.
- Фильтрация и модерация заявок.
- Управление номинациями премии.
- Управление партнерами премии.
