“Minotaur,” then, is the most corrosive version of this material imaginable, less the tale of a good marriage gone awry than that of a rotten one getting worse, plus something more: an icy study in the mechanics, and the erotics, of corruption and power. As ever with Zvyagintsev, who wrote the script with Simon Lyashenko, the pessimism isn’t limited to the domestic sphere. It’s the fall of 2022, and the grim consequences of Russia’s months-long assault on Ukraine are everywhere. On phones and computers, we see residential buildings being bombed and Russian cars fleeing toward the traffic-choked Georgian border. On the streets, billboards glorify the military’s efforts, even as some local graffiti (“FUCK YOUR WAR”) testifies to pervasive, if largely hidden, discontent. Gleb’s company is about to suffer the effects of the conflict in a particularly pernicious way. Krasnoborsk’s mayor (Vladimir Friedman) has ordered the city’s major employers to submit lists of male workers—the more physically fit the better—to be drafted into what Russia, avoiding the W-word, is calling its “special military operation.”

Gleb must provide fourteen men, a number that brings the film’s title, with its reference to Greek mythology, into crystalline focus. The Minotaur demanded that fourteen young noblemen and noblewomen be delivered to his labyrinthine lair, and Zvyagintsev’s film duly traps Gleb within his own moral maze. Faced with parallel dilemmas, one personal and one professional, he can address them, finally, only with the same banal disregard for human life. He may be a lesser monster than Putin, glimpsed here in a framed photograph on the mayor’s wall, but unquestioning complicity has made a monster of him nonetheless—one who profits from the blood of human sacrifice and perpetuates the most callous of the story’s innumerable betrayals.

Zvyagintsev, at sixty-two, has become a master at seeding the conventions of domestic melodrama with portents of sociopolitical catastrophe. It wasn’t always thus. His early features, including “The Return” (2003) and “The Banishment” (made in 2007 but not released here until 2018), were troubled-family sagas of a more spiritual than political bent, composed with a rapturous visual sublimity that earned lofty comparisons to the work of Andrei Tarkovsky. But Zvyagintsev’s pursuit of an uncompromising art-film purity could not, in the end, keep out an equal fascination with the malaise of modern life. In 2014, he directed “Leviathan,” about a husband and wife locked in a real-estate war with a small-town mayor, who, in his brutish overreach, clearly stood in for his country’s authoritarian leaders of the past, present, and future. (A photograph of Putin hung on that mayor’s wall, too.) Next came “Loveless” (2017), a bruisingly sad drama about the disappearance of a child, neglected and unmourned by his soon-to-be-divorced parents—a couple so bitterly at odds as to make Gleb and Galina look like honeymooners. “Loveless,” perhaps the most nakedly metaphorical of Zvyagintsev’s works, built to a blunt, summative image of a woman, in a conspicuously Russia-branded tracksuit, running on a treadmill—fierce, enraged, and going nowhere fast.

All of which is to say that Zvyagintsev has been here before, even though his sense of “here” has shifted. In 2022, while recovering from complications of a COVID infection that nearly killed him, the director moved with his family from Moscow to Paris, where he lives in self-imposed exile. France, long a haven for dissident artists and intellectuals, proved specifically instrumental in the making of “Minotaur”—and not merely because of its Chabrol-supplied source material. The film, which was shot entirely in Latvia, was mostly financed by French companies; it will represent France in the upcoming Oscar race for Best International Feature. (Another Gallic feather in the film’s cap: “Minotaur” won the Grand Prix, or second place, at this year’s Cannes Film Festival.)

Nine years, many of them fraught and full of upheaval, have elapsed between this film and its predecessor, and yet the sense of continuity between them is remarkable. In “Loveless,” the vanished child was an emblem of a lost Russian generation, cruelly abandoned by its elders. In “Minotaur,” and specifically in Seryozha—an ordinary, somewhat moody, clearly well-loved teen-ager—Zvyagintsev allows us a more hopeful vision of the future. There’s a moment when Gleb, learning of a potential bully at school, advises the kid to “never strike the first blow,” advice that he himself will swiftly disregard. His son, it becomes clear, already has a better head on his shoulders. In the film’s final moments, the emphasis shifts away from the fragile wreckage of Gleb and Galina’s marriage and toward Seryozha—seated with his parents yet slightly apart from them, happily lost in the clouds. You want the best for him, and hope that the only messes he’ll have to clean up are his own. ♦

items.title: Earth Was a Fixer-Upper
items.description: Every complex organism alive today—this includes not only you and me but also the mites that hang out in our hair follicles and the protozoa that lurk in our large intestines—is the product of an unlikely union. Roughly two billion years ago, a bacterium took
items.author: Elizabeth Kolbert
paragraphs: Every complex organism alive today—this includes not only you and me but also the mites that hang out in our hair follicles and the protozoa that lurk in our large intestines—is the product of an unlikely union. Roughly two billion years ago, a bacterium took up with a bacterium-like creature that belonged to a whole different domain, the archaea. From this microbiological meet-cute, a new kind of cell was born, one equipped with mitochondria, and, along with it, a new kind of organism: a eukaryote. (The term is pronounced “you-carry-oat.”) The particular eukaryote from which we and our mites descend is formally known as the “last eukaryotic common ancestor,” or, more affectionately, LECA.

By the time LECA entered the picture, archaea and bacteria had been grooving along, occasionally exchanging genes, for eons. But they, too, have a backstory. They are descended from a single organism, which, by the logic of phylogeny, also represents humanity’s unimaginably distant ancestor. This unicellular Eve goes by the acronym LUCA, for “last universal common ancestor.” A few years ago, a team of European researchers attempted to re-create LUCA—on paper, that is—by looking at genes that are shared among existing species of archaea and bacteria. LUCA seems to have liked it hot—probably more than a hundred and twenty degrees. The team decided that she was capable of synthesizing some twenty-six hundred proteins and made do on a diet of dissolved hydrogen and carbon dioxide. According to the researchers’ calculations, LUCA lived some 4.2 billion years ago.

For a one-celled creature, LUCA was pretty sophisticated. Her genome comprised some three million base pairs, and she possessed a rudimentary immune system, which implies that she already had to contend with pathogens, eager to attack her. By the time she emerged, then, life had been kicking around for a while. At some point even further back, a first universal common ancestor—FUCA—must have come into being. The weird thing is, there isn’t much further back to go.

Earth was created some 4.5 billion years ago, when a cloud of interstellar dust contracted to form our solar system. In its early days (and days were much shorter then, because the globe was spinning faster), the planet was a horrifyingly inhospitable place. There was no free oxygen and no protection from ultraviolet radiation. Asteroid impacts were frequent—some of these may have generated enough heat to boil the oceans—as were intense volcanic eruptions.

How did FUCA get by? Perhaps the explanation is simply that life is adaptable. Today, living things occupy steaming vents on the floor of the Pacific, frozen peaks in the Himalayas, and just about every space in between, so, clearly, they are flexible. As the movies teach us, life finds a way.

But perhaps that still doesn’t give life enough credit. This is the argument of two recent books, “The Co-Creation: How Earth Made Life and Life Made Earth,” by Olivia Judson (Penguin Press), and “Earth and Life: A Four Billion Year Conversation,” by Andrew H. Knoll (Princeton).

Judson is a science journalist who earned a doctorate in biological sciences from Oxford. Her previous book, “Dr. Tatiana’s Sex Advice to All Creation,” which was written as a series of advice columns to species like fig wasps and seaweed flies, explored the evolutionary dynamics of sex in a breezy, comic key. In “The Co-Creation,” Judson attempts something more ambitious: a work of popular science organized around not hanky-panky but the interplay of geology and biology, or, as the subject has become known, geobiology.

The book opens with a meditation on sand dunes. Though obviously not alive, dunes possess many of the attributes of life. They can move. They can grow. They can even, in a certain sense, reproduce; sometimes a large sand dune will spin off a smaller one. What dunes and life have in common, according to Judson, is that they “arise from, and are maintained by, an ongoing flow of energy and matter.” Life differs from dunes in that it actively seeks energy and, occasionally, reinvents itself to gain access to more of it. Judson ignores the conventional geological timescale, with its eons and eras and periods, in favor of a scheme of her own devising. The planet’s history, she writes, can be divided into five “epochas,” each defined by the emergence of a creature that could “intercept a new source of energy.” Living things, in Judson’s scheme, become “energons,” while inanimate objects—including corpses—are “statigons.”

The first epocha, the rock epocha, began when the earliest organisms learned how to extract energy from the chemical soup in which they floated. Judson believes that this skill was acquired in the sea, in places where a mineral called olivine was coming into contact with water and releasing hydrogen. “If you follow the thread of your forebears all the way back across the eons, you will find that your original ancestor was a fracturing wet, iron-rich rock,” she writes.

Judson’s second epocha commenced some 3.4 billion years ago, with the invention of photosynthesis. This was obviously a big deal, and it enabled life to greatly extend its reach. In the third epocha, a subset of photosynthesizing bacteria—cyanobacteria—developed the capacity to split water and liberate oxygen.

Next up in Judson’s scheme is an era she calls the flesh epocha. This started when groups of energons evolved the ability to dine on other energons. The fifth and final epocha is the age of fire, which began when some enterprising hominin figured out how to cook over an open flame.

Judson’s epochas and energons can be difficult to keep up with. (Her epochas have beginnings but no ends, so the energons keep piling up.) To help the reader out, she periodically interrupts her narrative to visit the office of a fictional “planetary accountant,” a harried, Nutty Professor type whose job it is to track the world’s growing complexity. Judson’s overarching argument, though, is fairly straightforward. Since FUCA first emerged, life has had to adapt to conditions on planet Earth. But life has also had a hand in determining those conditions. Life, in other words, can give as good as it gets.

Consider, once again, photosynthetic cyanobacteria. (These are sometimes referred to as blue-green algae, although they are not, in fact, algae.) Oxygen is a waste product of the process they use to harness energy from the sun. But free oxygen is highly reactive, and its appearance thoroughly transformed the planet. It brought into being many minerals that hadn’t previously existed. It caused vast quantities of iron that had been dissolved in the oceans to precipitate out and accumulate in what are called banded-iron formations. (These formations constitute the world’s major deposits of iron ore.) Eventually, it produced the ozone layer, which shields the planet from UV radiation. The ozone layer, for its part, changed the tint of the sky. Before the ozone layer appeared, the sky probably turned an eerie yellow at dusk. “In altering the composition and mass of the air, lifeforms have reached out and painted the heavens above” is how Judson puts it.

Meanwhile, the addition of oxygen to the oceans and the atmosphere made possible aerobic respiration, which, in turn, made possible the evolution of animals. When animals developed habits like burrowing, they allowed oxygen to penetrate the seafloor. This, it’s believed, helped create conditions favorable for the accumulation of gypsum, vast amounts of which were deposited around five hundred million years ago. Nowadays, gypsum is used in drywall; thus, anyone who’s renovated a kitchen or put in a new bathroom has ancient wormlike creatures to thank. “Truly, the advent of burrowing would change the world,” Judson observes.

Or consider the advent of predation. By consuming and then excreting their victims, predatory creatures invented a new kind of recycling. This allowed more nutrients to circulate through the system, thereby enabling more (and more various) creatures to find nourishment. Predators also spurred their potential victims to develop novel defenses, like shells or, in the case of one-celled creatures called coccolithophores, minuscule calcite plates. Calcite plates piling up on the floor of the ocean eventually became a new kind of rock: chalk. “The white cliffs of Dover in England, of the German island of Rügen, of the Normandy coast of France, of the Smoky Hill River of Kansas in the United States—these are all built of chalk,” Judson points out. Under high pressure, chalk can be converted into marble, which can be quarried and sculpted—a case of life initiating art.

As for man’s mastery of fire, it, too, has proved world transforming. From burning sticks, we’ve moved on to fossil fuels, which power our cities, our factories, our smelters, our fishing fleets, our industrial-scale farms, and, increasingly, our farmland-gobbling data centers. “Humans are, without doubt, causing more changes to the life-Earth system—in more ways and faster—than any lifeform ever has before,” Judson writes.

At the end of “The Co-Creation,” Judson offers a catalogue of researchers to whom she owes “intellectual debts.” Near the top of her list is Knoll, the author of “Earth and Life.” Knoll, a professor at Harvard, was more or less present at the creation of geobiology, and he played a key role in the discipline’s development. As a working scientist, he’s a lot more interested than Judson is in the nitty-gritty of how geobiologists piece together the history of Earth (and life) from fragmentary clues—isotopes of sulfur, say, or traces of compounds called sterols. (Conversely, he’s a lot less interested in promulgating neologisms.)

The “conversation” of Knoll’s subtitle is his organizing metaphor. Chapter by chapter, he recounts what geology and biology have had to say to each other over the eons. Sometimes the dialogue has been balanced, at other moments lopsided.

Initially, life was quite reticent. It was, Knoll reports, probably “a local phenomenon,” confined to watery spots where hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and “the minerals to catalyze their interaction were available.” Then, around 2.4 billion years ago, it started to speak up. This was the beginning of what’s become known as the Great Oxygenation Event, or, as it’s referred to in the scientific literature, the G.O.E.

Exactly what happened during the G.O.E. remains something of a paleontological puzzle, and Knoll devotes a number of chapters to exploring its mysteries. (He calls this section of his book “The Story of O,” in a nod to the rather racier French bondage novel.) Among the mysteries is the timing. Various lines of evidence suggest that oxygen-producing cyanobacteria showed up several hundred million years before oxygen levels began to climb. So what caused the delay? One possible explanation is that a shortage of phosphorus in the oceans limited the bacteria’s numbers. Phosphorus began to wash off the land when the earliest large continents appeared, so cyanobacteria may have got their big chance owing to plate tectonics. If this is the case, the G.O.E. would be the consummate example of geology influencing biology and biology influencing geology. In any event, once oxygen started to build up there was no going back. “The stage was set for environmental revolution,” Knoll writes.

On occasion, geology has come close to shouting down life altogether. About two hundred and fifty million years ago, in what’s known as the end-Permian extinction, huge volcanic eruptions in what’s now Siberia released huge amounts of carbon dioxide; this led temperatures to spike and the oceans to become both anoxic and acidified. Something like ninety per cent of marine animal species died out. A similar, if somewhat less devastating, die-off occurred about two hundred million years ago, probably owing to another burst of volcanism, this time from what’s been dubbed the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. Sixty-six million years ago, a Manhattan-size asteroid plowed into the Yucatán Peninsula; roughly seventy-five per cent of species went extinct, including our distant relatives the non-avian dinosaurs. Catastrophe, Knoll writes, appears to be “sewn into the fabric of our planet.”

In recent centuries, the conversation has taken a strange turn. For the first time, an organism is not only changing the world but also looking on with dread as it does so. Fossil-fuel combustion is adding carbon to the air at a rate that exceeds the pace of the release during the end-Permian extinction. Now as then, temperatures are rising, and the oceans are acidifying. Meanwhile, people are rerouting rivers, messing with the global nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, and churning out so much stuff—concrete, plastic, asphalt, iPhones—that, measured by dry weight, human-produced materials now outweigh all living organisms combined. “Humans have become a dominant voice in the conversation between Earth and life,” as Knoll puts it. The result, he says, is “a distinct time in our planet’s history”—a new epoch, if not a new epocha.

If life on Earth has been partly, or even largely, responsible for rendering Earth habitable, what does this say about the possibilities on other planets? Knoll, who served on the science team for NASA’s Mars Exploration Rover mission, devotes the last part of his book to the prospects of what he calls “other conversations.”

Knoll is pretty confident that life is out there somewhere. The universe, after all, is ginormous. Our particular galaxy, which is just one among billions, is estimated to contain more than a hundred billion stars, most of which probably have planets orbiting them. “If only one planet (or moon) in a billion sustains life, the universe must be a lively place,” Knoll observes. But that doesn’t mean we’re going to encounter it. So far, at least, no signs of life have been detected emanating from any other planet (or moon) in our solar system, and other solar systems are awfully far away. After the sun, the star closest to Earth is Proxima Centauri. It would take a probe like NASA’s Voyager 1—the first craft to journey into interstellar space—about seventy-five thousand years to reach it.

And, even if life has emerged elsewhere, it hasn’t necessarily had time to generate creatures capable of sending out interstellar probes or messages. If not for plate tectonics, which has kept life’s key ingredients recirculating, evolution on this planet probably would have hit a wall billions of years ago. “It may be that what makes Earth unusual is not so much that life began here—that may happen widely in the universe—but that it has persisted so long,” Knoll notes.

Judson, too, ends her book contemplating the cosmos. Like Knoll, she believes that in the vastness of space there are many other planets where life could have emerged. And yet, also like Knoll, she thinks there’s no place like home.

In the final pages of “The Co-Creation,” Judson describes a fascinating experiment in applied evolution which has been running since 1988. That year, a biologist named Richard Lenski, then at U.C. Irvine, placed virtually identical populations of E. coli into twelve identical flasks. (This was a nonpathogenic strain of the bacteria, rather than the kind that causes recalls.) E. coli reproduce by splitting themselves in two, and, in Lenski’s flasks, the bacteria were free to keep doubling until they exhausted their supply of glucose. Every twenty-four hours, Lenski—or, more likely, his assistants—would remove a small number of the bacteria from each flask, provide them a new supply of food, and let the process repeat itself.

In addition to glucose, the growth medium contained a compound called sodium citrate. At first, the twelve tribes of E. coli ignored the citrate. But then, around the thirty-thousandth generation, something interesting happened: bacteria in one of the flasks developed the ability to consume it. That population gained a powerful advantage—the citrate-eaters had found their way to a new energy source.

By now, Lenski’s E. coli have gone through another fifty thousand generations. But the populations in the other eleven flasks still can’t consume citrate. The necessary mutations just haven’t been repeated. The lesson, according to Judson, is clear: major evolutionary innovations are fluky. This, she argues, should be kept in mind whenever talk turns to aliens. Even on Earth, the “conversation” between biology and geology could have played out very differently. There was no guarantee that it would have included LUCA, LECA, or oxygen-producing cyanobacteria. And, without all of these, it certainly wouldn’t have included us.

That we are in a position to study the history of life and wonder at its contingency is itself a contingency. It’s one that we (and our mites) ought to be grateful for, and also one that, Judson argues, ought to make us think carefully about how we treat our planet. “If humans really are the only technological species now, and perhaps ever, in the cosmos—what then?” she asks. “What responsibility might that bestow on us, should we choose to accept it?” ♦

items.title: Sotheby’s Sold the World’s Most Expensive Van Gogh for $190 Million
items.description: This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.
items.author: Nate Freeman
paragraphs: This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors, from New York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

One thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in New York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.
We’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this issue: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian

Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

Honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

So who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is currently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

The $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

— As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

The 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

— Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

— The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred said the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”

— For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

— Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

— After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

— The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.
THE ENCOUNTER: MICHAEL CHOW

On a Friday in November, I walk into Gagosian on Madison Avenue for a meeting with Michael Chow, the artist, collector, filmmaker, designer, actor, and founder of the restaurant Mr. Chow. There’s a portrait of Chow by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a portrait by Julian Schnabel, a portrait by Andy Warhol. There’s a drawing of Chow by David Hockney, made soon after Mr. Chow opened in London in 1968.

Michael Chow: So I opened that restaurant. You’ve got Hockney, you’ve got fashion, you’ve got every single thing. It’s almost like a Dada movement on the First World War thing. This one is in London—all happening.

He starts talking about duopolys: Christie’s versus Sotheby’s, Coke versus Pepsi. There was an Italian restaurant in London’s Soho, so he opened a Chinese restaurant in Soho with Italian waiters. He has a theory about name-dropping.
Chow: I hate people who drop names, and Lady Gaga agrees with me.
True Colors: That’s a good one.
Why is name-dropping important? Because the minute I say “Napoleon,” you will go there immediately. So it saves a lot of time. Okay, so why am I saying that? Do you know who Robert Fraser is?
The art dealer from the ’60s. Groovy Bob.

I was looking forward to meeting him, blah, blah, blah. He was sitting there. Name-dropping. Sitting in front is Jim Dine. Name-dropping again. I say, “I would like to borrow some paintings.” I said, “Just like”—do you know the Kronenhalle restaurant?
We walk over to the Hockney portrait of Michael Chow sitting in his restaurant.
Chow: The first person I went to is David. He drew one and I said, “Boy.” You know what he did? Tore it all up.

Simultaneously, I went to Peter Blake. I say, “Give me a painting that’s the antithesis of racism,” which he did. At that time he’s into the circus, he’s into all that shit. All right? So I asked him, “Why did you do that?” He did a portrait. So now Peter Blake is fucking crazy. He loves the circus, he loves wrestling and all that shit.

Larry Gagosian walks in and gives Chow a fist bump. Gagosian takes a long look at the Schnabel and then flips through a book of drawings made by artists for 57th Street’s Mr. Chow when it was the art world’s clubhouse. We walk up to the Basquiat.
True Colors: To have it as this sort of landscape, you have the horizon line here, but it’s almost like a Western. It’s almost cinematic.
Chow: Name me three classic Westerns.
Shane. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. High Noon.
I’m going to act out the first scene of each. Okay, High Noon.
He uses his hand to pull a finger gun on me, then gets distracted by the Ed Ruscha and the Warhol double portrait.
Chow: Andy said, “Oh, what do you want?” I said, “Hold the color and add lots of diamonds.”
Gagosian brings up Anselm Kiefer, and then Richard Serra.

Chow: If you look at the year 2000, Charlie Rose and Richard Serra, their conversation on the culture of China, and Richard Serra identifies very clearly what is fine art: poetry, music, sculpture, and painting.
The works in the show are for sale. I ask Chow if he’s emotional about parting with them. He seems very calm.
Chow: I’m only a temporary steward of the works.
“Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow” is up at Gagosian’s 980 Madison space until December 22.
Have a tip? Drop me a line at nate_freeman@condenast.com. And make sure you subscribe to True Colors to receive Nate Freeman’s art-world dispatch in your inbox every week.

items.title: Are the Royals More Relatable Now Than Ever?
items.description: Prince William and Kate Middleton’s visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony marked their first joint overseas tour in four years, and the couple used it as an opportunity to demonstrate their star power. Through their action-packed itinerary, which too
items.author: Katie Nicholl
paragraphs: Prince William and Kate Middleton’s visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony marked their first joint overseas tour in four years, and the couple used it as an opportunity to demonstrate their star power. Through their action-packed itinerary, which took them from Mumbai to New Delhi, the Prince and Princess of Wales have paved the way for a new style of royal tour.

From Kate unexpectedly presenting an award and delivering a speech at the star-studded Earthshot Prize event to her and William playing cricket and traveling around Mumbai in an electric rickshaw, there have been plenty of photo opportunities and headlines around the world about the environmental initiative William is so passionate about.

According to royals author Russell Myers, who followed the couple on tour, the speech Kate gave at the awards was kept top secret. “None of us knew she was presenting an award on the night, or that she was going to speak. The auditorium was packed. There were about 5,000 people there. It’s been the biggest Earthshot yet, and you could see Catherine was nervous, but she delivered an absolutely brilliant speech. I’d say her best yet.

“It’s been wonderful for her to be here, supporting William, and you can see they’ve really had fun. Because of ongoing terror threats, there have been less walkabouts, but it’s been a very successful and varied tour, and I think, being shorter than most tours, it sets a new blueprint when it comes to royal tours for the couple in the future.”
There are seemingly already plans for another royal tour, says Myers.

“William let slip that Australia is on the cards next, and if that’s the case, I imagine they will go as a family. They don’t want to be away from their children for too long, and what a way it would be to win support for the monarchy Down Under,” Myers says.

According to royals insiders, there had been some nervousness around the trip after the couple’s disastrous tour of the Caribbean in March 2022, when their visit was overshadowed by calls for the UK to apologize for slavery. Then some of their photo calls, including one that involved the couple riding in an open-top Land Rover, led to accusations of the royals appearing colonial and out of touch.

“I think there has been a slight nervousness about how this tour would be received, but the reception has been really good,” Myers says. “The fact that William and Catherine have included a visit to New Delhi to see Prime Minister Modi is a clever move. While this is a private trip to promote Earthshot, the Foreign Office was keen for William to meet with the Indian prime minister, so they have packed that into the itinerary too.”

The visit to India has come at a time when the royals are on something of a charm offensive following a difficult year for the royal family, from Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest to what one palace insider calls “the ongoing soap opera” with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has not been charged and has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.)

William and Kate are keen to carve out their own initiatives and projects focusing on their major priorities, including the environment, children’s early years, and mental health. With the challenge of having Harry and Meghan carrying out their own engagements, the Prince and Princess of Wales have been careful to establish clear parameters that set them apart as working royals. In one telling moment while on an engagement in Mumbai, Kate was asked for an autograph. She politely declined, so as not to breach protocol, a clear contrast to the Duchess of Sussex, who has signed autographs in the past.

“Catherine was asked to sign an autograph, but she was right not to. It wasn’t a snub; it was just adhering to protocol. An autograph could be sold for money,” notes Dickie Arbiter, former press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II.

According to author Tom Bower, the royals are more relatable now than they were during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, who famously never gave a press interview. In recent weeks, Prince William has appeared as a guest on The Graham Norton Show (to promote Earthshot), and he’s revealed how he drinks his cider and his love of wild swimming as part of his guest-editing stint for a recent issue of Country Life magazine.

“The royals are more relatable, perhaps, than they ever have been, but they are not celebrities. There’s a danger of being too relatable, too much ‘one of the people,’ which means they can lose some of their mystery,” Bower says.

“William will have been advised to do TV appearances and take on media opportunities to bolster his public image. Of course, it’s charming to hear these nuggets and see this side of the prince, but I do think there’s a need to see and hear more from William about his broader plans. Over the years, Charles has made huge efforts to appeal to all cultural aspects of society. I’m not sure William has done that. He’s got to find a way of connecting with everyone, not just the younger generation,” Bower adds.
The Earthshot Prize awards have been a powerful way of demonstrating that William doesn’t just talk the talk; he is insisting on action.

“The Earthshot is a master class in what needs to be done,” concludes Arbiter. “He’s pushing for environmental issues and climate change, and he’s getting people to do something about it. The fact that he is so well supported, and by so many high-profile people, shows his pulling power and influence.”

items.title: Lesley Manville, Pierce Brosnan, and More Celebrate Violinist Joshua Bell at the Langham London
items.description: At the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since. “I don’t remember falling in love with music,” says Bell. “Music has just been my life. I used to string rubber bands on my dresser drawers and make pitches by pulling
items.author: Bridget Arsenault
paragraphs: At the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since. “I don’t remember falling in love with music,” says Bell. “Music has just been my life. I used to string rubber bands on my dresser drawers and make pitches by pulling the drawers out. I was fascinated with strings. It’s the closest instrument to the human voice. And I find it the most expressive instrument.”

Today, the Grammy Award–winning musician is one of the most celebrated classical violinists of his era. By 14, Bell was performing with the Philadelphia Orchestra, and would soon be touring the world. “I live in hotels 250 days a year,” says Bell of the nonstop schedule he has maintained since his teens. Specifically, Bell has been “staying at the Langham for decades now,” he says, referring to the regal central London hotel that first opened in 1865. “I chose it on my own because it was near one of my favorite halls in London, which is the Wigmore Hall. And now I stay with them whenever I’m traveling.”

That kinship was solidified over coupes of Champagne and hand-dived Orkney scallops, with the hotel celebrating Bell, a “Langham Luminary,” in its London ballroom packed with writers, artists, designers, and musicians.

Attendees included actor Simon Callow, House of Dragon actor Emily Carey, former British culture minister Ed Vaizey, Saturday Night Live UK cast producer Susie Hall, stage and television actor Indira Varma, and Verity actor Ismael Cruz Córdova.

Held in partnership with Vanity Fair, the evening marked the latest iteration of the Langham’s Luminaries in Residence program. The event series is continuation of the hotel’s legacy that brings together a diverse, influential community—an evocative reminder of prominent guests from its storied past, including Charles Dickens, Winston Churchill, George Orwell, Oscar Wilde, and Mark Twain.

“I’m not going to put my name in the same sentence as Toscanini or Mark Twain—who has stayed here, or Churchill, who has stayed here. But it’s cool to be part of the history,” says Bell. “So maybe someday, in a hundred years, there will be a violinist who might say that—that I stayed here. I don’t know, maybe that would mean something.”

It certainly does mean something. Pierce Brosnan and his wife, Keely Shaye Brosnan, “have been huge fans of Joshua for many, many years,” Brosnan tells me. “Keely went to go see him…I don’t know how many years back. Unfortunately, due to the LA traffic, she got there late, five minutes late, and they wouldn’t let her into the concert. So tonight is one of those nights.”
Bell, who performed mid-dinner with members of the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields—with a surprise appearance from his wife, soprano Larisa Martínez—brought about a collective catharsis.

Dazzling, fiery, and flamboyant, the experience of watching Bell up close is impossible to replicate. “I just think he’s incredibly soulful, and there’s something really elegant,” actor Russell Tovey tells me, before explaining how he actually discovered Bell via his Instagram algorithm.

For actor Lesley Manville, the event marked her introduction to Bell’s music. “I’m a bit embarrassed that he was not on my radar. But isn’t that nice to have a surprise like that?” says Manville. “Schubert’s String Quintet is one of my favorite pieces of music. It’s unbelievably beautiful. You think of a violin, you think of those strings. And it’s instant emotion. They just make you cry.”
There is a great power in being able to access the emotions of others, as Bell does.

“I think it is the ultimate gift to be able to make people happy,” says Brosnan. “My job is being an entertainer—to take the words of great writing and try to transform it into something that is meaningful and memorable.”

Speaking of entertaining, the week’s announcement that Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond was front of mind. “I wish him every joy and every success. He and I made a movie a number of years ago called Remember Me. I played his father. So I was very, very pleased and joyful for his nomination and now his success, and I believe he will be magnificent.”

And that creative full circle is exactly what the night was advocating. “Our own Luminaries in Residence program reflects our belief that meaningful hospitality creates genuine connection with extraordinary talents with one another, and with arts,” Bob van den Oord, CEO of Langham Hospitality Group, explained as he took the stage. “The Langham isn’t simply a place to stay, but a place to gather, exchange ideas, and indeed celebrate.”

items.title: Rosalía Calls Taylor Swift a 'Master Songwriter,' Reveals Her Favorite Swift Track
items.description: Rosalía gushed that it was an “honor” for Taylor Swift to hail her Grammy-nominated Lux as a “perfect album” and said that she considers the pop star a “master songwriter.”
items.author: Cheyenne Roundtree
paragraphs: Rosalía gushed that it was an “honor” for Taylor Swift to hail her Grammy-nominated Lux as a “perfect album” and said that she considers the pop star a “master songwriter.”

“To me, she’s a master, honestly,” Rosalía said during a red carpet interview for the Los40 Music Awards in Barcelona on Friday. “I think she’s incredible.” The Spanish singer also revealed her favorite Swift track. “I prefer individual songs rather than albums,” she added. “There’s one I really love, “Wildest Dreams.” It’s one of the songs I’ve listened to the most in my entire life.”

Swift had sung Rosalía’s praise earlier this month during a press conference for the nominations for the Golden Globes, which she is up for Best Original Song for the Toy Story 5 track, “I Knew It, I Knew You.”

“Two perfect albums that I love and that I kept coming back to are from Olivia Dean and Rosalía,” Swift shared about what will likely end up on her Spotify Wrapped this year. “For Rosalía, she has created an ambitious and expansive concept album that could’ve only come from her vital life experience. Those albums are marvelous because they’re human, they’re made for people and are about the human experience; that’s why humans connect with them.”

The women’s camaraderie and mutual respect comes ahead of the 2027 Grammys where both are going up against each other in several categories, including Album of the Year for Rosalía’s classically experiment Lux and Swift’s glitzy The Life of a Showgirl, as well as Record of the Year for “Berghain” and “The Fate of Ophelia.”

items.title: The Best Music Moments and Surprise Cameos From 'GTA VI'
items.description: The world has been waiting to play Grand Theft Auto VI, and the video game is finally here. Music, of course, is integral to all of it. There’s a soundtrack full of stars — the 34-track release, which is out today, features Travis Scott, Keith Richards, Dua Li
items.author: Julyssa Lopez
paragraphs: The world has been waiting to play Grand Theft Auto VI, and the video game is finally here. Music, of course, is integral to all of it. There’s a soundtrack full of stars — the 34-track release, which is out today, features Travis Scott, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Arca, and more. In addition to that, there is a massive one-day festival inspired by the game, taking place in Miami on Nov. 21, with headliners Cardi B, Metro Boomin, and Justice, who also put together the game’s score.

Once you start playing, there’s even more music to discover through the game’s radio stations and celebrity DJ hosts. Here are some of the best music moments and surprise cameos from the biggest video game of the year.

- PinkPantheress and the Dare on the Radio The game is full of celebrity guest DJs, which Rockstar began sharing a few weeks back. There’s Cocoteo FM hosted by Bad Bunny and RaiNao, Back Country Radio hosted by Morgan Wallen and Lana Del Rey, and Radio La Ola with Gloria and Emilio Estefan, plus tons more. But one that may surprise people is Stockyard FM, featuring two DJs named Victoria and Harrison — better known as PinkPantheress and the Dare. Victoria and Harrison are their real names, and their radio station is dedicated to experimental, left-of-center pop, electronica, and indie sleaze.

- A Surprise Song in Spanish From the Nineties Makes an Appearance One of the GTA VI radio stations, Radio La Ola, plays homage to Latin classics from over the decades. But one hugely surprising one is “Sopa de Caracol,” a massive but somewhat forgotten hit from the Nineties by Honduran band Banda Blanca. The inclusion made headlines in Central America, with the lead singer Pilo Tejada saying he was honored to have his voice reach new parts of the world.

- King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard Share New Bits of Music Psych-rock band King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard is featured on the soundtrack: They’re one of several artists on the collaboration “Flower in a Hurricane,” which also earned them their first Billboard 100 entry. But that’s not the only place you can find them: Gizz fans noticed that throughout several parts of the game, you can hear snippets of what appear to be demos from the band, woven into the score. On Reddit, diehards have been pointing these out and playing guessing games as they wonder what projects these might be from.

- Justice Perfects the Score We’ve known that the French electronic duo Justice composed the original score for the game, but the official album won’t be out until Dec. 11. We’re getting to hear some of what they came up with the release of the game but there’s still more to come, including an anticipated collaboration with the Weeknd. The duo have since said this is the “first and last” video game they’ll ever score.
- The Soundtrack Is Full of Stars

The soundtrack, which dropped on Nov. 19, is packed, featuring 34 songs by some surprising artists and  stars. There’s new music from Travis Scott, the Fuerza Regida track “Suzuki,” which is charting in 15 countries, and there are also songs from Keith Richards, Kali Uchis and Helado Negro, and more. A lot of the music was inspired directly by Miami, which you can hear in new tracks from artists like JT.
- Tinashe, Noah Kahan, and More Are Loving ‘GTA VI’

Artists are getting into the game, too. Tinashe delighted fans with a hilarious livestream playing for the first time. The stream captured her making an epic getaway by flying an airplane and hysterically crashing it into the ground, then running out of ammo in a shootout. “I have no bullets!” she screams. “Holy shit, I’m going to have to beat the fuck out of them myself.” After several days of sold-out shows in the U.K., Noah Kahan stayed up late and wreaked havoc in Vice City while his wife was asleep.

- There’s an Unreleased D’Angelo Song The world lost D’Angelo back in 2025, but his legacy lives on in Vice City. GTA VI players discovered that an unreleased track called “Kamakazi,” as confirmed by D’Angelo collaborator DJ Dojah, is one of the songs you can hear on the radio station Worldwide FM. D’Angelo’s “Lady” also plays on the in-game Honey FM channel, which is hosted by Chilli and T-Boz of TLC.

- Pop Is All Over the ‘GTA VI’ World While the creators of the game spent a ton of time adding interesting radio stations and track to the GTA VI universe, there is plenty of love for pop stars and major pop hits. Dua Lipa appears on the soundtrack, but the radio stations also feature plenty of pop girlies: There’s Chappell Roan’s “Hot To Go!,” Charli XCX’s “Good Ones,” and Addison Rae’s “Fame Is a Gun,” just to name a few, which players can blast while driving through Vice City.

items.title: Trump Says He 'Can't Speak To' Whether Russia is a Friend to America
items.description: Donald Trump has returned from his trip to Asia, and in a press briefing before a White House press corps eager to learn what had taken place in his closed door summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, as well as Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the pre
items.author: Nikki McCann Ramirez
paragraphs: Donald Trump has returned from his trip to Asia, and in a press briefing before a White House press corps eager to learn what had taken place in his closed door summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, as well as Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the president gleefully referred to as “my friend” this week in front of a room full of cameras.

When CNN’s Kaitlan Collins pointed out that Russia is one of Iran’s biggest allies and asked Trump if Russia is a “friend to America,” the president of the United States of America said he ”can’t speak to America.”
So who can he speak for? Himself, of course, and the autocratic rulers like Putin whom he considered his close personal friends.

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, speaking from his position as the chief representative of the American people, government, and territory. “I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia-Russia-Russia hoax, and to be honest, he was very nice about it … and I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship [with].”

Russia has, for the better part of a century, retained an adversarial position to the United States. They continue to be the primary military and financial backer of Iran, which America is currently at war with and which U.S. intelligence recently found is developing plans to target senior Trump officials with a “dirty bomb” in Washington, D.C..
But Trump spent much of the press conference praising Russia and China, while denigrating the United States.

“Some of our cities are so embarrassing,” he said at one point. “I don’t want to mention New York because I actually get along very well with Mayor Mamdani. But I could if I wanted to — but I won’t do that — because I like relationships,” he added.

“What a job president Xi has done,” Trump gushed while describing Shenzhen, where the summit took place. “It’s clean. It’s immaculate … He’s done a fantastic job for the country. And when I look at our cities where they’re dirty — not I must say, mostly blue — where the roads are dirty and they have potholes all over the place, and railings are falling down. Everything’s rusty and disgusting, and the crime is through the roof.”

Many Americans voted for Trump in 2024 hoping that he would deliver vast improvements to their quality of life and economic conditions. They took him up on his promise to deliver a “golden age” of American prosperity. Instead of delivering, the president has spent his time in office padding his own bank accounts and building himself a personal granite and gold paradise at the White House. Trump may not be able to speak for America regarding Russia, but Americans certainly spoke for themselves in the midterm elections, and they left nothing up for interpretation.

items.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Fact vs Fiction: Butkus the Dog, Bloody Knuckles and Stallone’s Fight to Get ‘Rocky’ Made
items.description: The beloved classic “Rocky” premiered half a century ago this week. Five decades later, “I Play Rocky,” in theaters now, tells the story of how unknown writer and actor Sylvester Stallone shoulders his way into not just writing the script but playing the iconi
items.author: Pat Saperstein
paragraphs: The beloved classic “Rocky” premiered half a century ago this week. Five decades later, “I Play Rocky,” in theaters now, tells the story of how unknown writer and actor Sylvester Stallone shoulders his way into not just writing the script but playing the iconic lead role of boxer Rocky Balboa, culminating in a best picture Oscar.

In the year 2026, is it really possible to go back in time and depict the making of “Rocky” with perfect accuracy? The unvarnished truth doesn’t always make for the best dramatic impact in a movie — and Stallone and the filmmaking team have told somewhat varying stories over the past 50 years.
“I Play Rocky” effectively toes the line between hitting most of the events of the production with some degree of accuracy and buffing up others for the sake of more effective storytelling.
Here are some of the scenes that happened just as “I Play Rocky” depicts them — according to most participants — and a few others that use a healthy amount of dramatic license.
Did Stallone really write “Rocky” in three days and then turn down hundreds of thousands so he could star?

“I Play Rocky” shows Anthony Ippolito as Stallone marching into Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler’s office and playing hardball with the big Hollywood producers, hearing offers of more and more money to give up his starring role until the producers finally agree. The need for a tidy narrative leaves out several details, though, and makes Stallone seem like even more of a total unknown than he was at the time.

The real story was a bit more complicated and left out the pivotal role that talent agents typically play in Hollywood deal negotiations. Chris Rumar, the son of one of Stallone’s early agents, Craig Rumar, said his dad and Rumar’s agent partner Larry Kubik were integral to getting “Rocky” off the ground.

“Since my dad died nine years ago, Mr. Stallone has been on sort of a tour about these inaccuracies about how ‘Rocky’ was put together,” Rumar tells Variety. “This time it was the triple whammy — we got the book, ‘The Steps,’ ‘I Play Rocky’ and the rerelease of ‘Rocky’ all within a month. He has been doing interviews with some of the biggest names in media and nobody challenges him.”

Kubik explained on the “Sexy Boomer” podcast that he and Rumar helped plant the seed for “Rocky” by introducing his friend, producer Gene Kirkwood, who had a deal with Chartoff and Winkler, to Stallone. Kirkwood and the agents first tried to set up Stallone’s script “Hell’s Kitchen” (which later became “Paradise Alley”), but Stallone had already sold it to another company and was trying to double-dip. So he went home and started work on another screenplay, influenced by a boxing match he had watched.

As seen in “I Play Rocky,” Stallone did work day and night for 72 hours to sketch out the basics of the script about an aspiring boxer, with his wife typing up his handwritten lines. But he didn’t write a fully-formed screenplay that fast — he sketched out the first third or so of the story, then made dozens of revisions before it was ready to shoot.

The neophyte actor insisted on starring in the movie he wrote — an idea which seemed preposterous to the studio, which would have preferred James Caan, Nick Nolte or Ryan O’Neal. “We negotiated a deal, and in the first deal he got paid for the script,” Kubik said. “I was told by United Artists that Mike Medavoy loved the script. But he loves it for Jimmy Caan. So I said, ‘That is not going to happen.’”

As seen in “I Play Rocky,” United Artists reportedly did offer up to $250,000 if Stallone would step aside, but “Stallone held his ground,” Variety reported. Did he ever deliver the titular line “I play Rocky” to the producers during the discussion of who should star? It’s not clear if anyone can remember.
Did Stallone really sell his bull mastiff Butkus for $40 when he was broke, and then buy him back?

In “I Play Rocky,” Stallone treasures the stray dog he found on the street during one of his lowest periods. After moving to Los Angeles, he’s still struggling to make ends meet, and sadly decides to sell Butkus to a stranger who compliments the dog for some $40. As Stallone often recounts and as seen in “I Play Rocky,” when it comes time to shoot “Rocky,” Stallone wants Butkus to be in the movie, so he tracks down the new owner, who says his kids love the dog, and ends up having to offer him thousands of dollars (the story varies from $1,500 to $15,000) to buy him back.

Stallone has told a version of the Butkus story many times over the years, naming a man called “Little Jimmy” as the one who bought the dog when he was broke. Stallone implies Little Jimmy was a stranger he met in front of a 7-11, before he sold the “Rocky” script.

But Jimmy Gambina, a diminutive boxing trainer who worked on “Rocky,” has a much different recollection of what happened. Gambina told “Going the Distance” author Mike Sielski that he dog-sat for Butkus during the movie’s production, and then Stallone gave Gambina the dog after his son Sage was born because he saw how close they had become.

When it was time to shoot “Rocky II,” Stallone wanted the dog back so he could appear in the movie. Gambina says he told Stallone, “You come over and explain it to my son. If my son says it’s OK, I’ll let you have the dog back. But we’ve had the dog going on three years now, and we love the dog.” Gambina says the two had a falling-out sometime after Stallone insisted on taking the dog back.
Did Stallone break his knuckles on a frozen meat carcass at a Philadelphia meat packing facility during filming?

Many people think “Rocky” was shot all in Philadelphia. But only the iconic steps, Rocky’s apartment and some other exteriors were captured in the City of Brotherly Love over a frenetic five-day period. “I Play Rocky” shows Stallone’s Rocky Balboa training with sides of beef at a Philly slaughterhouse, but the 1976 original was actually shot at Shamrock Meats in the L.A.-adjacent meat mecca of Vernon. The beef was frozen solid, though, and after Stallone pummeled the icy meat for eight hours straight, he ended up breaking a knuckle, so that part of the movie is accurate.

The ice skating rink where Rocky woos Adrian after hours was the Ice Capades Chalet in Santa Monica, Calif., which later became a Fred Segal store, while the climactic boxing match was filmed at the Olympic Auditorium and the L.A. Sports Arena.

“To help keep budget down, Kirkwood made arrangements for merchandising tie-ins to lure unpaid extras to the Sports Arena Monday. A foreign auto was to be raffled off, in exchange for a plug in the film, and other merchandise was to be given away at 15-minute intervals to keep the extras from leaving,” Variety reported during production. Extras were also given meals from Kentucky Fried Chicken, one background player recalled.
Adding to his injuries during filming, Stallone did break a rib during his final bout with Carl Weathers, while Weathers suffered a broken nose.
Did the studio really try to sabotage the production to get Stallone out as star?

Stallone pushed himself to run an estimated nine miles the first day of shooting and 11 the second, wearing Converse sneakers the whole time and giving himself a case of shin splints, according to the recent book “Going the Distance” about the making of “Rocky.” It’s not clear whether he was really told by doctors to stay off his feet for two weeks, as “I Play Rocky” shows.

But Kubik said that although the contract required a tight shooting schedule and budget, as well as giving producers the right to replace Stallone, it wouldn’t have made much sense to get rid of him. “I knew if they were going to shoot half the movie with him, there was no way they were going to shoot for five days and then say we don’t like him,” said Kubik.

Stallone had a similar memory of the contract when talking to Howard Stern in 2005: “We have a 14-day thing where we can fire you any time and, more importantly, we can reduce it down to 900 grand, all in, and if you can do the thing in 30 days, OK. If not, it’s over.”

So although United Artists did write the contract with strict requirements in order to come in under budget, it wouldn’t have been in anyone’s interest to try to get Stallone to quit after shooting had already started.

Variety reported that director John Avildsen used numerous tactics to save money and come in under budget, including saving $200 by having Stallone provide voice work for three or four disguised voices issuing from bars and TV sets.
Did Stallone call his dad, Frank Stallone Sr., and ask him to appear in “Rocky?”

Sylvester Stallone had a difficult relationship with both his absentee mother and his abusive dad Frank Sr., who could never seem to show his approval no matter what Sly had accomplished. “I Play Rocky” shows him extending an olive branch by calling his dad and asking if he can play a small part as the man who rings the bell at the end of the boxing match. Is that how it really happened?

Not so much, Stallone recounts in his book “The Steps: A Memoir.” As he tells it, when he showed up on set to shoot a scene, Frank Sr. was already there waiting for him and insisted on being given a part. There was just one problem, Stallone says in his memoir: The part had already been cast. “There was no reasoning with him, so with apologies, I let go of the timekeeper,” he recalled. When it came time to shoot, Frank Jr. repeatedly missed his cue and didn’t ring the bell, and the result was a “big Italian drama” of a fight, Stallone said.

items.title: Bowen Yang Apologizes for Calling Regina Spektor an Antisemitic Slur, Didn’t Know It Was ‘Popularized by Far-Right Movements’
items.description: Bowen Yang has apologized after he received backlash recently for calling singer Regina Spektor an antisemitic slur on a past episode of his podcast, “Las Culturistas.” A resurfaced clip from his Oct. 14 podcast came under fire when Yang referred to Spektor as
items.author: Jordan Moreau
paragraphs: Bowen Yang has apologized after he received backlash recently for calling singer Regina Spektor an antisemitic slur on a past episode of his podcast, “Las Culturistas.” A resurfaced clip from his Oct. 14 podcast came under fire when Yang referred to Spektor as “Zio.”

“I want to genuinely apologize for using a word on the podcast without knowing its antisemitic history, especially since we’ve repudiated antisemitism on the show as recently as the last two weeks,” Yang wrote on Instagram on Friday (his handle is @fayedunaway but has no connection to the actress). “Particularly upsetting to realize that I adopted language popularized by far-right movements whose rhetoric we should be wary of and act against.”
“Zio,” short for “Zionist,” has been used as a derogatory slur toward Jewish people and Israelis. Its origins trace back to Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke and white supremacists.

On the Oct. 14 episode of “Las Culturistas,” Yang, his co-host Matt Rogers and guest Edy Modica were discussing Spektor, her alma mater SUNY Purchase and her music when Modica added, “And now she’s out to lunch.” Rogers asked if Modica was “upset with Regina lately,” to which she responded, “she’s just like a little Israel hardcore.” Yang added, “yeah, she’s Zio.”

In recent days, social media users found the resurfaced clip of the podcast and called out Yang for using the slur. “Bowen Yang using antisemitic slang that was popularized and mainstreamed by KKK leader David Duke is really just chefs kiss for the guy who got Shane Gillis fired from ‘SNL’ for racism,” wrote Meghan McCain on X. “Well done buying this hate mongering podcast Disney.” “Las Culturistas” began streaming on Disney+ and Hulu on Wednesday.

“Bowen Yang, Matt Rogers & soooo many people LOVE preaching inclusion, compassion & protecting the dolls. UNTIL IT COMES TO JEWS,” Michael Rapaport posted. “They dismiss the GREAT Regina Spektor for supporting Israel. Funny how it’s ALWAYS Jewish Zionists they single out. Never Black, Christian, Muslim or LGBTQ Zionists. The self-appointed COOL KIDS CLUB is judgmental, mean & needs fixing Girl….Faye Dunaway would NEVER.”

items.title: The 25 Best New York Movies of All Time, Ranked
items.description: Hollywood has always been synonymous with the movies, but film history buffs know that American cinema really started in New York — or, if you want to get picky, just across the Hudson River at Thomas Edison’s lab in New Jersey, where the Kinetoscope was inven
items.author: David Rooney; Jon Frosch; Jordan Mintzer; Leslie Felperin
paragraphs: Hollywood has always been synonymous with the movies, but film history buffs know that American cinema really started in New York — or, if you want to get picky, just across the Hudson River at Thomas Edison’s lab in New Jersey, where the Kinetoscope was invented.

One of the first narrative motion pictures, Edwin S. Porter’s The Great Train Robbery (1903), was shot partly at Edison’s studios in Manhattan. The earliest works of D.W. Griffith were also made in Manhattan, until Biograph built a bigger stage in the Bronx. “King of Comedy” Mack Sennett, who launched Charlie Chaplin’s career, started off at Biograph as well.

In other words, New York was Hollywood before Hollywood was Hollywood, and even if the studios soon moved west (although Netflix is now headed back east with its ginormous new facility in Jersey), the city has remained an ideal backdrop for some of the greatest films ever made, many directed by native New Yorkers. Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Spike Lee, Woody Allen, Sidney Lumet and John Cassavetes were all either born or grew up in one of the five boroughs. They shot some of their best work there, eschewing L.A. sunshine for the vibrance and grit of the Big Apple, which has no equal anywhere on earth.

To celebrate the release of three true-blooded NYC movies — Club Kid, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York and Queens boy James Gray’s latest crime drama, Paper Tiger (in addition to fabulous doc Once Upon a Time in Harlem) — THR critics have compiled and ranked a list of the 25 best films taking place in the city. To say there were more options than we had room for is an understatement; we started with a “shortlist” of around 100 titles we love or like, then debated and whittled down from there.

We’d like to think you can trust us — two of us are NYC-born-and-raised, one from Manhattan, one from Queens; one of us is a longtime transplant (25 years in Chelsea and counting); and one of us is a Californian with deep family roots in Brooklyn.

Our list could have consisted exclusively of works by the directors name-checked three paragraphs above, so we decided to limit the count to one film per filmmaker. We excluded documentaries (Welfare, On the Bowery and Paris Is Burning would have staked strong claims). And while we adore the classics that have stood the test of time, we also wanted to make room for some more recent films that are plugged in to the city’s ever-evolving set of joys and challenges.

There are countless beloved mainstream hits featuring NYC in significant ways — Tootsie, Kramer vs. Kramer, Ghost, Splash, Big, When Harry Met Sally, Ghostbusters, Moonstruck, Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, Working Girl, The Devil Wears Prada … we could go on. Those aren’t on our list, not because we don’t have affection for them (we do!), but because there were other titles we found more interesting, more distinctive in their use of the city as a setting and, in many cases, really a character in and of itself.

Some of our selections exude sheer energy. Others are marked by solitude and despair, chaos and murder, because New York is a town that has broken many a soul. Brooklyn-born Jay-Z may have said it best in “Empire State of Mind,” undoubtedly the NYC anthem of our time: “Eight million stories out there in the naked city; it’s a pity half of y’all won’t make it.”

That lyric references Jules Dassin’s 1948 noir The Naked City, one of 10 honorable mentions — films that could have made the list if we had finalized it another day. The others: All That Jazz, Escape From New York, Girlfriends, It Should Happen to You, Klute, Marty Supreme, Midnight Cowboy, Saturday Night Fever and Tiny Furniture.
And here are our 25 favorites.

- ‘A Thousand and One’ (2023) Set against the background of rapidly gentrifying 1990s New York — Brooklyn and Harlem in particular — debuting director A.V. Rockwell’s atmospherically charged Sundance winner gives Teyana Taylor a powerhouse showcase as Inez, a hair stylist and single mother fresh from a stint at Rikers and determined to get her 6-year-old boy out of the foster care system by whatever means necessary. Tracing a decade-plus in the marginalized lives of the mother and son, this moving character study watches Inez evolve from youthful bravado to hard-won self-possession. It also acutely observes painful rips in the fabric of New York City life for the economically disadvantaged and racial minorities, under the aggressive policies of Rudy Giuliani’s mayoral administration and on through the rampant development and discriminatory policing of the Bloomberg years.

- ‘Two Lovers’ (2008) Queens native James Gray made a trio of dark and eloquent outer-borough thrillers (Little Odessa, The Yards, We Own the Night) before switching gears with this romantic drama set in Brighton Beach — about as far as you can get from Manhattan without officially leaving New York City. The neighborhood’s windswept boardwalks and beaches are a perfect backdrop for a searing study of desire, in which a 30-something homebody (Joaquin Phoenix) is caught between two women: the nice local Jewish girl (Vinessa Shaw) that his parents want him to marry and the bewitching blond shiksa (Gwyneth Paltrow) that he spies on, Rear Window-style, from across the courtyard of their apartment building. With a mastery of tone and an eye for authentic detail, Gray turns the setup for a zany rom-com into an arrestingly intimate tale of longing anchored by three great performances. Set to the swooning arias of Puccini and Mascagni, the film takes on the emotional proportions of a small-scale Brooklyn opera by the final act.

- ‘Raising Victor Vargas’ (2002) Peter Sollett’s film is not only a radiant and delicate indie rom-com/coming-of-ager, in which a 16-year-old self-styled lothario (Victor Rasuk) learns to be worthy of his guarded, regally dignified crush (Judy Marte). It’s also an indelible portrait of the Lower East Side’s Dominican community that vividly captures the romantic glow and sweaty, sensual restlessness of summer in the city. From the cacophony of a public pool on a scorching day, to the cramped apartment where the protagonist spars with his siblings and grandma, to tender close-ups of the teenage characters seducing, rebuffing, confronting and then tentatively yielding to each other, it’s a modest movie that nonetheless brims with authentic New York swagger and soul.

- ‘Love Is Strange’ (2014) Revolving around a longtime gay couple (John Lithgow and Alfred Molina at their rumpled best) forced to sell their West Village apartment — and make less-than-ideal sleeping arrangements — when one of them is fired from his job, Ira Sachs’ understated heartbreaker is also an ode to the glories, aggravations and absurdities of life in the city. Lovingly shot and precisely observed, the film is imbued with a weary affection for a metropolis that’s changed in cruel ways but retains its inexorable pull on the eccentric, creative people who call it home — and go to often logic-defying lengths to do so. This is a movie that grasps the socioeconomic and logistical challenges of 21st century New York City (from daunting subsidized housing applications to the awkwardness of hosting guests in small apartments), folding them into an achingly wise story about loss, legacy and the imperfect ways we love one another, in life and beyond.

- ‘The Taking of Pelham One Two Three’ (1974) Made in an era when hijacking planes was a frequent occurrence, Joseph Sargent’s raw and riveting adaptation of a novel by John Godey (real name Morton Freedgood) revolves around an almost ridiculous premise: Bad guys hijack a subway car and threaten to kill one passenger per minute if the city doesn’t cough up $1 million in used bills within an hour. But the bad guys weren’t counting on the perspicacity of Transit Police Lieutenant Zachary Garber (Walter Matthau at his most deliciously Matthau-ian), among others. The dialogue’s abundant racism hasn’t aged well, and the command center’s walls of blinking Christmas light bulbs look absurdly quaint. But there’s real, palpable New York City grit in the movie — literally so, in the grimy tunnels used as locations standing in for the 28th Street station, where the titular 6 train stops while negotiations proceed over walkie-talkies between Matthau’s officer and the lead hijacker (a silken Robert Shaw). Watch and marvel at how fast the cops get across lower Manhattan traffic in order to hit the deadline.

- ‘Crossing Delancey’ (1988) Before the Lower East Side became an overpriced haven for hipsters, fashionistas and finance bros, its streets were lined with modest mom-and-pop businesses, many of them run by Jewish New Yorkers whose families had settled there at the turn of the 19th century. The last remnants of that Manhattan shtetl are lovingly portrayed in Joan Micklin Silver’s charming rom-com, which follows a bookshop employee (Amy Irving) and a pickle vendor (Peter Riegert) who can’t manage to hook up despite the pair of matchmaking bubbes trying to get them together. Adapted by Susan Sandler from her own play, the film captures a vibrant pre-Giuliani-era LES, in which working- and middle-class 30-somethings could still afford to pay the rent and, perhaps, fall in love. (Micklin Silver’s memorable debut, Hester Street, depicts the very same neighborhood back in 1896, when Jewish immigrants were first building a community that has all but disappeared by now.)

- ‘Frances Ha’ (2012) The fact that Noah Baumbach’s sharp, affectionate portrait of a very modern millennial woman (Greta Gerwig, also co-writer) is filmed in knowingly retro black-and-white is just one of its many charming contradictions, along with the way its sketch-comedy randomness builds to a perfect, cohesive ending. The monochrome palette also signifies that this is a particular kind of New York movie, harking back to screwball comedies and vintage Woody Allen. The city is a playground for the not-quite-grown-up heroine, and Baumbach and Gerwig punctuate Frances’ odyssey through it with title cards noting each address she comes to rest at — from the Prospect Park digs she starts out sharing with her bestie (Mickey Sumner) to the room in a Chinatown walk-up that she rents from more moneyed hipsters (Adam Driver, Michael Zegen) and beyond.
