That’s 34 percent over the initial offering price, and makes it a $2 trillion company.
Silicon Valley’s dancing plague?
At the San Francisco Standard, Theo Baker likens the mood in Silicon Valley to 1518’s biggest dance craze:

Are we barreling toward utopia or destruction or something in between? Prioritizing speed — because otherwise others get there first, because you need to justify your valuation day in and day out, or because, in the simplest sense, that’s where the technology is headed — seems like a way to guarantee the worst outcomes of the bunch.

In Strasbourg in the summer of 1518, a woman began to dance without music. Others soon joined in, mimicking her spasmodic, uncontrollable movements — and before long they were crying for help. They couldn’t stop. Dozens, even hundreds, joined this dancing plague, today understood by scientists as a form of mass psychosis, and could be released only by collapse or death, their bodies drenched in sweat and blood.
This is what it feels like to be living in Silicon Valley during what may amount to the most important week in its history. The music is getting faster, and no one thinks they can stop.
Sucks to be you, institutional investors without a prior relationship with Anthropic
CNBC says a bunch of big firms may be feeling FOMO today:

Anthropic prioritized allocating shares to institutional investors it had relationships with, according to people familiar with the details, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That meant roughly half of the firms that placed orders were left empty handed, they said.

It’s normal in most IPOs for some portion of institutional investors not to receive any allocation, but that happened to be a higher number than usual for this offering, one person said. Anthropic’s management team had experience working with institutional investors from raising capital through private rounds, so the company had a strong view of what would make up a good shareholder base construction, the person said.
The angst of the now-rich Ants
At the New York Times, Jasmine Sun sums up her many conversations with Anthropic employees ahead of the IPO

Juxtaposed with what they presume will be the imminent arrival of superintelligence, the upcoming payday seems parochial to many at Anthropic. Some employees describe the I.P.O. with a shrug, likening it to just another funding round.

This is a peculiar attitude for a crowd of young people who, in many cases, are about to become deca- and centimillionaires overnight. The Ants are not your average tech workers. They spend morning to night at rows of desks in the bare, high-security offices in San Francisco’s downtown, where the common books on display include Richard Rhodes’s “The Making of the Atomic Bomb” and paperback printouts of company writings, such as Mr. Amodei’s “Machines of Loving Grace” and the in-house philosopher Amanda Askell’s “Claude’s Constitution.”

No one is compelled to work the grueling “996” hours (9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week) that have become common in the tech industry, but a good number of Ants do so anyway out of their own feverish devotion. Many cram themselves into modest group apartments, host house parties where few, if any, drink and blank when I ask how they spend their lavish salaries, even with my prompts: “A wardrobe update, maybe?” “Ever considered flying business class?”
The money is secondary. The most common form of I.P.O. talk involves discussions of where to allocate the newly liquid stock in their charitable donation accounts.
And yes, of course, somebody brought up LOTR:

One former Ant referenced J.R.R. Tolkien’s parable in trying to explain Anthropic’s mind-set: Whomever builds superintelligence first will get Sauron’s ring. That person or company will possess the most dangerous cyberweapons in the world, the cures and recipes for every disease, and an army of tireless digital geniuses to do its bidding. The most load-bearing question, then, is the morality of the one who wields the ring. (Of course, in Middle Earth, the Ring was destroyed because even the purest soul couldn’t make it safe.)
And that, of course, started a whole thing on social:
The Wall Street Journal reports that it may be as high as $104 a share:
Shares in Anthropic are set to begin trading midday and could open at around $104 a share, roughly 25% above their IPO price of $83, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Pricing indications tend to shift before the opening and there is no guarantee the stock will open at that level.
Dude, where’s my billionaire car?
Did you know that Ashton Kutcher owns 0.5 percent of Anthropic? Now you do. Per Bloomberg:

Dario Amodei was arguably one of the least famous people in the Beverly Hills home he visited in 2023. The Anthropic PBC chief executive officer sat across from actor-turned-venture capitalist Ashton Kutcher, and Guy Oseary, the legendary music manager and industry broker who owned the house. Oseary’s framed art by rock legends like John Lennon and David Bowie hung on the wall behind them.

The group spent hours discussing AI safety, the global race to build better artificial intelligence models and the overall vision for Anthropic, then still an easily overlooked challenger to OpenAI. By the end of the meeting, Oseary, Kutcher and the team had decided to participate in the Claude maker’s first institutionally led funding round through their investment firm, Sound Ventures. …

The under-the-radar venture firm with Hollywood ties is now poised for a substantial windfall from Anthropic’s initial public offering, expected in the coming days. Sound Ventures owns roughly half a percent of the AI company, according to a person familiar with the matter. That stake would be worth approximately $7 billion at Anthropic’s current target IPO valuation of $1.4 trillion, according to Bloomberg estimates.
Inside the Anthropic office right now
Some investors plan to wait and see
Notes the team at Reuters:
Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, CEOs and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry’s growth is being fueled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.
Anthropic’s breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying.

“Anthropic is a one-trick pony. People compare it with Amazon because even Amazon lost money for several years, but Anthropic won’t have that luxury,” said Bill Gunderson, partner at GCG Advisory Partners.
“They’ve got to get to profitability soon.”
Will Anthropic still be Anthropic after this?
The Verge’s Hayden Field wonders:

Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.

One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.
What Amodei had to say before ANT hits the world
Here’s some of what the Anthropic CEO said at the Nasdaq this morning, per NBC News:
“I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.”
But Amodei says the technology has “very real risks,” too.
“These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or by nation states to economic disruption to losing control of AI systems.”
“We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control.”
“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.”
The Nasdaq is already up nearly 2 percent
The Nasdaq Composite surged 1.9%, while the S&P 500 added 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 191 points, or 0.4%. …

Anthropic is set to pop 25% when it opens for trading, according to indications from the perpetual futures markets. Retail trader demand is expected to be even stronger than seen during SpaceX, according to Vanda Research.

The higher-than-expected pricing for the IPO gave the broader tech sector a boost. Chipmakers Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices were up 4% and 2.7%, respectively. Micron Technology gained 6%. Tech giants Microsoft and Meta Platforms also popped around 2%. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius advanced 8% and 6%, respectively.
Lets (let CNN) do the math
A helpful CNN explanation of Anthropic’s eye-popping $1.5 trillion valuation:

As for valuation: Companies create new shares to sell in an IPO, so the valuation involves the total number of shares that will exist after the IPO. This includes the shares created for IPO, plus those not part of the IPO offering — like unvested employee equity, non-voting shares held by investors and convertible debt.
These post-IPO shares are called “fully diluted” shares, and it’s why you might hear the term “fully diluted valuation.”
Offering price per share X total number of post-IPO shares = Fully diluted valuation
For Anthropic, that’s: $83 offering price per share X 18.14 billion total shares = $1.5 trillion fully diluted valuation
Let the ANT trading begin?
It’s 9:30 a.m. ET and things are probably about to get nuts. But the Anthropic trading won’t start right away, as the New York Times explains:

Delaying the start of trading in shares in a newly public company is part of an elaborate effort to ensure that the stock’s introduction into the market goes as smoothly as possible. A key part of that is deciding at what price Anthropic should begin trading.

Bankers will spend Thursday morning trying to assess from traders how much demand there is to sell and buy Anthropic shares at various prices. They are looking for an “equilibrium” price: the price at which there is generally the same amount of sellers as buyers.
The goal is to make sure that the company’s shares are relatively stable when they begin to trade.
The next Speaker of the House speaks Claude?

And he may not even realize it. The Washington Sun reports that “A member of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ staff operated a custom-designed artificial intelligence–powered program dubbed ‘Caucus Pulse’ to surveil various factions of the Democratic caucus and suggest messaging for Jeffries”:

The Caucus Pulse program, which was largely produced and fueled by Anthropic’s AI agent Claude, also generated a detailed report recommending steps Jeffries could take as minority leader to address concerns about the rapid development of Anthropic’s AI technology.
In a statement to The Sun, Jeffries’ office said the minority leader himself wasn’t aware of Caucus Pulse and didn’t use material generated by the AI-powered program.
Has your job ever made you an overnight centimillionaire?
CNBC on this massive rapid wealth-creation event:
The average Anthropic employee could be worth over $40 million after the company’s IPO today, with over 400 employees likely to be worth over $100 million, according to SEC filings and investors.

Anthropic was founded just five years ago and has only 5,300 employees. According to SEC filings, the artificial intelligence company has generated 1.77 billion options for employees, with a strike price of $2.91 a share. It has also paid out over 1 billion restricted stock units.

If the stock trades at $83 a share, the combined wealth of Anthropic employees will be around $232 billion, based on their share count in the filings. The total works out to an average of $44 million per employee.

Yet because many of the employees are later hires, earlier employees could have supersized gains since they’ve accumulated more stock. According to investors in the company, at least 400 early employees will be worth $100 million or more at a $83 share price. Several could become billionaires, they said.
The employee total doesn’t include the seven founders, who each own between 230 million and 240 million shares, which will each be worth around $20 billion based on a $83 share price.
Just in case you just got rich
Curbed has some suggestions on how the world’s new very rich effective altruists could invest in this fine city we all call home:

There is, of course, only so much that private philanthropy can solve — some issues, such as New York’s homelessness crisis and the increasingly bad signal system in the subways, are too vast and too bureaucracy heavy. But there are many areas of city life where a private donation of $100 million or less could make a dramatic difference.

A few months ago, we loosed reporters across the city to speak to insiders about what some of these projects could be. They probed experts and practitioners in different industries, policy wonks, local nonprofit directors, and lawmakers. They almost immediately happened on a trove of projects that were all but ready to go yet had lost funding — including ones with detailed renderings that had gone through the necessary approval processes and feasibility studies and were just awaiting a benefactor.

One example from the guide is how you could give the city a floating pool for the East River for only $60 Million. $75 million would teach 70,000 second grade New Yorkers how to swim. Or you could spend only $20 million to create a massive welding-apprentice workshop in the Bronx for our low-income neighbors. Read the rest here.
You know what’s cooler than a billion dollars?
Here comes ANT. Anthropic raised more than $107 billion yesterday, and their record-breaking IPO values the company at roughly 1.5 trillion. NPR reports:

Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share. The company’s seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic’s prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia. The total haul is more than $107 billion.
This post was continuously updated.

items.title: Trump Kept Embarrassing Himself at Summit With Xi and Putin
items.description: Donald Trump kicked off his meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin on Thursday by declaring, “We are really making history.” Technically, that’s true. It was the first time the leaders of China, Russia, and the United State
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Donald Trump kicked off his meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin on Thursday by declaring, “We are really making history.” Technically, that’s true. It was the first time the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States have had a formal three-way meeting.

However, Trump’s critics say all he was really doing was embarrassing himself on multiple levels. Before the meeting, Trump said he wanted to make progress on nuclear weapons and the wars in Iran and Ukraine. But he walked away with nothing more than platitudes from Putin and Xi. Even worse, in exchange for some pomp and flattery from China, Trump gave his two autocrat pals plenty of propaganda to use back home, as Anne Applebaum argued in The Atlantic:

The meeting was brief, almost substance-free, and carefully choreographed for the maximum benefit of the Chinese hosts. Its true purpose was not to end any wars — and certainly not to end Russia’s bloody invasion of Ukraine — but to produce propaganda photographs and video clips that each of the three leaders will now use to mask their political failures.

The president’s Asia trip wasn’t just conceptually embarrassing. He also engaged in plenty of Trumpy bumbling, from gushing about his “friend” Putin to falling asleep during a big meeting. Here are some of the lowlights.
He showed up in Asia with a new hair color.
The meeting with Putin and Xi wasn’t Trump’s first stop in Asia. He initially headed to Manila on Tuesday, November 17, for a meeting of Southeast Asian leaders.

Trump was clearly trying to look his best, and it wound up backfiring. He left D.C. with his usual light-blond coif and stepped off the plane with a much darker hair color (which he paired with a goofy flag wave). The shades of brown faded over the next few days, as chronicled by USA Today, and he was mostly back to his usual color by the time he arrived in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
He told Imelda Marcos, “We love you.”
Trump and the former First Lady of the Philippines go way back, as the New York Times explained:

When Imelda Marcos and Donald J. Trump partied in New York in the 1990s, she was the exiled former first lady of the Philippines, the wife of an ousted dictator, and he was a real estate mogul facing multiple bankruptcies.

They met again in Manila on Wednesday in vastly different roles. Mr. Trump, 80, is, of course, the president of the United States. And Ms. Marcos, 97, is the mother of the president of the Philippines, her family ensconced again in Malacañang Palace.

So it makes sense that Trump gave Marcos a warm greeting. But did he have to tell his famously corrupt pal “We love you!” and then let White House communications adviser Margo Martin advertise that fact on social media? Perhaps not.
He took in a performance of “Y.M.C.A.” with Xi.

This is mortifying on two levels. First, the Chinese thought the president of the United States would be flattered by a performance of the Village People’s “Y.M.C.A.” paired with a montage of special moments from his relationship with Xi. Second, they were right. Martin proudly posted video of this moment from the APEC welcome banquet:
He bragged about saving Christmas.

Remember how saying “Merry Christmas!” was outlawed in America until Trump won the 2016 election? No? Well, Trump does, and he thought it was important to tell the assembled dignitaries in the Philippines all about it.
He repeatedly called Putin his “friend.”

Obviously, presidents need to be polite to every foreign leader they meet with. But there’s being cordial, and then there’s Trump spotting Vladimir Putin, chummily teasing “Who is he?,” and then declaring “He’s my friend!”
Later Trump said Xi is his “friend” too, though there was less genuine passion behind it:
Trump announcing that ruthless authoritarian leaders are some of his best buddies didn’t go over well, even on Newsmax:
He fell asleep while Xi was speaking.
Trump once declared that, unlike Joe Biden, “you’ll never see me sleeping in front of a camera.”

That is, arguably, untrue. In his second term, Trump has repeatedly been accused of sleeping on the job. However, the president insists he just likes to rest his “beautiful blue eyes” during meetings so he can “listen intensely.”
Unfortunately for Trump, the rest of the world is not familiar with his preferred terminology for his power-blinking:
To make matters worse, Trump didn’t shut his eyes during a presentation from the leader of, say, Papua New Guinea. He appeared to nod off right as Xi was addressing leaders at the APEC summit:
All in all, Trump didn’t look as powerful as he would have liked during his authoritarian boys’ trip. But hey, at least he didn’t achieve any of his policy goals either!

items.title: Kristen Bell, Andie MacDowell, Eva Longoria, and More Honor Community Builders at L’Oréal Paris’s Women of Worth Gala
items.description: L’Oréal Paris welcomed its latest Women of Worth honorees with an intimate, elegant gala in Los Angeles on Wednesday night. For the annual celebration, which honors unsung nonprofit leaders, guests gathered at The Ebell of Los Angeles, a venue with a rich hist
items.author: Kara Warner
paragraphs: L’Oréal Paris welcomed its latest Women of Worth honorees with an intimate, elegant gala in Los Angeles on Wednesday night. For the annual celebration, which honors unsung nonprofit leaders, guests gathered at The Ebell of Los Angeles, a venue with a rich history of its own.

The evening began with an outdoor cocktail hour, where guests enjoyed passed apps and specialty drinks like the “Parisian Refresher” and “Worth It Spritz” under sparkling bistro lights. As honorees and attendees mixed and mingled, they also had the opportunity to pose for a photographer and peruse a beauty bar stocked with L’Oréal-brand lipsticks, lip oils, and glosses, which were available for guests to take home in a plush velvet bag with “I’m Worth It” embroidered on it.

As the gala officially began inside The Ebell’s picturesque ballroom, longtime brand ambassador Eva Longoria gave the introductory remarks, noting that “this night always gives me goosebumps. I’m always crying.” She saluted her 20-plus-year partnership with the brand and joked that it made her “112 years old,” though she doesn’t look like it, the actor-director said, “because I use Revitalift.” She gave a shout-out to the many beauty influencers in attendance, including Laura Lee and Desi Perkins. “You guys really changed the game of beauty, and I just applaud you,” she said. “Put me in your TikToks.”

L’Oréal Paris USA president Laura Branik followed Longoria, emphasizing the brand’s commitment to and pride in its Women of Worth program, which continues to celebrate “the power of women who know their worth and use it,” she said. She then welcomed the company’s newest global ambassador, Kristen Bell, to the stage. Bell, who was attending her “first Women of Worth ever,” said she was “very happy to be here” and introduced moving presentations for the first two honorees: Vy Le of WhereWear, which transforms clothing donations into targeted support for women’s and housing-insecure shelters and the people they serve, and Amanda Rice of The Chick Mission, a nonprofit dedicated to ensuring that every young woman newly diagnosed with cancer has the option to preserve her fertility.

Actor and brand ambassador Aja Naomi King was up next, taking note of the room full of glamorous gowns and festive energy. “Everyone showed up and showed out,” she said, “and we appreciate that because these women deserve to be celebrated properly. I had the immense honor of helping select this year’s Women of Worth, and I keep thinking about how much it matters when someone believes in your potential.” King introduced two honorees: Maya Bird-Murphy of Mobile Makers, an award-winning nonprofit that expands access to design education through workshops, community engagement, public installations, and pop-ups, and Christy Vogel of Sounding Joy, a nonprofit dedicated to providing hearing aids to children whose families cannot afford them.

Longoria then returned to present another pair of honorees: Marisa Hamamoto of Infinite Flow Dance, an award-winning disability-led nonprofit and professional dance company with a mission to reimagine possibilities, one dance at a time, and Chanel Power of Mentor Me Collective, a technical institute transforming how emerging technologists are identified, developed, and positioned to lead.

During a break in the program, guests enjoyed dinner from a menu that included roast chicken, citrus-soy-and-apple-cider-braised short ribs, and vegan pan-seared “scallops.” Another highlight? The venue’s bathrooms were stocked with more coveted L’Oréal goods like lip oil, mascara, setting spray, and velour puff makeup applicators.

Following the break, ambassador, actor, and model Cara Delevingne led the room in a cheerful group proclamation of “We’re worth it!” before introducing her honorees: Emily Cho of Juvie for STEM (JSTEM), an international nonprofit dedicated to expanding access to high-quality STEM education for justice-involved youth, and Arielle Galinsky of The Legacy Project, Inc. (TLP), a national nonprofit connecting younger and older adults for multigenerational friendship and storytelling.

Legacy L’Oréal ambassador Andie MacDowell had the pleasure of introducing the event’s final honorees. “For 40 years I have been a part of the L’Oréal Paris family,” she said, with the milestone receiving enthusiastic applause from the audience. “After all these years, the thing that stays with me [about the Women of Worth honorees] is the determination to make life better for someone else. That kind of care is powerful.” MacDowell introduced Jordan Pine of Greenlight Operation, a Pennsylvania nonprofit that strives to strategically combat human trafficking and serve sex trafficked women through a continuum of restorative care, and Dr. Christie Brungardt, cofounder of Jana’s Campaign, a Kansas-based nonprofit dedicated to preventing gender and relationship violence through education.

Proud “newbie” Bell returned to the stage to offer closing remarks and thank all the honorees for their tireless efforts to make life better for others. “I will be thinking of all 10 of these stories and the women we met tonight for quite some time,” she said. “Even though their stories couldn’t be more different, they seem to have one thing in common: that they all saw what needed to change and they did it. They didn’t wait for someone else to do something; they stepped forward and they did it themselves. And honestly, I think that’s gonna be my biggest takeaway from my first Women of Worth celebration ever: Never underestimate what one woman can set in motion.”

Each of the 10 Women of Worth 2026 honorees received a $25,000 grant, mentorship, and national visibility. As the program concluded, honorees, their proud guests, and other attendees continued to soak up the special evening and shared in a few more hugs and photo ops. Before departing for the evening, guests were invited to enjoy a final “sweet moment” in a separate room where a colorful candy bar and glasses of Champagne awaited.

items.title: Joe Biden Has a Lot of Unknown Unknowns
items.description: Good afternoon from Washington, where Party Animals has not forgotten the 5 a.m. wake-up required last Tuesday to attend Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s first Pentagon press conference in six months. This was a peculiar one, arranged so Hegseth could brief
items.author: Aidan McLaughlin
paragraphs: Good afternoon from Washington, where Party Animals has not forgotten the 5 a.m. wake-up required last Tuesday to attend Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s first Pentagon press conference in six months. This was a peculiar one, arranged so Hegseth could brief the public on his own personal battle for career survival.

The briefing kicked off at 8 a.m., but the press had to be at the Pentagon by 6 a.m. for an extensive security screening. I’d like to think that this cruel early start was a consequence of Hegseth’s self-proclaimed sobriety. What kind of drunk drags his sorry carcass before a crowd of jackals before noon? Not any I know.

But sources I spoke with for a new piece on Hegseth’s war inside the Pentagon told me there was a more Machiavellian motivation for the presser: Donald Trump loves to watch Fox & Friends at 8 a.m. And sure enough, soon after the conclusion of Hegseth’s performance, its intended audience of one offered a review on Truth Social.
Read on for my investigation into Hegseth’s turbulent tenure at the top of the Department of Defense, and what it means for his survival as Democrats take control of Congress in January.

The reviews are in for Joe Biden’s new book, Promise Me, America. The Atlantic calls the book “unrepentant.” The New York Times calls it a 400-page “cover letter.” The former president offers the fantastical opinion that he should have stayed in the race in 2024 and faced Trump, quite a position to maintain given he couldn’t voice his own audiobook and limited his press appearances for the release to a soft-focus People magazine story (his publisher did not respond to Party Animals’ multiple requests for an interview). According to the reviews, the former president dedicates scant attention to one of the biggest debacles of his presidency, the war in Gaza, which he abetted thanks to near-unwavering support for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu as 2,000-pound bombs rained down on the densely packed enclave, killing more than 70,000 people. As president, Biden publicly questioned the death toll numbers. “Too many innocent Palestinians were killed,” he now writes, as if possessed by the passive-voice ghost of Donald Rumsfeld. Mistakes were made, indeed. In contrast with his remarkably clinical view of dead Gazans, he writes movingly about his friendship with Netanyahu, recalling his farewell to the prime minister days before leaving the White House: “I still love you, pal.”
Elon Musk is Sorry About All That

Just five months ago, Elon Musk was promoting a movie in which a gunman goes on a mass murder rampage targeting supporters of immigration. That this was barely noticed is a sign of just how extreme Musk’s rhetoric has become over the years, as he devolved Xeet by Xeet into the online equivalent of a bum who yells at strangers on the street about race science. Then the midterms happened. After blowing nearly $500 million in an effort to get Republicans elected and falling short in key races, particularly in Texas, the octocentibillionaire seems to be seeking some kind of public rehabilitation. In a virtual appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk told Andrew Ross Sorkin that he is “not MAGA”—despite the many photos of Elon wearing a certain conspicuous hat—and that he is actually “a moderate.” Don’t take the hat’s word for it, though, here’s Musk on the record in October 2024: “I’m not just MAGA, I’m Dark MAGA.” Ah, well, nevertheless. He expressed hope for incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, and said he felt “foolish” for blowing so many millions to achieve very little. What’s the over/under on how long Moderate Elon will last?

Miller and Marco: The Wall Street Journal has a great report on the close relationship between Stephen Miller and Marco Rubio, who have forged an unlikely alliance despite their past clashes over policy like immigration. It’s a revealing look at how Rubio’s Republican Party lost to Miller’s Republican Party, and how Rubio then jettisoned his entire worldview to join the winning team.

Trump of Wall Street: The Washington Post reports that Trump’s financial disclosure revealed he held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August. That’s considerably higher than the $615,000 to $1.3 million he held at the end of 2024.

French, Toast: No one should know who “Bo” French is. No one really did until the Republican candidate for Texas Railroad Commission went viral for complaining about a group of college kids celebrating a touchdown at a University of Texas football game. (Some of the kids were not white; French objected to this). He became whatever the opposite of a sensation is and ended up losing his election to a Democrat. Now Politico reports French has taken another blow: River Crest Country Club, the Fort Worth members institution he frequented, has kicked him out.

Garcia’s Hit List: Robert Garcia, the House Democrat who is expected to lead the Oversight Committee in the new Congress, has begun mapping out his targets. Per The Atlantic: “Garcia this morning sent a dozen letters to high-ranking Trump-administration officials and members of the president’s family, providing the clearest signal yet of which topics—and which people—will likely face the greatest scrutiny once Democrats take control of the House.”
Oversight O’clock: New York Magazine’s Ben Terris went deep on the new era of Democratic oversight, everything from the war with Iran to Trump’s big beautiful ballroom.
No Longer Satire: Read Joe Bernstein, writing for The New York Times Magazine, on how America is becoming more and more like Grand Theft Auto.
Bye-Bye Boebert: Annie Karni writes for The New York Times about the rise and fall of the MAGA Mean Girl Caucus, as Marjorie Taylor Greene, Lauren Boebert, and Nancy Mace all exit Congress.

items.title: Kate Middleton Wore Matching Amethyst Necklace and Earrings for Her First Engagement in India
items.description: The Princess of Wales touched down in India this Monday for a whirlwind three-day visit to the country with her husband, Prince William.
items.author: Stephanie Bridger-Linning
paragraphs: The Princess of Wales touched down in India this Monday for a whirlwind three-day visit to the country with her husband, Prince William.
The couple visited Mumbai for the sixth Earthshot Prize Summit, which took place on Tuesday. It marked the Waleses’ first joint overseas visit since Catherine’s cancer diagnosis.

The busy schedule of engagements kicked off with a game of gully cricket—an informal version of the game played on the street. For the occasion, the Princess of Wales struck a balance between polished and casual, opting for crisp white Alexander McQueen trousers, paired with a white top layered under a pistachio blazer by Veronica Beard.

The finishing touch? A matching set of green amethyst earrings and a drop necklace from one of Catherine’s favorite jewelry labels, Kiki McDonough. Catherine has at least 20 pairs of earrings from the jeweler, ranging from the blue topaz drops she wore to Royal Ascot to the green tourmaline, green amethyst and diamond earrings set in gold, designed specially for her to mark Princess Charlotte’s birth.
The apple green amethysts, which she wore in Mumbai, are among the lesser-seen designs in her collection but proved the perfect accessory for this first engagement.

While in Mumbai, the prince’s program focused on The Earthshot Prize and its mission to accelerate solutions to the world’s most pressing environmental challenges. The princess joined the prince for a number of engagements during the visit.
During their time in Mumbai, the prince and princess also celebrated several of the deep cultural connections between the United Kingdom and India: cricket, fashion, and cinema.
Beginning with an engagement focused on the uniquely Indian passion of gully cricket and
concluding with a visit to the heart of Mumbai’s film industry, their royal highnesses
celebrated the creativity, talent, and cultural influence that continue to shape modern India and
strengthen ties between the two countries.

The highlight of the visit was the Earthshot Prize ceremony on Tuesday, November 17. Five Earthshot leaders were given 1 million euros (about $1.1 million USD) to accelerate the impact of their innovative solutions. Mumbai made perfect sense as the host city; India is home to more Earthshot Prize winners and finalists than any other country.

Since founding the prize in 2020, Prince William has attended all of the awards ceremonies: in London, Boston, Singapore, Cape Town, and Rio de Janeiro. Catherine joined the prince in London in 2021 and again in Boston the following year, but has missed recent editions in the further corners of the globe. This was partly due to the princess’s restricted work schedule while she underwent treatment for cancer and spent time in recovery.

It marked a return to the country for Prince William and Kate, who carried out a state visit in April 2016. The week-long tour saw the then Duke and Duchess of Cambridge explore Mumbai, New Delhi, Assam, and Bhutan, racking up a total of 22 engagements that saw them try their hand at cricket, meet Bollywood stars and royalty, and champion charitable causes close to their hearts.

It was one of four overseas trips taken by the couple that year. Although William and Kate still travel, it is with far less frequency as the couple prioritizes a stable family life. Their last major overseas tour was to the Caribbean in 2022.
Originally published by Tatler.

items.title: The Surprising History of the Royal Walkabout
items.description: “I have to be seen to be believed,” the late Queen Elizabeth II once said. And on Christmas Day, the royal family will be seen en masse during their annual walkabout on their way to services at St. Mary Magdalene Church on the Sandringham estate. For years, th
items.author: Hadley Hall Meares
paragraphs: “I have to be seen to be believed,” the late Queen Elizabeth II once said. And on Christmas Day, the royal family will be seen en masse during their annual walkabout on their way to services at St. Mary Magdalene Church on the Sandringham estate. For years, the holiday stroll, which features major and minor royals mingling with the public, has been a milestone event on the royal calendar.

But three controversial royals, the former Prince Andrew, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, Duchess of Sussex, almost certainly will not be there. While Andrew has disappeared into his new life at Marsh Farm in Norfolk, Harry and Meghan have continued the tradition of the walkabout, reportedly infuriating the palace with a planned meet-and-greet with a small group of well-wishers in Nottingham. Although no longer working members of the royal family, it seems the couple knows the value and the power of this famous tradition, whose origins are far more recent than many believe.

For centuries, commoners were lucky to get a glimpse of royals riding a horse on a march across the country or nodding from a carriage on the way to the opening of parliament. The first Buckingham Palace balcony appearance was not until 1851, when Prince Albert came upon the idea of Queen Victoria appearing to celebrate the Great Exhibition of London.

The leading figure behind the idea of making the monarchy more visible to the public was a surprising one: the dour, but savvy George V, who ascended the throne in 1910. “I may be uninspiring,” he admitted, “but I’m damned if I’m an alien.”

These royal appearances ramped up significantly during the first World War, when the royal family came under scrutiny for their German lineage. George visited everyday soldiers on the Front, and Queen Mary and her children spent hours visiting the wounded in hospitals.

“George took ‘getting out and about’ to new levels. He visited industrial areas and poor housing, went down a coal mine and went on a relentless round of opening hospitals and inspecting regiments,” royal news website Royal Central notes. “Queen Mary once retorted to a princess complaining about yet another hospital visit: ‘We are the royal family—and we love hospitals.’”

However, these events were still carefully curated, with a distance maintained between the royal family and those they were visiting. It was not until 1939, that the first unofficial walkabout occurred, when King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (better known as the Queen Mother) went to tour Canada on a goodwill tour in the midst of the looming war. In May, the couple laid a wreath at Ottawa National War Memorial while an estimated 10,000 veterans looked on.

Overcome with emotion, the royal couple decided to go into the crowd to speak with onlookers. A CBC radio journalist watching the scene could hardly have sounded more in awe. “They all look most happy, most excited,” the reporter said. “One had the hand of the queen in one hand and the hand of the king in another. A delighted expression.”

George and Elizabeth were equally touched, and continued these meet-and-greets throughout the tour. “I lost my heart to Canada and to Canadians, and my feelings have not changed with the passage of time,” the Queen Mother recalled.

Known for her effusive personality and warmth, the Queen Mother became a pro at speaking with everyday subjects. During World War II, George and Elizabeth were praised for going among the people in bombed out areas devastated by the Blitz, listening to their woes and offering encouragement and strength.

But it was not until Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip toured Australia and New Zealand in 1970 that the modern walkabout was truly introduced into the British royal calendar. There are different origin stories about how the modern walkabout came to be. One version asserts that it was a spontaneous decision of the Queen to walk to her next stop in order to chat, shake hands and accept flowers from schoolchildren in New Zealand.

Others say that first walk was the brainchild of the modernizing Australian courtier William Heseltine, known as the “mastermind behind the monarchy.” A firm believer in making the family seem more approachable and normal, he was also behind the 1969 Royal Family documentary. But if that project proved to be controversial, the walkabout (a term coined as a result of the tour) was a smash hit.

According to Kitty Kelley, the first royal walkabout did not occur in London until 1972, during the celebration of Elizabeth and Philip’s 25th wedding anniversary. “People were agog; their sovereign had never been known to speak to ordinary people,” Kelley writes in The Royals. “This was the first royal walkabout London had ever seen, and flag-waving Britons cheered as the Queen, the Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Charles, and Princess Anne melted into the crowd, greeting people and trying to make the royal family appear less remote.”

While the Queen reportedly enjoyed the intimacy of the walkabout, not every royal family member was quite as thrilled. “At nineteen years old suddenly being dropped in the middle of the street, suddenly being told to pick someone and talk to them,” Princess Anne said. “Fun? No, I don’t think so. A challenge.”

Soon, the walkabout was a major part of every royal’s schedule, and family members had to learn how to do them—like it or not. “I learnt the way a monkey learns—by watching its parents,” King Charles once said.

During international tours, the walkabouts made a packed schedule even more tiring, but Queen Elizabeth II never faltered. “On a tour of Canada, visiting Saskatchewan, the Canadian minister Alvin Hamilton was concerned that the Queen had been on her feet all day and had not even requested a ‘health break,’” Karen Dolby writes in The Wicked Wit of Queen Elizabeth II. “Her private secretary breezily replied that the Minister for Northern Affairs and National Resources need not worry, ‘Her Majesty is trained for eight hours.’ It’s impossible not to wonder about the training sessions.”

She also leaned upon her sense of humor when meeting folks of all different stripes. “On a walkabout in Scotland, a helpful observer commented that she looked just like the Queen, to which she quickly replied, ‘How reassuring,’” Dolby notes.

According to Dolby, the Queen also developed a system to communicate with her staff while talking with the public. If things were going well, she held her handbag in the crook of her left arm. If she wanted someone to relieve her so she could move on, the handbag was dropped to her side.

But the person who truly transformed the modern walkabout was Princess Diana, much to her husband Prince Charles’s chagrin. “Charles was smart enough to see what a stunning political asset Diana had become—but he was also deeply disturbed by all the adoration coming his young wife’s way,” Tina Brown writes in The Diana Chronicles.

From the start it was clear the young Princess had a connection with everyday people unlike any other royal. During a walkabout while touring Wales in 1981, Charles joked, “I seem to do nothing but collect flowers these days, I know my role.”

As Dianamania swept the world, the Princess became more and more comfortable with connecting with her often-rabid fans. Far from a stiff gloved handshake, she would clasp hands gloveless, hug well-wishers, kneel to speak with children. Frustrated that Diana constantly pulled focus, Charles delivered pithy one-liners with a forced smile. At one walkabout, the crowd openly groaned when they realized Charles was coming to their side, not Diana. “It’s not fair is it?” Charles quipped to the crowd. “You’d better ask for your money back.”

But despite Charles’s jealousy, he could not deny the impact Diana had during these walkabouts. “Everyone was really buoyed up to see her and she was making an effort to go along and speak to people and people appreciated the effort she put into meeting them,” one person she spoke with remembered. “I know it was her job but she gave that little bit extra to people that made her different and stand out.”
“She made people happy,” he noted. “It’s a rare gift.”

Catherine, Princess of Wales, has followed in her mother-in-law’s footsteps as a walkabout all-star. According to historian Robert Jobson, Catherine was initially scared during the walkabout, offering up the stiff refrain, “Thank you so much. We are so delighted to be here,” over and over. But she quickly acclimated and has become known for her chatty and warm ways. “There’s a real art to walkabouts,” she has said. “Everybody teases me in the family that I spend far too long chatting. I still have to learn a little bit more, and to pick up a few more tips, I suppose.”

In fact, it has become a sport for the press to catch Prince William subtly attempting to move Catherine along, often eventually giving up. During the Christmas Day walkabout in 2024, she was the last royal to leave the receiving line, quipping “I think I’ve lost my family!”

According to royal author Robert Hardman, King Charles can also be unusually chatty. No one quite wants to go up and go, ‘Sir, can you get a move on?’ he says. “Instead, Queen Camilla will nudge him in the small of his back with the corner of her handbag.”

But the predilection is one Camilla shares as well. On a walkabout in Wrexham, an irritated Charles was overheard telling an aide “Can we try to get [Camilla] back again? Please? We need to go! I was trying to wait for her, but she goes on!”

Learning the art of the walkabout—what to say, what not to say—is a lesson every royal must figure out, often on the job. When Meghan Markle married Prince Harry in 2018, she admitted her ignorance. “I never saw pictures or videos of a walkabout,” she claimed.

And with the advent of cell phones, the job has become much more difficult. “I’m glad that I’m not starting now because at least you had people to talk to. Now you don’t really. Phones are bad enough, but the iPads—you can’t even see their heads,” Princess Anne said.

And these engagements can occasionally go south. In 2018, the Duchess of Sussex was rushed out of a market in Fiji after the walkabout got out of hand. There are also the occasional overzealous fans, including recently when a woman attempted to kiss Prince William on the cheek. And who can forget the supremely uncomfortable walkabout at Windsor after the Queen’s death in 2022, when a warring William, Catherine, Harry and Meghan greeted public mourners. It was, Catherine reportedly said, “one of the hardest things she’d ever had to do.”

Walkabouts are also a logistical headache for royal protection officers. “You are always aware of who is in the crowd,” former royal bodyguard Simon Morgan explained to Hello! “That is one of the positives of our royal family, they always want to go and meet people and as a protection officer, you have to accept what their wishes are. The current trend of hugs, high fives and selfies, that’s going to continue, so the protection officer’s job is really brought to the front then, because the protection officer is constantly looking for what could go wrong, you are constantly working things through your mind for the ‘what if, what if, what if.’

But the walkabout shows no sign of disappearing anytime soon. And come Christmas Day, there will be cheers, hugs, and an enormous amount of quick, polite chats about the weather that citizens who wait and brave the winter cold will never forget.

items.title: Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi
items.description: President Donald Trump promised a “historic trilateral meeting.” He failed to deliver.
items.author: Mac William Bishop
paragraphs: President Donald Trump promised a “historic trilateral meeting.” He failed to deliver.

The American president billed Thursday’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as an opportunity to resolve intractable conflicts and bitter economic disputes through his signature brand of personal diplomacy.

But Trump’s need for public validation has always been a vulnerability, and America’s smartest opponents know how to exploit it. In China, Trump made a spectacle of himself fawning over authoritarian leaders who view the United States as a rival. They left with diplomatic legitimacy and strategic breathing space. He left with little to show in return.
“Peace through strength,” the White House posted on official social media channels, over a video of the three leaders meeting in Shenzhen, a major financial and technology hub in southern China.

Why viewers were meant to understand three old men in suits — Xi, Putin, and Trump are 73, 74, and 80 years old, respectively — walking down a hallway in slow motion as a projection of American strength is anybody’s guess.
“A meeting in search of an agenda,” The Guardian dubbed it.
“A meeting that could have been an e-mail,” a former British diplomat observed.

Critics and supporters alike speculated the gathering might become a “New Yalta,” invoking the 1945 summit where the “Big Three” — Franklin Roosevelt, Joseph Stalin, and Winston Churchill — negotiated the shape of the postwar world. Those talks charted a course for a new international order, built around the United Nations, national sovereignty, and collective security — which despite immediately running aground on Stalin’s violated promises to permit free elections in Eastern Europe, had more or less survived to the present.

There were fears that a modern “Big Three” would formally abandon that system altogether in Shenzhen, in favor of classic Great Power competition and spheres of interest. Each leader has their own interest in limiting the reach of international institutions. Instead, Shenzhen was a snoozefest: long on photo ops, short on substance.

Yesterday’s crowning achievement was the “China-Russia-United States Heads of State Declaration toward Peace,” which having lived and worked in China, I can assure you sounds better in Mandarin. At least, you can say it faster —《中俄美三国元首和平宣言》or “Zhōng é měi sānguó yuánshǒu hépíng xuānyán” — which amounts to the same thing.

I’ve read it so you don’t have to. It says the three countries should cooperate on UN reform, stable energy markets, limiting abuses of International Criminal Court (ICC) jurisdiction, and avoiding nuclear war.
Sharp-eyed readers will note that one of those items is curiously specific.
Given Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, there are surely more pressing concerns than the ICC’s jurisdiction.

The court has no independent police force, and relies on member states to execute warrants. It has never issued warrants for American or Chinese citizens, but it did so recently for Putin and a crop of his cronies. That complicates his ability to travel, if nothing else, so statements decrying the ICC and calling on states to disregard its jurisdiction are a de facto gift to the Russian president.

It’s also a boon to Trump, whose administration has made opposition to the ICC a rallying cry. The court is a convenient punching bag for skeptics of “globalism,” from Trump and his MAGA base to revisionist powers like China and Russia. What authoritarian leader doesn’t want their state officials shielded from international prosecution?

Certainly it was easier for the three leaders to launch an attack on international law than tackle the contentious issues that could have been on the table. Consider the trade war sparked by Trump’s tariffs on China, the wars in Ukraine and the Persian Gulf, or competition over artificial intelligence.

The race to control advanced semiconductors, computing capacity, and the most powerful AI systems are already a major source of tension between Washington and Beijing. Control of semiconductor production could well become the proximate cause of a shooting war, while AI-enabled weapons are already killing humans on the battlefield. Meanwhile, rogue or maliciously employed AI agents pose a threat somewhere between “the website is down” and “civilization-ending.”

How the competition over AI plays out could well shape economic and military power for generations, and for the moment, the United States appears to be leading the race. Yet the summit produced no public commitment on AI, and certainly nothing to ensure America retains its lead.

That AI was discussed but didn’t make the final cut says a lot about the dangers of the Trump presidency, even in its lame duck twilight years. Trump isn’t good at the painstaking work of diplomacy. Even if he is not experiencing a serious age- and/or dementia-related mental decline — and there are indications he may be — he has never been good at focusing on details, or sustained attention. Under Trump, the world is missing out on opportunities for peace and progress.

Xi and Putin are playing a much longer game. They understand that Trump has been humbled by his party’s defeat in the midterm elections, that he is constrained, and that his presidency has a finite horizon. Theirs is not. Neither leader has reason to engage with Trump on contentious matters as they wait to see what will come next in Washington.

Trump, as ever, mistakes personal chemistry for leverage. He embraced Putin and called him “my friend.” Xi received center stage presiding over the proceedings, later berating Trump in their one-on-one over Taiwan, warning Washington to “keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in U.S.-China relations.”

In return, Trump received no commitments about issues that matter. No progress toward peace in Ukraine, no assurances about Taiwan, no help resolving the Iran war, no AI framework, no nuclear arms-control deal, no breakthroughs on tariffs or agricultural trade.

A former German diplomat observed ahead of the summit that the United States seemed to have forgotten one of its greatest strategic advantages: a global network of partners and allies, built over decades. Trump and his administration have worked tirelessly to alienate allies. In their place, he offers friendship to America’s rivals.

The Shenzhen summit was historic, in the narrow sense that it had never happened before. Trump put the authoritarian leaders of China and Russia on a pedestal beside the American president. He legitimized Putin, gave Xi a grand stage, and presented both as equal partners in managing the world.
He made concessions in exchange for spectacle. And he forgot that there’s a difference between historic and consequential.

items.title: Jessica Lange Thinks She Might Have Made Her Last Film: 'It All Was a Great Adventure'
items.description: T here are long, successful careers and then there’s the load-bearing portfolio of Jessica Lange.
items.author: CT Jones
paragraphs: T here are long, successful careers and then there’s the load-bearing portfolio of Jessica Lange.

From her very first screen appearance in King Kong (1976) to unforgettable turns in films like All That Jazz (1979), Tootsie (1982), Cape Fear (1991), Blue Sky (1994), and Big Fish (2003), Lange has become one of American cinema’s great treasures. Onscreen and onstage, Lange’s control and emotional range have made her sought after by auteur directors and earned her two Academy Awards and one Tony.

When she took a role in Ryan Murphy’s inventive anthology series American Horror Story in 2011, Lange didn’t know much about the boundary-pushing Glee creator. “He immediately convinced me that this would be a good thing to do,” Lange tells Rolling Stone. “He’s very good at that.” Lange took a starring role in the four seasons of the series, earning her two Primetime Emmy awards along the way — and a whole new generation of fans.

This year, Murphy’s powers of persuasion ensnared her once more. For the just-concluded Season 13 of American Horror Story, Lange returned to to portray all four of her iconic characters — Constance Langdon from Murder House; Sister Jude from Asylum; Fiona Goode from Coven; and Elsa Mars from Freak Show — alongside returning AHS cast members (and fellow Murphy regulars) Sarah Paulson, Evan Peters, Emma Roberts, Angela Basset, Kathy Bates, and Billie Lourd.

Ahead of last night’s season finale, Lange stopped by the Rolling Stone Studio to talk about returning to the Murphy-verse, her accidental start in showbusiness, and why she might be saying goodbye to Hollywood.
Ryan Murphy has called Season 13 of American Horror Story an Avengers-like collab. What was it like to return to these roles after so many years?

It was absolutely great. Why I said yes to this season was the idea of revisiting, reprising these four roles. Because when we originally did them, it was just so new and crazy and wild. There was so much to do with every single episode that it was a wonderful adventure. Working with really what was a repertory company — all of the actors returning every season and creating a new character in a new story in a new situation — it was a wonderful way to work. I loved it.

You think you finish a character and then you’re done with it. Certain characters that I’ve played through my career, you can feel them stay with you. I remember after finishing shooting [Frances], the film about [the 1930s actor] Frances Farmer, she just stayed with me for a long time. It was almost like a haunting. I don’t want to sound like crazy or something, but I felt her presence. When I played Blanche Dubois [in A Streetcar Named Desire] three different times, again, it felt like I was still holding on to something. The same with Mary Tyrone [in Long Day’s Journey Into Night]. She wouldn’t let me go.
What are the characters you enjoy playing more than others?

Well, my favorite character was the last one I played [in American Horror Story], Elsa Mars, just because of where the story was set. It was such a magical, poetic environment that was created. This down and out circus, the freak show. The fact that they let me sing was a lot of fun.

With these characters, it’s such an extraordinary opportunity to explore how much of them are still there, and how easily they are to bring up. I would listen to old scenes from the original series. Not look at them, but just listen to the voice. The voice is what always brought me back.
How did Ryan Murphy convince you to sign on?

I sat down with Ryan and he explained the idea for this season to me and immediately it felt like this is something I want to explore. All four of these characters presented me with an opportunity to do something wild and very baroque, gothic. It’s fun to work that way. I thought, “Why not?”
What kind of rapport have you and Ryan developed through these seasons?

I adore Ryan. We don’t see each other often, but when we do — [like when] he directed the first episode of this season — [it’s] great to be around him again. I love the way he directs. He’s an amazing force.
I can only imagine returning to the show brought back a flood of memories. Was there a season that was particularly hard or emotional to film?

I like playing emotional. So the more emotional, the better for me. That makes it even more interesting. Some of those monologues given to me in those first four seasons are amazing writing and great opportunities to explore extreme emotions and stories and backstories and memories. It was always rich.
Can you describe the energy on set working with so many legendary actors?

Even before American Horror Story, I knew Sarah Paulson really well. We did a stage play together. Nothing brings you closer than being onstage every night together. I’ve worked with Kathy Bates over the years on other things, and again, she’s just a phenomenal actor. Being in her presence and seeing what she’s willing to do and her bravery and her intelligence, it was thrilling. We were like a repertory company. Every year we would get a different character, a different story, different situations, but you could always count on them to come through. It was a wild ride.
What was it like acting alongside Stevie Nicks, who appeared in Season Three?

She is such a lovely person. So warm and beautiful. Then to do a scene where she sits down and plays and sings? I was like, “Oh, my god, this is great. Does it get any better than this?” She was lovely.

American Horror Story is a show that balances the dramatic and the hysterical in both meanings of the word. When you work hard on the emotional resonance of a scene, how does it feel when that scene gets turned into a meme online, and all of a sudden it has to live in a different context?

Gratefully, I’m not on any social media. So unless somebody makes a point of sending me an Instagram meme, I’m not aware of it. I don’t even understand social media, so I’m not the right person to ask.

Let’s do a power ranking of your iconic lines from AHS. I’m going to give you three, and then you’re going to rank them: least favorite to most favorite. First one, Fiona Goode in Coven: “Oh, God, I can’t spend eternity here. This place reeks of fish, cat piss, and what is this? Knotty pine?” Second, also Fiona: “This coven doesn’t need a new Supreme, it needs a new rug.” Third, Constance Langdon in Murder House: “There’s not going to be a swimming pool, you stupid slut!”

Least favorite is “This coven doesn’t need a new Supreme, it needs a new rug.” Then the “swimming pool, you stupid slut” because that was a line I had to do with Franny [Frances Conroy], so it was a great scene. At Number One, I would say, “What is this place?” This is where she’s going to spend eternity. And doing that scene with Danny Huston was just fabulous. I never watch my own work but I watched that scene again [for] “knotty pine.” I thought, “I got to get the voice.” So I watched the scene and he’s so incredible in it, the whole thing came alive.

Let’s go way back to the beginning of your career. Your very first role was in King Kong , which was a commercial hit and a critical flop. What are some of your strongest memories from that experience?

It’s the first movie I ever did. It was my first audition. I remember a dear friend of mine that was on the film too, Chuck Grodin, said to me, “It’s lucky this is your first film because you don’t know any better.” They would have me sitting in this hydraulic hand that could have gone wrong at any moment. It could have killed me. But I figured, “Well, they know what they’re doing.” It was that kind of naivete, that innocence, that I would do whatever they asked me to do. I really loved the director, John Guillermin. He was a very complicated man — English and incredibly smart.
How did you start thinking that acting was a viable career path?

I had been living in Paris studying mime. I came back to New York because I thought I should find something to do that has a future. Maybe mime might not be it. I came back to New York specifically thinking, “Maybe I’ll study acting. I’ve go to do something. Maybe I’ll study acting then get some off-Broadway regional theater job.” Then out of the blue, somebody contacted me. I was also trying to work as a model at the time, although I never had a paying model job. When they talk about “model turned actress,” that was just bullshit.

I was living in a fifth-floor walk-up down in the Village, making a few bucks a night working as a waitress. They offered me a trip to Los Angeles to audition for King Kong. Well, I’m not that stupid. “Yeah, I’ll go. Why not? This might be a lark.” So I went out there and they didn’t like the looks of me. At all. They were going to send me home. Then the modeling agent back in New York said, “Come on, you flew her out there. At least roll some film on her.” So they did and then they offered me the part. We were shooting within a matter of weeks. I had no idea what I was doing. I’d never been in front of a camera before.
How did that lack of experience show up on set?

It was a very weird experience and it went on for months and months. We would shut down because the mechanical stuff wasn’t working, and then we would start up again. We finished shooting [in] October, maybe November, and the film came out in December. It was just this frantic, crazy year, and the film came out, and suddenly it was horrible. It felt like such a terrible invasion, this publicity. I remember I was flying home to Minnesota for Christmas, getting on an airplane. Some guy was reading a Time magazine, and that was me on the cover in the big hand. I started to cry. I thought, “Oh, my God, my life is ruined.” Suddenly, I’m this public thing. Then the reviews, of course, completely dismissed me as being like some old dumb blonde thing. All except for one critic, and that was [The New Yorker’s] Pauline Kael. I was dismissed. I didn’t work again for three years.
How did that change the roles you took after?

It wasn’t the way I ever imagined starting — in some big extravaganza. But I always knew what was true to me and that I could go back and study painting or something. I could do something else. But I just knew that [doing those types of roles] wasn’t my destiny. Luckily, the next couple parts that came along were The Postman Always Rings Twice and then, of course, Frances, which changed everything for me.
Did deep friendships in Hollywood help with that mindset? I’m thinking of your relationship with Bob Fosse.

Fosse, bless his heart. Maybe two people, Pauline Kael and Bob Fosse, saw something in that performance they thought was worthwhile. When he was writing All That Jazz, he created that part specifically for me, and he fought for me to do it. It was symbolic, that role: the angel of death. That began to turn things around for me. I love Bob. We were great friends. He was an amazing talent. Sometimes when it’s on TV, I’ll watch part of All That Jazz and realize what a fucking genius he was.

In 1982, you went from being the blond in King Kong to the first performer in almost 40 years to receive acting Oscar nominations for two projects in the same year — a Best Actress nomination for Frances and a Best Supporting Actress nomination for Tootsie, which you won. Did your relationship to press and attention change at that point?

Yes, but also, with Frances, that was a part that meant so much to me. It was different than other roles. Frances was the first part that I really felt I could fulfill. I don’t know how to describe this, but sometimes there’s almost an alchemy that happens. That’s how I felt with Frances — she came to me at exactly the right moment in my life to play her
Is that how you feel about Long Day’s Journey Into Night?

First, let me preface by saying, Long Day’s Journey Into Night is the greatest American play ever written. Eugene O’Neill, in his introduction, talks about a play of old sorrows, written in blood and tears, with great pity, understanding, and forgiveness for all four haunted Tyrones. That just moves me. But the play itself is so extraordinary and beautiful. It’s a play of forgiveness and coming from such a deep sense of truth that there’s not a false moment in it. Everything is grounded in this kind of tortured honesty. Playing Mary Tyrone, there is no end to this character. I could do this part for the next 20 years and never, never, never come to the end of it. But playing it on three different occasions: the first time in London in the year 2000, and then on Broadway here in 2016…
Which you won a Tony Award for.

Yes. And then doing the film of it. We filmed in 2022 and it’s finally out now. It’s been a long, hard road. It’s been 22 years [since] the first time I did it. So much changes in your own life. There’s so much more loss, so much more grieving, many more regrets. [That] just continues to inform what you bring to the performance.
You’re receiving the Lifetime Achievement Award at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival. What are some career highlights and some career achievements that you feel proudest of?

Certainly, the first one would be Frances. That part hit me like a locomotive. I just got on board and went for the ride. But in those first 10 years of working, when I think of the directors I worked with: Fosse, Bob Rafelson, Costa-Gavras, Tony Richardson, Karel Reisz. I [had] extraordinary opportunities working with great artists.

And the actors I was working with! Dustin [Hoffman] and Kim [Stanley] and Jack [Nicholson]. We got to throw Scorsese in there, too. It was an extraordinary run. I think what I assumed was it was always going to be that exciting and thrilling, and the work was always going to be on that caliber. But then, the business changes. When I started work, the cameraman would set up the for the scene [and] the director would be standing right next to camera. You could be five feet from him, or even closer. There was a wonderful exchange of energy, this belief in each other, and this [willingness] to do better. Then, of course, video playback came in, and now it’s so, so removed. Oftentimes, you don’t even see the director on the set, which I think is very detrimental.
You’re clearly still incredibly devoted to cinema as a craft. What projects do you still want to tackle in your career?

I actually feel like I’m coming to an end. Maybe it’s not a bad way to end, that last film being Long Day’s Journey Into Night and playing Mary Tyrone. There are a couple projects that have been in the works forever that may or may not happen. I don’t know. It doesn’t seem easy to get things made anymore. At least not the kind of films that interest me.
In a sad world, in my opinion, where Long Day’s Journey Into Night was your last film, how would you want people to remember your legacy in Hollywood?

For some good parts. For some good films. For being an honest actor. I’ve been incredibly lucky. I love acting, and I’ve had decades of being able to do it, which has been a joy for me. Difficult at times, balancing family and career and locations and dragging my kids here and there. But it all was a great adventure. I’m so grateful that [it] came my way.
Watch the full Rolling Stone Studio interview with Jessica Lange at Rolling Stone’s official YouTube channel — or hit the play button above.

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Season-Finale Recap: The Last of Us
items.description: We are in for some highs and lows in part two of the finale. It’s all feeling a little Squid Games up in here given that 49 percent of people in this country are struggling to cover essential expenses, and we’re watching these players emotionally wreck each ot
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: We are in for some highs and lows in part two of the finale. It’s all feeling a little Squid Games up in here given that 49 percent of people in this country are struggling to cover essential expenses, and we’re watching these players emotionally wreck each other in the finale in order to have a chance at financial security. It’s not fun, man. This isn’t the fault of The Traitors, but a real indictment of how poorly the American system is doing by at least half of its population.

But why would we dwell on that when Wyatt has just learned that Victor got a shield earlier in the game? Let’s focus on what matters, people, and that is Wyatt, who weirdly gives off Arthurian knight energy, being emotionally betrayed by his Lancelot. Victor, Shane, and Wyatt are talking before the final roundtable, and Victor casually tells Wyatt that he got a shield at the haunted cabin, and he told Shane, but not Wyatt. Wyatt is a thousand percent crushed. Wyatt is sitting at the edge of the sea, listening to “The Sound of Silence.” Wyatt is standing on a misty mountaintop, gazing into his soul’s abyss. “Why was I not included?” he asks. “It doesn’t matter,” Victor replies, shredding Wyatt’s heart into tatters.

Shane is very hyped about this turn of events, because he finally has something to use against Victor with Wyatt. Victor, meanwhile, completely oblivious of the emotional storm he has wrought, is telling us he wishes he and Katie were Bonnie and Clyde instead of Romeo and Juliet. Your Juliet is in the next room, Victor, and you just destroyed him.

There are only six people left, so the whole secret shield thing makes the rounds pretty quickly before they head to the roundtable. Before they begin their final table banishment, Alan tells them that anyone banished from this point on will not reveal if they are a Faithful or a Traitor.

Victor, per usual, starts us off, and he goes after Kriste and Katie. Katie is shocked, shocked, she says, that anyone would suspect her. Kriste straight-up calls Victor a liar, and when Katie brings up the secret shield, Victor looks dumbfounded. Have none of these people watched Survivor? I’ve only seen like two seasons, but not telling people about any kind of token you find makes them suspicious of you. Victor’s defense is that he was trying to protect Shane. Wyatt finds this credible, but is still stuck on not being confided in. Kriste starts, from what we’re allowed to see, spinning out. Abbey does not love Kriste’s reaction towards Victor because Kriste has been so set on Wyatt until now, and Kriste says that if they do not vote off Victor in this roundtable, none of them deserve the money. Kriste, that was your death sentence right there.

It’s time to vote. Wyatt votes for Kriste, saying the emotion they are seeing from her is because of the weight of having to lie every day. Feels sexist, but let’s move on, sir knight. Shane votes Kriste, Kriste votes Victor, Victor votes Kriste, and Abbey votes Kriste, citing her “astonishing” behavior change. Once again, it would be great to have gotten to know these people better, but we are stuck with these paltry 42 minutes. Kriste is banished. And then there were five.

Trust between the Traitors is fraying, as Shane was expecting Katie to vote for Kriste. Why, Katie, why! I mean, there’s no way you’re winning because enough people are suspicious of you, but now Shane isn’t sure you’re on the same page. Who’s Katie’s ally now? Probably Kriste. But Kriste’s gone.

And now we come to the Fire of Truth! Or, almost. First, Alan has to interview people in his pope-slash-vampire outfit. Shane tells Alan that he wants to win with Katie. Katie tells Alan that she has nothing to her name, so winning would set her up with security for her family. Haha, again, America is broken.

The Fire of Truth is inside. Has this happened before? I thought it was always outside. Okay, the Indoor Fire of Truth time is upon us. Abbey talks about how she wants to vacation with her family. This sounds frivolous, but there is the context of Abbey staying at home to care for her daughter’s medically complex needs. I’m sure it’s not easy going on a trip. Wyatt says, “This is the hardest, most difficult experience of my life.” WHAT. WHAT. This is the most Andy Bernard thing he has ever said.

Everyone has a small chest with two ceremonial pouches. One says “End Game,” and one says “Banish Again.” The decision to end the game must be unanimous, so all pouches thrown in the fire must burn green, not red. Wyatt starts us off. His pouch burns red, so everyone has to vote to banish one of the remaining players. For what it’s worth, we find out that Abbey, Victor, Shane, and Katie also voted to banish again.

Victor votes Katie and Katie votes Victor. She calls him the hottest Traitor ever, like Rob and Maura don’t exist. Wyatt, Abbey, and Shane vote Katie. Abbey adds that she thinks Katie is in fact the hottest Traitor ever. Katie leaves to cry in the interview chair, saying she knows that wasn’t easy for anyone and it’s just a game and she’s gained so much from it, but she’s shocked and disappointed in Shane.

Pouch time again! Victor votes to end the game, as does Shane. Wyatt’s pouch, however, burns red again. Wyatt thinks there’s a small chance that someone could be a Traitor. Abbey’s pouch also burns red. Victor votes for Wyatt: “Because I had to.” Shane votes for Victor, Wyatt votes for Victor (or rather “Vic” with a heart), and Abbey votes for Victor. Victor is banished. He tells us that “sweet, sweet Wyatt” couldn’t shake his suspicion of Victor, and he respects it. Someone send these two on a quest.

Now we’re down to three: Wyatt, Shane, and Abbey. Wyatt votes to end the game and is crying because he thinks they won the game. This is horrible. Take away this dramatic irony from me. I don’t want to know what I know. Abbey and Wyatt are so happy. They’re so confident. It’s horrible. Shane votes to end. Abbey votes to end. Wyatt and Abbey reveal they are Faithfuls. Shane is covering his face, grabbing his hair, and crying so much. He says, “I…am…a Traitor. I’m so sorry,” he sobs. OH, NO. Abbey starts weeping. THIS IS WHY TRAITORS WITH REGULAR PEOPLE ISN’T AS FUN. Abbey and Wyatt mourn together while Shane apologizes, face in his hands. To their credit, they go over and hug him. Wyatt tells Shane that he would have done the same thing.

Abbey and Wyatt leave, and Alan talks to Shane, who says that this is life-changing money and he can finally feel like he’s not drowning. Good LORD. Can we fix this? Can we just make sure no one has to worry about housing or food or education? Is that too much to hope for? APPARENTLY. Why would we try to make others’ lives less miserable when just a few of us can have fourteen times more money than the bottom 50 percent of the nation? They need that money. For buying things.

In the interview chair, Abbey tells us that she is heartbroken and gutted, but she did the best she could with what she knew. She can’t imagine how hard it was for Shane to tell them he was a Traitor, and she is really happy for him. After the initial shock, everyone is taking this very well. Shane and Alan head outside and toast everyone. Shane says he is inviting everyone to his wedding. Everyone hugs, fireworks go off; it’s a nice finale. Other than the emotional devastation and the indictment of our country’s treatment of its non-billionaire citizens. Congratulations, Shane!

items.title: War Season-Finale Recap: No Hard Feelings
items.description: After weeks of cunning, backstabbing, loathing, and illegal maneuvers, War concludes with a friendly smile and a handshake. Carla and Morgan’s return to their senses is so complete, they don’t need their lawyers to agree on their final settlement terms: 50 per
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: After weeks of cunning, backstabbing, loathing, and illegal maneuvers, War concludes with a friendly smile and a handshake.
