Carla and Morgan’s return to their senses is so complete, they don’t need their lawyers to agree on their final settlement terms: 50 percent of Morgan’s Zephyr shares and monthly payments until Morgan’s retirement for Carla and joint access to Gabe. Plain and simple. Morgan and Carla were ready to agree to such fair terms at various points in their divorce proceedings; their lawyers were the ones insisting on going to battle. That helps explain why the finale feels so anticlimactic: In the end, the law firms don’t have anything to do with the settlement. They are met with no consequences and learn nothing.

War hasn’t quite figured out what kind of show it wants to be. It is at its strongest when indulging its soapier elements: the corporate espionage, the messy divorce, the leering tabloids. It falters when it purports to reflect on current events, as with the paper-thin idea of Zephyr and the half-baked portrayal of Morgan as a “good billionaire.” What is obvious is that War wants to be a rich-people HBO hit, like Succession and Industry, both shows that thrived on skewering the powerful. At the beginning of the season, War seemed to be going a similar route: Carla set up a honey trap, but Morgan cheated of his own volition; Cathcarts employed a mole; Taylor & Byrne paid off Flora. The show seemed to propose that, as Johnny says to Flora in the finale, “it’s impossible to be a good lawyer and a good person,” at least in this economy.

But at the last minute, War backtracks: There are good people, good lawyers, and good billionaires. Look how wistful and regretful everyone is! Speaking with Flora, Johnny admits that he messed up — in his attempt to become a shark, he “fucked it” for every woman in his life and also Saeed. But when he says the experience taught him it’s impossible to be a good person and a good lawyer, I don’t buy it, because we’ve never seen Johnny try to be a good person. I didn’t even know that was a way he considered being. The first thing we learned about him is that he is happy to cheat, at work as well as on his girlfriend. The consequences for his unscrupulousness are theoretically great — Nick and Serena threaten to blacklist him forever — but by the end of the episode, he seems more likely than not to return to Taylor & Byrne; we never see anyone make contact with the Solicitors Regulation Authority. War’s messaging swerve is so acute, Carla and Morgan’s “war” ends with them wrapping their arms around each other. This note of togetherness sounds as implausible as “social-media platform designed to spread positivity” or “junior associate mole whose revelation does not lead to consequences for anyone involved.”

Okay, but how do we get to Carla and Morgan smiling affectionately at each other at the beach in Normandy? The finale opens on “D-Day,” as the judge quips — the last day of the trial. It’s Carla’s turn to take the stand, but the firms are hoping to settle before they get to the courtroom, to ensure the many unethical shenanigans committed by them remain unknown. Beatrice, Smallwood, and Schill stop by Taylor & Byrne in the morning to sign the paperwork, but they are interrupted by the discovery that Morgan’s dalliance with Flora has become national news. With each side accusing the other of leaking the information, the settlement offer is off the table. Maybe you, like me and Beatrice, thought that Johnny was the one to leak the news, hoping to gain some leverage over the firms. But that would be too character-forward for this show, so in the final scene between Morgan and Carla, it’s revealed that it was Gillian who leaked to the press, hoping that the scandal would help push Morgan out of Zephyr. She deduced Morgan had cheated when she found that earring in his hotel room back in the first episode. Gillian was never onscreen for any longer than it took for some inane red herring to be established; with no motivation, personality, or history to speak of, she was something less than a character.

Johnny tries to convince Beatrice to recruit him to her ranks once and for all by offering to speak to Flora to make sure that, if she starts talking to the press, her version of the story will suit Cathcarts. But Beatrice doesn’t trust him, and his spying never produced any valuable information, so she doesn’t feel beholden to him. The contempt of the people he risked his career to impress compels Johnny to avenge himself. Snooping around Smallwood’s office, he finds the letter Morgan wrote to Carla, the one Smallwood ripped in half, which will turn out to be the only consequential piece of evidence he manages to get. He passes the letter on to Flora during that meeting in which he unburdens himself of his guilt. To him, the letter proves his point about the incompatibility between good people and good lawyers. Flora wisely advises him that “all you can do is do life your way; live by your standards, not theirs.” Inspired by all of this, later, when the trial has concluded, Johnny pens a letter for Bella. That’s an awful lot of letters for a show that takes place in 2026. Have any of these people ever heard of a long text? We never find out what Johnny’s letter says, or what happened in New York. If it’s not important enough to expound on, why include it at all? Johnny’s character would have worked just as well as a power-hungry recent graduate hoping to impress the tough guys. Bella’s existence didn’t impact his decisions, and neither, seemingly, did his mysterious past in New York.

As Johnny hustles to make something out of his predicament, Carla prepares to take the stand. Budgie encourages her to forget about Flora — they have prepared, and they have the upper hand. Before the session starts, Carla asks Nick and Budgie to change her terms to ask for shares in Zephyr, rather than a cash sum. On the other side, Morgan presses his lawyers about why they can’t clarify that he was honey-trapped (it’s because he isn’t actually supposed to know), but they assure him that it doesn’t matter. Prudence is confident she can break Carla, not that she needs to, given that Smallwood gets to her first. He catches Carla in the hallway and tells her about Johnny, presenting the information as if it were common knowledge. He is also apparently the only lawyer who knows about Carla’s affair with Johnny — he is the one who stationed a photographer outside her house. I don’t think that’s unusual in divorce cases, but it does seem odd that the photos wouldn’t have been shared with anyone else. As with most of the loose threads in the finale, it’s almost like the writers read through the previous seven scripts and thought up hasty payoffs for all the plants. During recess, Carla texts Johnny, “Hope it was fucking worth it.” It’s probably the fiercest she’s ever been.

On the stand, Budgie and Carla’s first order of business is to establish that Carla is now asking for shares: She wants a stake in the future of the company she helped build. She offers her version of the Normandy story, saying that she took Morgan’s dream of “kinder social media” and turned it into an actionable concept. She rallied her famous friends to sign up for Zephyr and raise its profile, since Morgan himself, an unknown, couldn’t bring in advertising and revenue. Carla’s argumentative trump card is to present Zephyr as her “baby” with Morgan, like Gabe — she expects them both to have a part in their respective futures. On cross-examination, Prudence proves that Carla has no real involvement in Zephyr. She might be able to recite the poem that gave Zephyr its name by heart, but she has never exchanged a single text with Morgan about the company, doesn’t know anyone who works there apart from Gillian and Eric, and can’t say how its revenue has trended over the years — all stuff she would have to know to be a majority shareholder with the rest of the board, which is composed of people whose names she doesn’t know. But all of that is small potatoes compared to Prudence’s announcement that after recess, she’s calling Flora to the stand.

It is Johnny’s idea. During recess, while Carla rips Nick and Serena a new one for allowing the espionage to happen, Johnny calls Smallwood to let him know Flora will take the stand for Cathcarts. Smallwood, Beatrice, and Prudence go over the potential risks and rewards of bringing Flora in. The most important thing they need her testimony to establish is that she slept with Morgan for money. We know right away this won’t work, because Flora has always maintained that she acted out of her own desire. Cathcarts consider the risk of exposing Morgan as a cheater, but when the news has already done that, the reward of proving Carla’s mean-spirited machinations seems worth the shot. So Prudence interrupts the judge’s Twix-eating break to convince him to admit Flora to the stand.

Serena loses it. She is so hopeless, she even snaps at Budgie, who is the only person to question why Flora would want to testify. Serena is ashamed to see her case “go down in flames” along with her firm and possibly her marriage. She blames Nick for taking the divorce to court, though as he points out, she was the one who pushed him to do so. As their fight escalates, they begin to sound like a real married couple. Serena admits to wanting to impress Beatrice, so Nick is going for the jugular when he reveals that when Beatrice and Serena worked at the same firm, Beatrice vetoed Serena’s name when she went up for partner.

By the time they return to the courtroom, Serena and Nick are in pieces, but they’re in luck, because that’s when their happy ending begins. Under Prudence’s examination, Flora pulls the rug out from under Cathcarts’ feet. She explains that Carla brought up the idea of the honey trap as a joke, but she was the one who offered to go through with it. She maintains that she didn’t trick Morgan; she wanted to sleep with him, even if she was Carla’s friend. She contains multitudes! Regarding the hush money, a lawyer did come to her house offering to pay for her mom’s conservatory, but he worked for Cathcarts, not Taylor & Byrne. A collective gasp is heard through the courtroom; Johnny, sitting opposite the Cathcarts bench, smiles. Flora continues that Cathcarts wanted to make it look like Taylor & Byrne were paying her off, the only untrue part of her testimony. Prudence is stumped, but Budgie and the judge want to hear what else Flora has to say. She reads Morgan’s torn-up letter, which makes both Morgan and Carla cry. Carla and Johnny exchange a knowing look, the one conclusion to their whole affair and betrayal.

After the session ends, Carla follows Flora out to thank her, but Flora is still mad at Carla for disappearing when things got bad. Like Gillian, Flora is less a character than she is a plot device. It’s frustrating that she has such a big part in the finale when we never got to know her or understand her motivations or what her idea of friendship is (she’s mad at Carla for ghosting but thinks it’s okay to want to sleep with her husband?), or why she liked Morgan at all. For three episodes in a row, we never even saw her! But by this point, the show has committed to its happy ending. Morgan and Carla agree to their settlement terms while Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts face each other with amusement. Serena quips that she would have torn up the letter, too, and they all chuckle as if they’re old mates returning to the manor after a game of tennis, which maybe they are. It makes you feel like a fool to get invested in their characters only for them to flatten out like that.

The courtroom is the last we see of Smallwood, Beatrice, and Schill. We never learn who the young man was who shunned Smallwood at the club, or why that detail mattered, given that Smallwood’s lonely bitterness is sufficiently evident from Pip Torrens’s performance. As for Nick and Serena, when they get back to the Taylor & Byrne offices, they are still making amends for that courtroom fight. Johnny arrives just then, and Serena agrees to talk to him. She asks him to plead his case: Why should she ever believe him again? (She shouldn’t.) He says he wants to be a good lawyer, meaning of the good kind, the kind that works at Taylor & Byrne and not Cathcarts. And then he reverts to the spiel he had perfected during his interviews in the first episode: Give me a month, a fortnight, a week. But before we see whether or not Serena is convinced, she goes into labor. I have to admit, the last scene between Nick and Serena, when they reassure each other they’re going to be okay, got to me. That’s because their relationship is the only believable dynamic in this otherwise deflating finale.

items.title: The Altruists Recap: For Efficiency’s Sake
items.description: As The Altruists moves into its second half, the balance between the two ongoing timelines is starting to shift. It has always been a bit unclear which was the “main” story; the 2018 and 2019 segments have played as flashbacks to the present-day 2022 narrative
items.author: Ben Rosenstock
paragraphs: As The Altruists moves into its second half, the balance between the two ongoing timelines is starting to shift. It has always been a bit unclear which was the “main” story; the 2018 and 2019 segments have played as flashbacks to the present-day 2022 narrative, but they’ve also tended to take up the bulk of the screen time. Now, though, the 2022 timeline is moving closer and closer to the total collapse of FTX and the inevitable downfall of Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, and the series seems more interested in that story than anything else.

FTX’s company game nights provide the loose structure for “Game Nights,” with the first one taking place in 2019. The company experiences some growing pains after Sam splits the office down the middle and divides the staff into two camps: Caroline is frustrated with the FTX safeguards that keep her from trading as hard as she’d like, which leads to a fight where Sam downplays Alameda’s value compared to FTX. Caroline, furious, says she’ll go back to trading on BitMEX.

This is also, of course, a big speed bump in the road to Sam and Caroline sleeping together again, which they clearly both want to do — I mean, playing footsy on a spreadsheet is as nerdy and romantic as these two can get. And they technically don’t work together anymore, so why not? But Sam has control issues, and he doesn’t respect what Caroline is trying to do at Alameda. Instead of doing something to address her issues, he enlists Constance’s help with finding a new fund to be their market maker. Of course, this doesn’t work, because apparently Alameda is the only fund that checks all Sam’s boxes, which include having a gorgeous poly CEO who’s down to take risks and do crimes.

Constance comes more into focus this episode, but pairing her professional drive with a sort of lovesick-puppy attitude doesn’t do the character any favors. The show can’t stop converting these professional jealousies into romantic ones. Take Claire, who later spends game night still miserable and obsessed with Nishad hooking up with Vanessa, something that didn’t even happen. (It mainly just gets used as a way of pushing Lily to inquire more about Voyager.) And Constance can’t merely be frustrated with Sam’s unending loyalty to Caroline and unwillingness to give anyone else a chance at being his right-hand person; her envy has to have a romantic flavor. If the Altruists trailer alone made the real-life Constance vomit, this episode must’ve had her puking Exorcist-style.

Anyway, Sam can’t find another good candidate for a new fund to acquire, and a trip to the arcade brings him clarity. Constance mentioning the famous Konami cheat code somehow gives Sam another of his thinly motivated epiphanies: He should make an exception for Caroline and remove Alameda’s auto-liquidation safeguard, creating an entirely different set of rules just for her. Like spreadsheet footsy, and like Caroline saying she wants to be “exclusive to FTX,” it’s a romantic gesture put into tech terms.

Yep, the age of poly Caroline is over! For now, at least. Caroline connects with a shockingly hot fellow LARPer (Daniel Malik) while everyone else is off at the arcade, and they share a genuinely interesting conversation about how role-playing lets people step outside their usual reality to experiment with a new personality — but kissing this Adonis somehow reminds her she’d rather be kissing her freakish boss, so she returns to Sam and suggests they be exclusive “for efficiency’s sake.”

A parallel power game plays out in a more substantial way during the 2022 scenes this time. (Again, the show’s efforts to draw one-to-one connections between the two ongoing stories make the timeline shifts more difficult to keep track of, not less.) Following Sam and Caroline’s break in understanding at the end of last episode, they’re now trying to destroy each other: Sam already has Constance drawing up documents to dissolve Alameda in order to merge it with Modulo, Lily’s company, and Caroline is pitching Nishad hard on “couping” Sam in return by threatening to sell their shares if he doesn’t relinquish control of FTX. On top of that, Sam, Caroline, and Lauren are all separately dealing with the ramifications of the new CoinDesk article releasing Caroline’s doctored balance sheet to the public. It’s not a problem yet — she did an adequate job making the numbers look good — but before long, a smarty-pants like Hannah will figure out something’s off.

All of this is happening during the company game night, and that’s not all, because Sam has an unexpected guest: Joe Bankman, in town to helicopter-parent. Well, actually, he’s surprisingly gentle with his son this time, owning up to his prior pridefulness in wanting Sam to still need him. Moved, Sam responds by offering his dad a job helping FTX with their taxes, and even makes a vulnerable admission himself: His dad was right to praise caution in the early days, and he should’ve listened to him. Joe doesn’t bite here, but he probably should, because Sam seems closer than ever to admitting what a mess he has made of things. Instead, though, his dad just offers some poorly timed advice and urges him to keep Caroline around.

But it’s too late for that now, and too late to get back what Sam and Caroline once had. The dominoes are starting to fall, and there’s distrust everywhere. Will Caroline and Nishad manage to convince Gary to turn on his old friend? What will come of Trabucco truthfully answering Lily’s questions about his departure from FTX, and how could Lily possibly help fix the company’s issues? What exactly does Trabucco mean when he says that it was his fault Sam and Caroline stole $8 billion in customer money? It’s often hard to tell what framing The Altruists will use to fill in the gaps of this story, but if the first five episodes are anything to go by, sex will somehow be involved.

• A lot of this show’s comedy doesn’t work for me, but occasionally there’s a small exchange that will really get me. Last episode, it was Sam replying “so cool” after Will McAskill told him his mate at Animal Alliance HK got arrested. This time, it’s Lauren telling Nishad about her chess games with pop-pop and him just responding, “Okay.”
• Anthony Boyle’s British accent really jumped out when he said “HR.”

• The show makes a pretty obvious point when Barbara admits that she stopped thinking about the FTX shadiness as soon as that check hit her account, but it’s an odd thing for her to say now when she and Joe still believe Sam’s lies.

• Now, if Sam and Caroline did eventually get together in an official and monogamous capacity, why do Lucy and Hannah give her so much shit for messing with his head during that bachelorette party three years later? But whatever.

items.title: ‘Home Alone’ Reboot in the Works at Disney from Macaulay Culkin, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg
items.description: A “Home Alone” sequel is in early development at Disney, Variety has learned. Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg are shaping the script with original star Macaulay Culkin and will produce through their Point Grey banner.
items.author: Jack Dunn; Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: A “Home Alone” sequel is in early development at Disney, Variety has learned. Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg are shaping the script with original star Macaulay Culkin and will produce through their Point Grey banner.
Plot details and casting remain under wraps. Disney declined to comment.
Before Rogen and Goldberg fully dig into “Home Alone,” they first have to finish prep for their original horror comedy film for Universal, which they plan to direct.

The original “Home Alone” premiered in 1990 and starred a nine-year-old Culkin as Kevin McCallister, the youngest of many in the McCallister household who wishes he never had to see his family again after a rough night packing for Christmas vacation. Kevin gets his wish when the McCallister clan forgets to wake him on the way to the airport. Kevin is forced to become the man of the house, and in the third act, he fends off the holiday burglars known as the Wet Bandits. Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern co-starred as the bumbling thieves. Directed by Chris Columbus with a screenplay from John Hughes, other cast members include Catherine O’Hara, John Heard and Robert Blossom.

A 1992 follow-up, “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York,” followed a very similar premise, except it takes place in the big city. The third film, essentially a reboot of the first, was released in 1997 to much less acclaim. Culkin grew out of the role, and Alex D. Linz took his place. Raja Gosnell stepped in as director, but John Hughes stayed on to pen the script. There have been three “Home Alone” movies since. The fourth and fifth were both made for TV, and the sixth, “Home Sweet Home Alone,” was a Disney+ release.

Reports arose last summer that Culkin was eyeing a return to the franchise. Chatter about a “Home Alone” sequel recently reignited after Culkin appeared in a Christmas-themed McDonald’s ad as a grown-up Kevin.

items.title: Bo Derek Is Still a ‘10’ at 70: “It All Worked Out, Didn’t It?”
items.description: Bo Derek was 21 when she came bounding down a beach in a flesh-colored bathing suit, beaded cornrows bouncing on her shoulders. The movie was 10, Blake Edwards’ 1979 comedy about a film composer, played by Dudley Moore, who’s in the throes of a midlife crisis.
items.author: Seth Abramovitch
paragraphs: Bo Derek was 21 when she came bounding down a beach in a flesh-colored bathing suit, beaded cornrows bouncing on her shoulders. The movie was 10, Blake Edwards’ 1979 comedy about a film composer, played by Dudley Moore, who’s in the throes of a midlife crisis.

Ten is also roughly the number of minutes Derek appears onscreen. A lot more happens in the movie. Derek and Moore smoke up and get down to the rump-pa-pa-pump of Ravel’s “Boléro.” Julie Andrews, Edwards’ wife, plays Moore’s girlfriend and sings several songs.

The beach sequence ends with them crashing into each other. But no one remembers the slapstick part. They just remember Bo. A blond, blue-eyed California surfer girl, she managed to look all-American and exotic at the same time. A few seconds in slow motion were enough to make Derek a superstar and 10 a smash hit. The shot belongs alongside Rita Hayworth peeling off a glove in Gilda.

On Nov. 20, Derek turns 70. She’s talking via Zoom from her ranch in the Santa Ynez Valley, just north of Santa Barbara, where she lives with her husband, John Corbett, 65, the easygoing star of Sex and the City and the My Big Fat Greek Wedding movies.

Rain is pounding outside the window behind her. Lying nearby is Bear, the 110-pound German shepherd who had previously belonged to Gene Hackman and wife Betsy Arakawa. Derek and Corbett adopted him after the couple died in early 2025 — a mutual publicist made the connection.
I ask her when she was happier: now or at the peak of her post-10 success?
“Now,” she says. “Thank God.”

Derek got her role in 10 thanks in part to Hugh Hefner. Her first husband, John Derek, was a good friend of Hef’s and spent a lot of time at the Playboy Mansion. Bo and John’s relationship caused a major scandal: They got together making a movie in Greece when he was 46 and she was only 16.

Bo was still just 16 the first time John brought her to the Playboy Mansion. According to Bo’s 2001 memoir, Riding Lessons, John showed Hef some photos he’d taken of his new girlfriend. “I’ve never seen anything I wanted to defile so much,” was his response. John told Bo to take it as a compliment. “He respected me,” she tells me of the Playboy founder. “We only talked about things that you might consider more important than the grotto.”

One night at the Mansion, John ran into Edwards, who told him he’d heard about Bo and thought she might be perfect for 10. He’d already seen hundreds of girls, and no one was quite right. John thought the rejection would do her good. He felt she lacked discipline when it came to her career. “I went in to meet Blake and came home with the part,” she writes.

She remembers the shoot with great fondness, particularly working with Edwards and the addition of the “brilliant” Moore, a last-minute casting change from George Segal, who clashed with the director.

The problems began after 10 had wrapped. The studio, Orion Pictures, didn’t have high hopes for it. But they negotiated a shoot with Life magazine, which was getting a reboot and wanted a young ingenue — a throwback to the days of putting up-and-comers like Hayworth and Marilyn Monroe on its cover.

The photographer assigned to the shoot was given strict orders: The magazine wanted to faithfully re-create vintage pinup shoots of Hollywood starlets, right down to Hayworth’s negligee and Monroe’s bed of red satin. They also wanted Derek to appear emerging out of a burlap sack for the actual cover photo. She hated the idea and stormed out of the shoot.

Derek, who was born in Long Beach and grew up surfing, was shopping for a new windsurfer in a store in Marina del Rey when, somehow, incensed Orion executives tracked her down. They demanded to be put on the surf shop’s speakerphone.
“At first it was pleading,” she recalls of their attempt to get her to return to the photo shoot. “Then it was threatening. Then I’d had enough. I wasn’t interested anymore.”
Edwards was overseas at the time, prepping his next movie. By the time she got home, Derek had a message waiting for her from his agent: “Blake is furious and you’ll never work for him again.”

Derek — 22 at the time and with no representation — demanded to see it in writing. And so she was sent a telegram stating that Edwards would never hire her again if she failed to do the promotional shoot for 10. The thing was, Edwards had an option on Derek for three more films. “So I got out of that,” she says.
The studio retaliated by cutting her out of the press materials and disinviting her to the movie’s premiere. But a TV spot featuring Derek aired during a hugely rated Muhammad Ali fight.
“It just started this buzz,” she recalls. “All of a sudden, people were trying to reach me, the press was trying to track me down.”

10 opened on Oct. 5, 1979, and became a box office smash, grossing $75 million domestically. (That year’s Alien made $79 million.) Derek, meanwhile, became an overnight sensation, with women around the world demanding the “Bo braids” from their hairdressers.

John Derek had suggested she spend the film with her hair slicked back — something that would stand out from the feathered hair Farrah Fawcett had made a sensation. They were shopping in Inglewood when they spotted the African American hairstyle and together thought it would be the perfect look for Jenny. One of Ann-Margret’s backup singers connected her with a braider in Compton. (The Viva Las Vegas star was an old family friend who had known Bo since childhood.)

“I only work from my dreams,” the braider told them, adding that she dreamed of a butterfly the night before, which served as the design’s inspiration. She also told them she had braided Cleopatra’s hair in a previous life.
In Riding Lessons, Derek remembers singer Roberta Flack criticizing her on The Phil Donahue Show for taking credit for a hairstyle Black women had worn for generations.

“For the record,” Bo writes, “I never, ever intended to take credit for the sensation that my hairdo caused.” There was a Bo Derek pinup poster in 1979, which featured her seductively kneeling in the surf, and a Bo Derek calendar by 1981.

All of this Bo-mania seemed to smooth things over with Orion. “All of a sudden, I start getting jewelry from the studio chairman, Arthur Krim,” Derek says. “I had people coming with suitcases of cash trying to get me to sign on the dotted line, telling me what I should and shouldn’t do.” Edwards, too, found it in his heart to forgive her, and the two remained friends until his death in 2010.
It wasn’t that Derek didn’t enjoy being famous. She was just less sure she wanted the career everyone else seemed to want her to have. She was in a hotel room in Paris when it all caught up with her.

“I remember sobbing and saying, ‘I’m so confused. I don’t know what to do,’ ” she says. “And my husband said, ‘Well, do what you want. Just because everybody would kill for this career doesn’t mean you have to love it.’ “

The handsome son of silent film actors, John Derek appeared in more than 50 films, most famously playing Joshua, a follower of Charlton Heston’s Moses, in 1956’s The Ten Commandments. When the roles dried up, he transitioned to independent filmmaking and photography, particularly of beautiful women. (He shot Bo’s 1980 Playboy cover and spread.)

“I said, ‘Well, I just want to go make little films like we were doing before,’ ” Derek continues. “So I called my agent Marty Baum, and he put together Tarzan.” A soft-core spin on the legend told from Jane’s point of view — the alternate title was Me, Jane — 1981’s Tarzan, the Ape Man was eviscerated by critics but a surprise hit at the box office, earning $37 million. Her husband directed it, while Bo also produced the film. “I cringe when I look at a lot of it now,” she says. “But it was beautiful. It was fun. It was a romp in the jungle.”

The first little film they made together was in Greece, another soft-core outing written and directed by John called Fantasies that involved an affair between a teenage girl and her adoptive brother. Bo, newly 16, was accompanied by her mother to the audition.
Bo went by Mary Cathleen Collins then. “He was the most beautiful man I had ever seen,” she writes of John in Riding Lessons. She adopted the nickname Bo shortly after John came into her life.

The 46-year-old John was married to Linda Evans at the time — his third wife, after Russian ballerina Pati Behrs and original Bond girl Ursula Andress. A TV actress since the 1960s, Evans was 30 at the time — Dynasty was still several years away — and was discouraged by John from pursuing acting work.
“She was beautifully independent,” Evans, now 84, recalls of Bo, adding that she had “zero, zero, zero” inkling her husband might have romantic designs on the teen.

At John’s encouragement, Evans gave the neophyte acting lessons several times a week at their home. Evans noticed the director and the ingenue would spar during rehearsals and worried the film would fall apart once they left for Greece.
When Evans arrived on set a few weeks into filming, she learned her husband had fallen in love with Bo. “To say I was devastated is an understatement,” she says.
Still, she never put the blame on Bo. “She didn’t break up my marriage,” Evans says. She’s equally emphatic about who pursued whom. “She did not go after him — he went after her.”

But she doesn’t hold much resentment for John, either. She describes him as an “exceptionally fascinating man” who wrote her a love letter every night for nine years. She’d wake up every morning and read it. “When he loved you, he was consumed with you.”
Once the press caught wind of the affair, it sparked a feeding frenzy. “They want you to be humiliated,” Evans says. “I refuse to be humiliated.”

While she held out hope John would come back and admit he made a huge mistake, that never transpired. She finally let go when he called her up at 3 a.m. one night and inquired if she was seeing anyone. “Oh my God,” Evans recalls. “I’m trying to figure out how to live here and he wants to know about dating.”

Evans thinks it all played out for a reason. “John didn’t want me to work a lot with other people,” says Evans, who went on to marry real estate executive Stan Herman in 1976. “He wanted me to mostly work with him. So if I’d stayed with John, I never would have done Dynasty.
“It was a favor they both did to me,” she continues, “because I ended up having an extraordinary life going off on my own.”

John took Bo from Greece to West Germany. He later told The Washington Post that he was concerned about statutory rape laws in the U.S. “It was definitely more acceptable there,” Bo says. They were married in the Wee Kirk Chapel in Las Vegas a few years later, a wheezing pug tucked under the minister’s arm. They spent their wedding night in an RV parked outside Caesars Palace. Bo was 19 and he was 49.

The following day, Bo set off for Newfoundland to play a victim in the Jaws knockoff Orca, her screen debut. (Producer Dino De Laurentiis offered her the part himself.) She’s listed in the closing credits as Bo Derek.

Bo has no children. I ask what she’d do if her own daughter came home with a man 30 years her senior. “If it were my daughter, I would have kidnapped her and taken her away from him, of course,” she says. “It’s not the natural way of things.
“At the same time,” she continues, “I was with him 25 years until he died. He was a very ridiculously honest, good man. And it all worked out, didn’t it?”

Bo never sustained a particularly memorable acting career. Edwards’ farce turned her into one of the most recognizable and desired women in the world, but her subsequent parts never lived up to her star power.

After Tarzan, the Ape-Man came Bolero in 1984 (whose title shamelessly capitalized on the famous scene from 10) and Ghosts Can’t Do It in 1990 — both of which were directed by her husband and disappointed at the box office. The films’ main draw involved Bo taking her clothes off.

Derek’s days as a leading lady mostly drew to a close by the early 1990s. She remained a fixture in popular culture over the decades, turning up in small roles on TV shows, in the occasional movie and in one startling cameo from 2015, playing Tara Reid’s mother in Sharknado 3: Oh Hell No!
“I didn’t always make the right career moves,” she says. “But God, it was fun.”
Corbett relishes telling the story of how he and Derek met.

It was 2002, and old-school agent Norby Walters, who lived in the apartment above him in West Hollywood, hosted Wednesday night poker games attended by the likes of Burt Reynolds, Sharon Stone, Richard Lewis and Harvey Korman.
Corbett was a regular attendee at those. But it was another celebrity get-together — Walters’ annual Oscar night party Night of 100 Stars — that brought him and Derek together.
The guy known to millions of Sex and the City fans as Aidan had no one to bring as a date. So Walters slid a sheet of paper under his door with the names of about 20 actresses on it.
“Give me your picks one through five,” Walters wrote.
Corbett circled Derek’s name and slid it under Walters’ door. Not long after, his phone rang.
“One name? Corbett, one fucking name?”

Corbett was mostly kidding. He was an 18-year-old high school senior in Wheeling, West Virginia, when 10 came out. He never even saw the movie, but he remembers the newspaper photo — a black-and-white close-up of Derek that took up a half page of the Sunday paper.
“She’s sort of staring into the camera,” Corbett recalls. “I remember thinking, ‘My God, I wish I had a girlfriend that beautiful.’ “

The pair met first for a dinner in Beverly Hills to see if they would hit it off. They did — big time. On Oscar night, they hit the Walters party, attended by a less-sizzling set, then Derek got them into the much hotter Vanity Fair affair. The celebrity circuit was kind of foreign to Corbett, who spent most of his time in Seattle.

“I had filmed Big Fat Greek Wedding, but it wasn’t out yet,” he recalls. “But they knew me from Sex and the City. I got to be kind of famous at this party, which was kind of cool. And it felt good, too, to be showing that off in front of Bo. I liked it.”

When he dropped her off, they made plans to see each other again. “We’ve kind of never been apart since then, really,” he says. Early in their courtship, he finally got to see 10 when they rented it from a Blockbuster on Sunset Boulevard. “Bo’s never been better in anything,” he says, praising her “nuanced little looks” and line readings. They married quietly in late 2020.

She keeps a packed schedule. An avid equestrian, she was appointed in 2008 by Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger to the California Horse Racing Board, where she served until 2015, advocating for the safety of racehorses and jockeys. She’s still on the board of Del Mar racetrack.

Corbett says she recently spent two weeks on the road, traveling between Kentucky for the Breeders’ Cup, Washington, D.C., and New Jersey for a tribute to Dudley Moore. She’s flying to Finland this winter to see the northern lights on horseback. Corbett, meanwhile, is happier hanging at home with the dogs. “She just loves to be around people, man,” he says.
He was 40 and Bo was 45 when they met: “I just can’t believe how quickly my life has flashed in front of my eyes.”
I ask Derek what works so well between them.

“I fall in love,” she says. “I fall hard, and I think that when someone else truly loves you, it’s such a gift to cherish. It’s kind of a miracle with all the billions of people in the world, so I cherish it.”

When a call came about a year and a half ago saying a dog named Bear belonging to Gene Hackman and his wife, Betsy Arakawa, needed a happy home, the couple said no. They already had two German shepherds, and one was a rambunctious puppy. Then they saw a picture of Bear.
“I was a goner,” Derek recalls.

In police bodycam footage taken the day their bodies were discovered, an officer describes a dog holding vigil by Arakawa’s side. Corbett says it was Bear. The couple’s death was still a mystery at the time. It would turn out Arakawa died of hantavirus and Hackman, who suffered from Alzheimer’s, died a week later from heart disease.

Bear made the 17-hour trip from New Mexico in the back of a Ford Explorer. The couple has raised many German shepherds over the years — but none nearly as big as the massive creature who came bounding out of the trunk.

“Oh no,” Corbett recalls thinking. “What have we gotten ourselves into?” But Bear turned out to be a “perfect gentleman,” as Derek says, and loves to sing along whenever Corbett plays piano or guitar.
Her birthday will be a quiet one — just Bo and John and a few intimates over dinner. I ask if she has any regrets.

“No,” she says. “I tend to be an optimist. And I’m grateful to the industry. It’s been so good to me and I’ve made the most amazing friends around the world. It’s an embarrassment of riches, honestly.”
This story appeared in the Nov. 18 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: ‘Home Alone’ Sequel in Development at Disney With Macaulay Culkin, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg
items.description: The Home Alone franchise is expanding. A sequel to the beloved holiday classic is in early development at Disney, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed.
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: The Home Alone franchise is expanding. A sequel to the beloved holiday classic is in early development at Disney, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed.

Macaulay Culkin, who portrayed Kevin McCallister in the original 1990 film and its 1992 sequel, Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, is expected to reprise his role. Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg, the longtime comedy duo behind Superbad, Pineapple Express, Neighbors, Sausage Party and The Studio, are writing and producing the film under their Point Grey banner. The duo is also working with Culkin on his idea for the sequel.
Chris Columbus directed the first two films, which grossed a combined $836.3 million worldwide. No director is attached at this early stage to the new installment.
Disney declined to comment.

The news comes after Culkin expressed interest in revisiting the character in recent years. During a stop on his A Nostalgic Night with Macaulay Culkin tour in November 2025, the actor said he “wouldn’t be completely allergic” to returning as Kevin, provided the project was right. He also shared his idea for a potential sequel, which would see Kevin as a widowed or divorced father raising a child of his own. In his proposed story, Kevin would find himself locked out of his house, with his son setting traps to keep him out — reversing the original film’s premise.
According to reports, Culkin later met with Disney Motion Pictures chief David Greenbaum over the summer to pitch his idea for a sequel.

The original Home Alone, written by John Hughes, starred a nine-year-old Culkin as Kevin, the youngest child in the McCallister family. After his family accidentally leaves him behind when they depart for a Christmas vacation in Paris, Kevin must defend their Chicago-area home from two burglars, played by Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern.

The franchise continued without Culkin in other installments. Mike Weinberg took over the role of Kevin in the 2002 made-for-TV movie Home Alone 4, while 2012’s Home Alone: The Holiday Heist followed a new protagonist, Finn Baxter, played by Christian Martyn. Disney most recently attempted to revive the franchise with 2021’s Home Sweet Home Alone, starring Archie Yates.

items.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Hunts Down $21M in Box Office Previews
items.description: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is ready for battle in its opening weekend at the box office.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is ready for battle in its opening weekend at the box office.

The sixth film in the Lionsgate franchise grossed $21 million in Thursday previews before hitting 4,018 North American theaters on Friday. This gives it the second-best previews figure for the franchise, behind only the $25.2 million that 2013’s The Hunger Games: Catching Fire collected and besting the $19.7 million that the original Jennifer Lawrence-led film The Hunger Games earned when launching the franchise in 2012. The first Hunger Games went on to gross $152.5 million domestically in its debut frame, while Catching Fire holds the top-grossing launch in the series by opening with $158.1 million.

Lionsgate had projected The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to gross north of $80 million, but other sources expected that it would open much higher and potentially earn between $100 million and $130 million, which now appears the more likely outcome. Adapting author Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel that was published last year, director Francis Lawrence‘s movie carries a production budget of roughly $150 million as it revitalizes the franchise in telling a story set 24 years before the events of the original 2008 book.

In the new film, Joseph Zada stars Haymitch Abernathy, providing the backstory for the character whom Woody Harrelson brought to life in the first four movies. The cast for Sunrise on the Reaping also includes Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, Kieran Culkin and Maya Hawke.

The Hunger Games franchise’s five films have surpassed $3.3 billion at the global box office, with the series coming off of its lowest-performing entry with 2023 prequel The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. Starring Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer, that one disappointed in opening to $44 million domestically before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million.

Sunrise on the Reaping holds a 67 critical score on Rotten Tomatoes as it lags behind the franchise’s first four movies but bests the 64 percent approval for Songbirds & Snakes. In his THR review, chief film critic David Rooney wrote that the new film “delivers on emotion and brutal spectacle.”

The weekend’s competition includes Amazon MGM Studios’ I Play Rocky going wide after two frames in limited release for Peter Farrelly’s origin story of the 1976 Oscar-winning Rocky. Also fighting for attention spans this weekend is the highly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto 6, which launched Thursday after a 13-year wait since the franchise’s last title.

items.title: ‘GTA 6’ Sales Have Already Surpassed Christopher Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey’
items.description: For those wondering why Rockstar Games hasn’t licensed Grand Theft Auto for a movie or TV show, this is probably why.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: For those wondering why Rockstar Games hasn’t licensed Grand Theft Auto for a movie or TV show, this is probably why.
Grand Theft Auto VI has already generated an incredible $1.84 billion in sales, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.
That’s more than Christopher Nolan‘s blockbuster The Odyssey made during its entire global run ($1.80 billion).

What’s more amazing, is GTA 6‘s eye-popping sales figure may already be outdated. While Sensor Tower updated its tracker Thursday, the underlying charts appear to only show pre-sales through Tuesday — meaning that $1.84 billion estimate doesn’t yet account for yesterday (when all those glowing reviews were published) or today (when the game was actually released).
Therefore, current GTA 6 sales is very likely over $2 billion (in case you’re curious, the revenue split is 75 percent from PS5 sales and 25 percent for Xbox).

And GTA games tend to have very, very long tails. GTA 5 was released 13 years ago and has generated an estimated $5.4 billion in lifetime revenue (plus an additional $5.4 billion in revenue during that period from GTA Online), according to The Wall Street Journal. Even over the last four years, GTA 5 has averaged $400 million in sales … for, again, a game released in 2013. The top-grossing movie in 2013 was Disney’s Frozen, which made $1.28 billion … now imagine if last year Frozen was still averaging $400 million a year in ticket sales.
So needless to say, GTA 6 is just getting started.

Going back to that question up top, Rockstar Games is likely disinclined to risk its brand value or reputation through a movie or TV project given the revenue for the company would probably end up being a pretty small fraction of what they already make from the game itself.

As Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of Rockstar’s parent company Take-Two Interactive, told The David Rubenstein Show earlier this month: “We’re very careful about line extensions because this is a creative company and our goal is to make the best entertainment on earth, entertainment we’re always proud of. We would make a movie or television show based on our intellectual property if our creative teams were passionate about it, if they thought they would somehow engage and delight our consumers. It’s a high bar to do that. And of course, there’s always a risk of failure. So we don’t rule it out, but we’re very, very selective.”

items.title: How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space
items.description: Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.
items.author: Alyssa Bereznak
paragraphs: Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” says the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

The first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”

But embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman says. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.
Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

First and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.
I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

About five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

It was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

It’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

We had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very important for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

For emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

Then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

And so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I said, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we launched, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance plans were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

It was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we launched, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very quickly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We launched overwhelmingly at peace.
Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

It’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

For quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics issues, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

We set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some issues we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process showed with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

Then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was important: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.
That’s very well said. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

Yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

In the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really showed through when we were out there.

I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

It is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around New York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

We saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

We only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.
Yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

It’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on issues “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

items.author: Simon Hill
paragraphs: We see tempting Black Friday phone deals every year, and in 2026 the sales have kicked off early. I spotted phones we have tested and already recommend at a cheaper price than usual, and collected them below. It’s possible some of these prices will dip lower as day-of Black Friday deals, and more phones will definitely be on sale for the event, but we’ll update this guide as we spot them.

Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Amazon, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and Black Friday Deals at Home Depot. Plus, read our related shopping guides, including how to avoid scams and sketchy wares on Amazon.
Best Black Friday iPhone Deals

The iPhone Air impressed us with its super-svelte form factor. A lovely 6.5-inch OLED screen and excellent performance, courtesy of Apple’s A19 Pro chipset, are wrapped up in a body that’s just 5.6 millimeters thick and only weighs 165 grams. Battery life isn’t stellar, and the main camera is a lone 48-MP shooter, but it’s so thin. Discounts on iPhones can be hard to find, so if you’ve had your eye on the iPhone Air, this deal is worth grabbing.
Best Black Friday Samsung Phone Deals

Our top pick of the best folding phones pulls all of Samsung’s experience together into a fresh form factor that feels just right. The 5.5-inch cover screen is usable, and the 7.7-inch inner screen is perfect for opening two apps side by side. This is also a powerful phone with a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset and has plenty of stamina thanks to the 4,800-mAh silicon-carbon battery. This $350 discount brings it to the lowest price we’ve seen so far.

If you prefer a compact flip phone, the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 is calling. Samsung’s eighth-generation clamshell is wonderfully refined, slimmer than ever, and offers a 4.1-inch AMOLED cover screen with a 6.9-inch display inside. Performance and battery life are excellent. The camera will be enough for most folks, and there’s a healthy dose of AI. Best of all, this discount deletes the annual $100 price bump and knocks another $100 off. It has never been cheaper.

Samsung’s most powerful phone is the pick for professionals. It combines excellent performance, great battery life, and a reliable quad-camera system. The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra has a special Privacy Display to keep folks from peeking over your shoulder at what’s on your screen. The Ultra is also the only Samsung phone with the integrated S Pen stylus. It has dipped as low as $950 before (and may do so again), but this is a decent discount.
Here are a couple of other Samsung phones on sale:
Best Black Friday Nothing Phone Deals

While we prefer the Google Pixel 10a as a midrange phone, the Nothing Phone (4a) Pro is a full $200 cheaper with this Black Friday discount, making it a better pick today for folks on a budget. It promises good performance, a nice screen, reliable battery life, and a solid triple-camera system with 3.5X zoom. You also get to enjoy Nothing’s unique software design with the fun Glyph Matrix pixelated screen on the back.
Find other Nothing phones on sale right now below:
Consider Black Friday Carrier Deals

While it usually makes more sense to buy your phone outright and then shop around for service, several carriers are offering discounted phones or extras such as earbuds and smartwatches if you sign up for new contracts with them. Popular budget carrier Mint Mobile is offering some solid discounts; Verizon has some interesting bundle deals; you’ll find deep discounts as incentives to switch to T-Mobile, and there are lots of trade-in deals at AT&T. Just make sure you crunch the numbers to understand how much you’ll pay over the course of the contract.

items.author: Chinea Rodriguez
paragraphs: Black Friday is a little over two weeks away, but we know you can’t wait for the good deals and neither can your favorite retailers. If you’re ready to start your holiday shopping or just want to grab a few things for your closet before the holiday party season kicks off, now’s the time. You can save on everything from beauty and skin-care tools to home appliances and bedding. So far, retailers including Ulta, Net-a-Porter, Nordstrom, and Target have early Black Friday deals you won’t want to miss, below. Last year, Glossier, Tatcha, Gap, and more joined in on the early discounts, so check back here for updates throughout the month.
Updated on November 19, 2026: Updated prices and checked stock for all products.
Holiday glam essentials for less
The Best Early Black Friday Beauty Deals

The clean-beauty retailer has everything you need to smell good all over. Start with DedCool’s fragrant and gentle detergent and finish up with Ceremonia’s alcohol-free shimmer mist with rich notes of guava and tonka bean that you can use on your body and in your hair.

Ulta’s early Black Friday deals have already kicked off in stores and online. Not sure what’s worth buying? Why not save on the big-ticket items? Laifen dryers and BaByliss Pro straighteners are on sale. Want to skip the heat? The curly tie helps you get the perfect heatless curls.
Amazon is always good for a skin-care restock, but don’t pass up the beauty tools. Consider a water flosser at nearly half off or a makeup bag set that’s perfect for gifting.
Save on fall loafers and winter coats
The Best Early Black Friday Fashion Deals

Levi’s does denim well, and every style imaginable is on sale. Make your way to the top-rated selvedge jeans with the perfect fit or opt for looser, boyfriend-fit styles like the baggy boot-cut. They also have jackets if a Canadian tuxedo is your thing.
Now’s the time to stock up on your gym gear. Old Navy’s activewear is an affordable Cut Shop favorite. It’s durable and stretchy, whether you’re wearing it to the gym on just on the weekends.

Gap does basics and denim really well, and both categories are currently on sale. Consider the brand’s CashSoft, an affordable blend that feels like cashmere, and cotton jeans with a little stretch for the perfect fit.

Get more off the more you buy. The code SHOPMORE will get you 20 percent off purchases of $200 or more, and that’s on top of the already discounted pieces. Invest in warm wool, relaxed sweaters, and lots of denim.

Clear out some space for discounted designer from Bloomingdale’s. Willing to spend a little more? Brands like Burberry, Tory Burch, and Stuart Weitzman have discounted fall favorites. Save more with discounted jackets from Avec Les Filles — I have this faux shearling in my cart.

Whenever Nordstrom has a sale, I can’t help but gravitate toward the ever-evolving fashion section. If you need some new fall and winter pieces, start here. I have my eye on these Vince Camuto penny loafers and a Damson Madder trench I can layer over my sweaters and cardigans this season.

Madewell makes some of our favorite denim, but the brand’s accessories section is full of gems too. Consider this red woven tote to brighten up a dreary fall outfit. When you use the code SALEONSALE at checkout, you get an extra 40 percent off select items.

It takes a lot of browsing, but a Net-a-Porter sale is always worth it. If you don’t have the patience to sort by price and your favorite brands, I suggest checking out the jackets, coats, and denim. There are plenty on sale from brands like Agolde, Frame, Khaite, Toteme, Mother, and more.
