- Two Weeks Later, the Blue Midterms Wave Is Still Rising

items.title: We Need to Talk About Markwayne
items.description: You might think that someone who took over for Kristi Noem would have a solid sense of why saying and doing dumb things is unwise. The former Department of Homeland Security secretary was such an embarrassment that she earned the honor of becoming the first ou
items.author: Chas Danner; Benjamin Hart
paragraphs: You might think that someone who took over for Kristi Noem would have a solid sense of why saying and doing dumb things is unwise. The former Department of Homeland Security secretary was such an embarrassment that she earned the honor of becoming the first ousted Trump 2.0 Cabinet member, lost her plane, got exiled, no longer even has a job in MAGA Siberia, and was last seen shooting more animals with Greg Bovino. Senator Markwayne Mullin got the call to replace her, but as we’ve now seen over the past several days, he may not have reviewed Noem’s Wikipedia page as closely as one of his aides probably recommended.

Mullin is having a big moment in the national spotlight, thanks to last weekend’s epic FAA air-traffic debacle, plus an assortment of other apparently coincidental tech outages that are now causing alarm. It hasn’t gone well. Here’s some undoubtedly unwanted advice for the Homeland Security secretary about the lessons to be learned since Friday.
Don’t try to make “SI” happen during a national emergency, even if Trump is watching

On Friday, soon after the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop for as of yet unknown reasons, you spoke with reporters in an attempt to calm Americans’ nerves and assure them that the Trump administration had things well in hand. That was a good idea! But then you took the opportunity to correct a reporter who used the term “AI” instead of the Trump-mandated rebrand for artificial intelligence. This was not something a serious person does.
Avoid saying “this isn’t another 9/11” in almost all circumstances

We get it: It’s not unreasonable to assume that people old enough to remember September 11, 2001, may be worried about another nationwide departure ban. Still, though, you can probably just say something else to communicate the same idea, particularly if you run the agency that was created because of 9/11.
Don’t start a White House press conference during a crisis by saying, “Welcome to Friday the 13th, right?”

Yeah, okay, it’s a joke, and you’re the kind of head Homeland Security honcho who likes to cut the nervous tension of a confusing nationwide transit emergency with a little humor. But the problem is this: It’s a confusing nationwide transit emergency during which there has been scant official information from the government officials who release information, and what people have been waiting for someone to say, out loud, from some place like behind a podium in the White House briefing room, is this: The cause of the emergency has been identified; it has been or is being fixed; planes can fly without any additional risk; and the nationwide ban on flights taking off has been lifted. All of this information could have been bullet points written on and read from your hand (though reading notes off your hand at the White House would have looked even more amateurish).
Also, watch the face of your colleague, Transportation secretary Sean Duffy, after you say that line. That was not a good reaction!
Thanks, though, for not also coming to the podium wearing a Jason hockey mask. It was smart to leave that backstage.
Think about how things look before saying, “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like”
Outside of Trump’s inner circle, we call this common sense.
Don’t throw the Transportation secretary under the bus while he’s standing right next to you blaming everybody else
Well, unless he deserves it. You do you, Markwayne.
Don’t take your government plane to a college football game in the middle of an air-travel crisis you just fumbled

According to the New York Post of all places, “While thousands of Americans were stranded in airports around the country on Saturday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was on a government plane, flying to Baton Rouge, La., to take in the Texas-LSU college football game.” It’s okay, though, because he paid for the flight, his spokespeople told the Post.

This was not a good idea! Sure, you deserve to watch a Texas-LSU game as much as any American — but sporadically, on your phone, when you can steal away glances at the score because you are so damn busy managing a national crisis. And for goodness’ sake, don’t fly to Louisiana on a government plane to see the game in person when average Americans are re-creating their own private Odyssey fueled by snacks from Hudson News and stuck in a car rental line at their third airport in 24 hours while their suitcase (unbeknownst to them) has somehow ended up in Wichita and (also unbeknownst to them) they still have another 40 hours to go until they’ll finally be able to get home, get three hours of sleep, and then go to work — all because, you know, they don’t have their own government plane.
Markwayne, it would much cooler if you did not try to live like Matthew McConaughey in this situation.
Do not, under any circumstances, claim your football-game flight was leading by example

Just apologize! Why can’t Trump officials ever just apologize for doing something stupid instead of digging an even bigger hole? Comments like “We still gotta live our lives” — or worse, suggesting that your trip was necessary to prove air travel was safe — are not a good defense.
Here’s what Mullin told the Homeland Security Committee on Tuesday:

I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece who has never been to an LSU game and she’s a huge LSU game fan to a game. We had discussions at ten o’clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it, and it came in that if we cancel something with the airspace was completely open, it could bring confusion. Because I was meeting the governor there, I was meeting other people there, that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly. There was a lot of stuff going on in the news saying, “Is it safe to fly?”
Markwayne Mullin took a government plane to a college football game over this weekend for you, America.
Don’t be the DHS guy who shares some random other guy’s theories about AI suddenly breaking everything
Especially when you used to be the guy assuring everyone that “SI” wasn’t to blame:
Don’t make such of a fool of yourself that your new boss has to give you a TV timeout from abroad

On Thursday, Politico reported that Mullin’s various media appearances since the ground stop had gone so poorly that newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had intervened to yank him off the airwaves:

Mullin’s missteps hit a fever pitch Tuesday afternoon Washington time when White House chief of staff Stephen Miller intervened in the early morning hours from Manila, where he was traveling with President Donald Trump, to swap the floundering DHS secretary for the steadier hands of DNI Jay Clayton and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to message for the administration, three people close to the White House told Playbook.

It wasn’t just Mullin’s string of strange gaffes that landed him in trouble with Miller, though; per Politico, Mullin had already provoked his ire last week by floating a possible immigration deal that would give legal status to American residents brought to the country unlawfully as children. Read the (xenophobic) room, Markwayne!
This post has been updated.

items.title: San Francisco’s Congressional Earthquake
items.description: This year’s contest between Scott Wiener and Connie Chan to succeed Nancy Pelosi as San Francisco’s U.S. representative didn’t get much national attention on Election Night, partly because it was a Democrat-on-Democrat battle (thanks to California’s top-two pr
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: This year’s contest between Scott Wiener and Connie Chan to succeed Nancy Pelosi as San Francisco’s U.S. representative didn’t get much national attention on Election Night, partly because it was a Democrat-on-Democrat battle (thanks to California’s top-two primary system) and partly because we count votes very slowly in the Golden State. But it’s worth looking back on. The race to represent CA-11 was a fascinating microcosm of the California Democratic Party’s love-hate relationship with the tech community and the still obscure but important internal dynamics of the companies involved in AI. That the story also involves the legendary House Speaker Pelosi (who held this seat for 20 terms) and Wiener, the OG pioneer of the Abundance movement that has swept some Democratic precincts and alarmed others, makes it even more compelling.

Back in late 2022, Pelosi formally stepped down as Democratic House leader after 20 years (eight of them as Speaker of the House, the other 12 as minority leader). But she chose to remain in Congress for two more terms as potential successors waited for her to announce her retirement.

State Senator (and former San Francisco supervisor) Scott Wiener was long interested in moving up the ladder to Congress, having already established a statewide and then a national reputation as the author of up-zoning legislation seeking to force local governments in California to accommodate multifamily-housing development instead of endlessly prioritizing the mythic single-family-house-with-a-yard residential land-use pattern. Wiener’s battles with powerful NIMBY forces added to the local fame he had already achieved as a champion of LGBTQ+ rights. Meanwhile, Pelosi was perceived by many observers as keeping her seat warm until her daughter, Christine Pelosi, a political consultant and veteran staffer in both the federal and local governments, was ready to occupy it.

Then other would-be successors ran out of patience. First, tech mogul, Justice Democrats co-founder, and AOC chief of staff Saikat Chakrabarti declared for the seat in October 2025. He was quickly followed by Wiener, with both entering the fray before the former Speaker had publicly announced her retirement. This formidable field chased Christine Pelosi out of the race and, by all accounts, deeply annoyed her mom, who felt disrespected by the rush to force her to step down. Before the June 2 primary, Nancy Pelosi decided to back a third candidate, San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan, a more conventional liberal than either Chakrabarti or Wiener.

In the primary, the well-known Wiener finished first and Chan second with Chakrabarti being the odd candidate out. But the ensuing general election took on a whole new dimension when Wiener got some high-life money and backing from one faction of an AI industry that haunts San Francisco like a rich but demanding uncle.

Even as the Abundance Agenda was filled out by doers and thinkers who viewed Wiener as an inspiring figure, he had established a strong foothold in the AI-safety movement and its philosophical allies in the effective-altruism community, both closely associated with Anthropic. Wiener and New York legislator Alex Bores had become West and East Coast anchors of a group of state legislators committed to AI-safety measures who privately coordinated with each other on AI policy and how to handle pressure from industry lobbyists.

Bores’s congressional campaign in Manhattan became a national lightning rod and proxy war for battling schools of thought in the AI industry. An Anthropic-funded AI-safety-focused PAC (Public First Action) spent $12 million to back him, and a rival AI PAC opposing state regulation (Leading the Future, funded by big dogs representing OpenAI and the AI investor Andreessen Horowitz) spent $8 million to defeat him. In the end, Bores narrowly lost the Democratic primary to Micah Lasher. Restlessly looking for another champion in Congress, Public First Action decided to go big on Wiener, tossing $3 million into his campaign in mid-October. That gave the already well-funded legislator a crucial home-stretch advantage over Chan, who had lots of endorsements (from Pelosi, Senator Adam Schiff, and most unions) but not much dough.

As Wiener and Chan battled for votes, however, his relationship with AI firms became the campaign’s central issue with Wiener touting himself as an AI-safety watchdog of the industry and Chan and her allies labeling him a lapdog. Fortunately for Wiener, the Anthropic rivals who helped take down Bores did not get involved in the race; nor did Pelosi fix her candidate up with the resources necessary to win. Wiener ultimately defeated Chan by just over 6 percent of the vote.

Despite all the attacks on Wiener for both his up-zoning initiatives and his AI friends, he’d be considered a pretty rigorous progressive anywhere other than San Francisco. He was endorsed by the California Democratic Party, after all, and his actual campaign (rather than the shadow campaign that dwelled on his associations) focused on pledges to honor Pelosi’s legacy and fight Donald Trump tooth and nail. After Chan conceded the race, Pelosi pledged cooperation with Wiener, and in a final touch of irony, Christine Pelosi announced her candidacy for Wiener’s soon-to-be-vacated state-senate seat (though Wiener himself endorsed his Sacramento legislative ally Matt Haney).

Meanwhile, Nancy Pelosi’s successor is heading to Washington as an iconic figure in two separate movements that could be near and dear to the hearts of centrist Democrats going forward: the Abundance Agenda and the effort to thread the needle on AI via safety and guideline measures that regulate the industry without putting it down like the rabid beast so many progressives fear it has become.

That a man like Wiener will represent San Francisco in Congress is the product of both the perceived excesses of the city’s fractious progressive groups during their long dominance of the city’s political culture and the complex influence of the tech industry, which includes but transcends AI. More generally, San Francisco reflects California in its ambivalence toward the immensely powerful and wealthy spawn of Silicon Valley. Even as Wiener won the battle to succeed Pelosi with backing from some (but not all) tech titans, other tech titans massively funded the successful effort to defeat Proposition 40, the billionaire tax backed by Bernie Sanders and his allies but opposed by most of California’s leading Democrats. While the blue wave said a lot about what voters care about nationally, the upheaval that played out in San Francisco reflects the shifting tectonics of this Democratic-dominated but ideologically diverse state. It’s not entirely the Left Coast any more.

items.title: Want to Smell Bisexual? A Hit Podcast Has the Perfume for You
items.description: You Must Remember This is a podcast dedicated, as its host Karina Longworth says in every intro, to exploring the secret and/or forgotten histories of Hollywood’s first century. Longworth, who is an LA–based writer and film preservationist, usually tells her s
items.author: Marisa Meltzer
paragraphs: You Must Remember This is a podcast dedicated, as its host Karina Longworth says in every intro, to exploring the secret and/or forgotten histories of Hollywood’s first century. Longworth, who is an LA–based writer and film preservationist, usually tells her stories in themed seasons. Those include Erotic 90’s, spanning the introduction of the NC-17 rating to Eyes Wide Shut; Dead Blondes (Marilyn Monroe, Jean Harlow, Veronica Lake); and a whole series exploring the web of connections Charles Manson had to Hollywood. It’s addictive, exhaustively researched, and narrated in a way that is both soothing and trancelike.

Longworth is a native Angeleno who has been writing about film for years. She was a film editor and critic at the LA Weekly for three years until 2012; wrote books on Al Pacino and Meryl Streep; and then started You Must Remember This is 2014. She’s also part of a film-loving couple: her husband of 8 years is the Knives Out writer and director Rian Johnson.

The latest season of the podcast is called The Bisexuals, spotlighting the stories of actors and actresses whose love lives were often much more diverse than anything sanctioned by a studio. One star that the season discusses is Libby Holman, a singer and socialite who married the tobacco heir Zachary Smith Reynolds in 1931. Not only did she have a fruitful sex life with Tallulah Bankhead and Montgomery Clift, but she was known for her signature scent called Jungle Gardenia.

In honor of that bombastic perfume that wafted off of her, Longworth, 46, collaborated with Joey Rosin, who formulated a fragrance, Bisexual. Vanity Fair spoke to Longworth about moviegoing in Los Angeles versus New York, what she smelled like as a teenager, being in grad school in your 40s, and her thoughts about Quentin Tarantino’s film programming.
The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.
Vanity Fair: What was the first perfume you remember wearing?

Karina Longworth: Coco Mademoiselle was really a big deal for me when I was 18, 19. It was one of the first perfumes that I ever knew about. I started with The Body Shop’s Tea Rose oil. I didn’t really have any female adult influences because my mom died when I was 11, and so I had to sort of figure out that whole world.
Have you always wanted to make a perfume? Are you a perfume nerd?

So I never had an ambition to make a perfume, but over the past 10 years, I’ve become really into perfume. I used to rent an office space in the same building as an independent perfumer, Jacqueline Ella Steele, whose brand was called Goest— which doesn’t exist anymore—but she made a perfume called Silent Films. She was the first person I contacted about trying to formulate this perfume. But she’s out of business. So that’s when I started asking around and I got led to Joey Rosin.
The idea came from your research?

I got the idea because, in reading and writing about Libby Holman, there are all these anecdotes of her walking into a room in a cloud of Jungle Gardenia, to the point where, people who were attracted to her were attracted to it, and people who didn’t like her found it so disgusting. I thought there was something really interesting about that, how the same scent could be either attractive or repellent, depending on how you felt about the person wearing it.
Personalities, voices and clothes all depend on who’s doing it.

There’s this really incredible anecdote in Patricia Bosworth’s Montgomery Clift biography about how one of Montgomery Clift’s friends was at a party at Treetops, Libby Holman’s estate, and she was looking for the bathroom, and accidentally walked into her bedroom, and the bed was a tangle of white satin sheets, and there’s a giant bottle of barbiturates on the nightstand and everything just reeked of Jungle Gardenia. She was grossed out, but then she also got the impression this is Libby and Monty’s sex lair.
Were you trying to recreate the smell?

We didn’t try to copy the exact old fragrance. Joey does his research, and he did research into what the original notes were. But we talked about not wanting it to be a slavish copy, and instead just trying to evoke for both of us what jungle would smell like with gardenia, and how that could evoke Libby’s story. And so we played around with adding different types of smoke to it.
Have you ever been in a jungle?

I’ve been to Tahiti. I’m trying to think if I’ve ever been to a jungle. We talked a lot about tropical plants and what the dirt would smell like, and the heat. It’s like hot weather almost has a smell. But then pairing that with this kind of old lady scent of gardenia. I went to visit his studio in Brooklyn a few times and he mailed some samples to me in Los Angeles. And by that point, it was like four iterations that were almost exactly the same. So it was just about what was giving me the best vibe.
You were living in LA for the process?
I was living alone in Rochester, N.Y. in a depressing situation because of the weather and being very alone, having no social life.
But you loved your grad school program, right? I forget the name but I know it’s long.

L. Jeffrey Selznick School of Film Preservation at the George Eastman Museum. I got so much out of the program, but it was grueling, physically, and mentally, and emotionally. It was really difficult to suddenly be living alone in a place where I felt like I had no one I could really talk to.
So you were in an entirely new, but temporary situation.

I started relying on scented candles to improve my mood and to change my mood. If I got home feeling terrible, the fragrance was helpful. I also had nowhere to wear perfume. At first I thought I would just make a candle, and then as I started learning more about fragrance, I learned that candles have to go through a much more rigorous process. And it takes a lot longer. We were not going to be able to get it done in time to have a presale like we have during the podcast season. But in the future, I would like to do a signature scent for You Must Remember This and have it available as a perfume and a candle.
What would that smell like?
It would be classic, but in a different way. I’m very inspired by the signature scent that they have at the Chateau [Marmont].
There has been a lot of talk about moviegoing being back. How has your tour been?
It has been great. In Savannah they sold 400 tickets to a very obscure, pre-code movie on a Friday night.
People must ask you a lot of podcast questions. What are your tips?
I say I don’t know what form yours is going to take, but mine takes the form of writing an extremely detailed script, and then sitting by myself in a room and reading it into a microphone.

I built a recording studio. I bought a little house in Laurel Canyon at the end of a private road, like at the end of a cul-de-sac, but you feel like you’re in the middle of the forest. I bought it from this woman who had lived there for 15 years and was kind of an all-purpose healer. She basically built a soundproof room with clay on the walls and crystals embedded into the clay, where she would do sound baths with them. When I saw this house, it was just perfect.
Which city has a better movie scene, New York or LA?
New York’s way better than LA, but LA is getting better.
Did someone buy the Vista? I loved that theater.

[Quentin] Tarantino owns the Vista. Because it’s Tarantino, he won’t let them show anything digital. It has to be a film print, and so he’ll show a new movie if there’s a print, like The Odyssey played there, Sinners played there. But when there isn’t a new movie out that is on a print, he programs whatever he wants to see. He also does a lot of like Saturday morning matinees of classical Hollywood cinema that is just his taste, you know. Sometimes it’s my taste, sometimes it’s not. It’s a lot of Jerry Lewis. But one thing I will say for Tarantino is that when he discovers a filmmaker or genre or something from the past, he shows. He’s been showing all these William Beaudine silent films, and I think that’s great because silent film has really fallen out of fashion in LA.
I was leaving to interview you today and someone said, “Oh, I love that podcast,” and was talking about the Manson series. Is that your most popular?
It changes. Increasingly, people are asking about the Polly Platt series.
Do you know what the next series is going to be?

I have two ideas that would involve talking to people or family members of subjects who have passed away, but who could give me access to sort of the family lore. I am in contact with both of those families, but I need to kind of do the legwork, talking to them more and figure out which story makes the most sense. I also sketched out a very long season about the three stars of Rebel Without a Cause. That is something that people have been asking me to do for years. But the thing that stops me from doing it is that we still don’t know exactly what happened to Natalie Wood. But that’s kind of in my back pocket.

items.title: Joe Keery and Julia Louis-Dreyfus Are Insanely Tired
items.description: Joe Keery and Julia Louis-Dreyfus Are Insanely Tired
items.author: Julia Louis-Dreyfus
paragraphs: Joe Keery and Julia Louis-Dreyfus Are Insanely Tired

For 10 years, Joe Keery was best known as the guy with the great hair on Stranger Things, eventually becoming one of the most beloved characters on Netflix’s game-changing show. When it wrapped, “End of Beginning,” the song from his musical project, Djo, rocketed up the charts, cementing him as a bona fide double threat. Now he’s doing the least predictable thing a star in his position could: eight shows a week on Broadway as the peacemaking younger brother Trip, in an all-star revival of Other Desert Cities at the Hudson Theatre. Hours before curtain, he got on a call with castmate Julia Louis-Dreyfus, also making her Broadway debut, to talk about stage fright, personal lore, and the crazy grind they’ve gotten themselves into.
TUESDAY 2:30 PM OCTOBER 27, 2026 NEW YORK CITY
JULIA LOUIS-DREYFUS: I like your background.
JOE KEERY: Thank you. This is my apartment.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I love the brick. Do you own this place?
KEERY: I do. I got it in 2023, and it took a year and a half to finish it. Is that the park behind you?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah, that’s the park.

KEERY: Amazing. Julia, last night I did [The Tonight Show Starring] Jimmy Fallon, and I met Billy Crystal, who told me to ask you two questions. He told me to ask you about the Prince sketch, and about the sketch where Martin Short knocked his wig off.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Well, I’m sorry to disappoint, but I have no memory of anything he’s saying. In my defense, I was 23 years old.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I was in a Prince sketch?
KEERY: He said maybe he played Prince. I did not realize he also was on SNL for a year.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: My third year. And Marty Short and Chris Guest.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: So how are you? How was your day off?
KEERY: It was good. Did Jimmy Fallon. That’s always a nice little shot to the arm.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Do you get nervous doing those things?
KEERY: Certainly, but I felt a little more loose this time. What else did I do yesterday? I got a soap dish.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Breaking news: Joe Keery gets a soap dish.
KEERY: What did you do on your day off?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I saw You Can See Everything.
KEERY: What did you think? I’m glad we can talk about it.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah, we can. I don’t know if we want to talk about it for Interview, but I’m going to talk to you about it when I see you.
KEERY: Why don’t we sidebar directly before the curtain comes up?

LOUIS-DREYFUS: [Laughs] Yeah, directly before. But about doing the talk show thing, I’ve found nailing the panel—the shit you talk about on a talk show is called panel—and nailing awards banter, they all fall into this space of trying to nail it every time. Do you know what I’m talking about?

KEERY: I do. It’s a stressful thing to do well, and there’s two ways you can do it. You can either be like Andy Kaufman and try to do something absolutely ridiculous, or you can just tell a story really well. My dad is very good at telling a succinct story. I did not get that.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I find this hard to believe. I would imagine you’re very good at telling a story.

KEERY: I’m pretty good, but I’m not very succinct. And the way TV works nowadays, it’s all moving at such a pace. Not to destroy anybody’s idea of what TV is, but it’s planned out. It would be very fun if it was off the cuff.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Podcasts have stepped into this arena now. You can have an hour-plus conversation and it can meander all over the place.

KEERY: Going back to being succinct, you’ve had to give a bunch of speeches at award shows. For the first two or three, I’m sure you’re nervous, but for the next ones, do you feel like, “I have to do something different here?”

LOUIS-DREYFUS: It’s enormous pressure. It’s almost more pressure than winning or losing. I’ll never forget when I was getting ready, I was in the shower, and I got hit with a lightning bolt of something I thought would be funny to do if we won for Veep.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I called Tony Hale from my bathroom and was like, “I just thought of this. Would you be into it?” We worked it out on the phone, and then it came true, and we did it.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: It was where he followed me up on stage and was talking into my ear like his character on the show.
KEERY: Oh my gosh, that was off the cuff like that?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah. God bless him because he went for it. He could have easily said no.
KEERY: I’ve not met him, but I’m a fan.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Joe, you have no idea what a great person he is. This is somebody you want to work with.
KEERY: And so down. If he’s down to just on a dime do that, that’s so cool.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: He’s a total team player. Okay, I’m going to ask you one question they did give me.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: What strikes you as the most significant difference between doing a play eight times a week versus doing television or film?

KEERY: Certainly the washing machine cycle of emotions that go along with working on the same piece of writing for as long as we already have, and will continue to work on for even longer. It runs the gamut of feeling, like some nights you have it, some nights you don’t. But every single time you get up there, you will find something, which is cool.
KEERY: And it’s hard. You have to really focus, and that’s different.

LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yes. I’m constantly being surprised by something, which is a delight, either in the actual material itself or in the audience reaction. Certain lines in the show make me anticipate a certain reaction from the audience, but sometimes we don’t get that reaction. The communal aspect of doing this is what I find particularly unusual.
KEERY: And the audience is definitely the last member of the band. Everything changed when we started to do it in front of people.

LOUIS-DREYFUS: There’s no question about it. They’re a part of the performance, whether they know it or not. Isn’t that interesting to think about in terms of you as a musician? When you’re on tour, you’re doing essentially the same set every night, I’m assuming. Are you?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Is there overlap or not really?

KEERY: Certainly, but here’s a conversation every band will have with their members, about whether they’re going to use these things called in-ear monitors or not. It’s modern technology that gives everybody headphones while they’re playing live onstage. You can choose to use it or not, but using it puts everything in a bit more of a rigid system. Unlike that, there’s nothing between you and me and Lily [Rabe] and Ed [Harris] and Allison [Janney] and the people who are right there. With music, the audience is a part of it, but it’s not like there’s a comedic give and receive. This feels more intimate.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: That’s interesting.
KEERY: I would imagine if you’re Bruce Springsteen and you’re doing your one-man show, that’s maybe a little closer to what this experience might be.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: One-man show. How about that idea?
KEERY: I think you could definitely do that.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: But I like to be with actors.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Being onstage together, it’s unsurpassed in terms of pure-ass fun. Did you read reviews?
KEERY: No, not really. My mom sent me one or two, so I’ve got this wonderful filter of my mother to send me the good ones.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Oh, how nice.
KEERY: I think Ed was like, “Don’t send me anything.” And I was like, “That’s probably a good thing,” don’t you think?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I do, particularly when you’re going to be in bed with this material for months on end. Even if you’re lauded and they love it or love you, that can get in your way.
KEERY: It can disconnect you from what you’ve been establishing.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah. Hey, I’m enjoying this piece of art behind your head. What is that?
KEERY: I got it from this woman named Paula Rubenstein. She has a little shop. I think this was hanging in some Upper East Side spot for a while. Isn’t it beautiful?
KEERY: It’s chaotic and nice. We also have this whole Chicago connection we haven’t talked about. You went to Northwestern [University].
LOUIS-DREYFUS: That’s right. I went to Northwestern, and you were in Chicago. From when to when?
KEERY: I went to DePaul University from 2010 until 2017. I left to go do Stranger Things.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: You got cast for Stranger Things out of Chicago?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Oh, that’s a big break.
KEERY: At the time, it was certainly a big break. Is that why you moved to New York from Chicago? For SNL?
KEERY: Talk about a big break.

LOUIS-DREYFUS: That was also a big break. So that means you and I were in Chicago at the same time because my youngest son, Charlie, was at Northwestern when you were in Chicago. Isn’t it a great city?
KEERY: It is so great. I love to go back and hang out. I still have a fair amount of friends who live there, and band stuff will take place there.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Are your band mates from Chicago too?
KEERY: A lot of them are friends from after I graduated. I think I told you this, but Japhet [Balaban] and I worked at the same burger restaurant.
KEERY: Japhet is my understudy. A fantastic actor.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Great actor.
KEERY: He worked there and right as I started working there, he left the job. We have a bunch of mutual friends, and through that job I met all these guys who ended up being part of this band.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: So cool. How old were you when you first did Stranger Things?
KEERY: It went from when I was 24 until 33.
KEERY: How long was Seinfeld total? Was that a similar time of your life?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: No, I was a little older, but I did Seinfeld for nine years. I was in my twenties when I started, and then, let’s see, Charlie when I was 37, so I was 28 to 37 during Seinfeld.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: It’s pretty cool to have a series over a long period of time, isn’t it?

KEERY: It’s very cool. And also at that age there’s so much happening in your life developmentally. It felt huge. I don’t know if you do this, but when you think about your life, you’re like, “When did we go to my sister’s graduation? Oh yeah, that was season two.” I’ll judge things by when we were filming the show.
KEERY: And then you had a similar thing with Veep.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Veep was seven or eight years.
KEERY: Do you think you’ll complete the trifecta and do one more long show run in your life?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah, I see that happening. Would you do another one?
KEERY: It’s a pretty fun lifestyle, and it’s really fun if you get a group of people you really care about and are into working with.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: That’s the critical piece. Otherwise you’re fucked.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I love doing series work because it’s an opportunity to work on a character over a long period of time in a way you wouldn’t in the same way, like if it’s a film.

KEERY: Series stuff is very character-forward, which is always so fun. Obviously, if you’re doing a movie, the plot in some ways takes precedence, but you get to really dig in when you’re doing a series.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Have you ever been stuck doing something you hated?
KEERY: You feel stuck in certain moments in a lot of different things, but never in a punishing way. What about you?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah, maybe a little. But if you’re paying attention, you’re going to find ways to learn something.

LOUIS-DREYFUS: For example, when I was doing SNL, which was very difficult—that’s a punishing schedule for sure. It’s also a punishing environment, and it was not a lot of fun at the time. But I sure learned a lot from it, so I don’t regret it.
KEERY: To be frank, the first few weeks of this were really hard for me, especially because I came in a little later than you guys.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Oh yeah, that must have been so strange.

KEERY: I had been working on the material, but it very quickly became, “I need to get this script out of my hand as quickly as possible.” I was just living and breathing this, and it’s not necessarily the most fun to try to memorize lines for all hours of the day. You want to take a break or cook dinner. Work is not always going to be fun, but it will allow you to have fun once you get past that.

LOUIS-DREYFUS: When I was little, I took piano lessons, and it’s like scales. You’ve just got to do them well, and learning the material falls into that category. I had the same anxiety about it coming in. Before we came to rehearsal, I was like, “I have to memorize this, otherwise I’m not going to be able to fall asleep ever again,” because I lie there in a deeply anxious state.
KEERY: I feel like you knew your stuff very well.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I did know it well, but that was out of anxiety, because I worked on that pretty religiously. It’s a very wordy play.
KEERY: All that stuff, that “like,” “you know,” “I mean,” is written in there, so it does not need superfluous—
KEERY: How did you do it? Were you working with a partner?

LOUIS-DREYFUS: Well, [Allison] Janney gave me the name of an actor who does this with other actors, so I got on Zooms with her and started chipping away at the material. Then I got the app I told you about.
KEERY: Yeah, that helped me a lot.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: It’s not a perfect app, but it helps. I would also run the material with my husband, Brad, just pounding it. How did you do it before coming in?

KEERY: A little bit with my friend Wes, who I was on tour with. But the best work was when we started rehearsing and we were doing it all day. Then walking to work and walking home after work, focusing on individual chunks every day. Something about the walking—the stepping and the moving gets you, for whatever reason.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah. And aren’t you finding that right now sleep is everything?
KEERY: Oh my god. Are you so tired?
LOUIS-DREYFUS: So freaking tired.
KEERY: Why am I so exhausted? I was just talking to a friend about this.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Deeply tired.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Have you tried to nap when you have a matinee?

KEERY: I’ve tried. I just can’t quite go down. That dressing room I have, I feel like I’m on the Titanic. It’s a little slim and I’m like, “I got to get out of here.” I get outside a lot but I always regret it.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah, you get outside a lot.
KEERY: I do. I try to get energized in that way. But on those two-show days, the second act of the second show, that’s always a hard moment.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Oh my god, it’s so unbelievable. Once you get your big blowout speech in the second act and you say, “That’s it, I’m out,” I think is your last line—
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Then you can just sit back and enjoy the rest of the program.
KEERY: I’m still in the scene. I still have to focus and react. It may be the most challenging part for me right now.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: I think you’re nailing it.
KEERY: Well, thank you, Julia, for taking your precious off time before the show.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Well, Joe, thank you for taking your precious off time. Do you have any closing remarks for the people who are reading Interview magazine?
KEERY: I would say break a leg, because we’re about to do this in four hours and 30 minutes. Or no, excuse me, my math is wrong here. I’m an actor, not a mathematician.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: In about three hours and 20 minutes, we’ll be having a dance party to prepare for our performance.
KEERY: You got a song lined up? Maybe I’ll pick today. Maybe.
LOUIS-DREYFUS: Yeah, look for something. It’s on you.
Grooming: Rheanne White at Tracey Mattingly Agency.
Fashion Assistants: Paris Talbott and Carter Bright.
Production Director: Alexandra Weiss.
Photo Producer: Georgia Ford.
Production Coordination: Nicole Marquez.
Production Assistant: Camilo Flores.
Location: The Blank Space NYC.

items.title: Alexandre de Betak Helps Mel Ottenberg Find His Light
items.description: Alexandre de Betak Helps Mel Ottenberg Find His Light
items.author: Mel Ottenberg
paragraphs: Alexandre de Betak Helps Mel Ottenberg Find His Light

Alexandre de Betak knows that the right lighting can change everything. The French artist has spent the last thirty years meticulously demonstrating that fact as the man behind the design of unforgettable runway shows for brands like Dior, Saint Laurent, and Fendi. His work is an interplay of light, shadow, glass, metal, and reflection, transforming every space he takes over into something straight out of a cinematic masterpiece. Earlier this month, de Betak brought this signature expertise to Salon 94 in New York with a show titled TRUSS LIGHT SCULPTURES 01, featuring twelve sculptures based on the trusses and stage lights that are the backbone of all those fashion shows he worked on. Interview Editor-in-Chief Mel Ottenberg stopped by the exhibition where de Betak gave him a personal tour of the show while discussing trial and error, classicism versus punk, and when art becomes fantasy.
TUESDAY 11AM NOVEMBER 10, 2026 NEW YORK CITY
MEL OTTENBERG: A little sound is fine for my heightened experience, but turning it down a bit for the recording is great. Did you design the sound as well?
OTTENBERG: Fabulous. When did you decide to quit your career for this new career?

DE BETAK: To be honest, it just happened. I always thought I was going to do this. I never really felt I needed to sync it so concretely to do it. But the reality is that, yes, I did. Three years ago, I decided to completely leave the fashion show-making world and dedicate myself 100% to doing this, which in a way, is the continuation of the same thing but in a completely different context with a different objective.
OTTENBERG: Wow. Tell me about this story. This is the aluminum? So beautiful.

DE BETAK: There are two series. This one is the aluminum series. It’s made of nine unique pieces inspired by the most obvious and first tools I used when I started doing fashion shows a million years ago—aluminum trusses and stage lights, which no one really uses anymore. Those things were made to light other people’s work and be hidden in order to do so, and they very intentionally and very honestly were the first thing I worked with in my personal artwork. I completely redesigned, rebuilt, and rethought all of those elements. The systems that make the light are custom-designed and concealed so there’s no bulb. It’s just a combination of weird electronic elements that together we can play with and program in similar ways. The goal was to take what normally takes truckloads of very large equipment and many, many people and put them into a very small box that you can artistically, personally control yourself.
OTTENBERG: Very James Bond.
DE BETAK: Well, this one is aluminum. The bronze series is very heavy.
DE BETAK: So the idea was to basically continue with similar tools and ways I’ve always done, but take it to a completely uncompromised context, both commercially and artistically.
OTTENBERG: This is the one that controls this?
DE BETAK: This is the one that controls this one.

DE BETAK: See for example, I go on dancing and dancing is a sound reactive mode. So there are microphones inside of the sculpture and it’s got an evolutive sensibility. And I can change here—that’s warm white to cold white, so you go very warm here to very cold here.
OTTENBERG: Do you prefer warm or cold light?

DE BETAK: This can basically follow the sunlight through the day, the temperature of the sun from very cold in the morning to really warm at night after sunset. I actually like the combination alone, and I like the fact that you can control the temperature of the light to go together with the sun or to go against the sun, whichever way you want. It’s something that’s always obsessed me, to have the perfect temperature of white. It’s very rare. And with this control unit, now you can do it yourself.
OTTENBERG: What’s the technology in these lights? Do you believe in LED lights? Is this old school? What is this?

DE BETAK: It’s basically a mix. It is made of micro LEDs on electronic components that are designed and custom-built in a way that you can control them very specifically, like we were able to before with tungsten light, which you can no longer use.
OTTENBERG: Tungsten light?

DE BETAK: Yeah. Tungsten was what was before LED. And normally with LED, when you buy even a warm white LED, when you dim it, it becomes a bit green and a bit flickery. See, if I’m on glowing, you can go down really, really softly and it doesn’t go green, it doesn’t flicker. You see what I mean?

DE BETAK: It’s a very, very, very sensitive system. Then there’s a breathing mode, which will take a second to go. I put it colder so you see. It’s going to just slowly breathe. Then there is a sparkling mode, which is a little bit inspired by the The Eiffel Tower—on the hour at night it sparkles. Then there is the one that I call the dancing mode, which is basically sound-reactive. But it’s very sensitive. You can whisper to it. You can talk to it. [Coughs] You can cough to it. I have a cold.
OTTENBERG: Me too. I’m so upset about it.
DE BETAK: It’s so annoying.
OTTENBERG: I know. I woke up okay and now I don’t know. My friend that I was with on Saturday has a fever. Everyone is sick in New York.
DE BETAK: Anyways, let’s fight it.
OTTENBERG: Did you become an expert on this through trial and error when you were doing shows, or were you just always good at it?

DE BETAK: I still am trial and error. But in doing the shows, it gave me the means and the resources to experiment. I liked to play with light in particular, and I always felt it was very important to choreograph the synchronization of the light with the sound, music, choreography, and everything else in a very specific way. So I guess it is a combination of extensive trial and error and also extensive use.
OTTENBERG: Decades of both.
OTTENBERG: Are you more aluminum or bronze, personally?

DE BETAK: Let me show you the bronze. I thought I was more aluminum, maybe I am more aluminum as a person, but once we discovered the bronze, it was very touching. I was afraid that it would be too classic for me, and instead I find it almost more vitalistic and punk than the aluminums are because the aluminums are, of course, inspired directly by the original aluminum industrialist elements. But in a way, taking the industrial, ephemeral, and light essence of the original aluminum ones and making it in bronze—the most durable, heavyweight and artistically classic material—makes it extremely elegant, but still very punk in a way that I actually relate to. The combination is cool. It’s really fun.
OTTENBERG: I really like this. Do you have LED light bulbs at home?

DE BETAK: It took me a very long time and I had them special ordered when I decided to actually switch from the old incandescent to LED because I was never happy with them. I do have LED at home now, like we all do, because you can’t find the—
OTTENBERG: I always find the old ones, but I have to learn about the good ones because my supply will run out. There are places in New York that you can get them.
DE BETAK: Yeah, you still can get the very low-wattage ones, but at some point you can’t. Sustainably and ecologically thinking, you have to switch.
OTTENBERG: Oh, wow. They really are incredible.
DE BETAK: It’s really crazy that one.
SPEAKER 1: That’s another one, Ignorance we call it.
OTTENBERG: Yes. But it’s bronze. It’s really good.

DE BETAK: It’s crazy to create these bronze ones—30 molds per unit. We molded every single screw, every string, every part. Literally the screw itself, which functions for the filter, is made out of bronze. The glass is a specially-designed glass that I did to get the perfect diffusion of the light. And everything obviously functions from these lights, but made out of bronze. When I sent the first image of this to the foundry, they were like, “You’re completely mad. It’s going to be impossible. There’s too many pieces.”

DE BETAK: So this is a remote for this one. See, and you can go super low, almost like this. I can go super warm to super cold like this, and then raise really slowly. And then there’s a very slow breath. No, that’s the dancing. Hold on. That’s the breathing, which you can make warmer.
OTTENBERG: They look so good in Salon 94. Where else do you think they would look good?

DE BETAK: Hopefully, in many different settings because, as you saw, downstairs is a more modern, lofty kind of room and it works. And this one is very classic, grand mansion-y, which was where we dreamt of seeing them. And I think that kind of old-world classic is really where they take most of their value.
OTTENBERG: Yeah, I see it. It’s beautiful.
DE BETAK: I find them quite romantic as opposed to what one would have imagined they would be. Let’s see, that’s the sparkling.
DE BETAK: And then, if I go to dancing…See, it’s a very sensitive reaction to the sound. [Stomps feet]
OTTENBERG: I like it. I’m an aluminum guy, but I see the vision. I want a castle.
OTTENBERG: It would look so great. I mean, I want a castle for this. An Upper East Side castle is good too.
DE BETAK: An Upper East Side castle is not bad. Where do you live?
OTTENBERG: Washington Square.
DE BETAK: Have both. You can have the aluminum on Washington Square and then the castle on the Upper East Side.
OTTENBERG: Yes. What you’re doing downstairs is the art in my fantasy. I love art and I love light.
DE BETAK: An illumination of the room and the art.
OTTENBERG: Have you bought lots of lights over the years? Are you always buying a light or are you just making a light?

DE BETAK: I’ve been making a lot and accumulating pieces of old stuff. Some vintage pieces are just remnants of things I had designed and shows I have done. But I don’t know if I buy a lot of lights. At some point I did. There was a time when I had a lot of them, and then I got rid of a lot of things, and now I’m in a more bare environment.
OTTENBERG: Your house looks great. Can I take some pictures of you?
DE BETAK: Yeah, of course.
OTTENBERG: Your stuff looks so good here. It’s so space age, but not retro.

items.title: Sara Boustany and Kristina Bogic Can Keep a Secret
items.description: The Body’s Sara Boustany and Kristina Bogic on Kissing Girls and Keeping Secrets
items.author: Interview
paragraphs: The Body’s Sara Boustany and Kristina Bogic on Kissing Girls and Keeping Secrets

“Everybody start kissing,” Sara Boustany admits to thinking during her first watch of Netflix’s new must-see TV show, The Body. The actress plays Elise Zakaria, a bitch with a heart of gold, in Quinn Shephard’s sapphic, psychological thriller set at a Northeast Catholic high school in the early aughts. The genre-bending series centers around a girls dance troupe that start having strange religious hallucinations following an initiation-mishap. Drugs, Satan, and lesbians—The Body is a coming-of-age story unlike you’ve ever seen. And according to the actresses, the process of making the show also possessed a cult-ish undertone. “Everyone’s getting sick and you’re in sub-40 degrees and they’re like, ’We’re going to put you in this little bikini,’” confesses Kristina Bogic, who plays Anya Butler on the show—the dance team captain and Elise’s other half. Ahead of the show’s release, with Boustany calling from Mexico and Bogic from Australia, the pair braved a 17-hour time difference to discuss slickbacks, dance rehearsals, and magical thinking.—ISABELLA SOCCI
MONDAY 6PM OCTOBER 19, 2026 MEXICO
SARA BOUSTANY: Sorry, I’m in Mexico right now in the middle of nowhere. Are you in Australia?
KRISTINA BOGIC: I’m in Australia now. I went on a little trip.
BOUSTANY: Where was your little trip?
BOGIC: Hamilton Island. It’s in the north of Australia, this little island where you can only drive around on golf buggies.
BOGIC: What are you doing in Mexico?
BOUSTANY: Just for a vacation.
BOGIC: Beautiful. Do you want to talk about our audition experience?
BOUSTANY: I’m down. Everybody had a crazy experience getting the role.
BOGIC: It’s all weirdly a little spiritual as well.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, for sure. You go first.

BOGIC: Okay. I got the original audition, I think a few months before I even got a callback. It was a really long audition process for me. I did the first audition, I did a callback, and then I didn’t hear back for maybe a month or so. I was like, “You know what? I’m going to go to Europe with my best friend.” I was at this tiny, little airport and I got a call from my agent saying, “Hey, you need to get on this callback. It’s with Sara.” And I remember looking Sara up and going, “Oh my god.”
BOGIC: And then we did maybe four—
BOUSTANY: We did three. Was it four? I thought it was three.
BOUSTANY: Maybe your auditions were different.
BOGIC: I did one with Geena [Meszaros] too, who plays Lisbeth.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, I did too. With Anya, it was a long process for me, but I remember it so vividly. Do you?
BOGIC: Yeah, I remember it really well.
BOUSTANY: You had your hair back in a little pony and you were in Italy, right?

BOGIC: Yeah, I was in Italy, in Taormina. They were like, “Can you slick back your hair and wear no makeup for the audition?” Then, I wake up and I’m slicked back. For half of the auditions I was traveling around and it was at 3:00 AM for me because of the different time zones.
BOGIC: I was in the most random hotels. My best friend who traveled with me, she’s like, “I watched a tiny clip of the show. I remember this script so well from how many times I was doing it.”
BOUSTANY: Yeah, my friends as well. I had a couple of my friends audition too.

BOGIC: I actually knew a lot of people that auditioned for this. I remember getting lunch with some of my actor friends in Melbourne and they were all like, “Oh, there’s this open call for The Body.” As soon as I heard about it, I wanted it immediately.
BOUSTANY: Me too. But wait, we’re getting sidetracked.
BOGIC: Let me ask you the proper questions. Can we talk about our rehearsal period and how we all got close? Because it was eight weeks of dance rehearsals.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, there was a really intense week where it was every day, every day, every day. I really think each of us was almost hospitalized at a certain point.

BOGIC: We had Ryan Heffington putting us through boot camp. He was so patient, so graceful and kind when we were all getting to know each other. There was so much energy, but I’m so happy we all had that time because it warmed us up to each other.

BOGIC: I’ve made a point in every interview or conversation I’ve had about the show to say it has never once felt competitive. You’re coming into a group of 12 young girls and it was honestly the most supportive environment.

BOUSTANY: It really was. We just bonded so quickly. I’d never experienced something like that. I just feel so happy and proud to be a part of a group of girls who just love each other. It’s not rare. Women are amazing. But it’s rare in a workplace to be so close.
BOGIC: Yeah. As coworkers, you’re all put together and they’re like, “Okay, now be friends.” And it’s always a little awkward, but we all just clicked.
BOUSTANY: I have a question for you. How did you decompress after a disturbing or challenging scene?
BOGIC: I was going to literally ask you this.
BOUSTANY: Well, you had more of those, so you should answer it.
BOGIC: Honestly, at the beginning, I was very good at shaking off whatever scene I had to do that day. But there were times, I don’t know if you remember, I was in the trenches.
BOUSTANY: What do you mean, do I remember? I was traumatized for you. It was crazy. We were in the freezing cold.

BOGIC: If I’d had one moment of sun throughout the entire six months of filming, it would’ve saved me. But imagine you’re always together. It’s a huge group. It’s a huge crew. Everyone’s getting sick, and you’re in sub-40-degree weather, and they’re like, “We’re going to put you in this little bikini, and you’re going to walk around.”
BOUSTANY: And then also cry and lose your mind.
BOGIC: How to decompress? On the weekend, I would just rot away, but I needed that. I needed time to not speak, to not be touched or anything, and just fade away.
BOUSTANY: Yeah. I don’t think the show would’ve even been what it was if none of us leaned on each other as much.
BOGIC: Yeah. Even when it comes to press stuff, I’m so thankful I get to do it. We’re very lucky. Every time I’m with you guys, I’m like, “I’m safe.”
BOGIC: Okay. I’m going to ask you a question. What was your high school experience like?

BOUSTANY: I truly blocked a lot of it out. I didn’t have a negative experience. Emotions are so heightened when you’re a teenager and your body processes it as some kind of trauma, so it gets stored away.
BOGIC: Everything feels amplified at that age as well. Any experience I had with school was not a good one at all.

BOGIC: I was homeschooled from seventh grade, and then when I got to tenth grade, I went to an art school for three weeks. Imagine those formative years not growing up in a school system. You can go to the bathroom whenever you want. You’re treated like an adult in society because there’s not this hierarchy. When I went back to that, it shook me so much, and I ended up just leaving school. It was the best thing I could have done. If you give teenage girls the chance to just figure out what they want to do and who they want to be, they’re not going to waste that chance. That’s when we have the most excitement for life and innocence about the world. I’m very lucky I had those years to figure out what I wanted to do with my life.

BOUSTANY: Yeah. I also barely went because freshman year was just hell mentally for no reason. So for half of that semester, I was homeschooled. I went back sophomore year, and then I went to Lebanon, and then the revolution happened, and then none of us were going to school for six months. Got back to L.A., COVID hit, no school. I spent senior year at a normal school. I feel like my life just started a couple years ago.
BOGIC: We’re both very lucky we had enough time to figure our shit out.
BOUSTANY: Yeah. My parents were extremely supportive, and I wouldn’t have been able to figure out what I wanted to do without them.
BOGIC: Me too. What was your first impression of me? Tell me everything.

BOUSTANY: At first, you were pretty reserved and I loved it. I had an immediate connection with you. When we first met, we were doing dance stuff. I remember glancing at you and then you would glance at me and then we’d just be like—
BOGIC: I couldn’t believe everyone was real. Imagine walking into a room of 12 of the most beautiful women you’ve ever seen.

BOGIC: When we started filming, Geena and I had a conversation. We were like, “Isn’t Sara so amazing? She’s so amazing. Everything she does.” Whenever I was in a scene with you, I was like, “Girl, I got to fucking bring it.”

BOUSTANY: Oh, that’s so sweet. I love that. We only had one audition scene and I thought our chemistry was so amazing. But I was just curious about how you were going to play Anya because we talked so much about her bad decision making. I was curious about how you were going to bring that warmth to her, and I really felt it. What’s funny is that the only thing we would bicker about on set was Anya and Elise, but now we’re so on the same page about them.

BOGIC: But you know what? That’s such a good sign that we both trusted and believed in our characters so much. You would be able to feel it instantly watching the show if I couldn’t justify one of Anya’s decisions. I had to defend her through everything.

BOUSTANY: We’re in pretty bad shape most of the season. Someone asked me, “What do you think Anya and Elise love about each other?” And I’m like, “We didn’t even have the chance to explore their relationship outside of something happening so abruptly.”

BOGIC: Yeah. You see their dynamic as friends, but I would love to see Anya and Elise have more best friend moments. You get a sense of it in episode one, but once you see a lot of the issues in the show and how they talk, you can tell they’re very comfortable with each other.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, it was the girlness and the gossip of them. I don’t even know what the word is. It’s the conspiring that all girls love to do.
BOGIC: What should we talk about next? Do you have any superstitions? Irrational fears? Psychic experiences? Do you believe in curses? Astrology?

BOUSTANY: It’s more so words having power and what you put out is what you get. I’m going to get real vulnerable right now. When you’re struggling so much with yourself, sometimes you just want to talk about it to the people you care about. But when you tell people something they start focusing on it. So basically, keep what you doubt about yourself to yourself, because what you put out is what people will inevitably feel.

BOGIC: Not putting weight behind words is a big thing, which is basically just what you’re saying. I’m an anxious person in general, and as soon as I tell someone I’m anxious, all of a sudden it’s ten times worse.

BOUSTANY: Yeah, but it needs to be a specific person, because I remember talking to Geena about this and telling her something that was upsetting me. She was just like, “I see you being upset and it makes me feel like you’re human.” I guess it’s kind of superstitious of me to feel that way. I have random ones as well. My OCD comes out in random things, like clenching my teeth for a certain amount of time.

BOGIC: Yeah. This isn’t a superstition. This is weird shit that I do. If I’m eating and I only chew on one side of my mouth, I have to even it out with the other side. It’s a sensory thing. You know what? Say I do an audition and I really want it, I used to manifest and smother it with my hopes and dreams. I’d put all of my energy into it, and then I felt like I wouldn’t get the role because I would suffocate it. As soon as I let them go, they’d come back to me. I’m like, “Okay, I’m very grateful for this,” but I try not to invest so much spiritual energy into it.
BOUSTANY: Yeah, The Body felt that way for me.
BOGIC: I think if I didn’t get The Body, I would’ve dwindled away. I was so obsessed with Anya. I would’ve been heartbroken if I didn’t get her.
BOUSTANY: Oh my god, I would’ve lost my fucking mind.
BOGIC: I can’t even imagine my life without meeting everyone. It’s not even something I can fathom.

BOUSTANY: Me too. Sometimes you feel like these things were bound to happen. Sometimes I’m just like, “I knew that it was going to happen for me,” but it happens and then you’re, like, imposter syndrome to the fucking max. Would you have been friends with the characters in high school?

BOGIC: I feel like Anya would’ve been the girl to be like, “Have you ever made out with girls?” And I would’ve been like, “Girl, okay, I know where this is going.” Or I would’ve shaken her a couple times. [Laughs]
BOUSTANY: I would’ve been friends with Elise for sure, but this bitchy defense mechanism—cut it out. You have a good sense of yourself. You do not need to be doing all that. But it’s funny, I would.

BOGIC: But you know what? I think you thought that about Elise as well. And I think it’s good that you did because you made her so much softer than I ever read her on the page. I think she was always going to be lovable because she’s witty and funny and cheeky. But you gave her such a soft little heart where you’re, like, baby Elise. You just want to hold her.
BOUSTANY: Nobody’s a bitch just because they’re a bitch. It’s always something. Like an unrequited love.
BOGIC: Oh. Well, yes. I have no idea what you’re talking about. [Laughs]
BOUSTANY: I would’ve been friends with Anya.
BOGIC: Me too. I would love to explore her funny, girly side because I didn’t get to explore that as much. I did with Lisbeth a little bit too.
BOGIC: What I love is that although our trope is focused on, there are so many relationships in the show that I really root for. Not always romantically, but platonically.
BOUSTANY: I like everyone to be romantic.
BOGIC: Everyone’s romantic.
BOUSTANY: I’m like, “Everyone, start kissing now.”
BOGIC: The first time we watched it, we were like, “Smash, smash. I want these two together. Everyone has chemistry.”
BOUSTANY: Kind of wish Lisbeth and Anya kissed really quickly.
BOUSTANY: Just really quick, and then nobody ever talked about it ever again.
BOGIC: That would be a Lisbeth thing to do. She’d come up and kiss Anya as a threat.
BOUSTANY: She totally would. I love Lisbeth.
BOGIC: Me too. She’s probably one of my favorite characters.
BOUSTANY: Are you good at keeping secrets?
BOGIC: You are not good at keeping secrets. It eats you up inside.
BOUSTANY: No, I’m not. If I feel guilty about something, I can’t do it. But if it’s a secret that I’m keeping and it doesn’t hurt anybody, my lips are sealed.
BOGIC: I tell everyone everything. Ever since I was little, even people I don’t know very well have told me their deepest, darkest secrets.
BOUSTANY: Me too. I think it’s because we are very vulnerable with people.
BOGIC: True. I don’t remember the last time I lied. You know what? I exaggerate stories.
BOGIC: Not big things, but if it’s something funny, somehow the story gets bigger and bigger each time. But I’m like, “I’m an actor. That’s reasonable.”

BOUSTANY: Yeah, that is reasonable. Everybody’s lied. But I believe in confessing for sure. This is maybe controversial, but if someone tells me something fucked up, I’m like, “Okay, you better tell them before I do.”

BOGIC: Yeah. If I feel guilt for holding a secret, it makes me feel sick. I can’t keep it in. But I’m like Anya in that way where it literally will eat me up inside until I crack, and then I’m like, “Ugh, this is it.” And I just vomit it out.
BOUSTANY: Yeah. It’s weird. I can’t do it.

items.title: Photographer Natalie Curtis on Time, Memory, and Minions
items.description: Photographer Natalie Curtis on Time, Memory, and Minions
items.author: Dora Sahbazovic
paragraphs: Photographer Natalie Curtis on Time, Memory, and Minions

Photographer Natalie Curtis has a knack for transience. Her sentences are pithy and her pictures are taken as if captured in mid-air. The first time I met her, we’d agreed to have a drink by the Gare du Nord before she headed back to London. When she approached me on the cold, crowded terrace, the first thought I had was how she appears to have mastered the realm of time in the way only a true photographer can; I registered dignity, relief, and a shy curiosity. The last-minute hangout ahead of our scheduled interview had been Curtis’s idea, brought out of a desire to ensure I was normal, I gathered. She’s the daughter of Ian Curtis of Joy Division fame, and such an addendum can complicate one’s relationship with vulnerability.

But I don’t care much for biographical facts. I wanted to know how Curtis—whose work incites the same emotional impulse in me as a full-blooded bass line—dreams. Imagination and space are closely connected, and her work is a sublimation of the two rooted in memory, history’s affective peer.

As we glossed over the conspicuous fact that I’d shown up to our conversation with a freshly-bleached head of crunchy 2b hair, we got to talking about logistics the way only two strangers with a talent for never cutting to the chase can. After setting up her new photography show Tower at Galerie Arnaud Lefebvre, Curtis was off to Milan for a work trip. I asked whether she finds it tiring spending so much time on the road.
FRIDAY 1PM NOVEMBER 6, 2026 PARIS
NATALIE CURTIS: It’s alright. Could always be worse.
DORA SAHBAZOVIC: I guess. Could be a gig in Siberia.
CURTIS: Or another town in England.
SAHBAZOVIC: Scary. You also recently had your work shown at the Venice Biennale. How was that?

CURTIS: I had an image in ART-ICON’s Static Cinema exhibition, which took place during the film festival. It was very cool to be a part of something like that. Mostly, since I wasn’t there, I had FOMO. It looked like a great time to be in Venice.
SAHBAZOVIC: You described Tower as an exit project coinciding with you leaving Manchester for good. What has been drawing you back over the years?
CURTIS: I have very good friends in Manchester and it’s close to where I’m from, Cheshire, where my family are. And Manchester’s less expensive than London, though it has gone up in recent years.
SAHBAZOVIC: It feels like much artistic novelty has come out of this not too enormous city. I wonder how something like that occurs, or whether it’s mere chance?
CURTIS: Probably the weather has something to do with it, perhaps people are indoors more. Also, in a non-big city, everything’s less on a plate.
SAHBAZOVIC: When you think of Cheshire, what image comes to mind?
CURTIS: Hills. I really miss seeing the hills.
SAHBAZOVIC: I’m really in awe of the English countryside. It looks so lush. I imagine people still get around on horseback there.
CURTIS: I had a choice once to either save money for driving school or sign up for riding lessons. I still can’t drive.
SAHBAZOVIC: Aw. Was this in childhood?

CURTIS: Oh, this was like ten years ago. [Laughs] I was really passionate about it for a while. The first stable I took classes in though, in the hills, was a children’s riding school. I was the only adult in class.
SAHBAZOVIC: Did they give you a bigger horse?
CURTIS: Not necessarily! We’d always be switching horses. I remember one that was really scared of minions, you know, the small, yellow things.
CURTIS: Yeah, there was an obstacle course with minion cartoon cutouts for obstacles for some reason. And for this horse not to freak out, it was a whole affair of having to move the minions.
SAHBAZOVIC: Sure, happens every day.

CURTIS: There was also one that got demoted from working at the police to this riding gig. He was scared of traffic. Another one just hated bridges. Like he’d come up to a bridge all normal and then just freeze.
SAHBAZOVIC: I love that a horse can be unemployed. Why did you stop riding?
CURTIS: Among other things, there was just a lot of falling involved. There’s a saying one of the children’s moms at the riding school taught me: “Seven falls makes a horse woman.”
SAHBAZOVIC: That’s very strange and beautiful.

CURTIS: I know. Where I’m from in Cheshire, there’s a lot of cows as well—milk cows. You know that’s where the Cheshire cat got its name? They say she grins because she had a lot of cream from the milk cows.
SAHBAZOVIC: Oh, I wondered.

CURTIS: But don’t quote me on that. Anyways, I went to a village school. In the morning, before class, these dairy cows would always be in your way. The cows are crossing the road was the most normal excuse for being late.
SAHBAZOVIC: That’s grand. So, does London feel like home now?

CURTIS: As a person from the northwest, I feel that the southeast should not feel like home, but weirdly it does. When I returned to London, for this my third stint, I was walking through the neighborhood where I lived the first time, in 2010 I think it was, and it felt like I’d never left. As though the subsequent time in Manchester never happened, as though it was just something I dreamt.
SAHBAZOVIC: Do you find you’ve searched out comfort or novelty more as you’ve matured?

CURTIS: I like to be as comfortable as possible! I think novelty is important. But being comfortable helps to get things done. It’s harder to concentrate if you’re physically uncomfortable. When I’m away, I feel so glad that I have my desk at home set up properly, everything in the right place, at the right height, and that I have a mattress I like. Also, if you’re comfortable—physically, in your surroundings, in yourself—there’s a kind of active relaxation. It can happen if I’m taking photos somewhere very familiar, and also I can be doing something, like the washing up, and I’ll get an idea or something I’m working on will make sense. I think routine gives you space to find or see the novelty.
SAHBAZOVIC: You said you were already toying with your grandfather’s camera as a child. How did you get back to it as an adult?

CURTIS: Although sporadic, it never really went away. Then, as an adult, I took the Art Foundation course at my local college and realized photography was a real option and that I could study at art school.
SAHBAZOVIC: What or who did you find inspiration in back then?

CURTIS: Once, I photographed dolls. Mostly photographed my younger brother. I do tend to photograph parts of my life. I was always interested in locations and landscapes. But when I was younger, I couldn’t get my head around how to do what I wanted to do.
SAHBAZOVIC: Why photography?
CURTIS: It’s kind of magical as a medium.
SAHBAZOVIC: You mean the way it works?
CURTIS: Yeah, the science of it.
SAHBAZOVIC: What compels you to take a picture?
CURTIS: It’s a feeling that’s a need.
SAHBAZOVIC: Have you ever felt like getting into cinema as well? You had a part in Control, but that must have been quite an uncommon on-set experience.

CURTIS: Sometimes. Though I think film sets involve too many people for me—amazing people, but it’s just not my kind of thing. Yet I do like to play with moving image. I was an extra on Control, a friend from high school wanted to do it and for me to do it with her, and possibly I should’ve said no! It wasn’t a normal extra experience in that I’d already spent time on set and met everyone. But it was interesting to see different aspects of the filmmaking process in that I went to wardrobe and to hair and make-up—that I really enjoyed, and I guess is maybe special treatment for an extra. However, the actual filming of a riot scene was brutal. It was fun explaining to my dentist how exactly my tooth got chipped.

But when I was a student, with a friend from my photography course and my brother, we had what I think is a more typical extras experience for 24 Hour Party People. We wore our own clothes and most of it was just sitting around waiting in a pub near the set. We didn’t know what to expect and so weren’t prepared, all the other extras had books or work to get on with. My brother curled up and went to sleep. Though at various points actors did pop in, which was ace. During the actual filming—it was a much smaller location than the scene in Control and not a riot—we loved watching the director and cinematographer at work, being in that space is very different to observing during a standard set visit. A dream of a day’s work for a pair of photography students!
SAHBAZOVIC: What did an average night with friends look like in your twenties?

CURTIS: We either watched telly or listened to music, then we went to the pub. After the pub, more telly or music, maybe we played cards. There was a game called Shithead. Often we watched a film, sometimes we’d just drive round the countryside—or not. I remember waiting forever for a badger to move out the road. Everyone smoked and drank loads of tea. I remember laughing a lot. Mid to late-twenties was in Manchester, so I guess I maybe danced more, saw more live music, but it’s not as vivid as the late 90s/early 00s small town days.
SAHBAZOVIC: What’s your favorite photograph of yours?
CURTIS: It changes. As I write, “Union” in the Tower project.
SAHBAZOVIC: Your photographs feel to me as if already being captured from a future moment while being taken. Like an instantaneous, fundamental contortion of time.
CURTIS: I like that. I think maybe that’s what photography is.
SAHBAZOVIC: Talk about melancholy. Which of the four Ancient Greek temperaments do you correspond with best? There’s sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic, I gather.
CURTIS: So I did an online quiz once! The result was something like 75% melancholic, 17% sanguine, and 8% phlegmatic.
SAHBAZOVIC: This is very real. I don’t remember the last time I felt choleric.
CURTIS: I do feel angry sometimes, though maybe anger is too strong a word. Extreme frustration?
SAHBAZOVIC: What’s your relationship with memory?

CURTIS: I suspect that I often take photos in order to process and then not remember. I’m interested in memory in that everyone remembers differently, has their own version. There are facts but the truth varies. I think photographs can be both document and myth—something in between.

SAHBAZOVIC: Now that you mentioned myth, I find that myth-making is one of the most fascinating ways of understanding the modern age. It’s been around forever, but you don’t have to be a god to be the stuff of legend anymore.
CURTIS: Thinking about truth versus myth, I’m glad that people have stopped saying that the camera never lies. I always hated that.
SAHBAZOVIC: Are you at peace with not knowing?
CURTIS: Yes. [a Roma guy playing the accordion really loudly passes by, but not before lingering in front of our table first]
SAHBAZOVIC: What do forties feel like?

CURTIS: Amazing in that I feel very sure of what I’m doing creatively, I know how I want to spend my time and so on, and rubbish all at once. Maybe less pressure because I don’t give a shit, I just want to do what I want to do and have more experience and the confidence that brings. I feel like an adult teenager, actually. It’s like being a teenager, but with knowing things.
SAHBAZOVIC: If your body of work were translated into text, would it largely consist of questions or answers?
CURTIS: Both probably. But short sentences.
SAHBAZOVIC: Yeah. I find a good question is hard to come by.
CURTIS: For me, right now, I am concerned that I don’t give good answers.
SAHBAZOVIC: Who needs those? [Laughs] One more thing: where is beauty?
CURTIS: In good and honest intentions.

items.title: Tinashe Crashes a Plane and Belts Out 'Melatonin' During Hilarious 'GTA VI' Stream
items.description: The whole world has been counting down to Grand Theft Auto VI finally being released, and now that it’s here, people are calling out of work and school to play. One person who wasted no time? Tinashe, who dove straight into the video game for her fans through
items.author: Julyssa Lopez
paragraphs: The whole world has been counting down to Grand Theft Auto VI finally being released, and now that it’s here, people are calling out of work and school to play. One person who wasted no time? Tinashe, who dove straight into the video game for her fans through a hilarious livestream. The singer hopped on X right after midnight, tweeting: “Streaming GTA on twitch lets gooo.”

Once she was locked in, she got to work. The stream captures her cracking fans up by trying to make an epic getaway by flying an airplane and hysterically crashing it into the ground. She also screams her head off as she gets in a shootout but quickly runs out of ammo and has to rely on hand-to-hand combat. “I have no bullets!” she screams. “Holy shit, I’m going to have to beat the fuck out of them myself.”

At one point, during another shootout, she gets so stressed out that she starts singing the bridge of her own hit “Melatonin,” yelping, “Fucking with me, hope you know I’m what you asked for, asked for! Back door, back door!”

Tinashe is a big gamer; in the past, she’s played a lot of Call of Duty: Warzone under the name SniperNashe and streamed it on Twitch and YouTube for gamer fans. She’s also talked about being a fan of Mortal Kombat and Diablo IV. Plus, she’s chronically online — she was all over X earlier this month to clap back at conservatives during the midterms — so it makes sense she’d be celebrating GTA VI‘s big arrival on social media with everyone else.

She wasn’t the only celebrity excited about the video game: After several days of sold-out shows in the U.K., Noah Kahan kicked back after his shows and stayed up wreaking havoc on Vice City while his wife was asleep. F1 champion Lewis Hamilton and actress Millie Bobby Brown also shared how excited they were for the game’s sixth edition.

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Recap: The Penultimate Peril
