items.description: How is this show getting good right at the end? It took you this many episodes to make me feel something other than irritation with Victor? The Traitors loves to use a helicopter and a beaming Alan Cumming to show the triumph of the human spirit, and dammit if
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: How is this show getting good right at the end? It took you this many episodes to make me feel something other than irritation with Victor? The Traitors loves to use a helicopter and a beaming Alan Cumming to show the triumph of the human spirit, and dammit if it doesn’t work on me.

We are down to eight players at the start of this two-part finale: Kriste, Abbey, Katie, Victor, Shane, Wyatt, Clyde, and Jay. Clyde remains very suspicious of Katie and Shane, which is bananas. How is this cast so bad at getting Traitors out, but two of them have been 100 percent right about both their guesses? Victor’s unstoppable personality pushed through Tomica’s and Joe’s eliminations, but can Clyde meet that same level of fruit-based confidence with the remaining players? We’ll see.

Clyde floats Shane’s name to Katie, Abbey, and Jay, which Katie immediately reports to Shane. Their new plan is to get the other players onto Jay. Victor, the zebra from Madagascar, agrees to go after Jay. He is taking his winning streak and running in the completely wrong direction. Meanwhile, with Katie out of the room, Clyde floats her name to Kriste, Jay, and Wyatt. Clyde’s main evidence is that Katie is bad at puzzles. People make “that is a compelling argument” faces because no one knows what the fuck to do anymore.

At the roundtable, Kriste is in a dachshund sweater that’s really radiating mom energy. I didn’t think I needed the insane, Panem Capitol–style fashion we’re trending toward on D-list celebrity Traitors, but I miss it. Not that I wouldn’t buy that sweater. Jay tells the audience that he wants to get Victor out, then states that “if my life is threatened, kitty’s got claws.” Jay, I know sexuality is complicated, but damn. Alan, in a semi-bejeweled lilac suit, sets the stage for their penultimate roundtable and leaves them to it. Shane goes after Jay, which Katie backs him on. The way they talk to him makes me think everyone hates Jay. Is that the case? Katie says that with him, it’s always too little, too late. Ugh, this is why we need more time in these episodes. What have the actual tensions and dynamics been between the cast? We never would have gotten an MJ pants moment with this edit.

Clyde tries to pull focus from the Jay accusations and accuses Katie, then awkwardly laughs and weakly accuses Shane. Clyde! Where’s that fruit confidence?! Victor wants to focus on evidence, and he claims that Jay has voted with the Traitors in past roundtables. I will take his word for it. All I know is that Jay consistently voted for Victor. Jay thinks that Katie and Victor are Traitors. There’s no way that Katie is winning at this point, right? Enough people are suspicious of her that they’re going to be too paranoid to let her survive the sparkle flames at the end.

The voting goes: Abbey (Jay), Clyde says he’s really conflicted but votes (Jay), Wyatt (Jay), Jay (Victor), Shane (Jay), Kriste (Jay), Katie (Jay), Victor (Jay). Jay looks really emotional! Then he walks to the Circle of Truth and does a weird reveal that lands really awkwardly with everyone. It feels like we’re missing a piece of context, but after Jay proclaims, “When I first came in here, I was a Faithful, but now I! Am! A! Faithful.” Wyatt asks, “What the hell was that?” and Alan deems it “a rather different roundtable exit.” Is it because of the misdirect? Or is it because Jay is constantly as dramatic as he can be? Everyone looks awkward and confused.

Before they all disperse for the night, Kriste cries about not being part of a clique and everyone group-hugs her, then Wyatt immediately tells Abbey he still suspects Kriste. Clyde tells the men he is almost 100 percent certain that it’s Katie. Victor stammers in response to this and goes to talk to Katie in the bar. Nothing of substance is said. Everyone goes to bed, and the Traitors meet in the turret.

It’s the last murder! Wyatt and Abbey have shields, so that leaves Victor, Kriste, and Clyde. They’re concerned that murdering Clyde is too obvious, but also, what do they have to lose at this point? Murdering Kriste would maybe put heat on Wyatt, since she’s been saying his name for a while. They briefly consider Victor, and then mutually promise not to rug pull each other in the final eliminations.

The next morning, everyone is really sure that Victor is going to be murdered. Well, guess what, guys, it’s Clyde. Abbey is very disappointed to have lost her buddy, and now is more suspicious of Shane and Katie. But there’s no time for her suspicion, because Alan enters the room in an autumnal ensemble and tells them to get ready for the final mission. Before heading out, Shane tells Wyatt that it could be Victor. “I don’t know, bro,” says our eloquent Wyatt. That’s Wyatt’s one true love, Shane.

The prize pot is at $186,300, and the final mission can add $60,000 to it, getting the players very close to $250,000 if successful. The mission consists of the prize-money gold being in two underground bunkers. The players have to find the bunkers and break into them with dynamite. They’ll split into two teams: Four players will ride in buggies and two will be in a helicopter. The helicopter team has to locate the dynamite, and the ground team has to find the bunkers and identify which should be blown up.

Abbey and Katie immediately volunteer to go in the helicopter. They have one hour to get all this done. They are flown to the dynamite, find the location of the first bunker, and use walkie-talkies to tell the other team where to drive. Abbey is going to deliver the dynamite to them, so she is standing on the helicopter’s landing skids and then has to rappel down 80 feet (no thank you). To decide which bunker, the ground team has to remember whether Joe or Tomica received the most votes at the roundtables. Victor insists it’s Tomica, and he is correct.

For the second and final bunker, the explosives are already set, but the detonator is in the middle of the loch. Katie flies there, also on one of the landing skids, as the ground team races to remember the order in which players were eliminated. They have ten minutes left. Up on the helicopter, Katie is so happy. Alan is so happy. Then, when she starts to rappel down, Katie flips upside down and is just hanging there below a midair helicopter and over a large lake. This is truly a nightmare. Ninety seconds remain. Somehow, she rights herself and slides down, landing in the loch. She gets onto the platform with a minute left and detonates the dynamite. It’s so joyous! It’s so triumphant! “YOU WERE UPSIDE DOWN,” someone yells.

There we have it: the uplifting part one of The Traitors: New Blood finale. They have to raise us so we can be all the more devastated as everyone inevitably betrays each other in part two. Excelsior!

items.title: Southern Charm Recap: Allie Oops
items.description: To paraphrase one of Jacqueline Laurita’s taglines from The Real Housewives of New Jersey, “Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, you better run.” We know that Whitner has been spending lots of time in the gym, so he most likely has his running shoes on a
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: To paraphrase one of Jacqueline Laurita’s taglines from The Real Housewives of New Jersey, “Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, you better run.” We know that Whitner has been spending lots of time in the gym, so he most likely has his running shoes on already, because he’s in danger of fooling us. Why do I feel like this season is setting him up to be West Wilson 2.0? Well, the joke’s on him that he can’t pull a West Wilson because none of the guys on the cast can hold down a woman, and most of the women on the show don’t have any best friends. Instead, he’s just going to fuckboy his way through the hearts of Charleston. I hate to lose an imaginary husband, but it’s not looking great for the heir to Itchy Grass Farm.

Before we can get to all of that, we have to talk about Allie’s confrontation with Austen at the party that kicked off the season. She sits him down and says that Shep told her that Austen called off their romance because he didn’t want to commit. She does not remember it that way. She says she’s the one who ghosted Austen because she didn’t want to insert himself into the throuple of Austen, Salley, and an extraneous E that won’t go away. Austen stutters his way through saying that he never characterized their breakup like that, but even in confessional he says that Allie gave him an off-ramp and he took it because he didn’t want to commit. Sorry, but it doesn’t sound like he had as much of a choice as he’d like to let on. Also, this is all coming from Shep, who is a narrator as reliable as your roommate with the ketamine problem. (“So did you pay the rent or not, Spencer? No, I don’t want to trip balls with you. I would like to not get evicted!”)

The next confrontation is between Salley and Charley, who I didn’t even think was on this show anymore. Is she? Is she just waiting for her demotion to Southern Hospitality with her boyfriend Justin? She asks Salley why they’re not hanging out as much, and Salley says that it’s because Charley only wants to chill with Justin, and even when they do hang, he’s always there with his fine-ass face and his hot-ass body and his gorgeous scraggly facial hair and sexy tattoos just taking up all the attention. Then, right on cue, Justin walks up and says, “Salley, don’t take advantage of Charley.” First of all, he wasn’t there; how did he know that was happening? Second of all, thanks for literally proving the point. God, why is every hot man on this show an absolute nightmare? Is this all men in Charleston? Are the ugly men obnoxious, too? Oh yeah, they are. Remember Thomas? (ZING!)

Salley and Charley ask Justin to leave, and he’s telling them that they like each other and to talk it out, but they can’t while he’s there. Even though they dismiss him, he lingers like the smell of cheese in a broken refrigerator. Salley exits the conversation and tells Madison that Charley said that they always hang out without her and she feels left out. Madison walks right over to Charley and Justin and speaks to Charley and then looks at Justin and says, “Should you leave?” He tucks his head down and trots away, which is exactly why Madison is the only person on this whole cast who knows how to handle a man. Charley then tells Madison she doesn’t feel like anyone reaches out to try to be friends with her, and Madison is like, “Where are your texts? Where is your effort?” I think Charley thinks she has her place on the show solidified thanks to Justin, but I think it’s just the opposite; I think she’s blown her berth on not one but two shows and now she’s scrambling. Madison expertly clears her, and Charley goes crying in the ladies’ room, which, honestly, leave her there. I’m on Team Madison.

After a check-in with Whitney and his mother and then a check-in with Allie and her mother, we get to coffee with Craig and Whitney. Craig is upset that at the reunion Whit called him a narcissist, a word that Craig needs ChatGPT to look up for him because Craig is too busy thinking about himself to learn what a narcissist is. When they sit down, Craig says that he deserves an apology from Whit. For what? For speaking the truth? For saying a thing that was absolutely factual? This is like the sky raining down on us for 40 days and 40 nights because we dared to say it was blue. That Craig can’t even see that maybe he has narcissistic tendencies is crazy. Even ChatGPT says that narcissism is only a problem when it affects your relationships, and Craig makes a face that says, “Well, that is why Paige left me,” so even he knows it’s a problem.

Whit doesn’t apologize for saying it, but he does apologize for instigating a pile-on, but sorry, what he said did not instigate the pile-on; Craig’s narcissistic behavior did. Everyone can’t keep giving Craig a pass because he’s handsome and charming and can sew and has decent style and likes to take care of his home and seems like a nurturing carer for the bees and he’s been working on his fitness and have you seen him with his shirt off and he can’t be that bad … STOP! This is what we all keep doing.

The rest of the episode is spent in Madison’s backyard, where she invites all the girls (feat. Rodrigo) over for a little pool party mostly to show off her new GLP-1 post-baby body that is so good I want to look like that and also maybe sleep with her. I’m a lesbian now, just like Venita. Yes, there are lots of wacky revelations at the party, including that Venita and Salley make out when they’re wasted, and Salley hooked up with a girl in Canada and Venita was so upset that she cried. Wait, wait, wait, wait, wait. Salley has a Canadian girlfriend? Did the dog also eat her homework? Did her parents then take that dog to a nice home upstate? I mean, this is the biggest lie imaginable. But yes, this puts Salley and Venita’s friendship into a whole new perspective. Also, is Venita really bi or fluid or whatever, or is this just a stunt she’s pulling? I am so incredibly confused.

Salley is a little bit mad at Venita because Venita brought Allie to Madison’s party, and we all know that Salley hates Allie because Austen took her out on dates and wouldn’t go out on dates with Salley. But no. That’s not why. Salley says that Allie told Austen that the sexiest thing about him is that he hadn’t slept with Salley yet because everyone else has. How did she learn this? Did Austen tell her? How else would she know? Also, we all know that Austen lies. One of the things he lies about? That he and Salley have never had sex, because come on. You really expect us to believe that? No shade, nothing wrong with it, but these two have had more bangs than a dozen hair salons. Absolutely none of this story is real. Salley may believe it, but the Catholic Jesus does not because he is incapable of telling a lie except to Mormons, whom he has been punking for more than a century now. (Your own planet? Come on. He made that shit up.)

While Salley is talking to Venita about Austen and Allie, she’s saying that there’s no way Austen would lie to her about how their relationship ended, while Madison is on the other side of the pool talking to Allie about how Austen is totally lying about their breakup because that is what he does. If anyone has a Ph.D. in Austen’s shitbaggery, it is Madison LeCroy, so who do you think we’re going to believe?

As everyone is sitting around drinking Modelo with hot sauce in them (grody max), they all start talking about Whit and Allie and how they’re going on a date shortly. Then it comes up that Venita is also into Whit, and they’re all like, “Girl, no, he’s not. Stop it right now.” Yes, Venita. Knock it off. She has already expressed interest, and he has not followed up. This is not a man who is going to make it happen. Do not cook him a branzino; he does not want to pick tiny bones out of his teeth.

Molly and Rod, who are close with Whit, tell Allie that he may have been acting like a ho for the past year since his breakup, but that he’s quite serious about dating her. This is not what Venita wants to hear and not what Salley wants to hear. It’s not that Salley wants Whit; she just wants Allie to be miserable because she is jealous that she walked away from the man that Salley can’t seem to force to love her. (Has she tried an Etsy witch?) Salley keeps saying that Whit is a playboy and is going to break Allie’s heart.

That is when Allie tells us a story that I found a little confusing at first. She says that she and Whit made out and then he went and slept with a good friend of hers. She says that the friend knew Allie was interested in Whit and even told Allie that she should date him, and then slept with the dude. Now, I am not usually one to blame women for men’s bad behavior, but yes, this sounds like a friend that you don’t want to keep around. (Was her name Amanda, by chance?) This would make Whitner look bad, but only if he knew about Allie and Not-Amanda’s relationship before he slept with Not-Amanda. After all, this is Charleston. The pool of young, attractive, eligible people is quite small. There is going to be overlap that may be unintentional. But this girl? No way. She needs to go.

Salley hears this and gets incensed because if it’s true, that means that Whit is pretending like he’s better than Shep, Craig, Austen, and Whitney but doing all the same terrible shit that they’re always doing as well. She’s right on that account, but can Salley be right about anything? We’ve seen her be wrong about so many things: Austen, Craig, getting chickens, that terrible white dress where she can’t raise her arms, letting someone almost drown in her pool, dating Gaston, stealing the E out of her sister’s name and never giving it back. She’s not someone I trust, but as the sun sets on Madison’s poolhouse, as everyone collects their cover-ups and jangles all the empty bottles of Veuve into an already ripping Glad bag, as they call their Ubers and give their forced hugs thinking about their boys and their girls and their dates and their illusions and their loins, she may somehow be right about Whit, and that makes the sun set just a little bit faster.

items.title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: Brad Pitt Hits the Aura Jackpot in a Very Fun Tarantino Hangout Movie That Feels Like QT TV
items.description: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” gives you a highly pleasurable, shaggy heat-of-the-moment buzz. I’m not sure what I was expecting from a sequel to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” but I dug just about every ambling, low-down minute of this one. (I
items.author: Owen Gleiberman
paragraphs: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” gives you a highly pleasurable, shaggy heat-of-the-moment buzz. I’m not sure what I was expecting from a sequel to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” but I dug just about every ambling, low-down minute of this one. (I realize that low-down is an ancient phrase, but this is a movie that ends with Boz Scaggs’ “Lowdown” playing over the closing credits. That’s how 1977 it is.)

The film is Quentin Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay, going wherever the day (or night) takes him. And that will do just fine. But it’s also Tarantino honed and manicured, given a polish of precision by the film’s director, David Fincher. As an artist, the hot-blooded, motormouth Tarantino is Dionysian; the rigorously controlled, ice-in-his-veins Fincher is Apollonian. Together, the two merge in a divertingly odd way. “The Further Mis-Adventures” is an enjoyable contradiction — a meticulous hangout movie. It hops from one thing to the next, but it’s disarmingly placid and even-keeled about what it’s doing. In spirit, it’s almost as if someone had slipped the movie half a Quaalude. It’s got no worries, and neither does its hero, Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt), the most sexy-cool aging ex-stuntman you’ll ever see.

“The Further Mis-Adventures” sprawls over one week in Los Angeles in June of ’77 (the specificity has meaning; it’s supposed to be just after “Star Wars” has changed the force of the movie universe), and the tone is less sunlit intense than the 1969 of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” The counterculture has now evaporated, and everyone is stuck in a lackadaisical limbo of diversion, with one foot in the past. That doesn’t mean “The Further Mis-Adventures” is snobbish about the pop-culture era it’s rooted in. The film is brazenly and ever-so-slightly-ironically approving, whether it’s reveling in the throb of disco or the grand orchestral pomp of ELO’s “Tightrope,” smacking its lips at a tacky margarita bar that features mud-wrestling night, or opening with a last-days-of-blaxploitation movie called “Soul Brothers Die Hard!,” in which a couple of mack daddies sit around talking about the libidinous challenge of keeping their stables happy.

There’s a trick that Tarantino and Fincher spring several times here, and that’s to lure us into a piece of entertainment — a movie, a TV show — as if it were actually happening. That’s their tribute to the canny power of this stuff. Yet even as “The Further Mis-Adventures” embraces all this, you can feel a certain what’s-next? affectlessness hanging in the smoggy air. The only one who doesn’t feel it is Cliff, who lives in the eternal present. You might say that Cliff has become something of a loser. His old buddy Rick Dalton, who kept him supplied with stunt-double work, is now history (Rick has moved to Australia), and Cliff, with a slight limp and aching joints, is a man pushing 50, living with his cranky pawn-shop-owner dad (Peter Weller) in Marina del Rey, working odd jobs, driving around in his muscle-car jalopy. Yet in his slightly grizzled way he’s still a dreamboat, not to mention the most comfortable man in his own skin God ever invented.

Bringing Cliff back and expanding him into a more central presence, Brad Pitt hits the aura jackpot. With a Redford mustache and killer grin and golden sweep of honey-blond hair, parading around in gaudy short-sleeve bartender shirts with three or four buttons open, he makes Cliff high on his own supply of flinty good vibes. Cliff takes whatever comes at him, and that’s a life that suits him fine. He’s chivalrous and polite, but that’s connected to how comfortable he is with violence. He has no anxiety about it, and no anxiety about anything else. Pitt takes his own slightly seedy movie-star nobility and turns it up to full irresistible throttle. Even his voice is yummy — the sandy baritone directness of it, with that hint of a SoCal drawl. His Cliff puts everyone at ease, including the audience, but he keeps you guessing because he’s a paradox: a himbo with brains who can read anyone in the room — a sexy cowboy handyman who, if need be, will cut your throat.

The film’s opening episode is an appetizer of violence. It’s Tuesday night, and Cliff is working his shift as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema (the first of the film’s Tarantino Easter-egg in-jokes — there will be more, including a TV commercial for Red Apple cigarettes featuring Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate). The theater is showing “Soul Brothers Die Hard!,” and Cliff talks along with some of the tastier dialogue as he changes reels. But his real job comes after the theater closes. That’s when he has to rendezvous with a scurvy criminal (Karren Karagulian) accompanied by a twink hustler (Corey Fogelmanis), who is out to blackmail one of Cliff’s old director pals, who picked him up on Santa Monica Boulevard. Cliff is supposed to pay them $50,000 for stolen items. Instead, he gets rid of the crook and puts the hustler on a bus back to Ohio. The shock — and joke — of it is that Cliff kills a man as casually as if he were mixing a banana margarita on his bartending night. That’s the Zen of Cliff Booth.

Fincher has referred to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” as “‘Shampoo’ with violence” (an ace description), and that’s to say: It’s all about Cliff drifting around L.A. It isn’t necessarily trying to be a movie story. But the film is fixated on Hollywood, to the point that each new location is identified with an onscreen title that will say (for instance) “Beverly Hills, 4.3 miles west of Hollywood.” And what’s telling about “Cliff Booth” is that it treats Hollywood as the nucleus of the universe, but in its random anecdotal hangout way it’s rooted in the world of television.

Rick moved to Australia because he’s starring in a TV series there called “Dingo Dan.” Those items stolen by the hustler include a best director Oscar statuette, which suggests that that trophy is a relic of a lost age. And the plot of “The Further Mis-Adventures” centers on Cliff getting summoned for a meeting with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a garishly obnoxious star of TV Westerns and combat series. Charlie, who thinks he knows everything, does all his own stunt work (which indicates that he might be a Tarantino tweak of Tom Cruise — though the two characters, aside from being of average height, don’t have much else in common). Charlie, though, needs Cliff for something else: to get him out of an underworld jam. This is, after all, the stuntman who beat up Bruce Lee.

So Cliff meets with Charlie’s agent, the imperially tall and coldly sexy Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki). These two get a flirtation going — one so frosty that in spirit it feels more 2026 than 1977. You can see that there’s a mutual attraction. And you really see it after Cliff confesses his feelings, and their gamesmanship turns weirdly kinky. (The weird part is that the kink stays so casual.) But she’s classy and standoffish, and the most revealing conversation the two have is about the movies.

It’s one of those freewheeling Tarantino digressions (built on what sounds like a scrap from his abandoned script for “The Critic”), in which Karen tells Cliff that she was briefly a film critic who had gotten to know Pauline Kael (who Cliff dismisses because she didn’t like “Butch Cassidy”). Karen, sounding like a corrupt studio executive, says she now thinks of movies strictly as entertainment, and never as art. Cliff asks: Even “The Godfather”? Yes, she says, that’s just a gangster movie with artistic airs. It’s strange that the film never counters this view; it’s almost as if Tarantino agrees with it. Has he gone that far into pulp fetishization? (The author of “Cinema Speculation” is actually a great critic.) Or maybe he’s saying: Now that “Star Wars” has arrived, the movies as we knew them are dead.

I’m going on about this because I think it helps explain the enjoyably random, slightly disjunctive air of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” It’s the first Tarantino film that feels, in its structural DNA, like a glorified television series. At one point, the movie was supposed to be a series, and in spirit that’s kind of what it still is. Call it QT TV. The incidents hook you, but with less consequence than they’d have in a full-blown, let-it-rip Tarantino movie. “The Further Mis-Adventures” looks like a movie (Fincher gives it a stately sheen), and it’s way too violent for television. But the hangout factor, in this case, feels one small step removed from the characters-on-a-TV-series-are-your-family factor.

Driving the action forward are a pair of Filipino hitmen, the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), who are singular in their viciousness; one employs a scary hatchet hammer he calls Esmarelda. Scott Caan does a blustery job of playing Charlie, the blowhard TV star (I enjoyed the scene where he uses a live round of ammunition to put the fear into Timothy Olyphant as a fellow actor playing a Nazi), but given how central the character is, I wish he were less of a putz. I also wish we didn’t have to watch Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II), Charlie’s football-player-turned-actor costar, get not simply beat up but maimed for no good reason. On the other hand, I appreciated the quick reference to Cliff doing porn films, which becomes a punchline to the fact that everyone he meets feels like they’ve seen him before. Speaking of porn, there’s a shoutout/tweak to PTA when “Best of My Love,” the Emotions track that opens “Boogie Nights,” comes on the car radio and Cliff flips the channel.

How is the ultraviolent climax? It’s kind of spectacular. Tarantino doesn’t use it to rewrite history this time, but in a funny way he does a mini version of that. What happens to Cliff in the big fight is so extreme it should have eliminated him from the earth. But it doesn’t. It’s just a scratch. He doesn’t give a fuck, and he’s still there. To put it in QT TV terms: When’s the next episode?

items.title: ‘Gilded Age’ Scores Early Season 5 Renewal at HBO
items.description: “The Gilded Age” has been renewed for Season 5 at HBO, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: “The Gilded Age” has been renewed for Season 5 at HBO, Variety has learned.

The news comes after the period drama has aired just three of its eight episodes for Season 4. This marks the earliest renewal announcement for the show to date, which has continued to grow its audience season to season. Per HBO, Season 4 is averaging 5.9 million U.S. multiplatform viewers per episode to date, with episode three hitting 4.3 million viewers in three days time. The episodic average is up nearly 20% over Season 3, though there are still five more episodes to air.

“Julian Fellowes and the cast of ‘The Gilded Age’ have once again captured the zeitgeist this fall, delivering another captivating, unmissable season, and we love how our growing audience has continued to embrace the series year after year,” said Francesca Orsi, president of HBO Drama Series and Films. “We can’t wait to return to 61st Street, as the Russells, van Rhijns and Kirklands continue to wrestle with the cost of ascent, while we expand the canvas and deepen the operatic stakes for these beloved characters.”

The show’s expansive ensemble cast includes: Carrie Coon, Christine Baranski, Cynthia Nixon, Morgan Spector, Louisa Jacobson, Denée Benton, Taissa Farmiga, Harry Richardson, Blake Ritson, Ben Ahlers, Ashlie Atkinson, Dylan Baker, Kelley Curran, Jordan Donica, Jessica Frances Dukes, Amy Forsyth, Jack Gilpin, Simon Jones, Celia Keenan-Bolger, Ben Lamb, Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Debra Monk, Hattie Morahan, Donna Murphy, Kristine Nielsen, Kelli O’Hara, Taylor Richardson, Douglas Sills, Erin Wilhelmi, John Douglas Thompson, Taylor Trensch, James Scully, Dennis Haysbert, Maggie Kuntz, Neal Huff, Bonnie Milligan, Jim Gaffigan, Dallas Roberts, Andrew Burnap, Elizabeth Marvel, Adrienne Warren, with Bill Camp and Phylicia Rashad.

“It’s very exciting and deeply satisfying to see audiences fall more in love with ‘The Gilded Age’ every season,” said Erin Underhill, president of series producer Universal Television. “Our remarkable cast, writers – led by Julian Fellowes, and the entire creative team continue to make this world feel both timeless and resonant while keeping us on the edge of our seats season after season. We can’t wait for audiences to see what’s in store for Season 5.”

The official description of Season 4 states, “Bertha Russell (Coon) changed Society at a cost. Now, her family must reckon with the consequences as Agnes van Rhijn (Baranski) seizes an opportunity to regain her position. Meanwhile, Marian (Jacobson) forges a new path for herself, and Peggy (Benton) works to be accepted by her future in-laws. In this new era, you must be careful what you wish for.”

Julian Fellowes is the creator, writer, and executive producer of “The Gilded Age,” with Sonja Warfield also writing and executive producing. Salli Richardson-Whitfield serves as director and executive producer. Additional executive producers are Gareth Neame, David Crockett, Robert Greenblatt, Kate Churchill, Davita Scarlett, and Elaine Aronson. Erica Armstrong Dunbar and Holly Rymon are co-executive producers. The series is co-produced by HBO and Universal Television.

items.title: Brooks Nader Joins ‘Playmates’ Movie at Searchlight (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Brooks Nader is the latest addition to the cast of the upcoming Searchlight movie “Playmates,” Variety has learned exclusively.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Brooks Nader is the latest addition to the cast of the upcoming Searchlight movie “Playmates,” Variety has learned exclusively.

The film is inspired by writer and director Lorraine Nicholson’s childhood experiences at the Playboy Mansion. Nader will appear alongside previously announced cast members Lily-Rose Depp, Bill Pullman, Jessica Biel, Indiana Elle, and Anna Van Patten.

The official logline for “Playmates” states, “Elle (Elle), a thirteen-year-old know-it-all who considers the Playboy Mansion her second home, meets Anna (Depp), one of seven hopefuls vying to be Playmate of the Month. The two form an unlikely friendship and try to help each other get what the other wants most, a magazine cover and a boy.”
Pullman will star as Playboy founder Hugh Hefner, with Biel playing Hefner’s wife. Exact details on Nader’s character are being kept under wraps.

Nader will next be seen in Fox’s reboot of “Baywatch,” which will debut on the broadcast network on Jan. 6. She originally found success as a model, including appearing in the iconic Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue. She also currently stars in the Freeform reality series “Love Thy Nader,” which is prepping a second season, and also appeared in the 33rd season of “Dancing with the Stars.”
She is repped by WME, Dixon Talent, Inc. and by Leigh Fidler, Chief Brand Officer of Nader Sisters Inc.

Searchlight Pictures is the studio behind “Playmates.” As mentioned above, Nicholson will write and direct. Alex Orlovsky and Duncan Montgomery will produce via High Frequency Entertainment, with Depp producing in addition to starring. Searchlight vice president of production Richard Ruiz and creative executive Cornelia Burleigh will oversee the project for the studio. Ruiz and Burleigh report into the Heads of Production and Development, DanTram Nguyen and Katie Goodson-Thomas.

items.title: New ‘Serendipity’ Movie Casts Auli‘i Cravalho (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Auli‘i Cravalho is the latest addition to the new “Serendipity” movie in the works at Amazon MGM Studios and Miramax, Variety has learned exclusively.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Auli‘i Cravalho is the latest addition to the new “Serendipity” movie in the works at Amazon MGM Studios and Miramax, Variety has learned exclusively.

The project is described not as a reboot of the 2001 romantic comedy but rather an update in a modern setting featuring new characters. Cravalho joins previously announced cast members Milo Manheim, Whitney Peak, and Stephen Kalyn. Exact character and plot details are being kept under wraps.

Cravalho is best known for her starring role in the hit Disney animated film “Moana” and its sequel, while she was also an executive producer on the live-action version released in 2026. She has also starred in films like “Zootopia 2,” 2024’s “Mean Girls,” and “Crush.” In TV, she is known for roles in shows like “Rise,” “The Power,” and for voicing Jessica Cruz, a.k.a Green Lantern, in multiple DC animated projects. It was recently reported that she will appear in the series adaptation of “Icebreaker” for Netflix. She was named to Variety’s Power of Young Hollywood Impact Report in 2025.
Cravalho is repped by Gersh, Artists First, and Goodman Genow.

Michael Showalter is attached to direct “Serendipity.” Marc Klein, who wrote the original film, will pen the screenplay and executive produce. Showalter is also a producer alongside Jordana Mollick for Semi-Formal Productions. Simon Fields, who produced the original, is also a producer. Jonathan Glickman, Alexandra Loewy, and Thom Zadra will executive produce for Miramax. Arianna D’Andrea is overseeing the project for Miramax, while Emily Crook is overseeing for Semi-Formal.

The original “Serendipity” starred John Cusack and Kate Beckinsale. In the film, their characters meet one night in New York and decide to leave the chance of meeting again up to fate. They ultimately go searching for each other years later despite being in relationships with other people. The film was a box office success, grossing over $77 million on a reported budget of $28 million.

items.title: Judge Allows Trump to Sue New York Times Reporters Over Tax Fraud Claims
items.description: A judge has allowed President Trump to proceed with a $15 billion suit against the New York Times, finding a plausible claim that its reporters acted recklessly in accusing Trump of tax fraud.
items.author: Gene Maddaus
paragraphs: A judge has allowed President Trump to proceed with a $15 billion suit against the New York Times, finding a plausible claim that its reporters acted recklessly in accusing Trump of tax fraud.

Judge Steven Merryday denied the defendants’ motion to dismiss the lawsuit, holding that the book “Lucky Loser” includes a series of claims about Trump’s business dealings that are potentially defamatory.

Though the book cites tax experts who stated that Trump’s conduct was “highly suspicious” and “smells like a crime,” the judge ruled that was not enough to state outright that Trump had committed tax fraud or tax evasion. Such a clear-cut judgment would require “an explicit opinion from a qualified source after a thorough examination of pertinent facts,” the judge ruled.
Absent such a statement, the judge ruled that the reporters were venturing into risky territory.
“They know that they don’t know, but they are undeterred,” he wrote.

The book, published by Penguin Random House, included the allegation that Trump had obtained the equivalent of $400 million from his father, Fred, “much of it through fraudulent tax evasion schemes.” The book also asserted that Fred Trump had engaged in “likely tax fraud” when he gave his son gifts disguised as loans; and that the arrangement was designed to avoid gift and estate taxes.
In his lawsuit, Trump argued that the statements were false because neither he nor his father had ever been charged with a tax crime.

The New York Times published two articles drawn from the book in 2024. In the ruling, Merryday dismissed the claims pertaining to the first article, which focused on Trump’s relationship with TV producer Mark Burnett and the development of “The Apprentice.”

The judge also tossed statements from the second article that focused on Trump’s school record. But the judge allowed Trump to sue over a statement from that article that authorities had investigated his “ties to the Mafia” and had found “violations of money laundering laws.”
In response, a New York Times spokesperson said the paper was “encouraged” that almost all of the claims against the paper were dismissed.

“We continue to believe the remaining claim in the filing has no legal merit,” the spokesperson said. “We look forward to making this argument as we continue to defend ourselves against this baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country.”
The same judge dismissed an earlier version of Trump’s lawsuit last year, finding it overlong and full of colorful but irrelevant detail. Trump’s lawyers refiled a more concise version a month later.
The suit can now proceed to discovery and motions for summary judgment. The defendants in the case are the Times, three of its reporters, and Penguin Random House.

items.title: How High Can ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Reach in Its Box Office Opening?
items.description: The odds look to be in favor of the Hunger Games franchise, as it is likely to gobble up a box office debut on the level of its impressive hits from more than a decade ago.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: The odds look to be in favor of the Hunger Games franchise, as it is likely to gobble up a box office debut on the level of its impressive hits from more than a decade ago.

Lionsgate releases The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping in 3,900 North American theaters on Friday, with the studio projecting it to gross north of $80 million domestically. However, sources expect that the film will actually open much higher, likely surpassing $100 million and potentially reaching upwards of $130 million. Adapting author Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel that was published last year, director Francis Lawrence‘s movie carries a production budget of roughly $150 million as it brings new life to the franchise that launched with the initial Jennifer Lawrence-led The Hunger Games in 2012.

In the new film, Joseph Zada plays Haymitch Abernathy, whom Woody Harrelson portrayed in the character’s later years for the first four movies. The expansive cast of Sunrise on the Reaping includes Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, Kieran Culkin, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Billy Porter, Ben Wang, Maya Hawke and Iris Apatow.

Sunrise on the Reaping takes place in Panem on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Hunger Games, 24 years before the events in The Hunger Games, the initial novel that published in 2008. The franchise’s first five movies have surpassed $3.3 billion at the worldwide box office, with the initial four films led by Lawrence as Katniss, Josh Hutcherson as Peeta and Liam Hemsworth as Gale.

With its box office opening, the latest movie is expected to mark a significant uptick over that of 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. That prequel film featured Tom Blyth as the young Coriolanus Snow — the villainous character played by Fiennes in Sunrise on the Reaping — alongside Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer. The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes opened to a disappointing $44 million domestically before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million.

Sunrise on the Reaping should open with a haul much closer to the debuts for the first four movies that starred Lawrence. After 2012’s initial The Hunger Games opened to $152.5 million domestically and was followed by 2013’s The Hunger Games: Catching Fire with an even stronger $158 million, the next two films started a bit softer. In 2014, The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 launched with $121.8 million domestically, while the second film’s debut fell to $102.6 million in North America.

The critical response for Sunrise on the Reaping has delivered a 67 Rotten Tomatoes score from critics, which puts it behind the ratings for the franchise’s first four movies but just above the 64 percent approval for Songbirds & Snakes. In his THR review, chief film critic David Rooney wrote that the new film “delivers on emotion and brutal spectacle.”

Another entertainment option this weekend comes with Thursday’s highly anticipated release of the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, arriving 13 years after the launch for the beloved Rockstar Games franchise’s previous installment. GTA 6 has already surpassed $1.84 billion in sales, meaning that it has made more money that Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, which hit theaters over the summer and became Universal’s highest-grossing title ever globally.
As for whether the game could impact box office numbers, it’s likely that both Hunger Games and GTA will manage to thrive.

“I can certainly see GTA 6 keeping some people on the couch Friday night, and I’d imagine there is some crossover between folks who can’t wait to play the game and those who can’t wait to see the movie,” Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian tells THR. “But Friday night is just one night, and there’s a whole weekend of potential moviegoing. I think people who are excited about both will find the bandwidth for the game and the movie, so I don’t see GTA 6 taking much of a bite out of the Hunger Games opening.”

Among the other films looking to draw moviegoers this weekend is Amazon MGM Studios’ I Play Rocky, as director Peter Farrelly’s origin story about 1976’s Oscar-winning boxing drama Rocky goes wide after two weekends in limited release. Anthony Ippolito stars as a young Sylvester Stallone in the project that Rooney describes as a “big-hearted movie about moviemaking, if not an artful one.”

items.title: Rose Byrne on What Lured Her to ‘The Good Daughter’ and Why That Complicated Ending Wraps the Series
items.description: [This story contains major spoilers from The Good Daughter finale.]
items.author: Ronda Racha Penrice
paragraphs: [This story contains major spoilers from The Good Daughter finale.]

Rose Byrne keeps outdoing herself. Her explosive limited series The Good Daughter co-starring Meghann Fahy quickly became the top show on Peacock. Just last year, she grabbed a best actress Oscar nomination and won both the Golden Globe and Independent Spirits Award for If I Had Legs I’d Kick You — the film nobody saw coming. She also wrapped season two of her Apple TV comedy Platonic.

Even for an actress with a pedigree like Byrne’s spanning over 30 years, projects like The Good Daughter are rare opportunities, she shared last year while still filming in the Atlanta Metro area. “Sam is the sort of role written for a man,” the Australian actress confessed. “It’s very dominant, kind of self-possessed, and she has physical trauma. Like she has scars, and she has a history. She has all this rich stuff that’s not always the case with the female roles you read.”

It’s the kind of story that Byrne, who also serves as executive producer alongside fellow Aussie, Big Little Lies Emmy winner Bruna Papandrea, sees as bestselling author and fellow EP Karin Slaughter’s superpower. “She writes incredibly rich female characters who are complicated and complex, and not all good and not all bad, and who have a lot to work with,” Byrne continued.

For the first time ever, Slaughter, who has had other books grace the screen with Pieces of Her for Netflix and, of course, Will Trent for ABC, adapted her own work and served as showrunner. The psychological thriller revolves around estranged sisters Samantha and Charlotte Quinn who, as teens, suffer a brutal attack in response to their father Rusty’s (an excellent Brendan Gleeson) work as an attorney that has left them scarred. Partial blindness and a permanent limp serve as enduring physical reminders for Sam. Spared many of the physical scars, Charlie’s show up in other ways. And they both lost their beloved mother Gamma (an effective Olivia Williams).

As the older sister, Sam sacrificed herself to ensure Charlie would be hurt the least, but that act created emotional and physical distance between the two. Rusty’s failing health has brought Sam back home from New York City, where she is a patent lawyer, to Pikeville, Georgia. It’s his defense of Kelly Wilson (impressive newcomer Shayna Benardo), a special needs high school girl seemingly behind a horrific school shooting that killed the school’s principal and a freshman girl that keeps her there.

What seems like an open-and-shut case is anything but. Because Charlie witnessed part of the shooting and is also an attorney, the two women can’t avoid each other. Any degree of separation disappears in a small town, especially for a polarizing case like this one, so emotional landmines abound. As the mystery surrounding Kelly’s actions lingers, the attack that the sisters survived years before also figures more prominently, forcing both Sam and Charlie to tackle all they have left unsaid and unresolved.

“One of the pleasures of this is that I wrote everything from the perspective of two women. So much to probably Meghann and Rose’s dismay, one of them always has to be in every single scene, because we get their perspective, and it’s a very internalized kind of storytelling,” Slaughter said on set. “But also, in a way, it shows their growth as sisters and as daughters, and gives me an opportunity to frame something that happens every day in America, basically through these very personal stories of these sisters who have been victims of violence before.”

On set when speaking to The Hollywood Reporter, Byrne noted “it’s rare you get to work side by side with a fellow actress.” That female energy is also directly sustained behind the camera with Oscar and Emmy-nominated director Steph Green (New Boy, Duster, Watchmen) and Australian cinematographer Zoë White (The Handmaid’s Tale). Below, she probes beyond the many plot twists to delve into aspects of the series that move her professionally and emotionally. Of course, we asked if there would be more and if she felt what happens to Kelly, the young girl at the center of the mystery, is fair.
In addition to playing Sam, you’re also an executive producer. What made you want to take on roles in front and behind the camera?

Being an EP was really like more of a seat at the table, particularly with casting. Getting Meghann Fahy on board was a huge deal for us. She’s so effervescent as Charlie; so magnetic and funny and heartbreaking. You just believe her straight away. She jumps. She lights up the screen, and she’s just gorgeous. I adore her. She’s so extraordinary, so talented.

And then Brendan Gleeson, who’s a legend at this point — so extraordinary and such a gifted storyteller — and so magnanimous with his work. I’ve known him since I was 23 when I did Troy. So that was a great thread. I worked with his son Domhnall Gleeson, so it was a lovely full circle to then have him playing my father. And that’s a tough character; it’s very polarizing. There’s a lot of fury that my character has at her father, a lot of anger and disappointment, and Brendan makes that hard because he’s so charming, but that’s what makes it interesting.

Reading the screenplay and the novel… it’s a classic origin story for Sam, where going back to where she came from, she’s dealing with all of her truths and all of the lies, and trying to uncover the past through this case; understanding her father more, but it felt to me almost a role written for a man, not particularly something you would see necessarily for a female character. That really intrigued me.
How did you pull off Sam’s physical transformation to convey her disability or disabilities?

Well, she has dysarthria, [her] speech disability from her trauma, and so I worked with my voice coach Kate Wilson, who’s extraordinary. She’s the head of voice [and speech] at Juilliard. I’ve worked with her for years and she’s incredible. She’s the most alive, passionate, compassionate teacher, and she’s really very sage. She and I delved in with what that would sound like, listening to tapes and recordings, and also working on the accent of Georgia and how my character had lived in New York for 20 years, and what it would sound like returning, and when it would return, and in what situations. When I return to Australia, my accent becomes a lot broader, and you know how you’re influenced by your environment.

Then with the limp, I worked with this wonderful PT trainer who works in rehab with people who’ve suffered injuries and so on. We homed in on what her limp would look like, and then did a million videos and would send them to Steph and figure out how far to go with it because we didn’t want it ever to be comical. Sometimes what reads on screen is very different in real life.
The younger Charlie [Drew Ann Cheek] and Sam [Audrey Grace Marshall] really match the older Charlie and Sam.

I was very front seat with the casting of that, so there was a lot of weighing in with everybody about who we felt the best lead was and, also, physically you have to have a lot of resemblance to them. I thought the girls were so wonderful, and that’s again a very hard job to do. I thought they just captured both Meghann and myself in really specific ways, and we watched a lot of footage of them as well. With Sam, obviously there’s a real before and after physically with what she goes through, so that was something I had to separately have work on. But establishing them as young women was so important.

While Sam and Charlie, in particular, experience extraordinary circumstances, the series seems to center on this whole idea of women holding onto very traumatic events or violations but still functioning in their lives.

Which we do every day. If you read the statistics about it, like one in six women have been sexually assaulted. A lot of people in America have suffered gun violence in their families. These statistics are horrific, and we worked very closely with RAINN who work with survivors of rape and incest and other horrific things, and they were incredible. We always had resources on set if people were being triggered or needed to talk. It was a safe space.

To Steph Green, our director, my first question was: “How will this be portrayed? I’m not interested in anything gratuitous or exploitative.” And Steph was so determined to tell the story in a way that had none of those tonal qualities in it. So absolutely the story has elements of trauma, but it’s dealt with in a very delicate way that I think is powerful but never gratuitous or exploitative.
Speaking of Steph, the way she, and Zoë White the cinematographer, handle the traumatic flashbacks is such an innovative technique that I don’t think I’ve seen.

I agree. I remember her telling me about that, how she was going to focus on hands and this and moments and shoot close-ups of various things to sort of link the story. And it’s beautifully told. The sense of memory was really vivid, I felt, [in] a lot of those flashbacks to me. I feel like they achieved something quite innovative.
When Rusty dies, everything is understandably sad. But the coffin scene at the funeral home manages to be both light and heavy. Did it come at a time when you guys kind of needed a break?

Meghann was so heartbreaking in that scene, and she’s so funny, too. That was actually great because what was harder was the flashback scene when we’re in New York, and it precipitates the estrangement. That scene was a lot harder because we’re through a closed door, sort of screaming a monologue and it’s a flashback, and I’ve got a wig on. That to me was more of a leap of faith. I think that was a harder needle to thread. Whereas the coffin scene, as you called it, was so gratifying to be able to look at her and really have a scene like two actors opposite one another and have such rich material. It was definitely strange for Brendan because he was in the coffin for a little bit. That’s no fun. But that was a scene I was both scared and excited to do.
There are so many powerful scenes, what are some of your favorite moments, or what stands out most to you?

The scene that haunts me so much is when Charlie confronts Judith over the kitchen table. I remember reading it in the novel, and I remember the first one I read in the screenplay, and my hair on my body was just standing on end. It was so suspenseful, so tightly drawn, and the history alone between these two women across each other from this table to then reach this boiling point of this scene was just masterful storytelling.

And it’s interesting because Sam and Charlie don’t have that traumatic relationship with them that Kelly has. Then considering that she’s special needs. So it’s unfathomable that the Pinkmans could do something like this to Kelly, right?

Yeah Karin, she’s a master storyteller, and just when you think you know where something is going. I found myself reading the novel and reading the screenplay [drawn to] the turns of what these people do and the perspectives that she puts on each situation. But that scene still haunts me.
Do you think Kelly’s punishment is fair?

I think it’s a very, very complicated answer and question. It’s such a nuanced and complicated story that has led her to this horrific situation that we made her in at the beginning. I really was fascinated with the process of that. I spoke to many lawyers who work in the criminal justice system about the process and how it works, and where you end up, and how you interrogate a witness, and like the defense team, and all of that. And Karin so beautifully captures how hard that system is and how it fails again and again and again for people, but how also you can have some wins. But it’s very nuanced and it’s very complicated.

It was a learning curve for me to even begin to understand that. So I think [Karin] has such a great understanding of that, and also the genre of a thriller, you know, and creating the suspense of that. Right until the very last episode, you’re really on the edge of your seat, as she just twists and turns and uses the perspective of one character then the other, and you constantly have shifting alliances, and she’s just very unflinching in her portrait of things. And that’s brave.
That’s why I ask if what happens to Kelly is fair because it’s very clear in the end how manipulated she was. And given her mental capacity, she wasn’t really aware of what she was doing.
Absolutely. None of it is fair.
Do you see a continuation to The Good Daughter?

I don’t. It feels contained to this series, like the novel, to me. I have hope for the characters that they would, I mean, selfishly, continue to have a better relationship with one another after all the trauma and all the things they’ve weathered or the storms they’ve weathered. But it felt, to me, pretty contained about this specific thing they had to go through.
I’m sure you take lessons from each project that you do. What is your biggest takeaway from this one?

I think diving back into this genre was really interesting for me [because] I hadn’t done it for many years. [There are] tropes that are really fun in there, and the challenges of a very complicated plot at times, and being ahead of it for myself. But Karin, the author, is really ahead of everybody. So, it was interesting. Also to work with an author who then wrote the screenplay, that was also something I’d never done creatively, and how fun that was. Also, we would have rigorous conversations where we would disagree about things, and that was fun too. I think I learned a lot.
All six episodes of The Good Daughter are streaming on Peacock.

items.title: Billy Evans Will Secure His Cut of ‘You Can See Everything’ Profits After All — and Give It to Charity (Exclusive)
items.description: It looks like Billy Evans will get paid for the success of You Can See Everything after all. He just won’t keep the money.
items.author: Steven Zeitchik
paragraphs: It looks like Billy Evans will get paid for the success of You Can See Everything after all. He just won’t keep the money.

Evans and his representatives have negotiated for the backend share he gave up to be paid out, according to two sources not affiliated with him or his partner Elizabeth Holmes. The money will go to an unnamed children’s charity instead of to Evans, the sources said.

While the exact percentage is unknown, the total payout will be a lot bigger now than it would have been even a few weeks ago. The film has grossed $89 million domestically to date, a jaw-dropping sum for a documentary.

Subject payment is a key plot point in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s hit about the convicted Theranos founder and her life partner Evans. The film shows Evans back in 2023 seeking money from A24 without Holmes’ knowledge, casting him in a greedy light; the filmmakers reluctantly then agree to pay him in order to secure access and make a deal. But a title card at the end says that “Billy Evans ultimately relinquished his negotiated share of the film’s profits and would not receive backend compensation.”

It is unclear if Evans at the time of that relinquishing secured a payout to charity with the title card omitting that point, or if Evans had fully given up on the possibility at the time and had a change of heart after the film was released and started raking in cash. Supporting the latter timing, Page Six reported on Oct. 23, a week after the movie opened, that Evans had contacted lawyers to try to restore his deal, with no word in that story that he had even succeeded in retaining counsel let alone striking a deal.
A representative for Evans did not provide comment.
A spokesperson for A24 did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Documentary subjects these days often ask to be paid, and distributors sometimes agree, usually without giving up control of a film’s final cut. That is what happened here until Evans decided to relinquish what he’d negotiated.
Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter this week, Evans said he made that decision “maybe five months ago” because the filmmakers “said it would help the project”
“I am totally stubborn, but if there’s anything that I can do to help Liz regardless of the cost, I will do it,” he said.

(He explained his earlier push for money this way: “I’m a single dad with two kids whose best friend’s about to be sent to prison. And at that time I didn’t have a job. I’m trying to provide for my family and I’m really scared about what’s to come.” Evans is a member of the family that owns Evans Hotels, which operates three high-end Southern California properties including The Lodge at Torrey Pines, the Bahia Resort Hotel and the Catamaran Resort Hotel.)
The new deal means A24 will be cutting a profit-participation check for Evans’ role, just not to the entrepreneur himself.

The move could still possibly help Evans’ image. The entrepreneur has become a pop-culture villain thanks to moments like a domineering scene in which he shows Holmes how to whisk eggs, along with diatribes at filmmakers over questions he doesn’t like.

Amanda Seyfried, who plays Holmes in the film’s reconstructions, challenges Evans on camera and tells Fielder she wants to break up the couple. Fan boards, meanwhile, routinely debate his level of villainy.

items.title: How to Grow a Beard
items.description: So you want to learn how to grow a beard. First off, you should know that it helps to have the right genetics. Second, you have to stay committed to the endeavor. Too often, beard-growing attempts end before they’ve even had a chance to establish itself.
items.author: Adam Hurly; Tyler Chin
paragraphs: So you want to learn how to grow a beard. First off, you should know that it helps to have the right genetics. Second, you have to stay committed to the endeavor. Too often, beard-growing attempts end before they’ve even had a chance to establish itself.

“I’d say give it at least three to four weeks of solid growth before you even think about touching it with clippers,” Victor Mendoza, co-founder of beard care brand Viking Revolution, says. “Your beard needs time to actually show you what it’s going to look like, and that growth period lets you see the natural direction everything’s growing in. Plus, some hairs take longer to come in than others, so patience is key.”

There’s a sweet spot between letting your facial hair grow out and knowing when it’s time to take the trimmers for the best results possible, even if you can’t go full lumberjack. These are the best tips to maximize your hair follicles’ potential whether this is your first beard or your fiftieth.
There are many different beard styles to choose from; you don’t need to stick to neatly manicured, uniform look. Let your growth be influenced by the style you want to achieve.
“Your genes determine hair thickness, growth rate, density, and color,” Mendoza says. “If your dad or granddad had a thin beard, you’re probably dealing with the same hand, and that’s just life.”

If your beard is patchy, or if it has a unique growth pattern (sparse on the cheeks, full on the goatee, for example), then you should set your expectations properly. This goes for beards big, small, and medium alike. And while nutrition is important for hair growth, you can’t cheat genetics with your diet.

Patience is a virtue. Not only can a little time help fill in some patchiness, but it’s also requisite for almost any style. A beard transforms into something new every week. So, if it’s seeming like you’ll never reach your goal—in particular if it’s a long beard—then you honestly might wake up one morning and realize that you’ve arrived at the destination.

Mendoza says to wait at least two weeks before you start to do a cleanup, but only around the ends, i.e. the hairs that aren’t within the perimeter in which you want your beard to grow. That’ll help you figure out your beard’s natural shape.

One of the tenets of beard maintenance is to keep it defined. In short: shave the neckline and clean up the cheek lines. These keep it more beard-like and less neckbeard-like—unless, for some reason, a wooly stoner beard is your aim. In that case, let it grow wild and free.

The second way to keep things looking intentional is to sculpt and trim your beard as it grows. It might feel counterproductive—and counter to #2—but it’s the same way you need to get haircuts while growing out your hair. As Mendoza says, this helps direct the hair exactly where it needs to be: Fuller in some spots, less so in others. The styling products in the next tip can of course help influence things, but you foremost want to keep hairs in check as needed: This can mean spot-checking strays, snipping away split ends, or simply taking out some bulk. You’ll want a beard trimmer or a sharp pair of scissors.

There are a handful of beard products you should consider picking up if you’re serious about proper care and maintenance. A few drops of beard oil will absorb quickly and give your hair the right nutrients (plus a pinch of shine), while also making it less wild and frizzy. You can also swap in a beard balm or cream, something slightly heftier than an oil, to help style the beard and keep it in place all day. What’s important is that you clean your beard every day with an actual beard wash and not just a regular shampoo, which Mendoza says will dry out your beard and your face.

Weekly maintenance will consist of a deep condition, which you can do in the shower. “If you’re doing those things consistently, your beard is going to look way healthier and fuller than most guys out there,” he says.

Beard brushes help exfoliate the skin beneath the beard, for starters, which lifts dead skin cells and prevents future flaking. Moreover, brushing your beard at the end of each day will ensure its health and tame-ability in the long haul. This distributes the natural oils produced in the skin, which otherwise collect at the base of the shaft and only nourish the bottom of each hair. This oil distribution prevents breakage, frizzing, and split ends. (This is a great time to apply a few drops of beard oil as a booster, especially after a shower.)

Once your base has grown out—this can take months—it’s time to really make it yours. One of our favorites is to snip the bridge between the mustache and the chin, thus marooning the mustache. Or, pare back the beard itself, leaving a fuller mustache. You have lots of options, and it’s your privilege as a beard grower to flaunt it.

items.title: John Mulaney Wore Joe DiMaggio’s Watch to Host 'Saturday Night Live'
items.description: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.
items.author: Cam Wolf
paragraphs: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

Between sniffing out paternal autism and perfecting his Robert F. Kennedy impression, you may have noticed that John Mulaney was wearing an extraordinary watch while hosting Saturday Night Live this weekend. It’s a beauty—a gold vintage Patek Philippe with swoopy Breguet numerals—but its backstory is even more impressive. On December 12, 1948, New York Yankees legend Joe DiMaggio purchased this timepiece and owned it until his death in 1999.

The Patek Philippe, a ref. 130 circa 1947, is already a rare bird before you add in its Joltin’ Joe provenance. The model is one of just 180 made in yellow gold with Breguet numerals, and only 55 with this same combination have ever reached the secondary market. In late October, dealer Eric Wind of Wind Vintage put this specific watch up for sale with a $1.2 million asking price. “I think it’s the greatest Patek that’s known and tied to any athlete,” Wind told Robb Report last month.

For his seventh time hosting SNL, Mulaney came to Wind in search of “an important watch,” the dealer explains now. After surveying Wind’s entire catalog, the comedian landed on this piece, whose ties to a legendary New Yorker felt right for helming one of the city’s most hallowed institutions. To be clear, Mulaney only borrowed the watch for the show, which means its legend will have only grown by the time it reaches an eventual buyer. Talk about an illustrious provenance: A DiMaggio-owned Patek that also appeared on Saturday Night Live. “It was a very special moment and another cool moment of history for this important Patek Philippe,” Wind says.

As a known history buff and devoted baseball fan, the watch likely appealed to Mulaney on several levels. But its eggshell-hued dial also happened to go perfectly with the brown suit Mulaney sported during his opening monologue. “John has classic styling,” Wind says, “and the Joe DiMaggio Patek Philippe was the chef’s kiss on his wrist.”

Over the past several years, Mulaney has emerged as one of Hollywood’s most prolific and tasteful watch collectors. He is an eager and omnivorous admirer, bouncing between his beloved Rolex Air-King, loud Chopard chronographs, and glamorous Grand Seikos.

During our watch-focused interview last May, Mulaney told me that he steers away from more obvious models like your garden-variety Rolex Submariner. “I don’t ask any questions about it, I know what it is,” he explained. “And I’m just more interested in watches that [are a little more] mysterious.” As an example, Mulaney specifically referenced a Patek Philippe Calatrava his wife Olivia Munn bought him.

The DiMaggio Patek is full of intrigue. The watch obviously has important provenance, but it’s historic on its own accord, too. The ref. 130 is named for the movement inside, known as the Calibre 130. That engine was the basis for Patek’s 1518, the first serially produced watch to combine a perpetual calendar and chronograph.

Funnily enough, this isn’t the first Mulaney, DiMaggio, and SNL crossover. In his 2018 special Kid Gorgeous at Radio City, the comedian explained what it was like working with famous SNL hosts during his time as a staff writer. “It’d be like if you went into your childhood bedroom and Joe DiMaggio was sitting there,” Mulaney quipped. “Yeah, he’s Joe DiMaggio, he’s a legend, he had sex with Marilyn Monroe, but only you know where the bathroom is.” And only Mulaney has had DiMaggio’s watch on his wrist, for now.

items.title: 40 More Million-Dollar Watches Just Sold at Auction
items.description: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.
items.author: Cam Wolf
paragraphs: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

Back in June, I reported on the bonanza of watches crossing the million-dollar-plus mark at auction. What once felt like a unicorn price for watchmakers, auction houses, and the industry as a whole no longer feels so magical. “I joke with people that $1 million is like the new $250,000 of five years ago,” Paul Boutros of Phillips auction house said over the summer.

In just the first half of 2026, the number of million-dollar watches sold nearly eclipsed the total from all of 2025. Now, after a raft of high-profile auctions in Geneva a couple of weeks ago, the industry has set yet another record. In just the last month alone (including Monaco Legend Group, which kicked things off in late October), 40 million-dollar watches hammered, according to numbers provided by EveryWatch. That’s more sold than in any entire year before 2020.
If you’re keeping score at home, we’ve seen 133 watches sell at or above seven figures this year. And we’ve still got plenty of year left.
The question is: How much steam does the auction world have left? And what’s driving this radical spike in big-ticket timepieces?

Mike Nouveau, WatchTok King and dealer, has told me that if more kids knew how much growth potential there is in the vintage market, they’d put down the creator-style tiny microphones and start studying reference numbers. The vintage market spiked in the middle of the pandemic, when prices on sport watch grails like the Patek Philippe Nautilus and Rolex Daytona went crypto-mode as a new wave of speculators flooded the high-end collecting scene.

But while the steel sport watch craze has cooled—or at least leveled off—the market has continued riding a remarkably durable wave, helped in part by the arrival of a previously quiet category: the insiders-only independent brands. “For many years at auction, we always said, ‘You have Patek Philippe and Rolex. What’s the third brand that can compete?’” Alexandre Ghotbi, a deputy chairman at Phillips auction house, told me in 2024 for a story on the beloved watchmaker Rexhep Rexhepi. “Today’s third brand is not a brand—it’s a genre: independent artisanal watchmakers.”

Think F.P. Journe, Berneron, Phillipe Dufour, Rexhepi’s Atelier Akrivia—companies helmed by watchmaking auteurs turning out hyper-limited runs, most of which sell out long before a perfectly-lit product photo ever hits the web. Oftentimes, the only way to get your hands on one of their wares—if you haven’t yet achieved friend-of-the-brand status—is by raising a paddle at auction.

When I asked dealer Eric Wind if he thought the indie insanity would remain strong, he was unequivocal: “At the top end, yes.” The dealer Zoe Abelson, of Graal Watches, actually believes we haven’t reached the peak yet. “I do think there's still room for the pieces that are actually rare to continue to grow in value with a continuance in new interest in collecting watches and the yearning to build the most impressive collection,” she said.

Two weekends ago, a new independent brand joined the list of million-dollar watchmakers. Sylvain Pinaud cut his teeth restoring antique watches and established his eponymous brand in 2018. He’s known for showing his work—the instrumental components of his watches are often highlighted on the dial. A unique version of his Origine, a model that only launched in 2022, sold for 1,011,200 Swiss francs (roughly $1,211,500).

Pinaud’s success is indicative of what happens to the elite independent brands that hit the big time. Compared to many of the heavyweight Swiss makers working at scale, independent watchmakers are seen as artisans who hand-produce their designs in extremely limited quantities. It’s why a watchmaker like Kari Voutilainen, considered a master of his craft, has sold more million-dollar pieces this year than many of the big fellas getting rap lyric shoutouts. “There's a growing appreciation for what these watchmakers are producing,” said Ben Horesh, EveryWatch’s CEO. “It’s great to see more independents challenging the old guard."
The million-dollar dollar diagram

Look at that list above. Voutilainen ranks just after Rolex and Patek Philippe but ahead of Cartier for the most million-dollar watches sold at auction in 2026. The list is heavy on independents, including Rexhepi’s Akrivia, George Daniels, Philippe Dufour, and Vianney Halter. The real headline, though, is seeing F.P. Journe—the godfather of the indie scene—at the very top. If one area of the market doesn’t feel entirely sustainable, it’s the inferno around FPJ’s pieces. For deep-pocketed newcomers to the “hobby” of catching big-ticket whales, the Geneva-based maker has come to represent the grailiest of grails. Nearly every Journe piece that comes to auction sells for multiples of its estimate. And I mean everything: an empty watch box made for a set of FPJs sold for $230,000 at Christie’s! “The less rare—or in Journe's case, current production—pieces that get swept up in the overall market growth will slow down soon,” Abelson said. “I don't think it's sustainable; at a certain point the values will price out enough people that there should be a correction.”

If six-figure watches were once rare, 10-million-plus pieces were true spectacles. Between 2020 and 2023, not a single watch crossed that threshold. In the last decade, from 2015 to 2025, there were just seven 10-million watches total. But with some time still on the clock, seven watches have already topped that threshold in 2026. A solid chunk of that is thanks to the wild one-of-one Daytonas that Rolex made for a charity auction—three out of the four sold for seven figures—but it’s still an astounding feat. The rest of the list is filled out by:
- An F.P. Journe Chronomètre à Résonance "Régence” with a hand-engraved pink-gold dial ($13,922,000)
- An F.P. Journe Chronomètre à Résonance “Souscription, No. 007”—one of 20 in this foundational series ($10,583,960)
- A Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Chronograph ref. 2499, a defining model for the historic house and one of only five known made in pink gold ($10,255,325)
- A Patek Philippe World Time ref. 2523, a rare version of this complication with a golden enamel dial ($10,245,605)

These days, it’s hard to find a category of watches that isn’t doing well at auction. Cartier hasn’t fallen off—in fact, the brand keeps setting records: a very cool clock known as Portico No. 4 hammered for approximately $5,768,400 at Phillips the weekend before last, becoming the most expensive Cartier ever sold in the process. Breguet is, rightfully and finally, on the rise. And after relaunching just last summer, Urban Jürgensen’s vintage pieces are hotter than ever. A super sexy pink-gold version of the brand’s Reference 2 went for 358,400 Swiss francs (about $430,000) at Sotheby’s.

To put a fine point on all this, just look at how overall sales are soaring. Last year, Phillips set the record with $83,018,538 worth of timepieces sold in a single auction. It only took 12 months to shatter that number. This month saw Phillips reset the record with a $112.3 million auction. I would say 2026 is an inflection point for the industry…if I didn’t anticipate that we’ll be back here talking about even more record-setting sales every year for the foreseeable future.
