items.title: The Style 101 on 007: The Enduring Visual Legacy of James Bond
items.description: There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.
items.author: José Criales-Unzueta
paragraphs: There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.

That is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes. And yet, as Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Sean Connery, and other dangerously handsome men have proven, a mere suit does not a 007 make. This is why, despite Bond being one of the most popular film characters of all time, you will rarely see ordinary men dare to take him on as a Halloween costume. There’s simply more to making Bond than a good tux.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953. In the announcement clip for Pattinson’s casting, the actor looks the part in a black tuxedo and white shirt, but it’s his eyes, which pierce through the camera rather than down the barrel of his gun, that do most of the talking and offer a suggestion of what Pattinson’s Bond may have to offer. Will he be a little darker and tortured, like his take on Batman? Or perhaps his Bond will be louche and somewhat pricklier.

A safer bet to make is that he will look good. One of the most enduring legacies of the James Bond franchise is how stylish both the character of Bond and the universe built around him have always been. Bond has appeared classic and timeless in style during each of the franchise’s eras, but hindsight offers a much richer perspective.

As portrayed through the decades in the property’s famous title sequence, Bond is a silhouette—a classic, timeless silhouette. Fleming established the look in his development of the character when he made the suit his primary uniform. But it is Terence Young, the director of the first 007 films, who is responsible for the visual definition of Bond.

When Connery was cast as Bond for the first film, Dr. No (1962), Young, an avid wearer of suits himself, took him to his own tailor, Anthony Sinclair. We can credit Sinclair with developing the original silver screen Bond look: The suit was lighter in fit and tailoring than most other English suits at the time. The Bond suit had a soft shoulder and waist, but a strong, wide chest and a low button stance that elongated its wearer. Every Bond suit that’s followed has been measured to the standard of Sinclair’s work, and every Bond actor has had to compete with Connery’s charisma while wearing it.

Brosnan and his Brioni suits were indicative of the 1990s corporate look of the time. Craig wore Brioni too, but only for Casino Royale; Tom Ford created his subsequent suiting, which often stood out for the slim fit popular in the 2010s. Most memorable sartorially is Roger Moore’s take through the ’70s and ’80s, which often deviated from the sleekness that had come to define Bond by creating a little frisson with lighter, brighter fabrics and a bolder sense of playfulness.

The character of Bond, and the actor personifying him at a given time, have also become representative of a certain male standard: Connery in the ’60s, tan and athletic, or Brosnan in the ’90s, polished with lithe elegance. And then came Craig, whose casting was met with skepticism, to put it lightly. His arrival was marked by the image of the actor walking out of the ocean in tight swim trunks in Casino Royale. His strong legs, rounded shoulders, and sculpted, hairless chest cemented then and there the idea of what a leading man had become and would look like for the next two decades.

Also synonymous with Bond are his watch and many vehicles. Most recently, Bond cars have all been made by Aston Martin, though Brosnan drove some spectacular BMWs. The official Bond timepiece since Brosnan’s turn has been Omega. But before such kinds of commercial partnerships were commonplace in Hollywood, Connery wore watches by Rolex, Gruen, and Breitling, while Moore wore pieces by Seiko.
With the news that Pattinson is taking on the mantle, an equally pressing question emerges: Who will be the first new Bond girl?

Some of the most memorable moments in the franchise’s history have been anchored by women. Halle Berry’s emergence from the ocean in an orange bikini and a white belt safekeeping a knife was only made better by the fact that this moment was an homage to the first Bond girl, Ursula Andress, and her ivory two-piece featuring a belt for her own weapon. Then there was Eva Green as Vesper Lynd in a slinky Versace dress in Casino Royale. But it didn’t get better than Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. As May Day, a fabulous femme fatale, Jones wore costumes designed for her by Azzedine Alaïa. How could anyone measure up?

Of course, we will have to see how stylistic choices play out in the 26th Bond film, which, like Bond movies of the past, will become emblematic of the era in which we live. It will also, as a creative project, have to contend with the way Hollywood operates today. The fact that Amazon now has full creative control over the franchise—the company acquired MGM, a co-owner of the Bond franchise rights, for $8.45 billion in 2022 and later struck a deal with the other co-owners in regard to creative authority—is the primary indication of that.

Pattinson will also be the first Bond with airtight fashion-brand deals. Craig was an Omega ambassador as an extension of his role as Bond, which made him a household name, and the 007s who came before him operated within a film industry that was not as closely connected to fashion.

Also unlike his predecessors, Pattinson is stepping into the role as a bona fide movie star who has appeared in three other major franchises (Harry Potter, Twilight, and Batman). He’s already one of the most prolific and bankable stars of his generation, and an undeniable part of being a movie star today is becoming the face of a franchise, a brand, or a product.

In September, Pattinson was announced as a global ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, a Swiss watchmaker. But 007 has worn Omega watches onscreen for decades, a partnership between the brand and the franchise that dates back to the Brosnan years. If Omega’s partnership with the franchise remains for this new installment, it could present a potential conflict if Pattinson’s contract with Jaeger stipulates that he is not allowed to wear another brand’s watch onscreen or front related campaigns for competitors. It may sound like a banal preoccupation, as Pattinson has only just been cast, but there are millions of dollars at play, and actors today often make as much money from brand deals as they do from their turns onscreen.

Pattinson has also been an ambassador for Dior since 2013, serving first as a fragrance ambassador and subsequently as a face for ready-to-wear Dior Homme; he was originally tapped under Kris Van Assche, with his ambassadorship extending through Kim Jones’s tenure at the renamed Dior Men and now continuing with Jonathan Anderson at the helm of the French mega-brand. Will Anderson be providing his suits? The Irish designer has costumed films before, working with Luca Guadagnino on Challengers, Queer, and the upcoming Artificial. To design for the big screen would hardly be a stretch for him.

The real question is more existential: Should Bond wear high fashion? To return to the idea of the 007 silhouette, that in itself is counterintuitive to Pattinson saving the world in one of Anderson’s menswear takes on the famous Dior Bar jacket, with its nipped waist and slightly flared hem. And yet in this brave new world of brand deals, anything is possible.

items.title: Lux Pascal and Ella Rubin Talked ‘Mad Men’ and Vintage Jeans at Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry Dinner
items.description: “That is the highest compliment you could give anyone!” Lux Pascal says after I tell her she looks like Megan Draper from Mad Men. We’re at Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner, held at Daniel Humm’s new eponymous restaurant, Humm, in the West Vill
items.author: Elise Taylor
paragraphs: “That is the highest compliment you could give anyone!” Lux Pascal says after I tell her she looks like Megan Draper from Mad Men. We’re at Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner, held at Daniel Humm’s new eponymous restaurant, Humm, in the West Village. Pascal is in a ’60s black modish leather minidress that she’s paired with a cat eye. On her wrists are Chanel’s Première Galon watch and Coco Crush bracelets, which, like her rings and earrings, are all dotted with diamonds. As I look around, most of the celebrities dressed by the brand are wearing looks that show off their French fine accessories. Ella Rubin, the Gen Z star of the hit teen TV show Sterling Point, has upgraded a simple pair of vintage Levi’s with a sleek black-and-gold Première Ribbon watch and several diamond rings. This is not a night for hidden gems.

The Pierre Yovanovitch–designed restaurant is a verified New York power room at the moment: There’s Derek Blasberg talking to Sarah Pidgeon about books—War and Peace gets a name-check—and Architectural Digest’s Amy Astley in a corner with Metropolitan Museum of Art board member Robert Denning. Indrė Rockefeller is here, as is stylist Vanessa Traina. In a feat of fun seating arrangements, the Chanel team has sat Rubin next to another young Ella: Beatty, the recent star of Monster and daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening. (Although, with all due respect to those lovely Ellas, the two neighbors I’d most like to eavesdrop on are Devon Lee Carlson and Jack Harlow.) At the bar I hear two fashion people gossiping about industry hiring rumors: “Lauren Sherman says there’s two people in the running,” they whisper about some gig. I think I know what they’re talking about, but not enough to print it.

Guests mill about because there’s much to mill about: Humm’s filled his restaurant with dozens of notable, site-specific artworks. Louise Bourgeois supplied 24 watercolor paintings, as well as a fantastical sterling silver cast of one of her sculptures, situated by the bar. (Tonight it’s serving mezcal sours with guava and an apple brandy highball.) Francesco Clemente painted not one, not two, but four celestial murals across two months, with motifs of abstract stars, animals, trains, and clocks. On the walls in the main dining room are 12 pigment drawings by Roni Horn. Then there’s all the work by Rashid Johnson: In the lounge—which for this event doubles as a red carpet—hangs his painting Untitled Homes. With Yovanovitch, he also built a custom host stand cast in aluminum and painted red. It’s so textural that you can see the fingerprints, and a number of guests gather around it as the maître d’ explains Johnson’s artistic process like he’s a docent at The Met.

Chanel has decorated the tables with long taper candles and arrangements of deep fuchsia peonies and burgundy garden roses. Waiters serve Humm’s signature everything caviar bagels. When I think about ordering something other than the chicken, a waiter tells me not to. He’s right.

At the end of the night, after most guests are a few glasses of red wine (or martinis) deep, Pidgeon herself grabs a microphone. The event, as it turns out, has a surprise performer: girlsweetvoiced. “She captures something that’s very honest,” Pidgeon says of the emerging singer-songwriter, who then belts out a cover of Joni Mitchell’s “California.” Title aside, it’s been a very New York night.

items.title: New Scientific Analysis Suggests Jeffrey Epstein Was Murdered. His Brother, For One, Feels Validated.
items.description: One day in August 2019, Mark Epstein was having breakfast at a Virginia hotel when he looked at the TV and saw CNN reporting that his older brother, Jeffrey Epstein, had died by suicide in a Manhattan federal prison. As jarring as the report was, he had no rea
items.author: Dan Adler
paragraphs: One day in August 2019, Mark Epstein was having breakfast at a Virginia hotel when he looked at the TV and saw CNN reporting that his older brother, Jeffrey Epstein, had died by suicide in a Manhattan federal prison. As jarring as the report was, he had no reason to doubt it.
“I knew he wouldn’t want to live the rest of his life in jail,” Mark told Vanity Fair this week. “He had no children to worry about. Our parents were gone. He knew he didn’t have to worry about me.”
Mark says he finished his omelet and headed back to New York. Then, like so many other Americans, he started to become skeptical of the official narrative.

Over the last seven years, the endless conspiracy theories surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death have largely been relegated to the backwaters of YouTube and Reddit, while local and federal authorities have stuck to the suicide story. But this week there was a breakthrough. On Monday, Michael Freeman, a leading forensic scientist who testified for the prosecution in the trial of Derek Chauvin for the murder of George Floyd, issued the most legitimate challenge to date to the prevailing consensus.

Freeman presented his findings at a historic London legal society, saying, “The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging.” In a New York Times story published the same day as the presentation, Freeman told the publication that he had no view on who might have killed Jeffrey: “All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” Along with several global news outlets, including CBS and the BBC, the paper covered the presentation with a straight face even as it noted that Freeman’s efforts to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal had thus far been rejected.

In his thick Brooklyn accent, Mark Epstein, who has long been trying to prove that his brother was murdered while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges, excitedly recounted this new development over the phone the day after Freeman’s presentation, which he attended.
“This crosses all party lines,” Mark said. “Most people believe he didn’t commit suicide. So it’s a mystery. People want an answer to that. I think now they have the answer.”

Mark emphasized that the story of the recent findings was not about him but rather about his brother’s death and Freeman’s work. It was Freeman who reached out to him, Mark said, based on what the scientist independently thought was shoddy work on Jeffrey’s autopsy, and Mark agreed to turn over all the records, reports, and photographs he had as next of kin.

“I want to make it really clear,” he said. “I didn’t pay for this. He’s never asked me for anything other than the information, which I gave him willingly. And he’s been studying this. As a matter of fact, the night before last was the first time I ever met him face-to-face.”

Still, Mark has made his suspicions both his calling card and his personal mission in recent years. After working in real estate investing and serving as the chair of Cooper Union’s board of trustees, he had his own business dealings come under some scrutiny as Jeffrey’s life and crimes dominated political and cultural discourse beginning in the late 2010s—Jeffrey allegedly housed models and employees in an Upper East Side building that was predominantly owned by his brother’s real estate holding company. In the years since his brother’s death, Mark has said that Jeffrey “definitely had dirt” on Donald Trump, and he became a minor fixation amid the Epstein files rollout on account of emails containing banter between him and his brother. (Trump has denied any prior knowledge of Jeffrey’s crimes and said that the release of the Epstein files “totally exonerated” him.) Mark has dismissed a suicide note purportedly written by Jeffrey as a fabrication.

Jeffrey’s death certificate initially said “pending further study” in regard to the cause of death, rather than ruling it a homicide or suicide, but the chief medical examiner ruled it a suicide days later. “All the pathologists I’ve spoken to,” says Mark, “they said, [if] an initial death certificate says ‘pending further study,’ you don’t get an answer usually for weeks or more because something’s being studied.” Mark hired the celebrity forensic pathologist Michael Baden to observe and evaluate the autopsy, and Baden previously stated that “the evidence points to homicide.” Federal officials’ handling of the matter in the years to come only amplified Mark’s concern.

“You know a suicide when you see one,” FBI director Kash Patel said last year while he was under fire for not producing any proof of the Epstein conspiracies he had been touting during his time as a mere conservative podcast personality, “and that’s what that was.”
“I actually laughed out loud when I heard that,” Mark said, “because I thought, How many suicides has this fucking jackass actually seen?”
So who does Mark think killed his brother?

“It’s like in a Mob hit,” he said. “You try to find who the hit man was, and then you try to find who ordered the hit.” The hit man, he figured, could only be someone among a limited number of people: prison employees and other prisoners who had been on Jeffrey’s security tier. “Then the question becomes,” said Mark, “who would have the ability to orchestrate this in a federal prison, and who would have the ability to have the DOJ cover it up?” He couldn’t think of anyone besides Trump. (Trump has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection to Jeffrey’s death; in a 2023 interview with Tucker Carlson, when asked whether Jeffrey could have been killed, he said, “Oh sure, it’s possible. I mean, I don’t really believe—I think he probably committed suicide.”)

I thought Mark and I had developed some rapport over the conversation, particularly after I mentioned that I’d attended the same Coney Island middle school where he and his brother had been students; I emphasized that I was trying to listen to him carefully and take him seriously. But there was a bit more rancor in his tone after I said it was still difficult to believe that the Department of Justice could have successfully covered up the murder of the most high-profile prisoner in the world.
“If you don’t think that after what I just told you,” Mark said, “then you, sir, are a fucking idiot also.”

items.title: Victorian Psycho Author on Witnessing “the Fictional World Inside My Head” Become a Reality
items.description: The writer is the lowest form of life on a movie.
items.author: Virginia Feito
paragraphs: The writer is the lowest form of life on a movie.

When I finished editing my second novel, Victorian Psycho, I could not imagine we would be shooting the film adaptation the following year, mere months after the book’s publication. Generally, making a movie is one big miracle produced by an amalgamation of thousands of other tiny miracles. But when I met Zach Wigon, I understood that this was a joyfully tenacious person who was going to make this movie if it cost him his life.

I decided then to undertake this journey that would take me metaphorically to Hollywood but geographically to a county just outside of Dublin, where we would recreate the Ensor House of my novel. Among film stars, an Irish crew, and (rumored) ticks, the adaptation of Victorian Psycho—based on my screenplay, which is based on my novel, which is based on my ego, I guess—was born. Throughout the shoot I kept a sort of pseudo diary in order to remember every surreal detail from which I still haven’t recovered. I’ve chosen to reproduce some of it here.

Director Zach Wigon and producer Lisa Kelly call me from the set on the first day of shooting (Zach and I have agreed I won’t visit the set until after the first week so the cast and crew can acclimate without me hovering over them, because I am an intense fame whore, and also, I suppose, to signal I’m not important enough to pull a P.L. Travers and attempt to boycott the movie).
Over the phone, the producer says she can’t wait to meet in person. I tell her I’m underwhelming.
They promise to send me the dailies. I spend all day waiting for the dailies. The dailies never come.
At around 9 p.m., I spiral because I don’t know whether to celebrate with Champagne or KFC. I decide to have both.

I finally get the dailies. I fall in love with Maika Monroe’s character so hard it’s like I have an obsessive crush circa 2006 whose Facebook photos I’m compulsively looking at. But in this case it’s the same scene throughout five almost identical takes of Maika calling a 10-year-old boy a little idiot.

Over the phone, Zach mentions concerns about a specific scene because we don’t have the budget for that many extras. I get carried away and suggest shipping over a whole battalion of free extras from Spain because, in my head, it’s going to be me and my friends, drunk and decked out in period clothing like we’re at a cheesy bachelorette party. One friend starts making childcare arrangements and another cancels her Holter monitor appointment so she can come to the shoot. What could go wrong?
I start to realize what could go wrong.
I am informed we are probably no longer going to need the extras, and I feel a huge wave of relief as I uninvite my excited friends. I pack a suitcase for Ireland. It weighs 57 pounds.
I have a steak on the plane to Dublin at, like, 3 p.m., because when you’re flying business and somebody offers you steak, you take it.

The hotel room is wonderful, but I jokingly tell Zach over the phone that it’s on a first floor, so someone might crawl up and break in through the window and rape me, and he laughs at first but then is concerned and tells me to request a room on a higher floor, and I tell him it was a joke, but it wasn’t really.

I fill up the hotel room bathtub and call reception for a glass of red wine because I am a queen and I am queening. The glass doesn’t come, so in my anxious impatience I attempt to open a bottle of red wine sitting above the minibar. The cork crumbles because I’ve never understood how to use a corkscrew—like the compass in math class, I just faked my way through it my entire life and hoped for the best. So I call reception for another glass of red wine. They bring me all the glasses of wine and also properly uncork the bottle, and I watch Seinfeld in the bathtub while I drink red wine. I get drunk and paint my nails.

I arrive on set slightly Bromazepamed. It is extremely surreal to exist in a set labeled “Mr. Pounds’s Bedroom.” I am used to living in the fictional world inside my head but not used to it becoming more real than real life itself.

Maika hugs me when we meet, and I swallow a sob and refrain from smelling her hair (partly because it is, in fact, a wig). Everyone on set appears so happy to meet me, I suspect a Good Bye, Lenin! situation in which I have been diagnosed with cancer and for some reason the cast and crew all know but I don’t know. This isn’t the plot of Good Bye, Lenin!, but you’ll know what I mean if you’ve seen it.
Zach asks me to read the VOs in every scene, which means I’m in the scene with Ruth Wilson, Jason Isaacs, and Maika, and I’m about to have a stroke.
Jason eats for real in every single take and has already gulped down seven sausage rolls, so if I fuck up my VO, I will kill myself.
Suddenly experiencing fiction collectively feels very superior to experiencing it privately. This does not bode well for the rest of my career as a novelist.

There is a scene in a cramped drawing room in which I must read the VO, but I’m supposed to hide from the camera, so I crawl on all fours behind an antique couch and grovel my way around the room while the boom op steps on my hands. I secretly think the boom op hates me because I’m always in his way and have an irritating habit of apologizing when he slams into me.
I start developing Irish inflections, so I say it, “I start developing Irish inflections,” but the Irish seem happy about it, so I pursue it.

Jason Isaacs starts doing card tricks between takes because Jason Isaacs is actually magic and also indefatigable. Only one thing could ever defeat Jason Isaacs, and it’s the ghost allegedly living on the third floor.

Even though Zach asked me to oversee the second unit, I don’t think anyone believes I’m actually going to do this—and between you and me, I don’t really even know what a second unit is. It doesn’t help I can’t concentrate on what we’re shooting because we’re in the middle of the woods and someone said there were ticks, so I’m wrapping Sellotape around my ankles, hoping this way they won’t be able to crawl up my legs.

Like your worst trauma, I insert myself into the movie forever via a small cameo. I literally just have to stand in a wig while I smile and nod, but I do it in such a way that I ruin every single take. “Just smile…like a normal person,” the second-unit director says. I reason Zach can just cut me out of the movie, and I will only have wasted everybody’s time and money. There are worse things, like smiling normally but having no cameo. I cope by chewing on another Bromazepam and another chocolate bar. (Every morning I take the chocolate bar from the hotel minibar. It will invariably become an asset in the long afternoons on set, kind of like in prison or high school.)

I change hotel rooms because I have developed an intense FOMO with which I’m always fearing there is a better hotel room for the same price somewhere in the vicinity. This FOMO is also rampant on set between the different units—in the first unit, you have the cinematographer, Nico Aguilar, laughing in the sunlight, talking about color palettes, while in the second unit, we’re shooting clocks and screaming at each other because we still have 17 establishing shots to go.

Anyway, I change hotel rooms, and the new room is so superior to my previous room it’s like an entirely new hotel. I consider changing hotel rooms further. Perhaps I can somehow upgrade my way into a presidential suite.
My parents visit the set. My dad peers over his glasses at the fake lobster cake, and when I tell him the toilets are in trailers, he sighs gravely.

Jason Isaacs convinces my dad to take up tennis again even though my dad’s not supposed to play tennis after his seven hernias. But my dad is so inspired by this actor, who is not a doctor but whose performance in The Patriot my dad can’t help but praise at least once a month, that he will immediately start playing tennis again upon his return to Spain, and whatever medical issues arise henceforth shall all be Jason Isaacs’s fault.

At the Shelbourne restaurant that night, my mom tells the sommelier how she can’t drink red wine anymore because it makes her anxious, and he kneels on the floor beside her and places a hand on his heart as if she were confiding something intimate to him like her fear of death.
Suddenly, real life feels less real than fictional life.

Obama is visiting Dublin and he’s booked the entire floor, so he essentially kicks me out of the Shelbourne (probably to stay in the JFK Suite next door to my room, which is disappointingly predictable), so I go to The Hoxton, because what is life if you’re not constantly changing hotel rooms? The Hoxton is really lovely, but I get OCD about the light bulbs in the room because they appear mismatched, so I ask housekeeping to change them, but they claim not to have any extra light bulbs, which sounds suspect—like, what do they do if a light bulb suddenly goes out? Do they just never replace it?

We end the shoot at 5 a.m. I am wearing a thick puffer coat and a thermal T-shirt and a furry hat, plus fur-lined boots over my Sellotaped ankles, although I wonder, If ticks can survive this temperature, they kind of deserve to live off my blood. Nobody else seems as concerned about the cold as me, but then again, most of them are Irish.

Sadly, when we wrap, we are all so exhausted everyone races to clean up and leave, and it is sort of anticlimactic. I don’t know what I was expecting, but balloons falling from the skies did flash through my mind.
In the car on the way to our respective quarters, Zach and I look out the window, wide-eyed, like kidnapped children. Zach starts discussing a new project for us. I wonder if he is a sociopath.

I type this over a year later, sitting at my desk in Madrid, striving to work on my next novel. I feel empty inside knowing there is no car to pick me up and take me to set and thereby escape reality for extended periods of time, until set becomes reality and reality becomes a limbo in which you wait for said reality.
I am working on a novel, but also on four new scripts. I hope to return to reality someday.
This story was originally published in Vanity Fair España.

Style Editor: Joana de la Fuente. Visuals Editor Director: Reyes Domínguez. Art Direction: Ángel Perea. Production: Lucía Pregigueiro. items.title: K8 Hardy and Leilah Weinraub on Needles, Nudity and Vibes
items.description: K8 Hardy and Leilah Weinraub on Needles, Nudity and Vibes
items.author: Leilah Weinraub
paragraphs: K8 Hardy and Leilah Weinraub on Needles, Nudity and Vibes

Years before the invention of #OOTDs and TikTok fit checks, there was K8 Hardy. In the early 2000s, the artist began documenting her looks, turning the daily ritual of getting dressed into an ongoing exercise in self-invention. Working at the intersection of fashion, photography, and performance, the artist has spent much of her career making a mockery of conventional forms of femininity, using wigs, thrift-store finds, deadpan poses, and over-the-top styling to poke fun at the ways women are expected to look and behave.

In her new book Positions, Hardy revisits her Position Series (2007–2012), a collection of 50 photographs in which she, her sister, and a cast of mannequins inhabit uncanny, cinematic personas in otherwise everyday settings. The publication arrived in September alongside the MoMA exhibition Taking Back Our Space: Photographic Perspectives, where Hardy’s work is currently on view alongside artists who are similarly challenging how women are represented and occupy space. It’s a fitting moment to revisit a practice that anticipated our collective obsession with recording ourselves, even as Hardy is beginning to question the very nature of this self-documentation. To help her get to the bottom of it, she called up her self-described “work wife,” fellow filmmaker and artist Leilah Weinraub, and the two got to talking about injectables, watching yourself on screen, and taking up space.
TUESDAY 12:30 PM, OCTOBER 6, 20226 NYC
WEINRAUB: Hello, Katherine. How are you?
HARDY: Hello, Leilah. I’m fine. A little cold, what about you? Are you working from home today?
WEINRAUB: I just came back to have this chat with you from my house. I was thinking about lots of stuff.
WEINRAUB: I’m looking at pictures of Emily, the editor, the person that just got off the phone with us.
EMILY SANDSTROM: You’re looking at pictures of me?
WEINRAUB: Yeah, I’m trying—
HARDY: She’s on right now. [Laughs]
WEINRAUB: Oh, well, are you going to be on or are you going to just only come on—
HARDY: No, she’s listening-
WEINRAUB: Do you want to be part of the conversation?
SANDSTROM: No, not at all.
WEINRAUB: Okay. Well, you can’t just pop on.
SANDSTROM: I’m sorry. I was scared.
WEINRAUB: It was a little Wizard of Oz-y. Do you know what I mean? Yes, I’m looking at pictures of you.
HARDY: It’s called creep-editing.
WEINRAUB: I kind of like it. It’s cool, but you have to be willing to withstand the uncomfortableness of people talking about you with you in the room.
SANDSTROM: It’s the first time it’s ever happened, but I’m dealing with it.
WEINRAUB: Okay. Well, welcome. Don’t edit this out now either. [Laughs]
HARDY: This should happen more often.
WEINRAUB: I like her instincts.
HARDY: They’re going to edit everything out.
WEINRAUB: “Single-use insulin.”
WEINRAUB: I’m focused. What peptides are you on? Name them.
WEINRAUB: When did you start?
HARDY: January or February.
WEINRAUB: Okay. How’s it going?
HARDY: I mean, I like it. Whatever. Inject me. It’s cool.
WEINRAUB: Are you going to ask me?
HARDY: I like the needle thing.
WEINRAUB: Tell me more. Why? Do you think it’s a 90s thing?
HARDY: It feels better than taking a pill for some reason.
WEINRAUB: Advanced medicine.
HARDY: It’s advanced. It’s new.
WEINRAUB: Do you think our generation’s more susceptible to the needle thing because of heroin chic in the ’90s and we never really got over that?
HARDY: I always thought with heroin, why would you want to put a needle in a vein? I think if I had to find a vein, no.
WEINRAUB: You like the idea of finding a fatty place and then shooting an anti-fat buster into that?
HARDY: Yeah. I like shooting needles in other people too.
HARDY: Yeah. Well, your shot of T, if you need help with that. Not you, but you know…
WEINRAUB: Are you saying it’s erotic?
HARDY: I think it’s about the abject. It’s about the barrier going in and out. Also, it’s related to pimple popping.
WEINRAUB: Oh, I’m not into that.
WEINRAUB: I’m not really a pimple person, so that’s never really been something I had to deal with, but I don’t like that.
HARDY: Are you on a GLP-1?
HARDY: And what black market peptide are you injecting yourself with these days?
WEINRAUB: I’m on a cocktail.
HARDY: Where are you getting it?
WEINRAUB: I get it from an online pharmacy.
HARDY: Does it make you feel good?
WEINRAUB: Well, when people say, “Oh my God, you look so great. I love the way you look, what are you doing?” I usually say, “Prayer.”
WEINRAUB: I mostly take stuff that’s for mood. I take DSIP, that’s for sleep. I take stuff for mood and sleep and stuff like that. So it is prayer mostly.
HARDY: Okay. I can’t do black market, I guess it’s a real pharmacy. Anyways, let’s move on. So my question is, are we divorced?
WEINRAUB: Me and you? No, we’re not.
HARDY: I was your work wife.
WEINRAUB: I know. We’re separated, I guess.
HARDY: Okay. Just checking in about that.
WEINRAUB: What do you miss about our marriage?
HARDY: Seeing you all the time, bringing you food, picking your brain, and body doubling.
WEINRAUB: Right. It’s hard to work alone all the time.
HARDY: Totally. You helped me edit the order of my photos for the book.
WEINRAUB: Do you think I see your work differently than other people?
HARDY: Yeah, you see it deeply, differently.

WEINRAUB: I feel like it’s always a bit embarrassing when I tell you this, but I see you as an anomaly in the lesbian world because you have something that I like, which is that you’re a show queen. You were always a show queen, which was a little bit outside of our shared culture. Do you agree with that?
WEINRAUB: You were very much into extravagance and facade and the superficial. But at the same time, you were doing LTTR and more classically lesbian cultural things. You know what I mean?

WEINRAUB: But then also you worked in fashion and in luxury, and that has a really particular vibe and sense of humor. I always loved that you were really adamant about taking up a lot of space, and that there was a lot of resistance to that even inside of queer culture. It was about being a gender dropout. So not being a woman or female would be less noticed in some way. I’m kind of simplifying on emotional terms.

WEINRAUB: But there was this thing of dropping out of that way of being performative in society. It was more about controlling how you were seen and not being—am I describing that well? Can you help me with that?

HARDY: No, I think it’s really helpful. And with the book release, I’ve also been screening Outfitumentary and having to connect those two because one is very real and authentic, and the other is facade and camp. So they’re sort of pushing apart and it’s like, how do they connect in a way?
WEINRAUB: They’re both real.
HARDY: Yeah, but the gestures are very different.

HARDY: Outfitumentary is diaristic. I wasn’t getting dressed up for the camera. I was just capturing myself during the day or at a certain time. And with the position series, the photos in the book, I was really trying to push that medium, the edges of dress and use these skills that I have to deconstruct how we look at each other and how we create representation, I guess.
WEINRAUB: So it was like an intellectual pursuit?
HARDY: Well, it was fun too, but there’s just thinking about the construction of image and consumption.
WEINRAUB: Did you watch Outfitumentary last time it was screened?
WEINRAUB: When was the last time you saw it?
HARDY: 10 years ago maybe.
HARDY: It’s hard for me to watch.

HARDY: It’s psychologically hard because I feel vulnerable, and I judge myself, and then I feel embarrassed for myself. Or you remember, you have a weird memory that pops up, at least for me. So watching it’s a lot of work, and I usually don’t do it.
WEINRAUB: So you haven’t seen it with an audience in a while?
HARDY: No, not in a while.
WEINRAUB: Did you like seeing the work at the show, at the opening, looking at the picture with the audience?
HARDY: It was exciting, but I think when it’s photographs of yourself, you definitely dissociate a little bit.
WEINRAUB: I understand that. What happens after that?
HARDY: After that night or the next day?

WEINRAUB: I mean, I think it’s really important to talk about what it feels like to make work where you’re the subject, where you’re in your own work and what it’s like to view that with other people in the room and be a show queen and have to continue that performance.
HARDY: I think I feel vulnerable, and I still have a little bit of nerves, like how will the public react and why did I do that?
WEINRAUB: I recently had to sit in a screening of a documentary and it was—
WEINRAUB: Yeah. I was overwhelmed, especially at the parts where I’m in it.

WEINRAUB: I was actually overwhelmed because I liked it so much. [Laughs] You know what I mean? It’s just a real moment in time, and it’s amazing to have the opportunity to see myself in that way too, to have that recorded. It’s just very real, and I can’t imagine a better thing to have. It’s just a real moment of your real life. And it’s amazing to sit through the screening and watch it with people and feel how they feel watching it. It still changes me and still affects me to feel what it feels like in that room with other people. So I feel like the exhibition part of the work is you learn about the work and how it’s working.

HARDY: Totally. The more time that passes, the easier it is to look at my younger self and appreciate it. I get dissatisfied with my original ideas of making work, because on the one hand, your old thesis for making a project gets repetitive to say over and over. So I’m always trying to look at things differently. Do you know what I mean?

WEINRAUB: No, not really. I like saying the same thing and it gets deeper and I understand it. I believe in what I always believed in. And the ideas that were important to me when I was a teenager are even more important to me now, and they’re even cooler. They resonate more. I think it’s about going deeper in.

HARDY: I mean, it’s not radically changing things, but maybe it is about going deeper. But one thing I’m having to deal with more with the book and the photos, and then the 10-year anniversary of Outfitumentary is the use of style and fashion. Because it’s the accumulation that I just haven’t really talked about a ton or intellectualized. Whereas I really just saw that work about photography, representation, creating identity, objectification of women, going into the dark room, and bringing the surface to the forefront to lay out the construction of image and to take away the belief in the narrative that was happening to now. And now, people are asking me questions about fashion, and I always see myself getting dressed, the clothing and the styling as equal to the posing and the location, as these elements that came together to mess with this kind of iconic type of photography. And now people are asking me so much about fashion and style, and I’m kind of trying to be able to articulate that more.
WEINRAUB: Do you watch the shows that come out?
HARDY: No, I didn’t watch the shows.
WEINRAUB: Do you have some performances coming up?
HARDY: I’m performing at the MoMA artist party on November 17th.
WEINRAUB: You’re going to do it?
HARDY: I’m going to do it.

HARDY: Well, am I going to actually be in it? I think so. I don’t know that I think through my performance in such a way that I want to give something to the audience. I definitely want to connect, but I only found that out once performing in a black box theater and then feeling no connection to the audience, and I was like, “Oh my God, this is crazy.” I don’t even know how to perform without feeling that connection.
WEINRAUB: Because in the black box theater, you didn’t know who was there, or do you need to know who’s there to perform?
HARDY: No, I just felt no vibes. I felt nothing.
WEINRAUB: So then what’s the situation where you feel something?
HARDY: I guess not in theatrical moments. I’ve had performances where I get more into my head and into the feeling of it, and I’ve had ones that are more mechanical.
WEINRAUB: Can you describe the performance that I saw at Reena Spaulings?
WEINRAUB: The one where you’re in blue.
HARDY: In blue? I’ve done three performances at Reena.
WEINRAUB: Okay, describe all three.

HARDY: I thought maybe you might mean the one, the more musical, crazy, weird one that I did with Stefan [Tcherepnin]. That was very sound-based, and it was almost like noise and dance, slightly artless.
WEINRAUB: No, describe what you’re doing in the performance.
HARDY: I was rolling, dancing around. I had a Britney Spears mic thing on and was sort of chanting, screaming, singing.
HARDY: “This is a performance. It’s how I communicate. Maybe you meditate. Maybe you are straight. Maybe you think critically. This is a performance. It’s how I communicate.”
WEINRAUB: What year was that?
WEINRAUB: And then what’s the next Reena performance?

HARDY: I think it’s the body painting one where you were at. That one, I hired a body painter and had a T-shirt and jeans body painted on, and I hired two female bodyguards, and I came into Arena and stood there and did close to nothing.
WEINRAUB: So it was like Trompe-l’œil. Can you describe the body paint a little bit?
HARDY: Yeah, Trompe-l’œil. It looks like I’m clothed, but I’m not.
WEINRAUB: So you came naked with two bodyguards?
WEINRAUB: Did you say anything for that one?

HARDY: No, it was about art and performance. I wish I had worked it out a little bit more than just standing there because that actually is harder to do than you think, to just do nothing. And I didn’t say anything.

WEINRAUB: I would love to talk to you more about that. I do think it’s harder to do nothing than to have an action and that dealing with that uncomfortableness was probably really difficult. Can you describe the first performance?

HARDY: The first one was a live performance with a video feed behind me, and it was choreographed and worked out in relation to this video and the sound on the video. And then because I really came from more of a band background, I did it at a gallery and then I booked a tour down the West Coast and I traveled with it and did the same thing.
WEINRAUB: I went with you. To Baltimore.
WEINRAUB: What did you say in that performance?
HARDY: Oh my God. It’s mostly just “ready” and “I am happy. I am here. I am hurt.”
WEINRAUB: Where does ready come in?
HARDY: It’s a cheerleader thing. Before you cheer, you say, “Ready. Okay.” And there was a cheerleader channeling element of the performance.
WEINRAUB: Okay, cool. Thank you for talking to me.

items.title: Lainey Wilson Debuts New Song 'Just a Woman' with All-Female Band at 2026 CMA Awards
items.description: Though she has yet to announce a new album, Lainey Wilson has been steadily dropping singles over the past few months. But Wednesday night at the 2026 CMA Awards, Wilson took a break from hosting to debut one of her most powerful songs yet, the country-soul ba
items.author: Marissa R Moss
paragraphs: Though she has yet to announce a new album, Lainey Wilson has been steadily dropping singles over the past few months. But Wednesday night at the 2026 CMA Awards, Wilson took a break from hosting to debut one of her most powerful songs yet, the country-soul ballad “Just a Woman” — for which she appropriately performed with an all-female string band and gospel chorus. Strong and sultry, it was one of Wilson’s best award show moments to date.
The performance was the second of the evening for Wilson, following her touching tribute to Dolly Parton alongside Vince Gill, which opened the 60th annual awards show.

Written with Luke Dick and Shane McAnally, “Just a Woman” is both tender and to the point: “I ain’t an actress playing a part/damn sure ain’t a mattress/in case you forgot.” Wilson is known for her quirky, sometimes goofy sense of humor (see her recent video for the John Mayer-accompanied “Phone, Keys, Wallet,” where she quite literally looses her head), but “Just a Woman” proves that she can just as easily tackle something far more topical and lyrically potent. And get a little raunchy in the lyrics when the occasion calls for it, too.

Wilson hasn’t been shy why it comes to speaking out about the double standards women are saddled with. At last year’s CMA awards, one of her acceptance speeches directly targeted those who seem to think there’s only enough room for one female artist in the room at a time. “The folks that are sitting at home in your mama’s basement eating your Cheetos,” she said, “trying to pit women against each other, y’all need to find something better to do.”

Wilson is nominated for three CMA Awards this year, including the coveted Entertainer of the Year, which she has previously won twice. If she takes the honor this year, she will make history as the only woman to do so three times.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Recap: Bad Times at Barad-dûr
items.description: You have to feel for Galadriel and Celeborn. They barely had any time together before Sauron’s forces pulled them apart. And as this sixth episode opens, they find themselves not only in deep trouble but, once again, separated. Sure, they’ve had some time to g
items.author: Keith Phipps
paragraphs: You have to feel for Galadriel and Celeborn. They barely had any time together before Sauron’s forces pulled them apart. And as this sixth episode opens, they find themselves not only in deep trouble but, once again, separated. Sure, they’ve had some time to get used to being apart. In fact, they’ve had thousands of years to get used to it. But that doesn’t make this situation any easier. Galadriel’s alone (at first) while being pursued by Orcs and wargs. But even that’s preferable to the pickle in which Celeborn finds himself.

In fact, an unexpected development suggests that Galadriel might not be in as much trouble as it seems at first, thanks to an ability to neutralize the wargs on which the Orcs are relying to track her. The arrival of a Nazgnagôl seems like a troubling development until he reveals himself as a terrified Theo. Theo’s actions — aiding Sauron, killing Arondir, generally being a jerk — don’t endear him to her, but he at least recognizes this as he asks for her help. It turns out he’s experiencing some serious buyer’s remorse about taking the Ring of Power from Sauron, who, Theo now understands, lied to him.

Is this genuine repentance? That’s unclear. But he wants to be rid of the Ring, and since he can’t remove it himself, he turns to Galadriel to do it for him. In return, he offers news: Celeborn’s alive and trapped in the dungeon of Barad-dûr, Sauron’s headquarters. He’s been allowed to live because Sauron believes Celeborn knows the secret of the three Elven Rings, the ones Sauron had no role in shaping and thus can’t control. And, as a further sign that he’s trying to change his ways, Theo tells Galadriel he’ll go with her. He seems sincere, too, but you can’t rule out a double cross in a situation like this.

At the very least, he’s not lying about Celeborn, who’s in a bad state at Barad-dûr. It turns out Sauron believes he knows the secrets of the Elven rings because he spent time (a lot of time) in a cell opposite the last of the Elven-smiths. Surely she told him everything she knows, right? What else did they have to talk about? Celeborn sidesteps the question by asking a question of his own of Sauron: “Why are you doing this?”

Short answer: because it makes him feel good. Specifically, making others submit to his will is his raison d’etre. (It’s tempting to say “kink,” but that concept seems antithetical to Tolkien.) Thus, having the One Ring, which would allow him to bend everyone and everything to his will, would be a dream come true. For now, he tries to bend Celeborn to his will by sowing doubt. Why did she put all that effort into looking for Sauron if not Celeborn? Maybe she’s really more into Sauron than she is her husband. Celeborn doesn’t bite, however, replying, “I offered her a hill, a few trees, and she bound her immortal soul to mine. You could have given her all of Middle-earth, but she sent you off to Mordor like a cur.” It’s a sick burn, but it does not go well. The scene ends with Sauron ordering his underlings to “Ready the machine.”

In Númenor, Anárion demonstrates that tormenting prisoners isn’t just Sauron’s thing by eating a meal while a hungry Kemen looks on. Anárion’s father, however, is a bit more merciful. After dismissing his son, Elendil offers Kemen a bowl — his own rations, we’ll soon learn — and asks a few questions about Pharazôn’s plan. Kenen says little beyond noting Elendil’s forces are sorely outnumbered and suggests they all “start praying.” That being said, Elendil has no intention of backing down, as he explains to an impatient Anárion outside the wagon. Outnumbered or not, they plan to charge the moment Míriel gives the order.

They might be waiting a while. Not far away, Elrond advises Míriel and Isildur not to attack because Elrond still believes that Pharazôn would prefer to fight Sauron rather than engage in a civil war. (He kind of has to; it’s his whole reason for coming to Númenor.) If the King and the Faithful can come to an understanding, wouldn’t that be better for everyone? Isildur and Míriel offer a counterargument. Elrond, they believe, is being naïve and insensitive. They’ve lost a lot to bad men. How could they conceivably make peace with them? It’s time to attack. As this plays out, a similar debate is taking place between Gil-galad (who argues to give Elrond time to broker a peace) and Pharazôn and Belzagar, who are equally psyched to get the fighting started. It seems like a battle is inevitable. But wait: maybe not? Gil-galad makes the powerful argument that all this in-fighting makes Pharazôn weak, then butters him up by saying he sees greatness within him. And just as Pharazôn begins to waver, a soldier arrives with a message from Míriel. She’d like to talk.

Speaking of in-fighting, the drama continues at Khazad-dûm, where King Thráin has ordered a thorough search for the seven Dwarven Rings. But despite the help of Stone Singers who are in tune with the song of the mountain, he’s had no luck. What he really needs is Disa, who’s better at hearing the song than anyone. But Disa is refusing to help. This should come as no surprise to Thráin given, well, everything he’s done. That he’s locked Durin up in a cave can’t help either.

It’s not the first time, either. After Thráin recounts a funny (well, funny to him) story of locking Durin in a cave as a boy, Thráin expresses his frustration that Disa won’t help, then issues some vague threats, to which Durin replies by recalling their father’s reasoning for passing Thráin over for the throne. (In short: He’s a selfish jerk.) Durin vows never to help, and he knows Disa won’t either. Then Thráin plays his trump card: Thráin can always take his frustrations out on Durin and Disa’s children.

He wouldn’t, right? After Disa finds Thráin hanging out with Gamli — and implying that Gamli might be his son, not Durin’s — Disa decides not to take any chances, especially after Thráin signals to his guards to do … it’s not clear what, but it’s probably not good. Soon, after a crowd has assembled to witness it, Disa begins singing. This produces what sounds like a simple and straightforward answer: Thráin can find the Rings “deep inside a rock wall down in the Elder Mines,” so deep that she’ll need to be part of the search if they hope to find it. If this sounds like a trap, that’s because it is. Disa’s actually leading them toward Durin. The two easily knock out Disa’s escorts, including the spectacularly bearded Lady Freyja, then make plans to head home and rescue their kids. Oh, and the Rings, which have been at Durin and Disa’s place all along. It won’t be easy, and the possibility that Lady Freyja (who’s maybe not that unconscious after all) has overheard their plans will surely make it that much harder.

While Sauron introduces Celeborn to “the machine” and promises that they’re about to go way beyond torture, Galadriel and Theo race toward Barad-dûr on horseback. Theo’s pain, caused by no longer wearing his Ring but still being near it, slows them down a bit, so Galadriel mercifully suggests they rest for the night in a quiet corner she knows. But rest doesn’t really help. Desperate for the Ring, Theo begins rifling through Galadriel’s saddlebag, only to be distracted by her singing.

Drawn to her, Theo listens to Galadriel explain that they’re resting at a spot where she and Celeborn once talked about settling down and how hard she searched for the evil she believed responsible for what she thought was Celeborn’s death after he disappeared. Weirdly, Theo understands her thinking, telling her it was “easier to chase the darkness than face what you’d already lost.” He’s been there too, after all. And when he spots his Ring around Galadriel’s neck, he doesn’t attempt to grab it. Instead, he asks Galadriel’s help in destroying it. Maybe there’s hope for this kid after all.

That said, there’s not a lot of hope in Barad-dûr, where Sauron explains to Celeborn in graphic detail how the Elf’s immortality will just make his machine’s tortures that much more, well, torturous. “We’re Elves,” Celeborn tells his captor. “We talked about the trees and stars.” This, for some reason, goes over well, if not well enough for Sauron to stop the torture. What he means becomes clearer a little later when Sauron asks Celeborn to beg for mercy. Celeborn spits in his face, then Sauron, never passing up the opportunity to do the worst thing at any given moment, licks some of the spit from his fingers before telling Celeborn, “Now are we one. Now we are joined. Now we can begin.” This does not sound good at all.

Back in Númenor, Gil-galad arrives in the Faithful’s camp with the terms of Míriel’s meeting with Pharazôn. They’re not satisfactory to Isildur, whom Míriel sends away to look at some of Elros’ old stuff at Elrond’s suggestion. While the grown-ups talk, Elrond and Isildur check out Elros’ possessions. Elrond takes the opportunity to explain why he believes it would be better to pursue peace rather than war while also admitting that he doesn’t have Elros’s faith and patience. But the real action is outside, where Gil-galad restores Míriel’s sight using his Ring. She fears she’s dreaming, but Gil-galad assures her she’s not, saying, “You are awake. Now go and awaken Númenor.”

Awakening Númenor certainly seems to be Míriel’s plan as she heads to the meeting, which is to be held in public in the capital. Pharazôn and Belzagar are, perhaps understandably, freaked out to learn that Míriel can see now, and the summit threatens to fall apart or erupt into violence until Míriel suggests she and Pharazôn have a private meeting, just the two of them. Míriel has a peace plan: She’ll stand down and allow her troops to join Pharazôn in the fight against Sauron if he’ll give the Faithful religious freedom. After all, a united Númenor is surely better than a divided one.

Skeptical, Pharazôn suggests that even if they want this, those who follow them will not, after all that both sides have been through. (He doesn’t seem to care all that much about getting Kemen back. This is also easy to understand.) But he has another idea he believes might work. What, exactly, he has in mind goes unsaid, but it becomes quite clear when Isildur returns to the Faithful and shares the news with Anárion and Elendil: Míriel and Pharazôn are getting married. Wasting no time, Elendil rushes off to the city to stop the wedding.

The episode concludes with one last act of deception: We see Galadriel rushing in to save Celeborn, who, even in his weakened state, is overjoyed to see her. For no clear reason — let’s just say he’s still woozy from torture — he chooses this moment to tell her that the Elven-smith did share the Rings’ secret with him. They’re a mix of gold and silver from Valinor, like the metals that make up Galadriel’s brother’s dagger. After they kiss, Sauron reveals that he’s been posing as Galadriel. Now he knows what he needs to forge the One Ring. There’s only one problem, the ghost of Celebrimbor tells him later. There’s no way to generate enough heat to melt such metals. Except maybe one, revealed in the episode’s final shot: Mount Doom.

Who do you trust? That’s the question underlying every plot strand in this episode. It’s also one that some characters should probably be considering more deeply than they do. Can Galadriel trust Theo? He seems truly repentant, but then Galadriel was no better at figuring out whether or not Marnûkh was on their side than anyone else. Can Míriel trust Pharazôn? That’s hard to say. On the one hand, she’s right about all the advantages that come with avoiding a civil war. On the other, this is Pharazôn, who’s given no indication that he’s more trustworthy now than before. Can Thráin trust Disa? We already have an answer: no. While he might be good at scheming, he’s simply not that bright. Can Celeborn trust Sauron? Also no, but to his credit, he never does.

It’s also the question that’s given this season its best moments so far. With all respect to Charlie Vickers, who remains a strong presence, Sauron is boring now. It turns out pure evil just isn’t that dramatically compelling, and The Rings of Power seems to be attempting to remedy this by making Sauron extremely gross. Any tension between Sauron and Celeborn is almost entirely literal, thanks to his torture device. For now, it’s the Númenor scenes that have the most heat to them because that scenario has no easy answers. Have both sides come too far to back down now? Will a royal marriage be enough (assuming it happens)? Where does that leave Elendil and his sons? There’s genuine suspense to this subplot that the others don’t have at the moment, apart from the Dwarf palace intrigue. But maybe the next episode will help remedy that.
• For all the build-up to “the machine,” it looks like an elaborate press. (And Sauron essentially admits that it is.) He’s really more evil than creative, that Sauron.
• At the moment, Kemen seems like the second-most irredeemable character after Sauron. It’s hard to imagine him being humbled or opening his mind.
• Theo giving his Ring to Galadriel creates some genuine suspense. If he doesn’t become a Nazgûl, who does? And how do they get the Ring?

items.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Recap: My Dinner With Pharazôn
items.description: Hey, remember when it looked like Marnûkh was dead at the end of the previous episode? Guess what? He’s not. That doesn’t mean he’s in good shape, however. In fact, at one point he wishes aloud that he were dead. Still, though he’s injured and stretched out on
items.author: Keith Phipps
paragraphs: Hey, remember when it looked like Marnûkh was dead at the end of the previous episode? Guess what? He’s not. That doesn’t mean he’s in good shape, however. In fact, at one point he wishes aloud that he were dead. Still, though he’s injured and stretched out on Sauron’s torture table, he’s maintained a defiant attitude, or at least a spiteful one. Asked by Sauron if there’s anything he wants to say before he begins, he asks for a blade so he can scratch his “arse,” then offers up a “Hail Adar” that’s sure to really piss off his captor.

However angry he might be, Sauron remains focused. He wants to know where Galadriel has gone, and Marnûkh remains determined not to tell him, at least at first. Then Sauron plays his trump card: He’s prepared to start killing off Marnûkh’s five children. In fact, Sauron tells him, he’s already started; it’s just a matter of how many he’ll have to kill before he gets what he wants. This breaks Marnûkh, or at least seems to. He spills that Galadriel and the others are headed south, specifically to the borders of the Eryn Galen, where Arondir had kin. As Sauron leaves, he delivers a horrible punctuation mark to the exchange: Marnûkh’s children are already dead. What’s more, he’s going to keep Marnûkh alive to torment him.

Wasting no time, Sauron then orders his minions to hunt for the Elves while a skeptical Theo looks on. Theo would like to make good on Sauron’s promise to talk to the dead by having a conversation with his mother. Sauron’s response, “Be not a fool,” does not go over well. Is it possible, in spite of the Ring and badass cloak he now wears, that Theo made a horrible mistake?

After the credits, the episode flashes back, once again, to “Thousands of Years Earlier” where, in stark contrast to the preceding scenes (and most of the preceding episodes), it’s sunny and green. It’s here we meet Elrond’s twin brother Elros (also played by Robert Aramayo), who speaks dreamily of the still-unnamed island kingdom of Númenor as “a new land for a new kind of Men.” It’s Elros’s hope that its inhabitants, after helping save Middle-earth from darkness, can be beacons of virtue and greatness. In fact, Elros believes in this so strongly he’s taken the Valar up on their offer of mortality. Pulling back his hair, he reveals he now has the rounded ears of Men. This also means he’ll live, by Elf standards, a short life, leaving Elrond behind. Elrond doesn’t try to hide the premature grief he’s already feeling, but he seems to understand the decision.

Yet, when we flash forward to the present, as Elrond approaches Númenor, his melancholy expression remains largely unchanged from how it looked when he said goodbye to Elros. This doesn’t escape Gil-galad’s notice, and when he asks what’s up, Elrond replies that his heart is “uneasily balanced between hope and dread.” Then he explains why. “Elros was so certain of what Númenor would become,” he tells the king. “I hope he was right.” As for the dread, he offers a simple, three-word response: “That I was.” (And, again, the question arises: How long did it take them to get there? Seemingly not that long, especially since not much time has passed between episodes for the season’s other subplots.)

In the forest, Galadriel and Celeborn use their long journey as a chance to get reacquainted. It’s at once sweet and awkward. “This is usually the part of the dream where you disappear,” Celeborn tells his wife as she tends to his wounds. Then he explains how he’s still alive despite reports that he’d been burnt by dragon-fire — a horse kicked him into some water — and what he’s been up to since they last saw each other, well, thousands of years ago.

After escaping death-by-dragon, Celeborn ended up in the hands of the enemy, where he passed the time telling stories about his beautiful wife and, once, making the mistake of showing them a strand of Galadriel’s hair, which caused a fight to break out. Other than remembering a moment when the two once passed each other, however, there’s not that much more to share. Their exchanges are intimate and warm but also a little off. Galadriel assures Celeborn there’s no one else in her life but doesn’t deny it when he suggests there’s something she’s afraid to tell him. Before Galadriel can answer, a band of cloak-wearing Orcs shows up.

Later that night, the couple will have a real heart-to-heart. “What happened to you?” Celeborn asks, to which Galadriel replies, “He’s not welcome in this moment.” It seems like all that emotionally intense business with Sauron has done a number on her. Even if Celeborn doesn’t know exactly what she’s talking about, he’s okay changing the subject and sharing the vision that sustained him in his prison: That Galadriel would build their dream home and become “The Lady of Lórien,” the “wisest of all Elves.” (Spoiler: She does.) This prompts Galadriel to confess she’d pushed him away, sure that they’d never be reunited. When she finally lets herself accept that her husband is back in her arms, they begin making out furiously.

Of course, we already know that Elrond has reason to be wary of what he’ll find at Númenor. Númenor’s a mess! This isn’t immediately apparent, however. Elrond describes the city as “breathtaking” but notes “there’s something uneasy about this place.” Did his brother really give up immortality for this? After some time sitting around, Elrond and Gil-galad meet Pharazôn, and it’s all a little awkward. Pharazôn’s courteous enough, but the other members of the court can’t stop staring at Elrond, whose image has been a part of their culture for as long as Númenor’s existed. Belzagar rudely insists on touching Elrond’s hairless face, then informs the visitors that the beyond-rare libation they’ve brought as a gift won’t pair with what they’re having for dinner, but they’ll be sure it gets a nice place in the palace’s wine cellar.

It just gets more uncomfortable from there: At dinner, Elrond uses a dish of sea-worm that Pharazôn speared himself — a meal clearly not to the visitors’ taste — as an awkward segue into why they’re there. Wouldn’t Pharazôn be happier spearing Sauron’s forces? Gil-galad lays out just how dire things have gotten in Middle-earth, then challenges Pharazôn to rise to the occasion and help the Elves save it. Belzagar offers a counter-argument: they’d rather not.

There’s a bit more to it, of course. When Elrond reminds them that Míriel has previously promised Númenor’s help, Pharazôn pounds the table in rage before trying to laugh it off. Then he presents the possibility of a bargain. Míriel leads a faction attempting to preserve the old way, meaning the Elven ways taught to them by Elros. A reprimand from Gil-galad would pretty much shut her down. If that were to happen, naturally Pharazôn would be more inclined to bring Númenor into the war. It’s a simple matter of quid pro quo! (Though there’s no Latin in Middle-earth, so it’s probably something else in Sindarin.)

It’s also the last thing Elrond wants to do. Talking it over after dinner, Gil-galad stresses the importance of Númenor’s support, which can only come from a united Númenor. If bringing the Faithful back into the fold is what it takes, it’s what has to be done. After all, isn’t that what Elros would want? (The situation allows Gil-galad to combine a sentimental appeal with some Elven realpolitik.) Elrond agrees that something has to be done but obviously hates this idea, so he heads off “to seek Elros’s counsel.” This, a later scene reveals, involves talking to a statue of Elros where he meets Isildur, who does not recognize him at first. Once he does, Isildur introduces himself, and it seems like this meeting might have some implications for Númenor’s future.

With this, the episode turns its attention to Rhûn. It’s been a while since we’ve checked in on Gandalf, who’s decided the best course of action is to go have some words with the Dark Wizard (or “Pallando the Blue” if he has his information straight). Gandalf tells him he’s been talking to the Secret Fire and that Pallando should know that, like Pallando, he’s one of the five servants the Secret Fire dispatched to Middle-earth. Furthermore, the Secret Fire would like Pallando to join Gandalf to fight Sauron instead of leaving the next day to team up with Sauron.

Pallando has also been talking to the Secret Fire, however, and it’s been saying something much different to him. As Pallando begins to share his vision, a Nazgnagôl reveals himself sitting on his throne. Then he tells Gandalf that he’s seen their destruction. He’ll die at the hands of a Ring-bearer, while Sauron will kill Gandalf. Unless, that is, they surrender to Sauron. They engage in an intense, but brief, wizard fight that ends with Gandalf realizing he’s outmatched. Looks like both his powers of persuasion and his magic skills could use some polishing. If, that is, he survives being brought to Sauron as a gift.

Back in the forest, Galadriel happily wakes up next to Celeborn, but her postcoital bliss proves short-lived. (It’s presumably postcoital. Both Galadriel and Celeborn are still fully decked out in armor.) If there was any doubt about who she was talking about, it vanishes when she sees Sauron’s face instead of Celeborn’s. She falls from the tree in shock, prompting an Orc to send up a flare alerting others that they’ve found their prey. As Galadriel lies unconscious nearby, Celeborn tells the Orcs that she’s gone on to Lindon via eagle.

It doesn’t take long for Sauron himself to arrive astride his flying beast. Celeborn continues to keep up the cover story that Galadriel is already leagues away. No matter, he’s told. He can take Celeborn prisoner. When Galadriel wakes up, she finds that Celeborn is gone again. Then she sees Sauron flying off into the night. Just when it seemed like things were getting better, they take a turn for the much, much worse.

If that wasn’t cliffhanger enough, the episode has two more before it’s over. In the Havens, Elrond meets with Míriel, who believes he’s come to help them in their battle. “What battle?” he replies shortly before a cut to Elendil and his army preparing to square off against Pharazôn’s forces. And as for Gandalf, he’s strapped to the back of an oliphaunt and headed toward Mordor.

A lot of strands begin to get pulled together in this episode. Elrond makes it to Númenor and immediately gets pulled into a civil war. Sauron captures Celeborn, presumably with the intention of bringing him to Mordor. Gandalf and Pallando are also on their way to Mordor. The episode builds a lot of suspense for what will happen next. That involves a fair amount of table-setting, but we also get to learn a bit more about the characters in the process. Gil-galad seems a lot quicker to compromise than might be expected. And it seems like Galadriel has been bottling even more emotions than it seemed like she was bottling up before. It should be memorable when what’s bottled up explodes, but we’re not there yet.

• Looks like we’re going with the name Pallando instead of Dark Wizard, which makes sense since Pallando is mentioned by Tolkien as one of the “Istari,” or blue wizards. His partner’s name in the original text is Alatar.

• The Gandalf-Pallando storyline continues to be kind of a drag on the rest of the series. It seems like the show is setting up something big. Hopefully it will be more exciting than this episode’s wizard battle.

• Every time The Rings of Power flashes back to the First Age, it looks pretty much like the Second Age of the main timeline, which looks pretty much like the Third Age as depicted in the Peter Jackson films. Do fashion and technology remain static over the millennia?
• Okay, this show requires a heavy suspension of disbelief, but “I survived because a horse kicked me into some water” asks a bit too much.

items.title: The Real Housewives of New York City Recap: Onion Dips
items.description: Who would have thought that the villain of the season would be Daisy? It’s like getting to the end of an episode of Scooby-Doo and ripping the mask off the ghoul haunting the ice-cream factory, only to discover it’s just the junior vice-president of marketing.
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Who would have thought that the villain of the season would be Daisy? It’s like getting to the end of an episode of Scooby-Doo and ripping the mask off the ghoul haunting the ice-cream factory, only to discover it’s just the junior vice-president of marketing. But here is Daisy, stirring drama with just about every faction on the show and storming out of yet another party while everyone stands shocked around her.

While she’s still in the aftermath of her ongoing feud with Sai, the main event this episode is between her and Hailey. It is kicked up at an unusually windy lunch where Daisy is bitching to Carole, Erin, and Hailey about Sai, how they met up, and how Daisy just wants Sai to start acting like a friend. Sai has no friends around this table (we’ll get to her and Carole in a bit), but Hailey sticks up for her, saying that, when she was in the midst of her emotional breakdown at Daisy’s Seder, Sai chased her out into the street and used her Rosie Perez accent to lure Hailey back into the action. Daisy says that she wants Sai to chase her out into the street, too, and that’s not happening, hinting at a bit of jealousy she feels toward Hailey. She also tells Hailey that Sai is not the friend she thinks she is.

Daisy then turns the whole thing on Hailey, saying that everyone is talking about how none of Hailey’s stories are consistent, that no one knows her, and nothing adds up. Hailey asks for examples, and Daisy says, for instance, where her money comes from, and Hailey finally insinuates that it’s coming from her parents. Great. Now we know! Thank you, Daisy, but also sorry that Hailey had to go through this. Daisy adds that everyone is asking that, including Sai, throwing everyone in the group into the same bonfire just so that she can singe Sai’s eyebrows. Right there at the table, as Erin stays silent, Daisy says, “Erin, you’re not saying anything, and now I look like the asshole.” Hailey says that she’s done with Daisy, who is just being a bitch to her, and, well, she’s right. Hailey is just collateral damage in Daisy’s jealousy of her old Scores co-worker. Oh wait, we’re not supposed to bring that up.

Daisy isn’t wrong about Hailey. While I still love her and her antics, there’s something fundamental that she’s not sharing with us. We see it when she goes to lunch with her mother, who has to sit in every chair in the restaurant to find the one that’s jusssssttttt riiiigggghhhhtttt like she’s suburban Goldilocks. Hailey’s mother is letting Hailey talk for a change, but even then, with Hailey being vulnerable about her issues with her marriage, it doesn’t seem like we’re getting the full picture. Hailey says she feels like she has to take care of Reuben like he’s a child, not like he’s her husband. She also says she’s been with him since she was 22 and doesn’t know what life is like without him. There’s a tense exchange where she talks about the reason she’s with Reuben is that her mother was disapproving of her having relationships with women, saying the reason that women are together is that they can’t get guys. Um, Gabby Windey, Parvati Shallow, Kyle Richards (maybe), and every other reality-TV convert would like a word.

While Hailey is letting us in, it’s leaving us with more questions than we had going in. Is the reason she’s dissatisfied with Reuben because she felt forced into the relationship? Would she rather be with a woman? Is she a lesbian caught in a “lavender marriage,” or is she bisexual and just wants to explore relationships with women beyond the nose-breaking sexual encounters she’s had so far? Is she joining a queer bird-watching group because she’s queer and she’s into bird-watching, or is she into bird-watching in the English definition of bird, where she’s just training her binoculars on the other female-presenting members of the club and going “Oooohhhh Gaaahhhh, Oooohhhh Gaaahhhh” like some kind of cartoon wolf? We don’t know, and it seems hard to get answers out of Daisy — and maybe Hailey doesn’t have the answers herself?

Naturally, this all comes back up again at Jessel’s birthday party, which was absolutely lovely except for Pavit’s terrible speech, not wanting to take pictures with his wife, recognizing that Hailey was wearing Jessel’s wedding dress, and eating food off the floor. (Sorry, Pavit. I love you.)

The best addition to the party, of course, is Summer House star Lindsay Hubbard’s audition for both a role on RHONY and as Erin and Abe’s first foray into polyamory. (With that many kids, you need to pool resources.) Let’s enumerate the great things about Lindsay at the party. (1) She looks absolutely stunning in her revealing dress, and her boobs are like an erotic thriller, always on the verge of popping out and potentially luring someone to their murder. (2) She and Carole get, and this is the technical term, schwasted, and when Carole says that Devyn is a matchmaker who could find Lindsay a husband, she slurs, “I don’t even want one, frankly,” and Carole concurs that wanting a (non-gay) man is embarrassing anyway. (3) When Erika gives Daisy a gift of memory supplements, she does the hard work of saying “Oh, that’s a fuck-you gift” for everyone too busy on their phones to fully watch the episode. (4) She then acts as a bone carrier, pushing the Erika-Daisy conflict all party, including telling Carole that Erika thinks that Daisy thinks she’s Martha Stewart. They then erupt into cackles and hold each other aloft like sorority sisters who are about to volunteer to lube wrestle for free T-shirts that don’t fit. Basically, Lindsay, a consummate practitioner of the reality television arts and sciences, does more in one scene than Devyn has done all season as a friend-of. Sorry to Devyn.

I do think that the Erika and Daisy conflict is a little silly. While I like that Erika brings a “fuck you” gift to the party, it lands like a bit of a wet slap, a spitball missing its target. She already used the joke about the memory supplements in a voice-mail. Like a potato-chip bag, that can’t be recycled. I also think that Erika, as gorgeous, rich, and lovely as she may be, is wrong about Daisy. I don’t think Daisy wants to be Martha Stewart; I think she’s just like that. Erika also says that Daisy doesn’t treat her like a real friend but as a courtesy friend because of Martha. That is correct; Daisy does treat her like a courtesy friend, but it has nothing to do with Martha, and it has everything to do with the show. Daisy is looking for allies and wants to count Erika as one of them without doing any of the work.

Sorry, sorry, sorry. I got sidetracked by one of Daisy’s other beefs. We need to get back to her and Hailey. So, at the party, Hailey is talking to Daisy’s sister Samona, the HomeGoods Ramona, and Daisy comes up to join, and Hailey gives her the full “Talk to the hand because the face ain’t listening,” like she’s a ’90s hip-hop diss track. When they finally reconvene later at the party in a larger group that contains Jessel and Sai, Hailey is talking with her hands, and Daisy tells her to calm down with her hands. Hailey then gets heated, saying Daisy was slapping her hands at Hailey at lunch, saying everyone talked shit about her. Daisy again says that everyone talked shit about her and is like, “Am I right, Sai?” wanting Sai to self-incriminate as if the Fifth Amendment doesn’t matter to Housewives.
